places.name: New York, NY

visits.text: New York: major metropolis of the East Coast where Fogg arrives late, forced to find an alternative solution to reach Europe.
Port of New York: negotiations and improvisations around a cargo ship to cross the Atlantic urgently.

Start at the Frick Collection, 1 East 70th Street. This 1914 mansion once belonged to Henry Clay Frick, a steel magnate who spent 40 years assembling European masterpieces. You'll see three of the 36 known Vermeers in the world - including Officer and Laughing Girl, where window light illuminates the young woman's face while the officer remains in shadow. Don't miss Bellini's St. Francis in the Desert, considered by many art historians to be the finest painting in America, or Fragonard's The Progress of Love series - rejected by Madame du Barry, Louis XV's mistress, then purchased by Frick from J.P. Morgan. The rooms are never crowded: you see the paintings up close, without barriers. Reserve your timed tickets online.

Walk up Fifth Avenue to the Metropolitan Museum of Art at 82nd Street. With more than 2 million works and 5,000 years of history, it is the largest art museum in the Americas. If you see just one thing, go straight to the Temple of Dendur, an Egyptian temple dating from 15 BC reassembled stone by stone in a glass hall overlooking Central Park. The Egyptian collection contains 26,000 objects, including the gilded sarcophagus of a priest of Amun. The Vermeers, Rembrandts and Caravaggios are on the second floor in the European galleries. Allow at least two hours, even at a brisk pace.

Continue to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum at 1071 Fifth Avenue. The building is itself a work of art: Frank Lloyd Wright spent 16 years designing it (1943–1959) and died six months before it opened. Its 400-meter spiral ramp takes you down through the collections. Look for works by Kandinsky, Picasso, Mondrian, Chagall and Modigliani. The building has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019. Take the elevator to the top and walk back down on foot - it's the best way to see the museum.

End the day at the Museum of the City of New York, at 1220 Fifth Avenue near 103rd Street. In this Georgian Revival building, the permanent exhibition New York at Its Core traces the city's growth and asks visitors to imagine its future. Watch Timescapes, the film showing how the city changed. If you visit before October 12, 2026, Joe Macken's model depicts New York building by building in the exhibition He Built This City. Outside, continue on foot through East Harlem, the neighborhood around the museum.

Begin at the American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th Street. Founded in 1869, it houses 34 million specimens. The star is the 28.6-meter blue whale suspended in the Milstein Hall of Ocean Life - a life-size model built in 1969. On the fourth floor, the dinosaur fossils include a nearly complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton and a 15-meter Barosaurus rearing up on its hind legs in the Theodore Roosevelt entrance hall. The Rose Center for Earth and Space, a 27-meter glass sphere, houses the Hayden Planetarium. Budget at least 2 hours, even moving quickly - the museum covers 19,000 square meters.

Directly opposite, at 170 Central Park West, the New-York Historical Society is the city's oldest museum, founded in 1804. Its collection includes all 435 original preparatory watercolors for John James Audubon's Birds of America. The basement's DiMenna Children's History Museum is an excellent stop for families. Less famous than its neighbors, the museum is seldom crowded.

If you're traveling with children, make a stop at the Children's Museum of Manhattan, 212 West 83rd Street. Across five floors, interactive exhibits cover science, health and the arts - everything can be touched, handled and tried out. The EatSleepPlay space for under-4s is particularly well designed. Even without kids, you can tour it in 30 minutes to understand the American approach to learning through play.

Finish the day in Harlem with the National Jazz Museum in Harlem, 58 West 129th Street. It's a small museum, but the story is enormous: Harlem was the birthplace of jazz in the 1920s-1940s, with the Cotton Club, Savoy Ballroom and Apollo Theater just blocks away. The museum offers guided listening sessions, rare archival recordings of Duke Ellington, Billie Holiday and Charlie Parker, and live sessions some evenings. The surrounding neighborhood deserves a stroll - the brownstones on Lenox Avenue haven't changed in a century.

Start at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), 11 West 53rd Street. Founded in 1929, it was the first museum devoted entirely to modern art. Van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889) is in gallery 501 on the fifth floor; go when the museum opens, as the room fills up within an hour. Nearby you can see Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), Monet's Water Lilies on the fifth floor and Dalí's The Persistence of Memory with its melting clocks. The Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden is a quiet retreat in Midtown. Allow at least two hours.

Walk to the Museum of Arts and Design (MAD), 2 Columbus Circle. This 5-story museum is devoted to contemporary craft - ceramics, jewelry, textiles, glass, wood. Exhibitions rotate frequently, but what never changes is the open studio on the 6th floor where you can watch artists work live. The top-floor restaurant offers panoramic views of Columbus Circle and the southwest entrance to Central Park.

Head down to Pier 86 on the Hudson River for the Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum. Board the USS Intrepid, a 270-meter aircraft carrier from World War II that also served during the Cold War and the Vietnam War. Around thirty aircraft are displayed on the flight deck, including an A-12 Blackbird. Beside the carrier, a British Airways Concorde stands on the pier; entry to its cabin requires a separate guided tour. You can also visit the USS Growler submarine. Allow 90 minutes.

If you're interested, stop by Madame Tussauds New York on 42nd Street, right in Times Square. It's pure entertainment: wax figures of American and international celebrities, from sports to cinema. The main draw is the building itself and the frenetic atmosphere of Times Square around it. You can do it in 45 minutes.

Start at the Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort Street, at the foot of the High Line in the Meatpacking District. Renzo Piano's 2015 building is a machine for looking at the city - the stepped terraces offer views of the Hudson and the New Jersey skyline. The museum holds over 26,000 works of 20th and 21st century American art: Edward Hopper (the world's largest collection of his work, with 3,600 pieces bequeathed by his widow), Georgia O'Keeffe, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol. The Whitney Biennial, organized since 1932, is the essential gathering for contemporary American art.

Take the subway to the Lower East Side for the Tenement Museum. The visitor center is at 103 Orchard Street; tours also take you into the building at 97 Orchard Street, built in 1863 and home to some 7,000 people until 1935. Guided tours, required and conducted in English, recreate the lives of families from Ireland, Germany, Italy and China. You will see apartments restored or recreated to represent different periods. Book ahead, as tour places fill quickly.

Head to the far south of Manhattan, at Bowling Green, for the National Museum of the American Indian. It occupies the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House (1907), a stunning Beaux-Arts building with ceilings painted by Reginald Marsh depicting the great explorers. Admission is free - it's a Smithsonian museum. The collections cover 12,000 years of indigenous peoples' history across the Americas, from Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial masks of the Northwest Coast to Navajo textiles.

End with the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, at the foot of the former World Trade Center towers. At ground level, the two square pools occupy exactly the towers' footprints - water falls 9 meters into a central void. Underground, the museum preserves the original tower foundations, an 11-metric-ton twisted steel column and the “Survivors' Staircase,” the stairway by which hundreds escaped. Plan 1.5 hours and prepare yourself emotionally - it's an intense visit.

Begin the day in Brooklyn with the Brooklyn Museum, 200 Eastern Parkway. New York's second-largest museum at 52,000 square meters, it's far less crowded than the Met - and that's a good thing. The Egyptian collections are among the best in the United States, with pieces dating back 5,000 years. Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party (1979), a monumental feminist installation with 39 place settings dedicated to famous women from history, has a permanent room on the 4th floor. The American art galleries and temporary exhibitions regularly receive critical acclaim.

Take the subway to Court Street station for the New York Transit Museum, housed in a decommissioned 1936 subway station in Downtown Brooklyn. On the original platforms, about twenty vintage subway cars are lined up - from 1907 to today. You can board, sit on the wicker benches of early 20th century cars and compare them with modern trains. The museum also traces the construction of the New York subway, begun in 1900: 380 km of track, 472 stations, 1.6 billion rides per year. Kids love it - and so do adults.

End your museum marathon at the Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration. Take the ferry from Battery Park: it stops at Liberty Island first, then Ellis Island. A standard ticket covers the ferry and both islands, but access to the Statue of Liberty pedestal requires a separate reservation. Between 1892 and 1954, 12 million immigrants passed through this building, and more than 40% of Americans today can trace an ancestor through Ellis Island. On the second floor, the Great Hall, with its Guastavino tiled vault, is where arrivals were inspected; those who failed the medical examination were sent back. Search the freely accessible family-name database - you might be in for a surprise. Admire the Statue of Liberty as you sail to the islands.

activities.text: Exploring Manhattan between emerging skyscrapers, docks and neighborhoods in full transformation of the late 19th century.

Between museums, take advantage of Central Park. The entrance at 72nd Street (Bethesda Terrace) is a stone's throw from the Frick. Late in the day, stroll down Madison Avenue for its galleries and grab a drink at one of the Upper East Side bars - Gilded Age atmosphere guaranteed.

After the jazz museum, if you're there on a Wednesday or Saturday evening, check the Apollo Theater schedule (253 West 125th Street) - the Wednesday Amateur Nights have been running since 1934. Ella Fitzgerald was discovered there at 17.

Take advantage of your Times Square visit to watch the city's spectacle at nightfall - the giant screens and crowds are part of the New York experience. Grab a slice of pizza standing at the counter, like a real New Yorker.

After the Tenement Museum, explore Orchard Street and the Lower East Side on foot. It's the historic immigrant neighborhood: Jewish delis, vintage shops, street art. Try a pastrami sandwich at one of the century-old delis in the area - it's a New York institution.

Before taking the ferry, stroll through Battery Park and walk along the harbor esplanade. The view of the Statue of Liberty, Governors Island and New Jersey is superb in the morning. On the way back, if you still have energy, walk across the Brooklyn Bridge - 1.8 km over the East River, with Manhattan as backdrop.

places.name: San Francisco Ca

visits.text: San Francisco: arrival in North America, a booming city where Fogg must quickly organize the crossing of the continent.
Waterfront and dock district: piers and nearby stations that symbolize the junction between sea and rail.

Head down Balmy Alley (37.751694, -122.412333), a narrow Mission District lane, to see 50 political murals painted on garage walls and fences since the 1970s. The Mission is San Francisco's historic Latino neighborhood—Mission Dolores (37.764389, -122.426611), a Franciscan mission founded in 1776 and still standing, is the oldest building in the city. Ticket $7. The adobe architecture contrasts absurdly with the surrounding Victorian houses.

Head up to the Castro (37.762, -122.435) to understand what San Francisco really is. Harvey Milk Plaza (37.762806, -122.434889) honors the first openly gay elected official in the United States, assassinated in 1978. The Castro Theatre (1922, Art Deco architecture, still operating) was screening films the very evening of Milk's assassination—management didn't cancel the show. The monumental rainbow flags remind visitors that this neighborhood was a political laboratory long before it became a tourist destination.

End the day at the Painted Ladies (37.776, -122.433) on Steiner Street facing Alamo Square—a row of colorful Victorian houses used in the Full House opening credits since 1987 and photographed millions of times. They're smaller than photos suggest, but the contrast with San Francisco's skyline in the background is genuine.

Take the ferry from Pier 33 (37.808056, -122.404722) to Alcatraz (37.826667, -122.422778)—a 15-minute crossing of the bay as the island slowly grows before you with its white walls and water tower. The federal penitentiary operated from 1934 to 1963: 29 years, 1,576 prisoners, including Al Capone (cell B-181), Machine Gun Kelly (17 years there), and the Birdman, who, in a documented irony, never had birds here—his birds were at Leavenworth. The French-language audio tour narrated by former guards and prisoners lasts 45 minutes and is of remarkable quality. Reservations 2–3 months in advance are mandatory at alcatrazcruises.com, $47 per adult. Allow 3–4 hours on the island.

Back on the mainland, Fisherman's Wharf (37.808, -122.413) and Pier 39 (37.808750, -122.409306) are worth a 30-minute stop for the California sea lions—150 to 300 can always be found sleeping on the docks, where they took up residence after the 1989 earthquake. The noise and smell are distinctive. The sourdough bread bowl with clam chowder at Boudin Bakery (an institution since 1849, the oldest continuously operating business in San Francisco) costs $18–25 and is better than you'd expect.

Head up to Lombard Street (37.802, -122.4187)—8 tight bends over 400 meters. Driving down is possible but involves waiting in line; on foot, it is free and quick. Coit Tower (37.802389, -122.405833) on Telegraph Hill has overlooked the bay since 1933, 64 meters, panoramic view, $10 ticket.

Walk the Golden Gate Bridge (37.819722, -122.478611) from the south visitor center—2.7 km one way in 45 minutes, views of the city and bay in both directions. The bridge has been red-orange since 1937, a color chosen by architect Irving Morrow under the official name "International Orange" because it harmonizes with the landscape and remains visible in fog. Since 2024, safety nets have been installed beneath the deck after 30 years of debate—more than 1,600 suicides since opening, and the nets cost $224 million.

Cross to Sausalito by ferry from Pier 41 (15 minutes, $12 round-trip)—the waterfront village on the north shore offers the best view of San Francisco from outside the bay. Colorful stilt houses, art galleries, Mediterranean cuisine. The alternative is biking (rental $12-15/hour at Blazing Saddles), crossing the bridge and descending to Sausalito.

Haight-Ashbury (37.770, -122.446) deserves an hour's walk for the Victorian houses and the memory of the Summer of Love in 1967—100,000 hippies converged here that summer. 710 Ashbury Street was the Grateful Dead house, 635 Ashbury was Janis Joplin's, 1812 Page Street was Jim Morrison's. The addresses still exist, in various states of gentrification.

activities.text: Traverse hills and quays to follow Fogg's trail at the moment when the wager still seems feasible.
Vol prochaine étape

Have dinner in the Mission—the burrito as we know it was invented here in 1961 in a 24th Street restaurant, and the neighborhood's Mexican cuisine bears no resemblance to what's served elsewhere in the United States. Taquerias open late, $15-25 per person.

First evening free in your hotel's neighborhood—San Francisco is best explored on foot rather than from a tour bus. Cable cars run until 10 PM and cost $8 per ride, but the Powell-Hyde line during peak hours means a 30-minute wait.

Ride the Powell-Hyde cable car (37.794, -122.412) at least once—a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the world's last manually operated cable car system, running since 1873, $8 per ride. The Powell-Hyde line descends through Russian Hill and Lombard with views of the bay at every intersection. Crowded during the day, less crowded after 6 PM.

Have dinner in Chinatown (37.794, -122.407)—the oldest Chinatown in the United States since 1848, and one of the few where Chinese cuisine is genuinely authentic rather than tourist-oriented. $20-40 per person in restaurants on Grant Avenue or side alleys.

Have lunch in Sausalito overlooking the water—fish and chips or seafood platters with direct views of the bay and Golden Gate. $25–50 depending on the restaurant. The return ferry passes within 300 meters of Alcatraz: a second perspective on the island after the one this morning.

Pick up the car tomorrow morning—you don't need one within San Francisco, and downtown parking costs $40–60/day. Last dinner in the city tonight before three days on the road through the Sierra Nevada.

visits.text: Day 1 - Two black pools carved into the exact footprints of the twin towers: the 9/11 Memorial commands silence, even amid the groups. Access to the pools is free and open continuously. The engraved names light up at nightfall; a white rose is placed on each name on that person's birthday.

Day 1 - The elevator to One World Observatory, atop the neighboring tower, climbs to 386 m in 47 seconds; tickets start at $31. If you'd rather save an observatory for Midtown tomorrow, stick to the Oculus here, the white station designed by Calatrava: free, and striking inside.

activities.text: The 9/11 Museum, beneath the pools, takes 2 hours and requires you to be emotionally prepared: save it for another visit if the day is already full.
Walk to Brooklyn Bridge: 1.5 km via Fulton Street, about 19 min, with the Oculus and Woolworth Building on the way.

places.name: Abilene, KS

visits.text: Abilene - From Cattle Town to Presidential Legacy: This central Kansas city traces its journey from Wild West cow town to the boyhood home of a five-star general and president.

Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library, Museum and Boyhood Home - Where a Hometown Boy Became a World Leader: Upgraded in 2019 for D-Day's 75th anniversary, this comprehensive complex uses multimedia to let Dwight and Mamie Eisenhower tell their life stories in their own words.
Old Abilene Town - Relive the Cattle Drive Era: This recreated frontier settlement brings Abilene's notorious cattle town days to life, complete with make-believe gunfights erupting in the streets.
Abilene and Smoky Valley Railroad - Vintage Rails Through History: Board historic trains at the original depot for scenic journeys through the Smoky Hill River Valley on restored vintage equipment.

activities.text: Historic Downtown Abilene - Where Presidents Walked: Stroll the streets where young Ike grew up, browsing antique shops and local eateries in well-preserved historic buildings.

visits.text: Discover Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness Study Area, a remote badlands landscape where extraordinary hoodoo formations called fairy chimneys rise from colorful sedimentary layers deposited millions of years ago. The dramatic erosional features, created by wind and water sculpting soft rock over millennia, create some of the most unusual scenery in New Mexico. Geologists and photographers find endless fascination in these bizarre formations.

Search for dinosaur bones, petrified wood, and other fossils exposed in the eroding hillsides of this paleontological treasure trove. The wilderness study area preserves a landscape virtually unchanged since the age of dinosaurs, where ancient seabeds and river channels left behind the sediments that now reveal prehistoric life. The vast, empty landscape provides profound solitude for those seeking escape from civilization.

activities.text: Photograph the surreal hoodoo formations during golden hour when warm light transforms the multi-colored rock layers into a spectacular display. The remote location requires careful planning but rewards adventurous visitors with landscapes rarely seen by tourists. Camping in this pristine wilderness offers exceptional stargazing opportunities.

visits.text: A memorial, with no ship to tour: the USS Arizona Memorial stands above a shipwreck. The boat takes you to a place for reflection, then returns to the visitor center. Reserve through Recreation.gov and arrive 1 hour before the listed time; enter “Pearl Harbor Visitor Center” into your GPS to avoid the military base entrance.

The 23-minute film at the Pearl Harbor Visitor Center provides context for your visit. The galleries complement the memorial, with no admission ticket required; the film is not included in the boat program. Watch it before boarding if your schedule allows, then save the galleries for your return.

places.name: Aiken, SC

visits.text: Discover Aiken's distinguished equestrian heritage along South Boundary Avenue, a magnificent oak-canopied road reflecting the town's long association with horse country. The Aiken Thoroughbred Racing Hall of Fame and Museum documents this sporting tradition that has shaped community identity for generations. This graceful town combines small-town Southern character with refined sporting culture.

activities.text: Stroll through Aiken's charming downtown, where historic buildings house boutiques and gathering places that reflect the town's genteel atmosphere. The rural setting and equestrian influence create a distinctive character unlike anywhere else in South Carolina. Aiken's peaceful pace and natural beauty make it perfect for travelers seeking authentic Southern relaxation.

places.name: Alamogordo, NM

visits.text: White Sands National Park—The world's largest gypsum dune field: 710 km² of pure white sand. The gypsum comes from the dried-up Lake Lucero—crystals break into fine grains carried by the wind. Take Dunes Drive (13 km), which leads into the heart of the dune field. The farther you go, the more surreal the landscape becomes—a pristine white desert stretching around you in every direction. Go in the late afternoon for golden light, or stay for sunset (check the closing time, as it varies by season).

New Mexico Museum of Space History—Head up into the hills above Alamogordo for this museum tracing New Mexico's space history. Bear in mind that the world's first nuclear test (Trinity, July 16, 1945) took place 100 km from here. White Sands Missile Range, adjacent to the park, is still active—if you find the park road temporarily closed, it's due to a test firing.

activities.text: Sledding on the dunes—Buy or rent a sledding saucer at the visitor center and slide down the dunes. It's fun, free (apart from buying the saucer), and kids love it. Gypsum doesn't heat up as much as normal sand—you can walk barefoot without burning your feet.

Alkali Flat Trail hike - If you are looking for complete solitude, this 8 km loop crosses the heart of the dune field. No shade, no landmarks - follow the trail markers. Bring at least 2 liters of water and do not set off in the middle of the day in summer. Allow for a round trip by car from Alamogordo, in addition to the walk.

visits.text: Climb Star Dune (229 m). These dunes formed 440,000 years ago when Lake Alamosa dried up and winds carried sand toward the bend in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains - where it still accumulates. Never go without water: the surface can reach 66°C in summer. Plan a round trip by road from Alamosa to the dunes parking lot, followed by a long hike on foot.

If you are here from May to June, do not miss Medano Creek: a snowmelt stream that creates a real sandy beach with running water at the foot of the dunes. Children wade and photographers set up for low-angle shots. In July–August, it has often dried up—check conditions beforehand. Plan a round trip by road from Alamosa.

Make a detour to Zapata Falls, 10 km south of the park: to reach them, walk upstream for 100 m with your feet in the water; a headlamp is recommended for the final section through the rock. The reward is welcome coolness after a morning in the dunes. Plan a round trip by road from Alamosa to the trailhead, followed by the walk to the falls.

activities.text: Try sandboarding or sand sledding on the dune slopes: boards can be rented outside the park for $15-20 per day. The descent is short, but climbing back up on foot is good cardio. Avoid 11 am to 3 pm in summer - the sand becomes literally scorching. Plan a round trip by road from Alamosa.

Great Sand Dunes is ranked among the quietest national parks in the United States. If you camp at Piñon Flats, walk 1.5 km into the dune field after midnight—the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye at an elevation of 2,290 m, and the silence of a sand desert under the stars has no equivalent.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

visits.text: Turquoise-blue water that looks photoshopped: Radium Springs releases 285 million liters daily at a constant 20°C. Nicknamed “Radium” after a 1925 analysis detected small traces—a false alarm that made its reputation. A 1920s casino-hotel burned in 1982, then was finished off by Flint River floods in 1994 and 1998. What remains: an 11-hectare botanical garden with ruins, fountains, and walkways around the basin. Free admission, Thursday through Sunday, 5 km south of downtown.

Housed in the former Mt. Zion Baptist Church, the Albany Civil Rights Institute tells the lesser-known story of the Albany Movement (1961-1962)—Martin Luther King was arrested here twice, and this is one of the few movements he publicly called a failure. Police Chief Laurie Pritchett's strategy (jailing protesters in neighboring counties to avoid media images) successfully stymied nonviolence. Strategic lesson for later actions in Birmingham and Selma. $6, Tuesday-Saturday.

The Flint RiverQuarium is dedicated to this ecosystem—a single central “blue pool”, 4.5 meters deep, recreates the river: Gulf sturgeon, alligators, alligator snapping turtles, and freshwater mussels. $12, designed for families but genuinely interesting if you enjoy nature.

activities.text: Southern buffet for $12 at Pearly's Famous Country Cooking, open since 1976—fried chicken cooked to order, slow-cooked vegetables. Touristy by Albany standards? More like local and packed daily by residents. No-frills dining room, vinyl booths.

days_plan.itin_title: From Jacksonville to Dallas in 15 days, through the Deep South

visits.text: The New York State Capitol dominates Albany from the State Street hilltop. Built between 1867 and 1899 by five successive architects (including Henry Hobson Richardson), it cost $25 million—making it the most expensive public building in the United States at the time. The "Million Dollar Staircase" is hand-carved: 300 faces, including Abraham Lincoln, Susan B. Anthony, and dozens of anonymous figures—Italian stonemasons who depicted themselves in the work. Free guided tours Monday-Friday (10 am, noon, 2 pm, 3 pm), Saturday 11 am and 1 pm. Reservation recommended.

Empire State Plaza, just south, is Governor Nelson Rockefeller's paranoid masterpiece. Built between 1965 and 1976 for $1.7 billion, it swallowed an entire Albany neighborhood. Rockefeller wanted "the most electrifying capital in the world" after Princess Beatrix of the Netherlands visited Albany in 1959 and he felt ashamed. The result: four marble towers, The Egg (an egg-shaped theater), and 92 modern artworks in the concourses. Brutalist, massive, unexpected—worth seeing.

The Corning Tower observation deck, on the 42nd floor, is free and offers the best view of Albany - the Hudson Valley to the south, the Adirondacks to the north, the Berkshires to the east. It is the tallest building in New York State outside New York City. Monday to Friday 10am-3pm, photo ID required at the desk. Allow 30 minutes.

The New York State Museum, at the Plaza base, is free and narrates one billion years of the state, from fossils to 9/11—the centerpiece being an FDNY fire truck found crushed under the Twin Towers, preserved intact. Period carousel on the roof, to ride with kids. Budget two hours for the essentials.

activities.text: Walk along the Hudson River in the Corning Preserve, a linear park that follows the river for 5 km. This is the exact spot where Henry Hudson arrived in 1609 and gave up the idea of finding a passage to China. Bike paths, floating restaurants, and the USS Slater moored on the Albany bank - the last World War II destroyer escort still afloat in the United States, visit $12.

Taste the local beer scene in the city's former water pumping station (1873), now home to the Common Roots Albany Outpost brewery. A brick and cast-iron building, house beers on tap. For something more straightforward, the Lark Street area packs some twenty independent bars and restaurants into 600 meters - the “Greenwich Village of Albany”, as locals call it.

days_plan.itin_title: Boston to Niagara Falls in 13 Days, Through New England and New York State

visits.text: Santa Fe—New Mexico's capital is approximately 103 km from Albuquerque, a 1-hour 5-minute drive. The Plaza, surrounded by adobe buildings, has been the city center since 1610—it is the oldest state capital in the United States. The art galleries on Canyon Road (more than 80 along one kilometer) are free to enter.

Meow Wolf (Santa Fe)—Plan on a round trip from Albuquerque within the day for this visit. A two-story Victorian house where every door, drawer, and passage leads into a parallel universe: a bioluminescent forest, a spaceship, a crystal cave. This immersive art experience was created by a local collective. Book online—it often sells out.

Albuquerque—Central Avenue—Drive down Central Avenue—Route 66 runs straight through Albuquerque here. Stop in the Nob Hill district, with its shops in 1940s buildings. In the evening, the vintage motels' neon signs light up along the avenue.

Petroglyph National Monument - Over 24,000 petroglyphs carved into volcanic rock by ancestors of the Pueblos and early Spanish settlers. The Boca Negra Canyon trail (3 short loops, ~100 petroglyphs) is the most accessible. Arrive early - there's no shade and it heats up fast.

Indian Pueblo Cultural Center—This museum, managed by New Mexico's 19 pueblos, is the best introduction to Pueblo cultures. You'll see pottery, turquoise jewelry, and weavings. On certain days, dancers in traditional costume perform on the patio—ask at the desk.

Old Town Albuquerque - Founded in 1706, this plaza surrounded by adobe buildings houses San Felipe de Neri Church (1793). The galleries sell Navajo and Zuni turquoise and silver jewelry - beware of imitations.

activities.text: Sunset from the Sandia Peak Tramway—The longest aerial tramway in North America (4.3 km) takes you to 3,163 meters. The view over Albuquerque and the desert at sunset is extraordinary—the city lights up below while the sky turns red. Bring a jacket: it's 10–15°C cooler at the top.

Taste New Mexico green chile - Here, they ask you 'Red or green?' with every order. Roasted green chile is the local pride - you'll find it on burgers, enchiladas, and even fries. Answer 'Christmas' if you want both.

places.name: Alexandria, LA

visits.text: A practical stop rather than a destination, Alexandria was burned in 1864 by Union forces (General Banks) during the Red River Campaign—90% of antebellum buildings went up in smoke. Kent Plantation House remains, 5 km west: a 1796 Creole farmhouse, one of the few 18th-century structures still standing in central Louisiana. Half-timbered construction, cypress-shingle roof, detached kitchen with outdoor oven. Guided tour $10, one hour.

In an early-20th-century historic bank on the Red River, the Alexandria Museum of Art is a respectable regional museum—Louisiana folk art collection, contemporary Southern paintings, rotating exhibitions. $5, budget one hour. Pair with a lunch break if you're passing through at noon.

activities.text: Crawfish étouffée (in season December–June), grilled boudin, and coleslaw—Critic's Choice has been a local institution since 1986, serving straightforward Cajun-Creole food. The dining room gets noisy at lunchtime, especially on Fridays.

days_plan.itin_title: From Jacksonville to Dallas in 15 days, through the Deep South

places.name: Alliance, NE

visits.text: 5 km north of Alliance on Highway 87, 39 vintage American cars from the 1950s and 60s stand upright in a circle 29 meters in diameter, all spray-painted gray. Carhenge is a full-scale replica of Stonehenge, built in the summer of 1987 by engineer Jim Reinders and roughly 35 family members as a memorial to his father, who once farmed this land. Reinders dedicated it at the summer solstice with songs, champagne and a play his family wrote titled Unhinged. The heel stone is a 1962 Cadillac. Some cars are planted trunk-down in 1.5-meter pits; the arch cars are welded onto them. Alliance nearly tore it down in the late 1980s - the city council was called after someone reported that a man was burying cars in a field - but public opinion swung in its favor, and in 2013 the city took ownership of the 4-hectare site. Enter free; donations welcome.

activities.text: Walk the adjacent Car Art Reserve - a sculpture park that has grown around Carhenge since the late 1980s, where local artists contributed pieces including The Fourd Seasons (a wheat tribute) and a Carnastoga Wagon built from car parts. There is a car on the hill that visitors can sign with a marker - a tradition since the site opened. The Carhenge site became one of the best viewing spots in the country for the 2017 total solar eclipse, drawing thousands of stargazers to this remote corner of the Nebraska panhandle. At night, with no light pollution for miles, the formation takes on an entirely different character - eerie, improbable, and somehow appropriate to the plains.

days_plan.itin_title: Nebraska Sandhills & Pioneer Trails: From Omaha to the Rockies

places.name: Alpine, TX

visits.text: The Museum of the Big Bend, on the Sul Ross State University campus, is the best entry point for understanding the region: geology, Native American history, arrival of Buffalo Soldiers, 1880s railroad expansion, and Chihuahuan Desert fauna are all covered in one well-designed building. Free admission. Allow at minimum 1.5 hours - don't miss the relief model of the region with its dozens of interactive light points.

The Holland Hotel is Alpine's historic heart: built in 1928 in Spanish Colonial style with its arches and ironwork, it already welcomed Southern Pacific Railroad travelers. The terrace at sunset, with the Davis Mountains as backdrop, is one of the day's finest moments. Even if you're not staying, the hotel's worth a stop for a drink.

Downtown Alpine, designated a Texas Arts and Cultural District in 2011, can be walked in 45 minutes. Murals on adobe facades tell stories of the frontier, ranches, and railroad history. Spot the “Greetings from Alpine, Texas” mural at the corner of Holland Avenue and 5th Street - the town's most photographed image.

activities.text: Climb to the summit of Hancock Hill, the rise behind Sul Ross State University, for a 360° view over Alpine and the surrounding mountains. The hike is short (under an hour) and undemanding - a tradition among students since 1981, who left an old desk at the summit where every visitor signs a logbook.

Spend the evening at Kokernot Field, Alpine's baseball stadium built in 1947 by rancher Herbert Kokernot Jr.: a wall of local stone and wrought-iron gates decorated with baseballs. The Sul Ross State University team plays here in spring; out of season, the stone wall and its gates can be seen from the street.

days_plan.itin_title: Desert to Alamo: West Texas & Big Bend - 10 Days from El Paso to San Antonio

places.name: Altoona, PA

visits.text: Stand on the observation platform and watch a railway curve 720 meters across set into the wooded slopes of the Alleghenies - every 20 to 30 minutes, a freight train sometimes two kilometers long rounds the entire bend, with both ends visible on opposite slopes. Opened on February 15, 1854 by the Pennsylvania Railroad, Horseshoe Curve solved a major problem: crossing the Alleghenies without gradients too steep for the locomotives of the day. Engineer John Edgar Thomson designed a continuous rising curve climbing gently for 19 kilometers from Altoona to the summit at Gallitzin - cutting the Philadelphia-Pittsburgh journey from 23 days by stagecoach to 15 hours by train. Dug by Irish immigrants with picks and shovels, the curve cost $2.5 million and was listed as a civil engineering marvel alongside the Panama Canal and the Empire State Building. In 1942, Nazi agents landed by submarine with a mission to blow it up, but the FBI arrested them in New York before they reached their target. More than 111 million tonnes of freight pass each year, or 45 to 50 trains a day. Combined admission with the Railroaders Memorial Museum: $12 adult.

You enter the Railroaders Memorial Museum, installed in the Pennsylvania Railroad's former locomotive maintenance building, and discover that Altoona was for a century the beating heart of American railroading. The PRR built its main workshops here in 1850 - at its peak, Altoona employed 15,000 railroaders in a city of 80,000, meaning one job in five directly tied to locomotives. The museum traces this history through full-size locomotives, models, uniforms, and thousands of artifacts. An entire room is devoted to Pennsylvania railroad popular culture: railroaders' lunch boxes, unions, strikes - and the identity of a city built around a single employer for four generations. Open daily May through October 10am-5pm, closed Monday off-season.

You drive 20 minutes west to the Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site at Cresson, and discover the ingenious and slow system that Horseshoe Curve replaced in 1854. Since 1834, Pennsylvania used a combination of canals and steam-powered inclined planes to cross the Alleghenies: wagons were hauled on cables to the ridges, then descended by gravity to the next canal sections. The journey took four days with dozens of transfers - versus 15 hours after the curve opened. Ruins of engineers' houses, steam engine foundations, and a reconstructed rail segment allow you to visualize what was, at the time, one of the technological wonders of the United States. Open daily 9am-5pm; free with America the Beautiful pass, otherwise $7 adult.

activities.text: You settle on the observation platform and wait - not long. Freight convoys pass 45 to 50 times daily; when such a train enters the curve, both ends are visible simultaneously on opposite hillsides - the most photographed image in American railroading. Helper locomotives of 3,200 kilowatts are coupled at the rear to push the heaviest convoys uphill. The only passenger train of the day - the Amtrak Pennsylvanian Pittsburgh-New York - passes mid-morning eastbound. Check the exact schedule on Amtrak's site before your visit and wait for it: it's a special experience at this place.

You visit Baker Mansion, a neoclassical marble residence built in 1849 by Elias Baker, iron master who ran the region's first major foundries before Bethlehem Steel. The house remained in the Baker family until 1914 without major modification, making it one of the best-preserved Victorian interiors in Pennsylvania: original furniture ordered from Philadelphia and Europe, period wallpapers, silverware, and clothing from the 1850-1900 period. The house is 10 minutes from the Railroaders Memorial Museum - the two visits naturally complement each other in a half-day.

days_plan.itin_title: Pennsylvania Loop: From Amish Country to the Appalachians - 12 Days

Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site Cresson

visits.text: You enter the Noé House, built in 1864 as a communal kitchen and now the main museum of the Heritage Society's three-building campus. The exhibits hold 12,000 artifacts and 10,000 archival records tracing the Community of True Inspiration back to its 1714 German roots in the Pietist movement. Don't miss the “Amana meteorite of 1875,” a genuine fragment of the meteorite whose fiery fall was visible as far as Chicago. Open April through October; admission charged.

You step into Iowa's only surviving operational textile mill, weaving goods continuously since 1859 - through the communal era, the Great Change of 1932, and every decade since. Five full-time artisans still produce blankets, scarves, and table linens on historic looms. The adjacent Warped and Woven shop sells directly from the production floor. The larger mill complex now houses the Hotel Millwright, which opened in 2020. Shop open daily; mill tours by arrangement on Maifest and Oktoberfest Saturdays.

The Amana churches express Pietist humility through architecture: no steeple, no stained glass, plain brick walls, simple wooden benches arranged without ornament. The church in Main Amana is the most accessible and best-preserved example. Services are still held by the Amana Church Society. Visitors are welcome outside service hours. The contrast with mainstream American church design is immediate and striking.

activities.text: You follow the 5-kilometer Kolonieweg (Colony Way) trail from the Amana depot along the Mill Race canal that once powered the colonies' mills. The route connects Main Amana to Middle Amana and circles the 69-hectare Lily Lake, where trumpeter swans and river otters make frequent appearances. A second trail cuts through the Amana Forest along an Iowa River bluff. Both trails are flat and easy; free access.

You stop by Ackerman Winery, operating since 1956—Iowa's oldest active winery, run by the Wyant family since 2015. Village Winery and White Cross Cellars both offer tastings within the same tight cluster of villages. For dinner, the Ronneburg Restaurant—named after the 13th-century German castle where the Inspirationists took refuge from persecution—serves traditional German and American dishes in a converted communal kitchen. The entire circuit covers less than five kilometers of driving.

days_plan.itin_title: A Different Side of Iowa: From Glacial Lakes to Mississippi Bluffs
Iowa Backroads: From the Missouri Cliffs to the Mississippi Bluffs

visits.text: Rock Cafe (Stroud, OK) - Stop for breakfast at this cafe built in 1939 with local stone - it inspired the character Sally in Cars. Burned down in 2008, it was rebuilt stone by stone by the community.

Round Barn (Arcadia, OK)—Take a look at this 1898 round wooden barn, the only one of its kind on Route 66. It nearly got demolished in the 1980s before being saved by a former carpenter who volunteered to restore it single-handedly over four years.

POPS 66 (Arcadia, OK)—You can't miss the 20-meter-tall soda bottle sculpture marking the entrance—this gas station and restaurant offers over 700 varieties of soda from around the world. Try something weird: you won't find it anywhere else.

Oklahoma Route 66 Museum (Clinton)—The best museum dedicated to Route 66 along the entire route. The exhibit is organized by decade, from the 1920s to the 1980s, with reconstructions of period diners, gas stations, and motels. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: Dinner and atmosphere in Amarillo—The historic downtown on 6th Street has antique shops, bars, and restaurants far better than the tourist zone along the Interstate. If you like challenges, a famous steakhouse offers a free 2 kg steak if you finish it in an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Thelma & Louise Route: Grand Canyon
Route 66: Chicago to Santa Monica

visits.text: Stop on the way at Jekyll Island (about 104 km north of Amelia Island, 1 hour 15 minutes' drive) - the former private retreat of America's richest families. From 1886 to 1942, the Jekyll Island Club brought together Rockefeller, Morgan, Pulitzer, Vanderbilt and their guests, who together owned one sixth of the world's wealth. It was here, in 1910, that the plan to create the US Federal Reserve was secretly drawn up. The restored Club Hotel can be visited. $25 for the island pass.

Driftwood Beach, on the north tip of Jekyll, more than an hour's drive from Amelia Island, is a graveyard of trees - oaks bleached by salt and felled by erosion, forming a landscape of white skeletons on the sand. One of the most popular photo spots in Georgia. Free access, allow 1 hour for the walk and photos. Best light at sunrise.

Amelia Island has flown eight different flags through its history - French, Spanish, British, Patriot, Green Cross, Mexican, Confederate, American - the only US territory with this distinction. Fernandina Beach, the historic center, aligns 50 blocks of Victorian wooden houses on Centre Street. The Palace Saloon, open since 1903, is Florida's oldest bar still in operation.

activities.text: Amelia Island beach at sunset - 21 km of soft sand, one of the few Atlantic beaches in Florida that allow cars on certain stretches, as at Daytona. Several rental shops on the island offer beach bikes, ideal for riding along the beach at low tide.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys
Washington to Miami in 16 Days Along the American East Coast

visits.text: Gaze at Amicalola Falls, Georgia's tallest waterfall tumbling 222 meters over a series of rock ledges into a lush forested gorge. The Cherokee name meaning “turbulent waters” perfectly describes this spectacular cascade, one of the tallest waterfalls east of the Mississippi River. Trails to both the base and summit provide dramatically different perspectives of the thundering waters.

Hike through the surrounding state park where hardwood forests, mountain streams, and abundant wildlife create ideal conditions for nature photography and peaceful contemplation. The park serves as the southern approach to the Appalachian Trail, attracting hikers from around the world preparing for long-distance adventures. On-site naturalist programs offer archery, animal encounters, and guided wilderness exploration.

activities.text: Follow the 13-km Approach Trail connecting Amicalola Falls to the official southern terminus of the Appalachian Trail at Springer Mountain. Even short sections of this legendary pathway provide unforgettable hiking through pristine mountain wilderness frequented by deer, wild turkeys, and occasionally black bears.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Disneyland Resort - Where Dreams Have Come True Since 1955: Walt Disney's original Magic Kingdom continues to enchant visitors with its blend of nostalgia, innovation, and impeccable showmanship. The adjacent Disney California Adventure celebrates the Golden State's landmarks and culture.

Disneyland Park - The Happiest Place on Earth: Eight themed lands transport guests from Main Street USA to the jungles of Adventureland, the futuristic Tomorrowland, and the fairytale castles of Fantasyland. Classic attractions like Pirates of the Caribbean set the standard for immersive themed entertainment.

Disney California Adventure - California, Imagined by Disney: This sister park celebrates the state's culture through attractions like Cars Land, a life-size recreation of the Pixar film's desert town, and the Incredicoaster whipping along the Paradise Bay waterfront.

activities.text: Downtown Disney District - Entertainment Without a Ticket: This outdoor promenade connecting the parks and hotels offers shopping, dining, and entertainment accessible to all visitors without theme park admission.

visits.text: Day 1: Ship Creek - This stream runs along the north side of downtown Anchorage before flowing into Cook Inlet, a few minutes' walk from the Alaska Railroad depot. In summer, king salmon and then silver salmon swim upstream, and the footbridges offer a view of the fish as well as the anglers lined up along the banks.

Day 1: Lake Hood - This seaplane base next to Ted Stevens Airport sees bush floatplanes taking off and landing all day long in summer. On its shore, the Alaska Aviation Museum displays historic bush aviation aircraft.

Day 2: Anchorage Museum - The state's largest museum houses comprehensive collections spanning Alaska's art, history, and science. Galleries explore Alaska Native cultures through extensive artifact collections and contemporary art, while the Smithsonian Arctic Studies Center provides access to hundreds of objects representing indigenous peoples across the circumpolar north.

Day 2: Alaska Native Heritage Center - This cultural facility on the outskirts of Anchorage introduces visitors to Alaska's eleven distinct Native cultural groups through traditional village sites, demonstrations of crafts and customs, and performances of song and dance. The 26-acre campus includes a lakeside trail connecting authentic reproductions of traditional dwellings representing coastal, interior, and Arctic peoples.

Day 2: Downtown Anchorage - Alaska's largest city with over 290,000 residents serves as the state's economic and transportation hub. The walkable downtown features public art, historic buildings from the city's 1915 founding, and views of the Chugach Mountains rising immediately to the east.

activities.text: Day 1: Cook Inlet Beluga Viewing - The waters along the Seward Highway between Girdwood and Anchorage provide opportunities to observe the endangered Cook Inlet beluga whale population from roadside pullouts, particularly during salmon runs.

Day 1: Turnagain Arm Scenic Corridor - This dramatic fjord southeast of Anchorage features some of the world's highest tides, frequent Dall sheep sightings on adjacent cliffs, and tidal bores that can reach several feet in height during extreme tidal exchanges.

Day 2: Tony Knowles Coastal Trail - This 11-mile paved trail follows the coast from downtown through Earthquake Park and Kincaid Park, offering views of Cook Inlet, opportunities to observe moose and other wildlife, and access to Anchorage's extensive trail system.

Day 2: Departure Preparation - Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport serves as a major hub for travel between North America and Asia, with comprehensive facilities and services for departing visitors.

places.name: Angel Oak, SC

visits.text: Contrary to what many think, the Angel Oak isn't named for its beauty but for the Angel family, who owned the land. This Johns Island live oak is thought to be 300 to 400 years old, stands about 20 meters tall and shades nearly 1,600 m², about a quarter of a soccer field. Free entry, closes around 5pm, and climbing on the branches is strictly forbidden.

places.name: Ann Arbor, MI

visits.text: You enter the University of Michigan's central campus and reach The Diag—the broad paved diagonal walkway surrounded by red brick academic buildings constructed between 1840 and 1940. Keep your eyes on the ground: an “M” engraved in granite sets a trap—tradition holds that any student who steps on it before their first exam will inevitably fail that exam. Founded in Detroit in 1817 and moved to Ann Arbor in 1837, the University of Michigan enrolls 48,000 students across 3,207 acres and has 30 libraries and 16 museums. UMMA (Museum of Art, free admission) and the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology (also free) are the two most accessible to visitors passing through. Join a free student-led guided tour from the Michigan Union at the corner of South State Street.

You stand outside North America's largest college football stadium. Michigan Stadium opened in 1927 with 72,000 seats, then expanded in successive stages by digging ever deeper: the playing field now lies 9 meters below street level, and official capacity is 107,601 spectators. The Michigan Wolverines hold the all-time record for the most victories in NCAA Division I college football. Fall game days draw crowds exceeding 110,000 - book months ahead if you want to attend a game.

You push open the door of a former firehouse in the Kerrytown neighborhood and find yourself in one of America's most celebrated delicatessens. Ari Weinzweig and Paul Saginaw opened Zingerman's in 1982 with an obsession: the finest products possible, sourced directly from artisan producers. The Reuben—hand-sliced corned beef, house-made lacto-fermented sauerkraut, Swiss Emmental, and Thousand Island dressing on rye bread baked in their own bakery—is regularly cited as one of America's ten best sandwiches. Barack Obama orders the Reuben every time he passes through Ann Arbor. Lines sometimes extend out the door at lunch—arrive at 11:15 a.m. to be served before the rush.

activities.text: You descend into The Arb along paths dropping from the campus toward the Huron River, and the city disappears within minutes. Nichols Arboretum is a 50-hectare natural area jointly managed by the University of Michigan and the city since 1907, with glacial slopes, meadows and mixed forests crossed by students all year round. The deer you encounter at dusk in the lower meadows pay little attention to visitors. Avoid weekdays between noon and 2 p.m. - students gather on the lawns and the quiet vanishes.

You cross the threshold of UMMA without paying a cent and enter one of America's largest university museums—over 20,000 works spanning 5,000 years of art history across 94,000 square meters of space. The Asian collection on the second floor, with its 7th-century Tang dynasty ceramics and Japanese prints from the Edo period, rivals what much more famous museums charging admission offer. The galleries of African art and contemporary African American artists complete a breadth of coverage rare for an entirely free museum. Come on Thursday evenings—the museum closes at 8 p.m., with musical programming in the central atrium.

visits.text: The United States Naval Academy has trained officers for the Navy and Marines since 1845. The 138-hectare campus, nicknamed "the Yard," can be toured with a guide ($12, photo ID required). The Chapel houses the crypt of John Paul Jones, naval hero of the Revolution repatriated from Paris in 1905; Bancroft Hall is the world's largest dormitory with 4,400 rooms for the midshipmen. If you catch the "Noon Meal Formation" at 12:05pm, you'll see 4,000 students march in uniform in five minutes - pure military spectacle.

The Maryland State House is the oldest state capitol in continuous legislative use in the United States, in service since 1772. The Continental Congress met here in 1783-1784, making Annapolis the nation's temporary capital. George Washington resigned his military commission here on December 23, 1783 - a founding gesture establishing civilian authority over the military. Free tours, open daily.

City Dock, at the foot of Main Street, has been Annapolis's beating heart since the 17th century. Nicknamed "Ego Alley" because Chesapeake yachtsmen come to parade their boats, the wharf also holds the Kunta Kinte-Alex Haley Memorial - marking the 1767 arrival of the slave ship carrying the ancestor whose story writer Haley traced in "Roots" (1976), a worldwide bestseller with 8 million copies sold.

activities.text: Taste Chesapeake blue crab at an old-school crab house - Cantler's Riverside Inn, 10 minutes from downtown, has been the institution since 1974. Maryland blue crabs arrive steamed by the bucket, blanketed in Old Bay (the region's fetish spice blend, created in Baltimore in 1939). Wooden mallet provided, you crack them yourself. Count on $50 per person for a dozen, bib recommended - it's messy and that's the point.

visits.text: Anza-Borrego Desert State Park - California's Largest State Park: Over 640,000 acres of Colorado Desert wilderness spread across mountains, palm oases, and badlands. In wet years, spring wildflower super blooms carpet the desert floor in impossible colors.

Galleta Meadows - Sky Art in the Desert: Over 130 enormous metal sculptures by artist Ricardo Breceda populate this private estate, free and open to the public. Giant serpents, dinosaurs, and fantastical creatures emerge from the desert landscape.

Borrego Springs - An International Dark Sky Community: With minimal light pollution, this small town earned official designation for its pristine night skies, making it one of the best stargazing destinations in Southern California.

activities.text: Slot Canyon Hikes - Walk Between Narrow Walls of Stone: Several easily accessible slot canyons offer otherworldly experiences as you navigate between towering walls of sedimentary rock carved by flash floods over millennia.

Palm Canyon Trail - Oasis in the Desert: This 3-mile hike descends into a grove of native California fan palms, the state's only indigenous palm species, creating a green haven amid surrounding desert.

places.name: Apalachicola, FL

visits.text: Inside a one-room brick building on Gorrie Square, a three-quarter-scale replica shows you the machine that made Florida liveable. Dr John Gorrie arrived in Apalachicola in 1833, when it was the third-largest port on the Gulf. In 1841, watching yellow fever claim up to 70% of his patients, he began hanging basins of ice from hospital ceilings - and when ice from northern lakes arrived too slowly by ship, he invented a mechanical system to make it himself. US patent no. 8080, granted on 6 May 1851. One of only two Floridians honoured with a statue in the US Capitol. Admission $2; open Thursday to Monday.

The Apalachicola Historic District survived because money ran out. The Civil War blockade killed the cotton trade, the railroads bypassed the town, and nobody had the capital to tear the antebellum buildings down. Walk the result: intact Greek Revival commercial blocks, the Orman House (built 1838, original furnishings still inside), Trinity Episcopal Church from the same year. A two-story height limit has governed the city ever since. Hit Commerce Street along the waterfront at dusk - the Victorian storefronts in that light explain why the town still looks like 1870.

Apalachicola Bay once supplied 90% of Florida's oysters and 10% of the national harvest - the 'Oyster Capital of the World' wasn't marketing. Then came 2013: drought, a harvesting rush triggered by the 2010 Deepwater Horizon scare, saltwater predators flooding a low-flow bay. Landings collapsed from 1.4 million kilos to near nothing. The state closed wild harvest in 2020. The bay is in slow recovery now, and aquaculture farms like Water Is Life Oysters have emerged in the gap. Farmed Apalachicola oysters are back on local menus - ask your waiter which farm they come from.

activities.text: The oysters that made Apalachicola famous are back, in a new form. Aquaculture farms growing Crassostrea virginica in the same bay produce the same salty-sweet flavour - same mineral-rich water, farmed rather than wild-harvested. Boss Oyster, on Water Street, sources locally. Order the half shells, grab a cold beer, find a waterfront seat. That's the right sequence. Arrive before 7 p.m. at weekends.

The Apalachicola River drains 50,800 square kilometres from three states before meeting the Gulf here, and the floodplain it builds is one of the most biodiverse in North America. A kayak puts you inside it: cypress swamps, bottomland hardwood forest, osprey, anhinga, river otter working the banks. Local outfitters launch from the city marina on Water Street. Half-day trips run about three hours. Book 24 hours ahead in spring.

days_plan.itin_title: Florida Panhandle: Tallahassee to Pensacola on the Emerald Coast

map_keywords: John Gorrie Museum State Park Apalachicola

visits.text: Pass through the west entrance and drive 3 km to Apgar Village, the historic heart of Glacier National Park. The village dates to 1892, when Milo Apgar settled here to welcome the park's first visitors. You'll find a visitor center, gift shops, and a kayak and rowboat rental station. The Cedar Tree Gift Shop has the distinction of an old cedar growing literally through its roof.

Walk down to the shore of Lake McDonald—the park's largest lake at 16 km long, 1.6 km wide, and 144 meters deep. The water runs so clear you'll see multicolored pebbles on the bottom, a sight that's become famous on social media. Take time to walk the shoreline hunting for the prettiest specimens of red, green, and blue stones.

Continue by car on the Going-to-the-Sun Road to Lake McDonald Lodge, 15 minutes north. This Swiss-chalet-style wooden lodge dates to 1913. Push through the door and admire the great hall with its massive timbers, fireplaces, and hunting trophies—cowboy painter Charles M. Russell spent summers here telling stories to visitors by the fire. You can grab a meal or simply stroll the dock behind the lodge.

A few minutes from the lodge, stop at the Trail of the Cedars. This 1-km loop on wooden boardwalks winds through a forest of western red cedars, some 500 years old and over 2 meters in diameter. This marks the eastern edge of their range—normally these trees grow in Pacific rainforests. The trail is wheelchair-accessible and takes about twenty minutes.

activities.text: If you want to see Lake McDonald from a different angle, board the DeSMet, a two-deck boat built in 1930 that runs narrated tours from the lodge dock. The cruise lasts about 1 hour and gives you views of the snow-capped peaks along the Continental Divide from the middle of the lake.

Late in the day, settle onto Apgar Beach for sunset. The lake faces west and the reflections on the water with mountains in the background are spectacular. Bring your picnic—there are tables and grills by the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Rockies Loop: Glacier & Waterton

visits.text: Day 4 - In Harlem, the Apollo Theater launched Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and Stevie Wonder from its stage on 125th Street. The façade with its red neon sign can be photographed at any hour.

Day 4 - Around the Apollo, explore Harlem on foot: Strivers' Row brownstones, Sunday morning gospel (arrive early, appropriate attire required), soul food at Sylvia's or Amy Ruth's. The neighborhood has changed a lot in twenty years; 125th Street remains its beating artery, with historic businesses alongside chains.

activities.text: Chicken and waffles or mac and cheese at a soul food restaurant: the proper meal for Day 4; budget $20 to $30 per person.
Subway to Morris-Jumel Mansion: 3 km, C line from 125th Street to 163rd Street, about 20 min.

places.name: Arco, ID

visits.text: The black basalt at Craters of the Moon starts without warning - you're driving through sagebrush high desert and then the lava is simply there, covering everything. President Coolidge established the national monument on May 2, 1924, to preserve what he called “unusual and weird volcanic formations.” The Great Rift - an 84-kilometer crack in the Earth's crust - produced 60 distinct lava flows from 15,000 to just 2,100 years ago, making this one of the youngest lava fields in North America. In August 1969, astronauts Eugene Cernan and Joe Engle trained here with NASA geologist Ted Foss; Cernan later walked on the Moon during Apollo 17, while Engle was originally assigned to that mission but replaced by geologist Harrison Schmitt. Admission is free. Start at the Robert Limbert Visitor Center.

Climb the Inferno Cone - a steep 1.3-kilometer round trip up a 244-meter cinder cone - for a panoramic view of the lava field, and on clear days, the Teton Range 161 kilometers east. Then pick up a free cave permit at the visitor center and head to the Cave Trail, where lava tubes descend into the rock. The tubes stay near freezing year-round regardless of outside temperature; bring two light sources and a jacket. They formed when lava surfaces hardened while molten rock kept flowing inside, then drained, leaving hollow tunnels up to 9 meters high.

The Devils Orchard trail (800 meters, paved, free) winds through a kipuka - an island of older terrain completely surrounded by newer lava, hosting some of the oldest juniper trees in Idaho. The spatter cones visible along the loop road are among the best examples anywhere: steep chimneys formed where gas-rich lava blobs welded together above the rift into towers that look, from a distance, like broken teeth.

activities.text: After dark, watch the sky at Craters of the Moon, an International Dark Sky Park. On clear nights, the Milky Way stands out above the lava flows. Rangers sometimes hold telescope evenings in summer; check the park schedule. Lava Flow Campground lies within the monument among the lava formations. Its sites are first come, first served and cannot be reserved. Arrive early enough if you plan to spend the night.

Thirty kilometers east of the park, Arco is the closest town - and 29 kilometers beyond that, EBR-1 (Experimental Breeder Reactor No. 1) is a National Historic Landmark where, on July 17, 1955, Arco became the first town in the world powered by atomic energy. The original reactor, control room, and instruments are all intact. Self-guided tours are free from Memorial Day through Labor Day. Allow 45 minutes.

places.name: Arrow Rock, MO

visits.text: Pull off I-70 at Exit 89 and drive 21 km north to Arrow Rock—a National Historic Landmark whose entire town is the attraction. Lewis and Clark passed the limestone bluff here on June 9, 1804; Clark noted “the Prairie of Arrows” in his journal. Indigenous cultures had used the bluff as a flint quarry for 12,000 years, and “pierre à flèche” appeared on French maps as early as 1732. Today you'll find 45 permanent residents, wooden sidewalks, the 1834 J. Huston Tavern—Missouri's first state-preserved historic site—and the home of painter George Caleb Bingham, separately designated a National Historic Landmark in 1968. Thirty minutes is enough for a quick walk; the tavern serves lunch.

visits.text: Explore Asheville's celebrated downtown Art District, where world-class galleries and museums showcase an impressive array of artistic expression. This mountain city in western North Carolina has earned a reputation as a cultural haven, perfectly described as having an urban creative energy ringed by majestic mountain scenery.

Wander through Asheville's diverse art galleries, which feature works ranging from traditional Appalachian crafts to cutting-edge contemporary pieces. The city's thriving arts scene attracts creative talents from across the nation, making it one of the premier cultural destinations in the American Southeast.

activities.text: Experience the unique blend of city sophistication and mountain wilderness that defines Asheville's character. The surrounding Blue Ridge Mountains provide a stunning backdrop for this vibrant community, where natural beauty and cultural richness combine to create an unforgettable destination for both art lovers and outdoor enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Appalachian Road Trip: Great Smoky Mountains & Blue Ridge
North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

activities.text: Prepare for the climb to Paradise in Ashford, before the Nisqually Entrance. The village lies on SR 706, the western access route used here to reach Mount Rainier. Use this stop to organize meals, fuel, and offline maps; services become more spread out once you enter the park.

days_plan.itin_title: Olympic, Rainier and North Cascades: 11 Days in Nature

visits.text: Spend an hour in downtown Aspen to feel the atmosphere of this Victorian town set at 2,438 m in a valley framed by four ski resorts. The Wheeler Opera House, opened in 1889, still hosts concerts, and art galleries line the main street. The atmosphere is surprisingly peaceful for such a renowned town.

Detour to the Maroon Bells—Maroon Peak (4,317 m) and North Maroon Peak (4,273 m)—the two most photographed peaks in Colorado. Maroon Lake in the foreground creates the perfect reflection. In summer, a shuttle bus is mandatory between 8 AM and 5 PM from the Aspen Highlands parking lot—take it early for morning light.

Take time to drive up Independence Pass (3,687 m) on CO-82: the road follows the Roaring Fork River, passes through spruce forests and emerges onto open tundra. At the pass, the Sawatch Mountains stretch as far as the eye can see. Closed from November to late May - motorhomes over 35 feet are prohibited. Plan a round trip by road from Aspen.

activities.text: Rent a bike and cruise down the Rio Grande Trail, a former railroad bed turned bike path that follows the Roaring Fork River for 40 km toward Glenwood Springs. In the right direction, you descend with hardly any pedaling—take the RFTA shuttle back up.

After the drive, try Meat & Cheese on Hopkins Ave: a fine board of Colorado charcuterie and cheeses with a selection of natural wines. Aspen also has several MICHELIN-recommended restaurants for those who want to explore further.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

visits.text: Stop at Ruby Beach (47.7100, -124.4119) and let the engine idle a few minutes before getting out—the landscape deserves mental preparation. Emerged sea stacks, entire 30-meter trunks deposited by winter storms, permanent mist, nobody around. Beaches 2, 3, and 4 (47.886, -124.553) farther north share the same spirit. This is the wildest Pacific coast in the continental United States, and it proves right everyone who says Oregon and Washington have nothing to envy California.

In Astoria, cross the Astoria-Megler Bridge (46.2034, -123.8242) to see the Columbia estuary and both banks. Return to the Oregon side to see the wooden Victorian houses and the fishing port. From town, the bridge also provides a landmark for following the river towards the Pacific.

Head down to Aberdeen (46.9756, -123.8157) to see Kurt Cobain Memorial Park (46.9783, -123.8105) at the foot of the Young Street Bridge. The town has been in decline since the sawmill closures of the 1980s—a genuine sadness that fits the image of Cobain's adolescence. The statue, the bench, and the bridge he slept under as a teenager when he had no roof: not recreated, just there.

activities.text: Cross the Astoria-Megler Bridge (46.2034, -123.8242) in late afternoon—6.5 km over the Columbia, the longest continuous truss bridge in North America built in 1966, views of both banks and the estuary on clear days. You enter Oregon via this bridge. Astoria (46.1879, -123.8313) waits on the other side: 9,500 inhabitants, Victorian wooden houses, active fishing port, founded in 1811 as a fur trading post by John Jacob Astor—the oldest American city west of the Rockies.
Dine in Astoria on seafood pulled from the Columbia and Pacific—dungeness crab, Chinook salmon, Willapa Bay oysters. The active port guarantees a freshness you won't find in inland cities. $35-60.

days_plan.itin_title: 9-Day Pacific Northwest: Uncovering Hidden Gems and Cult Locations

places.name: Athens, GA

visits.text: It all began with a single light bulb. Curtis Crowe threw a Halloween party in his College Street apartment in 1978, the only illumination a 40-watt bulb, and the 40 Watt Club was born. By May 1980 it had actual walls and a stage at 100 College Avenue. Five locations later, it's at 285 West Washington Street—a former thrift store that Barrie Buck, ex-wife of R.E.M.'s Peter Buck, has run since 1987. R.E.M., the B-52's, Nirvana, Widespread Panic—all played here before they were household names. VH1 ranked it the second most legendary rock club in America. Check the calendar at the door.

Two blocks of downtown Athens—bounded by Pulaski, Washington, Lumpkin, and Clayton—hold the Athens Music Walk of Fame. The first ten stars went in September 2020; the 40 Watt Club got its own star in 2024, right outside the front door. Find the B-52's plaque and do the math: these people played their first gig at a Valentine's Day party in 1977 at 653 N. Milledge Avenue, eight hundred meters from where you're standing. The whole walk takes fifteen minutes. It's a short route for an enormous story.

Monroe Bowers Morton built the Morton Theatre around 1910—one of the country's first vaudeville theaters built, owned, and operated by African Americans, and one of the few still standing, at 195 West Washington Street. Duke Ellington, Armstrong, Cab Calloway, and Bessie Smith came through in the 1920s, 30s, and 40s. In the 1970s B-52's members were literally working in the restaurant downstairs and rehearsing in the back rooms upstairs. Restored in the early 1990s, it's a community arts center today. Look for the show listings inside.

Five kilometers from campus, the State Botanical Garden of Georgia covers 130 hectares along the Middle Oconee River - Georgia's official botanical garden and headquarters of the Garden Club of Georgia. Eight kilometers of trails wind through the Piedmont forest. The Alice Hand Callaway Conservatory rises three stories above the International Garden. The newest building - a porcelain and decorative arts museum from 2021 - adds eight exhibition spaces combining botanical art and conservation. Admission is free; closed on Mondays.

America's oldest state university - chartered in 1785 - sprawls across a hilly campus that connects East to North in about a 20-minute walk. The privet-hedged Sanford Stadium seats 93,000 and is sometimes unlocked on non-game days. More interesting than the stadium: the corner of College Avenue and Clayton Street, where Michael Stipe and Peter Buck first met in the late 1970s. Stipe was an art student; Buck was clerking in the record store below. That encounter produced seven studio albums before 1995.

A steeple standing alone in a small green space - that is all that remains of the church built in 1871 where R.E.M. rehearsed before anyone outside Athens knew their name. Services ended in 1899. The building became Red Cross headquarters, then a county museum, then student apartments, then nothing. R.E.M. played in this space before it was demolished. The steeple is free to visit, quiet, and easy to miss - precisely why it is worth finding.

The building at 215 North Lumpkin started as the YMCA in 1889, spent decades as a furniture store, and became the Georgia Theatre in 1977. The B-52's played here in 1978—the condition for booking them was that they pre-sell $1,500 in tickets themselves. The Police came the following year on their first American tour. R.E.M.'s “Shiny Happy People” video was shot here. A 2009 fire gutted the structure; full restoration finished in 2011. The rooftop bar opens at 5 p.m. and the view over downtown is the best in Athens.

activities.text: Georgia's official state art museum sits on the UGA East Campus and charges nothing to walk in. Founded in 1945, it holds nearly 20,000 works—American painting, Southern decorative arts, outsider art, a Kress Collection of Renaissance and Baroque pieces, and a sculpture garden dedicated to rotating work by women artists. The building is a 15-minute walk from the 40 Watt. Open Tuesday through Saturday; Thursday until 9 p.m., which is the best slot on a busy day.

Pick up the free music history map at the Athens Welcome Center (280 East Dougherty Street) and retrace the same three-kilometer route that R.E.M. and the B-52's followed between 1977 and 1982. Then find the Murmur railroad bridge on the North Oconee River Greenway: built in 1833, it appears on the cover of R.E.M.'s first album from 1983. The detour is worthwhile.

Athens had a music bar crawl before the term existed. The 40 Watt, the Georgia Theatre, and the Foundry - an iron foundry from 1850 turned concert venue - all book shows almost every night of the week. College radio station WUOG 90.5 FM has broadcast local and national bands since October 16, 1972; listen during the morning rush hour and it will tell you who is playing tonight. The Flagpole, a free weekly newspaper, publishes comprehensive listings available in every bar and record store in town.

Oconee Hill Cemetery on the North Oconee River is a Victorian burial ground that served as a late-night haunt for the Athens creative crowd through the 1970s and 1980s. B-52's guitarist Ricky Wilson is buried here. R.E.M.'s song 'Stumble' references those wanderings directly. Walk through at dusk before the evening shows - 20 quiet minutes that put the music scene in a different kind of context.
