visits.text: You stand above the world's largest effigy mound: the Great Serpent Mound of Adams County measures 411 meters in length, between 1.2 and 1.5 meters in height, and 6 to 7.6 meters in width - an earthen serpent that undulates in seven curves and ends with a tail coiled in a spiral, with a wide-open mouth around an oval mound. The site sits on the edge of a 300-million-year-old meteorite crater. The serpent's head is aligned with the sunset at summer solstice, and the tail points to the sunrise at winter solstice. The identity of the builders remains debated - Adena culture (800 BC) or Fort Ancient culture (1000-1650 AD) - but both cultures inhabited and used the site. The observation tower offers the only accessible aerial view. Arrive at opening at 10am to avoid school buses.

You enter the museum opened by the Ohio Historical Society in 1967 and discover that the debate over the mound's builders is far from settled. The exhibits present the soapstone-carved pipes of the Adena culture - some traveled to quarries in Illinois - and pottery from the Fort Ancient culture. Then comes the plot twist: carbon-14 dating done in the 1990s suggests construction around 1070 AD, which coincides exactly with the appearance of the Crab Nebula supernova in 1054, visible to the naked eye for twenty-three days. You leave with more questions than when you entered - which is the sign of a good museum.

You arrive in Athens descending from the Appalachian foothills of Ohio, a university town of 24,000 whose red brick campus is organized around a College Green planted with century-old elms - Ohio University, founded in 1804, is the oldest university in the Old Northwest Territory. You stroll down Court Street, the main artery lined with cafés, independent galleries, and lively restaurants that student life keeps animated even outside class hours. Push open the door of Little Professor Book Center on Court Street to find a title on Ohio's Native American mound history. If you're here in late October, Athens hosts one of the Midwest's largest street Halloweens: 20,000 people in costume flood the sidewalks.

activities.text: You join archaeologist Bill Kennedy of the Ohio History Connection for the 90-minute guided walk around the mound - the only way to get the complete scientific context, and the rare opportunity to hear a specialist debate the builder theories live. You learn how workers transported tons of earth in baskets from nearby borrow areas, how they shaped the serpent's curves without any metal tools, and why the head is precisely aligned with the summer solstice sunset. Bill Kennedy organizes these tours on the 2nd and 4th Fridays of the month from May to October - if you can time your visit to this schedule, don't miss it.

You leave Court Street on foot toward the Hocking River, and ten minutes later find yourself on a path lined with weeping willows and giant sycamores beside calm water framed by wooded hills. The Hocking River takes its name from the Wyandot word 'hockhocking', meaning bottle-shaped river, a name used by the Delaware and Shawnee peoples who fished here for centuries before colonization. In spring, pink redbud blossoms and wild magnolias brighten the banks, making this an especially rewarding time to walk.

places.name: Atlanta, GA

visits.text: The Sweet Auburn neighborhood holds an opening chapter of civil rights history. Walk to Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park—admission is free. Across the promenade stands historic Ebenezer Baptist Church: the building where King was baptized and where he and his father served as co-pastors still stands and holds Sunday services. Stop at the reflecting pool in front of Freedom Hall and read the inscriptions at the crypt of King and Coretta Scott King, set at water level. The Birth Home at 501 Auburn Avenue is currently closed for renovations.

Down the hill from Sweet Auburn, the Georgia State Capitol stands on the site of Atlanta's original City Hall - Federal troops camped here in 1864, three years before the building began rising. Completed in 1889, its gold dome is plated with gold from Dahlonega, Georgia. On the fourth floor, the Capitol Museum holds Confederate-era flags, portraits, and a famously beloved two-headed calf. Outside, look for the bronze statue of the Original 33 - the thirty-three Black legislators expelled from the Georgia General Assembly in 1868, a story the building rarely volunteers. Free admission; open Monday through Friday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Before or after the Capitol, walk along Auburn Avenue and visit Sweet Auburn Curb Market—operating since 1918, with fresh-produce vendors and a changing selection of food stalls. The neighborhood's dual history—as the birthplace of Atlanta's Black business community and King's birthplace—shows in its churches, old storefronts and park facilities. On a weekday, stop at historic Fire Station No. 6 on the park grounds: it was one of the first integrated fire stations in the Deep South and is now staffed by National Park Service volunteers.

activities.text: The Civil Rights Walk of Fame runs along Auburn Avenue within the King Historic District. Walk it slowly: bronze footprints are embedded in the sidewalk honoring inductees including Rosa Parks and Coretta Scott King. The whole stretch from the Visitor Center to the King Center and back is about 800 meters. Plan for late afternoon when the light is lower and foot traffic thins.

Dinner in Atlanta before tomorrow's early departure east on I-85. The Ponce City Market on North Highland Avenue brings together local restaurants in a restored 1920s Sears building - a comfortable place to decompress after a day heavy with history. Alternatively, the small restaurants on Edgewood Avenue are a ten-minute walk from the park.

places.name: Augusta, GA

visits.text: Built in 1845 to harness the Savannah River, the Augusta Canal is the only fully intact American industrial canal still running for its original purposes—power, water supply, transportation. Congress made it Georgia's first National Heritage Area in 1996. During the Civil War, Confederate Colonel George Washington Rains chose Augusta for the only gunpowder works ever designed, built, and funded by the Confederate States of America—28 buildings stretching three kilometers along this same waterway. The Discovery Center is inside Enterprise Mill at 1450 Greene Street. Guided boat tours aboard replica Petersburg cargo boats depart daily. Book ahead.

Two floors, 12,000 years. That's what the Augusta Museum of History represents. Founded in 1937, it opens downstairs with the full sweep of regional history—a 1917 steam locomotive, a Civil War cannon, the story of the Georgia Railroad (modified in 1835, the most important company in the state). Upstairs: the largest dedicated James Brown collection in the world. Costumes, family photographs, original vinyl, his “King of Soul” crown from the 1950s, kiosks playing the hits. Brown grew up in Augusta. He never really left. Paid entry.

Meadow Garden at 1320 Independence Drive is the oldest documented house in Augusta - built probably in the 1750s, expanded in the 1790s by George Walton, who at 26 became one of the youngest men to sign the Declaration of Independence. He signed his letters 'George Walton of Meadow Garden' from 1791 until his death here in 1804. The Daughters of the American Revolution bought the house in 1900 and opened it to the public on November 21, 1901 - making it one of the oldest house museums in the United States. National Historic Landmark since 1981. Paid entry.

activities.text: Eleven kilometers of flat towpath run from downtown Augusta out to the locks at Savannah Rapids Park—the original route used by mules pulling canal boats upstream. The most dramatic stretch is the first three kilometers, past the King Mill and the Sibley Mill, a Gothic Revival industrial building from 1882 built on the former Confederate Powderworks site. Herons, otters, and the occasional alligator work the banks. Bike and kayak rentals are at the locks on weekends in spring and fall.
The Augusta Riverwalk along the Savannah River, eight hundred meters from Broad Street, is the best place to catch the evening light.

visits.text: Augusta is the easternmost state capital in the United States, and the Maine State House that sits at the top of State Street has been here since 1832. Charles Bulfinch - the same architect who designed the US Capitol before Benjamin Henry Latrobe took over - drew the original plans, built in granite quarried from nearby Hallowell. C. Henri Desmond doubled the building's size in 1910, raising the copper dome to 185 feet. Free guided tours are available weekdays year-round through the Maine State Museum; just call ahead.

Down the hill on the east bank of the Kennebec River stands Old Fort Western, the oldest surviving wooden garrison in North America. It went up in 1754, during the French and Indian War, to serve as a supply depot for Fort Halifax further upriver. Benedict Arnold used it as a staging point in 1775 before leading 1,100 men up the Kennebec toward Quebec. The main structure is the original 1754 building; the two blockhouses were reconstructed in the 1920s. Costumed guides bring the place to life with demonstrations of 18th-century life.

Capitol Park, directly between the State House and the Kennebec, is Maine's earliest documented designed landscape - Augusta residents donated the 34 acres in 1827, and the Olmsted Brothers redesigned it in the 1920s. The park runs right down to the river with wide gravel paths between rows of old maples. It's been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1989. A short walk along the riverfront south of the park reaches the Kennebec River Rail Trail.

activities.text: The Maine State Museum on State Street sits directly behind the State House and covers 12,000 years of Maine history in a single building - from Ice Age mastodons found in a Scarborough marsh to the state's industrial heritage in logging, fishing, and granite quarrying. The “Made in Maine” gallery reconstructs a complete 19th-century mill town interior. Budget at least two hours; the natural history section alone is substantial.

Augusta sits at the head of tide on the Kennebec River - meaning the tidal influence stops right here. Walking or cycling the Kennebec River Rail Trail from the Capitol Park down toward Hallowell gives you 6.5 miles of flat riverside path through industrial-era warehouses and scenic river bends. The trail runs on a former railroad bed and connects Augusta to the historic town of Hallowell, worth a 20-minute wander for its antique shops.

places.name: Austin, TX

visits.text: Texas State Capitol: built from 1882 to 1888 in local pink granite, the capitol measures 92 m tall - 4.5 m taller than the one in Washington. At the time of its inauguration on April 21, 1888 (anniversary of the Battle of San Jacinto), it was the seventh-largest building in the world. Workers from Granite Mountain supplied the granite free of charge; in exchange, the contractors received 3 million acres in the Texas Panhandle - which became one of the country's largest ranches. The free tour takes you up to the dome through 400 rooms and 900 windows.

South Congress Avenue (SoCo): Austin's most photographed avenue packs everything that defines the city's personality into a few kilometers—secondhand clothing shops, food trucks, independent galleries, and the now-famous “I Love You So Much” mural on a café facade. If you're here on a Sunday morning, the flea market and brunches on outdoor patios are perfect for getting a feel for the local atmosphere.

Barton Springs Pool: fed by natural springs at a stable year-round temperature of 20°C, this 280-meter-long pool in the middle of Zilker Park has been the Austinites' gathering spot for a century. In the heat of a Texas summer, it's a godsend. There is a modest admission fee—arrive early on weekends as crowds can make entry difficult by late morning.

Blanton Museum of Art: on the UT Austin campus, this museum houses Texas's largest university art collection. You'll find European paintings from the Renaissance through the 18th century, a leading Latin American art collection, and remarkable prints. The building itself, designed by Kallmann McKinnell & Wood and opened in 2006, is worth the visit - the central nave is impressive.

Mount Bonnell: at an elevation of 238 m, the panorama opens onto the hills stretching westward. There are 106 steps to climb from the parking lot - allow 10 minutes. It's a popular sunset spot with Austin locals: arrive 30 minutes beforehand to find a good place.

activities.text: Live music night on 6th Street: Austin has over 250 concert venues and claims the title “Live Music Capital of the World.” Thursday night is often the best time—many local bands play with no cover charge. Walk into any bar from 9 PM onward: country, blues, indie rock, jazz—there's bound to be something for you within a few meters.

Bat-watching at Congress Avenue Bridge: since the bridge's 1980 renovation, cracks between the concrete beams have become North America's largest urban bat roost—between 750,000 and 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats settle here each spring. Every evening at dusk, they fly out in a column visible over 1 km away. Position yourself on the bridge's east side or on the Bat Observation Center lawn for the best view. The phenomenon runs from March to November.

Kayak or paddleboard on Lady Bird Lake: 16 km of urban lake framed by the 8 km Trail lining both shores - it's Austin's green heart. Outfitters offer kayak, pedal boat and stand-up paddleboard rentals directly on the banks. Early morning, the lake surface is perfectly smooth and the skyline reflections are spectacular.

BBQ circuit in Lockhart: dubbed the 'BBQ Capital of Texas' by the State Legislature, Lockhart sits 45 minutes from Austin. Four legendary institutions - some over 100 years old - are concentrated within a three-block radius. The brisket is smoked over post oak for a minimum of 14 hours, sliced to order with no plate or silverware - just kraft paper. If you've never eaten real Texas BBQ, this is where it happens.

visits.text: Exceptional day ahead: you're driving the Going-to-the-Sun Road, one of America's most spectacular highways. This 80-km road connects the west entrance to the east entrance by crossing the park over the Continental Divide. Built by hand between 1921 and 1933—dynamite, picks, and chisels—it's a National Historic Landmark. The road climbs to Logan Pass at 2,025 m elevation, snaking along vertiginous cliffs. Drive slowly (25 mph in the alpine section) and stop at the overlooks.

At the summit, stop at Logan Pass Visitor Center. This is the road's high point and the trailhead for two of the park's most renowned hikes. Take the Hidden Lake Overlook Trail—4.5 km round-trip with 140 m of elevation gain on wooden boardwalks through alpine meadows. At the end, you overlook Hidden Lake and its turquoise waters. You'll likely spot mountain goats and bighorn sheep—they're accustomed to hikers. Warning: parking at Logan Pass is limited to 3 hours in summer, plan to arrive early morning.

Descending the east side, make a stop at Jackson Glacier Overlook. This is the best spot on the road to view a glacier from your car. The interpretive sign shows comparative photos of the glacier over the decades—the retreat is striking. Continue to St. Mary and take the road toward Many Glacier (40 minutes from US-89).

Arriving in the Many Glacier valley, you'll discover a postcard landscape: Swiftcurrent Lake in the foreground, Many Glacier Hotel by the water, and the snow-capped peaks of Mount Grinnell (2,698 m) and Mount Wilbur (2,841 m) as backdrop. Circle the lake late in the day—the low-angle light turns the mountains golden. This is also the park zone where grizzly sightings are most frequent, especially in summer when wild berries ripen.

activities.text: If you still have energy after the drive, take the easy walk around Swiftcurrent Lake (3.8 km). Keep your distance from wildlife—at least 100 meters from bears and 25 meters from other animals.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Rockies Loop: Glacier & Waterton

activities.text: You will resume your drive on Bainbridge Island after arriving by ferry from Seattle. The ferry also carries cars, allowing you to continue toward Port Angeles without returning to the mainland via Seattle. Keep your ticket handy and follow the disembarkation instructions; buying a ticket does not reserve a space on board.

visits.text: Arriving in Baker, you can't miss the world's tallest thermometer: 41 meters of steel structure, visible from Interstate 15. Its height—exactly 134 feet—is a tribute to the temperature record set at Furnace Creek on July 10, 1913: 56.7°C. It was Willis Herron, a local businessman, who financed it in 1991 to draw travelers to his town. Desert winds toppled it shortly after its unveiling; it was rebuilt with 125 cubic meters of concrete in its structure. The Temp 134 shop at its base tells the whole story, including a frying pan left outside permanently to test whether the heat is enough to cook eggs (it takes 70°C to do so).

From Baker, plan a return trip during the day to reach the Kelso Dunes in Mojave National Preserve. These dunes cover 120 km² and rise nearly 200 meters above the desert floor; the return hike is about 6 km with 200 meters of elevation gain. The sand, made of quartz and feldspar, comes from deposits of the ancient Mojave River and accumulated here about 25,000 years ago. When grains slide down the slopes in dry winds, they produce a low hum audible from afar, an acoustic phenomenon linked to the specific grain size and the area's extreme aridity. Bring water, as the heat builds quickly. There are no markers on this terrain: choose your route and head straight for the ridge.

Kelso Depot, a historic 1924 station built in Mission Revival style by the Union Pacific Railroad, supplied steam locomotives with water and coal in the heart of the desert. The restored building can be seen from outside, but its visitor center is currently closed for renovation. Stop in front of the station before or after the dunes; do not plan on visiting the exhibits about railroad history and the preserve's geology.

activities.text: To reach the lava tube in the Cima volcanic field from Baker, take Aiken Mine Road: the track currently requires a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle. From the parking area, a rocky trail leads to the metal ladder descending into the basalt tunnel. Bring a headlamp: the cave is dark at first, although natural openings illuminate its central sections. Take a light jacket, as it stays cool even in summer. Check the track conditions before setting out; this is not a short walk from the Kelso Dunes.

places.name: Baker, NV

visits.text: In 1885, rancher Absalom Lehman began guiding neighbors through this cave for a few cents. Today you pay a little more, but it is still worth it. Lehman Caves is Nevada's longest known cave—3.2 km through marble and limestone—with 'parachute' formations. It stays at 10°C inside year-round: bring a jacket. Two ranger-led tours: 60 or 90 minutes. Reservation required on recreation.gov.

The Wheeler Peak Scenic Drive climbs 19 km from the visitor center up to 3,013 meters. You cross five ecological zones in one hour of driving—from sagebrush desert to alpine meadows. Stop at Mather Overlook: the view plunges across 150 km of empty valleys. Closed to vehicles over 7.3 meters, closed in winter—check conditions at nps.gov.

Stop at the Great Basin Visitor Center in Baker before entering the park. You will find current conditions, available tours and an exhibit on Great Basin ecology. Another display tells the story of the 'Forgotten Winchester', an 1882 rifle found leaning against a juniper in the park in 2014—still loaded, still standing.

Stella Lake and Teresa Lake sit perched above 3,200 meters beneath the north face of Wheeler Peak. The trail from the top of the Scenic Drive is 3.7 km round-trip—short but stunning. The water is ice-cold even in August. At dawn, the reflection of Wheeler Peak on Stella Lake is disturbingly sharp. Arrive early to have the lake to yourself.

The Baker Archaeological Site, accessible from a track east of the village, preserves the remains of a prehistoric Fremont village occupied about 1,000 years ago. 1990s excavations revealed a structured community organization—granaries, communal hearths, shared spaces. Interpretive panel on-site. Free access.

Lexington Arch is a 22 m natural limestone arch in the southern part of the park—very rare in the American West, where almost all arches are sandstone. From Baker, allow much of the day for a return trip via Lexington Creek Road, south of Garrison, followed by a hike. This badly eroded dirt road requires a high-clearance vehicle; four-wheel drive is recommended. Vehicle access to the old trailhead has not been restored. Avoid the road after rain and check conditions before leaving.

activities.text: The Bristlecone/Glacier Trail starts at 3,012 meters from the Wheeler Peak Campground parking lot: 6.9 km round-trip to the base of the rock glacier, passing through a grove of bristlecone pines. Some of these twisted trees are over 4,000 years old—they were already here when the pyramids were being built. Start early: thunderstorms often roll in around 2 p.m. in summer.

Great Basin is one of the darkest parks in the continental United States—designated an International Dark Sky Park. On clear nights, the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye from Wheeler Peak Campground at 2,999 meters. Rangers lead astronomy evenings on Fridays and Saturdays in summer at the Lehman Caves amphitheater. Schedule at nps.gov/grba.

The Baker Creek area is one of the park's least visited corners. The Baker Lake Trail, about 17 km round-trip from the Baker Creek trailhead, climbs through white pine forests to a lake you may often have to yourself. It is a long hike, not a short loop. Look for mule deer and marmots, and sometimes—with luck and quiet—a black bear among the rocks.

visits.text: Start your journey in Fells Point rather than the Inner Harbor—this is the real Baltimore. Founded in 1763, this waterfront neighborhood boasts over 300 buildings on the National Register, making it Maryland's first designated historic district. Frederick Douglass worked here as a caulker in the shipyards until his escape in 1838. Walk the Belgian-block cobblestones of Thames Street in the morning, before the sidewalk cafes fill up.

Fort McHenry deserves half a day, not just a photo from the parking lot. Picture the night of September 13-14, 1814: 25 hours of relentless British bombardment, and the fort held. It was from his own American sloop under flag of truce—detained by the British fleet—that Francis Scott Key scribbled the verses that became the national anthem in 1931. Arrive early in the morning to avoid school groups.

If you only have time for one thing in Baltimore, choose the National Aquarium on Pier 3. Opened in 1981, it draws 1.5 million visitors annually—20,000 animals representing 800 species, including a 500-pound green sea turtle named Calypso. Admission is timed: book online. On Fridays after 5 PM, tickets are half price.

At the Reginald F. Lewis Museum on Pratt Street, spend 60 to 90 minutes in the "Things Hold, Lines Connect" gallery—400 years of African American history in Maryland, with an in-depth section on Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman. Free admission on the first Sunday of each month.

The American Visionary Art Museum at 800 Key Highway isn't the art museum you expect. Self-taught artists with no formal training—their works fill seven galleries, plus a 55-foot outdoor windmill covered in mirrors. Plan 90 minutes and leave your usual reference points at the coat check.

activities.text: Walk the Inner Harbor waterfront for 1.5 kilometers to the Historic Ships in Baltimore: the USS Constellation, an 1797 frigate, and the USS Torsk, a World War II submarine, are the two most immersive. Combination ticket around $16.

Broadway Market has been open since 1786. Walk down Thames Street to the Horse You Came In On Saloon - this is where Edgar Allan Poe had his last drink before his mysterious death in October 1849. Try the crab fritters and a local beer.

visits.text: Discover Bandelier National Monument, a 13,000-hectare preserve protecting the ancestral homes, petroglyphs, and ceremonial sites of the Pueblo people dating back 11,000 years. The dramatic cliff dwellings carved into soft volcanic tuff allow visitors to climb ladders and explore actual ancient living spaces used by communities centuries ago. Hiking trails wind through canyon landscapes where archaeological treasures reveal the sophisticated civilization that flourished here.

Walk among the impressive ruins where the Ancestral Pueblo people built multi-story structures using natural cave formations and hand-carved chambers in the canyon walls. Interpretive programs explain how these communities adapted to the challenging environment, developing agriculture, crafts, and social structures that influenced later Pueblo cultures throughout the region.

activities.text: Watch for the distinctive Albert's Squirrels with their characteristic ear tufts while hiking the monument's scenic trails through ponderosa pine forests and canyon bottoms. The diverse ecosystems support abundant wildlife and provide insights into how ancient peoples utilized natural resources for survival and cultural expression.

places.name: Bangor, ME

visits.text: The house at 47 West Broadway is unmistakable: blood-red Victorian mansion, wrought-iron fence decorated with bats, spiders, and a three-headed dragon, designed and built by local metalworker Terry Steel in 1982. Stephen King bought the place in 1980 for $135,000 and lived here for over 40 years, writing many of his most famous novels inside. The neighborhood - Bangor's Whitney Park Historic District - inspired the fictional town of Derry in IT. King no longer lives here full-time; the house is now his foundation's archive and a writers' retreat. Visitors are welcome on the sidewalk for photos. Quiet and respectful, please: it's a residential street.

Three blocks from the waterfront on Main Street, the Paul Bunyan statue has been staring down at traffic since February 12, 1959 - Paul's 125th birthday, according to Bangor's official birth certificate on file at City Hall. The 31-foot fiberglass figure weighs 3,700 pounds and is engineered to withstand 110 mph winds. Bangor was the self-proclaimed “Lumber Capital of the World” in the late 1800s, when sailing ships lined the Penobscot River loaded with Maine timber. Stephen King worked Bunyan into the plot of IT in 1986, animating him with an evil spirit. A time capsule inside the pedestal is scheduled to open on Bangor's 250th birthday: February 12, 2084.

The Maine Discovery Museum on Main Street is the largest children's museum north of Boston, with three floors of interactive exhibits covering Maine's sciences, nature and arts. Even if you are not travelling with children, the floor devoted to nature is genuinely impressive - it traces the food chain of a Maine forest ecosystem from soil microbes all the way up to moose. It is also one of the few rainy-day options in Bangor.

The Penobscot River Walkway runs along the downtown waterfront, connecting the Paul Bunyan statue to the riverbank park. In the late 1800s this stretch of river was choked with log drives - thousands of trees floating from Moosehead Lake to the paper mills downstream, guided by “river pigs” with peaveys. The waterfront has been cleaned up into a pleasant park; interpretive panels explain the industrial history. Early mornings bring kayakers and the occasional osprey.

activities.text: Bangor has built a reputation as a surprisingly serious craft beer town. Geaghan Brothers Brewing on Main Street has been pouring its beers since 2013 and works with Maine farmers to source its ingredients - their Spinnaker Blonde is a local staple. 2 Feet Brewing, downtown, favours hoppy IPAs. Both are easily reached on foot from the waterfront. Pair a pint with a stop at Gerald Winters & Son Bookstore on Main Street, which specialises in signed Stephen King first editions and King collectibles.

For a proper immersion in King's Bangor, the SK Tours guided driving and walking tour covers the Jackson Street storm drain (the inspiration for IT's iconic opening), the Thomas Hill Standpipe (which appears in several novels), Mount Hope Cemetery (used as a filming location for Pet Sematary), and a dozen other real-life locations mapped to King's fictional Derry. Tours run seasonally and last about two hours.

places.name: Bar Harbor, ME

visits.text: At low tide, a natural sandbar connects downtown Bar Harbor to Bar Island—you've got about an hour before the sea reclaims it, so don't dawdle. The Abbe Museum, in the village, is devoted to Wabanaki culture and worth a quick visit. Bar Harbor was the late 19th-century summer retreat of the Rockefeller and Vanderbilt families—their wooden cottages survive on the heights.

Climb Cadillac Mountain early in the morning: at 1,530 feet, it's the highest point on the entire East Coast of the United States, and from October 7 to March 6, it's the first place in the country where the sun rises. The 360° view embraces Frenchman Bay, the Porcupine Islands, and on clear days, the Schoodic Peninsula. The summit road winds for 3.5 miles. Hikers will prefer the Cadillac North Ridge Trail (4.4 miles round-trip).

Thunder Hole is a crevice in the pink granite where waves crash with a dull roar—arrive at mid-rising tide for maximum effect. Just north, Sand Beach is one of Acadia's rare sandy beaches, framed by pink cliffs. The water hovers between 50 and 59°F even in August: bring a jacket.

Jordan Pond House is the park's only restaurant—settle on the terrace facing the South and North Bubbles, those glacier-rounded hills framing the pond. The tea house has served popovers since the late 19th century: order them hot with butter and jam, an unchanged tradition from the days of wealthy summer visitors.

Otter Cliff, at the southeastern tip of Mount Desert Island, is a 100-foot granite wall dropping straight into the Atlantic. It's one of the most popular sea cliff climbing sites on the East Coast—if you're not climbing, the view from the trail's edge toward the Cranberry Isles is striking.

If you didn't see the sunrise from Cadillac Mountain the day before, this is your last chance before the long drive to Vermont. Otherwise, have a typical Maine breakfast at Café This Way before leaving Bar Harbor—eggs, lobster hash, and strong coffee.

activities.text: Dine on the waterfront facing the Porcupine Islands: the village restaurants serve lobsters and mussels caught that very morning. Take the opportunity to reserve your Cadillac Mountain access for tomorrow—the summit road requires a reservation on recreation.gov from mid-May through late October, and sunrise slots sell out in minutes.

Rent a bike in Bar Harbor and explore Acadia's carriage roads: a network of 45 miles of gravel paths financed by John D. Rockefeller Jr. in the 1910s-1940s, with 16 hand-cut stone bridges. The Eagle Lake Loop (~5.5 miles) is ideal for a half-day in the spruce woods. Count on $30-40 per day for rental.

Go sea kayaking from Bar Harbor: local guides run 3-hour excursions around the Porcupine Islands with passage past seal colonies. The Atlantic is calm on the Frenchman Bay side most summer mornings—several outfitters are clustered on the Village Green. Reservation recommended in July-August.

visits.text: Devil's Lake State Park - Wisconsin's most-visited park, and for good reason: a glacial lake trapped between two 150-meter quartzite bluffs. These rocks, 1.6 billion years old, are among the continent's oldest. The contrast between turquoise water and pink cliffs is striking.

East Bluff Trails - Climb the East Bluff Trail (2.5 km) for plunging views over the lake and Baraboo Hills. The trail passes through "talus fields" - piles of quartzite blocks stacked by erosion - a rare habitat for certain moss and lichen species.

Circus World Museum - Baraboo was headquarters of the Ringling Brothers (America's greatest circus) from 1884 to 1918. The museum, housed in the original buildings, preserves decorated circus wagons, posters, and memorabilia. In summer, live circus performances are given under the big top.

activities.text: Swimming and Picnic at Devil's Lake - Both beaches (north and south) are well-maintained. The water is cool but pleasant in summer. Pack a picnic and settle in facing the bluffs - it's the perfect ending to this road trip.
Quartzite Climbing (optional) - Devil's Lake bluffs are a renowned Midwest climbing spot. Over 1,600 routes on quartzite, all levels. Outfitters offer introductory lessons.

places.name: Barstow, CA

visits.text: Needles, CA—You enter California through the Mojave Desert. Needles, named after the rock spires overlooking the town, is the last stop before 250 km of desert. Fill up on gas and stock up on water here—stations are scarce until Barstow.

Roy's Motel & Café (Amboy)—In the middle of nowhere, literally. This 1930s motel in the heart of the Mojave is being renovated for Route 66's centennial in 2026. The Googie-style neon sign is one of the most photographed on the route. Temperatures often exceed 45°C here in summer—stay in your car if you're not prepared.

Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch (Oro Grande)—Plan on a round trip from Barstow for this visit. Stop in front of these 200 “trees” made from metal pipes topped with colored glass bottles that chime in the desert wind. You have never seen anything like it—this folk art installation, created by one man on his own land, is mesmerizing.

Calico Ghost Town—If you're traveling with family, stop at this 1880s former silver mining town. Restored in the 1950s, it's a historic park with period buildings, a mine you can visit, and a small train. Allow 1 hour for the visit.

activities.text: Crossing the Mojave - The most desolate and spectacular part of the Route. Lunar landscapes, railroad tracks stretching to the horizon, purple mountains. Plan on having music - radio doesn't pick up much between Needles and Barstow.

places.name: Baton Rouge, LA

visits.text: At 137 meters tall with 34 floors, the Louisiana State Capitol is the tallest state capitol in the United States - and it has no dome. Huey Long insisted on a skyscraper, drawing inspiration from Nebraska's 1920s tower. The Art Deco building was completed in 1932, with floors cut from Italian volcanic stone and 26 types of marble throughout. Long is buried in the garden outside, marked by a 3.70-meter bronze by Charles Keck. Inside, ask to see the assassination hallway: a display case marks the ground-floor corridor where Long was shot on September 8, 1935, by Dr. Carl Weiss, whose father-in-law Long had just gerrymandered out of a judgeship. Bullet holes in a granite column are still visible. Take the elevator to the 27th-floor observation deck for views of Baton Rouge and the Mississippi.

The Old State Capitol, 800 meters toward the river on North Boulevard, is a Gothic Revival castle built in 1847 and rebuilt in 1882 after an accidental fire. The second version added the famous spiral staircase and a stained glass dome. Mark Twain called it a “monstrosity.” It now houses the Museum of Political History. The contrast with Long's skyscraper a few blocks away - one a Victorian fantasy, the other a Depression-era tower of ambition - tells you something about Louisiana's political imagination.

The USS Kidd, a Fletcher-class destroyer from the Second World War, is currently in Houma for repairs: it cannot be toured on the Mississippi riverfront in Baton Rouge. The ship fought at Leyte Gulf and survived a kamikaze attack in April 1945 that killed 38 men. The veterans museum remains open and holds aircraft and personal accounts from several conflicts. The Louisiana State Capitol on the hill and the Old State Capitol behind you offer two further scales of Louisiana history.

activities.text: The Capitol Park Museum on River Road covers Louisiana history from pre-Columbian cultures through Hurricane Katrina. The “Experiencing Louisiana” gallery has a full-scale oil platform section, a French Quarter streetscape, and one of the stronger Mardi Gras artifact collections in the state. Free admission.

Dinner in Baton Rouge before the final leg to New Orleans tomorrow. The stretch of Government Street between downtown and Mid-City has a concentration of local restaurants that aren't aimed at tourists. Book ahead - Baton Rouge is a university city and good tables fill quickly on weekday evenings.

visits.text: Day 1 - Start at Battery Park, the southern tip of Manhattan. Arrive before 8:30 AM: this is where ferries depart for the Statue of Liberty, and the security line behind Castle Clinton can exceed an hour in summer. The park takes twenty minutes to walk through, offering a first view of the bay and Lady Liberty in the distance.

Day 1 - Before boarding, take a look at Castle Clinton, an 1811 fort that now serves as the official ticket office for the Battery Park ferries. A very full day: the Statue of Liberty + Ellis Island loop eats up half a day with the lines, so adjust the rest of the itinerary accordingly.

activities.text: Book ferry tickets online at Statue City Cruises: $25.50 per adult in 2026, Ellis Island included in the same ticket. Without reservation, morning slots fill up fast.

Board the ferry to Liberty Island: a 2.8 km crossing; allow 25 to 30 min including the wait at the dock. Ferries run every 20 to 30 min, with the first departures between 8:30 and 9 AM depending on the season.

places.name: Bayfield, WI

visits.text: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore Visitor Center - Start here in Bayfield to understand the archipelago: 22 islands, 21 within the national park, carved by Lake Superior over billions of years. Rangers give briefings on sea conditions and visiting options. Maps and camping permits available.

Meyers Beach Sea Caves (trail view) - If weather doesn't permit kayaking, take the coastal trail above the caves. Budget 2.5 km to reach the first cavities, then another 1.5 km for the most spectacular ones. From atop the cliff, you'll see the arches, passages, and the famous "land bridge" spanning the Fissure. The 500-million-year-old Cambrian sandstone takes on almost surreal shapes.

Bayfield - This small Lake Superior harbor town (population under 500) was built on the lumber industry then reinvented itself as a tourist destination. Stroll the sloping streets lined with colorful Victorian houses. The marina is the launching point for all island excursions.

Bayfield Orchards - The peninsula is known for its apples, cherries, and berries. Several farms open their doors to visitors for pick-your-own (in season) or tastings of cider and preserves. It's particularly beautiful in May (apple blossoms) and October (harvest).
Lake Superior Views - Head up to the heights of Bayfield to see the Apostle Islands archipelago spread before you. On clear days, you can make out lighthouses on the nearest islands.

activities.text: Kayaking the Sea Caves - Bayfield's grand adventure. Outfitters offer guided trips of 2.5-3 hours from Meyers Beach. You paddle along the cliff face then enter the sandstone caverns - some large enough to glide through in your kayak. In summer, amber light from the setting sun illuminates the caves' interiors. You must be able to swim and sea conditions must be calm. Book ahead in July-August.

Apostle Islands Cruise - If you're not a kayaker, the 2.5-3 hour cruise tours the islands, passes the lighthouses of Raspberry Island and Devils Island, and skirts the sea caves. Departs from Bayfield harbor.

Big Top Chautauqua - If you're here in summer (June-September), don't miss this performance venue under a blue big-top tent on the Bayfield heights. Concerts, musical shows about Lake Superior history, comedies. Laid-back atmosphere, picnics welcome.

Madeline Island Ferry Crossing - The largest Apostle Island (the only inhabited one) is 20 minutes by ferry. Historic village of La Pointe, Native American museum, Big Bay beach, and 16 km of roads to explore by bike.

The road crosses a high plateau before descending in switchbacks toward Red Lodge; snow can still close the route during the tourist season. places.name: Beatty, NV

visits.text: In Beatty, visit the Beatty Museum & Historical Society on Main Street to learn about the Bullfrog Mining District before heading to Rhyolite. Its collections trace the rise of the area's mining camps, their residents' daily lives and the journeys that shaped this gateway to Death Valley. Take time to look at the photographs and objects preserved there: they give a human face to the abandoned buildings you will later see in Rhyolite. The museum is in your overnight town, with no detour through the Las Vegas area. It provides a concrete introduction to what prospectors sought in the Bullfrog Hills before you continue to the ruins and the Goldwell Open Air Museum.

4 km west of Beatty on SR-374, take the marked BLM road that leads to the ruins of Rhyolite. This mining town erupted from nowhere in 1905 after gold was discovered in the Bullfrog Hills: 5,000 residents in six months, three banks, a stock exchange, an opera house, a hospital, concrete sidewalks, and electricity. The John S. Cook & Co. bank, completed in 1908, cost more than $90,000 (approximately $3.2 million today) with its Italian marble stairs and stained glass imported from Europe. By 1916, the lights went out for good. What remains is the bank facade, the train depot, and the famous Bottle House—built in 1906 by Tom Kelly with 50,000 bottles salvaged from saloons, for lack of wood in the desert. Just below, the Goldwell Open Air Museum presents a dozen outdoor sculptures installed starting in 1984, including the haunting Last Supper by Belgian artist Albert Szukalski. Free admission, open dawn to dusk.

activities.text: On US-95 between Las Vegas and Beatty, keep an eye on the roadside: wild burros regularly roam the Amargosa Valley, descendants of pack animals abandoned by miners. Don't approach them and don't feed them—they remain wild animals. Allow about two and a half hours of driving from Red Rock Canyon to Beatty.

places.name: Beaufort, NC

visits.text: Discover the Beaufort Historic Site, a remarkable museum complex featuring nine beautifully preserved historic houses that offer vivid insights into coastal Carolina life in the 18th and 19th centuries. Once ranked among America's coolest towns by Budget Travel Magazine, Beaufort is rich in historic sites and Southern heritage.

Explore the North Carolina Maritime Museum, which chronicles the state's rich nautical heritage through diverse artifacts spanning centuries of seafaring history. The museum's extensive collections include shipwreck treasures, shipbuilding exhibits, and displays documenting the vital role the sea has played in shaping coastal North Carolina culture and commerce.

activities.text: Visit the Rachel Carson Reserve, a pristine coastal sanctuary offering an excellent atmosphere for relaxation and wildlife observation. This protected natural area features stunning water views and the chance to spot herds of adorable wild horses roaming freely. The reserve exemplifies the unspoiled coastal beauty that makes Beaufort a perfect weekend retreat.

visits.text: Beaufort (pronounced “Byoo-furt,” unlike North Carolina's Beaufort, “Boh-furt”) is South Carolina's second oldest town, founded in 1711. The historic center of 304 antebellum buildings has been listed in its entirety on the National Register - one of the densest concentrations in the country. The pre-1861 houses survived because the town surrendered without a fight to Union forces in 1861. “Forrest Gump” and “Le Grand Saint Nicholas” were filmed here. Self-guided walks, free maps at the Visitor Center.

Hunting Island State Park, 30 minutes east, is one of the wildest beaches on the East Coast - 8 kilometers of shoreline with scrub palmetto and oaks bleached by salt, a subtropical jungle atmosphere literally pressed against the ocean. The opening scene of "Forrest Gump" on the Vietnam beach was filmed here. The 1875 lighthouse (50 meters, 167 steps) can be climbed for $2. Park entrance $8.

Penn Center, on Saint Helena Island, was one of the first schools for formerly enslaved people in the United States, founded in 1862 by Pennsylvania missionaries during the war. Martin Luther King stayed here several times to plan the March on Washington (1963) and the Selma march (1965) - it was one of the few places in the South where Blacks and Whites could safely meet. Now a museum of Gullah heritage. $10.

activities.text: Taste Lowcountry cuisine at Old Bull Tavern on Carteret Street - a small chef-driven restaurant, local products, serious but unpretentious. For something more traditional, Q on Bay serves mustard-based barbecue sauce typical of the Carolina midlands, accompanied by hash (a thick stew made from hog's head meat) - a regional preparation little known elsewhere.

activities.text: Boulevard Park offers one last break by the water before you finish in Bellingham. The park sits right on the bay, with places to walk and relax near the shore. Stay within the park if a pedestrian connection is closed; adjust the length of your walk to your departure schedule.

You’ll finish the route in Bellingham, with the option of departing from Fairhaven station, served by Amtrak. Ending in the northern part of the state avoids immediately adding a long drive to Seattle. Arrange your vehicle return and onward connection before the trip; train reservations are separate from the driving itinerary.

visits.text: Pilot Butte — Climb this volcanic cone in Bend to see the high desert and the Cascade Range. From the summit, pick out Mount Hood among the volcanoes on the horizon; the Timberline Trail and Timberline Lodge lie at the foot of that mountain, far from Bend.

Smith Rock State Park — From Bend, plan a return drive to hike among steep 200-meter cliffs of welded volcanic tuff above the Crooked River. The park pioneered American sport climbing in the 1980s and offers high desert scenery with more than 1,800 climbing routes.

High Desert Museum — Explore regional natural and cultural history through indoor galleries and outdoor living exhibits. The museum features native wildlife, Old West artifacts, and interpretations of indigenous cultures across 135 acres.

Old Mill District — Browse this shopping and dining district built around preserved 1909 lumber mill smokestacks. The Deschutes River-front development represents Bend's transformation from lumber town to outdoor recreation hub.

activities.text: Deschutes Brewery visit — Tour one of Oregon's oldest craft breweries founded in 1988, instrumental in establishing Central Oregon's beer culture. The original pub serves flagship Black Butte Porter and seasonal specialties.
Deschutes River Trail cycling — Pedal along paved paths following the river through pine forests and lava rock formations. The 12-mile trail system connects parks, breweries, and downtown Bend.

Sunset at Pilot Butte — Climb this 150-meter cinder cone for 360-degree views across the high desert to Cascade peaks. The extinct volcano offers panoramic vistas of Mount Bachelor, Three Sisters, and surrounding volcanic landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Oregon Natural Wonders: Crater Lake to Pacific Coast Road Trip

places.name: Bentonville, AR

visits.text: Crystal Bridges opened on November 11, 2011, funded by Alice Walton, daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton. She chose Bentonville - the town where her father opened his first store - to build a world-class museum with free admission. Moshe Safdie designed eight pavilions of wood, concrete, and copper nestled around two ponds fed by a natural spring called Crystal Spring. The collection spans five centuries of American art - from 17th-century colonial portraits through Andy Warhol and Norman Rockwell - plus a Frank Lloyd Wright Usonian house relocated from New Jersey in 2013. Allow at least 2.5 hours, and don't miss the outdoor trails that connect the museum to downtown.

The Momentary is Crystal Bridges' satellite space dedicated to living art and performance. Inaugurated in 2020 in a converted Kraft cheese factory, the space mixes contemporary art exhibitions, concerts, artist residencies, and screenings. If you don't know what to expect, go in anyway - the programming is often more surprising than the industrial address suggests. Admission is free.

The Walmart Museum occupies the very first store opened by Sam Walton in 1950 on Bentonville Square, under the name Walton's Five and Dime. Archives, photos, and objects from the original shop trace the birth of what became the world's largest company by revenue. Allow 45 minutes and you'll leave with a clear sense of the distance between the 1950 shop and today's giant.

Bentonville Square is the central plaza with its early 20th-century brick facades, including Sam Walton's original Five and Dime. Walk the square after the museum: cafes, restaurants, and independent shops have moved in, and the atmosphere is far from what you'd imagine in Walmart's hometown.

activities.text: Crystal Bridges trails: over 3 miles of marked trails through the forest surrounding the museum, dotted with outdoor sculptures including a James Turrell skyspace. The Art Trail follows the ponds and passes the pavilions from the water side. Free, accessible year-round.

places.name: Berlin, OH

visits.text: You drive along the Amish Country Byway, a 264-kilometer scenic route designated Ohio Scenic Byway in 1998 that crosses the rolling hills of Holmes County to the rhythm of black buggies. Holmes County has the highest concentration of Amish population in the world: in 2023, estimates put the Amish population in the community centered on Holmes County at 39,525, half the county's total population. The first Amish settled here in 1809, coming from Somerset County in Pennsylvania, attracted by hills that reminded them of their Swiss ancestors' homeland. Driving these roads, you'll pass buggies (the most conservative, the Swartzentruber Amish, without orange warning triangles), women in pinafore dresses shopping, children walking to school.

You enter a circular room and find yourself enveloped by a 265-square-meter mural painted by hand by artist Heinz Gaugel between 1992 and 1998 - a panoramic chronicle of 500 years of Anabaptist history, from the first persecutions in 16th-century Switzerland to Holmes County farms today. The title Behalt means 'retain' or 'remember' in Pennsylvania German dialect. The guide stops you before each scene: the drowning of Anabaptist martyrs in Swiss rivers in 1527, the embarkation to America, the settlement in Ohio's hills in 1809. You leave with an understanding of why these people still live as they did in the 18th century - and why it's not ignorance, it's a theological choice.

You arrive in Millersburg and come to a stop before the red-sandstone Victorian courthouse of 1885, one of the most beautiful public buildings in rural Ohio. Nineteenth-century storefronts line the central square in a remarkable state of preservation. Step into one of the general stores: you may see men in black hats and green coats buying farm supplies beside a tourist quilt shop, without anyone finding the scene unusual. Before leaving, try a slice of Holmes County Swiss cheese: the county is the leading US producer of this cheese, made from recipes brought by nineteenth-century immigrants from the Bern region. From June to October, a farmers' market sets up near the courthouse on the first and third Saturdays of the month.

activities.text: You climb into a black-topped buggy pulled by a Quarter Horse and take the county's gravel roads at a trot, at the speed of local residents since 1809. The Amish driver explains in English the rules of his community - the Ordnung - and why some groups (the Swartzentruber) don't display the orange road safety triangle on their buggies, considered too ostentatious. From the buggy, the landscape takes on a different character: you see farms from the inside, giant vegetable gardens, clotheslines stretched between buildings, and children watching you pass.

You drive along the gravel roads of Holmes County and spot a painted wooden sign in front of a farm - 'Open', and nothing else. You stop. Perhaps a woodworking shop where a man in an apron assembles a solid oak tray without nails or chemical glue, perhaps a bakery where still-warm shoofly pies cool on the counter, perhaps a cheese dairy that just released a wheel. Direct purchases are the rule here: no credit cards, cash only - bring cash. This kind of improvised encounter, at a farm without a sign or Instagram page, is what you'll tell people about when you return.

places.name: Bethlehem, PA

visits.text: You arrive at SteelStacks and the five blast furnaces stop you in your tracks: two columns of rusted steel rising 70 meters, a row of industrial structures stretching nearly 400 meters along the Lehigh River - and at their feet, an outdoor amphitheater, lawns, and art galleries. Bethlehem Steel, founded in 1857 on this 1,800-acre site, was America's second-largest steel producer for nearly a century. Steel from these furnaces built the Golden Gate Bridge, the Chrysler Building, the Empire State Building, Madison Square Garden, and World War II warships. Blast Furnace A, the oldest, dates from 1915; each produced 2,600 to 3,000 tonnes of pig iron daily. They shut down for the last time on November 18, 1995, leaving 30,000 jobs vacant and a city in mourning. Rather than demolishing the structures, the city converted them into a cultural campus that opened in 2011 - a decision inspired by Ruhr Valley industrial conversions in Germany. Campus access is free; paid events are posted on steelstacks.org.

You climb onto the Hoover-Mason Trestle, the elevated half-kilometer walkway built on the former railroad that supplied the blast furnaces with iron ore and coke - and you walk at the level of the loads that fed the furnaces, just meters from the mouths of the vats. The plunging view of the industrial structures and Lehigh River is unmatched in the region. Panels explain each step of the steelmaking process, from Minnesota ore arrival to pig iron pour. Paid guided tours are organized in season by Historic Bethlehem Museums - the guided version lasts 90 minutes and accesses areas closed to the general public. Come in the morning for the low light on the rusted steel.

You enter the only national museum dedicated to American industrial history, affiliated with the Smithsonian Institution and installed in 2016 in one of Bethlehem Steel's original buildings. Permanent exhibitions trace successive American industrial revolutions with working 19th-century machines. The Bethlehem Steel section presents rare artifacts: original bridge structure plans, 1940s worker photographs. A documentary exhibition recounts Operation Pastorius of 1942: Nazi saboteurs landed by submarine had the primary mission of destroying Altoona's Horseshoe Curve and Bethlehem Steel plants - arrested in New York by the FBI before reaching their target. Open Wednesday-Sunday 10am-5pm, admission $10 adult.

activities.text: You travel back two centuries crossing the Moravian Historic District, Bethlehem's founding core traced in 1741 by German Moravian immigrants fleeing religious persecution in Saxony. These Protestant dissenters built an exemplary self-sufficient community: collective housing, communal farm, tannery, mill - all original brick buildings still stand and are listed on the National Register. The 1741 Gemein Haus now houses the Moravian Museum with its period musical instruments and furniture. The 1758 Sun Inn, a former tavern that hosted George Washington, John Adams, and Benjamin Franklin during their travels between Philadelphia and the northern front, is restored and open for tours.

You settle on the lawn at Levitt Pavilion, a stage designed so the illuminated blast furnaces form the natural backdrop for every concert - an industrial version of Red Rocks, as performing artists describe it. ArtsQuest programs more than 1,000 concerts and eight festivals per year, including the annual MusikFest in August: ten days of concerts with more than 500 bands on eleven simultaneous stages, one of the largest free music festivals in the United States since 1984. The evening atmosphere, when spotlights illuminate the rusted steel of the five blast furnaces while a band plays at the foot of the structures, is one of Pennsylvania's most singular experiences.

places.name: Bettles, AK

visits.text: Bettles has about a dozen permanent residents and lies 35 miles north of the Arctic Circle. The NPS ranger station, close to the airstrip, is your gateway to the 8 million acres of Gates of the Arctic, the least visited and wildest national park in the United States. Rangers lend bear-resistant containers for free and provide topographic maps; consult them before heading into the backcountry. Bettles Lodge, listed as a National Historic Site, has fed and housed explorers, geologists and photographers since the 1940s.

The Koyukuk River runs just a few meters from Bettles Lodge—it was this river that conservationist Robert Marshall ascended in 1929 to discover the two peaks flanking the northern passage: Frigid Crags and Boreal Mountain. He named them the “Gates of the Arctic.” The river can be floated from Bettles by canoe or raft for 160 km to the village of Huslia—local outfitters provide gear.

The North Fork Koyukuk is the park's signature river—it originates at the Gates proper and descends 160 km to Bettles in Class I-II water. From the air or from banks accessible by bush plane, the river's meanders between the Brooks Range walls give one of the most striking images of Arctic Alaska. If you've booked a floatplane drop-off, this river is where the real Gates of the Arctic begins.

The ridges and open valleys around Bettles, still technically outside park boundaries, host herds of caribou from the spring migration through autumn. The Central Arctic caribou herd—tens of thousands of individuals—regularly crosses the corridor. In August-September, bulls carry full antlers. Observe from high ground with binoculars to avoid disturbing their movements.

activities.text: Flightseeing from Bettles over the Brooks Range—in a Cessna or Super Cub, local pilots know every valley and peak of this range that forms the northern terminus of the Rockies. The Gates of the Arctic themselves (Frigid Crags and Boreal Mountain) are visible from the air. Budget 1.5 to 2 hours of flight for a loop over the main peaks. The evening light in summer is golden and endless.

Off-trail hiking north of Bettles into the tundra and birch-spruce forests bordering the park. There are no marked trails—you walk on moss and lichen, follow valleys. Grizzlies, caribou, moose, and wolves are all present in this transition corridor between boreal forest and Arctic tundra. Go with compass, topo map, bear spray, and satellite communication.

Rafting or canoeing on the North Fork Koyukuk: reach this remote river by bush plane from Bettles and allow several days for the expedition. The river is generally calm with a few easy rapids, and wooded slopes of the Brooks Range line the route. Arrange the drop-off, equipment and pick-up with a Bettles operator before setting out.

Fishing at Iniakuk Lake or on the Alatna River from Bettles—two spots accessible by bush plane for a day trip, with pilots dropping you off and returning at an agreed time. Rainbow trout, arctic grayling, and northern pike are the main targets. This region has one of the lowest angler densities on Earth—fish have the naive behavior of having never seen an artificial fly.

visits.text: Experience Big Bend National Park, an expansive wilderness covering over 324,000 hectares where the Rio Grande carves dramatic canyons through ancient mountains. The park's vast, open spaces encompass stunning desert landscapes, diverse ecosystems ranging from the Chihuahuan Desert to forested highlands, and some of the darkest skies in North America for exceptional stargazing. This remote sanctuary offers solitude and natural beauty on a scale difficult to find elsewhere in the continental United States.

Explore Santa Elena Canyon, where sheer limestone cliffs rise 450 meters above the Rio Grande, creating one of the most photographed and awe-inspiring landscapes in Texas. The canyon trail leads visitors through a dramatic corridor where Mexico rises on one side and Texas on the other, separated only by the flowing river below. Morning light illuminating the towering rock faces creates particularly stunning photographic opportunities.

activities.text: Venture into the Chisos Basin, the only mountain range in the United States entirely contained within a national park, offering spectacular views and notably cooler temperatures ideal for summer visits. The Window Trail provides a moderate hike to a natural rock window framing stunning sunset views over the desert below. For more challenging adventures, the South Rim trail rewards experienced hikers with 360-degree panoramas across the vast Big Bend landscape.

Take advantage of Big Bend's designation as a Dark Sky Park, offering some of the best astronomical viewing opportunities in North America thanks to its remote location far from urban light pollution. The park's rich cultural heritage includes evidence of Native American habitation, Spanish explorer routes, and pioneer settlements. Fossils dating back millions of years dot the landscape, making this region a geological wonderland for those interested in Earth's ancient history.

visits.text: Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone—Marvel at this 366-meter-deep canyon carved by the Yellowstone River, with waterfall views from multiple overlooks. The yellow volcanic rock that gave the park its name forms dramatic walls plunging toward the rushing river.

Artist Point — Photograph the Lower Falls plunging 94 meters into the canyon from this iconic viewpoint. Thomas Moran's 1872 painting of this scene helped convince Congress to establish the national park.
Hayden Valley — Drive through this prime grizzly habitat where bison herds graze and wolves hunt. The glacial valley along the Yellowstone River offers wildlife viewing rivaling Lamar Valley.

Norris Geyser Basin—Explore the park's hottest and oldest hydrothermal area with acidic geysers and colorful hot springs. Steamboat Geyser, the world's tallest active geyser, erupts irregularly to heights of up to 90 meters.

activities.text: Big Sky Resort Area — Visit Montana's premier ski destination, offering summer hikes. The resort at the base of Lone Peak provides mountain recreation year-round.

Gallatin River fly fishing—Try casting for wild trout in this blue-ribbon stream flowing through the Madison Range. The river featured in A River Runs Through It illustrates Montana's fishing culture.
Montana ranch dinner — Feast on grass-fed beef at working ranch restaurants. The agricultural heritage shapes Montana cuisine emphasizing quality meat and local ingredients.

visits.text: Bixby Creek Bridge — Photograph this 218-meter arch bridge suspended 80 meters above the canyon since 1932. An emblematic structure of Big Sur, it stands majestically against cliffs plunging into the turquoise Pacific.

McWay Falls—View this 24-meter waterfall, which drops directly onto an isolated sandy beach in Julia Pfeiffer Burns State Park, from the small viewpoint beside Highway 1. The Overlook Trail is closed for construction work; access to the beach remains prohibited. Allow for a round trip from Big Sur village and use only permitted parking spaces.
Pfeiffer Beach — Descend to this secret beach with sands tinted purple by manganese garnets. Pierced rock formations create natural arches where the setting sun projects spectacular golden rays.

Andrew Molera State Park — Hike in this wild 1,900-hectare park where trails wind between coastal meadows and redwood forests. The Beach Trail leads to a deserted beach perfect for observing gray whales and dolphins.

activities.text: Lunch at Nepenthe — Savor an Ambrosia burger on the panoramic terrace of this legendary restaurant perched 244 meters above the Pacific. The establishment opened in 1949 was frequented by Henry Miller and Orson Welles.

Exploring craft galleries—Discover artists' studios housed in former pioneer cabins. Potters, painters and sculptors draw inspiration from the changing light and dramatic natural surroundings of Big Sur to create their works.

Meditation at Esalen Institute—Book a workshop or stay in advance at this personal development center founded in 1962, the birthplace of the Human Potential movement. The natural hot springs overlooking the ocean are accessible under the terms of your reservation; simply dropping in at sunset is not possible. Allow for a round trip from Big Sur village.

visits.text: You start your road trip at Pictograph Cave State Park, 8 kilometers southeast of downtown Billings. Walk the 1.2-kilometer loop trail to three sandstone alcoves carved from Eagle sandstone 80 million years ago, and look closely at the walls of the largest cave: 106 pictographs painted in red, white, and black between 200 and 2,100 years ago. Excavations from 1937 to 1941 pulled over 30,000 artifacts from the site - one of the most significant archaeological digs on the Northern Plains. Bring binoculars; the paintings are faint and the distance matters. National Historic Landmark. Fee applies for non-Montana residents.

Step inside the Yellowstone Art Museum (YAM) in downtown Billings. Opened in October 1964 inside the former Yellowstone County Jail - a red-brick building dating to 1884 - it's now Montana's largest contemporary art museum, with over 7,400 works in its permanent collection. The Montana Collection covers regional artists from Will James's cowboy illustrations to abstract paintings by Rudy Autio and Deborah Butterfield. In 2009, the YAM received 50 works of minimalist and conceptual art through the National Gallery of Art's 50 Works for 50 States program. The Visible Vault - a publicly accessible art storage room - is rare in any museum. Free for Yellowstone County residents; paid entry for others.

You're standing in front of the Moss Mansion, a red sandstone 28-room house built in 1902-1903 for banker Preston Boyd Moss. The architect was Henry Janeway Hardenbergh - the same man who designed the original Waldorf-Astoria and the Plaza Hotel in New York City. Inside, the mahogany woodwork, onyx fireplace, rose silk and gold leaf wallcoverings, and the electric bell system for servants are all original and untouched. The family owned the home for over 80 years; Melville Moss, the last resident, died in 1984 while arranging for it to become a museum. Paid entry; guided tours at 10am and 1pm in summer.

activities.text: Head up to the Rimrocks at Zimmerman Park and follow the trails along the cliffs. They rise 60 to 150 meters above the valley, and from the top you can take in the whole panorama: the Yellowstone River below, the city nestled between the rock walls, and the Beartooth Mountains on the horizon. The Rimrocks formed from sediments laid down 80 million years ago on the shore of the Western Interior Seaway - a shallow sea that stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic. Free access; dawn or late afternoon brings the best light.

End the evening along Montana Avenue, the city's historic main street running parallel to the old Northern Pacific Railroad tracks. Many brick buildings date from the 1880s when Billings was founded as a railroad town. Walk to the Western Heritage Center, housed in the 1901 Parmly Billings Library building, which tells the story of the Yellowstone River corridor through photographs and rotating exhibits. Free admission at the Heritage Center; restaurants and bars on Montana Avenue fill up by 7pm on weekends.

visits.text: Day 1: Embark on a culinary world tour without leaving Birmingham at the Pizitz Food Hall, a stunning transformation of the city's former department store into a buzzing international food emporium. Sample Ethiopian injera at Ghion Cultural Hall, slurp Vietnamese pho at PhoPho, or build a rainbow bowl of Mediterranean salads at Eli's Jerusalem Grill beneath soaring ceilings and exposed brick. The central bar pours craft cocktails while the upstairs apartments hint at the building's glamorous retail past.

Day 1: Stand in solemn remembrance at 16th Street Baptist Church, where a white supremacist's bomb shattered Sunday morning peace in 1963, killing four young girls preparing for services. The guided tour weaves through this still-active congregation's sanctuary, pausing at the stunning stained glass window depicting a Black Christ, donated by the people of Wales in solidarity. This sacred space crystallizes the brutal reality faced by civil rights activists and the resilience that carried the movement forward.

Day 1: Take in the weight of history at Kelly Ingram Park, where powerful bronze sculptures freeze pivotal moments of Birmingham's civil rights struggle as enduring witnesses. Four little girls play eternally in innocent joy, forever captured in the instant before tragedy struck across the street. Walk past snarling police dogs straining at their leashes, children huddled against the force of fire hoses, and young protesters behind jail bars, each sculpture a visceral reminder of courage in the face of hatred.

Day 1: Deepen your understanding at the Birmingham Civil Rights Institute, a world-class museum that traces the African American journey from the humiliations of segregation to the ongoing fight for equality. Step aboard a replica Freedom Riders bus, sit at a recreated segregated lunch counter, and hear firsthand accounts that bring the movement's heroes to life. The institute's position facing Kelly Ingram Park and 16th Street Baptist Church creates a powerful trinity of remembrance and education.

Day 2: Discover the strategic nerve center of Birmingham's civil rights movement at Historic Bethel Baptist Church, where the fearless Reverend Fred L. Shuttlesworth organized resistance against segregation despite constant threats on his life. Outside, information boards mark the ghost outline of the parsonage destroyed by Klan bombers in an attack that miraculously left Shuttlesworth unharmed. His courage in repeatedly facing violence while advocating nonviolent protest epitomizes the movement's moral power.

Day 2: Celebrate African American athletic excellence at the Negro Southern League Museum, an intimate treasure trove honoring the baseball heroes who played with passion and skill while barred from the major leagues. Stand at home plate as a hologram of legendary pitcher Satchel Paige winds up and fires fastballs that helped him eventually break baseball's color barrier. The lovingly preserved uniforms, equipment, and photographs reveal how sports provided both escape and pride during the segregation era.

Day 2: Wander world-class galleries at the Birmingham Museum of Art, where the glass-fronted facade opens onto a serene sculpture court with pools reflecting a sinuous reclining nude. The eclectic collection spans continents and centuries, from American masters to a delightfully unexpected collection of English Wedgwood ceramics that somehow found their way to Alabama. Entry is free, making this an accessible cultural gem.

Day 2: Ascend to the top of Vulcan, the world's largest cast-iron statue, for panoramic views across the city this mighty Roman god helped build. Created for the 1904 World's Fair, the bare-bottomed blacksmith stands atop Red Mountain as an eternal tribute to Birmingham's iron and steel heritage. The museum below chronicles how deposits of iron ore, coal, and limestone in miraculous proximity fueled the Magic City's explosive growth.

Day 2: Escape to Railroad Park, a 19-acre urban oasis that has become Birmingham's beloved backyard since opening in 2010. Wander boardwalks through restored wetlands, cross bridges over shallow lakes, and join families gathering on the great lawn as trains rumble past on the adjacent tracks. As twilight descends, the park transforms into a magical landscape of soft lights and long shadows.

activities.text: Day 1: Join the locals lining up outside Saw's Soul Kitchen in the artsy Avondale neighborhood for BBQ that embodies Birmingham's culinary renaissance. The signature Pork & Greens layers impossibly tender pulled pork over creamy stone-ground grits and sweet-and-sour collard greens, crowned with crispy onion rings that shatter satisfyingly with each bite. Arrive early because once the meat's gone, it's gone.

Day 2: Experience a uniquely Southern snack at the Alabama Peanut Company on charming cobblestoned Morris Avenue, where vats of peanuts bubble away in Cajun spice and dill pickle brine. These boiled peanuts, a beloved beach-trip tradition, achieve a tender texture and intense flavor that converts skeptics with the first bite. The airy shop also sells roasted varieties and cheeky Southern and Salty merchandise.

Day 2: Photograph the iconic Magic City sign, a faithful replica of the neon beacon that once welcomed visitors to Birmingham's train station during the city's industrial heyday. The sign now marks the start of the Rotary Trail, a half-mile green corridor that connects to the city's expanding trail network and is perfect for an evening stroll or morning jog.

Day 2: Settle into the warm glow of Bottega Cafe, the casual sibling in James Beard Award-winning chef Frank Stitt's empire, where the spirit of Italian trattorias meets Alabama hospitality. The buzzing dining room with its rich red walls draws foodies seeking wood-fired pizzas, handmade pastas, and an Italian-leaning wine list that rewards exploration. Reservations are recommended, but bar seating offers prime people-watching.

Day 2: Enjoy a restorative lunch at The Essential, a neighborhood gem where globally inspired small plates arrive at prices that encourage ordering freely. The niçoise-style salad features barely seared tuna over farm vegetables, while the buttery croissant ice cream reaches an indulgent richness that begs to be shared. The eclectic crowd of artists, professionals and families reflects Birmingham's evolving character.

visits.text: The Queen Mine Tour takes you 450 meters inside the Mule Mountains aboard a small mining train. For over a century (1877–1975), 8 billion pounds of copper were extracted from these shafts. The guides are former miners—some worked here for decades. Underground temperature is constant between 8 and 15°C, regardless of the heat outside. A yellow slicker, hard hat, and headlamp are provided at the entrance. Book online in advance.

The Lavender Pit is a former open-pit copper mine 300 meters deep, opened in 1950 and closed in 1974 after producing 86 million tonnes of ore. Its wine-red and burnt-orange hues at sunset are spectacular. This is also where “Bisbee Blue” was extracted, a turquoise of intense blue considered one of the finest in the world. A roadside pullout with an interpretive panel allows a five-minute stop.

The Bisbee Mining & Historical Museum is affiliated with the Smithsonian Institution—a rare distinction for a town of 5,000 residents. The permanent exhibit "Bisbee: The Urban Outpost on the Frontier" traces the town's history from the earliest prospectors through the Bisbee Deportation of 1917, when Phelps Dodge expelled 1,300 striking miners in cattle cars. An inglorious episode in American labor history, addressed without flinching.

The Copper Queen Hotel, built in 1902, is the oldest continuously operating hotel in Arizona. Teddy Roosevelt, John Wayne, and General Pershing all slept here. A journal kept at the front desk records guests' encounters with its three supposed ghosts. Even if you're not staying here, step inside to see the Victorian lobby and bar.

activities.text: Old Bisbee is best explored on foot: the town is built into a hillside, linked by staircases carved into the rock—there are said to be more than 1,000 in all. The Brewery Gulch neighborhood was once the haunt of miners' saloons and brothels; today it's a colorful street of art galleries, craft bars, and cafés. Climb up to Tombstone Canyon Road to see the Victorian houses clinging to the slopes.

The galleries of Old Bisbee are worth a detour: the town has attracted artists since the 1970s, when the miners' departure left hundreds of houses vacant and cheap. Today, ceramicists, jewelers, and painters have taken over the alleys. Browse the Main Street shops to find "Bisbee Blue" jewelry—the local turquoise, recognizable by its black veining and color depth.

places.name: Bismarck, ND

visits.text: Start at the North Dakota Heritage Center and State Museum on the capitol grounds - North Dakota's largest museum and one of the best free museums on the Northern Plains. The 2014 expansion brought it to 11,800 square meters across four galleries. The paleontology hall holds a life-size T. rex cast, but the showstopper is Dakota - a mummified Edmontosaurus discovered in 1999 near Marmarth, ND, and housed at the Heritage Center since 2008. Dakota is one of only a dozen fully mummified dinosaurs known to science, preserving extensive fossilized skin intact. The Early Peoples gallery displays over 1,000 artifacts from the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara nations. Free admission every day.

Drive 11 kilometers south to Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park, North Dakota's oldest state park, established in 1907 when Theodore Roosevelt signed over the land. Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer commanded the 7th Cavalry here from 1873 until he left for the Little Bighorn campaign in May 1876. At its height the fort held 650 men across 78 buildings; all were dismantled by settlers after its 1891 abandonment. The reconstructed Custer House is furnished as it would have been when Custer and his wife Libbie lived there. The On-A-Slant Village - a reconstruction of a Mandan earthlodge settlement occupied from around 1575 until a smallpox epidemic in the 1780s - completes the picture of who lived here before the fort arrived. Paid entry.

Walk along the Missouri riverfront at Keelboat Park, where a full-size replica of Lewis and Clark's keelboat stands by the water. The Missouri at Bismarck is broad, brown and powerful — a route of exploration and westward expansion for two centuries. Free access.

activities.text: Take the self-guided tour of the North Dakota State Capitol - a 19-story Art Deco tower completed in 1934, the tallest building in either Dakota. The observation deck on the 18th floor gives a 360-degree view over the Missouri River valley and the rolling farmland. The guided tour covers the legislative chambers, murals, and the memorial hall. Free admission; observation deck closes at 4:30pm on weekdays.

Spend the evening in Bismarck's downtown around Main Avenue, where Laughing Sun Brewing and several other local spots sit alongside restaurants serving Northern Plains comfort food. If this is the last night of the road trip, it's a good place to eat well and look back at the week: a 1,600-kilometer arc through battlefields, badlands, dinosaur bones, and the two states where the American West still feels most like itself.
