visits.text: Columbus - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. The “Athens of the Prairie”. This city of 47,000 people has more than 60 modernist buildings by world-renowned architects. In 1954, the Cummins Foundation began paying architects' fees for public buildings - provided the designers were chosen from among the best. The result: schools, churches and banks designed by I.M. Pei, Eero Saarinen or Robert Venturi. Stop at the Visitors Center on 5th Street for a map of the walking tour.

North Christian Church (Columbus) - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. The last building designed by Eero Saarinen before his death in 1961, completed in 1964. A stone hexagon topped by a 59-meter spire with a golden cross. Natural light enters the interior through a central oculus.

Nashville and Brown County - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. As you continue west, you'll reach Nashville, an artists' village nestled in the wooded hills of Brown County. Galleries and shops line the main street. The atmosphere is relaxed—this is the sort of place where you stop for coffee and stay for two hours.

Brown County State Park - Indiana's largest state park (6,500 hectares), 20 minutes from Nashville and 30 minutes from Bloomington, where you'll stay tonight. The overlooks along the scenic road offer views of forested ridges. In October, fall colors attract crowds—arrive early if you're there during that period.

Indiana University Bloomington - IU's campus is one of the Midwest's most beautiful. Enter through the Sample Gates on Kirkwood Avenue, cross the lawns bordered by buildings in local limestone, and descend to the Jordan River (a creek, not a river). The Jacobs School of Music is one of the nation's finest - check if there's a free concert during your visit.

Marengo Cave - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. This cave, designated a U.S. National Natural Landmark, offers two underground tours: the “Dripstone Trail” (40 min, easy, suitable for families) and the “Crystal Palace” (1 hour, more varied, with stalactites, stalagmites and calcite columns). The formations were discovered in 1883 by two local children. The underground temperature stays at 13°C - bring a sweater.

Spring Mill State Park - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. Halfway between Bloomington and Marengo, this park contains a reconstructed pioneer village with a working watermill. The memorial to astronaut Gus Grissom (a local native who died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967) displays his Gemini III spacecraft capsule, “Molly Brown”.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Miller House (Columbus) - Plan a round trip by car from Bloomington. The private residence designed by Eero Saarinen (1957) for the Miller family is one of the few examples of a single-family home designed by the architect. Interiors by Alexander Girard, gardens by Dan Kiley. The “conversation pit” set into the living-room floor became a model copied everywhere in the 1960s. Visits by reservation only.

Bloomington Farmers Market (Saturday morning) - If you're there on the right day, the market at Showers Common brings together local producers, cheesemakers, and artisan bakeries. The rest of the week, Kirkwood Avenue between campus and downtown abounds with bookstores, cafes, and restaurants from around the world—the international student population is reflected in the menus.

places.name: Bloomington, MN

visits.text: Mall of America—The largest shopping mall in the United States: 520 stores, an indoor amusement park with roller coasters (Nickelodeon Universe), an aquarium, and a mini-city. Even if shopping doesn't appeal to you, the spectacle of this outsized place is worth seeing. Allow at least 2 hours.

Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge—Ten minutes from the Mall, the scenery shifts dramatically. Take the trails through this 5,600-hectare refuge along the Minnesota River—you might spot bald eagles, herons, and migrating pelicans. Free admission.

activities.text: If you're traveling with family, the indoor amusement park at Mall of America easily fills half a day. For adults, the craft breweries on the south side of the Mall offer an alternative to shopping.

places.name: Blowing Rock, NC

visits.text: Scale the legendary Blowing Rock, the high-altitude rock formation for which this scenic Blue Ridge Parkway town was named. This unique natural wonder features winds so powerful they seem to return thrown objects to the person who threw them, while the summit delivers unbeatable panoramic views of the surrounding mountain landscapes.

Embrace the challenge of hiking Glen Burney Falls Trail, a strenuous 2.6 km route that rewards adventurers with the discovery of gorgeous waterfalls at the end of the trail. This wilderness adventure exemplifies the exceptional outdoor experiences available in this beautiful mountain destination.

activities.text: Explore local heritage at the Blowing Rock Art & History Museum, a celebrated center exhibiting diverse artworks that illuminate the overall heritage of Southern Appalachia. The museum's collections provide fascinating insight into the cultural traditions and artistic expressions that have shaped this mountain region for generations.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

map_keywords: Blowing Rock Art and History Museum

visits.text: Cave of the Mounds - This limestone cave is 488 million years old. Discovered in 1939 during a quarry blasting operation, it remained intact and contains remarkable formations: stalactites, stalagmites, helictites (growing in all directions), and soda straws (hollow, translucent formations). The guided tour lasts about one hour and the underground temperature is constant at 10°C - bring a jacket.
Surface Karst Trail - Above the cave, a trail through restored prairie explains the region's karst geology: sinkholes, fissures, and underground water circulation. Well-designed and educational.

Blue Mound State Park - Southern Wisconsin's highest point (521 m). Two observation towers offer views across the Driftless Area - this Wisconsin region never covered by glaciers that retained unique rolling topography.

activities.text: Driftless Area Hiking - Blue Mound's trails cross wildflower prairies and oak forests. The contrast with the flat lands of the rest of the Midwest is striking.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: On your way south, stop at Newspaper Rock—plan a day trip from Bluff. It is a 15 m² petroglyph panel covered with over 650 carvings accumulated over 2,000 years by Fremont, Ancestral Puebloan, and Ute peoples. The site is right beside the road, 20 km from Highway 191 on the road to Needles. Admission is unrestricted and free.

Don't underestimate Bluff—this tiny village of 250 people on the San Juan River, surrounded by red cliffs. The Bluff Fort Historic Site tells the story of Mormon pioneers' arrival in 1880, after an epic expedition through a gap in the cliff called Hole-in-the-Rock. It's also the gateway to Bears Ears National Monument—sacred land to the Navajo, Hopi, Ute, and Zuni nations.

activities.text: If you have time, do the Valley of the Gods loop (28 km of dirt road, passable in a regular car in dry weather). It's Monument Valley in miniature—isolated buttes and mesas, no tourists and no entrance fee. Allow 1–1.5 hours for the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Utah-Arizona Road Trip: National Parks and Canyons

visits.text: Mission San Francisco Solano, Sonoma Plaza: plan a round trip from Bodega Bay. The 21st and last of California's Franciscan missions, founded in 1823. It is the last of California's 21 Franciscan missions, founded in 1823, and winegrowing at the mission continued here until secularization in 1834—the prehistory of everything you have been drinking over the past four days. Much of the present building dates from 1840. Small museum, $3 admission, 30 minutes is enough to understand the context.

Buena Vista Winery, 18000 Old Winery Road: plan a round trip from Bodega Bay. Founded in 1857 by Agoston Haraszthy, a self-proclaimed count and Hungarian winemaker who brought over 100,000 cuttings of European grape varieties to California in the 1860s. It is California's oldest commercial winery still in operation. The original stone building was restored in 2011 by Jean-Charles Boisset, a Burgundian owner (DeLoach, Raymond in Napa). The history of the place is more interesting than the wines—but the wines are decent.

Gundlach Bundschu, 2000 Denmark Street: plan a round trip from Bodega Bay. Founded in 1858, it has remained in the same family for six generations—an all-time record in California. Less touristy than Buena Vista, more rural, with its family estate spirit intact. The value for money is among the best in Sonoma County. Gewurztraminer and Pinot Noir are the two wines to ask for.
Bodega School (17110 Bodega Lane), the red-and-white school on its hill, appears just as it is in The Birds, filmed by Hitchcock in 1963 - you can stop on the road to photograph it.

activities.text: Lunch at The Girl & the Fig, Sonoma Plaza: plan a round trip from Bodega Bay. Provençal-Californian cuisine at a restaurant founded in 1997 that has become a local institution. The menu changes with market deliveries, while the wine is almost exclusively from the Rhône (on the French side) and Sonoma (on the local side). Book the day before for lunch.

Dinner at Spud Point Crab Co., Bodega Bay: clam chowder served in a sourdough bread bowl, a sandwich with Dungeness crab caught that morning. Informal, no reservations, no fuss—exactly what's needed after two days of starred tastings. Allow $15–20 per person.

days_plan.itin_title: California Wine Country in 10 Days: San Francisco to Los Angeles Through the Vineyards

places.name: Bodie Island Lighthouse, NC

visits.text: Black and white horizontal stripes above the cedars: you can't miss Bodie Island Lighthouse from NC 12. Completed in 1872 and about 48 meters tall, it retains its original Fresnel lens and has just over 200 steps to the balcony, the height of a ten-story building. Climbing tickets are sold same-day only on recreation.gov, from 7am, in season; children must be at least 1.07 m tall.

activities.text: Even without climbing, follow the wooden boardwalk across the marsh behind Bodie Island Lighthouse to an observation deck. You can watch birds and aquatic life in a calm that the site's rangers describe as soothing. After dark, the lighthouse still sends its beam some 30 km out to sea.

visits.text: Grove Street in downtown Boise is a single block that packs in the largest Basque community in North America - an estimated 16,000 residents whose ancestors left the Pyrenees in the late 1800s to herd sheep across Idaho's mountains. The cornerstone is the Cyrus Jacobs-Uberuaga House, built in 1864 and Boise's oldest surviving brick building; it served as a Basque boarding house from 1910 to 1968 and is now part of the Basque Museum & Cultural Center. The 1914 Anduiza Fronton next door still hosts handball and pala. Bar Gernika, opened in 1991 in a former 1912 Chinese laundromat, is the place for a pintxo and a glass of txakoli. The block is free to walk; the museum charges a small fee and closes on Sundays.

Steel doors clang shut behind you at the Old Idaho Penitentiary, and the sandstone walls - quarried by the inmates themselves from nearby Table Rock starting in 1872 - close in. The prison ran for exactly 101 years, housing over 13,000 people, including Harry Orchard, who assassinated Governor Frank Steunenberg in 1905 with a bomb wired to his front gate. Back-to-back riots in 1971 and 1973 burned the chapel and dining hall; the place closed in December 1973 and was left exactly as it stood that day, calendars still on the walls. Summer guided tours run daily from 10 AM to 5 PM for a fee - go at opening to avoid the wait.

Between 8th and 9th Street downtown lies Freak Alley - the Northwest's largest open-air mural gallery, born in 2002 when local artist Colby Akers painted a single alley doorway and the neighboring businesses asked for more. The project has since swallowed an entire city block and a gravel parking lot, with contributions from more than 200 artists. A $500,000 city renovation in 2018 expanded the space. Every August the murals are painted over during a week-long event and the whole thing starts again. Free and open 24 hours.

The Idaho State Capitol on Jefferson Street was completed in 1920 and is the only state capitol in the United States heated by geothermal water, drawn from a 914-meter well directly beneath the building. The interior dome rises 63 meters and is lined with four types of marble, including local Boise Basin stone. Self-guided tours are free on weekdays - check capitol.idaho.gov for guided tour times if you want the full context.

Julia Davis Park, on the south bank of the Boise River, contains the Idaho State Museum and Boise Art Museum. Walk through the park, then follow the Greenbelt to the Idaho Anne Frank Human Rights Memorial near the public library on 8th Street, outside the park. This free outdoor memorial includes texts about human rights. Thomas Davis donated the parkland in 1907 in memory of his wife Julia.

Boise Depot, at 2603 W Eastover Terrace, stands above the city and offers foothill views from its grounds. Built for Union Pacific in 1925 in a Spanish-inspired style, it recalls the trains that carried visitors toward Sun Valley. The building hosts open houses and organized tours; check dates with the City of Boise before planning to go inside or climb the bell tower. You can still view the facade and gardens when the interior is closed.

activities.text: Rent a bike or lace up your shoes and head to the Boise River Greenbelt - 47 kilometers of paved path tracing both banks of the river through the heart of the city. The trail was born in 1967 from three donated parcels of land; the 1971 Greenbelt Ordinance forced new buildings to set back at least 21 meters from the riverbank, protecting the corridor you're on today. The stretch between Ann Morrison Park and Barber Park is the most scenic, with great blue herons working the shallows in the early morning. Bike rentals are available from several downtown outfitters.

The Basque Block alone gives you two dinner options: Leku Ona, a boutique hotel and restaurant opened in 2005 inside a historic boarding house, and Bar Gernika, where the beef tongue sandwich sells out by noon on Saturdays. For a broader choice, the 8th Street strip packs in everything from wood-fired pizza to craft cocktails within a few blocks. Book ahead for dinner in summer - Boise fills fast in July.

Rent a tube at Barber Park and float 8.9 kilometers back through the cottonwood corridor of the Boise River Greenbelt to Ann Morrison Park - 2 to 3 hours depending on current, with great blue herons overhead and the city skyline in the background. The water comes from Lucky Peak Reservoir and runs cold; late June through August is the sweet spot. Tube rentals and shuttles back to Barber Park operate on summer weekends from the downstream parks.

The loop closes on 8th Street, where Bittercreek Alehouse has been serving locally sourced Idaho food and regional craft beer since 1997. For a Basque send-off, Bar Gernika is open for lunch Tuesday through Saturday - the lamb sandwich and a Basque cider is the right order. Book a late-afternoon flight from BOI. Nine days and Idaho still has more to give.

visits.text: Opened in 1846, Bonaventure Cemetery spreads over more than 40 hectares along the Wilmington River, under Spanish moss. Composer Johnny Mercer and poet Conrad Aiken are buried here, and the book “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” made it famous. It lies outside the historic district: plan on a car or a taxi.

places.name: Boone, NC

visits.text: Challenge yourself at Rocky Knob Mountain Bike Park, a popular recreation haven covering more than 180 acres with trails designed for all skill levels. This premier destination for hikers and bikers offers exciting outdoor opportunities amid the picturesque Blue Ridge Mountain landscape that defines this charming mountain town.

Browse world-class art pieces inside the Turchin Center for the Visual Arts at Appalachian State University. This celebrated center showcases a stunning blend of creations by national and international artists, establishing Boone as a significant cultural destination in the North Carolina mountains.

activities.text: Experience Boone's thriving craft beverage scene, where local breweries showcase the art of creating refreshing craft beers. Touring the production facilities offers an opportunity to witness the brewing process firsthand and then taste the results, providing a unique conclusion to your exploration of this mountain community.

places.name: Boston, MA

visits.text: In Boston, you can literally walk the history of American independence—a 4 km red line marked on the ground connects 16 sites of the Revolution from Boston Common (the oldest public park in the United States, established in 1634) to Charlestown. The Massachusetts State House opens the trail: its dome, covered in genuine 24-karat gold, cost $8 million to restore in 1997. Architect Charles Bulfinch built it in 1798. Free audio guide at freedomtrail.org, or join the Freedom Trail Players in period costume—$15, 90 minutes, and a level of detail you won't find on the signs.

At the Granary Burying Ground (1660), the Puritan gravestones are carved with winged death's heads. Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock and the 5 victims of the Boston Massacre are buried here. The neighboring King's Chapel Burying Ground (1630) is older still: Mary Chilton, the first woman from the Mayflower to step ashore at Plymouth in 1620, is buried there. Thirty minutes in each is enough, but people tend to stay longer.

In front of the Old State House (1713), look for the plaque on the ground—it marks the exact spot of the Boston Massacre on March 5, 1770, five deaths that triggered the Revolution. The Declaration of Independence was read publicly from this building's balcony on July 18, 1776, and the reenactment takes place every Fourth of July. Faneuil Hall (1742), further along, is where Samuel Adams climbed onto a table to convince his fellow citizens to break with the Crown.

Two sites close the Trail. The Paul Revere House (circa 1680, ticket $6) is the oldest residential house in downtown Boston—Paul Revere lived here when he made his night ride on April 18, 1775, to warn the Minutemen. The Old North Church, whose steeple displayed the two lanterns signaling “One if by land, two if by sea”, is a 5-minute walk away. Push on to Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown: a 67-meter obelisk on the site of the first major battle, fought on June 17, 1775.

Acorn Street in Beacon Hill is Boston's most photographed street—uneven cobblestones, gas lamps, closely spaced facades in two rows. Fifteen minutes is enough to understand why. Just next door, the Boston Public Garden (1837), America's first public botanical garden, is worth lingering in: look for the “Make Way for Ducklings” statue, a tribute to Robert McCloskey's 1941 book that, for generations of Americans, is their first memory of Boston.

Harvard Yard is home to what students call the "Statue of Three Lies": the inscription reads "John Harvard, Founder, 1638"—but John Harvard was not the founder (merely a major donor), the university dates from 1636 not 1638, and the face sculpted in 1884 by Daniel Chester French is that of an anonymous student, as no portrait of John Harvard survived. Students touch the statue's left foot for exam luck, which has polished it down to bare metal. An additional unofficial tradition surrounds this foot that guides mention with an embarrassed smile.

At the Harvard Museum of Natural History (ticket $15), one collection alone is worth the admission price: the Glass Flowers. Between 1887 and 1936, Czech glassmakers Leopold and Rudolf Blaschka, father and son, created 4,300 botanical specimens in blown glass with perfect scientific accuracy—veins, stamens, growth stages. You'll find more famous butterfly collections, but nothing in the world resembles this. An hour and a half.

Mount Auburn Cemetery in Cambridge (1831) inspired Central Park in New York - this is where the idea of a cemetery as a public green space first took shape in the United States. Longfellow, Buckminster Fuller and Winslow Homer are buried here. An hour and a half, at least.

Howard Phillips Lovecraft (1890–1937) was born in Providence, lived his entire life there, almost never left, and is buried there. College Hill, on the east bank of the Providence River, appears by name in The Call of Cthulhu, The Shadow over Innsmouth, and The Dreams in the Witch House—the streets, the 18th-century brick houses on Benefit Street, the cemeteries. Stephen King, Neil Gaiman, and Guillermo del Toro have all named Lovecraft as the primary influence on modern horror fiction. His texts also contain racism and xenophobia that contemporary readers confront with embarrassment—Providence didn't give him a commemorative plaque until 2013. Walking tour map downloadable at lovecraftartsandsciences.com.

The Providence Athenaeum (251 Benefit Street, ticket $5 for non-members) is a private library dating from 1838, its Victorian beauty intact and still in use. Lovecraft frequented it. Edgar Allan Poe had frequented it before him between 1845 and 1849, when he came to court Sarah Helen Whitman—who inspired his poem Annabel Lee. Open to the public at certain times, allow 30 minutes.

Lovecraft's grave at Swan Point Cemetery (585 Blackstone Boulevard) isn't easy to find without a map. From the main entrance: straight ahead to the Barnaby monument, left on Junction Avenue, right on Pond Avenue, to the T-intersection with Avenue B—the Phillips family plot is ahead, with a large central obelisk; Lovecraft's small gravestone is behind it, to the right. Inscription: “I Am Providence”. The grave is regularly covered with pens, Cthulhu drawings, plastic octopuses, and letters—from fans who come from all over the world for this.

activities.text: The North End, the neighborhood of the Paul Revere House, is the place to eat Italian in Boston. Mamma Maria (3 North Square, $60-100) in an 18th-century house, or Pizzeria Regina, Boston's oldest pizzeria, open since 1926. A stop at Mike's Pastry (300 Hanover Street) for cannoli is a must - there is always a line, $5-8, and it is worth the wait.

Boston is one of the few places in the United States where gas streetlights still operate—Beacon Hill has dozens, maintained by the city. The cobblestone streets, 18th-century brick houses, Louisburg Square with its $5–15 million homes: an evening in the neighborhood is enough to understand why Bostonians don't leave.

The Cheers Bar at 84 Beacon Street is the bar that inspired the 1982 series. Packed with tourists, burgers $18–25—but if the show was part of your childhood, spending an hour here is less about tourism than a Proustian trip down memory lane.

Cambridge can be explored entirely by T from downtown (Red Line, 15 minutes). Massachusetts Avenue between Harvard Square and Porter Square is lined with the independent cafés and specialty bookstores that Bostonians actually frequent. In the evening, Quincy Market, operating since 1826, offers dozens of food stalls for $15–30—the least stuffy spot of the entire week.

Olneyville New York System (18 Plainfield Street) has been a Providence institution since 1946: the “wieners” (hot dogs with meat sauce, 3 for $7) were featured by Anthony Bourdain on Parts Unknown. This is Providence's version of the authentic local experience. Fancier alternative: Al Forno (577 South Main Street), which invented grilled pizza in 1980 and charges $50–90.

Return to Boston Logan via I-95 North, a 1-hour drive. Return the car at the airport—all major rental companies are on-site. Total car rental budget for the trip: $600–800 for 8 days with an automatic sedan. Smartphone GPS required.

visits.text: At Hoover Dam, concrete plunges between the walls of Black Canyon, in a landscape where each structure seems to change the scale of the Colorado. Power plant tours show the dam’s hydroelectric function, with options distinct from simply viewing it from outside. Check the tickets offered and allow time for security checks.

The Boulder City/Hoover Dam Museum puts faces to the construction site you have just seen. Testimonies and objects tell the story of the workers and families who came to settle here during the Great Depression. This visit complements the technical explanations of the dam. Check opening hours before leaving the site and allow a margin to return to Las Vegas.

days_plan.itin_title: Las Vegas in 10 Days: Zion, Bryce, and the Grand Canyon

visits.text: Stroll Pearl Street Mall, pedestrianized since 1977: four blocks of red brick lined with independent shops, cafes, and award-winning restaurants, with the Flatirons as a backdrop. More than 70% of the businesses are local. Food & Wine ranked it among the ten best food streets in America.

The Flatirons—five tilted slabs of sandstone more than 300 m above the city—are impossible to miss for any visitor to Boulder. Chautauqua Park, at their base, gives access to about twenty trails. The First Flatiron Trail (3 km round trip) offers a bird's-eye view of the city—start at dawn to beat the crowds.

Wander the University of Colorado Boulder campus, founded in 1876—its red sandstone buildings and red-tiled roofs make it one of the most beautiful campuses in the country. A stroll through the University Mall is enough to grasp the atmosphere of this town at 5,430 feet that has made the outdoors its identity.

activities.text: If you're here on a Saturday morning from May to October, don't miss the Boulder Farmers Market: local producers, food trucks, and artisans at the corner of 13th and Canyon Blvd. It's where the community gathers—ideal for assembling a picnic before the Flatirons.

Boulder has several taprooms steps from Pearl Street. Avery Brewing and Twisted Pine are the local favorites—order a pint on the patio with the Flatirons in the background. It's the end-of-day ritual for locals, and you'll understand why this town is so appealing.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

visits.text: Whitaker Point (Hawksbill Crag) - Arkansas's Most Photographed Natural Wonder: This dramatic rock outcropping extends over a 100-foot drop into the Ozark wilderness, featured in Disney films and gracing countless magazine covers. The 3-mile round-trip hike rewards hikers with vertigo-inducing views across miles of unbroken forest stretching to the horizon.

Roark Bluff - Where Twin Waterfalls Plunge into Paradise: Two spectacular cascades-Roark Bluff Falls and V-Notch Falls-thunder over 100-foot limestone cliffs into the Buffalo River below. Access by canoe or kayak transforms the journey into adventure.

Buffalo National River - America's First National River: Flowing 150 miles through the Ozarks, this pristine waterway remains wild and free, protected since 1972. Towering 500-foot bluffs, hidden caves, and abundant wildlife make every bend a discovery.

activities.text: Buffalo River Float Trip - Paddle Through Living Geology: Multi-day canoe and kayak journeys pass beneath massive bluffs, through swimming holes, and past riverside campsites where elk now roam the restored bottomlands.

Lost Valley & Eden Falls Cave - Underground Waterfall Wonder: A short trail leads to a natural rock shelter harboring a waterfall that disappears into a cave system. The adventurous can scramble inside to witness Eden Falls plunging into complete darkness.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Butte Historic District — Explore this former copper-mining capital, where 100 kilometers of underground tunnels form a honeycomb beneath the hill, under Victorian mansions and miners' cottages. This national historic landmark preserves the architecture of the boom years when Butte was the richest hill on Earth. Allow for a round trip by car from Bozeman to reach Butte.

Berkeley Pit — View this massive open-pit copper mine, now filled with toxic acidic water. This 540-meter-deep pit operated from 1955 to 1982 and demonstrates the environmental impacts of hard-rock mining. Allow for a round trip by car from Bozeman to reach the site in Butte.

Museum of the Rockies — Discover Montana's natural history including the world's largest Tyrannosaurus rex skull collection. Jack Horner's dinosaur research center houses fossils from Montana's Hell Creek Formation.
Montana State University—Visit this public university founded in 1893, with its brick buildings and campus framed by mountains. This Gallatin Valley institution enrolls 16,000 students.

activities.text: Bozeman Main Street—Browse outdoor recreation shops, galleries, and restaurants in this thriving mountain town. Bozeman balances Old West heritage with modern amenities for recreation enthusiasts.
Brewery and distillery tasting—Sample craft beers and spirits made with Montana grains and glacial water. Bozeman's beverage scene reflects the state's agricultural bounty.
Gallatin Valley sunset — Watch alpenglow paint the surrounding peaks pink and orange. The valley's mountain rim creates spectacular evening light displays.

places.name: Branson, MO

visits.text: Silver Dollar City isn't your typical theme park. Beneath its 40 hectares of wooded hills lies Marvel Cave, a natural cavern known to the Osage for generations and commercially operated as early as 1894. The park opened in 1960 around it, designed as an 1880s mining town. A hundred resident craftspeople work in public—glassblowers, blacksmiths, potters. The roller coasters are serious business: Outlaw Run is a wooden coaster with an 81-degree drop that set a world record when it opened in 2013. Plan a full day.

The Titanic Museum is a half-scale replica of the ocean liner planted right in the middle of Highway 76—you can't miss it. More than 400 authentic artifacts from the 1912 sinking are on display, including recreated first- and third-class cabins. At the entrance, you receive a boarding pass for an actual passenger. You find out at the end whether they survived.

Branson Landing runs along Lake Taneycomo in the heart of downtown—shops, restaurants, and a water-and-fire show scheduled every hour in the evenings. This is where tourists gather after the shows to walk along the waterfront. Of little interest in the morning, much better after 8 PM with the lights on the lake.

Table Rock State Park lies 8 km southwest of Branson, on the north shore of the lake. This is Branson before the shows: wooded trails along limestone bluffs, white-tailed deer at dawn, kingfishers on the rocks. The marina rents boats and points out diving spots on wrecks deliberately sunk to create artificial reefs. Go before 9 AM—you'll have the trails to yourself.

The Shepherd of the Hills Historic Homestead is the original farm described in Harold Bell Wright's 1907 novel - the book that sparked tourism in the Ozarks and the first American bestseller to exceed a million copies. Old Matt's Cabin is still standing. The 60-meter observation tower offers a 360-degree panorama of the surrounding hills.

The Branson Scenic Railway departs from the historic 1905 depot right downtown. Eighty minutes through the White River Valley gorges, tunnels, steel bridges, and sharp turns along the hillside. This is genuine vintage rolling stock. Take a window seat on the right as you depart—the river views are on that side.

activities.text: Table Rock Lake was created in 1958 by a dam on the White River—196 km² with 1,350 km of shoreline. Book a spot on the Showboat Branson Belle, a paddle-wheel steamboat launched in 1994: to lubricate its launch into the water, engineers used two tonnes of bananas. The cruise lasts 2 hours on the lake and includes a three-course meal and a variety show. Unapologetically kitschy, but genuinely enjoyable.

Branson has dozens of dinner shows along Highway 76—country, gospel, comedy, magic. If you only do one, choose the Shepherd of the Hills Outdoor Drama over the generic shows: performed outdoors since 1960 in an amphitheater facing the hills, it tells the story of Harold Bell Wright's 1907 novel—the book that put the Ozarks on the American tourist map, the first American bestseller to exceed one million copies.

Rent a boat on Table Rock Lake for the morning—powerboats, jet skis, and kayaks available at the marinas. On weekdays in the off-season, the rocky coves along the east shore are quiet and the water is clear enough for swimming. Largemouth bass fishing is good on this lake—ask the rental operator which areas are open for the day.

If you're traveling with kids, Fritz's Adventure is Branson's second attraction after Silver Dollar City. Seven stories of zip lines, climbing walls, and tunnels in a 4,600 m² building, opened in 2014. Without kids, skip it—but if you have them, it's two hours of peace for you.

visits.text: Ascend Brasstown Bald, Georgia's highest peak at 1,458 meters, where an observation tower provides 360-degree panoramas across four states on clear days. The summit trail passes through misty forests draped in wildflowers during spring and brilliant foliage in fall, rewarding hikers with some of the most spectacular mountain views in the American Southeast. Interpretive exhibits at the visitor center explain the region's ecology and Cherokee heritage.

Explore the vast Northeast Georgia Mountains region, a landscape of forested ridges, waterfalls, and crystal-clear streams that has attracted nature lovers for generations. Scenic byways wind through quaint mountain communities where local artisans create traditional crafts and family-owned vineyards produce award-winning wines. The area offers world-class hiking, fishing, and wildlife observation.

activities.text: Visit Château Élan winery for tastings of Georgia wines accompanied by vineyard tours explaining traditional winemaking techniques. The rolling hills, elegant tasting rooms, and relaxing atmosphere make this an ideal introduction to the state's emerging wine region.

places.name: Breaux Bridge, LA

visits.text: Leave Baton Rouge via I-10 heading west. After 40 minutes, you'll cross the Atchafalaya Basin on a 29 km elevated highway bridge over America's largest swamp—the view is striking, especially in the morning when mist floats above the cypress trees. Exit at Henderson (exit 115) for a bayou boat tour. Local operators offer tours lasting 1 hour and 30 minutes to 2 hours through the basin's channels: you'll see alligators, great blue herons, egrets, and turtles in a landscape of bald cypress draped with Spanish moss.

After the bayou, drive 15 minutes to Breaux Bridge, which Louisiana's legislature named the “Crawfish Capital of the World” in 1959. The small downtown on the banks of Bayou Teche has authentic Cajun charm: painted wooden houses, art galleries, music shops, and restaurants that smell of roux and cayenne. Walk across the bridge spanning the bayou—the first bridge here was built in 1799 by Acadian pioneer Firmin Breaux.

activities.text: Make a detour to Lake Martin, between Breaux Bridge and Lafayette (10 minutes). This nature preserve harbors a colony of herons, egrets, and ibis—during nesting season (March-June), the trees are literally covered with white birds. You can drive along the lake on Rookery Road or rent a kayak to weave between the cypress trees. Alligators are common—keep your distance.

In the evening in Breaux Bridge, look for a restaurant with live Cajun music. On Saturday mornings, several venues offer a “zydeco breakfast”—breakfast accompanied by live zydeco music, with people getting up to dance between tables. If you're here on a weekday, inquire about evening “Cajun jams.”

visits.text: Drive the last 5 kilometers to Bodie State Historic Park (38.2125, -119.0119) on an unpaved track - slow and rough, 15-20 minutes from CA-270. No fuel or food on site: fill up in Bridgeport beforehand. As you reach the parking lot, 110 gray wooden buildings spread across the hills, silent beneath the Sierra Nevada sky. The park’s policy is called “arrested decay”: nothing is restored, but nothing collapses. The interiors are left exactly as the last inhabitants left them in the 1940s-1960s - dishes on tables, tools on workbenches, open books on shelves, toys on the floor in family homes. $8 ticket.

In 1879, Bodie had 8,000 to 10,000 residents, 65 saloons, several brothels, 200 restaurants, a bowling alley, and daily newspapers. The town was known as the most violent in the West—a gunfight a day, a murder a week on average. An 8-year-old girl whose family was moving here scribbled in her diary: “Goodbye God, I'm going to Bodie.” The phrase became a proverb throughout the American West. Visit the schoolhouse (38.2128, -119.0144)—blackboards with writing still on them, desks, open books, inkwells, as if class had been interrupted—and Bodie Bank (38.2114, -119.0156), whose safe, a blackened metal cube, is the only object that survived the 1932 fire.

Finish at Bodie Cemetery (38.2150, -119.0172)—19th-century graves bearing the names of people whose violent deaths are documented, and the adjacent Boot Hill where the “unworthy” were buried: prostitutes, criminals, people who died by suicide, and Chinese people in the same mass grave. The Chinese community ran the laundries and supplied the town with wood from a Chinatown northwest of Main Street—they faced discrimination in the mines but were indispensable outside them. The Standard Mill (38.2128, -119.0169) offers a guided tour on weekends at 1 PM ($6 extra, excellent quality).

activities.text: Bring a picnic—there's nothing to eat in Bodie or within a 30-kilometer radius. Get it in Bridgeport before leaving in the morning. Allow 4-5 hours on site total: the self-guided tour brochure ($3) at the visitor center ensures you don't miss anything.

Return to Bridgeport (38.2557, -119.2298) for the night - motels and guesthouses, $90-180/night. An unpretentious little mountain town, but Bodie cannot be visited in the evening (closed at 6 pm in summer, 3 pm in winter).

visits.text: Two rearing stallions guard the entrance to Brookgreen Gardens: the Fighting Stallions by sculptor Anna Hyatt Huntington. Founded in 1931 by Huntington and her husband Archer, the site claims the largest outdoor collection of American figurative sculpture, on former plantations. Follow the Live Oak Allée and its roughly 250-year-old oaks, and note: the gates close at 4:30pm for day admission.

activities.text: Round off Brookgreen Gardens with the Lowcountry Zoo, accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums: alligators, a butterfly house and red foxes. The site also offers a trail devoted to Lowcountry history and programs on Gullah Geechee culture. Ask at the entrance about boat rides on the day of your visit.

visits.text: Day 1 - End the day on the Brooklyn Bridge: steel cables dating from 1883 and a wooden walkway above the traffic. Start on the Manhattan side and walk at least to the first tower; the view over the harbor at sunset is your reward for the day. Allow 30 to 45 min round trip, with dense crowds in the late afternoon.

Day 1 - The Brooklyn Bridge pedestrian path is now bike-free, with cyclists moved to the roadway: it's easier to walk along than before. The neo-Gothic arches frame the skyline; the best photos are taken early in the morning or at blue hour. A tripod is unnecessary; the structure vibrates as subway trains and cars pass.

activities.text: If your legs hold up, cross all the way and head down on the Brooklyn side for dinner in Dumbo facing Manhattan's lights, before returning by subway.
End-of-day option: head to the Whitehall terminal, at Manhattan's southern tip, for the Staten Island ferry. Subway from Brooklyn Bridge, about 9.5 km, 40 to 45 min with transfer.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Day 5 - Suspended above the expressway, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade unfurls the classic panorama over Lower Manhattan, the bridges, and the statue in the distance. Benches, old trees, residential calm: locals walk their dogs facing the skyline. Free, any hour; sunset is superb there.

Day 5 - Behind the promenade, Brooklyn Heights has rows of 1840s brownstones on streets named after fruits: Cranberry, Pineapple, Orange Street. Truman Capote wrote here. A ten-minute detour along Willow Street gives you the America of the movies you came looking for.

activities.text: Artisanal ice cream at the foot of the bridge, to enjoy along the promenade: the quintessential Brooklyn combo.
Subway to Brooklyn Museum: 4 km, 2/3 lines from Clark Street or Borough Hall to Eastern Parkway-Brooklyn Museum, about 25 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Day 5 - The Brooklyn Museum, often eclipsed by its Manhattan cousins, houses one of the city's richest collections: remarkable ancient Egyptian art, Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party, specialized pop exhibitions. No lines compared with the Met. Allow 2 hours; on the first Saturday of the month, there's a free, festive evening.

Day 5 - Adjacent to the museum, the Brooklyn Botanic Garden makes the combined ticket worthwhile in spring: the cherry esplanade in bloom in late April is an event in itself, with a Japanese garden too. If time is short, simply choose: the garden in good weather, the museum in the rain.

activities.text: Possible detour through Prospect Park, designed by Central Park's creators, which many Brooklynites judge more successful than the original.
Subway to Green-Wood Cemetery: 3 km, about 20 min; 25th Street station (R line) brings you right to the main entrance.

places.name: Brooks Camp, AK

visits.text: Brooks Falls is a 1.8-meter drop on the Brooks River—nothing spectacular in itself. What is spectacular is that dozens of brown bears, some exceeding 400 kg, position themselves here to catch sockeye salmon returning to spawn. The NPS viewing platforms, equipped with ramps and waiting areas, are limited to 40 people at a time with hourly rotation in July. In peak season, expect 90-minute waits—come at 5 a.m. or after 7 p.m. to avoid crowds.

The Valley of 10,000 Smokes, reached from Brooks Camp by the park’s only drivable road, resulted from the 1912 eruption of Novarupta, the largest eruption of the twentieth century worldwide. Millions of tonnes of ash covered 120 km² of the valley. Today the landscape looks lunar: valleys carved through pumice, with almost no vegetation. The park bus makes the round trip from Brooks Camp.

The Katmai Visitor Center at Brooks Camp—modest but well-designed—traces the park's volcanic history and its designation as a national monument in 1918, long before bears made it famous. The daily ranger talks (free) are often among the best you'll hear in the entire U.S. national park system.

The Riffles Platform—the second viewing platform, downstream from Brooks Falls—is often overlooked in favor of the falls. That's a mistake: dominant bears that can't secure a spot at the falls fish here in the shallows, often just about ten meters from the platform. The atmosphere is different, more intimate, and there's almost no wait.

The shore of Naknek Lake from Brooks Camp is a discreet but effective observation post to watch bears stroll the beach, especially late in the day. Naknek Lake is the park's largest (about 625 km²) and feeds the Brooks River where salmon concentrate. Settle on the rocks in the evening with binoculars—don't attempt to go down to the beach if bears are present.

activities.text: The Brooks River has been a world-class fishing river since the 1950s. Rainbow trout, king salmon, and sockeye salmon can be caught with light flies from the banks, in waders. There's one absolute rule: if a bear approaches your spot, you leave—no discussion. Rangers on-site review the protocols upon arrival. Licenses available at the lodge.

The Dumpling Mountain trail (7 km round-trip, 450 m of elevation gain) starts at Brooks Camp and climbs above treeline to panoramic views over Naknek Lake, the Alaska Peninsula mountains, and on clear days, all the way to the Pacific. Go early in the morning—bears are active on the slopes in the evening.

Kayaking on Naknek Lake from Brooks Camp—kayaks are available for rent through Katmailand. On the water, you're at the same level as bears on shore, at a safe distance. Early morning, the lake is often mirror-flat and the reflection of the volcanoes breathtaking. Avoid outings after 6 p.m.—wind picks up quickly.

Katmai's Fat Bear Week is an internet phenomenon that drew over 800,000 votes in 2021—but before voting online, come observe in real life. In September, bears that spent the summer fishing accumulate fat reserves at an astonishing rate. Some individuals, like the famous Bear 747, can weigh over 600 kg by the start of winter. Rangers at Brooks Camp know the names and histories of every regular bear—ask them.

visits.text: Discover Brunswick, the historic mainland gateway to the Golden Isles, where Victorian architecture, tree-lined streets, and scenic tidal rivers create understated coastal charm. The century-old Lover's Oak, a massive oak beneath which couples have traditionally pledged their love, spreads its ancient branches over a peaceful park. The Old Town district preserves authentic small-town Georgia character.

Tour Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation, a remarkably intact antebellum rice plantation documenting the complex history of agriculture, slavery, and Southern society along Georgia's tidal rivers. The quiet marina and working waterfront reflect Brunswick's enduring connection to the sea. Cross the stunning Sidney Lanier Bridge for spectacular views of the coastal landscape.

activities.text: Taste local craft spirits at the rum distillery, where small-batch production creates distinctive rums with notes of black cherry and caramel. The mainland location provides convenient access to all the Golden Isles while offering more affordable accommodation than the islands themselves.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Day 3 - Bryant Park, a lawn set between towers, serves as Midtown's open-air cafeteria: movable chairs, kiosks, pétanque, and ping-pong. In winter, there's a free ice rink (skate rental costs extra) and a Christmas market. It's the natural lunch stop on Day 3, midway through the day.

Day 3 - With its back to the park, the New York Public Library's entrance is guarded by its two marble lions, Patience and Fortitude. Go up to the Rose Main Reading Room, a 90 m-long reading room with a painted ceiling: free access, silence required. It was used as a setting for both Ghostbusters and The Day After Tomorrow.

activities.text: Sandwich or salad to go, green chair in the sun: the most New York lunch there is, for under $15.
Walk to Times Square: 500 m via 42nd Street or Broadway, about 6 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Bryce Amphitheater—Bryce Canyon isn't technically a canyon but rather a collection of amphitheaters carved into the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The rocks, deposited at the bottom of a lake 55 million years ago, get their colors from the oxidation of iron and manganese. Start at Sunrise Point for the overview: thousands of orange, pink, and cream-colored hoodoos rise like a petrified army. This is where the Queen's Garden trail begins.

Sunset Point—800 m from Sunrise Point via the Rim Trail, this is the starting point for the Navajo Loop. From the rim, you'll spot Thor's Hammer, a 10 m hoodoo topped by a balanced block that defies gravity. The view down into Wall Street, a slot canyon lined with Douglas firs, is dizzying.

Continue to Inspiration Point and Bryce Point for even broader amphitheater panoramas. Bryce Point, at the end of the road, offers the most spectacular perspective - you take in the entire amphitheater in a single sweeping view.

activities.text: Queen's Garden - Navajo Loop—Bryce's essential hike. Descend via Queen's Garden from Sunrise Point (the gentlest descent), walk among the hoodoos and the Queen Victoria formation—a pinnacle resembling a crowned queen—then climb back up via the Navajo Loop and its tight switchbacks between the walls of Wall Street, accessible only outside its winter closure. The loop is 5 km with 200 m of elevation gain; allow 1.5 to 2 hours. The park is at an altitude of 2,400 m: take your time, the air is thinner than it seems.

If you're here between April and October, stay for sunset from Sunset Point - the hoodoos shift from orange to deep crimson in minutes. The park is also certified Dark Sky: on clear nights, the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye. Bring a warm layer; it can get chilly at this elevation even in summer.

places.name: Buffalo, NY

visits.text: Frank Lloyd Wright's Darwin Martin House — Tour this Prairie School masterpiece completed in 1905, considered Wright's most important work before Fallingwater. The complex features 394 art glass windows and doors creating geometric light patterns throughout interconnected spaces.

Albright-Knox Art Gallery — Explore this museum renowned for its contemporary and modern art collection spanning Impressionism to Pop Art. The 1905 Greek Revival building houses works by Picasso, Matisse, Pollock, and Warhol.

Buffalo City Hall — Ascend to the 28th-floor observation deck of this 1931 Art Deco skyscraper for panoramic city and lake views. The 115-meter tower features intricate Native American motifs and Art Deco ornamentation throughout its limestone facade.

Canalside — Stroll along Buffalo's revitalized waterfront where the Erie Canal met Lake Erie beginning in 1825. The harbor development features historic ships, kayak launches, and winter ice skating on refrigerated outdoor rinks.

activities.text: Buffalo wings at Anchor Bar — Taste the original Buffalo wing invented here accidentally in 1964 by Teressa Bellissimo. The deep-fried chicken wings tossed in cayenne pepper hot sauce and served with celery and blue cheese became a global phenomenon.

Elmwood Village neighborhood walk — Browse boutiques, galleries, and cafes in this vibrant historic district listed on the National Register. Tree-lined streets showcase Victorian and Colonial Revival architecture dating from Buffalo's prosperous Gilded Age.

Sunset at Times Beach Nature Preserve — Observe migrating birds and watch sailboats on the Niagara River at this 37-hectare urban wilderness. The preserve's wetlands and meadows attract over 200 bird species along the Atlantic Flyway.

places.name: Burlington, VT

visits.text: Church Street Marketplace makes itself known the moment you set foot in Burlington: a four-block pedestrian street voted best public space in the United States by USA Today in 2022, with over 100 shops and restaurants and street musicians on every corner. The ECHO Leahy Center for Lake Champlain, on the waterfront, is an interactive museum featuring the lake's 81 fish species—worth seeing if you're traveling with children.

Waterfront Park opens onto Lake Champlain with New York's Adirondacks as backdrop—settle on the boardwalk at sunset. Named by Samuel de Champlain in 1609, the lake stretches for 120 miles and contains 6.8 trillion gallons of water. The Burlington Bike Path follows 7.5 miles of shoreline and joins the Island Line Trail, a converted railway running for miles above the lake's waters.

If you are there on a Saturday morning, the Burlington Farmers Market sets up at 345 Pine Street, in the South End: local growers, artisan bakeries, cheesemakers and maple sugar shacks side by side. Try a creemee—the local maple soft serve—before hitting the road to Providence.

activities.text: Burlington is regularly ranked among the cities with the highest density of breweries per capita in the United States—try Foam Brewers on the waterfront, Zero Gravity, or Switchback Brewing Company. In the evening, the Spirit of Ethan Allen offers dinner cruises on the lake with views of the Adirondacks at sunset.

6 miles to the south, the Shelburne Museum holds one of the most comprehensive collections of Americana in the country: 150,000 objects spread across 39 historic buildings, including a steamboat that once sailed Lake Champlain. Allow at least 3 hours—open from May to October, admission ~$30.

visits.text: Leave Los Angeles via the Pacific Coast Highway heading north. The first Malibu beaches begin 30 kilometers from downtown—this is where movie stars' homes have clustered since the 1920s. Stop at Zuma Beach for a break before continuing to Santa Barbara.

Santa Barbara calls itself the 'American Riviera.' Mission Santa Barbara, founded in 1786, is one of California's 21 Franciscan missions and one of the few never abandoned since its founding. The neoclassical facade you see today dates from 1833. Stearns Wharf, California's oldest working pier built in 1872, extends 650 meters into the sea—ideal for spotting dolphins and seals.

activities.text: Arrive in Cambria by late afternoon. This small village of 6,000 residents is wedged between wooded hills and Pacific cliffs. Moonstone Beach is scattered with translucent pebbles—the moonstones that gave the beach its name. Dine facing the ocean.

visits.text: The gallery at Cameron Trading Post deserves a close look before you continue toward the Grand Canyon. Navajo rugs, Hopi pottery, and jewelry offer a chance to observe different craft traditions beyond standardized souvenirs. Ask about the origin of the pieces that interest you and the artisan’s name, without assuming that all the objects have the same origin.

Cameron Suspension Bridge recalls a time when crossing the Little Colorado River was a stage of the journey in itself. The old metal bridge remains a landmark near the trading post and today’s roads. View it from an authorized public spot, without trying to cross it or climbing down to the riverbanks.

visits.text: Scout the Goonies locations in Astoria—the sets from Richard Donner's 1985 film are almost all still there. Drive up to 368 38th Street to see Mikey's house (46.1898, -123.8405): Victorian on the hill, private property, residents have nailed a "No Trespassing" sign because they've had enough. Photo from the sidewalk, gate closed. Astoria High School (46.1898, -123.8264) served as the high school in classroom scenes, still in operation. The Oregon Film Museum (46.1894, -123.8284), 732 Duane Street, is housed in the old jail used for the Fratelli escape sequence—ticket $6, 30 minutes, with sections dedicated to other Oregon shoots (Free Willy, Stand By Me, Kindergarten Cop, Twilight).

Climb to the Astoria Column (46.1801, -123.8232), 1 Coxcomb Drive—38-meter tower built in 1926, spiral frieze retracing the region's history, views over the Columbia and estuary. Buy a $1 balsa glider at the tower's base and launch it from the top: local tradition since the 1980s, the gliders spiral for a long time before getting lost in the trees. Parking $5.

From Cannon Beach, plan a round trip to see Fort Clatsop in Lewis and Clark National Historical Park (46.1342, -123.8772): a wooden replica of the fort where Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1805-1806 after traveling 6,700 km from Missouri. It rained on 95 of their 106 days there, much like the conditions here in November. A 20-minute film is included; admission $7.

Haystack Rock (45.8851, -123.9686) at Cannon Beach commands attention before you've even left the car—72 meters of black basalt emerging 100 meters from shore, a nature reserve where tufted puffins nest from April to July. This is where the final Goonies scene takes place, One-Eyed Willy's ship offshore. The photo is the one you'll find twenty years from now remembering the trip.

activities.text: Bowl a game at Lower Columbia Bowl (46.1881, -123.8298), 826 Marine Drive—the bowling alley where Chunk does his "Truffle Shuffle" in Goonies, still operating and open to the public. $15-20 per person, more authentic than a plastic souvenir.

Drive down US-101 to Cannon Beach (35 minutes south) for the night. Dine facing the ocean on Hemlock Street, seafood, $35-65. Book a beachside hotel with Haystack Rock views if you're coming in season—$180-380, and sunrise from the room is worth the price.

visits.text: Discover the works exhibited at Cold Mountain Art Collective in Canton, where local artists draw inspiration from Appalachian landscapes. Explore their creations and different techniques, then browse the handmade products at Willow Hill Soap Company. This visit offers a firsthand look at the work of makers in this Haywood County town near Asheville.

Explore Graveyard Fields, a distinctive high-altitude area offering mysterious and captivating views of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Plan a round trip by car from Canton to the trailhead, followed by a visit on foot. This popular hiking destination features unusual landscapes and abundant wildflowers, offering outdoor enthusiasts unforgettable mountain experiences.

activities.text: Discover local crafts at Cold Mountain Art Collective, where regional artists showcase their creative works inspired by the surrounding mountain landscape. Browse handcrafted items at Willow Hill Soap Company, known for its artistic and decorative candles that make perfect souvenirs of your mountain adventure.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Kennedy Space Center - Where Humans Reach for the Stars: Allow for a round trip from Cape Canaveral to visit this historic launch complex, which has sent all American astronauts into orbit since the 1960s. The visitor complex offers encounters with real astronauts, displays of full-size rockets, and the actual space shuttle Atlantis.

Rocket Garden - Walk Among Giants: Allow for a round trip from Cape Canaveral. Stand beneath authentic rockets from every era of American spaceflight, from Mercury to Apollo, and discover the scale of humanity's greatest engineering achievements.

Canaveral National Seashore - 24 Miles of Preserved Atlantic Coast: Allow for a round trip from Cape Canaveral. NASA's need for privacy created this unexpected benefit—an unspoiled refuge protecting sea turtle nesting beaches and more than 1,000 plant species.

activities.text: Rocket Launch Viewing - Watch History Being Made: Multiple companies now launch from Cape Canaveral, with public viewing areas offering front-row seats to thundering liftoffs that shake the ground miles away.

IMAX Theater and 4D Experience - Immersion in Space Exploration: Allow for a round trip from Cape Canaveral. State-of-the-art theaters showcase the wonders of space exploration through footage filmed by astronauts aboard the International Space Station.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

visits.text: Provincetown, about 48 miles from Hyannis, 1 hour 15 by road, is worth the drive—don't skip it. The Pilgrim Monument (1910) recalls that the Pilgrims anchored the Mayflower here in November 1620, before Plymouth, and drew up the Mayflower Compact. The granite tower rises 253 feet. North of town, Race Point Beach spreads its 100-foot dunes along the open Atlantic.

Chatham, about thirty minutes' drive from Hyannis, is the postcard image of Cape Cod: Main Street lines up shops, art galleries and seafood restaurants in white clapboard buildings. The Chatham Fish Pier comes alive early in the morning as the boats come in—you can buy fresh tuna directly from the fishermen. Chatham Lighthouse (1878) overlooks the beach from the top of a bluff.

The Cape Cod National Seashore has protected 50 square miles of coastline since 1961: Atlantic beaches, dunes, pine forests and salt marshes. Start at the Salt Pond Visitor Center in Eastham, about thirty minutes' drive from Hyannis, for a trail map. Coast Guard Beach and Nauset Light Beach are wild beaches—cool water, few people on weekdays.

The moment the ferry docks in Oak Bluffs, head to Trinity Park: over 300 painted wooden cottages in vivid colors form a unique ensemble, the "Gingerbread Houses" built from the 1860s onward on the site of a Methodist camp meeting. The central cast-iron Tabernacle (1879) still hosts summer concerts. Circuit Avenue, the main street, is lined with shops and restaurants.

Edgartown, founded in 1642, is the island's historic center. The 19th-century whaling captains' houses line up their white façades along Water Street. A 3-minute ferry crosses the channel to Chappaquiddick Island.

At the island's western tip, the Gay Head Cliffs of Aquinnah rise 200 feet above the Atlantic. Step to the edge to watch the clay change color with the light—ochre, red, white, gray. These lands belong to the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), which regained them in 1987. The Gay Head Lighthouse (1844) is reachable on foot from the parking lot. Caution: erosion is rapid.

activities.text: Head out whale watching from MacMillan Pier in Provincetown, about 48 miles from Hyannis, 1 hour 15 by road: 3-4 hour trips to the Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, 5 miles north of the Cape, let you spot humpback whales, rorquals and dolphins. The Dolphin Fleet runs daily departures from May to October—book online, ~$50 per person. Morning trips have the best sea conditions.

The Cape Cod Rail Trail winds for 25 miles along a 19th-century railway bed—rent a bike and go: the path crosses dunes, glacial ponds, and scrub oak forests. Rental points dot the route. It's the most pleasant way to cross the Cape without a car.

Rent a bike as you leave the ferry in Oak Bluffs and ride across the island on State Road to Aquinnah, at the far end of the island: the road runs through oak forests and meadows and skirts Tisbury Pond. The cycle network is well developed - allow ~$30 a day.

In the evening, go eat in Menemsha, the small fishing port on the west side of the island. The lobster is caught that very morning and cooked to order—eat on the docks watching the boats come in and the sun set over Vineyard Sound.

places.name: Cape Elizabeth, ME

visits.text: Portland Head Light bears Portland’s name but is located in Cape Elizabeth. You can view the lighthouse from Fort Williams Park; its museum occupies the former keepers’ house. The tower opens only on rare occasions, and the museum’s season differs from the park’s: check the operator’s calendar before planning an indoor visit.

activities.text: Extend your visit in Fort Williams Park, among lawns, rocky shoreline, and military remains. The park is open from sunrise to sunset year-round, unlike the lighthouse museum. Follow public paths and check the parking signs: several areas charge for parking even when park admission is free.

places.name: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, NC

visits.text: In 1999, Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was moved about 880 meters inland, in 23 days. Built in 1870 some 450 meters from the surf, the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States stood only about 30 meters from the water by then. The keepers' quarters, moved along with it, house a free museum.

activities.text: If you visit in 2026, forget about climbing Cape Hatteras Lighthouse: restoration has fallen behind schedule and the lighthouse stays closed to climbing all year, partly under scaffolding. The grounds remain open 24/7 and you can walk to the beach from the lighthouse, facing Diamond Shoals, the sandbars that earned this coast the nickname "Graveyard of the Atlantic".

map_keywords: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, Buxton, North Carolina

visits.text: Explore Capulin Volcano National Monument, where an extinct cinder cone volcano rises dramatically from the surrounding plains, providing a remarkable example of geologically recent volcanic activity in the American Southwest. The paved road spirals to the crater rim, where hiking trails circle the edge and descend into the volcanic crater itself. From the summit, views extend across four states on clear days, revealing the vast grassland plains that characterize this corner of New Mexico.

activities.text: Watch for diverse wildlife including elk, coyotes, and black bears that inhabit the volcanic slopes and surrounding grasslands. The monument preserves not only geological features but also prairie ecosystems that once supported vast bison herds and continue to shelter numerous species adapted to this high plains environment.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Ancient Pueblos, White Sands and Ancestral Volcanoes

visits.text: Descend into Carlsbad Caverns National Park, where more than 100 limestone caves beneath the Chihuahuan Desert reveal spectacular underground formations created over millions of years. The famous Carlsbad Cavern features the Big Room, one of the largest cave chambers in North America, where massive stalactites and stalagmites create an otherworldly landscape 230 meters below the surface. Guided tours reveal increasingly remote sections of this subterranean wonderland.

Marvel at Lechuguilla Cave, the nation's deepest limestone cave at 478 meters and fourth longest, containing rare mineral formations found nowhere else on Earth. While this cave is closed to general visitors due to its scientific importance, exhibits explain the extraordinary discoveries made within its pristine passages. The park protects over 300 caves beneath the desert surface.

activities.text: Witness the spectacular evening bat flight from May through October, when hundreds of thousands of Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral from the cave entrance at dusk to hunt insects across the desert. Ranger programs explain the ecology of these remarkable creatures and their importance to the cave ecosystem. Drive Walnut Canyon Desert Loop to experience the Chihuahuan Desert landscape above ground.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Ancient Pueblos, White Sands and Ancestral Volcanoes

visits.text: Carlsbad Caverns - Descend through the natural entrance: a gaping opening in the rock where a 2 km trail drops to a depth of 230 m. The route passes monumental limestone formations before reaching the Big Room, the largest underground chamber in North America - 33,000 m², the area of 6 soccer fields. The temperature is 13°C year-round, so bring a jacket. If your knees cannot handle the descent, an elevator takes you directly to the Big Room. Allow for a round trip by car from Carlsbad to the cavern entrance, in addition to the underground visit.

Carlsbad Museum and Art Center - If you still have energy after the caverns, swing by this small free museum in town. You'll see Permian fossils, Southwestern art, and a collection of Native American pottery.

activities.text: Bat Flight Program - From May to October, between 200,000 and 500,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats emerge from the caverns at dusk to hunt insects. Take a seat in the stone amphitheater facing the cave entrance. The spectacle begins when the black spiral starts swirling into the sky - it lasts 20 to 40 minutes. Rangers give a presentation before the flight. Free, no reservation required. Allow for a round trip by car from Carlsbad.

days_plan.itin_title: Desert Parks of Texas and New Mexico: Big Bend, Carlsbad, White Sands, and Guadalupe

visits.text: Carmel-by-the-Sea is best explored without looking for an attraction at every intersection. Around Ocean Avenue, galleries and small courtyards form an arts-focused downtown; the street then slopes down toward the beach, giving your walk a natural direction. Browse a few storefronts, then follow the passages open to the public. Park once and check the time limit before extending your stop.

activities.text: Explore 17-Mile Drive by choosing your stops rather than getting out at every sign. The private road runs through Pebble Beach and connects Spanish Bay, Bird Rock, and The Lone Cypress, among other sights; its 17 miles amount to approximately 27 km. The map provided at the entrance helps you follow the route past residential turnoffs. Check the day’s fee and restrictions, then leave time for a walk along Spanish Bay.

Light-colored sand and cypress trees immediately set the scene at Carmel Beach. At the end of Ocean Avenue, the beach opens the town onto the bay, while the coastal path lets you continue walking without staying on the sand. Head down for a break toward the end of the day, then walk back uphill to downtown. Keep your distance from the waves: this stop is planned for walking, with no guarantee that swimming will be possible.

If you prefer trails to storefronts, set aside the early part of the following morning for Point Lobos State Natural Reserve. Coves, cypress trees, and kelp forests continue Carmel’s scenery, with access on foot; the Lace Lichen Trail connects the entrance to the Sea Lion Point area. Check at the entrance for open trails and limit the length of your loop. Visit before continuing toward Big Sur, without returning to downtown Carmel.

places.name: Casper, WY

visits.text: Pull off I-25 for the National Historic Trails Interpretive Center—free admission, and one of Wyoming's best history museums. Casper sits at the crossing of four westward migration corridors: the Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, and Pony Express trails. The museum covers the 400,000 emigrants who crossed this ground between 1841 and 1868, with interactive exhibits including a virtual covered wagon crossing and a treadmill that simulates pulling a handcart. A 27-minute film addresses US treaty violations with Plains tribes. Allow 75–90 minutes.

Fort Caspar Museum sits on the banks of the North Platte River in a reconstructed 1865 military post - named for 2nd Lieutenant Caspar Collins, killed at the Battle of Platte Bridge Station that year. A typo in the 1889 town registration swapped the 'a' for an 'e' in Casper, which is why the town and the fort are spelled differently. The museum covers prehistoric Plains Indians, the frontier army, and the energy industry. Open daily May through September.

visits.text: The nickname "Grand Canyon of the East" is a bit presumptuous—but when you're standing on the rim, 180 meters above the Genesee River, you stop arguing. Letchworth State Park was even named the best state park in the United States by USA Today in 2015. The gorge stretches 27 kilometers, the park covers 14,350 acres, and 66 miles of trails wind through it. Three main entrances: Mount Morris to the north, Castile in the center, Portageville to the south. A car is essential to move between them.

This is where William Pryor Letchworth, a Buffalo industrialist, lived from 1859 until his death in 1910, before bequeathing his 1,000-acre estate to the state to become a park. Middle Falls, the widest and tallest of the three main waterfalls at 33 meters, is visible from the esplanade behind the Glen Iris Inn—his house transformed into an inn in 1914. The restaurant still operates; you can have lunch without staying overnight. Direct view of the cascade from the terrace.

Upper Falls, 21 meters high and 90 wide, sits beneath the imposing Portageville railroad viaduct—a 250-meter-long steel arch bridge completed in 2017, replacing the 1875 wooden trestle. Norfolk Southern freight trains still cross several times daily. If you wait a bit, it's worth it for the photo.

Lower Falls, accessible via a 127-step trail descending into the gorge, marks the end of the three-waterfall stretch. Modest height (21 meters) but wilder setting, with a footbridge spanning the river mid-slope. Often deserted compared to the other two, so pleasant in summer.

activities.text: Picnic at Tea Table Overlook, a developed viewing point on the gorge rim in the park's northern section, accessible by car. Stone tables, a view down onto the river 150 meters below. This is the postcard photo spot, and it's free. Self-serve ice cream at the Trading Post at the Castile entrance.

Whitewater rafting with Adventure Calls Outfitters. A 5 km trip on Class II–III rapids depending on the season, about 90 minutes on the water, guides included. Available from April to October, more intense in spring after the snowmelt.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Berkshires to Niagara Falls: 10 Days of Waterfalls, Villages, and Wide-Open Spaces

places.name: Cave City, KY

visits.text: Welcome underground. Mammoth Cave is the world's longest known cave system - 686 km of mapped passages to date, 1.5 times the length of the world's second-longest system. The limestone rock began forming 330 million years ago when Kentucky was still at the bottom of a tropical sea. Native Americans explored these passages 4,000 years ago: their woven moccasins and reed torches have been found several kilometers from the entrance. Stop at the Visitor Center first to pick up your tickets - the cave stays 12°C year-round, bring a layer even in summer.

Do the Historic Tour first (2 hours, 3.2 km, about 540 steps): it is the benchmark visit. You descend into the Rotunda, where slaves mined saltpeter for gunpowder during the War of 1812. Stephen Bishop, a slave who later became a freed guide, mapped a large part of the system in the 1830s; his grave can be seen near the entrance.

In the afternoon, follow up with the Frozen Niagara Tour (1h15, 400 m, easy): a different section of the system, visually very different. Here formations dominate - stalactites, stalagmites, and the great cascading rock draperies that look like a petrified waterfall. Two tours in one day are enough to get a complete picture of the system's diversity.

If you want to go deeper, the Violet City Lantern Tour (3 hours, 4.8 km) completely changes the atmosphere: rangers turn off all electric lighting and you advance by lantern like in the 19th century. The immensity of the passages becomes palpable when artificial light disappears. It's the favorite tour of several park rangers - and one of the most powerful underground experiences of this road trip.

In Bowling Green, less than an hour's drive from Cave City via Interstate 65, Lost River Cave is worth a stop: it is one of the largest cave openings in the eastern United States, with an underground river navigable by boat. The cave was used as a nightclub in the 1930s - a sign at the entrance recalls this unlikely period. The boat tour lasts 45 minutes.

activities.text: Between tours, enjoy the surface: the Green River Ferry (free, NPS-operated) crosses the river every 10-15 minutes. On the other side, the shaded banks are nearly deserted on weekdays. The First Creek Lake Loop trail (2.5 km, flat) follows a wet prairie frequented by deer and wild turkeys - a good way to decompress between underground plunges.

In the evening, Cave City a few miles south has decent restaurants and affordable motels. If you prefer sleeping in the park, The Lodge at Mammoth Cave is right on-site - convenient for being there first thing when tours open the next morning.

For thrill-seekers, the Wild Cave Tour (6 hours, 8.8 km) is the park's most demanding tour: six hours crawling through tight passages, climbing in the dark, and squeezing through sections the standard tours never visit. Bring old clothes - you'll emerge covered in mud. Minimum age 16, reservation required well in advance.

If you prefer staying above ground, the park's 110 km of trails traverse the karst hills of Kentucky - a landscape of sinkholes, springs, and depressions typical of this limestone terrain. The Sal Hollow Trail (7 km) follows a wooded valley along a creek, nearly empty of people.

places.name: Cedar Rapids, IA

visits.text: You enter a 4,645-square-meter Smithsonian Affiliate on the Cedar River's south bank, which began in 1978 as the Czech Fine Arts Foundation. Its crown jewel is the largest collection of traditional Czech and Slovak kroje (folk costumes) outside the Czech Republic and Slovakia, including pieces dating back to the 16th century. The Immigrant Home exhibit—a 19th-century Bohemian house relocated to higher ground after the devastating 2008 Cedar River flood—walks you through five generations of one family's American story. Admission charged.

Cedar Rapids native Grant Wood painted American Gothic in 1930 in a studio right here in downtown Cedar Rapids. The museum holds the world's largest public collection of Wood's work, from early Impressionist experiments to the regionalist paintings that made him a national figure. The Grant Wood Studio itself is a separate site a few blocks away - advance booking required for studio access. Admission charged.

You drive 50 kilometers south to Iowa's first capitol, which housed the legislative assembly from 1842 until 1857, when the seat of government moved west to Des Moines. The building then became the anchor of the University of Iowa campus—a National Historic Landmark standing at the heart of the Pentacrest. The cornerstone was laid in 1840, and the restored period rooms inside represent the building's appearance in the 1840s–1850s. Free admission; closed Sundays and Mondays.

activities.text: Plan a day trip from Cedar Rapids to Iowa City. You step into Prairie Lights, founded in 1978 by Jim Harris and moved in 1982 to its current 1,022-square-meter premises—the same building where Iowa City's literary society met in the 1930s, hosting readings by Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Langston Hughes. Seven Nobel laureates in literature have read here, including Toni Morrison and J.M. Coetzee. The Live from Prairie Lights reading series takes place four or five evenings a week. Check the calendar before your visit.

You wander along 16th Avenue SW through Cedar Rapids' Czech Village, passing the NCSML, where North America's only Orloj—a working replica of Prague's medieval astronomical clock—stands in front of the museum. The adjacent NewBo (New Bohemia) district has converted old industrial buildings into a food market, microbreweries, and galleries. You can walk both neighborhoods in under an hour.

visits.text: Cedarburg Historic Downtown - Over 200 nineteenth-century buildings line the streets of this small town north of Milwaukee. Old woolen mills converted into shops and galleries at Cedar Creek Settlement, a covered wooden bridge (Wisconsin's last), and cobblestone streets full of charm. This is one of the state's best-preserved downtowns.
Cedarburg Covered Bridge - Built in 1876, this is Wisconsin's last remaining covered bridge. It spans Cedar Creek in a wooded setting north of town.
Cedar Creek Settlement - The former woolen mill (1864) now houses a winery, art galleries, and craft shops. The limestone building is impressive.

activities.text: Craft Breweries and Distilleries - Cedarburg has embraced the craft trend. Several breweries and a distillery offer tastings. This is Wisconsin - beer is serious business here.
Cedar Creek Walk - Easy, shaded trail following the creek through town. Pleasant in late afternoon.
