visits.text: Day 4 - Central Park starts the day: 341 hectares of landscaped nature in the heart of Manhattan. Focus on the south and center: the Mall and its elms, Bethesda Terrace and its angel, Bow Bridge, Strawberry Fields in Lennon's memory. Two hours on foot, much less on a rental bike.

Day 4 - Belvedere Castle, the Alice in Wonderland statue, rowboats on the Lake: Central Park is a place to enjoy rather than simply visit. A warning about today's deliberately packed schedule: two enormous museums border the park, and you'll have to choose. Save some energy for the afternoon.

activities.text: A rental rowboat on the Lake or just a bagel eaten on a rock: a break is in order before tackling the museums.
Exit on the west side of the park toward the American Museum of Natural History: 600 m, about 8 min on foot.

visits.text: Explore Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserving the most remarkable concentration of ancient Pueblo architecture in North America. Between 850 and 1250 CE, Chaco Canyon served as the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of a vast regional network spanning thousands of square miles. Massive great houses containing hundreds of rooms and multiple stories demonstrate sophisticated engineering and astronomical knowledge.

Visit Pueblo Bonito, the largest and most famous of Chaco's great houses, featuring over 600 rooms arranged in a perfect D-shape aligned to celestial events. The precision construction using millions of carefully shaped sandstone blocks continues to amaze archaeologists and visitors alike. Petroglyphs throughout the canyon document the spiritual and practical knowledge of these ancient peoples.

activities.text: From the canyon road, take in the silhouette of Fajada Butte, the isolated butte that holds the famous Sun Dagger, where spirals carved into the rock marked the solstices and equinoxes. The butte has been closed to the public since 1989. The solar calendar cannot be visited, but the butte can be admired from the canyon floor. The park's isolated location, far from light pollution, makes it exceptional for stargazing, and it has been designated an International Dark Sky Park. Hiking trails link the main ruins while revealing the raw beauty of the desert canyon.

places.name: Chamberlain, SD

visits.text: Pull off I-90 at Exit 263 and walk onto the keelboat-shaped balcony of the Lewis and Clark Welcome Center—the Missouri River stretches below you in both directions, and the replica of the Corps' 17-meter keelboat gives you a sense of scale. Just outside, *Dignity: Of Earth and Sky* by sculptor Dale Lamphere rises 15 meters in stainless steel—a Lakota and Dakota woman with outstretched quilt-patterned wings, facing the river the expedition traveled up in 1804. The Akta Lakota Museum at St. Joseph's Indian School, three kilometers east, holds one of the most comprehensive collections of Lakota art and artifacts in the Great Plains. Free admission.

visits.text: Paisley Park—Book ahead: Prince's studio and residence, opened to the public in 2016, is by appointment only. Inside this 6,000 m² white building, you'll see his recording studios, private concert hall, costumes, and instruments. The guided tour lasts 90 minutes.

Minnesota Landscape Arboretum - A 15-minute drive from Chanhassen, take time to explore this 480-hectare botanical garden. You can visit on foot or by car along a 5 km loop. If you come in autumn, the colours are exceptional.

activities.text: Make a detour through Excelsior, a village on the shores of Lake Minnetonka. The lake covers 58 km² with 125 km of shoreline—it's been the site of summer estates since the 19th century. Stroll the pier and watch the boats pass.

places.name: Charging Bull, NY

visits.text: Day 1 - Three and a half tonnes of bronze planted on Broadway: Arturo Di Modica's Charging Bull, left without permission one night in 1989, has become Wall Street's totem. A photo without the crowds is almost impossible during the day; stop by early in the morning or in the evening. Two minutes are enough, but it's not to be missed.

Day 1 - Steps from the bull, Wall Street is home to the New York Stock Exchange and Federal Hall, where Washington took the oath in 1789. You can photograph the colonnades from Broad Street. Trinity Church, at the end of the street, holds Alexander Hamilton's tomb in its cemetery.

activities.text: Break at Bowling Green, the city's oldest park (1733), just behind the bull; the National Museum of the American Indian, free, occupies the monumental former customs house across the street.
Walk up to the 9/11 Memorial: 700 m via Broadway or Trinity Place, about 9 min.

places.name: Charleston, SC

visits.text: Starting at the International African American Museum gives context to the plantations you will visit later. At Gadsden’s Wharf, the exhibits connect the transatlantic slave trade with African American experiences and cultures, while the African Ancestors Memorial Garden extends the visit outdoors. This garden is part of the museum’s message, not simply its setting. Set aside time for it after the galleries, and reserve your admission before planning the day.

Pastel facades, then the harbor breeze: Rainbow Row and The Battery flow naturally into a single walk. The houses on East Bay Street recall Charleston’s trading past before the promenade opens up views of the harbor. The contrast between the narrow street and the waterfront brings variety to this exploration. Walk the route, and keep residential entrances clear while taking photos.

Middleton Place contrasts the geometry of its gardens with the free-flowing Ashley River. The estate combines landscaped grounds, a museum, and areas devoted to plantation trades, with tours addressing the lives of enslaved people. Heritage-breed animals offer another perspective on how this agricultural operation worked. Start by checking the schedule of talks, then plan your time in the gardens around the one devoted to slavery.

Beautiful gardens, but a history that calls for looking beyond the flowers: Magnolia Plantation & Gardens was a rice plantation. The From Slavery to Freedom tour uses former dwellings to explore the lives of enslaved people and their later lives in freedom. The buildings thus tell a story that extends beyond the family who owned the property. Pick up your ticket for the guided tour, distributed on-site, as soon as you arrive, before exploring the gardens.

1936: at Boone Hall Plantation & Gardens, the main house is much newer than its appearance suggests. The former brick homes of enslaved people date from a different period and house the Black History in America exhibition. This gap changes how you interpret the estate. Give these dwellings as much attention as the main house, then explore the areas open to the public rather than limiting yourself to the entrance drive.

activities.text: Take time to watch artisans at work at Charleston City Market, beyond the souvenir stalls. Sweetgrass baskets belong to a Gullah tradition; their shapes recall objects used to winnow rice on plantations. A decorative object thus also tells a story of labor. Ask the artisan to explain their technique and the price before handling a piece.

If you prefer woodland to flower beds, set aside time for the Audubon Swamp Garden at Magnolia. This self-guided route offers another perspective on the estate, focusing on the swamp rather than the house and landscaped gardens. Here, water and vegetation become the focus of the walk. Stay on open paths, bring insect repellent, and observe wildlife from a distance without trying to attract it.

Settle in to listen to Exploring the Gullah Culture at Boone Hall instead of walking through the entire estate without a pause. Gullah descendants share their culture through storytelling, song, and dance. These living voices offer a different perspective from the exhibition panels. Check the presentation time on the day of your visit, and leave enough time before your next scheduled activity.

A plate of shrimp and creamy grits offers another way to experience Charleston City Market and its surroundings. Shrimp and grits is among the Lowcountry specialties served in this area; recipes vary from kitchen to kitchen. Corn forms the foundation of the dish, rather than serving as a mere side. Check the ingredients and listed extra charges before choosing, then enjoy the meal as a proper break.

visits.text: You're discovering one of the most beautiful state capitols in the United States: the 46-meter dome covered in pure gold leaf has dominated the Kanawha River since construction was completed in 1932 to plans by architect Cass Gilbert, who also designed the Supreme Court building in Washington DC. The interior is covered in Italian and Hungarian marble, and the Rotunda chandelier weighs two tonnes. The free guided tour (45 minutes) recounts the story of West Virginia's separation from Virginia in 1863, in the middle of the Civil War—one of the most unusual state births in American history. Don't miss the 1930s murals in the Senate and House chambers.

You enter the West Virginia State Museum, adjacent to the Capitol, and walk through galleries that trace the region's history from Native American cultures to the mining strikes of the 1920s. An entire gallery is dedicated to Appalachian folklore: traditional musical instruments, storytelling traditions, and the craft of quilting. Admission is free. The museum bookstore offers an excellent selection of works on regional history—the best place to buy a reference book on Appalachia before getting back on the road to Washington.

You're entering a converted freight depot where producers from the Kanawha Valley and neighboring farms display their goods: vegetables, goat cheeses, Allegheny honey, wild fruit jams, and local meats. On weekdays, the permanent stalls sell fruits and vegetables, spices, and artisan products from all over West Virginia. It's the best place to buy edible souvenirs before heading back to DC—pawpaw jam, mountain honey, hickory-smoked sausages.

activities.text: You're walking along Kanawha Boulevard for several miles facing the downtown skyline and the Capitol crowned with its golden dome. The promenade lined with century-old elms is frequented by residents in the evening after work. You'll pass several contemporary murals that tell the story of the state's labor history—mining unions, the Kanawha Valley chemical industry. At the end of the day, the reflections of the golden Capitol in the river are striking—this is the photo of Charleston that nobody shows in the guidebooks.

You're entering the Clay Center, inaugurated in 2003, and you're discovering under one roof a science museum, an art museum, a 1,800-seat theater, and a digital planetarium. The science collections trace Appalachian geology with specimens of coal, limestone, and oil shale. The art gallery presents contemporary Appalachian artists. The building itself, with its glass facades on Charleston's riverfront, is one of the state's finest architectural achievements.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

places.name: Charlotte, NC

visits.text: The NASCAR Hall of Fame opened on May 11, 2010, for $160 million in the heart of Uptown Charlotte—and even if you're not a racing fan, you'll spend 3 hours without realizing it. The story begins with 1930s bootleggers who modified their cars to outrun the police; NASCAR was founded in 1948. The "Glory Road," a ramp banked at 33 degrees like Talladega, displays 18 historic cars.

The Harvey B. Gantt Center for African-American Arts + Culture on South Tryon Street is named after the first Black student admitted to Clemson University (South Carolina) in 1963, who was also Charlotte's first Black mayor from 1983 to 1987 - don't walk past without going in. Its rotating exhibitions explore African-American art and culture with genuine curatorial rigor. The building by the firm Gantt Huberman Architects is itself a fine piece of architecture.

If you only have time for one museum in Charlotte, choose the Mint Museum Uptown in the Levine Center for the Arts. Its 145,000 square feet house, among others, its collections of American art, contemporary art and craft + design.

The Bechtler Museum of Modern Art, right across from the Mint Uptown, is devoted to mid-20th-century European avant-garde art—and you'll find Miró, Giacometti, and Warhol assembled by a Swiss family with remarkable taste. Mario Botta's sandstone building is itself an architectural sculpture.

activities.text: Uptown Charlotte is compact and pleasant on foot—start from Romare Bearden Park, named after the great collage artist born in Charlotte in 1911, and walk up Tryon Street to 7th Street. In the evening, South End and NoDa (North Davidson) await with the city's best tables and a live music scene almost every night.

End this journey with a real North Carolina barbecue meal: slow-smoked pork shoulder, vinegar-pepper sauce, mayo-free coleslaw. It's a distinct style from Texas or Tennessee. Several recognized pit masters operate within 30 minutes of Uptown. Don't leave without trying it.

days_plan.itin_title: Baltimore to the Outer Banks - Historic America from Chesapeake Bay to Charlotte

map_keywords: Bechtler Museum of Modern Art Charlotte

visits.text: You stop in Staunton and discover one of Virginia's best-preserved Victorian downtowns—the town was spared by the Civil War, and its red-brick façades from 1880–1900 are almost intact. Staunton is the birthplace of Woodrow Wilson, the 28th president of the United States, born here in 1856; his birthplace has become a presidential museum. The Beverley Street district is lined with independent restaurants, galleries, and shops in historic commercial buildings. It is an ideal lunch stop—allow 1 hour 30 minutes to stroll without rushing before heading back toward Charlottesville. Allow for a round trip by car from Charlottesville to visit Staunton.

You're climbing the hill at Monticello and standing before the house that Thomas Jefferson himself designed, modified, and perfected over forty years starting in 1768. The facade is familiar to all Americans: it has appeared on the nickel, the five-cent coin, since 1938. Jefferson—architect, inventor, philosopher, 3rd president of the United States—lived here until his death on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the signing of the Declaration of Independence that he drafted. The estate has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Book your guided tour online in advance—morning slots fill quickly during high season.

You're walking along the Lawn—the central lawn of the University of Virginia—framed by the red brick pavilions that Jefferson himself designed between 1817 and 1826 to embody his ideal of “a university based on freedom and reason”. The Rotunda that closes the axis to the north is inspired by Rome's Pantheon, at half scale. The campus was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site at the same time as Monticello—it's the only university campus in the world to share this distinction with its founder's home. Self-guided tours are free at any time; free guided tours depart from the Welcome Center several times daily.

activities.text: You visit the white wooden Presbyterian house where Woodrow Wilson was born in 1856—the only American president to have earned a doctorate, who received the Nobel Peace Prize (1919) for his role in creating the League of Nations after the First World War. The adjacent museum recounts his presidency (1913–1921): the progressive New Freedom legislation, entry into the war in 1917, the Fourteen Points, and the U.S. Senate's failure to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, which ruined his health. His 1919 presidential Pierce-Arrow is displayed in the original garage. Allow for a round trip by car from Charlottesville for this visit to Staunton.

You're walking along the Downtown Mall, an 8-block pedestrian street paved with red brick in the 1970s, which has become one of the liveliest pedestrian shopping streets in the American South. Hundreds of independent restaurants, galleries, bars, and art-house cinemas bring this corridor to life year-round. UVA students, longtime residents, and tourists from Monticello mingle here. At the end of the day, take a seat in an outdoor seating area to observe local life before getting back on the road to Washington the next morning.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

visits.text: Rock City Gardens — Explore this 1930s attraction on Lookout Mountain, with huge rock formations, gardens, and views of seven states from Lovers Leap. The Swing-A-Long Bridge spans a 55-meter gorge.
Tennessee Aquarium — Explore freshwater and saltwater ecosystems in this aquarium, home to 12,000 animals. The $45 million complex has two buildings that follow environments from river to ocean.

Walnut Street Bridge — View this historic bridge, built in 1891 to link downtown with the North Shore arts district, from the riverbanks. While it remains closed for renovation until October 3, 2026, cross the river on foot via Market Street Bridge for views of the water and mountains.

Hunter Museum of American Art — View American art from Colonial to contemporary in this clifftop museum. The 1904 classical mansion and 1975 brutalist addition house works by Mary Cassatt, Ansel Adams, and regional artists.

activities.text: Incline Railway ride — Board the funicular climbing a 72.7% grade on Lookout Mountain. This 1895 railway offers panoramic views of Chattanooga and the Tennessee River.
Riverfront dining — Enjoy farm-to-table Southern cuisine at restaurants overlooking the Tennessee River. The revitalized waterfront features local ingredients and mountain views.

days_plan.itin_title: Tennessee Music & Mountains Road Trip: Nashville to Great Smoky Mountains

visits.text: Chauvin Sculpture Garden - At the end of a narrow road hugging Bayou Petit Caillou, 100 km south of New Orleans, this sculpture garden is one of the most striking works of outsider art in the United States. Between 1990 and 2000, Kenny Hill, a solitary mason, created about a hundred life-size concrete statues: angels with light bulb halos, cowboys, self-portraits with faces painted black and white, and a 14-meter-tall brick lighthouse with figures clinging to its sides. Kenny Hill abandoned everything one day in 2000 and disappeared. The site, restored and managed by Nicholls State University, is free and open from 8 AM to 5 PM.

Bayou Petit Caillou - Driving to Chauvin, you'll cross one of the most authentic landscapes in deep Louisiana. Houses on stilts, moored shrimp boats, herons on fence posts. This is the Louisiana tourists never see—the Louisiana of fishermen and Cajun communities living at water level.

activities.text: Watch the shrimp boats on the bayou - Chauvin is a shrimping community. The colorful boats moored along the bayou are a spectacle in themselves. If you're there in spring, the Blessing of the Fleet is an annual event that brings the Cajun community together at the sculpture garden.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Louisiana Road Trip: Jazz and Bayous

visits.text: Day 2 - In the former Nabisco factory where the Oreo was invented, Chelsea Market packs in about thirty food counters: lobster rolls, tacos, Fat Witch brownies. The day's lunch or afternoon snack is sorted. Crowds peak between noon and 2 PM; tables are fought over, and you often eat standing up.

Day 2 - Amid Chelsea Market's brickwork and neon lights, take time for the shops too: a bookstore, the Italian grocery Buon Italia, a fish shop with a food counter. The upper floors house Google offices: the tech district is nibbling away at Chelsea without, for now, changing its character.

activities.text: Try the tacos at Los Tacos No.1, the fastest line and safest bet in the market.
Walk to Little Island: 400 m to the Hudson via 15th Street, about 5 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

places.name: Cheyenne, WY

visits.text: The Wyoming State Capitol's gold-leafed dome has been gilded five times since 1900—seen from the north, it floats above the city like a European building. Inside, the ground-floor rotunda has checkerboard marble floors and a cherry-wood staircase shipped from Ohio. The building was finished in 1890, the same year Wyoming became the 44th state, and the third-floor chamber is where delegates voted to enshrine women's suffrage in the state constitution—Wyoming women had held that right since 1869, five decades before the 19th Amendment. Self-guided tours are free, Monday through Friday during business hours.

Cheyenne was nothing but open plains until 1867, when Union Pacific laid its tracks there and the city sprang up in a matter of months. That story is told at the Cheyenne Depot Museum, housed in the original 1886 railroad station—a National Historic Landmark. The third floor holds a wood-carved Big Boy locomotive model and a full-scale model railroad display; labels cite their sources like footnotes, which is unusual and worth taking your time over. Allow 90 minutes if you read everything.

The Cheyenne Frontier Days Old West Museum holds one of the largest collections of horse-drawn carriages in the country and thousands of rodeo artifacts tracing the event to its first day: September 23, 1897, when Union Pacific agent Frederick W. Angier organized a one-day cowboy roundup that drew 4,000 people. By year two, 20,000 showed up. Today it draws 300,000 visitors over 10 days and pays out more than $1 million in prize money. Worth 60-90 minutes even outside rodeo season.

Thirty minutes north of downtown, the Quebec 01 Missile Alert Facility State Historic Site is the only publicly accessible Peacekeeper missile alert facility in the world. Above ground is a self-guided museum of Cold War daily life; underground guided tours take you into the actual launch control room—codes, safes, escape hatches designed to fill with sand after a nuclear blast. The 90th Missile Wing at F.E. Warren Air Force Base still operates Minuteman III missiles today. Free above ground; admission is charged for the underground tour.

The Wyoming Historic Governors' Mansion at 300 East 21st Street is a Colonial Revival building from 1904 that housed 19 Wyoming First Families - among them Nellie Tayloe Ross, the first female governor in United States history, elected in 1924. Docent-led tours move through rooms decorated to represent different eras of occupancy. Open Tuesday through Saturday; free admission.

The Nelson Museum of the West downtown holds one of the largest collections of saddles, wagons, and Old West memorabilia in the region—cowboys, lawmen, Native Americans, and soldiers throughout the frontier period. Free admission for most of the year. Allow 60 minutes and combine your visit with a walk through the nearby historic district.

activities.text: Scattered across downtown Cheyenne are dozens of 2.40-meter cowboy boots painted by local artists, each depicting a different slice of Wyoming history—the Big Boots art trail. Pick up a location map at the Depot Museum visitor kiosk, or call (307) 316-0067 for a cell phone audio tour where artists explain their own work. The main cluster near the historic district takes 45–60 minutes to cover, and you'll see more of the old town than any guided bus tour would show you.

Curt Gowdy State Park sits 38 kilometers west in the foothills of the Laramie Mountains—granite outcrops, rainbow trout in Granite Springs Reservoir, pronghorn grazing in sight of the trail, and over 56 kilometers of mountain biking trails. It's one of the few spots near Cheyenne where the city genuinely disappears. A day-use fee applies.

The Cheyenne Street Railway Trolley runs a narrated 90-minute loop through the historic district - the railroad district, Capitol Hill, historic homes and Fort D.A. Russell. The best way to get your bearings before deciding which buildings to revisit on foot. Operates year-round; admission charged; departs from Depot Plaza.

Finish the loop at Westby Edge Brewing downtown—local craft beer in the same city where the itinerary started nine days ago. Denver is 90 minutes south on I-25; factor that into your departure time and don't book a flight before noon.

places.name: Chicago, IL

visits.text: You enter Millennium Park from Michigan Avenue and Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate stops you in your tracks—110 tonnes of polished steel shaped like a giant bean, reflecting Chicago's skyline and passersby in its curved surfaces and turning every visitor into a participant in a permanent installation. The park opened in 2004 after a $325 million budget overrun, for a final cost of $475 million, and welcomes over 25 million visitors a year. Frank Gehry's Jay Pritzker Pavilion hosts free Grant Park Orchestra concerts every summer evening from June to August. Free admission.

You climb the steps guarded by two bronze lions dating from 1894 and enter the American art museum with the highest concentration of major works per square meter. Founded in 1879, the Art Institute holds the world's second-largest collection of Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist paintings after the Musée d'Orsay: Seurat's “A Sunday on La Grande Jatte,” Picasso's “The Old Guitarist,” Edward Hopper's “Nighthawks,” and Grant Wood's “American Gothic” are less than a 10-minute walk from one another. Renzo Piano designed the Modern Wing in 2009, adding 25,000 square meters of naturally lit galleries. Open daily, 11 a.m.–5 p.m., until 8 p.m. on Thursdays; admission: $35 per adult—book online, as weekend lines are long.

You descend the stairs from Wacker Drive to the Chicago River and find yourself in another city—a 2.5-kilometer promenade at the base of the Loop's skyscrapers, at water level. From this perspective, Willis Tower, the Gothic Tribune Tower of 1925, and Mies van der Rohe's steel-and-glass towers from the 1950s form a complete panorama of the history of modern architecture in a single glance. Orange water taxis cross your path, and transparent kayaks can be rented at the main dock to explore the river's branches. Come in the evening for the tower lights reflected in the water—the Riverwalk stays lively until 10 p.m. in summer.

You push open the door of what looks like a marble palace at the corner of Randolph and Michigan—and enter one of America's most beautiful civic buildings for free. Built in 1897 as Chicago's first public library, the building houses two halls with Tiffany stained-glass domes 13 meters in diameter—American Art Nouveau masterpieces in colored glass that diffuse changing light depending on the time of day. The floors and columns are made of Guatemalan green onyx and Carrara marble. Since its conversion to a cultural center in 1991, admission has been entirely free. The vast majority of tourists walk past without entering—don't make this mistake: it's one of Chicago's most beautiful interiors, open Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–7 p.m.

You cross Hyde Park to the neoclassical building housing the Western Hemisphere's largest science and technology museum, housed since 1933 in the Palace of Fine Arts from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Its treasure is the German submarine U-505, captured on the high seas in the Atlantic in June 1944 by the U.S. Navy—America's first capture of an enemy warship since the War of 1812. The 77-meter submarine has been displayed inside the museum since 1954 in a gallery built around it. Open daily, 9:30 a.m.–5:30 p.m.; admission: $21 per adult—book online to avoid weekend lines.

You get off the L train at Damen and walk on Milwaukee Avenue - lined with BYOB restaurants, alternative bookstores, art galleries, and vintage boutiques in Victorian houses built by Polish and Ukrainian immigrants in the late 19th century. The neighborhood was the center of Chicago's alternative rock scene in the 1990s - the Smashing Pumpkins played their first concerts here. The adjacent Ukrainian Village preserves several 1910s-1920s Ukrainian Orthodox churches with gilded domes, including Holy Trinity Cathedral designed by Louis Sullivan in 1903. Come on weekends for cafe terraces spilling onto sidewalks and farmers' markets in Wicker Park square.

activities.text: You board at the Michigan Avenue dock and the boat heads up the Chicago River, passing under drawbridges every two minutes. In 90 minutes, a Chicago Architecture Center guide describes 50 buildings spanning 130 years of modern architecture—from the world's first skyscraper (Home Insurance Building, 1885, demolished in 1931) to the 1964 Marina City tower, whose circular apartments are shaped like an ear of corn. Chicago invented vertical architecture because the city was devastated by a fire in 1871 and rebuilt in twenty years by architects who had no precedents to follow. Book 48 hours ahead in July–August—cruises often sell out on the morning of departure.

You push open a blues club door and the smell of warm beer and electric amps hits your nostrils—you're in the city that transformed acoustic Delta blues into urban electric blues in the 1940s. Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf settled in Chicago after the war, plugged their guitars into amps in South Side clubs, and created a sound that would influence the Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin. Kingston Mines, open since 1968, is Chicago's oldest blues club still in operation—bands alternate between two stages without a break until 4 a.m. Buddy Guy's Legends (700 S. Wabash) is the most reliable venue for consistently high-quality music.

You grab a Divvy e-bike at Millennium Park and set off along the 29-mile paved path running along Lake Michigan's shore, with the Loop's skyscrapers as a constant backdrop for the first five kilometers. The Lakefront Trail was honored as one of North America's best bike routes—flat, with a succession of public beaches for swimming in summer. On clear days from the north shore, you glimpse Indiana's dunes 50 kilometers to the southeast—visually bringing the entire road trip full circle. Avoid Saturdays between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m. in summer: the path gets so crowded it becomes dangerous for cyclists.

Allow for a round trip from Chicago to reach Gene & Jude's in River Grove. You begin at Gene & Jude's for a Chicago-style hot dog—a Vienna Beef sausage in a steamed bun, yellow mustard, bright green relish, raw onions, tomatoes, pickles and a sport pepper, but NEVER ketchup, an uncompromising rule since it opened in 1941. Then you head to Al's Beef (1079 W Taylor Street, open since 1938) for Italian beef: roasted beef rump sliced paper-thin, served in a roll dipped directly into the garlic-and-herb cooking juices, a dish born in the 1930s in the Italian neighborhoods of the West Side to feed construction workers cheaply. Order each dish in its classic form: a hot dog without ketchup, Italian beef “dipped and hot” with spicy giardiniera. These two dishes are the true hallmarks of Chicago's popular food culture—deep-dish is for tourists, these are for locals.

visits.text: Day 1 - optional: Hidden gem: the New York Chinese Scholar's Garden, on the Snug Harbor grounds on Staten Island. A scholar's garden assembled by artisans from Suzhou: rockeries, pavilions, bamboo, a carp pond. A modest admission fee, almost always deserted. Half an hour of classical China 40 minutes from Wall Street.

Day 1 - optional: Around the Chinese garden, Snug Harbor has repurposed a former 19th-century sailors' retirement home as a cultural campus: colonnaded façades lined up like Greek temples, botanical gardens, an urban farm. You can walk around the park for free; only certain gardens charge admission. You'll encounter more locals than tourists, and that's just fine.

activities.text: Picnic on the lawns facing the colonnaded façades, before taking the bus back to the ferry.
Return to Manhattan by free ferry, then subway: Day 2 starts in Chinatown, at the Mahayana temple. About 11.9 km; allow nearly an hour including the crossing.

places.name: Chinle, AZ

visits.text: South Rim Drive reveals a depth to Canyon de Chelly that the map cannot show. The overlooks reveal the walls, cultivated canyon floors, and, at the end of the route, the spire of Spider Rock. Notice the paths and plots of land as well: people still live in this landscape. Preferably set aside the afternoon for this rim, as the NPS recommends for photography, and keep children close near the cliffs.

If you want to compare the canyon's branches, continue exploring along North Rim Drive, starting from Chinle. The overlooks offer views of Canyon del Muerto and its archaeological sites, visible from a distance in the canyon walls. Binoculars are more useful than a phone's zoom alone for understanding what you are seeing. Stop only in designated areas, and do not look for a way down from the rim: access to the canyon floor is regulated.

activities.text: You will descend toward White House on the White House Trail, subject to confirmation at the Canyon de Chelly visitor center that it is open. The out-and-back hike drops into the canyon before returning to the same overlook; the uphill return is the main physical challenge. The NPS's recent visitor information page lists the trail as open, but conditions may change. Set out in the morning with water, allow extra time for the climb back, and respect the boundaries around the ruins.

The best complement to the overlooks is a guided tour of Canyon de Chelly from Chinle. An authorized Navajo guide takes you into permitted areas on the canyon floor, where the walls, ruins, and present-day uses take on a different scale. Choose a short tour to leave room for the morning hike. Ask which permits are included, confirm the local time, and clarify the cancellation policy if rain makes the terrain impassable.

places.name: Cincinnati, OH

visits.text: The road trip begins in Cincinnati, where Charlie and Raymond start their journey in Rain Man. Walk across the Roebling Suspension Bridge—it's the prototype for the Brooklyn Bridge and was built in 1866 by the same engineer. At 322 meters, it was the world's longest suspension bridge at the time. When cars drive over the metal grates, the bridge “sings”—a sound that locals love. The view of Cincinnati's skyline from the middle of the bridge is perfect in the morning.

At the foot of the bridge on the Ohio side, head to the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center. The museum tells the story of slavery and the clandestine network that helped enslaved people escape to the North. Cincinnati was a key stop—the Ohio River marked the border between slave states and free states. Allow 1 hour and 30 minutes.

Head up to Over-the-Rhine, the old German neighborhood. The 19th-century brick facades now house craft breweries, galleries, and cafés. Vine Street and Main Street are the liveliest. The neighborhood gets its name from German immigrants who, when crossing the Miami and Erie Canal to work, said they were "crossing the Rhine."
Stop at Fountain Square, the heart of downtown. The Tyler Davidson Fountain (1871) is the city's symbol. This is where the opening scenes of Rain Man establish Cincinnati's atmosphere.

activities.text: Swing by Findlay Market, Ohio's oldest covered market (1852). Try Cincinnati chili—a chili served over spaghetti, topped with shredded cheese and onions. Locals call it a "three-way." It's strange and delicious.

days_plan.itin_title: The Rain Man Route: A Road Trip Across the United States

map_keywords: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center Cincinnati

visits.text: You turn off Route 66 at Foyil and drive four miles east to find a 90-foot concrete totem pole rising from the back of a sandstone turtle - built entirely by one retired woodworking teacher, Nathan Edward Galloway, who moved to this farm in 1937 and spent eleven years on the project from 1937 to 1948. He collected most of the materials himself from a nearby stream: 28 tons of cement, 6 tons of steel, and 100 tons of sand and rock. The 200 bas-relief images spiraling up the pole include four 9-foot Native American figures near the top and tropical reptiles near the base, drawn from old National Geographic photographs. The adjacent Fiddle House holds hundreds of handmade fiddles - none playable - that Galloway carved at night after long days on the totem. Free admission, open daily.

You pull up to an 80-foot grinning blue whale beached beside a pond - and the story behind it is stranger than the object itself. Zoologist Hugh Davis spent two years welding steel rod and applying hand-mixed cement, one five-gallon bucket at a time, to build this as a surprise 34th-anniversary gift for his wife Zelta, revealed to her on September 7, 1972. Zelta collected whale figurines and had never seen a live one. What started as a family swimming hole became one of Route 66's most photographed landmarks. The City of Catoosa purchased the property in 2021 and a new visitor center opened in early 2026, ahead of Route 66's centennial. Entry is free; the interior of the whale is open for exploration.

You stand on the 20-acre hillside Will Rogers bought in 1911 with plans to retire here. He never made it - he died in an Alaska plane crash alongside aviator Wiley Post on August 15, 1935. His widow Betty donated the land and his papers to Oklahoma, and the memorial opened November 4, 1938, his 59th birthday, built from locally quarried limestone. Route 66 was officially renamed the Will Rogers Highway the same year he died. Inside: 12 galleries of ropes, saddles, radio transcripts, and a theater showing his films. Outside, his tomb reads: “I never met a man I didn't like.” Twelve galleries take about 90 minutes.

activities.text: You leave Tulsa on the original Route 66 alignment - not the interstate - passing through Catoosa and the string of small towns that kept the Mother Road alive after the bypass. Oklahoma holds more miles of original drivable Route 66 alignment than any other state on the route. Between Tulsa and Claremore you watch for vintage neon signs, original narrow-lane concrete sections, and the turnoff to Catoosa where the Blue Whale waits. Pull over whenever something catches your eye - that's how this road has always worked.

You wind down the day on Claremore's compact Main Street, within walking distance of the Will Rogers Memorial. Hammett House Restaurant has been a Claremore institution since 1969 - classic American fare and homemade pies in a room that hasn't tried too hard to reinvent itself. It's the kind of place where regulars know their server's name and the menu hasn't needed a major overhaul in decades. Book a table if you're arriving on a weekend evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Oklahoma Route 66 & Native Heritage: Tulsa to OKC

visits.text: Three oversized electric guitars rise from a concrete island at the corner of North State Street and DeSoto Avenue - the old intersection of Highways 61 and 49. The sign reads 'The Crossroads.' Whether Robert Johnson really met the Devil here around 1930 is unprovable, but what's documented is the transformation: Son House heard Johnson play in 1930 and described him as near-unlistenable; two years later Johnson returned with a technique that left House speechless. His fewer than 30 recordings became foundational to the blues and influenced everyone from Eric Clapton to the Rolling Stones. Worth a stop, a photo, and a minute of silence.

Inside a 1918 freight depot built for the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley Railroad, the Delta Blues Museum has been running since 1979 - Mississippi's oldest music museum. Its collection centers on the culture that produced the music: the sharecropper cabin where Muddy Waters lived on Stovall Farms sits in the main gallery. Exhibits trace the migration of bluesmen north along Highway 61 to Memphis, St. Louis, and Chicago. Don't miss the listening stations and the artifacts annotated in Son House's own hand. The museum is at 1 Blues Alley Lane. Allow 90 minutes; pick up the printed Clarksdale walking map at the desk.

Ground Zero Blues Club opened in May 2001 in a former cotton-grading warehouse, deliberately unrefurbished. Mismatched chairs, Christmas lights, graffiti walls: it looks like it's never been cleaned up, which is exactly the point. Academy Award-winning actor Morgan Freeman co-founded it with then-Clarksdale mayor Bill Luckett and Howard Stovall to give local musicians a regular venue. Live music runs Wednesday through Saturday, usually from around 9 p.m.; cover is typically $10. Freeman still shows up occasionally. Come for dinner too - the Southern food is genuine.

activities.text: Ten minutes south of downtown, Hopson Plantation is where the first successful mechanical cotton picker was field-tested - the machine that made hundreds of thousands of Delta sharecroppers redundant and set off the Great Migration north. One of the original pickers stands on the property. The old commissary is now a bar; the Shack Up Inn next door rents genuine sharecropper shacks as accommodation. An hour here gives the blues its economic and social backstory more concisely than any museum exhibit.

Red's Lounge on Sunflower Avenue is the real thing: a cinderblock juke joint with a wood-burning stove and no stage, musicians set up in the corner. Smaller, rawer, and more local than Ground Zero, it's where Delta residents actually go on Friday and Saturday nights. Red Paden has been running it for decades. No cover most nights, no cocktail menu - cold beer and loud music in a room the size of a living room.

days_plan.itin_title: Mississippi Delta Blues Trail: Memphis to Jackson

visits.text: Clearwater Beach - Sugar Sand and Turquoise Water: Consistently rated among America's best beaches, this Gulf Coast gem offers powdery white sand and the calm, crystal-clear water the region is famous for.

Clearwater Marine Aquarium - The Center Made Famous by Winter the Dolphin: Made famous by the 'Dolphin Tale' films, this rescue center rehabilitates marine animals while educating visitors about ocean conservation.
Pier 60 - Sunset Celebration Capital of Florida: This famous pier extends into the Gulf of Mexico, hosting nightly sunset celebrations with street performers, artisans, and spectacular views.

Caladesi Island State Park - Florida's Most Pristine Beach: Accessible only by boat, this Gulf island remains one of the last undeveloped barrier islands in Florida, offering unspoiled beaches and nature trails.

activities.text: Sunset at Pier 60 - A Nightly Festival: Join locals and visitors for the daily celebration of Florida's legendary Gulf Coast sunsets, complete with entertainment and crafts.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

visits.text: Experience Clemson's charming college-town atmosphere, where the walkable downtown centers on College Avenue with its shops, cafes, and historic character. Outside major university events, the area maintains a relaxed pace perfect for leisurely exploration. The Clemson Area African American Museum presents important regional history through thoughtful exhibits.

Visit Clemson University's beautiful campus, where historic buildings blend with modern facilities amid landscaped grounds. Memorial Stadium and other landmarks reflect the university's prominent role in South Carolina culture. The campus provides pleasant walking paths and architectural interest for visitors exploring the Upstate.

activities.text: Browse local boutiques and galleries reflecting the creative energy of this academic community. The downtown district offers an authentic college-town experience with regional character. Clemson's position near both mountain wilderness and larger cities makes it an excellent base for exploring the Upstate region.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Road Trip: From Lowcountry Beaches to the Blue Ridge Mountains

places.name: Cleveland, OH

visits.text: You enter the building designed by architect I.M. Pei—a 46-meter-high glass and steel pyramid perched on the Lake Erie shore, opened on September 1, 1995, in the presence of Yoko Ono and Little Richard. Cleveland beat New York, Memphis, and Chicago to host this museum in 1986, notably because this is where disc jockey Alan Freed popularized the term “rock and roll” in the 1950s on radio station WJW. The 14,000 square meters of exhibition space house thousands of artifacts—John Lennon's handwritten lyrics, Michael Jackson's stage costumes, Janis Joplin's Porsche—as well as The Garage, an interactive space where you can play drums, guitar, or keyboards on real stages. Book your time slot online to avoid waiting; allow at least 2.5 hours.

You enter one of the oldest and most vibrant public markets in the United States. The yellow brick building with its 42-meter clock tower was inaugurated in 1912, designed by Hubbell & Benes at a cost of $680,000, but the market's history dates back to 1840 when two Ohio City mayors gave this land to the municipality with the obligation to keep it as a public market forever. Today, 70 merchant families - of Irish, German, Slovenian, Italian, Hungarian, Greek, and Middle Eastern origin - sell meats, cheeses, breads, fish, and flowers in its 100 indoor stalls and 82 outdoor arcade stands. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973, it's open Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday from 8am.

The Cleveland Museum of Art, founded in 1913 and expanded several times, possesses a collection of 61,000 artworks spanning 5,000 years of human history—and admission to the permanent collection is free. Its white marble Beaux-Arts building on the edge of Wade Lagoon in University Circle is flanked by a contemporary glass wing designed by Rafael Viñoly in 2012. The museum's strength lies in its medieval armor, East Asian art, and a beautiful Impressionist section. Gallery One, at the entrance, is an interactive space where you can create your own compositions from works in the collection.

activities.text: The Ohio City neighborhood, just west of downtown Cleveland, is one of the best examples of urban rehabilitation in the American Rust Belt. Around the West Side Market, a concentration of craft breweries, restaurants, and cafes has moved into Victorian houses and converted warehouses. Great Lakes Brewing Company, founded in 1988, is one of Ohio's first craft breweries and its beers - notably the seasonal Christmas Ale - are a local institution. Continuing north along Detroit Avenue, you reach the Detroit Shoreway neighborhood and its independent art galleries.

Cleveland's North Coast Harbor stretches along Lake Erie's southern shore—the fourth largest of the Great Lakes by surface area but the smallest by volume and the shallowest, which also makes it the most susceptible to storms. The promenade takes you between the Rock Hall, the Great Lakes Science Center, and Voinovich Bicentennial Park, with views of the harbor and the Erie Islands in the distance. In summer, sailboats and kayaks crisscross the bay; in winter, the lake can freeze along its shores and the view is spectacular.

places.name: Cocoa Beach, FL

visits.text: Kennedy Space Center remains one of the sites from which American crewed rockets lift off. All the Apollo flights (1968-1972) left from here, the Space Shuttle launched here 135 times between 1981 and 2011, and SpaceX launches its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy here today. The visit is huge: the bus tour passes the foot of the Vehicle Assembly Building (160 meters, one of the most voluminous buildings in the world), and the Apollo/Saturn V Center displays an intact 110-meter Saturn V rocket suspended above your head. Allow 4-5 hours minimum, more like 6 if you are an enthusiast. $75.

If a launch is scheduled during your visit, it's a singular experience - SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets lift off on average twice a month. The best free viewing points are Jetty Park (Cape Canaveral), Playalinda Beach, and the toll bridge at Bennett Causeway. The rumble passes through your chest for 30 seconds, the plume remains visible in the sky for 10 minutes. Real-time calendar at spaceflightnow.com.

Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge surrounds the space center - 56,000 hectares of preserved marshland precisely because NASA made it their security zone. Alligators, manatees, dolphins, over 350 bird species including ospreys. Black Point Wildlife Drive, an 11-kilometer driving loop, is the most accessible observation route. Entrance $10.

activities.text: Cocoa Beach Pier extends 250 meters into the Atlantic, standing since 1962. Bars, restaurants, surfboard rentals - the Cocoa coast is nicknamed "Space Coast Surf Capital." Kelly Slater, 11-time world surfing champion, was born in Cocoa Beach in 1972. Ron Jon Surf Shop, 800 meters away, is the world's largest surf shop - 4,600 square meters, open 24/7, free to visit as a tourist.

Beginner surf lesson at Cocoa Beach Surf School ($75 for a 2-hour session, board provided) - perfect school waves, rarely rough seas. For a casual dinner, Coconuts on the Beach serves fresh fish and burgers on a terrace with your feet in the sand.

Washington to Miami in 16 Days Along the American East Coast

places.name: Cody, WY

visits.text: Five museums share one roof at the Buffalo Bill Center of the West, 720 Sheridan Avenue - a Smithsonian Affiliate since 2008 and the oldest museum complex dedicated to the American West, founded in 1917. The five: Buffalo Bill Museum (Wild West show artifacts and personal effects), Cody Firearms Museum (7,000 individual firearms, the most comprehensive collection in the US), Whitney Western Art Museum (Remington, Russell), Draper Natural History Museum (Yellowstone geology and wildlife), and Plains Indian Museum (Arapaho, Lakota, Crow and Cheyenne objects; first curator was George Horse Capture of the A'aninin tribe). Your ticket is valid for two consecutive days.

Old Trail Town on the western edge of Cody brings together 26 historic frontier buildings gathered from original sites across Wyoming by archaeologist Bob Edgar, starting in 1967. The collection includes a trappers' cabin from 1883, a dance hall, a saloon, and the grave of mountain man John “Liver-Eating” Johnston. One of the few places in the West where the structures are original, not reconstructed. Admission is charged; open May through September.

The Irma Hotel on Sheridan Avenue opened in November 1902 - Buffalo Bill Cody's personal hotel, built for $80,000 and named after his youngest daughter. At the center of the dining room stands a cherrywood bar said to have been a gift from Queen Victoria in recognition of a performance of the Wild West show commissioned at her court; the hotel's current owner acknowledges that there is no documentary evidence, but the bar has been here since opening day. Stop in for a drink or meal without a reservation; the Cody Gunfighters stage a free shootout on the sidewalk outside the hotel at 6 p.m. in summer.

activities.text: Attend the Cody Nite Rodeo at Stampede Park—every night from June 1 through August 31 since 1938, making Cody the only town in the United States with a nightly rodeo. Former Wild West show performer Carly Downing founded it, originally calling it the “Pup Rodeo”. The 6,000-seat arena sits on a terrace above the Shoshone River west of downtown; gates open at 7:00 p.m., the rodeo starts at 8:00 p.m. A bus departs from most hotels for about $7 round-trip. Admission is charged; book ahead in peak summer season.

West of Cody, US-14/16/20 follows the North Fork of the Shoshone River through 84 kilometers of Shoshone National Forest that Theodore Roosevelt called “the most scenic 80 kilometers in the United States”. Dramatic volcanic formations line both sides. No Yellowstone entrance fee applies if you turn around at the East Gate—back in Cody in 2–3 hours.

places.name: Colorado Springs, CO

visits.text: Park at the Garden of the Gods Visitor Center and set out on foot—the park has been free since 1909, when Charles Perkins bequeathed it to Colorado Springs with one condition: "free forever." Its 300-million-year-old red sandstone formations were tilted vertical by the same tectonic uplift that pushed up Pikes Peak. Cathedral Spires, Kissing Camels, Balanced Rock—everything is within a 10-minute walk.

Drive up Pikes Peak via the Pikes Peak Highway - 31 km of paved road from Cascade to 4,302 m. The song America the Beautiful was composed after an ascent to the summit in 1893. At the summit, the cafeteria serves doughnuts fried at an altitude of 4,302 m. Toll $15/person; allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the round trip. Plan the drive from Colorado Springs to Cascade, followed by the ascent on the Pikes Peak Highway.

activities.text: Before heading back to Denver (1 hour 15 minutes on I-25) or Colorado Springs airport, take one last bike ride through Garden of the Gods. The park offers marked bike trails among the red formations—Pikes Peak as a backdrop, free entry, and 6 million visitors a year who'll confirm that you have every reason to return.

places.name: Columbia, SC

visits.text: Congaree National Park is 30 km southeast of Columbia. Don't be fooled: it's not a swamp, it's a floodplain. Floods from the Congaree River cover about 80% of the park ten times a year and that's precisely what feeds these giant trees - the park harbors champion specimens of 15 species, including a Loblolly pine over 51 meters tall. It's the largest old-growth bottomland forest in the United States, designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Start at the Harry Hampton Visitor Center to check boardwalk conditions.

Take the Boardwalk Loop (3.9 km, accessible): the elevated walkway first crosses a mixed forest of pines and hardwoods, then descends into the low section where bald cypresses and their conical knees emerge from the flooded ground. Weston Lake, a former river meander at least 6 meters deep, is accessible from the boardwalk - watch the banks: alligators have been spotted. Bring mosquito repellent: not optional.

If you have the energy, the Weston Lake Loop (7.4 km) pushes deeper into the forest and follows oxbow lakes where vegetation is especially dense. This is where wildlife photographers wait for herons, kingfishers, and woodpeckers - eight different woodpecker species live in the park.

At the corner of Main and Gervais Streets, the South Carolina State House bears visible scars: look for the bronze stars on the exterior façade. They mark the exact spots where artillery shells from General Sherman's troops struck the building during the burning of Columbia in February 1865. The African American Monument in the grounds traces the history of Black South Carolinians from the arrival of the first enslaved people.

The South Carolina State Museum occupies a former cotton mill from 1893, listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Four floors cover natural history, state history, science, and art. A digital planetarium, observatory, and 4D theater are integrated into the building. Allow 2 hours to tour it properly.

The Hampton-Preston Mansion (Historic Columbia) is one of Columbia's oldest surviving houses. The guided tour doesn't just recount the planter family - it also explores the lives of the enslaved people who ran the property. It's one of the most honest approaches to Southern history in the city.

activities.text: The Cedar Creek Canoe Trail (32 marked km) is one of the best ways to enter Congaree: you paddle under a canopy of cypresses and tupelos, in black water colored by tannins. Kayaks and canoes rent in Columbia for around $50 per day. Allow 3 to 4 hours for a round trip on the main section. Check water levels before you go.

Evening in Columbia, the Vista District is the liveliest neighborhood for dinner. The local barbecue sauce is mustard-based - very different from Louisville's bourbon barbecue. Try Doc's BBQ for the classic version.

Riverbanks Zoo & Garden is regularly ranked among the ten best zoos in the United States: nearly 2,000 animals on a site crossed by the Saluda River, with a suspension bridge over the rapids. The giraffe feeding station and the Kangaroo Walkabout are the most popular. Allow at least 3 hours, more with children.

If you're here on a Saturday, the Soda City Market on Main Street closes the road from 9am to 1pm. Up to 5,000 people gather: arepas, Korean bulgogi, bratwursts, Caribbean jerk chicken - Columbia counts residents from over 200 countries. It's the best quick introduction to South Carolina's capital city diversity.

places.name: Columbus, GA

visits.text: The CSS Jackson is a 68-meter ironclad hull in a museum at 1002 Victory Drive - the world's largest surviving Confederate warship, recovered from the mud of the Chattahoochee River in the 1960s. It was built at the Confederate Naval Shipyard less than a kilometer and a half from here and was nearly complete when General Wilson's cavalry captured Columbus in April 1865 and burned it. The National Civil War Naval Museum opened around it in 2001. Admission is charged.

Francis Joseph Springer, an immigrant from Alsace, opened his opera house at 103 10th Street on February 21, 1871. It was immediately the finest theater between New York and New Orleans. Edwin Booth played Hamlet here in 1876. Oscar Wilde lectured. Tom Thumb performed. Ma Rainey sang. Buffalo Bill came through. By 1959 the building was a movie house and nearly demolished five years later before a preservation campaign saved it. President Carter made it Georgia's State Theater in 1971, its centennial year. One of seven theaters in America with National Historic Landmark status. Tours Monday and Wednesday at 3:30 p.m., $5 per person.

Forty-eight kilometers north on US-27, Callaway Gardens covers 1,000 hectares of the Pine Mountain foothills—opened May 21, 1952, by Cason J. Callaway on exhausted former cotton land. The Cecil B. Day Butterfly Center opened within the gardens on September 25, 1988: a 680-square-meter glass dome, North America's largest tropical butterfly conservatory, maintained at 27°C year-round with over 1,000 butterflies of more than 50 species in free flight. Named for the founder of Days Inn, funded by his wife Deen Day Sanders. Blue morpho butterflies arrive in spectacular numbers every September. Paid entry.

activities.text: The Columbus Riverwalk connects the Naval Museum, the Columbus Iron Works Convention Center - second-largest iron producer in the Confederacy, completed in 1853 - and the 26-block National Register Historic District. On Broadway, a marker stands at the former pharmacy of Dr. John S. Pemberton, a Confederate Army captain who invented Coca-Cola in 1886. Cobblestone streets, old brick mill buildings, the Chattahoochee rolling past: this stretch of Columbus does more work than most history museums.

Plan on a same-day round trip from Columbus for this walk at Callaway Gardens. The Callaway Brothers Azalea Bowl and Chapel Trail is a 2.4-kilometer loop passing the Ida Cason Callaway Memorial Chapel from 1962—fieldstone walls, wooden beams, and 16th-century Gothic lines—and descending toward Mountain Creek Lake. A pioneer log cabin from the 1830s, moved here from Troup County in 1959, stands on the trail. For a longer route, the paved 16-kilometer Discovery Bike Trail connects all the major attractions. The one-and-a-half-kilometer white sand beach at Robin Lake is open in summer.

places.name: Columbus, OH

visits.text: You stroll beneath the 17 illuminated arches of High Street, the visual signature of the Short North - a district that didn't exist before 1980. In the 1970s, this stretch of High Street north of downtown was nothing but a succession of abandoned buildings with boarded-up windows. It was local police who gave the neighborhood its name: 'Short North', because it lay north of downtown and short of the Ohio State University campus. The renaissance began with a 'cooperative opening' of galleries in 1984, now known as the Gallery Hop and held every first Saturday of the month. Today, over 300 businesses animate this mile of High Street, most of them independent. Come on the first Saturday of the month for the Gallery Hop, or midweek to avoid the weekend crowds.

You enter the largest privately funded historic residential district in the United States to be entirely listed on the National Register of Historic Places: 233 acres of red brick houses built between 1840 and 1880 by German immigrants who then constituted 30% of Columbus's population. World War II marked the beginning of decline - having a German name became a source of shame - and demolitions began in the 1950s. In 1960, a group of residents founded the German Village Society, paid out of pocket for restoration, and secured historic protection in 1963. The result is remarkable: original paved streets, walled back gardens, and the Book Loft, a bookstore housed in a labyrinth of 32 rooms in connected houses. Arrive early to wander before the patio crowds arrive.

Founded in 1876 and housed since 1995 in a former red brick warehouse, the North Market is Columbus's oldest continuously operating public market. About 35 permanent merchants sell Ohio-local products: artisan cheeses, grass-fed sausages, honey from urban apiaries, vegetables from Franklin County farms and Ohio's Appalachian region. On Saturday mornings, the outdoor market brings together over 60 seasonal producers. It's the best time to buy provisions for the road - grab some local cheeses and sausages for upcoming picnics in Hocking Hills.

You push open the doors of the Columbus Museum of Art - founded in 1878, one of the oldest museums in the United States still operating in its original city - and immediately encounter the Wonder gallery, inaugurated in 2016: 700 square meters dedicated to creativity and imagination, the first permanent space of its kind in the world in a museum. The permanent collections gather 11,000 works including Picasso, Hopper, and Matisse, as well as paintings by George Bellows - a Columbus native, major figure of the Ashcan School. Admission is free on Sunday: if you can time your visit to this slot, it's the best time to go without spending the usual $18.

You enter beneath the glass canopies of the Franklin Park Conservatory - a grand greenhouse built in 1895 in the Crystal Palace style of the 1893 Chicago World's Fair - and find yourself wandering among seven different biomes under 13 acres of glass. Then you look up at the chandelier dominating the main hall: 1,400 pieces of glass blown by Dale Chihuly, the colors changing with daylight. Chihuly installed a permanent collection of his sculptures here, from orange glass trumpets emerging from water basins to cobalt blue glass towers lining the walkways. In the outdoor Japanese garden - 1.2 hectares created for Columbus's bicentennial in 1812 - allow at least thirty additional minutes.

You walk down to the Scioto River in central Columbus and discover the Scioto Mile, a 3.2-kilometer linear park opened in 2011 following a $38 million investment. From the Broad Street bridge, the city presents itself as a postcard: the Statehouse and its stone drum in the background, the Scioto reflecting the evening lights, and pedestrian bridges connecting the two banks. In summer, cafés and food trucks set up by the river, and free concerts take place on weekends.

You walk on The Oval - Ohio State University's central esplanade - surrounded by red sandstone collegiate Gothic buildings, and realize you're on the largest university campus in the United States by student enrollment: 61,000 enrolled in 2023. The Thompson Library, completed in 1913 and restored in 2009, raises its neo-Romanesque facade at the north corner of the Oval - enter to see the 12-meter-high atrium lined with marble. The university was founded in 1870 on land donated by William Neil, whose farm covered the entire area of what is today Victorian Village and the campus. If contemporary architecture interests you, don't miss the Wexner Center for the Arts designed by Peter Eisenman in 1989 - one of the first American deconstructivist buildings, all grids and colliding forms.

You travel north from Columbus to Highbanks Metro Park to see the earth mounds attributed to the Adena culture. The Coyote Run Trail crosses meadows and passes near one burial mound, while the Overlook Trail area offers a view of another. Stay on the marked trails: these remains are outdoors, with no burial chamber open to visitors or adjacent museum. At the park visitor center, displays about Highbanks' cultural history provide context before your walk. Continue to the Olentangy River overlook to see the mounds in their landscape of wooded ravines.

You park your car in a quiet residential neighborhood in northwest Columbus, descend a 1.5 km trail through a wooded ravine - and suddenly you hear the water before you see it. Hayden Falls plunges 12 meters over a sandstone escarpment surrounded by a forest of beeches and tulip trees that the suburban zone hasn't managed to swallow. It's one of the last preserved riparian forests in Franklin County, ten minutes from downtown Columbus, and almost no outside traveler knows it. Neighborhood residents jealously guard the secret - you'll understand why as soon as you're there. On weekdays, you have a good chance of being there alone.

activities.text: You enter one of the rare American capitols without a dome - Columbus's Greek Revival building, whose construction lasted twenty-two years (1839-1861), is topped with a stone drum pierced with windows instead of the usual dome. The central rotunda features a stained glass ceiling and a mosaic of Ohio's Great Seal. The Senate chamber and House chamber retain their original 19th-century furnishings. The Statehouse has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1972. Self-guided tours allow free access to all public rooms.

You push open the doors of COSI - Center of Science and Industry - a 320,000-square-foot glass building perched on the edge of the Scioto River, ranked among the ten best science museums in the United States. You move from one gallery to another: space, energy, health, Ohio's natural history, with dozens of hands-on experiments to manipulate rather than observe. The 300-seat digital planetarium projects shows every hour - book upon entry or you'll miss your time slot. The glass walkways overlooking the Scioto from the second floor offer the best free view of Columbus.

You enter the Brewery District via Sycamore Street and find yourself in a former neighborhood of ice warehouses and 19th-century industrial breweries, converted into a row of red-brick taprooms. Push open the door of Elevator Brewery & Draught Haus: you're in an 1897 building with cast-iron columns that was successively a brewery, a warehouse, and an elevator factory - the original pulleys and rails are still on the ceiling. Barley's Brewing Company, opened in 1992, was Columbus's first microbrewery; their rack of wooden casks behind the bar has a saloon vibe that fits the neighborhood perfectly. Over a dozen tasting venues within a 500-meter radius - take your time.

You stroll along the mile of High Street on the first Saturday of the month starting at 6pm and understand why the Short North Gallery Hop has become one of the most attended cultural events in the United States. In 1984, a few visionary gallerists organized a first 'cooperative opening' in half-empty premises - the neighborhood was then blighted. Forty years later, over 300 establishments simultaneously open their doors: openings with artists present, musical entertainment on sidewalks, cocktails in shops. Even if you're not there on a first Saturday, the Short North's permanent galleries remain open during the week - check their individual hours on the Short North Alliance website.

You pass through the entrance of Columbus Zoo to find 220 acres spread before you, divided into seven geographic regions - Africa, Asia, Americas, Australasia - with 9,000 animals and a freshwater aquarium inaugurated in 1999 among the largest in the Midwest. This zoo, founded in 1927, was the first in the world to breed gorillas in captivity: the gorilla Colo was born there in 1956, a world event at the time. Jack Hanna, director from 1978 to 1992, transformed the establishment from a decrepit zoo into a world reference institution for species preservation. Plan a full day: lines lengthen from mid-morning on summer weekends. Buy your ticket online to skip the ticket office.

You grab a bike from CoGo Bike Share - over 50 stations in Columbus, a few dollars for a half-day - and head north on the Scioto Greenways, a network of over 100 miles of trails entirely separated from traffic. The section along the Scioto from downtown to Griggs Dam, 16 km north, is the most spectacular: you follow the river between natural prairies, riparian forests where herons fish at low tide, and parks whose lawns descend to the water. Griggs Dam, built in 1906, forms an artificial lake of 8 km surrounded by wooded cliffs - total serenity less than 30 minutes from downtown Columbus. It's the best way to end this Ohio loop.

visits.text: If you are passing through on a weekday, continue to the New Hampshire State House visitor center in Concord. The building houses the state legislature and offers opportunities to tour it. The visitor center lists its hours as Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; check the arrangements before counting on an indoor visit.

A Concord stagecoach and paintings of the White Mountains come together at the New Hampshire Historical Society. These collections connect the landscapes you have traveled through with the history of their residents and transportation. Check opening hours before this final stop; if they do not fit your schedule, allow more time to reach Boston.

visits.text: Cement gave Concrete its name, and Silo Park preserves evidence that is hard to miss. The silos belonged to the former cement plant, several remnants of which survive around the park. View them from permitted areas: the appeal of this stop lies in the industrial landscape, rather than in exploring the buildings.

Henry Thompson Bridge deserves a short stop for its arch as well as the Baker River. This concrete bridge is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and continues the industrial history told by the silos. Use a nearby legal parking space, then view the structure without stopping in the middle of the roadway.

activities.text: You’ll follow the historic walking tour through downtown Concrete, connecting traces of the cement plant with the small downtown area. Building plaques and the historic route tell the story of the early settlements that formed Concrete. Pick up the local map before your walk; this stop also sets you up for the next day’s excursion to Diablo Lake, returning to the same base.

places.name: Coney Island Luna Park, NY

visits.text: Day 5 - Day 5 ends with your feet in the sand: Coney Island, its 1923 wooden boardwalk, Nathan's hot dogs served since 1916, and Luna Park rides. The beach and boardwalk are free; pay for attractions individually or with a pass. In the offseason, half of them close, but the faded atmosphere has its charm.

Day 5 - Two designated landmarks dominate Coney Island: the Cyclone, a wooden roller coaster from 1927 that really shakes you up, and the Wonder Wheel from 1920, with cars that slide along rails. Sunset from the pier, then a return trip on the elevated subway: the line offers a long tracking shot over Brooklyn's rooftops.

activities.text: A hot dog at Nathan's original Surf Avenue location, the venue for the world hot dog eating championship every July 4.
End of 5 days. Return to Manhattan by subway from Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue station, terminus of D, F, N and Q lines.

visits.text: Living through winter has shaped Cooke City as much as searching for ore: the Cooke City Montana Museum tells the story of both aspects of the region. Its collections also trace local schools, tourism, and the construction of the Beartooth Highway. Check seasonal hours before arriving; this short stop deserves more planning than simply fitting it in between fuel stops.

activities.text: You will take a short walk in Silver Gate before reaching Cooke City, after leaving Yellowstone. This village developed around tourism, unlike its neighbor, which was shaped by mining. Fit this short stroll into your arrival route from Lamar Valley, then continue to your evening stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Yellowstone and Grand Teton: 12 Days Among Lakes and Mountain Passes

visits.text: Day 1: Kenai River Corridor - The world-famous Kenai River flows from Kenai Lake through Cooper Landing and on to Cook Inlet, supporting legendary salmon runs that attract anglers from around the globe. The river's turquoise waters, colored by glacial flour, wind through a forested valley with mountain views.
Day 1: Kenai Lake - This 24-mile-long glacial lake fills a stunning mountain basin, offering scenic beauty and recreational opportunities including boating, paddling, and shoreline hiking.

Day 2: Kenai Peninsula Fisheries - The rivers and lakes of this region support some of the world's most productive salmon fisheries, with five Pacific salmon species returning in runs that can number in the millions. The Kenai River holds the world record for king salmon at 97 pounds, drawing anglers seeking trophy catches.

Day 2: Russian River Confluence - The junction of the Russian and Kenai rivers creates one of Alaska's most popular fishing destinations, with sockeye salmon runs so abundant that combat fishing, with anglers standing shoulder to shoulder, has become a cultural phenomenon.

activities.text: Day 1: Scenic Kenai River Float - Gentle rafting trips drift through the upper Kenai River canyon between Kenai Lake and Skilak Lake, passing through pristine wilderness with opportunities to observe eagles, moose, bears, and spawning salmon depending on the season. Guides share information about the region's natural and human history.

Day 2: Guided Salmon Fishing - Professional guides provide boats, equipment, and expertise for pursuing king salmon (May–July), sockeye salmon (June–August), and silver salmon (August–September) on the Kenai River and its tributaries.
Day 2: Trout and Char Fishing - Beyond the famous salmon runs, the region supports excellent populations of rainbow trout and Dolly Varden char, with fishing opportunities throughout the season.

places.name: Cooperstown, NY

visits.text: Even without knowing anything about baseball, you can spend two to three hours here without getting bored. The National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum opened June 12, 1939, based on a myth (Abner Doubleday supposedly invented the sport here in 1839—since debunked), and has since accumulated 40,000 artifacts, 3 million documents, and 140,000 cards. Across three floors, you work through the chronology: Babe Ruth's jersey, Joe DiMaggio's glove, balls from historic games. The Plaque Gallery, a bronze pantheon of inductees, functions as a very American secular memorial.

The Fenimore Art Museum, on the west shore of Otsego Lake, occupies the former 150-acre estate of James Fenimore Cooper. Inside, the Thaw Collection assembles over 850 objects of Native American art—Yup'ik masks from Alaska, Iroquois beadwork, Plains moccasins. The lawn behind the building slopes down to the lake, perfect for picnicking. Count on 1.5 hours if you want to really see it; closed January through March.

The Farmers' Museum, directly across from the Fenimore, recreates a New York State village circa 1845: working forge, print shop, pharmacy, one-room schoolhouse, tavern. The costumed artisans know their craft and aren't reciting scripts. Touristy, but well done. Great with kids, but adults happily linger for two hours.

activities.text: A one-hour cruise on Otsego Lake with Glimmerglass Queen. The lake, nicknamed Glimmerglass by James Fenimore Cooper in his novel The Deerslayer (1841), is 9 miles long and is the source of the Susquehanna River. From the water you can spot Kingfisher Tower, an 18-meter mock ruin in a neo-medieval style built in 1876 by Edward Clark to give the locals work during an economic crisis—a typical Cooperstown anecdote.

In the 19th century, the Cooperstown region produced 80% of America's hops and was called Hop City. A blight devastated everything starting in the 1920s, and the last commercial harvest was in 1942. On a former 136-acre hop farm south of the village, Brewery Ommegang was founded in 1997 by importers Don Feinberg and Wendy Littlefield with support from Belgian brewer Duvel Moortgat. Trappist style, bottle-conditioned. Three Philosophers, their classic, is a 9.7% quadrupel blended with Belgian kriek—to be savored slowly. Tour plus tasting $15.

places.name: Copper, AK

visits.text: Day 1: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park Visitor Center - The primary information facility for America's largest national park, this complex introduces the 13.2-million-acre wilderness through exhibits on the region's volcanic geology, massive glaciers, and historic copper mining heritage. The center serves as the gateway to understanding this UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Day 1: Ahtna Cultural Center - Adjacent to the visitor center, this museum preserves and shares the heritage of the Ahtna Athabascan people who have inhabited the Copper River basin for thousands of years. Exhibits include a traditional fish wheel demonstrating the ingenious technology used to harvest salmon runs.

Day 2: Copper River Basin Wilderness - This remote region offers access to some of Alaska's most pristine river systems, flowing through valleys flanked by glaciated peaks exceeding 16,000 feet. The watershed supports all five species of Pacific salmon, making it world-renowned among fisheries biologists and anglers.

activities.text: Day 1: Copper River Valley Orientation - The small community of Copper Center sits at the confluence of the Copper and Klutina rivers, surrounded by the Wrangell, Chugach, and Alaska mountain ranges. This strategic location has made it a crossroads for indigenous traders, gold seekers, and modern travelers.

Day 2: Copper River Rafting - Float trips through this wilderness basin range from calm scenic journeys suitable for families to challenging whitewater adventures. The glacier-fed rivers wind through landscapes of extraordinary beauty, with wildlife viewing opportunities throughout.

Day 2: Salmon Fishing Expeditions - The Copper River produces some of the world's most prized salmon, with king, sockeye, and silver runs occurring throughout summer. Guided excursions provide equipment and expertise, with catch processing and shipping services available.
Day 2: Klutina River Fishing - Tributary streams offer additional angling opportunities in more intimate settings, with runs of salmon and resident populations of rainbow trout and Dolly Varden char.
