visits.text: Letchworth State Park — Allow for approximately 115 km from Corning, a 1-hour-25-minute drive. Marvel at the Grand Canyon of the East, where the Genesee River plunges into a gorge 183 meters deep. Three major waterfalls tumble over ancient rock layers, while the gorge walls reveal 340 million years of sedimentary history.

Corning Museum of Glass — Discover 3,500 years of glass artistry in this world-class museum housing 50,000 objects. Live hot-glass demonstrations reveal the magic of glassblowing while contemporary galleries showcase works by Dale Chihuly and other masters.

Watkins Glen State Park — Allow for a round trip from Corning. Hike the gorge trail, which climbs 122 meters past 19 waterfalls carved into spectacular rock formations. The 2.4-kilometer trail winds through tunnels behind the waterfalls and past misty pools with rainbows in the narrow gorge.

activities.text: Scenic drive through the Finger Lakes — Allow for a round trip from Corning. Drive along the shores of Seneca and Cayuga lakes, where vineyard-covered hills descend toward crystal-clear waters. Stop at viewpoints overlooking the long, narrow lakes carved by glaciers more than 2 million years ago.

Farm-to-table dinner — Savor seasonal cuisine prepared with ingredients from surrounding farms and orchards. Regional restaurants showcase New York wines paired with grass-fed beef, artisan cheeses, and heirloom vegetables.

days_plan.itin_title: New York State Road Trip: From Manhattan to Niagara Falls

visits.text: USS Lexington (CV-16) is an Essex-class aircraft carrier commissioned in February 1943. At 872 feet long, she participated in virtually every major Pacific naval operation between 1944 and 1945, racking up so many missions that the Japanese declared her sunk four separate times - hence her nickname 'The Blue Ghost'. She remained in service until 1991, making her the longest-serving Essex-class carrier in all of American naval history. Since 1992, she's been permanently moored on Corpus Christi's waterfront. Five self-guided circuits cover 250,000 square feet spread across 11 decks. Allow a good two hours.

The Texas State Aquarium, facing the USS Lexington, focuses exclusively on Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean fauna. You'll observe bottlenose dolphins, sharks, rays, sea turtles and coastal birds in tanks recreating their natural habitats. Operators run dolphin-watching trips from the neighboring dock - the animals are often visible from the jetty's edge without even boarding.

A bronze statue of Selena Quintanilla-Pérez stands at Mirador de la Flor on the Corpus Christi waterfront. Selena, known as the 'Queen of Tejano music', grew up here and was murdered in the city on March 31, 1995, aged 23. Her death prompted mourning across Spanish-speaking communities nationwide. The small Selena Museum, run by her family, tells the story of her career in another part of town; make a separate trip there from the waterfront.

activities.text: Padre Island National Seashore stretches along 70 miles of coast between Corpus Christi and Port Mansfield; it is the world's longest undeveloped barrier island. Malaquite Beach, near the visitor center, is closed to vehicle traffic. To drive on the sand, use the separate access to South Beach; farther south, sand conditions may require a four-wheel-drive vehicle with tires deflated to around 16 psi. Check your fuel level and bring water before setting off: there are no services along the next 37 miles. In return, you may have the beach to yourself. From June to August, park staff release young Kemp's ridley turtles, the world's most endangered sea turtle, at Malaquite Beach around 6:45 AM. Call the Hatchling Hotline at (361) 949-7163 for times. Plan a round trip from Corpus Christi to visit this coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Gulf Coast: Lafayette to South Padre Island - 9 days

places.name: Cortez, CO

visits.text: Book your Cliff Palace visit ahead on recreation.gov ($5/person): 150 rooms and 23 kivas in a sandstone alcove, built between 1190 and 1270 by the Ancestral Puebloans. In 1888, two cowboys lost in a snowstorm were the first Europeans to see it. The one-hour guided tour descends into the site using stone ladders - exactly as its inhabitants did. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez to the site.

For Balcony House, be prepared: a 10 m ladder against the cliff, then a tunnel just 60 cm wide to crawl through - exactly how the Puebloans entered their homes for defense. The guided tour lasts 1 hour. Not recommended for people with claustrophobia, highly recommended for everyone else. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez to the site.

Visit the Chapin Mesa Archeological Museum before your guided tours: the 30-minute introduction to 1,400 years of Puebloan history - pottery, tools and reconstructions - radically changes how you understand the sites. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez to the museum.

Follow the Mesa Top Loop Road (10 km) to see the remains of 10th-century villages - far older than the cliff dwellings. Park Point, the park's highest point at 2,613 m, offers a 360° view of all four Four Corners states. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez to the park's sites.

activities.text: End the day on Petroglyph Point Trail (5 km, loop), which follows the canyon walls to a panel of petroglyphs carved into the rock. It is one of the few trails accessible without a guide in the Chapin Mesa area - collect a map at the museum before leaving. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez to the trailhead, followed by the hike on foot.
If you are curious, Four Corners Monument is 64 km to the west: the only place in the United States where four states meet at one point. Plan a round trip by road from Cortez.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

map_keywords: Cliff Palace Mesa Verde National Park
Mesa Top Loop Road Mesa Verde

visits.text: You step out of the 1881 Spring Hill Ranch visitor center and the wind hits you at once: this is what 170 million hectares of North America felt and sounded like before the plow arrived. Established on November 12, 1996 as the 370th unit of the national park system, this 4,400-hectare preserve protects the only site in the National Park System entirely devoted to tallgrass prairie. Less than 4% of the original prairie survives today, and most of it lies in the Flint Hills. The three-story German bank barn holds 1,765 m² of storage; the 1882 Lower Fox Creek School is reached by a short uphill trail. A bison herd roams the pastures; more than 65 kilometers of trails wind across the rolling terrain.

Stand at the base of Broadway Street and look up: the 34-meter red mansard roof of this 1873 courthouse lords over the entire town. Architect John G. Haskell - also the first architect of the Kansas State Capitol - designed it for 600 residents who approved a bond issue in 1871. Workers quarried local limestone by hand and hauled blocks weighing up to seven tonnes by horse-drawn wagon from a nearby quarry. Inside, a three-story walnut spiral staircase rises from logs cut along the Cottonwood River. Self-guided tours run Monday-Friday, free of charge.

Walk the three-block main street between the stone bridge over the Cottonwood River and the courthouse steps and you are in a town whose limestone went into the U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C. By 1885, six quarries near here were shipping magnesian limestone by rail to every state in the country. Art galleries, antique stores, and a few restaurants line the street. On select summer Friday evenings, the Emma Chase Café hosts Friday Night Music, with local fiddlers performing on the porch.

activities.text: Tune your radio to 1680 AM before you leave town - three transmitters along Highway 177 broadcast the history, ecology, and fire management of the Flint Hills as you drive. The 75-kilometer route from Council Grove south to Cassoday passes through uninterrupted tallgrass prairie with no billboards and almost no buildings. Spring burns (typically April) turn entire hillsides orange at night; the hills are vivid green through June and rust-red by October. Eight kilometers south of Cottonwood Falls, a designated scenic overlook gives the best panoramic view of the rolling rangeland.

Take the Southwind Nature Trail (2.8 km) and you will pass the bison pasture without needing a guide - just check the NPS website for current herd locations before you go. The preserve has over 65 kilometers of trails total, from short loops near the historic buildings to the 5.6-km Two Section Trail that climbs to a scenic overlook. Spring and early summer bring prairie wildflowers in waves: purple coneflower, prairie turnip, and Indian paintbrush. Mornings are best for birding; greater prairie-chickens are visible near the preserve in spring.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Flint Hills & Frontier: Wichita to Dodge City

places.name: Council Bluffs, IA

visits.text: You climb to a 1936 monument perched on a bluff in the Loess Hills. From this height, the Missouri River stretches below, Council Bluffs spreads to the east, and Omaha's skyline extends to the west across the water. The relief carved in stone depicts this historic meeting; interpretive panels enrich the account of this first diplomatic encounter during the Corps of Discovery expedition. Visit early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light softens and the heat subsides.

You step into Council Bluffs' 1905 Carnegie Library—a Beaux-Arts gem worth the visit on its own—which houses a museum that opened May 10, 2003, precisely 134 years after the transcontinental railroad's completion. The exhibits trace more than 150 years of American railroading, from the Pacific Railroad Act signed by Lincoln in 1862 through today's continental freight operations. Interactive displays and an HO-scale model railroad share floor space with historical photographs, period documents, and artifacts that bring the iron-horse era to life. Open Thursday through Saturday; confirm hours before you go.

About twenty kilometers north of Council Bluffs, this 513-hectare nature preserve offers a true immersion in the Loess Hills—a nearly unique geological formation found only here and in northwest China, sculpted from windblown glacial silt that forms ridges rising up to 90 meters above the Missouri River floodplain. Sixteen kilometers of trails range from easy boardwalks to steep ridge climbs. The 14-meter HawkWatch observation tower ranks among the top 25 raptor-monitoring sites in North America, tallying an average of 13,000 migrating raptors each year from September through December. Weekday mornings are the quietest; a vehicle entry fee applies.

activities.text: The Loess Hills Scenic Byway stretches more than 320 kilometers along the Missouri's eastern bank. You don't need to follow the full route—even the northern stretch between Crescent and Council Bluffs reveals why these wind-sculpted ridges matter: razor-edged crests, remnant tallgrass prairie, and views down into the river valley. Follow it south from Hitchcock Nature Center back into town, an ideal way to end the day in nature.

The blocks around Pearl Street reward a short walk on foot. You pass the Golden Spike monument marking the city's role as the eastern anchor of the transcontinental railroad. The RailsWest Museum and the preserved home of General Grenville Dodge - Union Army engineer and Union Pacific's chief surveyor - both sit within a few minutes' drive. Solid dinner options line the downtown streets, and the whole area is compact enough to cover on foot in an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Iowa Backroads: From the Missouri Cliffs to the Mississippi Bluffs

map_keywords: Union Pacific Railroad Museum Council Bluffs

visits.text: Crater Lake National Park — Marvel at America's deepest lake filling the caldera of Mount Mazama volcano that collapsed 7,700 years ago. The 594-meter-deep lake's impossibly blue water results from exceptional purity and depth absorbing all colors except blue.

Rim Drive — Circle the lake on this 53-kilometer scenic road climbing to over 2,100 meters with 30 viewpoints. The summer-only drive showcases constantly changing perspectives of Wizard Island, Phantom Ship, and surrounding peaks.

Wizard Island — Photograph from the lake rim this 230-meter cinder cone rising from the lake's western side, formed by volcanic eruptions after the caldera collapsed. Boat trips to the island are suspended for the 2026 to 2028 seasons.

Watchman Peak Trail — Hike 1.6 kilometers to this fire lookout offering the best sunset views over Crater Lake. The relatively easy trail climbs 128 meters to panoramic vistas encompassing the entire caldera.

activities.text: Crater Lake Lodge visit — Stop at this 1915 rustic lodge perched on the caldera rim with floor-to-ceiling windows framing lake views. The National Historic Landmark preserves original stone fireplaces and craftsman-style architecture.

Stargazing at dark sky — Observe the Milky Way arcing overhead in one of America's darkest national parks. The high elevation and remote location create exceptional conditions for astronomy and meteor shower viewing.

Ranger talk — Attend evening programs explaining the volcanic geology, formation, and unique ecology of Crater Lake. Rangers share the Klamath tribe's legend of Llao and Skell battling to create the sacred lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Oregon Natural Wonders: Crater Lake to Pacific Coast Road Trip

visits.text: Turkey Run State Park - Plan a round trip by car from Crawfordsville. Indiana's second state park (1916), Turkey Run hides sandstone gorges carved by glacial waters 20,000 years ago. Trail 3 is the most spectacular: 2.7 km through Bear Hollow, a narrow canyon where you climb wooden ladders fixed into the rock. The “Punch Bowl” on this same trail is a cylindrical hole carved by swirling blocks of ice. Wear shoes with good grip - the rocks are slippery even in dry weather.

Shades State Park - Along Sugar Creek; plan a round trip by car from Crawfordsville. The ravines are narrower and more shaded. Less visited than its neighbor, the park feels wilder. The trail to Silver Cascade Falls is worth the detour after rain.

Parke County covered bridges - Plan a round trip by car from Crawfordsville. Parke County has 31, a national record. They date from the 19th century, when the roof protected the wooden deck from rain and snow. The Narrows Covered Bridge, at Turkey Run, is one of the most photogenic.

activities.text: Combined hike on trails 3, 5 and 9 at Turkey Run - Plan a round trip by car from Crawfordsville to the park. This long 7.5 km loop links the park's three best-known trails: ladders, canyons, the Falls Canyon waterfall and the “Ice Box”, a rocky overhang where the air stays cool even in midsummer. Allow 3 to 4 hours with photo stops.

Canoeing or kayaking down Sugar Creek - Plan a round trip by car from Crawfordsville to the launch point. Rental operators offer trips of 5 to 21 km on the river that runs through both parks. From the water, you will see the sandstone cliffs from a different angle. Booking is recommended on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Indiana Road Trip: Dunes, Caves, and Cities

visits.text: Crystal River National Wildlife Refuge - The Manatee Capital of the World: Every winter, hundreds of manatees gather in the warm spring waters here, creating the most accessible manatee-watching experience on Earth.

Three Sisters Springs - Snorkel with Manatees: This unique opportunity allows swimmers to enter the water with these gentle giants, observing them feeding, resting, and socializing in their natural winter habitat.

activities.text: Manatee Snorkeling Tours - Face to Face with Florida's State Marine Mammal: Licensed operators guide small groups into the springs for close encounters with manatees.
Kings Bay Kayaking - Paddle Through Crystal Waters: Explore the spring-fed bay and its network of tributaries where manatees, dolphins, and sea turtles share the remarkably clear waters.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

visits.text: Discover Cumberland Island, Georgia's largest and wildest barrier island where 27 km of pristine beaches stretch beneath towering dunes and maritime forests of moss-draped oaks. Wild horses descended from colonial-era stock roam freely across 14,500 hectares of protected wilderness, creating unforgettable encounters along empty shorelines. The island remains deliberately undeveloped, accessible only by ferry from St. Marys.

Explore the haunting Dungeness Ruins, crumbling remains of Thomas Carnegie's Gilded Age mansion slowly being reclaimed by resurrection ferns and climbing vines. The grand Plum Orchard Mansion showcases meticulously preserved Carnegie-era architecture and furnishings. The historic First African Baptist Church and Stafford Plantation cemetery document the island's complex history of enslaved people and freed African Americans.

activities.text: Hike or bike over 80 km of trails winding through moss-draped maritime forests, past salt marshes teeming with wildlife, and along windswept beaches where loggerhead sea turtles nest each summer. Limited ferry capacity and minimal facilities preserve the island's remote, mysterious character for those who plan ahead.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

places.name: Custer, SD

visits.text: From Custer, plan a same-day round trip to Wind Cave. Before going down, read this figure: 95% of the world's known boxwork formations are in this cave. These calcite cells lining the walls—like a mineral honeycomb 60 to 100 million years old—exist almost nowhere else on Earth. Theodore Roosevelt made it the world's first underground park in 1903. Since then, 270 km of passages have been mapped, and cavers estimate that there is probably just as much left to explore.

Choose the Garden of Eden Tour if you want to see the formations without exhausting yourself: 1 hour, 400 m, 150 steps, intermediate level. If you're adventurous, the Historic Candlelight Tour descends into undeveloped sections by candlelight—$17, minimum age 16, reservation required. Either way, bring a jacket: the cave stays at 11°C year-round.

On the surface, don't leave without walking 30 minutes on the Elk Mountain Trail. Wind Cave is home to one of four genetically pure bison herds in North America—along with Yellowstone, Utah's Henry Mountains, and Alberta's Elk Island. You'll often see them from the trail, at a reasonable distance. Stay on the path.

Custer State Park begins just to the north—71,000 acres, 1,500 free-ranging bison. Sylvan Lake, framed by pink granite, is where Doane Robinson—South Dakota state historian—got the idea in 1923 to carve faces into the Black Hills. He was looking at the Cathedral Spires above the water. This is where it all began. Swim in the lake if you're here in summer; the water is crystal clear.

activities.text: The Wildlife Loop Road runs 29 km through the park's open prairies—drive slowly, windows down, preferably in the morning between 7 and 9 a.m. or in the evening before sunset. Bison, deer, pronghorn, and wild burros (descendants of animals abandoned by miners in 1874) often cross the road. No guarantees, but the success rate is very high.

Needles Highway (SD-87): 27 km of road winding between pink granite needles, passing through tunnels dynamited through solid rock and opening onto views you won't see anywhere else. Stop at Eye of the Needle. Warning: the road is narrow—maximum tunnel height 3.4 m, width 2.6 m. RVs and trailers, skip this one.

places.name: Cuyahoga Valley, OH

visits.text: You discover the most popular waterfall in Cuyahoga Valley National Park—a 20-meter cascade over sandstone slabs flowing into Brandywine Creek, forming a turquoise pool at the bottom of a forested hollow. The 2.5-kilometer loop trail leading from the parking lot passes the Brandywine Inn house, dating from 1848, which served as a stop on the old canal route. The national park itself, designated a national recreation area in 1974 then promoted to national park status in 2000, extends over 33,000 acres between Cleveland and Akron along the Cuyahoga River—a name of Mohawk origin meaning “crooked river.” Arrive early in the morning for mist on the falls; the parking lot is often full on weekends after 10 a.m.

You walk alongside the setting of one of the park's most remarkable stories of ecological resilience: this marsh was recreated in the 1980s by a beaver colony that moved in on its own among the remains of an abandoned vehicle lot after industrial waste had been removed. The beavers dammed a small stream, transforming wasteland into a wetland teeming with life—gray herons, wood ducks, kingfishers, and raccoons now live here side by side. A wooden boardwalk lets you observe the whole area without disturbing the ecosystem.

You walk or bike on one of the best-preserved towpaths in the United States - the former towpath of the Ohio & Erie Canal, built between 1825 and 1832 over 496 kilometers to connect Lake Erie to the Ohio River. Before the canal, Ohio was a transportation wilderness; after its construction, the state's agricultural products could reach eastern markets in days. Interpretive signs dot the 34 kilometers of trail in the park, explaining how mules towed boats at 4 km/h from this same path less than two centuries ago.

activities.text: The Cuyahoga Valley Scenic Railroad offers excursions aboard a historic train that follows the Cuyahoga River through the entire length of the park, from Akron to Rockside Road in the north. It's the most contemplative way to see the park's oak, maple, and beech forests without crossing roads—especially in fall when colors spread across the hillsides. The train is particularly popular with cyclists who board at a northern stop and pedal back down the Towpath Trail. In fall, book several weeks in advance.

The Ritchie Ledges are sandstone formations carved by retreating glaciers more than 10,000 years ago—cliffs and crevices covered in moss and ferns that contrast with the surrounding forest. In the 19th century, these rocks were already a playground and picnic spot for Cleveland and Akron residents. The trail passes Ice Box Cave, a narrow gorge where the temperature remains close to 0°C even in midsummer thanks to cold air trapped between the sandstone walls.

places.name: Dallas, TX

visits.text: Dealey Plaza and the Sixth Floor Museum: it was from the sixth floor of this red-brick building - the former Texas School Book Depository - that Lee Harvey Oswald fired at Kennedy on November 22, 1963. The museum, opened in 1989 and operated as a nonprofit, preserves over 90,000 items related to the assassination. You'll see the reconstructed sniper's nest, the life-size FBI model of Dealey Plaza used by the Warren Commission, and the teletype machine that announced the president's death to the world. Plan to book your tickets online - the museum is only open Wednesday through Sunday.

Dallas Museum of Art: founded in 1903, the DMA ranks among the ten largest art museums in the United States, with over 24,000 works spanning 5,000 years of human creativity - from ancient Egypt to contemporary American art. Permanent collection admission has been free since 2013: you have no excuse to skip it. Don't miss the Level 1 pre-Columbian collection or the Level 2 Impressionists - Monet, Degas, Van Gogh. The building itself, designed by Edward Larrabee Barnes and opened in 1984, is worth the visit.

Reunion Tower GeO-Deck: the geodesic sphere perched 561 feet (171 m) high has been Dallas's signature landmark since 1978. The GeO-Deck observation platform sits at 143 m - count on 65 seconds in the elevator. On clear days, you can see Fort Worth 50 km away. Inside, a 16-meter interactive screen called the Halo displays a 3D map of Dallas with information about the city's landmarks.

Pioneer Plaza: right in the heart of downtown, this garden features 49 life-size bronze sculptures depicting a herd of Texas Longhorns crossing a stream. If you want a Texan photo without traveling 50 km, this is your spot—the sculptures are life-size and kids can sit on them. It's also one of the few places in Dallas where you grasp why the region earned the nickname “Cowtown.”

Bishop Arts District: in the North Oak Cliff neighborhood, about a hundred independent shops, restaurants, galleries and bars occupy perfectly preserved 1920s buildings. It's the ideal place to finish this circuit—street art murals line the facades, and if you want one last BBQ meal or Texas craft beer, you'll find what you're looking for without having to look.

Perot Museum of Nature and Science: designed by architect Thom Mayne (Morphosis) and inaugurated in 2012, this concrete cube perched above ground on columns is one of Dallas's most daring buildings. The 11 permanent galleries cover paleontology (a fine hall on Texas dinosaurs), geology, space and human sciences. Allow a good 2 hours if you're curious—the interactive experiences take up far more time than you'd anticipate.

activities.text: Live music night in Deep Ellum: Dallas's blues, jazz and rock club district has been around since the 1920s - Blind Lemon Jefferson played here before becoming a legend. The massive murals on colorful building facades are unmissable even if you never step inside a bar. Arrive after 9 PM to catch local bands in full swing, and go Thursday or Friday for the best lineups.

Bike or walk around White Rock Lake: the 15 km cycling loop follows the lake shores amid oaks and cypresses—it's the “Central Park of Dallas.” Outfitters offer bike rentals at the boathouse on the north shore. Early in the morning, herons and ducks are everywhere and the lake is perfectly calm. Allow 1.5 hours for a leisurely bike ride or 3 hours on foot.

Texas Triangle: Dallas, Austin, San Antonio & the Hill Country - 8 Days

places.name: Davis, WV

visits.text: You head up to West Virginia's highest point, Spruce Knob; allow for a round trip by car from Davis for this excursion. At an elevation of 1,482 meters, the summit vegetation—spruce trees twisted by the prevailing westerly winds, stunted into flag shapes all pointing in the same direction—resembles the Canadian taiga more than the surrounding Appalachian forests. In clear weather, the observation tower offers a 360° panorama over the Allegheny Mountains. Arrive early in the morning to see the valley mist before it dissipates.

You descend the 214 steps of the wooden boardwalk to the Blackwater Falls observation platform: the river plunges 17 meters over a Pennsylvanian sandstone escarpment, tinted a characteristic amber-brown by tannic acid released from red spruce and hemlock needles fallen into the water. It's this singular color that gave the river—and the park—its name. Illustrator David Hunter Strother was the first to describe and sketch the falls for a wide audience, in 1852. Come early or late in the day for raking light on the gorge—the canyon is eight miles long.

You emerge at Lindy Point after 0.3 miles of easy walking from the parking area and discover what many consider the most beautiful view in West Virginia: from a ledge at an elevation of 915 meters, you overlook the full width of Blackwater Canyon, with the park's white lodge below and the Alleghenies stretching to the horizon. In October, the red leaves of maples, the orange leaves of hickories, and the yellow leaves of birches cover the canyon slopes in a spectacular array of shades. This overlook is particularly photogenic in late afternoon when the setting sun's light enters the canyon from the west.

activities.text: You follow the Elakala trail from the lodge for a five-minute walk and discover a series of four tiered waterfalls totaling 40 meters in height, carved into the walls of Blackwater Canyon. The water of Shay Run tumbles from ledge to ledge through ferns, hemlocks, and abundant mosses that create the atmosphere of a moist high-altitude forest. Elakala Falls is much less crowded than the main falls—you have a good chance of finding yourself alone, even in high season, if you come in the morning.

You walk along the canyon's south rim for several miles, looking down at the amber river snaking 200 meters below. The canyon is geologically young—the river has carved this 8-mile chasm in less than a million years through an Appalachian sandstone plateau. You pass through forests of balsam fir, a species usually confined to Canada and the Northeast's high peaks, with the oldest trees reaching 200 years of age. The best time is morning, when the mists from the canyon floor slowly rise toward the ridges.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

map_keywords: Blackwater Falls State Park Davis WV

visits.text: Daytona Beach - The World's Most Famous Beach: Twenty-three miles of hard-packed white sand have earned this Atlantic destination its legendary status. This is one of the few beaches where you can drive directly onto the sand and park steps from the surf.

Daytona International Speedway - The World Center of Racing: Home to the Daytona 500 and numerous NASCAR events throughout the year, this 2.5-mile tri-oval track also hosts concerts and special events. Tours take visitors behind the scenes of racing history.

Daytona Beach Boardwalk and Pier - Classic Americana: This oceanfront landmark features arcades, rides, shops, and restaurants stretching along the shore, anchored by the historic pier extending into the Atlantic.

activities.text: Beach Driving - A Florida Tradition Since 1903: Automobile pioneers raced on this hard-packed sand, and today visitors can experience parking their vehicle right on the beach with waves crashing nearby.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

places.name: Deadwood, SD

visits.text: From Deadwood, Mount Rushmore is about 79 km away, a 1-hour-15-minute drive. The first thing that strikes you about Mount Rushmore is not its size - it is that it was built without anyone dying. Between 1927 and 1941, Gutzon Borglum and 400 workers blasted 450,000 tonnes of granite while dangling in midair from a 9 mm steel cable. Each of the four faces measures 18 meters. Arrive before 9 a.m. - after that, the buses roll in. In the evening, the lighting ceremony run by the rangers is free and often surprising.

From Deadwood, plan a same-day round trip to Crazy Horse Memorial, under construction since 1948—and that is precisely what makes it fascinating. Lakota chief Henry Standing Bear wrote to sculptor Ziolkowski in 1939: “My people want the white man to know that the Red people, too, have great heroes.” The finished sculpture will be 563 m high and 641 m long. The face (87.5 m) was completed in 1998, the left hand in 2023. Not a cent of federal funding—everything comes from admission tickets and private donations.

Deadwood emerges at the bottom of a wooded gulch, and Main Street still looks like 1876. The entire town is designated a National Historic Landmark. On August 2, 1876, Wild Bill Hickok sat here, at Saloon No. 10, back to the door for the first time in his life. Jack McCall shot him in the back of the neck. Hickok was holding black aces and black eights—the Dead Man's Hand, known worldwide ever since. McCall was acquitted the next day by a miners' court, then retried and hanged.

The Adams Museum (100 Sherman Street) is free and worth an hour. Photo archives from when the town had 25,000 people, recreation of Hickok's card game, history of the 1875 gold rush—everything is well told and presented tastefully. It's the best antidote to the slightly too-kitsch reenactments on the main street.

Mount Moriah Cemetery sits on the hill above town, perched among the pines. Wild Bill Hickok is there, metal bust on his grave. Calamity Jane rests 50 cm away—she'd asked to be buried near him before dying in 1903. Seth Bullock, Deadwood's first sheriff and future close friend of Theodore Roosevelt, is higher up the slope. The view over the entire valley from the top is worth the climb.

Take US-14A north from Deadwood and let Spearfish Canyon pull you in. Limestone cliffs rise 460 meters above Spearfish Creek, covered in ponderosa pines and aspens. In fall, the colors are strikingly vivid. Stop at Bridal Veil Falls and Roughlock Falls—two waterfalls accessible from the roadside in less than 5 minutes' walk. Total: 32 km of scenery passing by.

In Lead (pronounced “Leed”), the Homestake Mine operated from 1876 to 2001—the most productive in North America, with more than 1,200 tonnes of gold extracted over 125 years. Today, 2,400 meters below you, the Sanford Underground Research Facility uses the old mine passages for dark matter detection experiments. The guided surface tour explains how a 19th-century open-pit mine became a particle physics laboratory.

Sturgis has 7,000 residents the rest of the year—and in August, between 400,000 and 700,000 bikers descend for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, held continuously since 1938. Outside rally time, Main Street keeps its leather shops and legendary bars. The Sturgis Motorcycle Museum & Hall of Fame is worth an hour: the event's history is well documented, and some machines on display are remarkable.

activities.text: At Saloon No. 10 (657 Main Street), actors reenact Wild Bill's death Monday through Saturday - 1 p.m., 3 p.m., 5 p.m. and 7 p.m., May to September. Settle in, order a beer, watch McCall shoot the Wild West's greatest gunslinger in the back. It is unapologetically touristy and, frankly, well done. Free admission.

Since 1989, gambling has been legal in Deadwood and slot machines and blackjack tables have invaded the historic hotels on Main Street. The Bullock Hotel (633 Main Street), built in 1895 by Seth Bullock himself, is the most distinctive place to end the evening: the building is intact, and the sheriff's ghost—they say—still roams the hallways.

In Spearfish Canyon, head to the Roughlock Falls Trail trailhead near Spearfish Canyon Lodge in Savoy; plan a same-day round trip from Deadwood. The trail follows Little Spearfish Creek through the trees to Roughlock Falls. View the waterfalls from the walkways and viewing platforms, then return the same way. Bring walking shoes and water, and stay on the trail and designated paths around the falls.

On Upper Main Street in Deadwood, the Broken Boot Gold Mine is a real 1876 mine converted into an attraction. Tunnels, ore carts, and panning technique—a few flakes guaranteed in your pan. Genuinely fun with kids, and honest about what real gold miners' lives were like in 1876.

visits.text: Death Valley National Park - The Hottest, Driest, Lowest Place in North America: This vast desert wilderness holds the world record for highest reliably recorded air temperature (134°F). Yet within its 3.4 million acres, life persists in remarkable adaptations, and landscapes of surreal beauty unfold.

Badwater Basin - Stand at 282 Feet Below Sea Level: Hexagonal salt flats stretch toward distant mountains at the lowest point in North America. The basin supports a unique ecosystem including the endemic Badwater snail.

Zabriskie Point - Sunrise Over Martian Badlands: These eroded mudstone formations glow gold and amber as first light strikes their contours, creating one of the most photographed desert scenes on Earth.

Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes - Saharan Splendor in California: These undulating dunes near Stovepipe Wells rise up to 100 feet, their pristine surfaces erased and redrawn by desert winds. Dawn and dusk light transforms them into sculptural masterpieces.

activities.text: Artist's Palette - A Mountain Painted in Minerals: This hillside showcases nature's full palette through oxidized metals creating stripes of pink, green, purple, and gold across barren slopes.

Zabriskie Point - Observe the Desert Landforms: From the overlook, examine the badland ridges and gullies stretching into Death Valley. Layers of eroded rock form golden and ocher folds whose shadows change with the light. Sunrise offers a chance to photograph the contours of this rocky landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Vesterheim Norwegian-American Museum—The largest museum of Norwegian heritage outside Norway. Across 12 buildings, it traces the history of Norwegian immigrants who settled this valley starting in the 1850s. Collections of rosemaling (decorative painting), textiles, farm tools, and a recreated farmstead. Plan 90 minutes.

Dunnings Spring—Right in the heart of Decorah, this 60 m waterfall drops from a limestone cliff into a shaded ravine. A staircase and footbridge bring you to the base of the falls. It's a 5-minute walk from downtown—perfect for a refreshing break.

Decorah Fish Hatchery—This state fish hatchery, nestled in a valley, raises rainbow and brown trout. The spring water feeding the pools is crystal-clear. Admission is free and kids love watching the fish. Right next door, a bald eagle nest is filmed continuously by a camera—Decorah became famous thanks to these eagles.

Ice Cave - On the outskirts of Decorah, this natural cavity in the rock contains ice in spring and early summer thanks to a natural ventilation system. Cold air sinks into the cave in winter and remains trapped there. A short trail leads to it from the parking lot.
Phelps Park—In the hills above Decorah, this park offers views of the Upper Iowa River valley and its limestone cliffs.

activities.text: Stroll downtown Decorah—Water Street is lined with independent shops, cafés, and craft breweries. The town has youthful energy despite its small size (8,000 people), thanks to Luther College, which has been here since 1861.

Biking or walking the Trout Run Trail—This 18 km loop circles Decorah following the Upper Iowa River, passing bluffs, prairies, and woods. It's one of Iowa's most beautiful bike trails. Bike rentals available in town.

Canoeing or kayaking on the Upper Iowa River—The river winds between 30 m forested limestone bluffs. Outfitters offer rentals with shuttle service. The Decorah–Bluffton section (15 km) is the most popular—plan 3 to 4 hours at a relaxed pace.

places.name: Delaware Water Gap, PA

visits.text: The Delaware Water Gap is where the Delaware River carved a spectacular breach through the Appalachian ridge, separating Mount Minsi in Pennsylvania (445 meters) from Mount Tammany in New Jersey (465 meters) across less than a kilometer at river level. This natural passage has been used for millennia by Lenape Native American populations, then by European settlers who traced the first road in 1793 - today followed by I-80. The National Recreation Area, created in 1965 on 27,000 hectares, attracts more than 4 million visitors per year, making it one of the most visited national parks in the United States. Admission is free and the park is open 24/7, allowing you to enjoy dawn light on the river.

Raymondskill Falls is Pennsylvania's tallest waterfall, with three tiers dropping a total of about 46 meters - nearly the height of Niagara Falls viewed from the side, as park rangers like to point out. It is at the northern end of the recreation area near Milford: allow for a day trip from Delaware Water Gap. The access trail from the parking area is short but steep over 400 meters and leads to viewpoints above the three tiers. In spring, after April rains, the flow is at its strongest. In summer there is less water, but the woodland of beeches and hemlocks makes the falls just as beautiful.

Millbrook Village is a preserved nineteenth-century village inside the national recreation area. Founded around a flour mill in the 1830s, it has about a dozen restored buildings - a forge, general store, church and barn - that show what rural life in New Jersey was like in the previous century. The National Park Service holds living-history days on summer weekends with craftspeople in period dress. The village is on the New Jersey side of the park, reached via Old Mine Road: allow for a day trip from Delaware Water Gap.

activities.text: Mount Tammany is the Delaware Water Gap's signature hike, and deservedly so. The Red Trail starts about ten meters from the I-80 bridge and climbs directly into the forest over exposed rocks. The 465-meter summit offers the most photographed view in the park: the Delaware Water Gap breach from above, with the river winding 400 meters below and Pennsylvania forests as far as the eye can see. More than 260 bird species have been recorded in the park, and peregrine falcons have nested on Milford cliffs since 2018, for the first time in 70 years. Arrive in the morning to avoid the crowds and have the views to yourself.

The Delaware is the East Coast's free-flowing river - one of the few major American rivers without a dam from end to end, earning its status as a 'National Scenic and Recreational River.' Canoeing through the park offers a unique perspective on the Water Gap from water level, with wooded cliffs rising on both sides. Several outfitters in Delaware Water Gap Borough and Dingmans Ferry offer half-day trips with return shuttle. Water is generally at its lowest in summer (ideal for beginners) and highest in spring after snowmelt.

places.name: Demopolis, AL

visits.text: Gaineswood at 805 South Cedar Avenue is one of the more unusual buildings you will see on this trip. General Nathan Bryan Whitfield started with a two-room dogtrot cabin in 1843 and spent the next 18 years redesigning and expanding it into a Greek Revival mansion - acting as his own architect, drawing from architectural treatises and his travels north. He was also a musician and inventor: the barrel organ he designed, which plays from large cylinders with pins, is still functional. The two front rooms have matching domed ceilings with cupolas; the mirrors in the ballroom are angled to reflect each other to infinity. By 1860, Whitfield owned 235 enslaved people and the plantation produced 600 bales of cotton a year. The house cannot be separated from that labor. Tours run with local docents who know every detail. Admission charged.

Bluff Hall, a ten-minute walk from Gaineswood, sits on a white limestone cliff above the Tombigbee River - that is where the name comes from. The Federal-style house was built in 1832 by merchant Allan Glover as a wedding gift for his daughter and her husband, cotton plantation owner Francis Strother Lyon. The Marengo County Historical Society has restored roughly 75 percent of the authentic furnishings. The textile and clothing collection is one of the stronger holdings. On the grounds, a log cabin saved from a demolition site was found to date to the original French expatriate Vine and Olive Colony settlement of 1817.

Lyon Hall on Main Street was built between 1850 and 1853 by enslaved workers for George Strother Gaines - the same Indian trader who originally owned the land Gaineswood was built on. The connection between these three properties maps a dense network of land ownership, political power, and forced labor in a small corner of the Alabama Black Belt. Check local hours before visiting.

activities.text: Demopolis City Landing on the Tombigbee River gives you a different angle on this town. The river was the economic artery that carried Demopolis cotton to Mobile and from there to global markets. A fifteen-minute walk along the riverfront connects the antebellum architectural legacy of the town to the water that made it possible. Fishing boats still use the landing; it's a quiet place in late afternoon.

Foscue Creek Park, just west of town on U.S. 80, offers a short walk down to the water - a good way to clear your head after a day of house museums. The park is operated by the Army Corps of Engineers and has a boat ramp and picnic area along the river. It's a place where the landscape reasserts itself.

visits.text: Day 1: Denali National Park Visitor Center - The primary orientation point for this six-million-acre wilderness preserve, featuring comprehensive exhibits on the park's ecosystems, geology, and the cultural history of the Athabascan people who have inhabited this region for millennia. Rangers provide daily programs and essential information for exploring the park's single 92-mile road.

Day 1: Denali Park Road (First 15 Miles) - The only section accessible to private vehicles, this scenic drive passes through taiga forest and offers the first glimpses of Denali when skies are clear. Pullouts at Savage River provide access to hiking trails and wildlife viewing opportunities.

Day 2: Tundra Wilderness Tour (62 miles) - This seven- to eight-hour narrated bus journey penetrates deep into Denali's wilderness, crossing Polychrome Pass with its multicolored volcanic formations and descending to the Toklat River basin. The route traverses prime habitat for grizzly bears, wolves, caribou, Dall sheep, and moose, with experienced drivers stopping for wildlife viewing.

Day 2: Kantishna Experience (92 miles) - The full-day twelve-hour expedition travels the entire length of the park road to the historic mining district of Kantishna. This immersive journey maximizes wildlife viewing opportunities and reaches the most remote accessible areas of the park, with Wonder Lake offering iconic Denali reflections on calm days.

Day 2: Eielson Visitor Center - Located at mile 66, this sustainable facility perched at an elevation of 3,500 feet provides panoramic views of Denali and the Muldrow Glacier. Exhibits explain glaciology and the mountain's unique weather patterns that make summit visibility a treasured occurrence.

activities.text: Day 1: Denali Flightseeing - Aerial tours departing from the park entrance reveal the immense scale of the Alaska Range, with glaciers flowing from Denali's flanks and vast expanses of untouched wilderness stretching to every horizon.

Day 1: Nenana River Rafting - The Nenana River paralleling the park entrance offers both tranquil scenic float trips through pristine canyon scenery and exhilarating Class III–IV whitewater sections through Nenana Canyon.

Day 1: Guided Wilderness Hiking - Naturalist-led excursions venture into roadless areas of the park, teaching backcountry navigation and wildlife awareness while exploring tundra ecosystems rarely seen by casual visitors.

Day 2: Transit Bus System - The National Park Service operates a hop-on, hop-off shuttle allowing independent exploration. Visitors can disembark at any point to hike unmarked wilderness routes, then catch a later bus to continue deeper into the park or return to the entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alaska Circuit: National Parks and Glaciers

places.name: Denver, CO

visits.text: Begin at Denver Union Station in the heart of LoDo. This Beaux-Arts building in carved granite opened in 1914 - exactly one hundred years before its reopening as a cultural hub in 2014. At its peak in the 1940s, the station welcomed over 50,000 people daily, including thousands of soldiers heading to World War II. Theodore Roosevelt and Franklin Roosevelt passed through here, as did Queen Marie of Romania. Today it houses a mix of restaurants, shops, and the Crawford Hotel on the upper floors. The Great Hall on the ground floor remains open to all - visit in the evening when the lighting is superb.

From there, walk up to Larimer Square, Denver's first historic district, whose 1870s brick facades were saved from demolition in the 1960s by a visionary developer, Dana Crawford. The street concentrates independent restaurants and bars in a preserved setting - it's one of the few places in Denver where you'll truly feel the city's history.

End the evening on the 16th Street Mall, the mile-long pedestrian artery running through downtown. The Daniels & Fisher Tower, built in 1910, rises 76 meters here - it was then the tallest building west of the Mississippi. Perfect for dinner and surveying the surrounding neighborhoods before heading to altitude tomorrow.

Take the Peak-to-Peak Scenic Byway (CO-7 then CO-72) to descend toward Denver - it's Colorado's oldest scenic route, created in 1918, covering 88 kilometers of ridgelines between Estes Park and Black Hawk. The road passes aspen forests, abandoned mining villages, and offers direct views of Longs Peak (4,346 m), the park's highest point. In autumn, it's a spectacle of golden leaves. Stop in Nederland at 1,700 m elevation for a coffee break before descending to Boulder.

Boulder, Pearl Street Mall - this several-block pedestrian street in old Boulder concentrates restaurants, independent shops, and street musicians. The University of Colorado is nearby, giving the area a young, international atmosphere. Stop here for lunch before continuing toward Denver.

On the way to Denver, make a detour to Red Rocks Amphitheatre in Morrison, even if you do not have a concert tonight. The venue is free to visit outside events. Two 90-meter red sandstone monoliths - Ship Rock and Creation Rock - frame the stage and naturally absorb sound, giving it some of the best natural acoustics in the world. The 9,525-seat amphitheatre was built by the CCC in the 1930s; the Beatles played here in 1964 and U2 in 1983 (the “Under a Blood Red Sky” concert). Climb to the top for views of Denver and the eastern plains.

Use this final day in Denver to explore what you missed on arrival. The Denver Art Museum holds one of the country's most important Native American art collections - the building itself, a prism-shaped extension designed by architect Daniel Libeskind and opened in 2006, is worth seeing from outside. Allow at least 2 hours to tour it.

The RiNo (River North Art District) neighborhood is Denver's liveliest area for murals and craft breweries. Denver counts over 400 breweries in Colorado, and several of the best known have their taprooms in this district. Stop by late afternoon before the airport.

activities.text: Prepare for your ascent to altitude: Denver sits at 1,609 meters (the famous 'Mile High City'). If you're coming from the coast, plan to drink plenty of water starting tonight - altitude sickness can appear above 2,400 m, and Trail Ridge Road exceeds 3,700 m. A night in Denver to acclimate before heading higher is genuinely useful.

Morning run or yoga at City Park - Denver's largest park (330 hectares) offers direct views of the Rockies on clear days. It's also home to the Denver Museum of Nature and Science and the Denver Zoo if you're traveling with family.

places.name: Des Moines, IA

visits.text: You approach the only five-domed capitol in the United States—built between 1871 and 1886 and crowned by a central dome sheathed in 23-karat gold leaf that rises 84 meters above the city. Inside, 29 types of imported marble line the walls and floors, while 12 hardwood species native to Iowa adorn the legislative chambers and corridors. Free guided tours run Monday through Saturday, covering the Governor's Suite, the law library, both legislative chambers, and the historic Supreme Court chamber. Arrive early on a weekday for the quietest tour.

The museum's centerpiece is a full-skeleton replica of a Hebior mammoth - a species whose bones have been unearthed from Iowa's glacial soil. Permanent galleries trace Iowa's story from pre-statehood territorial days through the Civil War - in which 76,000 Iowans fought for the Union - to the present, with a recent addition covering Iowa's surprising film history. Free admission, free parking in the garage across Grand Avenue. Of the museum's 80,000-plus artifact collection, roughly 1,500 are on display at any given time.

You cross into Western Gateway Park, where this 1.8-hectare sculpture park opened in 2009 thanks to a gift from Des Moines art collectors John and Mary Pappajohn—the largest single donation in Des Moines Art Center history. More than 30 works by artists including Louise Bourgeois, Jaume Plensa, and Ai Weiwei populate the green space. Plensa's monumental “Nomade” figure greets you at the entrance. Free admission; open dawn to midnight year-round.

Built between 1923 and 1928 for businessman Carl Weeks, this 42-room, 2,044-square-meter manor was modeled directly on the 15th-century King's House in Salisbury, England. English oak woodwork and roof timbers dating to the Elizabethan era were imported whole for the construction. Inside you encounter art, rare manuscripts, historic musical instruments, and tapestries assembled over decades of passionate collecting. The surrounding gardens are equally impressive. Admission charged; tours run on scheduled days.

What began as a greenhouse in 1939 has grown into a botanical center covering nearly three hectares in the heart of Des Moines. The geodesic dome conservatory shelters thousands of plant species from around the globe. Outside, themed gardens—water garden, hillside garden, Lauridsen savanna—reward unhurried walking. Admission charged; outdoor gardens peak in late spring and early fall.

Plan a day trip from Des Moines to Madrid, then reach the bridge on foot or by bicycle along the trail. This half-kilometer bridge spans the Des Moines River valley 40 meters above the water. Steel frames along the span are tilted to evoke the underground coal mine tunnels that once riddled Iowa's landscape. At dusk, blue LED lighting transforms the structure into something closer to an art installation than cycling infrastructure. The trail surface is paved and level. Free access, open year-round.

activities.text: You walk from the Capitol steps down to Court Avenue through the East Village—independent bookstores, craft microbreweries, the Raygun shop with its sharp Iowa-centric merchandise, and some of Des Moines' best restaurants packed into a few walkable blocks. Nearly all the neighborhood's historic buildings appear on the National Register of Historic Places. Return in the evening when the bar scene comes alive and continues late into the night.

Three separate buildings designed by Eliel Saarinen (1948), I.M. Pei (1968), and Richard Meier (1985) form a unified museum campus on Grand Avenue. The permanent collection spans American and European modern and contemporary art. The adjacent Clare and Miles Mills Rose Garden wraps around the building's south side, in full bloom June through October, and welcomes visitors free of charge at any hour.

Running Saturdays from May through October, the Downtown Farmers Market takes over Court Avenue with more than 300 local vendors—Iowa-grown produce, artisan goods, prepared foods, and live music filling the street. Arrive before 9 a.m. for the best selection and smallest crowds. On mornings without a market, East Village cafés offer a quieter version of the same local-food experience.

You drive just northwest of downtown to Urbandale, where Living History Farms covers 202 hectares and recreates Iowa farming life in three distinct periods: a 1700 Ioway Native American farm, an 1850 pioneer farm, and a working 1900 farm using horse power. Costumed interpreters work the fields from May to October—you may see them plowing, harvesting, or slaughtering livestock depending on the season. Admission charged; allow a full half-day to explore the site properly.

places.name: Destin, FL

visits.text: Destin's East Pass was an accident. A hurricane in 1929 blocked the original waterway; locals dug a trench and the storm surge widened it overnight into the only direct outlet to the Gulf from the 13,856 km² Choctawhatchee Bay. This pass now pushes tidal water twice a day through a narrow channel - producing the impossible emerald colour that fills every Destin photo. Walk the HarborWalk promenade along the working fishing harbour: charter boats, open-air restaurants, live music most evenings. Free entry.

Henderson Beach State Park exists because someone stopped the bulldozers. The last undeveloped coastal scrub in Destin was acquired by the state specifically to prevent what happened to the rest of the shoreline. The park's surface sand runs up to 106 metres thick - the same quartz that makes every beach on this coast white. A nature trail threads the scrub behind the dunes; 60 campsites connect by boardwalk to the beach. Get to the boardwalk at sunrise before anyone else does. Fee applies.

Crab Island is not an island. It's a submerged sandbar - 30 centimetres to 1.2 metres deep at high tide - sitting just north of the Destin Bridge where East Pass meets the bay. The Army Corps created it accidentally in the 1930s when dredging deposited spoil sand in the shallows; by the 1980s boaters had found it and turned it into a floating social scene. Today hundreds of pontoon boats anchor here on summer afternoons. At high tide, Gulf water flooding in through the pass turns the sandbar a Caribbean blue-green that makes every photo look like it was taken somewhere far more exotic.

activities.text: Renting a pontoon from HarborWalk and anchoring at Crab Island is the defining Destin afternoon. The water is 30 centimetres to 1.2 metres deep - enough to wade, float, and let the current work. The colour peaks at high tide when Gulf water pushes in through East Pass; check the tide table before you book. Alcohol can't be sold at the sandbar but you can bring your own cooler. Book before 9 a.m. in summer; boats are gone by 10.

The Choctawhatchee Bay dolphin population is large and resident - sunset cruises from Destin Harbor find them reliably from late spring through fall. Most operators run two-hour evening trips departing around 6 p.m. In summer the bay is also nursery habitat for juvenile bull sharks and cobia; a good captain will point them out near the surface. Book at least 24 hours ahead in July and August.

places.name: Detroit, MI

visits.text: You stand in front of the little blue-and-white house on West Grand Boulevard—Hitsville U.S.A., the birthplace of Motown. Here, Berry Gordy Jr., who came from an African American family in Detroit and had worked on Ford's assembly lines, founded his label in 1959 with an $800 family loan and a quality-control method inspired by the automotive industry. From 1959 to 1972, Diana Ross & The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, the Temptations, and the Jackson 5 recorded their hits in the tiny Studio A—whose equipment, instruments, and creaking floorboards have been fully preserved. Founded in 1985 by Berry Gordy's sister, the museum is currently undergoing an expansion to reach 50,000 square meters.

The Detroit Industry murals—painted by Diego Rivera from 1932 to 1933 on the four walls of the Rivera Court—are the DIA's centerpiece and one of the most important mural works of the 20th century. Rivera depicted Detroit's auto industry in a socialist-realist style that glorifies workers on Ford assembly lines—at the very moment when the Great Depression was ravaging the city. The work is listed as a National Historic Landmark. The museum itself, founded in 1885, holds over 65,000 works in a collection ranked among America's six finest—including the first Van Gogh to enter an American collection, a Self-Portrait from 1887. The German Expressionism collection is one of the most important outside Europe.

Michigan Central Station is Detroit's great ruined cathedral - an 18-story Beaux-Arts station inaugurated in 1913 by Reed & Stem, the same architects as New York's Grand Central Terminal, abandoned in 1988 and left to decay for 30 years until its purchase by Ford Motor Company in 2018. The restoration, completed in 2024, made it a technology and arts campus while preserving the grandeur of the main hall with its marble columns, vaults, and restored stained glass. The station is now partially open to the public - check the program on the Michigan Central website.

You enter the largest historic public market in the United States—43 acres of a bustling market district, whose heart is formed by five large brick halls built between 1892 and 1966. Eastern Market began in 1841 on Cadillac Square before being renamed and moved to this site in 1891 when area farmers needed a larger space to supply the rapidly expanding industrial city. The Saturday market, open from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. year-round, attracts between 30,000 and 40,000 people in summer—Detroit families buying directly from Michigan and Ohio farmers. The district includes over 150 permanent businesses and surrounding streets are covered with more than 100 murals commissioned during the annual Murals in the Market festival.

Belle Isle is a 4-square-kilometer island in the middle of the Detroit River, a few minutes from downtown via a bridge, and has been a Michigan state park since 2014. Frederick Law Olmsted—the same landscape architect who designed New York's Central Park—laid out its gardens in 1883. The island is home to an Art Deco aquarium from 1904 (the oldest public aquarium in the United States still operating), a tropical conservatory, and remarkable views of both riverbanks. On Sunday mornings, Detroiters run and bike there in a peaceful atmosphere that contrasts with the city's noise.

Founded in 1965 by Dr. Charles H. Wright, a pioneering African American from Detroit, this museum is one of the world's largest museums devoted to African American history and culture. Its permanent exhibition And Still We Rise traces 600 years of history from West African kingdoms through the slave trade, slavery, Reconstruction, and the civil rights movement to contemporary culture. The museum is located in Midtown, steps from the DIA—combining both museums in a single day gives a deep and moving understanding of America.

You visit the three-story red brick building where Henry Ford designed and assembled the first Fords between 1904 and 1910—notably the legendary Model T, the first automobile produced on an assembly line for the general public, which went on sale in October 1908. The factory is smaller than you'd imagine: Ford had set up a secret room on the third floor, accessible through a hidden door, to design the Model T out of sight of skeptical investors. The building, listed as a National Historic Landmark, is managed by an association of passionate volunteers who explain with remarkable precision how the Model T changed the world.

You descend below street level onto one of the most original urban promenades in the United States—a disused railway trench from the former Grand Trunk Railway converted in 2009 into a 3-kilometer bike and pedestrian path connecting Eastern Market to the riverfront. The concrete walls of the trench are entirely covered with high-quality street art—one of Detroit's largest legal graffiti spots. The path runs past community gardens established on vacant lots and passes under several bridges that give it the feel of an unusual urban tunnel.

Greektown is one of the few ethnic neighborhoods in downtown Detroit to have survived decades of depopulation—a handful of blocks on Monroe Street where Greek restaurants have stood alongside grocery stores and pastry shops since the 1920s. Greek immigrants began arriving in Detroit in the early 20th century, attracted by the auto industry. The opening of Greektown Casino in 2000 revitalized the neighborhood, which remains a popular dinner destination for Detroiters today. The Pegasus Taverna restaurant, open since 1980, serves baked lamb and spanakopita in a traditional Mediterranean taverna setting.

activities.text: The RiverWalk promenade runs along the Detroit River for 8 kilometers from the marina to Belle Isle, the island park in the middle of the river. Detroit's geographic curiosity: it's the only major American city where you look south to see Canada - Windsor, Ontario, sits directly across on the opposite shore. The riverfront rehabilitation project transformed former industrial wastelands into a corridor of walkways, gardens, and street art spots frequented by Detroit families. In summer, free concerts take place along the shore.

Detroit's Midtown is one of the American neighborhoods where post-industrial transformation is most visible and radical. The 2013 municipal bankruptcy crisis freed up immense urban spaces that artists, entrepreneurs, and associations have reclaimed. Over 100 international street art murals cover buildings around Woodward Avenue and adjacent streets—some commissioned by Cass Corridor galleries, others by the annual Murals in the Market festival at Eastern Market. The vacant lots between renovated houses still speak to the Motor City's industrial heyday in the 1950s.

The Henry Ford Museum, opened in 1929 by Henry Ford himself on 29 hectares in Dearborn, for which you'll need to allow for a round trip from Detroit, is one of the most unusual and impressive history museums in the United States. It houses the Lincoln Continental limousine in which John F. Kennedy was assassinated on November 22, 1963, the Rosa Parks bus where she refused to stand up in Montgomery in 1955, the chair in which Abraham Lincoln was sitting when he was assassinated, and hundreds of locomotives, automobiles, aircraft, and agricultural machines. A museum that tells America's story through its objects, not just its great figures.

Corktown is Detroit's oldest residential neighborhood, named after Irish immigrants from County Cork who settled there in the 1840s fleeing the Great Famine. Dominated by the restored silhouette of Michigan Central Station—the Ford campus opened in 2024—the neighborhood is experiencing a remarkable renaissance with restaurants, breweries, and artist studios moving into Victorian houses and former shops. Batch Brewing Company and City Winery have opened in former factories, and Michigan Avenue has become one of the city's liveliest streets.

Comerica Park, opened in 2000 to replace the legendary Tiger Stadium, is one of the American League's best-loved baseball stadiums for its family atmosphere and view of Detroit's skyline. The Detroit Tigers, founded in 1894, are one of the oldest franchises in American professional baseball and have produced legends like Ty Cobb and Al Kaline. The stadium is nicknamed “The Corner” by fans in homage to the original intersection of Michigan and Trumbull where Tiger Stadium had stood since 1912. Even if baseball leaves you indifferent, a game night at the stadium with a hot dog and a local beer is an authentic way to end your stay in Detroit.

The Guardian Building from 1929 is Detroit's Art Deco masterpiece—a 40-story tower of glazed brick from Pewabic Pottery whose interior hall stuns on every visit: gold and orange mosaic vaults, polychrome marble from floor to ceiling, brass light fixtures. Architect Wirt Rowland himself called it the “cathedral of finance”. When Detroit was the world capital of automobiles in the 1920s, its businessmen built as if prosperity could never end. This hall is the most striking proof—and admission is free.

visits.text: Rock ground into dust gives Diablo Lake its color: Diablo Lake Overlook offers a vantage point for understanding this glacial landscape. Suspended particles account for the turquoise hue, which is often more pronounced during the summer melt. Choose a bright time of day and use the designated overlook without stopping on SR 20.

activities.text: If you want to leave the roadside behind, Thunder Knob Trail climbs through the forest to views of Diablo Lake. The trail passes through varied settings, from damp stretches to drier areas exposed to the sun. Start at the marked trailhead at Colonial Creek, bring water, and allow enough time to hike back down before returning to Concrete.

places.name: Dickinson, ND

visits.text: Pull off at exit 72 and turn north to see Geese in Flight first - certified by the Guinness Book of World Records in 2002 as the world's largest scrap metal sculpture: 33.5 meters tall, 47 meters wide, weighing over 78 tons. Gary Greff built all seven sculptures alone over 30 years, welding flattened oil well tanks and salvaged steel into flying geese, a tin farm family, deer, grasshoppers, fish, pheasants, and Theodore Roosevelt on horseback. Drive the full 51 kilometers south to Regent to see them all. At the end of the road, Greff converted his former high school into the Enchanted Castle hotel. Free access to all sculptures; donations welcome at the gift shop.

visits.text: You are standing on the original Boot Hill Cemetery site - the burying ground for men who “died with their boots on.” Front Street around you recreates downtown Dodge City as it looked in 1876, and the 20,000-plus artifacts in the complex include more than 200 original firearms. The Long Branch Saloon here is modeled on period photographs of the original, which opened around 1874, burned in 1885, and hosted the June 1883 Dodge City Peace Commission photograph - one of the most reproduced images of the Old West. In summer, gunfight reenactments run at noon and 6 p.m. The Kansas Cowboy Hall of Fame and a Gunsmoke exhibit are also on site.

Walk through the only limestone house in Dodge City and you are in the oldest building in the city still standing on its original foundation. Bavarian immigrant John Mueller had 60-cm-thick walls quarried from Sawlog Creek, 19 km northeast of town - the same quarry that supplied Fort Dodge - and hired fellow German craftsman William Strubel to hand-build the walnut spiral staircase, its newel post inset with bird's-eye maple. Built between 1879 and 1881, the house passed to only one other family: the Schmidts, who kept it until 1968. The desk where Dodge City founder Robert M. Wright wrote his 1913 book Dodge City: The Cowboy Capital is still inside.

Drive fourteen kilometers west of Dodge City on US-50 and you reach a National Historic Landmark where 3.2 km of wagon ruts survive across 57 hectares of unplowed prairie - among the longest and best-preserved sections of the entire trail. For 60 years, wagon wheels cut this path through the sod, sometimes four abreast. The ruts are most visible when the sun is low; visit in late afternoon for the best light on the depressions. A short interpretive boardwalk explains the site; it also preserves remnants of the 1880s Soule Canal irrigation project.

activities.text: Walk Wyatt Earp Boulevard and you are on the route of the original Front Street, where 16 saloons operated simultaneously during the cattle trade's peak years. The Dodge City Trail of Fame embeds bronze boot prints and narrative plaques for Wyatt Earp, Bat Masterson, Doc Holliday, and other figures from the era. The El Capitan bronze sculpture nearby depicts a full-scale Texas Longhorn steer, commemorating the five million head that ended their drives here. The Wyatt Earp statue outside Boot Hill marks the spot where Earp enforced the “Deadline” at the railroad tracks - south of which anything went.

Book ahead and spend the evening in the Long Branch, where a variety show has run every summer since 1957 - one of the longest-running seasonal variety shows in the country. Miss Kitty, singing bartenders, can-can dancers, and gunfighters re-enact the entertainment that Chalk Beeson's five-piece orchestra once provided nightly at the original saloon. The original Long Branch, named by owner William Harris after Long Branch, New Jersey, served Anheuser-Busch beer kept cold in summer by ice shipped by train from Colorado, and hosted gambling from five-cent chuck-a-luck to thousand-dollar poker pots.

visits.text: Day 5 - Your exploration of Brooklyn starts in Williamsburg, at Domino Park: the former Domino sugar refinery converted into an East River waterfront promenade, with industrial gantries preserved and Manhattan as the backdrop. A playground, tacos, deck chairs facing the water. A free introduction, 30 to 45 min.

Day 5 - Around Domino Park, wander Williamsburg without a plan: thrift shops and record stores on Bedford Avenue, street art on the cross streets, coffee roasters' cafés. It's Day 5's planned breather. On Saturdays, Smorgasburg brings together dozens of street food stalls by the water.

activities.text: A bagel or specialty coffee on Bedford Avenue, then window-shopping at local designers' stores: Williamsburg is best savored slowly.
To Dumbo: 2.2 km. Most pleasant is the NYC Ferry, East River line, from South Williamsburg to Dumbo; otherwise subway, 15 to 20 min.

places.name: Dothan, AL

visits.text: Welcome to the “Peanut Capital of the World”: half of America's peanuts are harvested within a 160 km radius of Dothan. This identity is proudly displayed—since 2001, over 90 peanut statues decorated by local artists have been scattered throughout downtown. Each stands 1.20 meters tall, painted to a theme (firefighter, police officer, Elvis, doctor, soldier…). Free map at the Visitor Center for hunting them down. It's kitschy, it's unapologetic, budget an hour on foot.

Officially the state agricultural museum, Landmark Park isn't a museum: it's a reconstructed working farm from the early 20th century on 40 hectares—a 1900 farmhouse, one-room schoolhouse, barn, blacksmith shop, and planetarium. Animals roaming free. This is what the region looked like 100 years ago, before industrial peanut farming. $5, 10 km north of town, two full hours.

The world's largest number of military helicopters under one roof: the U.S. Army Aviation Museum at Fort Novosel (formerly Fort Rucker). 160 aircraft, including unique prototypes—Vietnam Hueys, AH-64 Apaches, OH-6 Cayuses. This is where the U.S. Army trains all its helicopter pilots. Free admission, but access is through a military base: ID required, security check, arrive 20 minutes early. 25 km west of Dothan.

activities.text: Buffet for $14 at Old Mill Restaurant, where regulars have had lunch since 1980—fried chicken, ribs, vegetables of the day. For something more contemporary, Poplar Head Mule Co. downtown reimagines regional cuisine: fried chicken with honey-pepper sauce, mac & cheese with local porcini mushrooms.

visits.text: Dry Tortugas National Park - A Remote National Park: Located 70 miles west of Key West, this small chain of islands can be reached by ferry or seaplane, rewarding visitors with unspoiled beaches, exceptional snorkeling, and a massive Civil War fortress.

Fort Jefferson - The Largest Masonry Structure in the Americas: This hexagonal fortress rises from Garden Key, with walls built from 16 million bricks, but was never completed despite 30 years of construction. Its most famous prisoner was Dr. Samuel Mudd, convicted of complicity in Lincoln's assassination.

activities.text: Snorkeling the Pristine Reefs - Caribbean Waters in American Territory: The clear, protected waters surrounding the islands offer some of the best snorkeling in North America, with coral formations and tropical fish rivaling any Caribbean destination.

Camping Under the Stars - Sleep in the Shadow of the Fortress: Limited primitive camping allows overnight visitors to experience the islands after day-trippers depart, with star-filled skies unspoiled by light pollution.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

visits.text: Plan a day trip north from Dubuque to this 1,022-hectare monument, established in 1949, which preserves 206 earthen mounds perched along the Mississippi bluffs in northeastern Iowa. Of these 206, thirty-one are effigy mounds built between 500 BCE and 1300 CE in the shapes of bears and birds—a ceremonial practice found nowhere outside the upper Mississippi valley. Great Bear Mound measures 42 meters long and 21 meters wide. The Marching Bear group—ten bear effigies and three bird shapes—stretches for nearly 400 meters along the top of a bluff. Twenty-three kilometers of trails crisscross the site; admission is free.

Iowa's most-visited attraction is a Smithsonian Affiliate covering the history and ecology of the Mississippi River across multiple buildings at the Port of Dubuque. Six aquariums hold river creatures from giant catfish to playful river otters. Indoor galleries trace the steamboat era, the construction of locks and dams, and the culture of riverside residents through artifacts and interactive exhibits. The preserved Fred W. Woodward riverboat sits docked outside. Admission charged.

You walk along the riverfront to the only surviving shot tower west of the Mississippi—a 37-meter masonry tower built in 1856, listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The tower produced lead balls for muskets for just two years before facing competition from a St. Louis rival. After standing abandoned since 1911, it was restored in 2006. A historical marker tells the full story of its brief industrial life.

You board what bills itself as the world's shortest and steepest scenic railway—built in July 1882 by former Dubuque mayor J.K. Graves, who grew tired of the long carriage ride up the bluff to his home. A fire destroyed the original structure in 1884; Graves rebuilt it and opened it to the public. The ride up the 90-meter bluff takes about a minute each way, and the view from the top takes in Dubuque, the Mississippi, and the states of Wisconsin and Illinois simultaneously. Fee applies.

activities.text: The 65-kilometer stretch between Dubuque and Guttenberg is particularly spectacular: sandstone bluffs plunge straight toward the river, lock and dam structures appear in roadside parking areas, and small river towns preserve intact nineteenth-century commercial streets. Free access; drive at your own pace and stop wherever the view calls for it.

The Port of Dubuque's revitalized riverwalk and entertainment district wrap around the Mississippi River Museum at the foot of the bluffs. Stone Cliff Winery, housed in the historic Dubuque Star Brewing Company building, ranks among the most atmospheric dinner options in town. The view of the river and old warehouse brick at nightfall makes a fitting close to a day spent on the Mississippi.

places.name: Duluth, MN

visits.text: Check the freighter schedule before arriving at the bridge: when a 300-meter laker passes under the Aerial Lift Bridge, the deck rises to 36 meters in under three minutes. It's one of the few lift bridges still operating in the United States. The Maritime Center hands out the schedule—or search online for Duluth ship schedule so you don't miss a passage.

Step aboard the William A. Irvin, a 1938 freighter converted into a floating museum. This ship holds a record: 13,856 tonnes of iron ore unloaded in 2 hours and 55 minutes. You'll explore the engine room, officers' quarters, and the hull from the inside—an immersion into the industrial era of the Great Lakes.

Glensheen has 39 rooms and was built on the shores of Lake Superior between 1905 and 1908 for magnate Chester Congdon—original furnishings intact, carved woodwork, family china. The story takes a dark turn with the 1977 criminal case; the guides don't shy away from it. Book online; the full tour lasts 90 minutes.

If you're interested in trains, the Lake Superior Railroad Museum is worth a stop. It's housed in the historic 19th-century train depot with steam locomotives and period railcars. In summer, you can board the North Shore Scenic Railroad for a ride along Lake Superior to Two Harbors—26 km of coastline seen from the windows.

activities.text: Walk the Lakewalk from Canal Park: 8 miles of paved trail along Lake Superior, from Bayfront Park to Brighton Beach. The lake covers 31,700 square kilometers and you need to walk alongside it to grasp its scale. Along the way, keep an eye out for pebbles—Lake Superior agates, red and orange semi-precious stones deposited by glaciers, turn up here.

The Great Lakes Aquarium is the only freshwater aquarium in the United States dedicated entirely to the Great Lakes basin. Sturgeon, river otters, lake trout—native species alongside information panels on invasive species threatening the ecosystem. Ideal if it clouds over during the day.
