places.name: Eagle River, WI

visits.text: Eagle River Chain of Lakes - Welcome to the Northwoods. Eagle River boasts the world's longest chain of navigable lakes: 28 lakes connected by natural channels spanning 116 km². You can boat from one lake to another without ever touching land. The landscape is a mix of pine forests, lakefront homes, and wooden docks.

Downtown Eagle River - Classic Northwoods small-town center with fishing tackle shops, burger joints, and Friday fish fries (Wisconsin's breaded fish tradition). Summer vacation Americana at its finest.

activities.text: Guided Fishing - The lakes teem with largemouth bass, muskellunge, and walleye. Local guides offer half-day or full-day boat trips. The musky is the ultimate trophy - some specimens exceed 1.2 meters.

Kayaking or Paddleboarding the Lakes - Quieter alternative to fishing. Rent a kayak or SUP and explore the channels between lakes. The water is clear and relatively warm in summer (22-25°C in July-August).

visits.text: Step back in time at the historic Chowan County Courthouse, a remarkable Georgian architectural landmark dating back to 1767 that dominates Edenton's charming downtown skyline. This beautifully preserved building represents one of North Carolina's finest examples of colonial-era civic architecture and offers insight into the region's early American heritage.

Tour the magnificent Penelope Barker House, an exceptional example of Greek Revival-Federal architectural fusion built in 1782. This elegant historic home showcases period artifacts representing life in colonial and early American Edenton, providing visitors with a fascinating window into the town's distinguished past.

activities.text: Enjoy a leisurely stroll through Colonial Waterfront Park while soaking up breathtaking views of Albemarle Sound. The park offers a peaceful setting to appreciate Edenton's scenic waterfront and historic charm. Browse local artworks at the Chowan Arts Council, which highlights the creative talents of regional artists in this picturesque historic community.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

places.name: El Paso, TX

visits.text: Mission Trail - Three Spanish missions from the 17th and 18th centuries line the Rio Grande south of El Paso. The oldest, Ysleta (1682), is the oldest mission still in use in Texas. Socorro (1691) preserves beams decorated by Native American craftsmen. San Elizario, a little further on, about thirty minutes' drive from downtown El Paso, is a former presidio (fort) with a pretty arcaded square. Allow half a day for all three.

Franklin Mountains State Park - The largest urban park in the United States: 10,000 hectares of desert mountains right in the city. The Ron Coleman Trail (5 km round trip) climbs to a pass with a view over El Paso, Ciudad Juárez in Mexico and New Mexico.

Downtown El Paso - Step inside the Plaza Theatre (1930), a Spanish Colonial Art Deco masterpiece, even without a show. The area around San Jacinto Plaza mixes 19th-century architecture and street art.

Hueco Tanks State Park (en route) - Fifty kilometers east of El Paso, detour to these syenite rock formations containing over 3,000 Native American pictographs (the Tigua, Apache, and Kiowa peoples succeeded one another here for 10,000 years). The “tanks” are rock basins that hold rainwater—a vital desert resource. Reserve ahead: access is limited to 70 visitors daily.

Scenic Drive - Back in El Paso, drive up this panoramic road winding along the flanks of the Franklin Mountains. At sunset, the view of illuminated El Paso and Ciudad Juárez is spectacular—two million lights spread across the Rio Grande valley.

El Paso Museum of Art - If you have time before your flight, this small free museum presents a fine collection of Southwestern art: desert landscape paintings, Spanish colonial sacred art, and contemporary border art.

activities.text: Border Tex-Mex cuisine - Try red or green enchiladas at one of the restaurants in Segundo Barrio, El Paso's old Mexican-American barrio.

Final Tex-Mex meal - Before leaving El Paso, treat yourself to one last border feast. Green chile enchiladas (New Mexico green chile sauce) are the local specialty. The red-versus-green sauce debate is taken very seriously here.

places.name: Elevated Acre, NY

visits.text: Day 1 - Another end-of-day option: the Elevated Acre, an elevated garden hidden at 55 Water Street. An inconspicuous escalator leads up to a lawn with views of the East River and Brooklyn Bridge. Almost no one goes up; many New Yorkers don't know it exists. Free access, perfect for catching your breath for fifteen minutes.

Day 1 - From the Elevated Acre terrace, the ballet of ferries and helicopters on the East River provides the show. Wooden amphitheater, manicured lawn, sea breeze: a late afternoon snack or picnic beats many Financial District restaurants.

activities.text: Head down to Stone Street, a cobblestone alley lined with outdoor seating between the towers: a beer or a slice of pizza to recover from the day.
Walk to the Charging Bull: 500 m via Water Street then Broadway, about 6 min.

places.name: Elkhart, IN

visits.text: You enter a museum devoted to the history of recreational vehicles and understand why Elkhart County produces more than 80% of the world's motorhomes. In 1931, a resident named Milo Miller built a trailer for his family - he sold it before even reaching his destination, built a second, then a third, and never stopped. Today, more than 1,000 manufacturers and suppliers are based in the county. The museum displays a 1913 trailer, Mae West's 1931 housecar and the trailer built for Charles Lindbergh in 1939. Open Monday-Saturday, 9 a.m.-5 p.m., Sunday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m.; admission: USD 12 per adult.

You ring the bell at a Beaux-Arts mansion in beige limestone built in 1910 for Albert Beardsley—heir to a pharmaceutical fortune—and a guide shows you through 38 rooms that seem frozen in the 1900 Paris Exposition. The decorative arts collection is exceptional for a city the size of Elkhart: Louis XV furniture, silverware, Sèvres porcelain, and paintings from American schools of the Progressive Era, in a carefully preserved period arrangement. The French formal garden, freely accessible in summer, contrasts with the working-class homes of the surrounding neighborhood—an immediate visual reminder of the economic gulf between industrialists and employees at the turn of the 20th century. Guided tours Tuesday–Sunday, 10 a.m.–4 p.m.; admission: $12.

You turn onto the first side road south of Goshen and settle into a different rhythm: black horse-drawn buggies trot along the shoulder, houses without power lines line the road behind neatly trimmed hedges, and roadside stands offer vegetables and jams on the honor system. Elkhart County is home to America's third-largest Amish community, with approximately 35,000 members. The Heritage Trail Driving Tour is a 145-kilometer loop with an audio guide available to download for free from the local tourism office's website. Download the audio before leaving Elkhart—cell service is spotty on the county's back roads.

activities.text: You enter Wellfield Botanic Gardens from a former industrial site restored in 2010 and are immediately surprised by the scale of the project: twelve themed gardens range from Indiana's native prairies to formal water gardens, with steel sculptures commissioned from regional artists that change twice a year. A wooden walkway spans the central wetland—wait until dawn or dusk to observe gray herons feeding there in silence. Tulips and magnolias burst into bloom in April, irises and peonies in June. On July weekends, hundreds of families flood the paths—come on weekdays for peace and quiet.

You put on a safety vest and step onto an assembly line where technicians build recreational vehicles almost entirely by hand—from small camper vans to 15-meter luxury motorhomes. Thor Motor Coach opens its production lines to visitors on weekdays. Some high-end models contain more than 50,000 different parts. You leave with a radically different idea of what “made in the United States” still means in practical terms today. Book several weeks ahead—places are limited and tours often sell out.

visits.text: Day 1 - Twelve million immigrants passed through Ellis Island between 1892 and 1954. The National Immigration Museum occupies the original building: the Registry Room, immense and silent, conveys the scale of the place. The 45 to 60 min audio guide is included in the ticket. Plan about 1.5 hours on site.

Day 1 - At Ellis Island's Family History Center, you can search for an ancestor in the landing records. Watch the clock: if you board after 2 PM from Battery Park, you won't have time to see both islands. Last return ferry around 5 PM in low season, around 7 PM in high summer.

activities.text: The Hard Hat Tour (90 min, guided, in English) gives access to the island's disused hospital, including the autopsy room. Spaces are very limited, so booking well in advance is essential.
Return ferry to Battery Park: 2.3 km, about 25 min including the stop. From there, you can walk to the Battery Maritime Building for a connection to Governors Island if you're ahead of schedule.

visits.text: Newport State Park - Wisconsin's only wilderness park and the state's only certified Dark Sky Park. Over 2,300 acres of forest, 11 km of Lake Michigan shoreline, and 48 km of trails. Here, no paved roads or developed campgrounds - just walk-in campsites. The atmosphere is radically different from the more touristy rest of Door County.
Lake Michigan Shoreline - The coast mixes sandy beaches and rocky shores. The water is cold (even in summer, expect 15-18°C) but remarkably clear. Sunrises over the lake are spectacular.

activities.text: Newport State Park Hiking - The Europe Bay Loop Trail (8 km) follows the coast through white cedar and birch forest before reaching Europe Bay beach - one of the peninsula's most secluded.

Night Sky Observation - If skies are clear, return to the park after dark. Light pollution is virtually nonexistent here. The Milky Way is visible to the naked eye, and August meteor showers (Perseids) are a highlight.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: At the International Wolf Center in Ely, the exhibition traces the history of wolf reintroduction in the northern forests. The resident wolves can be seen through the large observation windows throughout the day - take time to sit and watch them.

Dorothy Molter lived alone for 56 years on Knife Lake, 25 km from the nearest road—the last non-Native resident of the Boundary Waters. She made homemade root beer for the thousands of paddlers who stopped by her place. After her death in 1986, her two cabins were dismantled and rebuilt in town to form this museum.

activities.text: Take time to paddle on the lakes around Ely before leaving. Local outfitters - Piragis Northwoods, Ely Outfitting - offer day trips by canoe or kayak without committing to a journey into the Boundary Waters. The best taste of the million acres stretching beyond.

days_plan.itin_title: Minneapolis, Voyageurs, Isle Royale & the Upper Peninsula

places.name: Ely, NV

visits.text: The East Ely depot closed in 1983 when Kennecott shut down the copper operation. It's remained virtually untouched since—supply rooms, offices, steam locomotives still in the yard. The Nevada Northern Railway is now listed as a National Historic Landmark and the 'Ghost Train of Old Ely' still runs certain weekends on the original tracks. Check dates at nnry.com—it's Ely's most distinctive experience.

The White Pine Public Museum displays over 300 minerals from the region—gold, silver, raw copper—and the replica of a cave bear discovered in the county in 1982, extinct 10,000 years ago. On your way out, the Nevada Northern caboose parked by the entrance and the reconstructed pioneer cabin in the yard are worth a look.

The Ward Charcoal Ovens look like six giant igloos lost in the desert, 29 km south of Ely. Eastern European immigrants built them between 1873 and 1876 to fuel nearby silver smelters. Each kiln stands 9 meters tall and produced 35 tonnes of charcoal per load. Free entry, on-site parking.

activities.text: Walk the Ely Renaissance Society murals circuit: over 35 frescoes and sculptures on the brick walls of Aultman Street, painted by artists from around the world since 1999. Each piece tells a story—a Finnish miner, a Basque family, a Pony Express horse. Map available at the visitor center across from Hotel Nevada.

places.name: Empire, MI

visits.text: You climb on your hands and feet through fine white sand that gives way beneath each step—the Dune Climb is an ascent with an 87-meter elevation gain on a 30° slope, with no marked path, just sand and sky. Everyone climbs. Many run down, their knees giving way beneath them in an involuntary tumble. At the top, you're not yet at the summit of the main bluff—you must still walk 3 kilometers across a sand plateau to reach the edge of the cliffs that drop away from a height of 140 meters above Lake Michigan. The water below is turquoise. The forest of birches and maples encircles the promontory. The Ojibwe say that the two Manitou islands offshore are the cubs of the mother bear who fell asleep waiting for them on this shore after crossing the lake from Wisconsin.

12 stops over 12 kilometers of winding road through the national lakeshore—the Pierce Stocking Scenic Drive is named after the local logger who laid it out in the 1960s and donated his property to the park before dying in 1976. Stop 9 makes your head spin: a wooden platform perched at the bluff's edge at an elevation of 140 meters, Lake Michigan before you, wind in your face, and below, white sand beaches that seem to belong to another planet. Stop 10, the Sleeping Bear Dune Overlook, shows the dune that bears the name—a wooded hill shrinking decade by decade through erosion, which will have disappeared in a few centuries.

Glen Lake stretches just east of the dunes - a 7-kilometer inland lake with extraordinarily transparent waters. You'll easily see the bottom at 10 meters depth in calm weather. The lake formed about 10,000 years ago when glaciers carved a depression in the rock then retreated. The two arms - Big Glen Lake and Little Glen Lake - are separated by an isthmus that Route 22 crosses in five seconds. Stop at the public beach to swim or simply put your feet in the water before tackling the dunes.

activities.text: The Empire Bluff Trail is Sleeping Bear's secret trail: less known than the Dune Climb, it climbs 1.2 kilometers through mixed forest to a promontory overlooking Lake Michigan and the northern dunes. The vegetation is dense until the last 200 meters, then suddenly opens onto 180 degrees of lake. In October, red maples and golden beeches frame the view.

South Manitou Island is one of the two Manitou Islands—the cubs of the Ojibwa legend—offshore from Leland harbor. The island is part of the national park and has no cars. It is known for its giant 500-year-old cedars in the Valley of the Giants, its 1871 lighthouse and its abandoned farms from the 1900s. In 2026, dock closures for construction suspend ferries to both islands: do not plan a crossing. From Empire, drive instead to Leland harbor to explore Fishtown, its wooden fishing buildings and its docks along the river.

visits.text: Day 3 - Midtown begins at the world's most-filmed summit: the Empire State Building and its open-air 86th floor, 320 m above the street grid. Tickets start at about $44; booking online is strongly advised. One observatory is enough today: this one or Top of the Rock tonight, not both.

Day 3 - The Empire State Building's Art Deco lobby and 2nd-floor exhibits, King Kong included, are part of the ticket: don't skip them. Best slots: at opening in the morning, or late at night, the observatory closing very late. Plan an extra layer, the wind blows hard up there.

activities.text: Budget and line tip: a late-morning weekday slot avoids the noon crush and the extra charge for sunset slots, which sell out days in advance.
Walk to the Morgan Library: 400 m via Madison Avenue, about 5 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

activities.text: A walking break is welcome after the switchbacks: Cole Street in Enumclaw offers a pause before you get back on the road toward Everett. This downtown street brings together shops and cafés in the city at the western end of Chinook Scenic Byway. Park legally, stretch your legs, and time your departure around traffic near Seattle.

days_plan.itin_title: Olympic, Rainier and North Cascades: 11 Days in Nature

visits.text: Ephraim Village - This postcard village is a lineup of whitewashed buildings facing Eagle Harbor. Founded in 1853 by Norwegian Moravian immigrants, it has kept its character - no bars or liquor stores (the town stayed 'dry' until 2016). Browse art galleries, shops, and cafes along the main road.
Eagle Harbor Sunset - In the evening, head to the village pier or beach. The sun sets behind Green Bay, illuminating the harbor's calm waters. This is Door County's most celebrated sunset spot.
Moravian Church - The small white church at the village center dates from 1857. It's still active. The adjacent cemetery tells the story of the Norwegian community's early decades.

activities.text: Bonfire and Fish Boil - Door County tradition: fish boil involves boiling Lake Michigan whitefish with potatoes and onions in a huge outdoor cauldron. The show's climax: the 'boil over,' when the cook throws kerosene on the fire to make the cauldron overflow and eliminate the grease. Several Ephraim establishments offer it on summer evenings.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: Essex Steam Train & Riverboat - Journey Through Time on Rails and Water: Board a vintage steam locomotive at the historic 1892 Essex Station for a 2.5-hour round-trip adventure through the Connecticut River Valley. Two operating steam locomotives pull various passenger coaches, including a seasonal open-air car, on a 12-mile journey to Deep River Landing.

Becky Thatcher Riverboat Cruise - Glide Past Castles and Covered Bridges: Transfer to a classic riverboat for a picturesque cruise along the Connecticut River, taking in views of Gillette Castle perched above, the Haddam Swing Bridge, and the ornate Goodspeed Opera House along the tree-lined shores.

Connecticut River Museum - Celebrating 410 Miles of Living History: Housed in the historic Steamboat Dock building in downtown Essex, this museum explores the cultural and natural history of New England's longest river through artwork, memorabilia, interactive exhibits, and guided river cruises.

activities.text: Essex Village - Connecticut's Most Perfect Town: This carefully preserved village consistently ranks among America's most charming small towns, with Federal-era architecture, yacht-filled harbor, and quiet streets that embody New England's maritime heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

places.name: Estes Park

visits.text: Arriving in Estes Park, make your first stop at the Beaver Meadows Visitor Center at the park's east entrance - the building was designed by Frank Lloyd Wright's architecture firm. Inside, a 20-minute film provides park context before you enter. Purchase your pass here if you haven't already, and verify Trail Ridge Road status (info line is 970-586-1222).

Then head down to Moraine Park, a vast meadow shaped by glaciers over 15,000 years ago. It's one of the park's best locations for observing elk, particularly early morning and late afternoon. In September-October, you'll hear the bugling of males during the rut - Estes Park counts approximately 3,000 elk in its surroundings and has even renamed October 'Elktober'. Don't try to approach too closely: elk are massive and unpredictable.

In town, pass by the Stanley Hotel. Built in 1909 by Freelan Oscar Stanley - co-inventor of the Stanley Steamer automobile - this white Georgian hotel with 140 rooms dominates Estes Park from a hillside. Stephen King spent a night here in 1974, snowed in, and drew inspiration from the atmosphere to write 'The Shining'. Kubrick's film wasn't shot here, but King produced his own TV movie at the Stanley in 1997. Day tours and nighttime 'ghost' tours are offered if the subject intrigues you.

The three-lakes hike from Bear Lake Trailhead is Rocky Mountain National Park's most iconic trail. In 5.8 km round-trip with 215 meters of elevation gain, you'll visit Nymph Lake (covered with yellow pond lilies in summer), Dream Lake (turquoise waters reflecting the cliff face of Hallett Peak, 3,874 m), and Emerald Lake (nestled at 3,082 m at the base of the massif). The emerald color of the latter comes from glacial silt suspended in the water. Allow 2 to 3 hours depending on your pace. Arrive before 8am to avoid parking saturation - a free shuttle from the Glacier Basin overflow parking operates every 10-15 minutes in season.

If you have energy after the lakes, Sprague Lake is a few minutes' drive on Bear Lake Road - it's a flat 1.3 km loop around a lake with superb reflections of surrounding peaks, accessible to strollers and wheelchairs. It's also one of the park's best spots for sunrise photography.

activities.text: Stroll the Estes Park Riverwalk along Fall River - a flat path that crosses downtown and runs past local shops and restaurants. It's ideal for a first evening at altitude (2,286 m) before climbing even higher tomorrow.

Optional hike to Lake Haiyaha from the same area: a junction between Nymph and Dream Lake leads there by adding 3.2 km and 107 meters of elevation gain. This fourth lake is less crowded and offers a wilder character, with scattered granite blocks on the shore. Ideal if you want solitude after the crowds at the main three lakes.

places.name: Eureka Springs, AR

visits.text: Eureka Springs was founded on July 4, 1879, around springs reputed to have healing properties - within two years, the town already counted 10,000 inhabitants, making it Arkansas's fourth-largest city. Since 1970, the entire downtown has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Walk through Spring Street and Main Street: the 500 local stone buildings lining the winding streets nearly all date from 1890 to 1910. Eureka Springs' peculiarity: its streets never cross at 90 degrees - the chaotic topography of the Ozarks made a grid layout simply impossible. Some buildings have entrances on different floors depending on which side of the street you approach from.

Thorncrown Chapel rose from the ground in 1980, commissioned by a retired schoolteacher, Jim Reed, who wanted to offer a meditation space to passersby who stopped to admire the view from his property. Architect E. Fay Jones - a Frank Lloyd Wright apprentice at Taliesin - imposed an absolute constraint: no structural element could be larger than what two men could carry through the woods, to avoid damaging the site. Result: a 15-meter-high chapel, 425 windows, over 550 m² of glass, built entirely of local pine. The AIA ranked it the fourth-best building of the 20th century. Come early morning or late afternoon - the light playing through the wooden lattice changes every hour.

Christ of the Ozarks is a 20-meter (65-foot) white concrete statue inaugurated on June 25, 1966, on Magnetic Mountain, commissioned by evangelist Gerald L.K. Smith. You spot it from the road long before you arrive - it dominates the woods from a ridge and remains visible for miles. Access to the site is free; if you're there in the evening, the lights illuminating it after sunset give it a striking presence. Nearby, The Great Passion Play has been staged every summer since 1968 - the most-attended outdoor drama in the United States according to the Institute of Outdoor Theatre.

activities.text: The Eureka Springs trolley system covers four lines and serves the entire historic center. It is by far the best way to explore the town without wearing yourself out on the hills - the winding, steep streets are hard on unwary walkers. A day pass lets you hop on and off at every stop as often as you like.

Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge is a 450-acre sanctuary that shelters big cats rescued from captivity - tigers, lions, leopards, cougars, primarily former circus animals or private ownership. Guided tours of the enclosures are offered several times daily. Allow at least 2 hours to tour it properly.

visits.text: Jetty Landing Park offers a look at Everett’s port before you head back toward the mountains. The site combines boating access, places to relax, and marina views near the mouth of the Snohomish River. Stay on the shore for this stop; do not count on an impromptu crossing to Jetty Island.

activities.text: Follow a stretch of the Mill Town Trail along Everett’s waterfront. The walk connects several landmarks of the city’s port history, including the area around the Weyerhaeuser building and the marina. Choose a short out-and-back walk from your parking spot to enjoy the shoreline without turning the evening into a long walk.

visits.text: Everglades National Park - The River of Grass: This UNESCO World Heritage Site and International Biosphere Reserve protects 1.5 million acres of subtropical wilderness, home to the endangered Florida panther and millions of alligators.

Shark Valley - Fourteen Miles into the Wild: Cycle or take the tram through sawgrass prairie to an observation tower offering 360-degree views across seemingly endless wetlands teeming with alligators and wading birds.

Anhinga Trail at Royal Palm - Guaranteed Wildlife Encounters: This half-mile boardwalk trail at Royal Palm provides some of the most reliable wildlife viewing in Florida, with alligators, anhingas, herons, and turtles visible year-round.
Flamingo Visitor Center - Where Fresh Water Meets Salt Water: This southern outpost provides access to Florida Bay's mangrove estuaries, with kayaking, camping, and dolphin-watching opportunities.

activities.text: Airboat Tours - Skimming the River of Grass: These flat-bottomed boats powered by aircraft propellers are the traditional way to explore the Everglades, accessing areas no other vessel can reach.
Backcountry Camping - Sleep Among the Chickees: Platform campsites called 'chickees' allow overnight stays in the heart of the wetlands, an unforgettable wilderness experience.

places.name: Fairbanks, AK

visits.text: Start at the Morris Thompson Cultural and Visitors Center, 101 Dunkel Street downtown - it's your essential first stop in Fairbanks. Opened in 2008 and completely free, the building houses 840 m² of permanent exhibits on Interior Alaska's Indigenous peoples: life-size dioramas, a reconstructed fishing camp, Koyukon Athabascan artifacts. The center honors Morris Thompson, an Indigenous leader born in Tanana in 1939 who died in the Alaska Airlines 261 crash in 2000 while returning from vacation in Mexico. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours to see everything, and grab your maps and local tips before heading out.

Steps from the center, Golden Heart Plaza marks Fairbanks' historic heart. The central statue - 'The Unknown First Family' - was designed by sculptor Malcolm Alexander to honor the city's founding families. Fairbanks was born in 1901 when a merchant named E.T. Barnette accidentally ran aground here with 130 tonnes of goods meant for other goldfields. The Chena River runs alongside the plaza - this is where early 20th-century gold seekers moored their steamboats.

Drive the Parks Highway back north: the road parallels the Alaska Range for long stretches, with open viewpoints toward the mountain chain to the east. Several pullouts allow stops - if skies are clear, the view south may give you a final glimpse of Denali at 6,190 m from the highway. In Fairbanks, stop at the Museum of the North on the University of Alaska campus: the building itself is worth the visit - designed by architect Joan Soranno in 2005, its angular lines evoke alpine ridges and auroral curtains. Inside, allow at least 2 hours: the highlight is Blue Babe, a 36,000-year-old steppe bison mummy, recovered intact from the permafrost in 1979. The park's gold gallery is the largest public collection of Alaska gold.

Late afternoon, Creamer's Field Migratory Waterfowl Refuge 5 km from downtown is a former 890-hectare farmstead transformed into a refuge for migratory birds. It's also one of the best in-town spots to watch northern lights in season without leaving Fairbanks - vast open fields, no intrusive artificial light.

Final morning in Fairbanks depending on your flight time. If you still have time, return to the Morris Thompson Center to collect your aurora certificate if you saw any - rangers issue it free. The Antler Arch, right next door, is an arch built from over 100 caribou and moose antlers collected throughout Interior Alaska - obligatory farewell photo. Fairbanks International Airport is 11 km southwest of downtown.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll along the banks of the Chena River. What you will see depends entirely on the month: between 17 May and 27 July, it never gets truly dark - Fairbanks enjoys 70 consecutive days of continuous light. From 21 August until 21 April, nights turn dark again and the northern lights can appear - Fairbanks lies directly beneath the auroral oval at 65° north. If you are here during aurora season, head away from the city lights towards Cleary Summit (32 km) or along the Chena Hot Springs Road for a darker sky.

Free evening in Fairbanks: Pioneer Park (formerly Alaskaland) is an open-air historical park with period buildings from the 19th-century gold rush, restaurants, and Indigenous craft shops - open in summer only. If you're here during aurora season (August 21 - April 21) and skies are clear, head toward Cleary Summit 32 km out for a standard viewing site, or continue along Chena Hot Springs Road for darker skies.

If your flight is in the afternoon, Chena Hot Springs (90 km east on Chena Hot Springs Road, fully paved) deserves a final detour: natural geothermal springs in a forest setting, and in all seasons an Aurora Ice Museum carved from permanent ice. In winter, many come to soak in the hot pools while watching the northern lights - an experience few places in the world can offer.

places.name: Fayetteville, WV

visits.text: You're overlooking one of the world's largest steel arch bridges: 924 meters in total length, with a 518-meter arch span, 267 meters above the New River—higher than the Eiffel Tower from its base. Built between 1974 and 1977 in COR-TEN steel that develops a protective rust patina without ever being repainted, the bridge reduced gorge crossing time by a factor of 40: it once took 45 minutes on winding roads, now it takes less than a minute. The bridge was the world's longest steel arch for 26 years; it has appeared on West Virginia's state quarter since 2005. The Canyon Rim Visitor Center offers the best view from its observation deck north of the bridge.

You walk the Long Point Trail (4.5 km round trip) to an exposed overlook on the south rim where you see the bridge from a different angle: the rusted arch stands out against hills covered with deciduous trees, and 267 meters below, the green river glitters among the rocks. Inaugurated as a national park in December 2020—the newest in the United States at that date—New River Gorge protects 28,500 hectares of gorges and Appalachian forests around a river that is paradoxically among the continent's oldest, with an estimated age of 320 million years. Wear closed-toe shoes: the trail crosses rocky sections and exposed roots.

You're strolling through this Victorian town of 3,000 residents whose historic center dates from the 1880s, when the region's coal mines ran at full capacity. Today Main Street is lined with outdoor shops, cafes, and several craft breweries that depend on adventure tourism. The granite cathedral of the Methodist church, built in 1903, and the 1895 county courthouse dominate the central square. Stroll in the evening after your day of activities to dine in one of the restaurants brought to life by the community of local climbers and rafters.

activities.text: You navigate Class III to V rapids, depending on the flow, at the bottom of a 267-meter-deep canyon—the most powerful rapids in the eastern Appalachians. The New River flows from south to north, against the grain of the Appalachian terrain, which attests to its age, predating the tectonic movements that formed the mountains. Passing beneath the New River Gorge Bridge and seeing it from water level, 267 meters above your helmet, is an experience in itself. Be sure to book several weeks ahead in July–August.

You're walking on a 60-centimeter-wide catwalk suspended beneath the bridge deck—924 meters out, 924 meters back, safety harness required, the green river 267 meters beneath your feet. This catwalk was originally built for structural inspection; guides tell you the story of the 1970s construction, the technical challenges of the COR-TEN arch, and anecdotes from Bridge Day—the third Saturday in October, when the bridge is closed to traffic and hundreds of BASE jumpers leap from the deck.

places.name: Fish Creek, WI

visits.text: The limestone cliffs of Cave Point drop straight into Lake Michigan: you stand at the edge of a ledge and watch the waves slowly carving the caves beneath your feet, as they have for millennia. This is Door County's most photographed spot. By canoe or kayak, you can slip into the low caves when weather permits; from the ridge trail, you can see up to 15 meters deep into the turquoise water. Arrive early in the morning before the fog or late afternoon for golden light on the limestone.

To reach the Cana Island lighthouse (1870), you walk across a stone causeway sometimes covered by water. The 22-meter white limestone tower is one of the most photographed of Door County's 11 lighthouses. The lighthouse is managed by the Door County Maritime Museum and open from May to October—the tower can be visited for an additional fee.

Peninsula State Park is the peninsula's largest park with 1,500 hectares of forest and 13 kilometers of Green Bay shoreline. Climb the Eagle Tower—a wooden observation platform—to take in Chambers and Horseshoe islands offshore. The Eagle Bluff Lighthouse from 1868 offers guided tours from May to October: the keeper and his family lived in these six rooms for decades of near-total isolation. Arrive early for the cliff-edge trails, packed after 10 am in July–August.

From mid-July to mid-August, the Montmorency cherry orchards open for pick-your-own harvesting. Door County produces millions of kilograms of cherries each year thanks to Lake Michigan's moderating effect on temperatures—the cherry blossoms in May are as spectacular as the fruit in July. Outside the picking season, farm markets offer jams, pies and juices throughout the year. Allow the morning for this outing among the orchards before heading to Ephraim for lunch.

Ephraim is the only Door County village founded by Moravian settlers from Prussia in 1853, who banned alcohol sales until 1969. You find yourself among rows of white clapboard houses, a church from 1857 still standing, and Anderson Dock, whose graffiti-covered warehouse has become a local art gallery. The sunset from the dock, with the colors of Green Bay before you, is unanimously cited as the peninsula's most beautiful—plan to be there around 7 pm.

activities.text: The fish boil is Door County's culinary tradition: chunks of Lake Michigan whitefish, potatoes and white onions boil in a giant cauldron. The finale is spectacular—kerosene thrown on the flames makes them leap two meters high to eliminate the fish oil. Then comes cherry pie. The recipe comes from Scandinavian and Finnish immigrants who fished here in the 19th century.

Seen from a kayak, Cave Point takes on a different character: you enter the caves at water level, beneath limestone arches, and the lake bottom appears through water so clear it seems there's nothing beneath the hull. Door County has more than 200 recorded shipwrecks in its waters—a testament to the sinister reputation of the Death's Door passage.

Crossing the Death's Door passage takes 30 minutes and brings you to the peninsula's only island inhabited year-round. Washington Island is known for its concentration of residents of Icelandic descent, drawn in the 19th century by a landscape that reminded them of their homeland. Circle the island on a rental bike in 1 hour and 30 minutes, then catch the ferry back in early afternoon to return to Fish Creek in time for sunset at Ephraim.

places.name: Flagstaff, AZ

visits.text: Grand Canyon—Mather Point—Even though the Grand Canyon isn't on Route 66, it's 130 km north of Flagstaff and skipping it would be absurd. Mather Point, right next to the visitor center, offers the first view of the canyon. 450 km long, 1,800 meters deep, 2 billion years of geological strata. Nothing prepares you for what you see.

Bright Angel Trail—You don't need to descend to the bottom (2-day round trip). The hike down to the first rest house (2.4 km round trip, 1 hour 30 minutes) already gives you a dizzying perspective. Warning: it's always hotter at the bottom than the top, and the climb back up takes twice as long as going down. Bring water.
Yavapai Point - The best spot for sunset. The strata shift from red to purple as shadows descend into the canyon. Arrive 30 minutes before sunset - spots fill up quickly.

activities.text: Evening in Flagstaff—This college town at an elevation of 2,100 meters is cool and pleasant even in summer. Route 66 runs right through the historic downtown. Craft breweries are plentiful and downtown is pedestrian-only and lively in the evening.

visits.text: Push open the unassuming doors of Muscle Shoals Sound Studio and enter hallowed ground where the magic of American music was forged by four visionary session musicians. This modest building on a busy highway witnessed Cher reinventing herself, Rod Stewart finding his raspy soul, and the Rolling Stones laying down three tracks during a legendary recording session. Stand on the same porch where Mick and Keith posed for photos, or recreate Cher's iconic album cover shot at the entrance to 3614 Jackson Highway.

Experience Frank Lloyd Wright's democratic vision at the Rosenbaum House, the only Wright-designed structure in Alabama and a pristine example of his affordable Usonian concept. The house was built in 1939 for newlyweds Stanley and Mildred Rosenbaum, and every element from built-in furniture to clerestory windows bears the architect's revolutionary touch. The intimate guided tour reveals how Wright believed families should spend less time indoors and more time embracing nature's beauty.

Pay homage to one of history's most remarkable women at Ivy Green, the Tuscumbia birthplace where Helen Keller learned to communicate despite being deaf and blind from infancy. Walk the grounds where teacher Anne Sullivan's patient devotion unlocked a brilliant mind, and visit the pump where Helen first connected the sign for water to the cool liquid flowing over her hands. The preserved family home and gardens offer profound insight into the determination that made Keller a global advocate for the disabled.

activities.text: Dig into golden-fried Southern comfort at Champy's, a roadside institution where chicken is cooked to order and arrives sizzling in red plastic baskets. The no-frills atmosphere of melamine tables and checkered tablecloths sets the stage for seriously good eating, from succulent bone-in pieces to tangy coleslaw and beans cooked in butter. Check out the vintage jukebox and neon signs while you lick your fingers.

Cap your Shoals exploration with refined seasonal cuisine at Odette, Florence's destination restaurant where locally sourced ingredients meet Southern flair in an elegant yet relaxed setting. The charcuterie board is legendary, with over a dozen artisanal cheeses, house-pickled vegetables, and cured meats that the server recites from memory like poetry. Reserve a table on the terrace for golden-hour dining.

Rest your head at the GunRunner Boutique Hotel, a gloriously quirky retreat carved from a former car showroom where an original Harley guards the stairway. Each of the ten suites pays tribute to local legends, from the Sam Phillips room honoring the Sun Records founder to spaces celebrating Muscle Shoals musicians and Billy Reid fashion. Guitars wait to be strummed, the rooftop terrace beckons for nightcaps, and the central bar feels like a rockstar's private living room.

days_plan.itin_title: Alabama Road Trip: Civil Rights and the Gulf Coast

visits.text: James Cook named Cape Foulweather (44.7625, -124.0664) in 1778 during his passage, because the wind from this 150-meter cliff seemed worth a mention in his logs. It still blows. The view over the Otter Crest Loop from the lookout is among the best on Oregon's central coast.

Climb to the top of Yaquina Head Lighthouse (44.6764, -124.0786)—built in 1872, 28 meters, Oregon's tallest, still in service. Tufted puffins nest on offshore rocky islets and Steller sea lions sun themselves on the basalt. Newport (44.6368, -124.0535) is two minutes away: head down to the historic Bayfront, sea lions noisily occupy the underside of the piers permanently, and the 1936 Yaquina Bay Bridge with its green Art Deco arches is one of the coast's most beautiful structures. Lighthouse ticket $7.

Stop at Devil's Punchbowl (44.7392, -124.0683), 10 km north of Newport—circular natural basin in the rock, waves enter through two side openings and explode at high tide with a “boom” you can hear from the parking lot. Tourists have been swept away by unpredictable waves here: stay behind barriers, especially if the sea is rough.

Heceta Head Lighthouse (44.1369, -124.1283), built in 1894, gets photographed from the road before you've even looked for it—the white cliff, the red and white lighthouse, the Pacific backdrop, the combination imposes itself. Then descend to Sea Lion Caves (44.1199, -124.1297) by elevator: 95 meters long, 38-meter ceiling, 300 Steller sea lions in permanent residence. The smell warns you before you reach the bottom. Ticket $16.

activities.text: Drive through the dunes at Oregon Dunes National Recreation Area (43.9000, -124.1500) in Florence—80 km of sand reaching up to 150 meters high, an extraterrestrial landscape that Frank Herbert drove through in 1958 and drew from for inspiration for Dune (published in 1965). Rent a dune buggy at Sand Dunes Frontier for $60-90/hour, or walk freely from Honeyman State Park.

US-101 between Cannon Beach and Florence takes 5-6 hours with all stops—it's a scenic drive day, not a race. Tillamook (45.4561, -123.8442) at the halfway point offers the Tillamook Cheese Factory as a free visit: local cheeses are renowned throughout Oregon, and the artisan ice cream is worth the stop even in cold weather.

days_plan.itin_title: 9-Day Pacific Northwest: Uncovering Hidden Gems and Cult Locations

visits.text: Embrace the relaxed, bohemian atmosphere of Folly Beach, where wide sandy shores, gentle waves, and colorful surf shops create an irresistible coastal vibe. The fishing pier provides perfect sunrise viewing as the sky transforms into a pastel masterpiece reflected on the water. This barrier island maintains an authentic beach town character distinct from more developed coastal destinations.

Explore the Lighthouse Inlet Heritage Preserve at the island's northern tip for striking views of the historic Morris Island Lighthouse standing sentinel offshore. Quieter beaches stretch along this protected area, perfect for long contemplative walks. The preserve's maritime forest and salt marsh ecosystems showcase the natural beauty that once defined the entire Carolina coast.

activities.text: Kayak or paddleboard through the salt marshes surrounding Folly Beach, gliding past egrets, dolphins, and hidden waterways that reveal the Lowcountry's ecological richness. The island's surf breaks attract wave riders, while the funky downtown area invites evening exploration. Folly's laid-back energy blends natural beauty with creative spirit in equal measure.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Road Trip: From Lowcountry Beaches to the Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Climb to Hurricane Ridge (47.9692, -123.5167) via Hurricane Ridge Road—27 km from Port Angeles, 1,600 meters elevation, road closed in winter. At the summit, the Olympic Mountains open in panorama, Vancouver Island appears to the north across the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and on clear days glaciers are visible to the naked eye. The ranger station offers easy hiking trails from the parking lot. Park ticket $30/vehicle for 7 days.

Stop at Lake Crescent (48.0644, -123.7993) on the route toward the west coast—the water of this 19 km-long glacial lake has a disconcerting turquoise transparency for a lake this size, 190 meters deep, with centuries-old cedars right to the edge. Lake Crescent Lodge (48.0598, -123.7917) dates to 1916 and serves honest lunch on the terrace facing the water.

Walk the Hall of Mosses Trail at the Hoh Rainforest (47.8606, -123.9347)—1.3 km flat, 30 minutes, and it stays in memory for years after. The temperate rainforest receives 3.7 meters of rain annually, Sitka spruce reach 80 meters tall and 1,000 years old, and mosses hang from branches like green drapes filtering an almost submarine light. The silence is total. It's one of the most beautiful trails in the United States, and it's 1.3 km.

activities.text: Take the Seattle-Bremerton ferry (1h, $18 with car) rather than going around via I-5—Puget Sound from the deck, Seattle shrinking behind you, the Olympic Mountains growing ahead. The terminal queue can be long in high season. Alternative: I-5 then US-101 (4.5h), faster but less memorable.

Stephenie Meyer economically resurrected Forks (47.9510, -124.3852) by setting Twilight (2005-2008) there—a town of 3,800 inhabitants in post-logging-industry decline became a tourist destination. Free self-guided tour at the visitor center, recreated Bella Swan house, dedicated shop. If Twilight means nothing to you, Forks remains the best logistical base for the Hoh and coast.

places.name: Fort Benton, MT

visits.text: The Grand Union Hotel opened on November 2, 1882, at a total cost of $200,000—the finest hotel between St. Louis and Seattle, built at the very peak of the steamboat era, seven years before Montana became a state. U.S. Army officers, Canadian Mounties, and highwaymen all signed the same register. The Northern Pacific Railroad reached Helena in June 1883 and killed the steamboat trade almost overnight; the hotel went bankrupt in 1884. Restored and reopened in 1999, it is now Montana's oldest operating hotel, with 26 rooms, many overlooking the river. Dinner at the Union Grille is the best meal along the entire route.

The Steamboat Levee stretches two kilometers along the Missouri through the center of Fort Benton, and this is where the trail becomes visceral. A full-size keelboat replica is moored at the levee; interpretive signs tell the story of Lewis and Clark's passage on July 13, 1805—the farthest navigable point of the Missouri and the last flat water before the Great Falls portage. The remains of the original adobe fort from 1847, renamed Fort Benton at Christmas in 1850, stand at the levee's north end. The bridge across the Missouri, standing since 1888, frames the downstream view.

The Museum of the Upper Missouri and the Museum of the Northern Great Plains share a campus two blocks from the levee and together cover Fort Benton's full arc — fur trade, steamboat era, the Whoop-Up Trail to Alberta, homestead boom, and ranching culture. The Old Fort Benton site next door preserves two original adobe blockhouses from the 1840s trading post — the oldest standing structures in Montana. Allow 75 minutes for both; combined paid admission.

activities.text: Fort Benton is the launch point for the Upper Missouri River Breaks National Monument, 240 km of Wild and Scenic River corridor that the National Park Service describes as the most intact section of the Missouri River traveled by Lewis and Clark. Float trips ranging from half a day to weeklong expeditions depart from here. Upper Missouri River Guides and Missouri River Outfitters both operate from Main Street.

Walk Fort Benton end to end in the evening when the light hits the levee cottonwoods from the west. The story of Old Shep — the border collie who met every train for five and a half years waiting for his deceased owner, becoming national news in 1939 — is told in a bronze statue near the levee. The entire walkable town grid: three museums, two river outfitters, a saloon, and the Grand Union Hotel, all within six blocks.

places.name: Fort Davis, TX

visits.text: Guadalupe Mountains National Park deserves a stop even if you don't climb to the summit. It lies several hours' drive from Fort Davis: make the stop on the way from El Paso. From the Visitor Center car park, the face of El Capitan rises 600 metres above the plain like a ship's prow, with Guadalupe Peak (2,667 m, the highest point in Texas) behind it. The park protects an immense fossil reef, formed 265 million years ago in a shallow inland sea. The Pinery Trail (3 km return from the Visitor Center) passes the ruins of a Butterfield Overland Mail station (1858) with no difficult climbing - ideal for taking in the atmosphere of the park in an hour.

Fort Davis National Historic Site is one of the best-preserved frontier forts in the American West. Founded in 1854 on the Chihuahua Trail to protect wagon trains, it became the base for Buffalo Soldiers between 1867 and 1885 - infantry and cavalry regiments composed of formerly enslaved people, who served under white officers. The adobe and local stone buildings are carefully restored; weekend historical reenactments are worth catching.

Balmorhea State Park, about 51 km north of Fort Davis, a 35-minute drive, is home to the largest natural spring-fed pool in the United States, supplied by the artesian resurgence of San Solomon Springs. The flow exceeds 15 million gallons a day, and the temperature stays between 22 and 24°C all year round. The water is exceptionally clear - you will swim alongside endemic freshwater fish. Book ahead: the pool regularly sells out in season.

activities.text: McDonald Observatory sits atop Mount Locke and Mount Fowlkes at 2,070 metres elevation in the Davis Mountains, 25 km northwest of Fort Davis. Jeff Davis County laws strictly limit light pollution - the result: some of the darkest skies in the continental United States. The observatory was financed by banker William Johnson McDonald's bequest (died 1926) and opened in 1939; the 2.1-metre Struve telescope was then the world's second-largest. Star Parties (Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday evenings, about 2 hours) offer views of planets, nebulae, and star clusters through telescopes. Book several weeks ahead in high season - dress warmly, temperature drops 10°C once the sun sets.

visits.text: Fort Lauderdale - The Venice of America: Over 300 miles of navigable waterways have earned Fort Lauderdale its nickname, with yacht-lined canals and waterfront mansions creating a unique urban landscape.
Las Olas Boulevard - Fort Lauderdale's Downtown Heartbeat: This tree-lined thoroughfare extends from downtown to the beach, lined with boutiques, galleries, restaurants, and sidewalk cafes.

Fort Lauderdale Beach - Where Families Replaced Spring Breakers: The wide, clean beach along A1A has evolved from its wild spring break reputation into a family-friendly destination with excellent hotels and restaurants.

Las Olas Boulevard - Galleries and Cafés by the Canals: In Fort Lauderdale, explore Las Olas Boulevard to discover its galleries, shops, and outdoor cafés. Then head to the canals to watch the boats and see the waterfront homes.

activities.text: Water Taxi - Cruise the Canals: Hop aboard water taxis that navigate Fort Lauderdale's intricate canal system, connecting waterfront restaurants, shops, and attractions throughout the city.

places.name: Fort Macon, NC

visits.text: Free admission, and yet Fort Macon State Park draws about 1.3 million visitors a year. The pentagonal fort, built from 1826 to 1834, was retaken by the Union in 1862 after a bombardment that cracked its powder magazine. Explore its 26 vaulted rooms with walls nearly 1.4 meters thick, then climb the ramparts for the view over Beaufort Inlet.

activities.text: Often calmer water than elsewhere: the Fort Macon State Park beach faces south, somewhat sheltered from the northeast swell. Lifeguards in summer, showers, changing rooms and no parking fee. Perfect for a family swim after visiting the fort.

places.name: Fort Myers, FL

visits.text: Fort Myers and Sanibel Island - Gateway to Island Paradise: This Southwest Florida region combines historic Edison and Ford estates with some of the most beautiful barrier island beaches in the state.

Edison and Ford Winter Estates - Where Genius Took Vacations: Thomas Edison and Henry Ford were neighbors in Fort Myers, and their adjacent estates now form an 8-hectare museum showcasing inventions, gardens, and the friendship between two of history's greatest innovators.

Sanibel Island - A World-Famous Shell Collecting Destination: Allow for a round trip from Fort Myers. The island's unique east-west orientation acts like a net for Gulf shells, creating what collectors call the 'Sanibel Stoop' as visitors bend down to gather treasures along the shore.

J.N. 'Ding' Darling National Wildlife Refuge - 2,590 Hectares of Protected Paradise: Allow for a round trip from Fort Myers. This nature reserve covers nearly half of Sanibel Island, protecting crucial habitat for roseate spoonbills, alligators, and hundreds of other species.

activities.text: Fort Myers Beach - Tiki Bars and Gulf Sunsets: Allow for a round trip from Fort Myers. This relaxed beach town offers classic Florida experiences with seafood shacks, tourist shops, and kilometers of sandy shoreline.

places.name: Fort Peck, MT

visits.text: Fort Peck Dam—the world's largest hydraulically filled earth dam, built by the Army Corps of Engineers between 1933 and 1940—created a reservoir with 2,450 km of shoreline through the Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge. Lewis and Clark passed this stretch on May 8–11, 1805, noting the Milk River confluence. The dam's visitor center covers both the engineering story and the boomtown of 10,000 workers that appeared and vanished in eight years during the Depression. Stop for 45 minutes, then continue west toward Fort Benton.

places.name: Fort Raleigh, NC

visits.text: When help finally returned, around 1590, Roanoke's 117 colonists had vanished. Fort Raleigh National Historic Site commemorates these English attempts from 1585 to 1587, as well as Virginia Dare, the first child born to English parents in America. Start with the 17-minute film “Roanoke” at the visitor center.

More English than an English garden: the Elizabethan Gardens pay tribute to Elizabeth I across more than 4 hectares on the waterfront. Created in the 1950s by the Garden Club of North Carolina, they mix period statues and Roanoke plants behind a Tudor-style entrance. Admission is paid separately from the national site.

activities.text: Every summer since 1937, except during World War II, Paul Green's "The Lost Colony" has been performed outdoors at the Waterside Theatre of Fort Raleigh National Historic Site. The show tells the story of the vanished colony just steps from where it lived. Check the show's website for dates and prices, as the schedule changes with the season.

visits.text: Fort Smith National Historic Site - Where the Wild West Met Justice: Walk the grounds where 'Hanging Judge' Isaac Parker presided over the lawless frontier, sentencing 160 outlaws to the gallows including notorious figures like Cherokee Bill. The reconstructed courtroom, jail cells, and gallows bring the brutal justice of the 1870s-1890s to vivid life.

Trail of Tears Overlook at Belle Point - Sacred Ground of Sorrow: Stand at the confluence of the Arkansas and Poteau Rivers where thousands of Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole people passed during their forced removal from ancestral homelands. Interpretive exhibits honor this dark chapter with dignity and remembrance.

Historic Garrison Avenue - The Longest Main Street in America: Stroll this 5-mile boulevard where Victorian-era architecture houses independent boutiques, galleries, and eateries in buildings that once served soldiers, settlers, and frontier justice.

activities.text: U.S. Marshals Museum - Legends of Law Enforcement: This striking museum overlooking the Arkansas River chronicles 225 years of the nation's oldest federal law enforcement agency through interactive exhibits and artifacts from famous cases.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Shipshewana and Amish country - Heading southeast from South Bend, stop in this village at the heart of the third-largest Amish community in the United States. Plan a round trip by car from Fort Wayne. Black horse-drawn buggies share the road with cars. If you are here on Tuesday or Wednesday, the outdoor flea market (May to September) is one of the largest in the Midwest. On other days, the craft shops and cheese shops are worth a stop.

Fort Wayne - Riverfront and Museum of Art - Fort Wayne sits at the confluence of three rivers (St. Marys, St. Joseph, and Maumee). The riverside Promenade Park is landscaped with green spaces, water features, and a canal. Two blocks from the park, the Fort Wayne Museum of Art occupies a 1920s Art Deco building and displays a collection of American art from the 19th to the 21st century—a quick visit but a good complement to the walk.

activities.text: Lunch on an Amish farm - Plan a round trip by car from Fort Wayne to the Shipshewana area. Several farms around Shipshewana offer “family style” meals served at a shared table: fried chicken, mashed potatoes and apple pie. Advance booking by phone is required.

places.name: Fort Worth, TX

visits.text: Fort Worth Stockyards: between 1866 and 1890, over four million head of cattle passed through Fort Worth - the city earned its 'Cowtown' nickname during this era. Today, the historic stockyards district hosts the world's only daily cattle drive: twice daily at 11:30 AM and 4 PM, period-costumed cowboys drive a herd of Texas Longhorns down Exchange Avenue. It's free and surprisingly compelling right in the heart of the city.

Kimbell Art Museum: this building designed by Louis Kahn, opened in October 1972 (two years before the architect's death), is unanimously considered one of modern architecture's masterpieces. Kahn designed sixteen cyclonic concrete vaults pierced by plexiglass skylights that diffuse silvery natural light—what critics called “a lighting system unparalleled in the history of architecture.” The collection is remarkable: you'll find a Caravaggio, a Velázquez and a La Tour, among others. Take time to sit for a moment—the quality of light changes with the time of day.

Sundance Square: 35 blocks of Fort Worth's historic downtown with perfectly restored 19th-century red-brick facades. If you still have energy after the Stockyards, this is the best place to end the day on a patio—the atmosphere is more urban and elegant, with art galleries and independent restaurants within easy reach.

activities.text: Honky-tonk night at Billy Bob's Texas in the Stockyards: founded in 1981 in a former cattle exhibition hall, it's the world's largest honky-tonk - 6,000 m² of dance floor, 40 bars and an indoor rodeo arena. Professional rodeo takes place every Friday and Saturday night. Arrive before 8 PM for a good spot facing the ring.

places.name: Four Corners, NM

visits.text: Stand at the Four Corners Monument, the only point in the United States where four state boundaries converge, allowing visitors to simultaneously occupy New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, and Colorado. The quadripoint marks a unique geographical curiosity that draws travelers seeking to literally be in four places at once. Navajo Nation vendors offer authentic crafts and traditional foods at the monument.

Photograph the bronze disk embedded in granite marking the exact intersection of state boundaries surveyed in the 19th century. While the monument itself occupies a remote desert location, the opportunity to claim presence in four states simultaneously creates memorable experiences and unique photo opportunities for visitors from around the world.

activities.text: Explore the surrounding Navajo Nation landscape where traditional hogans, grazing sheep, and vast horizons preserve ways of life stretching back centuries. The monument provides a starting point for adventures into multiple states, each offering distinct landscapes and attractions within short driving distances.

places.name: Four Freedoms Park, NY

visits.text: Day 3 - End-of-day option: Four Freedoms Park, Franklin D. Roosevelt memorial designed by Louis Kahn at Roosevelt Island's southern tip. A white granite triangle pointed toward the UN headquarters, framed by linden trees. Free access; the park closes one day a week, check before crossing.

Day 3 - The journey to Four Freedoms Park is an attraction itself: the tramway flies over 59th Street and the East River in four minutes, red cabins skimming buildings. On the island, follow the west promenade for the Midtown skyline at sunset. Few restaurants on site: plan dinner in Manhattan.

activities.text: Photo from the memorial's tip: the UN and Chrysler Building aligned across the water, ideal light late in the day.
Head for Queens on the NYC Ferry, Astoria route, from the Roosevelt Island landing, or on the F subway line: the ferry drops you in Long Island City, right by Gantry Plaza.

visits.text: Same name, different setting: Echo Lake in Franconia Notch is not the lake you visited near North Conway. Here, the water lies in the mountain pass connecting the Flume Gorge and Cannon Mountain areas. View the lake from authorized access points and check seasonal beach conditions before settling in.

activities.text: In Flume Gorge, damp rock walls and the roar of the stream accompany you along the walkways. The full route is about 3.2 kilometers long and includes uphill stretches and numerous stairs; the shortcut is unavailable. Reserve your time slot and bring sturdy shoes: the walkways are removed during the off-season closure.

You’ll take a short break at The Basin before continuing toward Vermont. This natural site in Franconia Notch lets you observe the water and rock formations without hiking the entire Basin-Cascades Trail. Follow the signs from the parking lot and allow enough time to return to your vehicle before the light fades.

places.name: Fredericksburg, TX

visits.text: Enchanted Rock is a pink granite dome that rises 130 metres above the Hill Country and dates back more than a billion years. It lies about 29 km north of Fredericksburg via Ranch Road 965, a 25-minute drive. It is the largest pink granite monadnock in the United States - 260 hectares of exposed rock. The Comanche, Tonkawa and Apache held it sacred: the rock creaks at night as it contracts after a hot day, a very real phenomenon that is still impressive today. In 1841, Texas Ranger Jack Hays held out alone against a band of Comanches from the summit, keeping them at bay for three hours. Book your entry in advance - the park regularly reaches capacity on spring weekends.

The National Museum of the Pacific War, devoted entirely to the Pacific theatre of the Second World War, is located in Fredericksburg because Admiral Chester Nimitz, commander-in-chief of Allied naval forces in the Pacific, was born here in 1885. The exhibition runs from Pearl Harbor (1941) to the Japanese surrender (1945) through weapons, vehicles, uniforms and eyewitness accounts. Allow at least 2 hours.

Fredericksburg was founded in 1846 by John O. Meusebach leading a group of German immigrants - the first convoy included about one hundred pioneers. Main Street preserves the heritage: Hill Country limestone houses, Sunday Houses (small weekend cottages built by farmers to attend church in town), and architecture straddling the line between Rhineland village and Texas town. The nine blocks of the historic center can be walked in 30 minutes.

Pedernales Falls State Park offers one of the most pleasant natural swimming spots in the Hill Country: pools carved into the limestone by the Pedernales River, with cascades and a backdrop of Texas oaks. The park is a little under an hour's drive from Fredericksburg, via Johnson City. Water levels and swimming access vary with rainfall - check conditions on the park website before setting off. The Twin Falls hike (3 km return) follows the river to two secondary falls rarely mentioned in guidebooks.

Luckenbach is a hamlet of three buildings - an 1849 post office-store-bar, a blacksmith shop, and a barn - serving as an informal country music venue. Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings made the place famous in the 1970s. On weekends, local musicians play under the oaks starting in the afternoon, no reservation or tickets - bring your chair and your beer.

activities.text: The Highway 290 Wine Trail gathers some forty wineries along 50 kilometres between Fredericksburg and Johnson City. The grape varieties that do best on the limestone and clay-limestone soils are Tempranillo, Viognier, Mourvèdre and Sangiovese. Tastings take place directly at the producers', often outdoors under oak trees - avoid visiting too many estates in one day, as the road is winding.

The LBJ Ranch in Stonewall, 25 km east of Fredericksburg, is the family ranch of the 36th US president, Lyndon Baines Johnson, designated a National Historical Park. You can see LBJ's birthplace, his grave beneath a grove of trees, and the private airstrip he had built for Air Force One.

The Willow City Loop is a 21-kilometre loop on a private rural road (open to the public) north of Fredericksburg, traversing the hills and granite ravines of the Llano Uplift. In April, you'll find here one of Texas's finest bluebonnet displays - the Texas bluebonnet, state flower - and masses of Indian paintbrush along the roadway. Outside bloom season, the landscape of rolling hills and walnut trees remains handsome, but the road is mainly worth the trip in spring.

Hamilton Pool Preserve is a natural grotto where a 15-metre waterfall drops into a turquoise-green pool carved into the limestone, about 92 km from Fredericksburg, a drive of 1 hour 10 minutes. Swimming is subject to regular water quality tests and may be banned after heavy rain. Reservations are required to enter the park - slots go several weeks in advance.

visits.text: Along the Sunken Road, the 1862 stone wall still stands, partly restored. On December 13, 1862, seven Union assaults broke against the Confederate lines here on the Fredericksburg battlefield. Start at the Lafayette Boulevard visitor center, the starting point of the driving tour.

Chatham Manor, a Georgian-style mansion, is part of Fredericksburg's national military park. During the battle, the Union army used it as an artillery platform, a hospital and a headquarters. Combine it with the Sunken Road on the same tour: it is only a few minutes away by car.

activities.text: Fredericksburg's historic district is worth parking the car for an hour. Old houses and churches still line its streets, and the town saw some of the earliest urban combat in American history. Drop into the James Monroe Museum, dedicated to the fifth president, then finish at Carl's Frozen Custard, a local favorite.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

visits.text: The Tower District is the neighborhood that makes you want to linger in Fresno longer than you'd planned. Built in the 1930s as a streetcar suburb, it centers around the Tower Theatre - a 1939 Art Deco gem designed by S. Charles Lee, the architect behind several legendary Hollywood movie palaces. The building cost $100,000 during the Depression, a staggering sum at the time, and seated 900 in an auditorium oriented 45 degrees from the facade. Now converted into a live performance venue, it hosts jazz, comedy, and rock shows. Stroll down Olive Avenue in the evening - the street closes on Thursdays for the night market strung with fairy lights - and take the opportunity to prep your gear before heading up into the mountains tomorrow.

Return to Fresno via CA-41 along the Sierra foothills - past peach and orange groves you may have flown over on arrival. Stop in Coarsegold, a historic Gold Rush village whose antique shops and rustic architecture deserve a few photos before you hit the valley floor.

If you didn't have time to see them on Day 1, revisit the Forestiere Underground Gardens - 65 rooms, grottos, and subterranean gardens hand-dug by Baldassare Forestiere from 1906 to 1946 across 4 hectares, descending up to 7 metres below the surface. The guided tour lasts about an hour. The site is closed from December to mid-March and on Tuesdays, so check ahead.

Final day in Fresno - take the opportunity to explore downtown, often overlooked but dotted with numerous murals and outdoor sculptures. Pedestrian Fulton Street cuts through the historic core and concentrates a handful of restored Art Deco buildings. It's also a chance to visit Armenian Town, the historic neighborhood of the Armenian diaspora that helped develop Central Valley agriculture in the early 20th century.

activities.text: Detour to the Forestiere Underground Gardens before heading to your hotel. A Sicilian immigrant, Baldassare Forestiere, spent 40 years (from 1906 until his death in 1946) digging with a pickaxe - no blueprints, no architect - a network of 65 rooms, grottos, and subterranean gardens across 4 hectares, descending up to 7 metres below ground. He planted citrus trees and grapevines that still thrive today. The site has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1977. Plan for about an hour of guided tour - book online, as group sizes are limited.

If you have kids or are simply curious, Fresno Chaffee Zoo is worth a late-day stop. It's home to more than 190 species across 12 hectares and notably features an area dedicated to Sierra Nevada wildlife. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours depending on your pace.

Before you leave or return your car to the airport, take one last walk through the Tower District. On Thursday evenings, the Olive Avenue night market, strung with fairy lights, gathers local producers and artisans - if you're leaving another day, the street's cafes and art galleries are worth a stop for one last Sierra coffee.

places.name: Friday Harbor, WA

visits.text: San Juan Islands Ferry — Cruise through the scenic San Juan archipelago aboard Washington State Ferries, weaving between 172 named islands and countless rocks. The 3-hour journey from Anacortes offers chances to spot orcas, harbor seals, and bald eagles.

Lime Kiln Point State Park — Watch for orca whales from this rocky shoreline on San Juan Island's west side, one of the world's best land-based whale watching locations. Three resident pods totaling 75 southern resident orcas frequent these waters May through September.

American Camp National Historical Park — Explore this southern San Juan Island site commemorating the 1859-1872 Pig War boundary dispute between the US and Britain. Rolling prairies, historic buildings, and seaside trails reveal the peaceful resolution of this territorial conflict.

English Camp — Visit the British Royal Marines encampment on Garrison Bay featuring restored barracks, blockhouse, and formal garden. The peaceful setting with white picket fences belies the tense standoff that nearly sparked war over a pig.

activities.text: Kayaking among the islands — Paddle calm waters between rocky islets watching for harbor seals, river otters, and porpoises. The protected channels offer beginner-friendly sea kayaking with dramatic scenery and abundant marine life.

Friday Harbor exploration — Browse art galleries, boutiques, and seafood restaurants in this charming port town. The walkable downtown maintains its maritime character with fishing boats moored alongside whale watching vessels.

Fresh seafood dinner — Dine on Dungeness crab, Penn Cove mussels, and Pacific salmon caught in surrounding waters. Island restaurants emphasize local ingredients with water views and casual Northwest atmosphere.

places.name: Furnace Creek, CA

visits.text: Stop at Mono Lake (38.0107, -119.0040) - 20 minutes south of Bridgeport on US-395. This 180 km² salt lake is 760,000 years old, about 50 times the age of Lake Geneva. Its water is 2.5 times saltier than the ocean and its pH of 9.8 makes it alkaline - unpleasant with prolonged contact but not dangerous. The tufa towers - vertical limestone formations 1 to 9 meters tall - line the lake and emerge from the water: they form when fresh spring water meets the alkaline water beneath the lake’s surface. Exceptional sunset over the towers, but you will need to leave beforehand.

Make a stop at Manzanar National Historic Site (36.7280, -118.1494) on the route to Death Valley—a Japanese American internment camp where 10,000 people were detained from 1942 to 1945. 66% of them were American citizens, innocent of any crime, interned solely based on their ethnic origin. The visitor center and reconstructed barracks are free, the visit takes 1.5 hours. The site is silent and rarely visited by Europeans—which is exactly why it deserves this stop.

Arrive at Furnace Creek (36.4622, -116.8669) in late afternoon—the administrative headquarters of Death Valley National Park, with a visitor center, two hotels, and a restaurant. Park admission $30/car for 7 days. The Inn at Death Valley (36.4528, -116.8369), an Art Deco palace from 1927 set in the desert, is the most remarkable accommodation on the circuit if your budget permits—$200–650/night. The Ranch at Death Valley is more affordable at the same site.

Get up before sunrise and reach Zabriskie Point (36.4202, -116.8118) 30 minutes before the sun comes up. The Manly Beacon badlands are lake sediments from 5 to 10 million years ago, eroded by rare rains into undulating multicolored ridges: yellow, ocher, pink, manganese green. The raking light of sunrise reveals the colors better than full daylight. Five minutes' walk from the parking lot, and the view is what Ansel Adams photographed here in the 1940s.

Head down to Badwater Basin (36.2298, -116.7679), approximately 27 km from Furnace Creek, a 30-minute drive - the lowest point in North America, 86 meters below sea level. Walk on the salt flats: perfect hexagonal patterns formed by salt crystallization stretching over kilometers. The “Sea Level” sign fixed to the cliff above the parking lot provides a sense of scale. In March-April 2024, following Storm Hilary in August 2023, ancient Lake Manly, 13,000 years old, temporarily reappeared here - a shallow sheet of water over the salt flats, since evaporated, but liable to return during extreme rainfall. Devil's Golf Course (36.2769, -116.8503) is a field of chaotic salt crystals: “only the devil could play golf here,” the rangers say.

Drive Artists Drive (36.3683, -116.8050) - a 14-km one-way road in the Black Mountains, hills whose mineral pigments create a palette: iron oxides in red, pink and yellow, manganese in purple, chlorite in green. Late-afternoon light reveals the colors better than full sunlight. Finish at Dante's View (36.2206, -116.7269) for sunset, allowing for the drive from Furnace Creek - a viewpoint 1,668 meters above Badwater, with a panoramic view of the valley from north to south. George Lucas filmed shots of Tatooine here for Star Wars: A New Hope in 1977.

activities.text: The drive down US-395 from Mono Lake to Death Valley (CA-190) takes 3.5 hours, with the landscape gradually changing—you pass from Sierra Nevada pastures to the high plains of the Mojave Desert before plunging into the Death Valley basin. A stop for fuel and water in Lone Pine or Big Pine is essential: gas stations are scarce in the park and prices there are twice as high.
Dine in Furnace Creek - the restaurant at the Inn or The Ranch, $60-90 per person. Sunset over the Black Mountains from the Inn’s terrace is worth the price.

Hike Golden Canyon (36.4202, -116.8467) mid-morning—5 km round-trip, a golden canyon sculpted by erosion, accessible and varied. The complete loop to Zabriskie Point is 9 km and connects two of the day's most beautiful spots. Leave before 10 AM to avoid midday heat even in fall.

Death Valley covers 13,793 km²—equivalent to all of Lebanon—and is the largest park in the 48 contiguous states. Distances between attractions are 30 to 100 km: keep your gas tank more than half full at all times. In late September and October, temperatures are 20–30°C. In summer, 47–54°C and 1 to 3 tourist deaths per year.

visits.text: Gainesville - A Hip College Town with Serious Natural Wonders: Home to the University of Florida, this eclectic city combines vintage shops, neighborhood bars, and artisan coffee shops with some of Florida's most remarkable geological sites.

Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park - Wild Horses and Bison in Florida: This 21,000-acre savanna south of Gainesville is one of the few places in Florida where wild horses and bison roam free across grasslands that once fed cattle drives to the port of St. Augustine.

Devil's Millhopper Geological State Park - A Sinkhole Garden of Eden: This 120-foot-deep sinkhole creates a miniature rainforest ecosystem where 232 steps descend past waterfalls and ferns to a primeval world.
University of Florida Campus - Architectural Beauty and Gator Pride: Wander through expansive greens surrounded by red brick buildings at one of America's largest public universities.

activities.text: Devil's Den Spring - A Prehistoric Underground Pool: This private spring inside a dry cave offers snorkeling and scuba diving year-round in water at 22°C where ancient fossils have been discovered. Allow for a round trip from Gainesville.
