visits.text: You climb Bouthillier Street to an Italianate brick house built in 1859-60 and presented to Grant by grateful local Republicans upon his return from the Civil War on August 18, 1865. Grant used it as his official voting address during the 1868 presidential campaign and visited throughout his presidency (1869-1877), returning one last time in 1880. His children donated the house to Galena in 1904 as a public memorial. Original furnishings remain throughout the rooms. Interpreter-led tours run Wednesday through Sunday.

You wander along Main Street past the DeSoto House Hotel, opened in 1855, where both Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas lodged and spoke during the 1858 campaign. More than 125 shops and restaurants occupy intact 19th-century commercial buildings along the steep half-kilometer corridor. The Galena & U.S. Grant Museum holds Grant memorabilia including Thomas Nast's monumental 1895 painting Peace in Union—2.7 meters tall and 3.7 meters wide. Museum admission charged; walking the street itself is free.

activities.text: Galena Cellars Vineyard lies on rolling farmland in Galena's Driftless countryside. The Driftless region — spared by the last glacial advance — gives this corner of Illinois and Iowa its distinctive topography: limestone ridges and stream-cut valleys, unlike the flat plains stretching south and west. The vineyard grows cold-hardy grape varieties; an outdoor patio offers sweeping views of the hills. A downtown tasting room on Main Street is also open every day.

You drive 30 kilometers east of Galena to Apple River Canyon, where the river has sliced 60 meters deep through Silurian dolomitic limestone—geology roughly 430 million years old, with fossils exposed along the creek bed. Five trails cover the canyon rim and valley floor, offering some of the most spectacular vertical landscapes in the region. Fee applies for park access.

Iowa Backroads: From the Missouri Cliffs to the Mississippi Bluffs

visits.text: Kansas Route 66 - 13 Miles of Nostalgic Americana: The short stretch of the Mother Road that runs through southeastern Kansas comes pre-packaged with vintage delights celebrating the highway's golden age.

Cars on the Route in Galena - Where Tow Mater Was Born: This 1934 service station inspired the beloved character from the Pixar film, with Tow Tater himself welcoming visitors. Nearby, a 1951 Hudson Hornet modeled after Doc Hudson sits beside the 1939 gas station housing Gearhead Curios.

Nelson's Old Riverton Store - 98 Years of Route 66 History: Pull a glass-bottled soda from the red metal cooler at this store that predates the Mother Road itself, having served travelers since before Route 66 was designated.

Kansas Route 66 Visitors Center - Sign the Guest Book Walls: Inside a restored 1930s-era Baxter Springs gas station, leave your mark alongside thousands of Route 66 pilgrims who've passed through before.

activities.text: Route 66 Photo Safari - Capture Vintage Americana: The concentrated stretch of preserved gas stations, motels, and memorabilia creates one of the most photogenic Route 66 experiences in the country.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Tour: Prairies and the Wild West

visits.text: The Strand, Galveston's main historic district street, was nicknamed the 'Wall Street of the South' in the late 19th century - Galveston was then the largest city in Texas and the world's leading cotton port. On September 8, 1900, a Category 4 hurricane swept across the island with 130-mph winds and a 15-foot storm surge. The catastrophe claimed roughly 8,000 lives - estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000 - and remains the worst natural disaster in United States history. The Victorian buildings that survived along The Strand are now restored. Stroll the sidewalk and study the cast-iron facades: some details date from the 1880s.

Bishop's Palace, on Broadway Avenue, is one of the most spectacular Victorian mansions in the United States. Built between 1887 and 1892 by architect Nicholas Clayton for the Gresham family, then purchased by the Catholic Diocese of Galveston in 1923, it survived the 1900 hurricane thanks to its stone and steel structure. The interior - paneling in different precious woods, carved fireplaces, stained glass - has remained virtually intact since construction. Allow 45 minutes for the guided tour.

The Galveston Seawall, built starting in 1902 following the hurricane, now measures over 10 miles long and 17 feet high - one of the largest civil engineering projects in American history. Simultaneously, the entire city was raised several feet by sand pumping. The seawall runs along Seawall Boulevard, lined with seafood restaurants and bars. If you're there in the evening, the raking light on the Gulf from the seawall is magnificent.

activities.text: Galveston Island's beaches stretch 32 miles. East Beach and Stewart Beach, on the island's east end, are the liveliest with facilities and restaurants. Gulf water reaches 80-86°F from June through September. Watch out for jellyfish in summer - an anti-jellyfish spray sold locally can make swimming more comfortable.

Operators based at Galveston Harbor run boat tours to observe bottlenose dolphins in Galveston Bay. These dolphins are year-round residents in the Gulf's shallow waters. Morning tours offer the best viewing chances, before maritime traffic disturbs the pods.

visits.text: Hubbell Trading Post has been part of trade in Ganado since 1878; the historic store continues to sell goods and crafts. activities.text: You can try the visitor loom at Hubbell Trading Post if the area is accessible during your visit. visits.text: Yellowstone National Park North Entrance — Enter America's first national park through the Roosevelt Arch built in 1903. The Montana gateway provides access to Mammoth Hot Springs and Lamar Valley wildlife viewing.

Mammoth Hot Springs—Explore terraces of travertine formed by hot springs depositing calcium carbonate. The ever-changing formations create rainbow-colored steps where thermophilic bacteria produce brilliant hues.

Lamar Valley—Scan North America's Serengeti for wolves, grizzlies, bison, and moose. This glacial valley offers the park's best wildlife viewing, with herds visible across open sagebrush landscapes. Allow for a round trip by car from Gardiner to reach the valley.

Tower Fall — Photograph this 40-meter waterfall plunging from volcanic pinnacles. This waterfall is named after the tower-shaped formations that drop into the Yellowstone River canyon. Allow for a round trip by car from Gardiner to reach the site.

activities.text: Wildlife photography during golden hour—Get into position at dawn or dusk when animals are most active and lighting is optimal. Lamar Valley and Hayden Valley offer the best opportunities.
Gardiner riverside dining—Enjoy moose steaks and bison burgers at restaurants overlooking the Yellowstone River. This park gateway town retains its Western character.

places.name: Gary, IN

visits.text: You park in front of a 1930s Art Deco building facing Lake Michigan and discover one of America's least-known historic landmarks. This National Historic Landmark honors Octave Chanute—a French-American engineer who conducted the world's first glider flight tests here from the dunes of Miller Beach in 1896, laying theoretical foundations that directly inspired the Wright brothers. The second floor hosts an exhibition on the Tuskegee Airmen, America's first African American military pilots. The terrace overlooking the lake offers an unobstructed view of Chicago, 45 kilometers away, on clear days. Marquette Park beach is free and accessible at all times—one of Indiana's finest, five minutes from the highway.

You park in front of a 40-square-meter brick house on an ordinary residential street and read the commemorative plaque on the facade: this is where the nine Jackson family children were born and raised, including Michael in 1958. The family left Gary in 1969 for Los Angeles, the same year the Jackson 5 signed their first contract with Motown Records in Detroit. The address—2300 Jackson Street—likely inspired the siblings' stage name, though no source confirms this officially. The house is private and not open to visitors; the exterior can be freely photographed from the public sidewalk. The surrounding neighborhood provides a concrete illustration of Gary's economic decline since the 1970s.

You cross Miller Beach—a neighborhood of artists' bungalows sandwiched between the national park's dunes and the steel mills—and emerge onto a white sand beach within the national park's boundaries. The visual paradox is one of the Midwest's most striking: to your left, Gary Works' industrial towers smoke day and night; to your right, wooded dunes; before you, Lake Michigan. It was on these very dunes that Octave Chanute experimented with his gliders in 1896. Come at sunset—orange light reflects on the water between the steel towers, and the contrast produces one of Indiana's most astonishing photos.

activities.text: You head up Washington Street toward downtown Gary and look up at City Methodist Church—a 1926 neo-Gothic church built for 1,500 worshippers, abandoned in the 1970s, and since colonized by trees piercing its collapsed ceiling. Its Gothic arches overgrown with vegetation have been photographed by artists worldwide, making Gary one of America's most documented post-industrial sites. The former Union Station, Palace Theater, and rows of condemned Victorian houses bear witness to a city that had 100,000 residents in 1930 and has lost half of them. All this is visible from public streets during the day—stay on the main roads.

You follow Lake Shore Drive westward and glimpse, from the public road, the titanic structures of Gary Works—a forest of blast furnaces and cooling towers set directly on Lake Michigan's shore. Founded in March 1906 by U.S. Steel on leveled marshes and dunes, this mill was built in less than two years with an entire city constructed around it to house its workers. At its 1953 peak, Gary Works produced over 35 million tonnes of steel annually and employed 32,000 people. Today North America's largest steel complex, it has a workforce reduced to a few thousand. Stop at dusk—the scene of lake, dunes, and heavy industry resembles nothing else in America.

visits.text: Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Explore America's most visited national park protecting 2,114 square kilometers of ancient mountains. The UNESCO World Heritage Site preserves old-growth forests, diverse wildlife including black bears, and over 2,100 kilometers of streams.

Cades Cove — Allow a day trip from Gatlinburg to drive the 18-kilometer loop through this historic valley, with its preserved 19th-century farms, churches, and gristmills. White-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and black bears visit the mountain-framed meadows. From May to September, the loop is closed to cars on Wednesdays.

Kuwohi (formerly Clingmans Dome) — Take the seasonal road to the parking lot below the park’s highest point at 2,025 meters, then walk to the observation tower for 360-degree views. The paved half-mile trail climbs 100 meters through spruce-fir forest. The access road closes in winter.

Cataract Falls — From Sugarlands Visitor Center near Gatlinburg, follow the woodland trail to this waterfall on a 1.1-kilometer round-trip walk. Watch the water tumble over the rocks before returning to the visitor center. Laurel Falls Trail remains closed for renovation.

activities.text: Wildlife watching — Look for black bears at dawn or dusk in Cades Cove. At Elkmont, synchronous fireflies appear mainly in late May and early June; access to the area during their peak period requires a reservation. Allow for the journey from Gatlinburg to see them.
Gatlinburg strip exploration — Browse Appalachian crafts, moonshine tastings, and family attractions. The mountain resort town offers tourist amenities and Smoky Mountain access.

visits.text: Stroll along Georgetown's Front Street, the main corridor of this remarkably preserved historic district running parallel to the Sampit River. Eighteenth and nineteenth-century buildings frame the waterfront, creating one of the most relaxed and picturesque settings in the Lowcountry. The town's unhurried pace and architectural character transport visitors to an earlier era of Southern coastal life.

Visit the Rice Museum housed in the historic Old Market Building, examining the role of rice cultivation in shaping South Carolina's economy and culture. Georgetown once served as the center of the colonial rice industry, and the museum's exhibits illuminate this pivotal chapter of regional history. The bell tower overlooking the waterfront has become an iconic symbol of the town.

activities.text: Walk the Harborwalk Marina at sunset, where open waterfront paths provide views of the Sampit River and surrounding marshlands. The measured, unhurried atmosphere invites lingering strolls past historic buildings and working boats. Georgetown's authentic character offers an alternative to busier coastal destinations while maintaining easy access to surrounding beaches and natural areas.

places.name: Gettysburg, PA

visits.text: You begin your Gettysburg visit at the Museum and Visitor Center, the essential starting point for understanding the deadliest battle of the Civil War. From July 1 to 3, 1863, Union and Confederate armies clashed here on the hills and fields of Pennsylvania, leaving more than 51,000 dead, wounded, or missing in three days. The museum preserves the Cyclorama - a 360-degree panoramic painting 111 meters in circumference depicting Pickett's Charge on July 3. The introductory film, produced by History Channel, effectively prepares you for the battlefield visit. Book tickets online; the museum is open 8am to 5pm March through November, 9am to 4pm in winter.

The 24-square-kilometer Gettysburg battlefield is traversed by more than 64 kilometers of roads dotted with 1,300 monuments, 400 cannons, and 148 historic buildings, making it one of the largest outdoor sculpture collections in the world. You climb Little Round Top, the hill whose defense by Colonel Joshua Chamberlain on July 2 saved the Union line, then descend into the jagged rocks of Devil's Den, scene of fierce fighting by Confederate sharpshooters. The Virginia Memorial marks the starting position of Pickett's Charge, that desperate frontal assault across a kilometer of open field on July 3, which cost the Confederacy more than 6,000 men in less than an hour. Hire an official Licensed Battlefield Guide for a 2-hour car tour (about $80), or download the NPS app for a self-guided tour.

The Soldiers' National Cemetery, consecrated on November 19, 1863, is where Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address - one of the shortest and most powerful speeches in world political history, 272 words that redefined the meaning of the war and the nation. The cemetery holds more than 3,500 Union soldiers, including hundreds of unknowns identified by their state of origin. The headstones arranged in concentric semicircles create a particular solemnity. Come in late afternoon, when the tour buses have left and the place regains its calm - the low light on the rows of white stones is striking.

activities.text: The Gettysburg bike tour is a different experience from the car tour: you cross the same fields as the soldiers, you feel the slope of the hills, and you physically understand why Little Round Top was so strategic to hold, and why Pickett's Charge across a kilometer of open ground was a near-suicidal mission. GettysBike offers guided or self-guided tours with electric bikes for those wanting to conserve energy. The battlefield is dotted with interpretive signs and QR codes linked to the NPS app. Arrive early in the morning: battlefield roads are quiet before 9am and crossing the misty fields in the dawn light is memorable.

Gettysburg is reputed to be one of the most haunted towns in the United States, and it would be hard to doubt after three days of carnage on its soil. Candlelit Ghost Tours at night walk through downtown streets and around former field hospitals, recounting stories of soldiers who died on site and testimonies from current residents. Whether you believe in ghosts or not, the nighttime setting of historic downtown Gettysburg, its 19th-century houses, and the quality of historical narratives accompanying the paranormal anecdotes make the outing worthwhile.

visits.text: Alaska Marine Highway Ferry - The six-hour crossing from Valdez to Whittier traverses Prince William Sound aboard state-operated ferries that accommodate vehicles and passengers. This scenic voyage passes glaciers, forested islands, and abundant marine wildlife, with onboard naturalists during summer months providing interpretation.

Whittier - This unusual community is housed almost entirely in two large buildings, a legacy of its World War II military origins. The town serves as the main port for Prince William Sound cruises and gives access to the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel, the longest combined road-rail tunnel in North America at 4 kilometers. It is about 40 km from Girdwood, a 35-minute drive.

Portage Valley - The road from Whittier runs through this glacier-carved valley, home to the visitor facilities managed by the U.S. Forest Service. Portage Glacier, which has retreated considerably in recent decades, offers an example of the impacts of climate change.

activities.text: Girdwood Resort Area - Nestled in the Chugach Mountains 65 kilometers south of Anchorage, this four-season resort community offers aerial tram rides to an elevation of 700 meters for panoramic views, hiking trails through temperate rainforest, and access to alpine and coastal ecosystems.

visits.text: Glacier Point turns the valley into a scale model from nearly 980 meters above Curry Village. Half Dome stands out almost at eye level, while waterfalls appear in nearby valleys. Follow the short developed path to the overlook and check that the road is open before leaving: snow closes this access in winter.

If waterfalls appeal to you more than cliffs, stop at Washburn Point too. This nearby overlook offers a more direct view of Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall than Glacier Point does. Make this brief stop on the way down, using the designated parking area, then continue toward Wawona; do not try to find a walking route between the rocky ledges.

visits.text: You pull into Makoshika State Park - the name comes from Lakota, meaning “bad land” - and the landscape justifies it: hoodoos, caprocks, fluted hillsides, and natural bridges carved from Hell Creek Formation sandstone. Over ten dinosaur species have been found here, including T. rex and Triceratops. A 270-kilogram juvenile female Triceratops skull, excavated during a 1990-91 dig led by paleontologist Diane Gabriel, is on display at the visitor center. In 1997, Jack Horner and Bob Harmon found a nearly complete Thescelosaurus skeleton here. The K-T boundary line - the geological marker of the mass extinction 66 million years ago - is visible in the rock walls. Fee applies for non-Montana residents.

Stop at the Frontier Gateway Museum in downtown Glendive. It houses a full-size skeleton cast of “Margie”, a Struthiomimus found near Glendive, plus exhibits on the Yellowstone River, the town's railroad history, and the cattle era. William Clark described these badlands in his journal on July 30, 1806, calling them the “birnt hills” - the pale sandstone cliffs visible today from the river. Free or low-cost admission.

Walk down to the Yellowstone River at Jaycee Park. This stretch is one of the best places in Montana to find Yellowstone agates - semi-precious stones formed in gas pockets in volcanic rock and polished over millennia by the current. The river is broad and shallow with sandbars good for wading; late summer exposes the most gravel. No permit required for personal quantities.

activities.text: Drive the Makoshika scenic road through the heart of the badlands and stop at Sand Creek Overlook and Artist Vista Overlook. The light changes the color of the formations dramatically throughout the day; late afternoon turns the rock faces from gray-brown to deep orange. The disc golf course runs right through the badlands, which gives a sense of scale even if you don't play. Passable by regular vehicle in dry conditions.

Go agate hunting on Yellowstone gravel bars east of Glendive. Look for stones with translucent banding or a waxy sheen at public river access sites maintained by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks. Bring wading shoes and a bucket. The best bars are exposed at low water in late summer. No permit required for personal quantities.

visits.text: Leave New Orleans via River Road (LA-18) heading west—this route follows the Mississippi for 120 km between NOLA and Baton Rouge. Before the Civil War, this was one of America's wealthiest regions: sugarcane plantations stretched as far as the eye could see. First stop, 50 km away: Whitney Plantation in Wallace. This is Louisiana's only museum entirely dedicated to the history of slavery. Three memorials, period slave cabins, and an 1870 church built by formerly enslaved people tell the story of those forced to live and work here. The guided tour lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes—it's intense and necessary.

Continue 25 km to Vacherie for Oak Alley Plantation, Louisiana's most famous. Its avenue of 28 live oaks planted in the early 18th century forms a quarter-mile tunnel of greenery between the road and the house. The Greek Revival mansion dates from 1839, built by Jacques Roman. Six replica slave cabins have been reconstructed based on archaeological excavations, and the walls bear the names of more than 220 people enslaved on this property between 1836 and 1865.

6 km from Oak Alley, Laura Plantation offers a striking contrast. This is a Creole plantation—no white columns here, but a colorful cypress wood house raised on brick pillars in Louisiana vernacular style. The estate dates from 1805 and was managed by Creole women for four generations. The tour's narrative is based on the manuscript of Laura Locoul, born here in 1861. This is also where the Br'er Rabbit stories were collected, as told by the plantation's enslaved Senegalese people.

activities.text: Head to Gonzales for the night. Gonzales calls itself the “Jambalaya Capital of the World” - if you find a local restaurant open, order some and judge for yourself.

visits.text: Day 1 - Optional if time permits: Governors Island, a former military base turned park, a few minutes by boat from the Battery Maritime Building. The artificial hills of The Hills give a head-on view of the statue and harbor. Bike rentals, lawns, hammocks: the perfect breather after the morning lines.

Day 1 - Fort Jay and Castle Williams, two early 19th-century fortifications, are freely accessible on Governors Island. The island can be walked in a good hour. It closes early evening: check the last boat schedule before settling into the grass.

activities.text: Ride the giant slides of Slide Hill, among the longest in New York: free, and not reserved for children.
Return by boat to Manhattan, then head to the Elevated Acre: 1.7 km in total; allow about 25 min including the crossing and walk.

places.name: Grand Canyon Of The Yellowstone, WY

visits.text: At Artist Point, you hear the roar before your eyes settle on Lower Falls. The yellow and pink walls of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone frame a waterfall about 94 meters high, whose full shape is much easier to make out here than from its brink. Take time to look at the colors of the canyon walls, too. Approach only along designated paths and stay behind the barriers, even when a photographer is looking for a different angle.

Crossing to the other side is more rewarding than taking more photos from the same spot: Lookout Point offers another perspective on the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone. The overlooks along North Rim Drive complement Artist Point, while Upper Falls has its own access points farther upstream. The two waterfalls therefore call for separate stops. Follow the posted traffic directions and choose accessible viewpoints if you prefer to avoid steep slopes.

activities.text: If you are prepared for a strenuous climb back up, Brink of the Lower Falls brings you close to the exact point where the river plunges over the edge. The trail descends in switchbacks to the top of the waterfall; its short distance belies a demanding slope. The return follows the same route and takes more effort than the descent. Check that the trail is open, bring water, and skip the descent if your fitness or the ground conditions are unsuitable.

places.name: Grand Canyon Village, AZ

visits.text: Walk the Strip (36.111, -115.173) from Mandalay Bay in the south (36.0926, -115.1764) to the Stratosphere in the north (36.1473, -115.1561)—6.8 km, 45 minutes walking, several hours if you stop. The Venetian's gondolas (36.1211, -115.1700), on indoor canals with singing gondoliers, cost $35–50 per couple and are the first layer of a recreation of Venice that has never seen the sea. The High Roller (36.1175, -115.1683), the world's tallest observation wheel when it opened in 2014 at 167 meters, gives panoramic views of the entire Strip from above, $28.

Head down to Fremont Street Experience (36.1707, -115.1437)—old Las Vegas from the 1940s–1950s, a street covered by a 460-meter LED screen, the Viva Vision Canopy, the world's largest. Light shows run every hour from 6 PM to 1 AM. The Golden Nugget and Binion's are the historic founding casinos, less flashy than the Strip and more honest about what they are.

Go up the Stratosphere Tower (36.1473, -115.1561)—350 meters, five thrill attractions at the top including the X-Scream that tilts out over the drop and the SkyJump at 261 meters. A view of the entire Strip from a height other towers don't offer. For those who prefer to stay below, the nighttime view from the sidewalk at the tower's base is enough to understand the scale of it all.

activities.text: Leave for the Grand Canyon early afternoon—4.5 hours via I-40 then AZ-64. Hotels inside the park (El Tovar Hotel, Bright Angel Lodge) book 6 to 12 months in advance; otherwise, Tusayan south of the park for $150-280/night. Arrive at Mather Point (36.0617, -112.1083) for sunset—180° panoramic view, raking light revealing geological layers.

Have dinner on the Strip before leaving—Las Vegas is home to restaurants by Michelin-starred chefs (Joël Robuchon at MGM Grand, Guy Savoy at Caesars Palace) at prices that remain lower than at their Paris restaurants. Casino buffets cover the other end of the range: $15–50 depending on the standard. What Las Vegas doesn't do well is mid-range dining.

visits.text: Day 3 - Beneath Grand Central Terminal's turquoise vault, 2,500 painted stars overlook the ballet of commuters. You can walk through the hall for free at any hour. Look for the Whispering Gallery in front of the Oyster Bar: two people standing at opposite corners can hear each other whisper across the vault.

Day 3 - Grand Central hides a gourmet market, a basement food court, and the central kiosk's four-faced clock, the quintessential New York meeting point. Pass through at rush hour, 8–9 AM or 5–6 PM: that's when the station plays its true score. Fifteen minutes of guaranteed spectacle.

activities.text: Oysters at the Grand Central Oyster Bar counter, opened in 1913 under its Guastavino ceramic vaults: not cheap, but memorable by the half-dozen.

places.name: Grand Island, NE

visits.text: The Stuhr Museum of the Prairie Pioneer sprawls across 81 hectares southwest of Grand Island and is one of the most ambitious living history complexes in the Midwest. The centerpiece is Railroad Town - over 60 original structures relocated from across the Great Plains to recreate an 1890s prairie village complete with a blacksmith, a church, a general store, a Pawnee earth lodge, and the birthplace of Henry Fonda (born here in 1905; he personally helped relocate and restore the house in 1966). The circular Stuhr Building was designed by Edward Durell Stone - the architect of the Kennedy Center - opened in 1967 on a surrounding moat. Costumed interpreters bring the town to life from May through September. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015. Paid entry.

The Crane Trust Nature and Visitor Center, west of Grand Island along the Platte River, sits at the center of one of the world's great wildlife events. Each spring - mid-February to mid-April, peaking in late March - over one million sandhill cranes converge on a 110 km stretch of the Platte, representing more than 80 percent of the world population. Fossil records place cranes in Nebraska for nine million years, predating the Platte River itself. Each individual bird stays about 29 days, consuming nearly 1,600 tonnes of waste corn before continuing to Canadian and Alaskan breeding grounds. Guided sunrise and sunset tours during migration sell out weeks ahead - book early at the Crane Trust website.

activities.text: At dawn, travel from Grand Island to the free public viewpoints along the Platte River: the Fort Kearny Hike-Bike Trail bridge near Kearney or the Plautz Viewing Platform south of Gibbon. At the height of the migration in March, the predawn silence gives way to the calls of hundreds of thousands of birds; their mass takeoff at sunrise can darken the sky. At dusk, they return to the river in a stream lasting an hour, their silhouettes outlined against the setting sun. Outside migration season, the Platte corridor still attracts pelicans, herons and migrating waterfowl.

After the Stuhr Museum, follow the road along the south bank of the Platte on your way back toward Grand Island: the river is shallow, braided and broad here, and herons, white pelicans and deer can often be seen from roadside viewpoints. Stolley Park in Grand Island is a quiet place for a picnic before dinner. Downtown retains several well-preserved late nineteenth-century commercial blocks and dependable local restaurants.

places.name: Grand Junction, CO

visits.text: Start at Colorado National Monument, just outside Fruita. Rim Rock Drive winds 37 km along red sandstone cliffs carved by millions of years of erosion. Stop at Independence Monument View—this 137-meter monolith is the park's tallest, and every Fourth of July a flag is raised at its summit. If you only have time for one short hike, take Otto's Trail (1.6 km round trip): the plunging canyon views are worth every step.

Late in the day, cruise through downtown Grand Junction. This is mainly your chance to fuel up and stock water—once you pass Green River, services become scarce. Also locate a grocery store to pack picnic supplies for the coming days.

Before heading back to Grand Junction, allow yourself one last stop at Chimney Rock, visible from Highway 24 at the park's western entrance. This ochre sandstone chimney capped with a darker rock hat is one of Capitol Reef's icons. A 5.8-km loop trail circles the formation—the view from the top embraces the entire Waterpocket Fold.

On Highway 24 heading east, spot the Behunin Cabin right by the roadside. Built in 1882 by Elijah Behunin from red sandstone to blend into the landscape, this tiny one-room cabin sheltered a family of 13. The stop takes only a few minutes but the story is worth the detour.

The return via I-70 crosses the San Rafael Swell—and this stretch of highway is spectacular in itself. For about 50 km, the road cuts through geologic cross-sections of red and gray sandstone, with cliffs on either side. Several rest areas offer viewpoints. Take time to stop before returning to Grand Junction.

activities.text: If you cycle, ride Rim Rock Drive on a road bike: locals have nicknamed it “Tour of the Moon”. Otherwise, take a short walk from the Saddlehorn Visitor Center to look for the desert bighorn sheep that inhabit the cliffs.

If your flight or plans allow, save 1.5 hours at day's end for another pass through Colorado National Monument on the Fruita side—this time in late-afternoon light. The sandstone colors change completely compared to the morning of Day 1. The Devil's Kitchen Trail (2.5 km) is a good option for a final short hike.

places.name: Grand Lake, CO

visits.text: The day is dominated by crossing Trail Ridge Road, the highest continuous paved road in the United States at 3,713 meters in elevation. Over 77 kilometers total (including 11 miles above 3,350 m), it connects Estes Park to Grand Lake by crossing the Continental Divide. Built from 1929 to 1938 by the Civilian Conservation Corps, it receives up to 7.5 meters of snow in winter and requires an average of 42 days of snow removal each spring at a cost exceeding $30,000. Stop at Rainbow Curve (3,315 m) for the view over the glacial valley, then at the Alpine Visitor Center (3,595 m) - the highest National Park Service visitor center in the United States. Bring a jacket even in summer: temperatures at the summit are often 10°C colder than in Denver.

On the west side, Kawuneeche Valley follows the headwaters of the Colorado River - the river that irrigates seven states and supplies water to 40 million people begins in this park. Stop at the Kawuneeche Visitor Center, then look for elk and moose in the meadows beside the river. The Holzwarth Historic Site, reached from a parking area, preserves cabins from a ranch dating to 1917 - one of the country’s first “dude ranches”.

Grand Lake, founded in 1881, is Colorado's largest natural lake with a maximum depth exceeding 116 meters. The small town counts fewer than 500 permanent residents but its boardwalk concentrates shops and restaurants with no chains - it's one of the few small Colorado mountain towns to have resisted commercial standardization. Late afternoon, take the short walk to Point Park for panoramic views of the lake and surrounding peaks.

activities.text: Rent a kayak or canoe on Grand Lake - the Grand Lake Yacht Club, founded in 1902, is one of the world's highest yacht clubs at 2,551 meters in elevation. You can also take a motorboat to explore the two connected lakes, Grand Lake and Shadow Mountain Lake. Rental outfitters offer kayaks and boats by the hour or day from lakeside marinas.

places.name: Grand Marais, MN

visits.text: Grand Marais sits on a natural double harbor 65 km from the Canadian border, between the Sawtooth Mountains and Lake Superior. The Ojibwe called it Gitchi-Ba-Too-Biig, the double bay. Budget Travel Magazine named it America's Coolest Small Town. Downtown spans three blocks around Harbor Park—art galleries, artisan shops, fish restaurants—with the lake as a constant horizon.

Walk out to Artist's Point, the rocky promontory jutting into the lake east of town. From the point, you overlook both harbor basins on one side and the vastness of Lake Superior on the other. In bad weather, waves crash just a few meters away—the atmosphere changes completely. The walk from the harbor parking lot takes 15 minutes.

activities.text: The North House Folk School, located on the lakeshore since 1997, offers workshops in blacksmithing, timber framing, weaving, bread baking, or birch-bark canoe building. If your timing lines up with a one-day workshop, sign up: it's one of the most authentic North Shore experiences. Otherwise, browse the shop and tour the campus.

visits.text: The blue sometimes disappears behind the steam at Grand Prismatic Spring, then reappears between the orange fringes. From the boardwalks at Midway Geyser Basin, you remain at the level of this vast hot spring, near Excelsior Geyser. Never step off the wooden boardwalk to improve a photo; wait for the steam to shift.

activities.text: Climb to Grand Prismatic Overlook to appreciate the pattern that the boardwalks put you too close to see. The route starts at Fairy Falls Trailhead, in a separate parking lot. Expect a round-trip distance of about 1.9 km according to the NPS; check that the trail is open before leaving the basin.

days_plan.itin_title: Yellowstone and Grand Teton: 12 Days Among Lakes and Mountain Passes

visits.text: The day is devoted to Kings Canyon National Park, the lesser known of the two parks but just as spectacular. The canyon itself - carved into the granite by Quaternary glaciers - is more than 1,600 metres deep, making it one of the deepest canyons in the United States, ahead of the Grand Canyon. In 1891 John Muir described it as “a rival to Yosemite”. Take the Kings Canyon Scenic Byway (Highway 180) to Cedar Grove, about 50 km from Grant Grove, 1 hour by road - the road follows the Kings River for kilometres of rapids and rocky beaches.

On the way, stop at the General Grant Tree in Grant Grove. It's the second-largest tree in the world by volume, designated in 1926 as the “Nation's Christmas Tree” by President Calvin Coolidge. The 800-metre loop surrounding it is flat and accessible.

At Cedar Grove, hike the Zumwalt Meadow trail - a 2.4 km loop at the canyon floor, between granite domes, river, and open meadows. It's one of the most photographed spots in the park and notably less crowded than Sequoia's sites. Don't miss Roaring River Falls either, a waterfall accessible in barely 500 metres from the car park.

activities.text: If you have time on the return, stop at Boyden Cavern, just at the park boundary within Giant Sequoia National Monument. These limestone caves open onto the canyon wall and can be visited on a one-hour guided tour - a striking contrast to the granite landscapes dominating the rest of the circuit.

At the end of the day, in Grant Grove, head up to Panoramic Point. A narrow little road leads from the village to a car park, from which a short trail climbs to the viewpoint. The view stretches over the Sierra Nevada peaks that tower above Kings Canyon and, below, over Hume Lake. The road is closed in winter: in season, it is the perfect stop to unwind before dinner.

days_plan.itin_title: Sierra California Road Trip: Sequoia and Kings Canyon

visits.text: Great Bend and Cheyenne Bottoms - North America's Most Important Bird Migration Route: Arrive at sunrise to witness one of nature's greatest spectacles as hundreds of thousands of birds utilize this critical stopover on their continental journeys.

Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area - The Largest Inland Wetland in the United States: This 41,000-acre complex of marshy basins provides the richest wetland feeding grounds in the central flyway, critical to the survival of some 320 bird species that frequent these waters.

Kansas Wetlands Education Center - Understanding an Ecological Treasure: Exhibits explain the international importance of this freshwater marsh and its role in supporting migrating waterfowl and shorebirds each spring and autumn.

Quivira National Wildlife Refuge - A Rare Inland Salt Marsh: Allow for a day trip from Great Bend. This unusual Midwest ecosystem features trails offering closer views of ducks, geese and several threatened species in a landscape unique to Kansas.

activities.text: Sunrise Birding - Watch Pelicans Take Flight: Time your visit for dawn to observe pods of American white pelicans lifting off the water, beginning another day of their remarkable migration.

places.name: Great Falls, MT

visits.text: The Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail Interpretive Center is built into a bluff overlooking the Missouri, and the Corps spent more time here than anywhere outside of winter camp. The portage around five successive waterfalls took 33 days in June and July 1805, covering 29 km on improvised log-wheeled wagons through prickly pear cactus, grizzly bear territory, and coulees prone to flash floods. The centerpiece of the 2,300 m² center is a two-story diorama of the portage; you can test your strength at a simulated boat-hauling station. A 45-minute audio walk featuring an actor reconstructs the scene in William Clark's voice. Paid entry ($8 for adults); closed Mondays and Tuesdays outside peak season.

Giant Springs Heritage State Park is a 400-meter walk from the interpretive center along the River's Edge Trail, and it holds one of the largest freshwater springs in the world. Lewis described it on June 18, 1805, as “a most beautiful fountain”—the spring discharges 590 million liters per day through limestone. The Roe River, flowing just 60 meters from the spring to the Missouri, long claimed the title of the world's shortest river—a distinction that has since been contested and removed from the Guinness records. The park has picnic areas, trout ponds, and a wildlife center. Free admission.

The C.M. Russell Museum covers an entire city block and holds close to 1,000 original works by Charles Marion Russell—painter, sculptor, and self-described cowboy who arrived in Montana at age 16 in 1880 and spent the rest of his life documenting the West before it vanished. His log cabin, built in 1903 from western red cedar telephone poles, stands on the museum grounds alongside his family home—both National Historic Landmarks since 1965. More than 3,000 pieces of Western art fill 16 galleries. Paid entry; open daily in summer.

activities.text: The River's Edge Trail runs for 97 km as a paved, non-motorized path through Great Falls along the Missouri, connecting the interpretive center to Giant Springs, the five waterfall overlooks, and the CMR Museum district. Rent a bike in town and ride the section from Giant Springs past Rainbow Falls and Black Eagle Dam—about 13 km of riverside trail with the actual waterfalls that stopped the Corps for 33 days. The falls look modest now, controlled by hydroelectric dams, but the side canyons and cottonwood banks still tell the story.

First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park, 16 km south of Great Falls on I-15, is a 1.5 km sandstone cliff over which Indigenous hunters drove bison for at least 2,000 years—the remains of millions of butchered animals lie in the talus below. An interpretive trail and shelter explain the archaeology. It predates Lewis and Clark by millennia, but it gives the Great Falls stop a deeper Indigenous context that the expedition barely acknowledged during its grueling month-long portage. Free admission; 30-minute drive from downtown.

places.name: Green Bay, WI

visits.text: Green Bay is the smallest city in the United States to have an NFL franchise—the Packers, founded in 1919, are also the only professional football team collectively owned by its fans (approximately 360,000 shareholders). Lambeau Field, opened in 1957 and expanded to 81,441 seats, remains one of the league's most legendary stadiums. On non-game days, the guided stadium and Packers Hall of Fame tour lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes—you enter the locker rooms, walk on the field, and touch a replica Lombardi Trophy. Book online if visiting during the season (September to January).

The National Railroad Museum in Green Bay houses one of the largest collections of locomotives and railcars in the United States, including Union Pacific's Big Boy—the largest steam locomotive ever built, weighing 132 tonnes and put into service in 1941. You can board several restored railcars, including Eisenhower's presidential car used during World War II. Allow 1 hour and 30 minutes to explore the entire outdoor grounds and indoor exhibitions.

The CityDeck runs along the Fox River right in downtown Green Bay—a wooden boardwalk over the water with restaurant patios and benches facing the evening reflections. This is where locals gather after work, far from the bustle of Lambeau Field. Take the opportunity to dine on the riverfront before tomorrow's long leg to the Upper Peninsula.

activities.text: The Bay Beach Wildlife Sanctuary spans 280 hectares on the edge of Green Bay. This municipal refuge shelters deer, foxes, otters and injured raptors undergoing rehabilitation—all viewable from marked trails that are free to access. It's one of the few urban green spaces where you can find yourself alone with nature less than 5 minutes from downtown. Go in late afternoon for the best chances of spotting wildlife.

Green Bay is the perfect meeting point for Wisconsin's two sources of pride: beer and cheese. Downtown bars serve local craft beers accompanied by cheeses from regional cheesemakers—aged cheddar, colby, and the curious cheese curds, little pieces of fresh cheese that squeak when you bite into them. A simple and authentic way to end the day before the long transit to the Upper Peninsula tomorrow morning.

places.name: Green River, UT

visits.text: Drive to Wedge Overlook, nicknamed Utah's “Little Grand Canyon.” At the end of a well-maintained dirt road (passable in a regular car in dry weather), you'll reach the edge of a 360-meter drop above the San Rafael River. The panorama is staggering—and you'll likely be alone staring into the void. No services on-site, no water, no safety barriers.

On your way down through Buckhorn Draw, stop at the Buckhorn Wash Pictograph Panel. This Barrier Canyon–style rock art dates back more than 2,000 years—the life-size figures are among the most impressive in the Colorado Plateau. The site is accessible right from the road, about 5 km north of the San Rafael River bridge.

In Green River, step inside the John Wesley Powell River History Museum, perched on the riverbank. Don't miss the 25-minute film “The Great Unknown,” which traces Powell's 1869 expedition—three months and 1,600 km on rivers no one had ever mapped. Downstairs you'll find replicas of period boats and a small dinosaur exhibit.

activities.text: Green River is Utah's melon town. If you visit during the Melon Days festival in September, enjoy the events celebrating the harvest. At other times of year, ask about trips on the Green River: the Desolation Canyon run has Class II–III rapids and requires suitable preparation.

visits.text: Day 5 - Atypical option yet one of Brooklyn's most beautiful walks: Green-Wood Cemetery, 1838 garden cemetery, hills, ponds, and mausoleums under century-old trees. Basquiat, Leonard Bernstein, and Boss Tweed rest here. Free admission through the 25th Street neo-Gothic portal, where green parakeets nest.

Day 5 - From Battle Hill, Brooklyn's highest point in the heart of Green-Wood, the statue of Minerva greets the Statue of Liberty eye to eye, with the harbor below. In the 19th century, before Central Park, the place attracted more visitors than anywhere else. Free maps at the entrance, trolley tours on certain days.

activities.text: Allow 1 to 1.5 hours for a leisurely walk; in hot weather, it's also the coolest spot on Day 5's itinerary.
Subway to Coney Island: 9.4 km, R line then D or N to Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue, about 45 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Moosehead Lake stretches 40 miles long and up to 20 miles wide, at 1,023 feet above sea level in the boreal forest. Greenville sits at its southern tip, and from the public boat launch you can make out Mount Kineo, an 800-foot rhyolite cliff rising out of the water near the middle of the lake. The waterfront town centre is small but practical: outfitters, a diner, and Northwoods Outfitters, an equipment and guiding centre. Arrive before dusk and drive Lily Bay Road north of town - moose are often spotted in the ditches and beaver ponds along this stretch.

Berthed at the town dock, the SS Katahdin - locally called “the Kate” - is the oldest vessel afloat built at Bath Iron Works, launched in 1914. She carried tourists and supplies to the Mount Kineo Resort, then spent decades as a lumber towboat hauling log booms across the lake until 1975. The Moosehead Marine Museum rescued her in 1976 and restored her completely in the 1990s, including replating the hull at Bath Iron Works. She runs cruises from June through October - the three-hour version goes north past Beaver Cove and Sugar Island, with narration on the lake's history and wildlife.

Lily Bay State Park lies 9 miles north of Greenville on the eastern shore of Moosehead Lake. The 952-acre park has lakeside campsites, as well as a small swimming beach, hiking trails and a boat launch. Even for a day visit, the views across the lake towards Big Moose Mountain are worth the trip. Open all year; summer draws paddlers and anglers, winter brings snowshoers and cross-country skiers.

activities.text: Northwoods Outfitters on Lily Bay Road runs the moose safaris that Yankee Magazine voted best in New England. Registered Maine Guides take small private groups out at dawn and dusk - the times when moose are most active - either by vehicle on logging roads or by canoe on remote beaver ponds. Success rates are high: guides claim over 1,000 sightings a year. Book the early-morning tour for the best light and the highest probability of seeing bulls.

If the seaplanes at Currier's Flying Service catch your eye at the town dock, a 30-minute floatplane flight over Moosehead Lake makes the wilderness scale unmistakable - 40 miles of lake surrounded by nothing but boreal forest stretching to the Canadian border. Currier's has been operating bush-flying charters out of Greenville since 1947, making it one of the oldest floatplane operations in the Northeast.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Maine: Moosehead Lake, Mount Katahdin & the North Woods

visits.text: Leland, 16 kilometers east of Greenville on Highway 61, produced Jimmy Reed, Little Milton, Eddie Cusic, and blues-rock guitarist Johnny Winter, whose father ran a local cotton business. The Highway 61 Blues Museum on the main drag covers around 80 Delta blues artists from the surrounding area, with instruments, photographs, and hand-annotated festival posters. Blues musician Son Thomas lived here for decades; his son Pat Thomas still plays in the museum most days, unpaid and purely for love of the music. Leland is also Jim Henson's hometown - the Kermit the Frog exhibit is next door if the kids need a break.

Robert Johnson recorded 'They're Red Hot' about tamales in 1936, and that tradition runs deep. Greenville, which declared itself the Hot Tamale Capital of the World in 2012, is the best place in the Delta to taste it. Delta tamales are smaller than Mexican ones, made with cornmeal instead of masa, heavily spiced, and simmered rather than steamed - the recipe most likely crossed between Mexican migrant farm workers and Black laborers in the cotton fields in the early 20th century. Scott's Hot Tamales on MLK Boulevard uses a family recipe dating to 1950, wrapping each one by hand in corn shucks. Doe's Eat Place on Nelson Street has served tamales alongside its steaks since the 1940s. Budget an hour for lunch.

activities.text: The drive south from Clarksdale on Highway 61 is itself a full activity: flat Delta farmland, bayous, shotgun houses, grain elevators, Mississippi Blues Trail markers appearing every few kilometers. Stop at each one - they're brief, factual, and densely specific, each giving a name, a date, a story. By the time you reach Greenville you'll have covered the arc from Charley Patton through the Great Migration. Keep the windows down and drive slowly; the light over Delta cotton fields in the morning is worth photographing.

Lake Washington, about 32 kilometers south of Greenville, is an oxbow lake, one of those crescent-shaped bodies of water left behind when the Mississippi River changed course. Blues musicians played around its shores for generations, and the surrounding country roads seem largely unchanged since the sharecropping era. An evening drive around the lake, stopping to look at the old plantation structures, ends the day with a quieter view of the landscape that produced all this music. Bring mosquito repellent between May and September.

days_plan.itin_title: Mississippi Delta Blues Trail: Memphis to Jackson

visits.text: Marvel at Falls Park on the Reedy, an urban oasis where the Reedy River tumbles over a dramatic waterfall surrounded by gardens, stone pathways, and shady trees in the heart of downtown Greenville. The curved Liberty Bridge suspension walkway floats above the falls, offering sweeping views that never fail to impress. This transformed space represents one of the finest urban parks in the American South.

Stroll along the Swamp Rabbit Trail, miles of scenic pathway following the Reedy River through beautiful natural areas and charming neighborhoods. The trail connects downtown attractions to outlying communities, providing opportunities for walking, running, and cycling. Greenville's investment in green spaces and pedestrian infrastructure has created a remarkably livable city.

activities.text: Explore downtown Greenville's wide, walkable streets lined with boutique shops, art galleries, and diverse dining options. The city's vibrant arts scene includes world-class performances and exhibitions throughout the year. Flowering gardens, hidden nooks, and benches overlooking the river invite visitors to slow down and appreciate this mountain-ringed cultural destination.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Road Trip: From Lowcountry Beaches to the Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Greenwich - Where New York Sophistication Meets New England Charm: This affluent coastal community on Connecticut's Gold Coast offers pristine beaches, world-class shopping, and stunning waterfront estates. The town's 50-kilometer shoreline along Long Island Sound provides endless opportunities for sailing, swimming, and scenic strolls.

Bruce Museum - Science and Art Under One Roof: This regional museum showcases natural history, environmental science, and fine arts through rotating exhibitions and permanent collections that illuminate both the natural world and human creativity.

activities.text: Greenwich Avenue Shopping District - The Rodeo Drive of Connecticut: Browse upscale boutiques, galleries, and gourmet food shops along this tree-lined thoroughfare that has attracted discerning shoppers for over a century.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

visits.text: Gold explains part of Groveland’s appearance; the Groveland Yosemite Gateway Museum tells the story behind it. Its collections bring together local history and the natural environment, rather than reducing the region to a gateway to the park. Check its fairly limited opening days, and pick up any last essentials in town before continuing.

activities.text: Take a short walk in Mary Laveroni Park before the final climb toward Yosemite. This Groveland park adjoins the museum area, making it an easy stop along the main road without a detour. Take time to have a drink and stretch your legs; traffic may still slow down at the park entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: Conquer Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas at 2,667 meters, where breathtaking panoramic views reward determined hikers who complete the challenging summit trail. This ancient fossilized reef mountain, dating back over 260 million years, rises majestically from the Chihuahuan Desert floor. Reaching the top of Texas provides an unparalleled sense of accomplishment and a unique connection to the state's geological heritage.

Discover McKittrick Canyon, renowned for producing the most spectacular fall foliage display in West Texas when maples, oaks, and other deciduous trees transform the desert canyon into a blaze of autumn colors. The canyon's unique microclimate supports a surprisingly diverse ecosystem within the arid surrounding landscape. Crystal-clear streams and towering limestone walls create a hidden oasis that contrasts dramatically with the desert terrain.

activities.text: Hike the El Capitan trail for closer views of the park's iconic rocky outcrop, a massive limestone cliff that served as a landmark for travelers, including Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoaches, crossing the desert for centuries. The park offers exceptional stargazing opportunities due to minimal light pollution from surrounding areas. Over 300 species of birds have been documented here, making it a premier destination for wildlife observation.

days_plan.itin_title: Texas: An Epic Journey from Metropolises to Wild Canyons

visits.text: Day 4 - Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral is worth as much as the collections inside: at the Guggenheim, you ride the elevator up and walk down the gently sloping ramp, passing artworks along 400 m. Tickets are $30. After the Met or the Natural History Museum, an hour for an overview is more than enough; the architecture does the rest.

Day 4 - The Guggenheim presents Kandinsky in depth, the Impressionists of the Thannhauser collection, and major temporary exhibitions in the rotunda. Some evenings offer pay-what-you-wish slots; check online. Photograph the 1959 building's exterior with a wide-angle lens from the sidewalk across the street.

activities.text: If you're getting tired of museums, skip the interior without regret: take in the façade, snap a photo, and head straight to Harlem for a change of scene.
Subway to Harlem: 3.1 km, 4/5/6 lines from 86th Street station to 125th Street, about 20 min walk included.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Day 1: Trade city streets for coastal paradise as you enter Gulf State Park, a 6,000-acre sanctuary where pristine white-sand beaches meet freshwater lakes teeming with wildlife. Rent a bike at Lake Shelby and pedal along trails crossing bridges between three interconnected lakes, pausing at the Nature Center to learn about the alligators, herons, and sea turtles that call this preserve home. The Leave Only Footprints program protects nesting sea turtles along the shore.

Day 1: Sink your toes into the sugary sand of Gulf Shores Beach, where the Gulf of Mexico's emerald waters lap against Alabama's stunning 60-mile coastline. Unlike the crowded shores of neighboring Florida, these beaches offer space to breathe, with the state park providing particularly peaceful stretches backed by natural dunes rather than residential towers. A long fishing pier attracts anglers casting for the day's catch.

Day 1: Experience coastal luxury with a conscience at The Lodge at Gulf State Park, a striking wood-clad hotel run by Hilton but owned by Alabama, with all profits supporting state parks. Book a beach-view lunch at Foodcraft restaurant, where sustainable Southern cuisine celebrates local ingredients in a light-filled setting overlooking the dunes. Even day visitors can access the hotel's pristine stretch of protected beach.

Day 2: Set sail with Cetacean Cruises for an afternoon dolphin encounter, where bottlenose dolphins play in the wake of your vessel as you glide through the calm waters of Mobile Bay. The knowledgeable crew shares fascinating facts about these intelligent marine mammals while steering toward shrimp boats where dolphins congregate for easy meals. With the sail raised and a drink in hand, there's no better way to experience Alabama's coastal waters.

Day 2: Drive the scenic coastal road to Fort Morgan, a star-shaped brick fortress a good half-hour's drive from Gulf Shores that has guarded the mouth of Mobile Bay since the 1830s. This strategic stronghold witnessed fierce naval battles of the Civil War, including Admiral Farragut's famous cry to damn the torpedoes. Climb the ramparts for panoramic views across the bay to Dauphin Island, where its twin, Fort Gaines, stands guard on the opposite shore.

Day 2: Board the Mobile Bay Ferry for a scenic cruise to Dauphin Island, where Fort Gaines and quiet beaches await exploration. The 35-minute crossing offers dolphin spotting opportunities and gorgeous views of both fortifications that once defended this vital waterway. History buffs can explore the companion fort before catching the return ferry.

activities.text: Day 1: Start your beach day right at Woodside Restaurant, a laid-back cafe on the edge of Gulf State Park where the South Island Parfait layers fresh tropical fruit and banana bread with creamy Greek yogurt drizzled with local honey. The setting amid the park's natural beauty makes this more than just breakfast; it's the beginning of an adventure.

Day 1: Embrace beach club vibes at The Gulf, a buzzing waterfront gathering spot built from repurposed shipping containers painted in cheerful colors. Order shrimp tacos and fresh-squeezed lemonade from one of two outdoor kitchens, then claim a table overlooking the water as the sun begins its descent. Families, friends, and the occasional live band create an atmosphere that captures everything wonderful about Alabama's coast.

Day 1: Dress for a special evening at Cobalt, where an expansive patio overlooks Perdido Bay and the menu showcases Gulf seafood at its finest. The tuna salad features ruby-red fish barely kissed by heat, scattered over greens with goat cheese, pecans, and house-pickled vegetables. The BBQ Gulf Shrimp swimming in butter sauce demand crusty bread for sopping up every drop.

Day 2: Settle into the boutique Hotel Indigo Orange Beach, a stylish retreat just steps from the sand where ocean-hued decor and a minimum check-in age of 25 ensure peaceful relaxation. The suite-style rooms include full living areas and kitchenettes that feel like your own beach apartment, while the pool and lobby swings invite lingering. The Backcountry Trail begins just behind the property for morning bike rides.

Day 2: Browse for coastal treasures at Southern Grind Cafe next door to Hotel Indigo, where excellent coffee pairs with an eclectic collection of beach-inspired gifts and housewares. The dog-friendly patio welcomes four-legged travelers, while the cafe's breakfast and brunch offerings provide fuel for another day of Gulf Coast adventures.

Day 2: Reflect on your Deep South journey as the sun sinks into the Gulf of Mexico, painting the sky in shades of peach and amber. From rockets to civil rights monuments, recording studios to sugar-sand beaches, Alabama has revealed itself as so much more than a state to pass through. The Heart of Dixie beats with stories of innovation, courage, creativity, and hospitality that will stay with you long after you've returned home.

days_plan.itin_title: Alabama Road Trip: Civil Rights and the Gulf Coast

places.name: Gustavus, AK

visits.text: The Bartlett Cove Visitor Center—14 km from Gustavus via the area's only paved road—is NPS headquarters for Glacier Bay. Rangers give daily talks on the bay's extraordinary history: 250 years ago, everything was under 1,500 meters of ice. When Vancouver passed in 1794, the bay was largely filled with glaciers—he saw only a narrow arm of the sea at its entrance. Today the bay extends nearly 100 km—making it one of the fastest glacial retreats ever documented on Earth.

The Forest Loop Trail (1.3 km) and Bartlett River Trail (8 km round-trip) both start from the Visitor Center through a forest of hemlock and spruce recently colonized on old moraines. The phenomenon of plant succession is visible to the naked eye: you pass from bare rock to moss, then to young trees in the span of a few hundred meters—a living geology lesson.

Point Adolphus, at the mouth of Icy Strait across from the village of Hoonah, is one of the most renowned humpback whale watching spots in North America. More than 85 humpback whales return each summer to these waters extremely rich in krill and fish. Local boats from Gustavus get you there in 30 minutes. Group bubble-net feeding displays—a cooperative hunting behavior where several whales blow a curtain of bubbles together to trap prey—are observed almost daily in July-August.

The Nagoonberry Loop Trail from Gustavus, an easy 5-km trail through forests and coastal meadows, gives a sense of the region's unique rural landscape—Gustavus is one of the few Southeast Alaska communities where people grow vegetable gardens and houses have actual lawns. Wild raspberries and nagoonberries grow trailside. Views of the Fairweather Range peaks at the head of the bay are constant.

activities.text: The day-long bay cruise, organized by NPS aboard the catamaran Spirit of Adventure, ascends 100 km to the Grand Pacific and Margerie glaciers at the head of the bay. A ranger-naturalist narrates the wildlife and geology throughout the crossing. Bears, wolves, mountain goats, porpoises, and up to a hundred species of seabirds are frequently spotted. Calving seracs from the face of Margerie Glacier create waves perceptible onboard.

Kayaking from Bartlett Cove with Glacier Bay Sea Kayaks—an hour or two of paddling is enough to escape all human presence into quiet coves where seals rest onshore. Guided introductions are offered for non-paddlers, as well as independent rentals for experienced kayakers. Don't venture into the upper reaches of the bay without experience and radio communication.

Sport fishing in Icy Strait targets halibut and coho salmon from late June through September—the depths of the strait are among the richest in the Inside Passage. Local charters depart from Gustavus dock and provide all gear. If you're not an angler, the marine wildlife en route—sea otters, Dall's porpoises, harbor seals—is more than enough for a morning on the water.

Bike from Gustavus to Bartlett Cove—the 14 km of flat road between the two are ideal for observing meadows, wetlands, and transition forests. Local homeowners rent bikes by the day. Gustavus is one of Alaska's flattest and most bikeable places—take advantage, it's rare.
