visits.text: The drive from Cincinnati is 1,200 km—the longest leg of the trip. Leave at dawn. You'll cross Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri before entering Oklahoma. In the final stretches through Missouri and Oklahoma, I-44 parallels historic Route 66—watch for “Historic Route 66” signs and vintage gas stations along the roadside.

Guthrie is a town of 12,000 frozen in time. It was Oklahoma's first capital from 1890 to 1910, before losing that status to Oklahoma City overnight—residents woke up without their capital. The Victorian brick downtown is listed on the National Register and spans 400 buildings. Stroll along Harrison Avenue and Oklahoma Avenue.

Don't miss the Scottish Rite Masonic Temple, a massive neoclassical building that seems incongruous in a town this size. Built in 1919, it's one of the world's largest Masonic temples. The interior is open for tours—the painted ceilings and pipe organs are worth seeing.

activities.text: Guthrie is also the "bluegrass capital of the world." If you're there on a Friday or Saturday night, there's often live music at the bars on Harrison Avenue. Otherwise, enjoy the quiet—you're far from everything here, and that's the point.

days_plan.itin_title: The Rain Man Route: A Road Trip Across the United States

visits.text: The skull of a Hagerman Horse dominates the visitor center at Hagerman Fossil Beds - Equus simplicidens, Idaho's state fossil, the earliest known member of the genus Equus. Rancher Elmer Cook spotted bones eroding from the bluffs along the Snake River in 1928 and called the U.S. Geological Survey; the Smithsonian dug here from 1929 to 1934 and uncovered more than 200 individual horse specimens of all ages and both sexes, alongside mastodons, saber-toothed cats, and ground sloths, all 3 to 4 million years old. The fragile sandstone bluffs are restricted; the visitor center is the place to see the fossils. Free admission.

The Oregon Trail emigrants who passed through this valley in the 1840s and 1850s stopped and stared: springs poured straight out of the canyon walls by the dozens, cascading down basalt cliffs into the Snake River below. They were looking at overflow from the Snake River Plain Aquifer, recharged every year by snowmelt from the Rocky Mountains above. At Malad Gorge today, the Malad River drops through stairstep falls into the Devil's Washbowl then cuts a 76-meter gorge; the bridge crossing it gives you the best view. One park fee ($7) covers all six units of Thousand Springs State Park.

Ritter Island sits in the Snake River as a green anomaly - surrounded by water and canyon walls, with Lemon Falls cascading into view on all sides. In the early 20th century, Minnie Miller ran a state-of-the-art Guernsey dairy farm here; her original buildings are still standing. The Nature Conservancy bought the 156-hectare property in 1986. Access is Thursday through Monday, Memorial Day through Labor Day; a rental house on the island is bookable year-round through Idaho State Parks.

activities.text: Hagerman's stretch of the Snake River runs Class I-III whitewater through a canyon whose walls are the same fossil-bearing bluffs you visited this morning. Several local outfitters run guided half-day trips with the fossils above you the whole time. For something quieter, the Billingsley Creek unit of Thousand Springs State Park has excellent fly-fishing - the creek is fed by constant-temperature springs and stocked with trout year-round.

Clear Springs Foods, based near Hagerman, is among the region's trout producers. For dinner, ask at local restaurants, including Snake River Grill next to Hagerman Valley Inn. For breakfast, Bullets N' Brews serves coffee and burritos. Hagerman Valley Inn is a place to stay; check the available dining options rather than assuming it operates a restaurant.

days_plan.itin_title: Idaho: Sawtooth Mountains, Sun Valley & Craters of the Moon

visits.text: The roar of the waves sets the tone at Waimea Bay before you even reach the sand. This North Shore bay has been part of big-wave surfing history since the 1950s. Stop here before Haleʻiwa when arriving from Kaʻaʻawa; during heavy swells, stay back from the shore and skip swimming.

Haleʻiwa retains its low-rise facades while Honolulu builds upward. Its plantation-town past remains visible in the buildings, while surf shops and galleries occupy the center. Park in a legal space, then explore the old town on foot; take care when crossing Kamehameha Highway.

activities.text: You’ll stop at Matsumoto Shave Ice in Haleʻiwa to try a Hawaiian specialty. A machine shaves a block of ice into fine flakes, which are then topped with syrup: the texture differs from crushed ice. Choose a small serving to start and check the closing time before joining the line.

days_plan.itin_title: Oahu in 3 Days: Honolulu, Pearl Harbor, and the North Shore

visits.text: Haleakala National Park, Kipahulu District — Follow the Kuloa Point Trail, a short loop from the Kipahulu Visitor Center, to the Oheo pools where waterfalls tumble in tiers towards the ocean. This rainforest-covered coastal side of the park preserves remains of ancient Hawaiian villages. The district is about half an hour's drive south of Hana.

Road to Hana — Navigate 103 kilometers of winding coastal highway featuring 600 curves and 59 bridges through lush rainforest. Waterfalls, black sand beaches, and dramatic ocean views make this one of the world's most scenic drives.

Wailua Falls — Photograph this twin waterfall plunging 24 meters into a tropical pool accessible directly from the road. The cascade appeared in Fantasy Island's opening credits and flows year-round through rainforest vegetation.

activities.text: Black sand beach at Waianapanapa — Walk across volcanic black pebbles formed by lava meeting ocean creating dramatic contrast against turquoise waters. The state park features lava tubes, sea caves, and ancient Hawaiian burial sites.

Bamboo Forest Hike — Walk through dense bamboo groves along the Pipiwai Trail to the 122-meter Waimoku Falls. The 6.4-kilometer round trip passes banyan trees and crosses boardwalks through a magical cathedral of bamboo. The trailhead is at the Kipahulu Visitor Center, about half an hour's drive south of Hana.

Fresh fish plate lunch — Sample ahi poke, loco moco, or teriyaki chicken with rice and macaroni salad at roadside stands. Plate lunch represents Hawaii's multicultural fusion cuisine in generous portions.

days_plan.itin_title: Hawaii Trip: Volcanoes and Dream Beaches

visits.text: A crater open to the ocean: Hanauma Bay reveals its shape before you even descend to the beach. The sea breached the volcanic wall and filled this basin. Start at the overlook within the preserve; your admission time slot includes a mandatory educational video before you can access the shore.

activities.text: If sea conditions allow, explore Hanauma Bay with a mask and snorkel. Protected since 1967, the bay is home to corals that you must not step on. Book an admission-only ticket 2 days in advance, starting at 7 a.m. Hawaii time, for a visit Wednesday through Sunday; listen to the lifeguards’ instructions before entering the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Oahu in 3 Days: Honolulu, Pearl Harbor, and the North Shore

visits.text: Goblin Valley State Park is one of Utah's strangest places. Across roughly 5 km², thousands of sandstone mushrooms—the “goblins”—stand in a landscape that served as the set for the film Galaxy Quest. These formations were born from erosion of the Entrada Sandstone, deposited 170 million years ago when the region bordered an ancient sea. Unlike most parks, you can wander freely among the hoodoos. Arrive in the morning—on weekends and school holidays, the parking lot fills fast.

Before leaving the area, take a look at the Three Sisters, a trio of hoodoos in the park. A short path starts from the access road to the observation point. From the main overlook, go down the steps into the “first valley” and wander among the formations: the farther south you go, the larger the goblins become.

Factory Butte is visible from Highway 24, about 20 km west of Hanksville. This isolated monolith rises to 1,920 m and dominates an ocean of blue-gray badlands streaked with yellow. Come at sunrise or sunset—the raking light transforms the ravines into an abstract painting. The access road (Factory Butte Road) is passable in dry weather, but the slightest rain turns the clay into a vehicle trap.

activities.text: About 8 km from the entrance to Goblin Valley, Little Wild Horse Canyon is an accessible Utah slot canyon. No technical equipment is needed: the 5 km out-and-back trail winds between sandstone walls so narrow that you sometimes have to turn sideways. Allow 2 to 3 hours. For a longer hike, the full loop with Bell Canyon is 13 km and takes about 4 hours. Check the weather before you set out: if rain is possible, even in the distance, do not enter, as flash floods can be deadly in these slots.

If you have a high-clearance vehicle, push on to Moonscape Overlook, 30 minutes from Hanksville. This viewpoint looks over a valley of undulating gray hills that resemble the Moon's surface. The best time: at sunset, when the valley takes on silver hues. Photos never do the place justice.

days_plan.itin_title: Utah-Arizona Road Trip: National Parks and Canyons
Utah Canyon Loop: Capitol Reef & Goblin Valley

visits.text: You walk to Last Stand Hill at Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, and the white marble headstones stop you flat. On June 25-26, 1876, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors defeated the U.S. Army's 7th Cavalry - 263 soldiers killed out of 650, including Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer and all 209 men under his direct command. The site was renamed from Custer Battlefield by President George H.W. Bush in 1991; red granite markers now stand for fallen Native warriors alongside the white cavalry stones. A 7-kilometer self-guided tour road connects the Custer battlefield to the Reno-Benteen entrenchment where 350 soldiers survived. Paid entry.

Walk through Custer National Cemetery, adjoining the battlefield visitor center. It holds more than 5,000 veterans with interments from the Indian Wars era through the Korean War, and began as a repository for remains collected from abandoned frontier military posts across the region. The grave markers and the surrounding silence of the Montana prairie create a stark contrast with the battlefield just over the hill. Free access, included with battlefield entry.

Take the Deep Ravine Trail to understand the terrain the battle was actually fought on. The path follows the ridge where Custer's battalion made its final movements before collapse, and the dry grasses and rolling bluffs look much as they did in 1876. Don't miss the Indian Memorial on Last Stand Hill - a circular stone structure dedicated on June 25, 2003, the first formal acknowledgment of the Native American perspective built into the monument itself. Allow at least 30 minutes for this walk on top of the main visit.

activities.text: If you're visiting in late June, make time for the Real Bird family's annual Battle of the Little Bighorn Reenactment at Medicine Tail Coulee near Garryowen - on the actual ground where Custer's battalion was closest to the Native village. Run entirely by Crow tribal members since 1992, it tells the battle from an Indigenous perspective with roughly 170 horses and scenes depicting Sitting Bull's prophecy. Jim Real Bird created the event specifically because, as he put it, “at the other place, the Indians were invisible.” The 34th edition runs June 26-28, 2026, marking the 150th anniversary. Fee per vehicle.

At Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, take the tour road to the Reno-Benteen Entrenchment. In this part of the battlefield, read the interpretive panels and look across the hills where the soldiers held out after Custer's battalion was defeated. Then return to Last Stand Hill to compare the two parts of the site and see the combatants' markers. This visit complements the Indian Memorial and the national cemetery.

days_plan.itin_title: Montana East: Big Sky Country from Billings to Bismarck

visits.text: You're entering one of the most history-laden towns on the entire East Coast. Harpers Ferry is famous for John Brown's raid in October 1859: this radical abolitionist seized the federal arsenal with 21 men hoping to spark a slave uprising. The town changed hands eight times during the Civil War, and its Victorian Lower Town has remained virtually intact since 1865. Start early to visit before the school buses arrive, and don't miss the view from Jefferson Rock—Thomas Jefferson himself wrote in 1783 that this panorama of the confluence of two rivers was worth “a voyage across the Atlantic”.

You stop before this small red brick building—the only vestige of the 1859 raid still standing. John Brown and his men held out here for 36 hours before being captured by Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee—the same man who would lead the Confederate army two years later. The irony of history: the fort was dismantled stone by stone and rebuilt three times in three different locations before returning in 1968 to its original site, within a few meters. The adjacent museum traces the context of the abolitionist movement with documents and accounts from Brown's contemporaries.

You're standing on the point of land where the Shenandoah meets the Potomac—two rivers with slightly different hues that blend only gradually over several hundred meters. This place already fascinated Lenape tribes long before Europeans arrived, and it was the first natural site on the continent described as “sublime” by an American president, namely Jefferson. To the north, the 1894 truss railroad bridge crosses both rivers in a single span. In fall, the red and orange leaves make this viewpoint one of the most photographed scenes in the entire region.

activities.text: You climb through forest for 45 minutes on a rocky trail, then the vegetation opens onto the ruins of Confederate artillery batteries from 1862. At the summit—448 meters—the complete panorama unfolds below: Lower Town, both rivers, the railroad bridges, and the Virginia hills stretching to the horizon. It was from this very spot that Confederate General “Stonewall” Jackson's army observed the town before taking it in September 1862. Arrive in late afternoon for golden light on the village rooftops.

You're launching onto the Shenandoah just upstream from Harpers Ferry: a few beginner-friendly rapids, banks lined with giant sycamores and weeping willows, and the awareness that you're paddling on a river that Confederate and Union soldiers forded multiple times between 1861 and 1865, sometimes under fire. The view of Loudoun Heights cliffs from the kayak is one of the most spectacular in the region. River Riders and Harpers Ferry Adventure Center offer rentals with shuttle included.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

visits.text: Mark Twain House & Museum - Where American Literature Was Born: Tour the stunning Gothic-style mansion where Samuel Clemens penned 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn,' 'The Adventures of Tom Sawyer,' and other American classics. The elaborately decorated 25-room house, described by Twain as 'part steamboat, part cathedral,' reveals the author's creative genius and domestic life.

Harriet Beecher Stowe Center - The Home That Changed a Nation: Adjacent to the Twain House, this historic site honors the author of 'Uncle Tom's Cabin,' the novel Abraham Lincoln credited with helping start the Civil War. The center continues Stowe's legacy of literary activism.

Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art - America's Oldest Continuously Operating Public Art Museum: Founded in 1842, this castle-like institution houses over 50,000 works spanning 5,000 years across European, American, and contemporary collections. The stunning and diverse holdings rival those of major metropolitan museums.

Old State House - Where Democracy Took Root: This National Historic Landmark served as Connecticut's center of government from 1796 to 1878 and witnessed pivotal moments in American history. Now a museum, it preserves the chambers where early Americans debated the nature of liberty.

Connecticut Science Center - Interactive Discovery by the River: This striking modern venue overlooking the Connecticut River features hundreds of interactive exhibits exploring everything from space to the human body, along with a 3D theater.

activities.text: Bushnell Center for Performing Arts - New England's Premier Performance Venue: This historic theater hosts Broadway tours, world-class concerts, and cultural events in an ornate setting that has entertained Hartford audiences since 1930.

Connecticut Art Trail - 250 Miles, 21 Institutions, 500,000 Works: This statewide route showcases Connecticut's pivotal role in American Impressionism through museums from Greenwich to Hartford, including entry to the Wadsworth Atheneum and numerous specialized collections.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

places.name: Hattiesburg, MS

visits.text: One of the few museums in the world dedicated solely to African American military history is here—housed in a 1942 USO Club reserved for Black soldiers under segregation. Six wars covered, from the Civil War to Iraq. An entire room on the Tuskegee Airmen, African American pilots who flew 1,491 missions without losing a single escorted bomber in Europe. Free admission, open Tuesday–Saturday.

Funny and unexpected, the Hattiesburg Pocket Museum is a 90 cm-wide “museum” in a niche between two buildings on Front Street—miniature exhibitions changed monthly (Barbie dolls, Cold War objects, outsider art miniatures). Free, open 24/7. All around, the historic downtown has gained over 70 murals since 2014 through a municipal program that revitalized the former railroad district.

15 km south, Camp Shelby is the largest National Guard training base in the United States, active since 1917—and its military museum is one of the South's largest. An exceptional exhibition on the 442nd Infantry Regiment, the most decorated Japanese American unit in U.S. military history, trained here in 1943 while the soldiers' families were in internment camps. Free admission, ID check at the base entrance.

activities.text: You bike along the Longleaf Trace—a 66 km greenway built on a former railroad line, connecting Hattiesburg to Prentiss through longleaf pine forest. Flat, paved, shaded. Bike rental at Trace Station in Hattiesburg ($15 for a half-day). The urban section can also be explored on foot without renting a bike.

days_plan.itin_title: From Jacksonville to Dallas in 15 days, through the Deep South

Mississippi Armed Forces Museum Camp Shelby

visits.text: Chateau Montelena, Calistoga: plan a round trip from Healdsburg. The other winner of the 1976 Judgment of Paris, in the white wine category. The 1973 Chardonnay made by Mike Grgich—a Croatian who would later found his own winery, Grgich Hills—beat Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet in a blind tasting before a French jury. The stone château was built in 1888 by Alfred Tubbs, a merchant who had studied viticulture in Bordeaux. Jim Barrett's restoration in the 1970s returned it to its original appearance. Today's Estate Chardonnay is the direct descendant of the 1973. Reservations required.

Old Faithful Geyser of California, Calistoga: plan a round trip from Healdsburg. One of the world's three “faithful” geysers (alongside Yellowstone and one in New Zealand). It erupts every 10–30 minutes depending on underground pressure, up to 20 meters high, with water at 78°C. Not grandiose in the Yellowstone sense, but the phenomenon's punctuality is real—unlike many geysers that stray from their schedule. $15, 30 minutes is enough.

Healdsburg Plaza, your arrival point in Sonoma: a town of 12,000 inhabitants arranged around a central square planted with palm trees, with about fifty tasting rooms within walking distance. The contrast with Napa is immediate - less marble, more wood, fewer $100 labels, more winemakers serving you themselves.

Williams-Selyem, 10701 Westside Road: founded in 1979 by Burt Williams and Ed Selyem in a Fulton garage, this winery became the cult benchmark for American Pinot Noir. Their 2007 Litton Estate received 100/100 in Wine Spectator in 2009—the first North American Pinot to reach that score in a major magazine. The problem: visits are reserved for mailing list members, and the waiting list is several years long. If you get access, you're truly lucky. Otherwise, Gary Farrell Vineyards right next door (10701 Westside Road as well, separate entrance) offers a view looking down over the Russian River Valley from its tasting room.

Iron Horse Vineyards, Sebastopol: 25 minutes west of Healdsburg, on the edge of the Sonoma Coast. The estate founded in 1979 produces traditional-method sparkling wines served at the White House since Ronald Reagan—every president since has continued the tradition. Tastings take place outdoors on a terrace with 360° views of the vines. This isn't a winery to visit just because you're passing by: the trip from Healdsburg is worth the detour for the contrast in scenery and the style so different from Russian River reds.

activities.text: Crossing the Mayacamas Mountains via Highway 128: 1 hour of switchbacks between Calistoga and Healdsburg, through the range separating Napa from Sonoma. The road is narrow, the turns tight, and the views of both valleys are worth the effort. This isn't a road to be in a hurry on - that's exactly why it deserves to be savored.

First glass of Sonoma Pinot noir in Healdsburg: The Matheson (106 Matheson Street) is the Plaza's go-to restaurant and bar, with an impressive cellar of local wines available by the glass. It's the right way to enter Sonoma County: mentally compare them with the Cabernets of the last three days. The difference is immediate—less body, more fruit, pronounced acidity.

Westside Road drive: Sonoma County's most beautiful wine road. You follow the Russian River between Healdsburg and Guerneville for about twenty kilometers, under eucalyptus and redwoods. The sandy Goldridge soils—the secret of the valley's great Pinots—are visible in the roadside cuttings. Drive slowly, with no schedule.

Winemaker's picnic between tastings: buy bread, cheeses, and charcuterie at Big John's Market in Healdsburg (1345 Healdsburg Avenue), add a bottle of Pinot bought that morning, and find a spot at a table in the gardens of one of the wineries that allows picnics (Gary Farrell, notably). It's cheaper than a starred restaurant and often better than you expect.

places.name: Healy, AK

visits.text: Take the Parks Highway south from Fairbanks for about 195 km to the entrance of Denali National Park, via Healy. Keep your eyes open towards the end of the drive. Past Healy, shortly before the park entrance, the Nenana River canyon suddenly opens up: the glacial river cuts a gorge through the rock for several kilometres, and its turquoise waters contrast with the dark walls. Operators offer rafting trips on these waters from the village of Denali Park, right at the park entrance. At the Denali Visitor Center, pick up your maps and ask about the day's weather and conditions on the Park Road - Denali (6,190 m) is visible only 30% of the time from the entrance area.

The whole day is devoted to the transit bus into the park - book your seat on reservedenali.com, as seats go fast in July and August. In 2026, buses run as far as mile 43 (East Fork River) because of the works on the Pretty Rocks landslide. The green transit buses are hop-on/hop-off: you get off wherever you like along the road and continue on any following green bus. The road winds through open tundra - it is from the bus that you will spot grizzlies (300 to 350 individuals in the northern part of the park), herds of caribou (about 1,500 head in the Denali herd), Dall sheep clinging to the white ridges, and perhaps a wolf. Bring binoculars - the wildlife is often far away. On a clear day, the ridges along the road offer direct views of Denali.

Start the morning at the park's sled dog kennels - take the Kennels Shuttle from the Visitor Center. Demonstrations run at 10am, 2pm, and 4pm in high season (June-September) and last 30 minutes. This program began in 1922 when the park's first superintendent, Harry Karstens, bought the first 7 dogs for $45 each to patrol the wilderness. Today, about thirty dogs live and work here - the only active kennel in the entire National Park Service. You can pet most of the dogs in the dog yard between demonstrations.

Drive to Savage River (mile 15), roughly forty minutes by road from Healy - this is the end of the road open to private vehicles. Arrive early, as the parking lot is small. The Savage River Loop Trail runs 5 km on the flat along the river, with a footbridge crossing: on the slopes above, look for Dall sheep with the naked eye or binoculars - about 2,500 of them live in the park. The transition between boreal forest and open tundra happens precisely in this area, making it one of the best places near the entrance to grasp the typical Denali landscape.

activities.text: Early afternoon, take the free Riley Creek Loop shuttle from the Visitor Center - it serves Riley Creek Campground, the Bus Depot, and the Horseshoe Lake trailhead. The Horseshoe Lake Trail is 2.4 km round-trip from the bus stop: the descent through spruce forest leads to a horseshoe-shaped lake dammed by beavers. It's one of the best spots in the entrance area for moose watching, especially early morning. In the evening, if you arrive before 5pm, catch the sled dog demonstration at the park kennels (3 km from entrance) - rangers explain a program dating back to 1922, the only active kennel in the entire National Park Service.

Late day after your bus return, hike to Horseshoe Lake trail if you missed it yesterday, or try the Mount Healy Overlook Trail from the Visitor Center: 9 km round-trip with 520 m of elevation gain, it climbs through birch forest then emerges onto an open ridge with views across the entrance valley and, on clear days, Denali's summit on the horizon. Allow 3 hours round-trip and wear good boots - upper slopes can be slippery.

For hikers, the Savage Alpine Trail starts from the same car park: a point-to-point climb up to the ridge with plunging views over the valley. Be careful - bears have been reported on this trail, so carry bear spray and make noise. In the evening, before heading back to Healy, stop at the restaurants in the Denali Park Village area, about twenty minutes by road south of Healy, which serve local dishes. The weather changes very quickly in this area - always keep extra layers in your pack.

visits.text: Step into the charming Bavarian-themed village of Helen, where colorful Alpine architecture, flower-draped balconies, and cobblestone lanes create an unexpected European atmosphere nestled in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Over 200 specialty shops, authentic German bakeries, and traditional restaurants line the pedestrian streets beneath forested peaks. The town hosts the longest Oktoberfest celebration in America, spanning two full months of festive activities.

Hike to Anna Ruby Falls, a spectacular dual waterfall where two creeks plunge side by side into a misty pool surrounded by lush mountain forest. The accessible trail winds through hardwood groves and rhododendron thickets, offering a refreshing escape into pristine wilderness just minutes from town. Interpretive displays explain the area's unique ecology.

activities.text: Sample wines at local vineyards producing distinctive Georgia varietals, then explore the Helen Arts & Heritage Center documenting the town's transformation from a declining logging community to a beloved tourist destination. The Chattahoochee River flows directly through town and is perfect for tubing.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Atchafalaya Basin - The largest swamp in North America: 600,000 hectares of black water, bald cypress, and Spanish moss. Henderson, a small Cajun village on the levee, is the gateway to the basin. The landscape is otherworldly—cathedrals of cypress rise from dark, still water.

activities.text: Take a boat tour in the Atchafalaya Basin - Several operators depart from Henderson for 1.5- to 2-hour swamp tours. You'll navigate between century-old cypress trees, spotting alligators, turtles, great blue herons, and bald eagles. Early morning and late afternoon are best—the light filtering through the moss is spectacular.

Eat crawfish in Henderson - Levee restaurants in Henderson serve all-you-can-eat boiled crawfish during the season (January–June). You eat them on newspaper, spiced with cayenne, alongside corn and potatoes. Salt them with your hands—no utensils.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Louisiana Road Trip: Jazz and Bayous

visits.text: Visit the Henderson County Heritage Museum, which provides comprehensive accounts of local history and culture through engaging exhibits and artifacts. The museum offers visitors an excellent introduction to the heritage of this charming mountain foothill community.

Discover the Mineral & Lapidary Museum along Hendersonville's vibrant Main Street, featuring a varied collection of precious stones, minerals, and semiprecious stones found and mined throughout North Carolina. This fascinating museum showcases the geological treasures that lie beneath the Carolina soil.

activities.text: Engage young minds at Hands On! Children's Museum, where interactive exhibits and hands-on activities entertain and educate visitors of all ages. For a change of scenery, escape to the peaceful open surroundings of Saint Paul Mountain Vineyards, where you can sample sweet local wines while enjoying stunning mountain views.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Day 2 - The High Line brings the day to a beautiful close: 2.3 km of elevated railway converted into a garden, with wild grasses, artworks, and walkways above Tenth Avenue. Free, open into the evening. Allow 45 min to 1 hour for a leisurely walk north to Hudson Yards.

Day 2 - On the High Line, original rails still surface between the perennials planted by Piet Oudolf. Viewpoints follow one another: Hudson Yards' coppery Vessel, the Empire State in the distance, Zaha Hadid's building along the park. Very busy on weekends; weekday mornings it's nearly yours.

activities.text: Possible mid-route exit at 23rd Street for Chelsea's art galleries, free, concentrated between 20th and 27th Streets.
End of Day 2. Toward the Empire State Building for tomorrow morning: 1.6 km from Hudson Yards, on foot via 34th Street or by subway, about 15 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

places.name: Hilton Head Island, SC

visits.text: Explore Hilton Head Island's pristine beaches, featuring miles of soft, pale sand perfect for cycling, dolphin watching, and spectacular sunrise viewing. The island's coastline transforms into brilliant shades of pink and gold at dawn, creating an atmosphere of tranquility that defines this barrier island paradise. With gentle waves and wide-open stretches, this destination offers quintessential Lowcountry relaxation.

Discover Harbour Town, the island's iconic waterfront village crowned by the distinctive red-and-white striped lighthouse. Climb the lighthouse for panoramic coastal views stretching across the marshlands and harbor. The village combines maritime charm with boutique shopping and waterfront dining in a picturesque setting.

activities.text: Cycle through more than 100 km of scenic trails shaded by magnificent live oaks draped in Spanish moss. These pathways wind through maritime forests, past lagoons teeming with wildlife, and along beaches where the sand is firm enough for extended rides. The island's extensive trail network makes it one of the most bike-friendly destinations in the Southeast.

Paddle through the calm salt marshes by kayak, gliding past herons, dolphins, and jumping fish in some of the most pristine waterways in the Lowcountry. The Art League Gallery and the Gullah Museum of Hilton Head Island offer cultural enrichment, showcasing regional artistry and the rich heritage of the Gullah people.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Road Trip: From Lowcountry Beaches to the Blue Ridge Mountains

map_keywords: Gullah Museum of Hilton Head Island

visits.text: At the James Fort site, archaeologists are still scraping the soil right in front of you, near the 17th-century church tower. In 1607 the first permanent English colony in North America settled here, and the Jamestown Rediscovery project has already unearthed about 3 million artifacts. Plan on two tickets, sold at the visitor center: the island is managed by Preservation Virginia and the National Park Service.

Long believed to have been swallowed by the James River, the James Fort palisade was found on dry land in 1996. The Archaearium, Historic Jamestowne's archaeology museum, displays over 4,000 artifacts, and in 2013 researchers there documented the remains of a young Englishwoman who was a victim of cannibalism during the 1609–1610 famine. The Dale House Café is closed for renovation, so bring a picnic.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

places.name: Hocking Hills, OH

visits.text: You descend into the most famous of Hocking Hills gorges: Old Man's Cave is a recess cave carved into 150 feet of Blackhand sandstone - a red-orange sandstone deposited over 300 million years ago when Ohio was covered by an ancient ocean. The name comes from Richard Rowe, a hermit who migrated from Tennessee's Cumberland Mountains around 1796 and lived in this cave with his two dogs until his death in the early 19th century. He is said to be buried beneath the rock. The State of Ohio purchased the first 146 acres of the future park in 1924, including Old Man's Cave. Arrive before 9am on spring and fall weekends: the parking lot overflows very quickly and rangers limit access.

You enter Ohio's largest recess cave: Ash Cave measures 700 feet from one end to the other and 100 feet deep, large enough to shelter an entire church. A waterfall plunges from the edge of the vault in a streaming cascade that, in winter, transforms into a spectacular ice curtain. The name comes from the mounds of ashes found here by the first European explorers of the 19th century - traces of Native American occupation over thousands of years. The access trail is flat and paved for 0.8 km from the parking lot, accessible to strollers and people with reduced mobility.

You reach Cedar Falls from the Grandma Gatewood Trail - a 6-mile trail named after Emma 'Grandma' Gatewood, the first woman to hike the entire 3,500 km Appalachian Trail solo in 1955, at age 67. The falls plunge into a sandstone basin where aspens and hemlocks form a vegetal dome. In reality, Queer Creek feeds the falls - the cedars that settlers noticed here were actually hemlocks, a botanical confusion from the colonial era. It's one of Ohio's most photogenic waterfalls in any season.

activities.text: You set off from Old Man's Cave and walk to Ash Cave along 9.7 km of trail that forms part of the Buckeye Trail, a 1,400-mile route winding across Ohio. You pass through deep gorges where the air is ten degrees cooler than on the plateau, follow streams over sandstone beds, and walk beneath damp, fern-covered cliffs. The giant hemlocks along the trail have survived here since the last glaciation 15,000 years ago, sustained by a cool microclimate beyond the reach of Ohio's summer heat. On weekends from late May to late October, take the free park shuttle back to the starting point instead of retracing your steps.

You don a harness, climb onto a platform in the trees, and launch yourself on a cable stretched above the orange sandstone gorges - Hocking Hills has been designated the 'Canopy Tour Capital of the Midwest', and you understand why from the first departure. Hocking Hills Canopy Tours offers a SuperZip that reaches 100 km/h above the canyon and Nightflight evening tours. From the cables, you see the sandstone cliffs from inside, the hemlock crowns beneath your feet, and the gorge opening downward - a perspective hikers never know. Book ahead: weekend slots fill up weeks in advance.

activities.text: Hall of Mosses takes you beneath maple trees whose branches are draped in thick moss. This short loop in Hoh Rain Forest showcases a temperate rain forest, very different from a tropical jungle despite its lush appearance. Arrive early to reduce the wait at the entrance, and stay on the trail, even when photographing the roots.

Continue your walk on Spruce Nature Trail to reconnect with flowing water. The loop follows Taft Creek and then the Hoh River, passing through forest stands of different ages. It complements the moss-covered maples without repeating the same scenery. Bring a waterproof layer and keep your distance from any wildlife you encounter.

places.name: Holbrook, AZ

visits.text: The drive north from Tucson offers a worthy detour: Salt River Canyon, on US-60, plunges more than 300 meters deep and its red granite walls recall a miniature version of the Grand Canyon. Stop at the bridge spanning the river—several short trails begin there and the water is accessible.

In Holbrook, don't pass the Wigwam Motel without stopping. Built in 1950 by Chester Lewis on Route 66, this complex of 15 concrete tipis has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 2002—and it directly inspired the Cozy Cone Motel in Pixar's Cars. The small museum at the front desk houses a collection of petrified wood and Route 66 memorabilia that the Lewis family has maintained for three generations.

225 million years ago, northeastern Arizona was a humid tropical forest at the equator of the Pangaea supercontinent. Trees that fell into rivers were slowly mineralized, their cells replaced by quartz colored by iron, manganese, and carbon. You'll see these petrified logs scattered across the landscape, some several meters long, gleaming like ceramics under the sun. Enter from the north (exit 311 off I-40) to begin with Painted Desert panoramas from Tiponi Point and Tawa Point.

Midway through the park, make the Blue Mesa stop: the blue-violet sandstone hoodoos rising from the desert are among the park's most photographed formations. A 1.6-km pedestrian loop descends among these strange formations—allow 45 minutes and bring water, there's none on site.

Puerco Pueblo is the park's most accessible archaeological site: the ruins of this ancestral Puebloan village, occupied until around 1380, are surrounded by petroglyphs 650 to 2,000 years old carved into the dark sandstone. The trail is flat and loops around the remains in under 30 minutes.

activities.text: Explore historic downtown Holbrook, one of the most authentically Route 66 towns in Arizona. The Navajo County Historical Museum (in the old 1898 courthouse) traces the region's history with collections of fossils, Navajo crafts, and period documents. Admission is free.
If the road and sun have worn you down, Holbrook's few local restaurants serve Southwestern cuisine—burritos and green chile—before a good night's rest before the big park day tomorrow.

In the park's south section, don't miss Newspaper Rock: from an observation platform, you can make out hundreds of petroglyphs carved by Native peoples over several centuries. The park's main road (28 miles / 45 km) takes you from north to south without needing to backtrack—a considerable time-saver.

The Painted Desert Inn, designated a National Historic Landmark, deserves a stop: built in the 1940s and designed by architect Richard Neutra for the park's north entrance, it now houses a museum and exhibits on the history of Route 66, which once crossed through the park. The view of the Painted Desert from its terrace is among the park's finest.

visits.text: Day 1: Kachemak Bay - This 40-mile-long arm of Cook Inlet features dramatic scenery where forested mountains plunge to productive waters teeming with marine life. The bay's rich ecosystem supports commercial fishing, marine research, and exceptional wildlife viewing.

Day 1: Homer Spit - This narrow 4.5-mile finger of land extending into Kachemak Bay hosts the community's fishing harbor, charter operations, and eclectic collection of shops and services. Walking the spit offers views of volcanoes across Cook Inlet and opportunities to observe sea otters and eagles.

Day 1: Cook Inlet Volcanoes - On clear days, the skyline across the water reveals the dramatic profiles of Mount Augustine, Mount Iliamna, and Mount Redoubt, active volcanoes of the Aleutian Range rising to heights exceeding 10,000 feet.

Day 2: Kachemak Bay State Park - Alaska's first state park encompasses 400,000 acres of wilderness across the bay from Homer, accessible only by boat or floatplane. The park protects tidewater glaciers, alpine peaks, old-growth forests, and diverse marine and terrestrial ecosystems.

Day 2: Halibut Cove - This small artists' colony across Kachemak Bay from Homer is accessible only by boat, featuring boardwalk trails, galleries, and a peaceful atmosphere distinct from road-connected communities.

Day 3: Seldovia - This remote fishing village across Kachemak Bay maintains a slower pace and frontier character that has largely vanished from road-accessible Alaska. The 1964 earthquake and resulting tsunami devastated the original community built on pilings, but Seldovia rebuilt and preserves its distinctive character as an isolated outpost accessible only by water or air.

Day 3: Seldovia Boardwalk and Harbor - The small commercial harbor and remaining historic boardwalk sections offer glimpses of the community's past as a thriving fishing and Native village, while surrounding trails provide access to beaches and forests.

activities.text: Day 1: Homer Arts and Culture - This community at the end of the Sterling Highway has earned a reputation as an arts destination, with numerous galleries showcasing local painters, sculptors, and craftspeople inspired by the surrounding natural beauty.
Day 1: Bald Eagle Viewing - The harbor and beaches of Homer are home to bald eagles, drawn by the abundance of fish and marine carrion.

Day 2: Halibut Fishing Charters - Homer claims the title of Halibut Fishing Capital of the World, with charter boats departing daily for the productive waters of Cook Inlet and Kachemak Bay. Pacific halibut here can exceed 300 pounds.
Day 2: Salmon Fishing - Charter operations also target all five Pacific salmon species during their seasonal runs through Cook Inlet waters.

Day 2: Bear Viewing Flights - Scenic flights cross Cook Inlet to Katmai National Park and Lake Clark National Park, where coastal brown bears gather at salmon streams and mudflats. These day trips offer opportunities to observe bears at close range from safe viewing platforms.

Day 2: Kachemak Bay Hiking - Water taxis provide access to trailheads within the state park, where routes range from easy beach walks to challenging climbs reaching glacier viewpoints and alpine meadows.

Day 3: Fast Ferry from Homer - The 45-minute passenger ferry crossing offers panoramic views of Kachemak Bay's islands, wildlife, and the volcanic skyline beyond. Day trips allow several hours of exploration before returning to Homer.

Day 3: Seldovia Hiking and Kayaking - Trails radiate from the village through coastal forests and along beaches, while kayak rentals and tours offer ways to explore the surrounding waters and islands.

visits.text: Pearl Harbor National Memorial — Visit the USS Arizona Memorial commemorating the 1,177 sailors and Marines killed during the December 7, 1941 Japanese attack that brought America into World War II. The white memorial structure designed by Alfred Preis spans the sunken battleship's hull still leaking oil 80 years later.

USS Missouri Battleship — Tour the Mighty Mo where Japan surrendered on September 2, 1945, ending World War II. The Iowa-class battleship launched in 1944 served through Desert Storm before retiring to Pearl Harbor in 1999.

Diamond Head Crater — Hike 1.1 kilometers to the summit of this 232-meter volcanic tuff cone formed 300,000 years ago. The extinct crater offers panoramic views across Waikiki, Honolulu, and the Pacific from military bunkers constructed in 1908.

Iolani Palace — Explore the only official royal palace in the United States, completed in 1882 for King Kalakaua, blending American Florentine architecture with Hawaiian motifs. This National Historic Landmark features the throne rooms, the royal bedrooms and the tragic story of the overthrown Hawaiian monarchy.

Hanauma Bay Nature Preserve — Snorkel in this volcanic crater bay teeming with more than 400 species of fish, including parrotfish, tangs and triggerfish. The protected marine ecosystem, formed 32,000 years ago, creates ideal conditions for observing coral reefs and sea turtles. Allow about half an hour's drive from downtown Honolulu.

Nuuanu Pali Lookout — Stand at this windswept cliff edge 365 meters above Oahu's windward coast where King Kamehameha I won the decisive 1795 Battle of Nuuanu. Trade winds gust up to 60 mph through the mountain pass offering dramatic valley views.

Byodo-In Temple — Explore this replica of a 950-year-old Japanese Buddhist temple nestled in the Koolau Mountains. This 1968 concrete structure commemorates the centennial of Japanese immigration and houses a three-meter Buddha statue amid koi ponds and meditation gardens. Allow about half an hour's drive from Honolulu.

Lanikai Beach — Discover this pristine beach on Oahu's windward side with its powdery white sand and turquoise waters. The Mokulua Islands offshore create a picture-perfect landscape, ranked among the best beaches in the world. Allow about half an hour's drive from Honolulu.

activities.text: Waikiki Beach sunset — Relax on this world-famous crescent beach backed by high-rise hotels with Diamond Head providing dramatic backdrop. Surf lessons, outrigger canoe rides, and beachfront bars create the iconic Hawaiian vacation atmosphere.

Traditional Hawaiian luau — Experience ancient Hawaiian culture through hula dancing, fire knife performances, and kalua pig cooked in underground imu ovens. Cultural shows explain Polynesian navigation, legends, and aloha spirit.

Duke Kahanamoku statue visit — Photograph this bronze statue honoring Hawaii's legendary Olympic swimmer and father of modern surfing who won gold in 1912. The beachfront monument faces his beloved Waikiki waters with outstretched arms.

North Shore Drive — Travel Oahu's legendary surf coast past famous spots such as Pipeline, Sunset Beach and Waimea Bay. Roadside shrimp trucks, fruit stands and surf shops create a relaxed country atmosphere. Plan a full-day round trip from Honolulu.

Shave Ice at Matsumoto's — Taste this Hawaiian specialty of finely shaved ice topped with fruit syrups and condensed milk at the iconic Haleiwa shop, in business since 1951. This rainbow-coloured treat is the perfect refreshment on hot tropical days. Haleiwa is about three quarters of an hour's drive from Honolulu.

Watching at Sunset Beach — Watch winter swells build 9-meter waves at this world championship surf venue. From November to February, professional surfers take on the North Shore's massive waves, while summer brings calm swimming conditions. Allow about an hour's drive from Honolulu.

visits.text: Columbia River Gorge — Drive this 130-kilometer canyon where the Columbia River cuts through the Cascade Range at sea level. The National Scenic Area features over 90 waterfalls, dramatic basalt cliffs, and the only sea-level passage through the Cascades.

Multnomah Falls — From Hood River, plan an excursion to this waterfall, which drops 189 meters in two tiers linked by the historic Benson Bridge, built in 1914. The falls draw many visitors to their easily accessible viewing platform. Allow for a return drive from Hood River.

Vista House at Crown Point — From Hood River, plan a return drive to see this 1918 Art Nouveau observatory perched 223 meters above the Columbia River. The octagonal stone building offers views stretching 48 kilometers up and down the gorge from its clifftop setting.

Bonneville Dam — Tour this 1938 hydroelectric dam featuring underwater fish viewing windows where migrating salmon climb the fish ladder. The powerhouse generates 1,200 megawatts while allowing salmon passage upriver to spawn.

activities.text: Windsurfing observation at Hood River — Watch world-class windsurfers and kiteboarders ride consistent gorge winds accelerated by the Venturi effect. The Columbia River Gorge ranks among the world's premier windsurfing destinations.

Fruit Loop drive — Navigate the 35-mile loop through Hood River Valley orchards producing apples, pears, cherries, and peaches. Farm stands offer U-pick opportunities and fresh cider with Mount Hood backdrop.
Craft cider tasting — Sample hard ciders made from valley apples at local cideries. Hood River's orchards and craft beverage scene produce award-winning ciders showcasing heirloom apple varieties.

visits.text: Horicon Marsh - A vast freshwater marsh: 13,000 hectares of wetlands divided between a national wildlife refuge and a state wildlife area. In autumn (September-November), tens of thousands of Canada geese stop here during their migration - a striking sight. In spring, look for egrets, herons and sandhill cranes.
Boardwalk - A wooden walkway extends over the marsh offering close-up views of water lilies, reeds, and birds. Binoculars essential. You'll probably see turtles and, with luck, a bald eagle.

Auto tour - The driving loop at Horicon National Wildlife Refuge is on Highway 49, east of Waupun: allow for a round trip from Horicon. The 3-mile paved route crosses the marsh, with stops for birdwatching. It is open to cars from mid-March to late November, subject to conditions and hunting closures. The parking area and trails remain accessible in winter.

activities.text: Bird Watching - Over 300 bird species have been recorded at Horicon Marsh. The federal visitor center and state visitor center provide guides and maps of the best observation spots by season.

places.name: Hot Springs

visits.text: Hot Springs National Park is the oldest federally protected site in the United States: Congress created the Hot Springs Reservation on April 20, 1832, under President Andrew Jackson, 40 years before Yellowstone launched the national park concept. The park encompasses 47 springs that emerge at 62°C. Don't miss the public fountains on Central Avenue - the water is drinkable and free. What you're swallowing took about 4,000 years to percolate through the rock: it fell as rain in Roman times. Start here before heading down to Bathhouse Row - the walkway below the springs gives you the whole panorama in a single glance.

Bathhouse Row lines up eight bathhouses built between 1892 and 1923, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1987. Each has its own personality: the Buckstaff (1912) still operates exactly as it did originally - it's the only one. The Quapaw offers a more modern spa experience. The Superior now houses the only brewery in the world located inside a national park. The Maurice is undergoing restoration thanks to a $32 million grant. Take time to walk the full length of the facades: each building tells the story of a different decade of America's Gilded Age.

The Fordyce Bathhouse is the largest and most luxurious on Bathhouse Row - built in 1915 for over $200,000 at the time. Converted into the Visitor Center in 1989, it's the only one whose interior has been preserved intact: hand-laid tile, Italian marble, stained glass, Roman fountains in the hall, and a glass rendering of the Daughters of Neptune on the ceiling of the men's bath. Go inside even if you're not taking the waters - it's a museum in its own right.

activities.text: Thermal bath at the Buckstaff or the Quapaw: the only two bathhouses still operating on Bathhouse Row. The Buckstaff offers the most traditional experience - marble tubs, hot towels, the ritual hasn't changed since 1912. The Quapaw is more contemporary, with four pools at different temperatures. Book ahead on weekends, and arrive early on weekdays: the Buckstaff doesn't take reservations for simple baths but closes its doors at 3 PM.

Hot Springs Mountain Trail hike: 3 km round trip to the 65-meter observation tower with panoramic views across the Ouachita Mountains. The trail starts right from Bathhouse Row - no car needed. Allow an hour round trip at a good pace, but the summit is worth lingering.

places.name: Houghton, MI

visits.text: The Ranger III takes 6 hours to travel from Rock Harbor to Houghton—a crossing of open Lake Superior worth experiencing in its own right. From the deck, you watch the island disappear behind you and the Michigan shoreline gradually emerge. Houghton first reveals itself through its Portage Lake Lift Bridge, opened in the 1950s.

At Michigan Tech's A.E. Seaman Mineral Museum, native copper crystals weighing several kilos are displayed under glass. The Keweenaw Peninsula had been producing copper for millennia—the Ojibwe extracted it long before Europeans arrived. The display cases also hold meteorites, gemstones, and nuggets that tell the story of two centuries of mining.

activities.text: Head up to Quincy Mine to descend into the tunnels of what was one of the world's largest copper mines in the 19th century. The tour takes you by tram along the hillside. The Cornish miners who dug here left their culinary mark: pasties—small meat and vegetable pies they took underground—became the signature dish of the entire Upper Peninsula.

visits.text: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park — Explore the 9,200 hectares of bayous, swamps and marshes of the Barataria Preserve, representing the ecosystems of the Mississippi River delta. Boardwalk trails wind through cypress-tupelo swamps inhabited by alligators and wading birds. A good hour's drive from the stopover town.

Southdown Plantation House—Tour this 1858 Greek Revival mansion converted into a museum documenting Terrebonne Parish's sugar industry and Mardi Gras traditions. The house features original furnishings, Mardi Gras costumes, and local history exhibits.

Wetlands Acadian Cultural Center — Learn about the Cajun, Native American and African American cultures shaping Louisiana's coastal wetlands. The exhibits explain how communities adapted to life in America's largest coastal marsh system. About 26 km from the stopover town, 25 minutes by road.

Mandalay National Wildlife Refuge — Travel by boat through 17,500 hectares protecting coastal marsh habitat for wintering waterfowl and resident alligators, as most of the refuge can only be reached by boat. The refuge shows the coastal erosion challenges threatening Louisiana's vanishing wetlands.

activities.text: Airboat swamp tour — Skim across shallow marshes and bayous at high speed spotting alligators, nutria, and abundant birdlife. Local Cajun guides explain wetland ecology while navigating channels through sawgrass and water hyacinths.

Fresh Gulf seafood—Dine on boiled crawfish, fried catfish, and shrimp po-boys at seaside restaurants serving daily catches. Terrebonne Parish fishermen supply restaurants with Gulf shrimp, oysters, and blue crabs.

Cajun music at Jolly Inn—Hear traditional Cajun musicians playing accordion, fiddle, and washboard at this authentic dance hall. The family-friendly venue preserves musical traditions passed through generations of South Louisiana families.

Deep Louisiana: Jazz, Bayous & Plantations - 9-Day Loop from New Orleans

visits.text: The Henderson Levee, 30 minutes east of Lafayette, is the gateway to the Atchafalaya Basin - the largest river swamp in the United States. From the earthen levee overlooking the cypress trees, you have a clear view of the expanse of reeds and flooded forest stretching south as far as the eye can see. This is also where boat tour operators and catfish restaurants cluster - an essential stop before heading out on the water.

Space Center Houston is the only way for the general public to access NASA's Johnson Space Center. The showstopper remains the historic Mission Control, designated a National Historic Landmark in 1985 and fully restored in 2019 to its exact configuration on July 20, 1969 - the day Neil Armstrong set foot on the Moon. Cigarettes, ashtrays and period carpeting were all recreated identically from photographs and controller testimonies. The room guided nine Gemini missions and every single Apollo flight. Outside, climb aboard the NASA 905 Boeing 747 that dominates the courtyard: the high-fidelity Independence shuttle replica rests right on top. Allow at least 3.5 hours to see everything, and book the tram tour in advance during high season.

The Menil Collection, in Montrose, is one of the most surprising free museums in the United States. John and Dominique de Menil - Franco-American collectors based in Houston - assembled 17,000 works spanning antiquity to contemporary art. Renzo Piano's building, inaugurated in 1987, filters Texas natural light through its concrete 'leaves' so it never damages the canvases. You can easily spend an hour and a half without noticing time pass - it's one of those museums you keep coming back to.

The Museum of Fine Arts Houston ranks among the ten most important art museums in the United States, with more than 70,000 works divided between two buildings connected by a tunnel: Mies van der Rohe's Caroline Wiess Law Building (1958) and Rafael Moneo's Audrey Jones Beck Building (2000). The African art and Pre-Columbian collections are particularly remarkable. Arrive at opening on weekdays to avoid school groups - you'll have the galleries to yourself until 11 AM.

The Rothko Chapel is one of the most singular places in Texas. In 1964, collectors John and Dominique de Menil asked Mark Rothko to create a non-denominational meditation space. The painter, who never visited Houston and never saw the completed chapel - he took his own life in February 1970, a year before its inauguration - designed 14 immense canvases in deep violet and black for an octagonal structure lit by a skylight. The room compels silence. A $30 million restoration in 2021 restored the exact light Rothko intended. Free admission.

The Bellaire Chinatown, in Houston's southwest suburbs, is the most important Asian district in Texas. You'll find Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and Taiwanese restaurants whose quality rivals the great Asian American metros. Walk or drive along Bellaire Boulevard to spot the signs - several bakeries and markets merit a stop.

activities.text: From the Henderson Levee - barely 30 minutes from Lafayette - operators run boat tours into the Atchafalaya Basin, America's largest river swamp with nearly one million acres of cypress forests, bayous and lakes. Some use powerful airboats that penetrate areas inaccessible to any other craft; others opt for quiet motorboats, letting you hear the buzz of insects and the plunge of herons. Go early in the morning: alligators bask on the surface before the heat rises, and birds fish in the golden dawn light. Plan to lunch in Henderson afterward before taking I-10 to Houston - count on 3.5 to 4 hours driving.

Buffalo Bayou Park unfolds 160 acres of urban park along the bayou that cuts through Houston's heart. Vendors rent kayaks at Lost Lake - an unexpected way to see the downtown skyscrapers from the water. The park is also crossed by well-maintained bike trails. If you're there in the evening, the Waugh Drive bridge harbors a colony of over 250,000 Mexican free-tailed bats that pour out in a dense cloud at dusk.

Discovery Green, a four-hectare urban park in the heart of downtown, is Houston's outdoor living room. Free concerts when scheduled, food trucks, a lake and shaded terraces make it a pleasant late-afternoon stop. Walk around the lake and take time to see the green spaces and downtown buildings surrounding the park.

visits.text: Humboldt - Small Town, Big Revival: A devoted team of entrepreneurs has launched an effort to modernize this small eastern Kansas town in surprisingly innovative ways.
Base Camp Humboldt - Scandinavian-Inspired Glamping: Rental cabins perch around a large fishing pond, with bike rentals providing access to adjacent rail trails for multi-day adventures.
Southwind Rail Trail and Prairie Spirit Trail - 51+ Miles of Trail Adventures: These connected trails offer cycling and hiking through Kansas countryside, accessible right from Base Camp.
Humboldt Mercantile - Kansas-Made Goods and Craft Coffee: Browse a curated selection of Kansas-made products while enjoying locally roasted coffee drinks.
Water Tower Mural - Humboldt's Instagram Moment: Snap a selfie beside the colorful mural depicting the town's famous water tower proclaiming “Life is fine in Humboldt.”

visits.text: Bleached trunks lying in the sand: Boneyard Beach at Hunting Island State Park is the direct result of erosion. The island, South Carolina's most visited state park, retains a lighthouse made of detachable cast-iron sections, moved about 2 km inland in 1889. Check access to Little Hunting Island and the beach before you go: the park may close the bridge and beach because of tides and hazardous conditions. Also check whether the lighthouse is open for climbing: it sometimes closes for repairs.

activities.text: Hunting Island State Park regulars head for the lagoon, "the calm side of the beach". Herons, egrets and sometimes dolphins show up there, away from the crowds. This island is also where Vietnam scenes from Forrest Gump were filmed: bring water for the trails.

visits.text: Day 1: Step into humanity's greatest adventure at the US Space & Rocket Center, where towering Saturn V rockets pierce the Alabama sky and the dreams of space exploration come alive. Wander through the awe-inspiring Saturn V Hall, home to one of only three remaining moon rockets, and stand beneath the very engines that propelled astronauts to the lunar surface. Don't miss the meticulously recreated International Space Station module, where you'll discover the ingenious solutions astronauts use for everyday tasks in zero gravity.

Day 1: Channel your inner astronaut at Space Camp, the legendary program that has inspired generations of future scientists and explorers since 1982. Whether you're traveling with curious kids or harboring your own cosmic dreams, the center offers immersive experiences from simulated shuttle missions to underwater astronaut training. The gift shop is a treasure trove of NASA memorabilia and space-themed items you won't find anywhere else.

Day 2: Wander through the tree-lined streets of the Twickenham Historic District, where antebellum mansions draped in Southern grandeur transport you to a pre-Civil War era of cotton wealth and gracious living. This remarkable neighborhood boasts Alabama's finest concentration of historic homes, their columned porticos and wraparound verandas whispering tales of a bygone age. Pick up a self-guided walking tour from the Visitor Bureau and let the free audio guides bring each architectural treasure to life.

Day 2: Discover artistic treasures overlooking the serene waters of Big Spring Park at the Huntsville Museum of Art, a showcase of carefully curated collections. Marvel at the Buccellati silver menagerie, where semi-precious stones and gleaming silver are transformed into lifelike creatures of extraordinary craftsmanship.

Day 2: Find your peaceful center at Big Spring Park, Huntsville's beloved green heart where the city's founding spring still bubbles up from ancient limestone caves beneath your feet. Stroll across the graceful Japanese bridge reflected in lily-pad-dotted waters, or spread a picnic blanket on the manicured lawns where festivals and community gatherings have brought neighbors together for generations. The smaller park section features a dancing fountain fed by the original spring that drew settler John Hunt to establish his cabin here in 1805.

Day 2: Journey back to the summer of 1819 at Alabama Constitutional Hall Park, where delegates gathered in a humble cabinetmaker's workshop to forge the state's founding document. The meticulously reconstructed wooden buildings surrounding the central courtyard paint a vivid portrait of frontier life, from the postmaster's quarters to the blacksmith's forge. Join a guided tour to peek inside the furnished rooms and imagine the heated debates that shaped Alabama's destiny.

Day 2: Browse the nostalgic aisles of Harrison Bros. Hardware, where original wooden counters, brass cash registers, and floor-to-ceiling shelves evoke the general stores of yesteryear. Though the nails and tacks have given way to locally crafted treasures and Rocket City memorabilia, the store's authentic 19th-century character remains gloriously intact. This is the place to find that perfect American-made souvenir that captures Huntsville's unique blend of history and innovation.

Day 3: Lose yourself in 45 hectares of botanical wonder at the Huntsville Botanical Garden, a volunteer-driven project that has blossomed into one of the South's premier horticultural destinations. Glide through the gardens in a golf cart, pausing at the Damson Aquatic Garden where a Japanese pavilion floats serenely above pools carpeted with water lilies. Time your visit for summer when the Daylily Garden erupts in a sunset palette of gold, coral, and rose that will take your breath away.

Day 3: Watch children's imaginations take flight in the enchanting Children's Garden, where wading pools sparkle in the sun, dinosaur bones await discovery, and fairytale creatures peek from hidden corners. The butterfly house offers pure magic as kaleidoscopic wings flutter around you, landing on tropical blooms and sipping from shallow pools in a living rainbow of color.

Day 3: Ascend Monte Sano to discover Burritt on the Mountain, the eclectic retreat of homeopathic physician Dr. William Henry Burritt, who sought the cooler mountain air and woodland tranquility above the city. Tour the 1930s mansion furnished with period pieces, then wander the historic park where relocated log cabins and wooden farmhouses reveal how Alabama's pioneers lived and worked. Chat with costumed interpreters, meet the friendly farm goats, and try your hand at traditional handicrafts at the folk school.

Day 3: Step into a creative wonderland at Lowe Mill, the South's largest independent arts facility housed in a magnificently repurposed textile mill. Over 200 working artists have transformed this industrial cathedral into a vibrant village of studios, galleries, and cafes where you can watch potters throw clay, painters layer color, and jewelers craft wearable art. Check the schedule for concerts on the dock, where musicians perform on a raised walkway while audiences picnic around the iconic water tower.

activities.text: Day 1: Rise early and join the locals at the beloved Blue Plate Cafe for an authentic Southern breakfast that will fuel your adventures. Sink your fork into fluffy scrambled eggs alongside crispy bacon, impossibly creamy cheese grits, and the quintessential Southern duo of buttermilk biscuits smothered in rich sausage gravy. The bottomless coffee flows freely as regulars swap stories at the counter, offering a genuine taste of Huntsville hospitality.

Day 1: As evening falls, treat yourself to refined Southern cuisine at Connors Steak & Seafood, where Gulf Coast flavors meet prime cuts in an elegant yet welcoming atmosphere. The Cajun Red Grouper, mesquite-grilled to perfection and served with fluffy couscous and tender greens, showcases the region's culinary heritage. Start with the legendary Voodoo Shrimp bathed in a spicy remoulade sauce that'll have you reaching for another.

Day 2: Savor a leisurely lunch at Pane e Vino, Chef James Boyce's Italian-inspired haven with a terrace overlooking the park's shimmering waters. The handmade butternut squash ravioli, draped in sage brown butter, offer a delicate counterpoint to the hearty Southern fare you'll encounter throughout your journey. Pair them with a glass of chilled wine as you watch ducks glide across the lake.

Day 3: Fuel your creativity at Piper and Leaf, a Lowe Mill gem specializing in artisan tea blends crafted from locally foraged ingredients and organic herbs. Sample their signature Southern sweet tea reimagined with wild honeysuckle or choose from inventive blends that capture Alabama's seasons in every sip. The whimsically decorated shop invites lingering over a steaming cup.

Day 3: Hunt for Huntsville's vibrant street art, starting with the massive koi mural where giant fish seem ready to gulp you whole at the intersection of Spring and Spragins Streets. Stand on the marked spot to experience the stunning 3D effect, then seek out the playful Welcome to Huntsville rocket mural facing Big Spring Park. Art enthusiasts can extend their treasure hunt along the Clinton Row Color Walk and the mysterious Downtown Secret Art Trail.

places.name: Hurricane Ridge, WA

visits.text: The wind immediately changes the atmosphere at Hurricane Ridge, high above the piers of Port Angeles. From the edges of the meadows, views stretch toward the ridges and snowcapped peaks of the Olympic Mountains when the clouds part. Aim for a clear spell; pack water and a meal before leaving your base.

activities.text: Hurricane Hill is worth setting aside time for a hike beyond the view from the parking lot. The trail climbs through subalpine meadows, gradually opening up views of the surrounding terrain. The trailhead lies beyond the main Hurricane Ridge area: check access to this stretch of road before deciding where to park.

visits.text: Hutchinson - Where Space Race History Meets Subterranean Wonder: This central Kansas city delivers world-class attractions both above and below ground, from space exploration to salt mine adventures.

Cosmosphere - The World's Largest Combined Collection of U.S. and Russian Space Artifacts: Kansas's only Smithsonian-affiliated museum displays spacecraft that have flown in the first three crewed space programs—Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo—bringing the Space Race back to life through extraordinary exhibits.

Strataca - 650 Feet Below Kansas: A 6-tonne hoist lowers visitors through a frozen aquifer and layers of rock to a museum carved into a former section of an active salt mine, with detailed underground exhibits explaining the secrets hidden beneath the prairie.

Kansas State Fair - September Celebration of Sunflower State Pride: Each September, Hutchinson hosts the Kansas State Fair, celebrating all things Kansas with livestock exhibitions, carnival rides, concerts, and agricultural displays.

activities.text: Underground Salt Mine Tour - Experience a World Without Sunlight: Explore the vast chambers and corridors carved from ancient salt deposits, learning about this unusual underground world and its modern uses.

visits.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt's home at Springwood — Visit the Roosevelt family home in Hyde Park. The guided tour lets you discover the furnished rooms, the study, and the president's personal belongings. Then walk around the estate and through the rose garden where Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt are buried.

Vanderbilt Mansion — Tour this Gilded Age palazzo built in 1899 for Frederick Vanderbilt, grandson of Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt. The 54-room Beaux-Arts mansion showcases Renaissance Revival architecture and Hudson River School landscape design across 211 acres.

FDR Presidential Library and Museum — Visit America's first presidential library opened in 1941, containing Franklin D. Roosevelt's papers and artifacts from his unprecedented four terms. The museum chronicles the New Deal, World War II, and Eleanor Roosevelt's advocacy.

Walkway Over the Hudson — Cross this 2-kilometer pedestrian bridge suspended 65 meters above the Hudson River, the world's longest elevated pedestrian bridge. Built on a former 1889 railroad bridge, it offers sweeping valley and mountain views.

activities.text: Wine tasting in the Hudson Valley — Sample award-winning wines at family-owned vineyards planted in the rolling hills. Rieslings and Cabernet Francs thrive in the microclimates while tasting rooms offer farm-to-table pairings with Hudson River views.

Visit to the Culinary Institute of America campus — Explore this culinary school founded in 1946, housed in a former Jesuit seminary. The student-run restaurants serve exceptional cuisine prepared by future master chefs in training.

Antique shopping in Cold Spring — Allow for a round trip from Hyde Park. Browse the Victorian-era storefronts along Main Street, filled with vintage treasures, Hudson River School paintings, and handmade crafts. This charming village nestled beneath Storm King Mountain retains its character from the 1800s.

visits.text: Idaho City peaked in September 1863 with 6,267 residents - larger than Portland at the time and the biggest city in the entire Pacific Northwest. Gold had been discovered in the Boise Basin on August 2, 1862; within eight months, the area became the largest settled region on the Pacific coast. The town was first called Bannock City, renamed in late 1863 by the Idaho Territorial Legislature to avoid confusion with Bannack, Montana. Walk the old main street past original frontier-era buildings; the Boise Basin Museum, housed in a historic post office building, tells the whole story with artifacts and photographs. Free admission.

Boot Hill Cemetery is a short walk above town, and the names on the markers are a ledger of the gold rush: gunfights, mining accidents, diphtheria, freezing. An 1863 Kansas newspaper described Idaho City simultaneously as the next El Dorado and one of the most desolate places on earth. Beyond the cemetery, the surrounding foothills are still scarred by dredge tailing piles from operations that ran here until 1952 - ridges and furrows that look from the right angle like frozen waves.

Northeast of Idaho City, Highway 21 follows the Ponderosa Pine Scenic Byway. It crosses ponderosa pine forest, then meets the South Fork of the Payette River before continuing toward Lowman and Stanley. Stop at roadside viewpoints to see the canyon and forest. Check Idaho 511 for road conditions before driving in winter or spring.

activities.text: Reach Kirkham Hot Springs via Highway 21, about 60 km from Idaho City and around an hour's drive. Thermal cascades flow from the rocks into pools beside the South Fork Payette. Water at the source reaches 49–57 °C; test the temperature before entering a pool. The site is in Boise National Forest and is visited during the day; check access conditions before setting off. Arrive early on summer weekends to avoid the crowds.

Between Lowman and Stanley, Highway 21 crosses the mountains and reaches the Sawtooth Valley. Stop at accessible roadside viewpoints to see the forest and mountain scenery. In winter and spring, sections can close temporarily because of weather and avalanche risk; check Idaho 511 before leaving Idaho City. Galena Summit lies farther south on Highway 75, between Stanley and Ketchum.

days_plan.itin_title: Idaho: Sawtooth Mountains, Sun Valley & Craters of the Moon

places.name: Indiana Dunes, IN

visits.text: You park the car and immediately grasp the paradox of this place: before you, a white sand beach stretches along Lake Michigan; behind you, Gary's steel mill smokestacks rise into the sky. Indiana Dunes became America's 61st national park in February 2019, after half a century of conservationists battling industrialists who wanted to transform the dunes into an oil port. Botanist Henry Chandler Cowles formulated the concept of ecological succession here in 1899, after observing how plants progressively colonize bare dunes to create entire forests. The park counts over 1,100 plant species - a botanical density higher than most national parks. Start at the Visitor Center for a map and to check rip current alerts before any swimming.

You stand at the foot of a 37-meter dune slowly but inexorably moving inland at a documented rate of approximately 1.2 meters per year, swallowing trees in its path. Mount Baldy is one of the Great Lakes' most active moving dunes—in 2013, a child was swallowed by a hole that suddenly opened above a decomposing tree under the sand; since then, climbing without a guide has been prohibited and stabilization programs are underway. Comparative plaques on the beach show photographs from 1955 and 2020: the dune has advanced more than 70 meters in 65 years. The beach at its base is freely accessible and offers, on clear days, a direct view of Chicago's Loop towers on the horizon, 50 kilometers away.

You follow Lakeshore Drive and spot, incongruously amid dunes and pines, five Art Deco and modernist pavilions from the 1930s that seem to have landed here by mistake. These houses were pavilions from Chicago's 1933 “Century of Progress World's Fair”—a world's fair devoted to technological progress. The following year, developer Robert Bartlett had them transported by barge across the frozen waters of Lake Michigan in winter 1935. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, they're now rented by private individuals who undertake their restoration. Their sharp geometric forms contrast surreally with the dunes and boreal forest—photograph them from Lakeshore Drive in the morning for direct light.

activities.text: You walk 200 meters from the parking lot before the white sand beach comes into view, with Lake Michigan's blue-green waters before you and 50-meter wooded dunes at your back. The Dune Succession Trail—a 2.5-kilometer loop from West Beach—is the park's most educational trail: you pass from bare beach to pioneer grasses, shrubs, pines, and oaks, observing the ecological succession Cowles described in 1899. Lake Michigan reaches 22–25°C in July–August—clear water that is surprising to find so close to an industrial metropolis. Avoid swimming in strong north winds; rip currents form quickly in this area.

You start from the parking lot on Mineral Springs Road and plunge into a forest of northern white cedars alongside Cowles Bog—one of Indiana's most protected wetland habitats. The trail then climbs wooded dune ridges before emerging onto the Lake Michigan beach, far from the crowds at West Beach. Over 350 bird species have been recorded in the park. Bring lightweight gaiters in spring: the trail crosses wet areas that cannot be avoided after April's rains.
