visits.text: Monument Circle - At the heart of Indianapolis' street grid, this roundabout is home to the Soldiers & Sailors Monument, an 86-meter limestone monument inaugurated in 1902. Designed by Germany's Bruno Schmitz, it honors Indiana soldiers from the Revolutionary War onward. Climb the 330 steps (or take the elevator to step 290, then climb 49 more steps) for a panoramic view from 70 meters above the city. The statue at the top, “Miss Indiana,” brandishes a sword and a torch.

Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum - Indiana's most famous site. The museum, renovated in 2025, displays more than 75 race cars in a 3,500 m² building nestled between turns 1 and 2 of the oval. You'll see every car that has won the Indy 500 since 1911, a tire-change simulator, and a recreation of Gasoline Alley through the eras. Take the bus tour of the track—you'll ride over the famous “Yard of Bricks,” the starting line made of original bricks. Allow 2 to 3 hours on site.

Indiana War Memorial - Indianapolis' memorial district covers 10 hectares in the heart of downtown, one of the nation's most extensive memorial complexes outside Washington D.C. The main building, inspired by the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, houses a sanctuary on the top floor bathed in bluish light. Outside, the USS Indianapolis memorial recalls the 1945 sinking - of 1,200 sailors, only 317 survived.

Newfields - This 60-hectare campus combines the Indianapolis art museum with landscaped grounds. The collections range from classical European painting to contemporary American art. The outdoor garden changes with the seasons - in winter, light installations enliven it in the evening. Allow at least 2 hours.

Eiteljorg Museum - Dedicated to Native American arts and the American West, this museum along the canal presents both Western landscape paintings and traditional objects of indigenous peoples. If the subject interests you, it's one of the finest museums of its kind outside the Southwest.

Mass Avenue - This neighborhood runs diagonally through Indianapolis' street grid, a rare feature, and brings together galleries, independent restaurants, and cocktail bars. The brick facades and vintage signs give it a character missing from the rest of downtown.

activities.text: Canal Walk at the end of the day - Follow the White River Canal on foot or by pedal boat. The 2.5 km route passes through White River State Park and is lined with gardens and sculptures. In summer, the evening light on the water is very pleasant.

Evening at Fountain Square - Ten minutes southeast of downtown, this retro neighborhood houses a vintage bowling alley on the top floor of an Art Deco building, concert halls, and rooftop bars. The atmosphere is laid-back and local - far from the tourist circuits.

places.name: International Falls, MN

visits.text: Stop at the Rainy Lake Visitor Center first, before heading out on the water. The park covers 218,000 acres on the Canadian border and most of it is only accessible by boat—skip this step and you'll miss the best parts. Rangers will advise you on tours, boat access, and the day's conditions. The rocks visible from the dock are between 1 and 3 billion years old.

Rainy Lake is the largest of the park's four lakes: 97 km long, 1,495 km of shoreline. From the Visitor Center dock, you get your first sense of the landscape—dark water, dense pine forests, vast sky. These are the same waters that French-Canadian voyageurs paddled in canoes to transport furs northward as early as the 18th century.

The Ellsworth Rock Gardens exist nowhere else: Jack Ellsworth hand-carved more than 200 sculptures from granite on the shore of Lake Kabetogama between 1944 and 1965, surrounded by terraces of wildflowers. You can only reach them by boat from the Kabetogama Visitor Center—a 30-minute boat ride. A garden built single-handedly in the wilderness, and left intact.

Kettle Falls Hotel has stood since 1910 at the crossroads of four lakes in the heart of the park—you can only get there by boat or seaplane. Its bar is slightly tilted, a legacy of a century of ground settling. A Finnish postmistress is said to have stayed on after her husband disappeared. A stop between shores worth visiting for the atmosphere alone.

activities.text: Book the Grand Tour boat excursion from the Rainy Lake Visitor Center: 2.5 hours on the lake with an NPS ranger. The tour passes by Little American Island—where gold was discovered in 1893, triggering a rush—the Harry Overson Fish Camp, and historic cabins. It's the best way to grasp the park's history and geography in half a day.

In the evening, park on a forest road north of Rainy Lake and look up. Voyageurs is Dark Sky certified—no light pollution for tens of kilometers around. The Milky Way is visible to the naked eye on most clear nights from June through September. During strong solar activity, the northern lights appear even in summer.

The Kabetogama Peninsula—the heart of the park, inaccessible by car—can only be explored from the water. Look for moose at sunrise along the shallow shores, and common loons nesting on the islands. More than 55 miles of trails are accessible by boat.

Second night in the area—use it to try to see the northern lights. Park far from any lighting and wait. Voyageurs ranks among the best aurora viewing areas in the United States: International Falls has a population of just over 5,000. September nights are the most promising.

visits.text: En route to Iowa City, stop at the Amana Colonies (30 minutes north). Seven villages founded in 1855 by German Pietists who lived in a self-sufficient community until 1932. The brick and sandstone buildings have remained intact. You'll find woodworking shops, a communal brewery, a bakery producing wood-fired bread, and a distillery. The Woolen Mill, operating since 1857, still produces wool blankets. It's a National Historic Landmark.

Arrive in Iowa City, Iowa's first capital and a university town. The Old Capitol Building (1840) sits atop a hill at the center of the University of Iowa campus—this is where Iowa was admitted to the Union in 1846. The Greek Revival-style building is restored and open to the public (free). In 2008, UNESCO designated Iowa City a "City of Literature"—the first in the United States—thanks to the renowned Iowa Writers' Workshop, which has trained dozens of Pulitzer Prize winners.

activities.text: The downtown Pedestrian Mall is where students gather: independent bookstores (Prairie Lights is an institution), cafes, restaurants, and bars. The atmosphere is young, relaxed, and intellectual—a refreshing contrast after the small rural towns elsewhere on the circuit.

places.name: Islamorada, FL

visits.text: Windley Key Fossil Reef Geological State Park - A former coral quarry transformed into a geological park. The cut rock walls reveal cross-sections of fossilized reef dating back 125,000 years - you're literally looking at corals, shells, and sponges frozen in limestone. It's an open-air geology lesson wrapped up in a 30-minute walk.

Hurricane Monument - This Art Deco coral limestone monument beside US-1 honors the 423 World War I veterans who died in the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935. This Category 5 cyclone, with winds of 300 km/h, remains the most powerful storm ever to strike the United States. The evacuation train sent from Miami arrived too late—it was overturned by the storm surge.

Indian Key Historic State Park - This tiny island off Islamorada, accessible only by kayak or boat, served as a trading post for goods salvaged from shipwrecks in the 1830s. In 1840, Seminoles attacked and burned it. Today, foundations overgrown with tropical vegetation and an observation tower remain. It has the atmosphere of a forgotten island.

activities.text: Feeding the tarpon at Robbie's Marina - Buy a bucket of baitfish and toss them from the dock. Silver tarpon over a meter long leap out of the water to snatch the fish—the spectacle is guaranteed. Pelicans will try to steal your bait. Go in the morning to avoid the crowds.

Kayaking to Indian Key - Outfitters at Robbie's Marina rent kayaks for the paddle to Indian Key (15-20 minutes). The crossing is easy in light wind - check conditions before launching. On the island, a marked trail loops around in 30 minutes.

visits.text: Ithaca sits at the southern tip of Cayuga Lake, and the local phrase "Ithaca is gorges" is not an advertising slogan: it's topography. The town is carved by three glacial gorges that spill straight into downtown. Cornell University overlooks it all from 300 meters of elevation. The campus, founded in 1865, is one of eight Ivy League schools. Stroll through Sage Chapel and Uris Library—the A.D. White Reading Room is ranked among the world's most beautiful university libraries. Campus tours are free; maps at the Information Center.

Taughannock Falls, 15 minutes north of Ithaca, is one of the tallest single-drop waterfalls in the eastern United States: 65 meters, taller than Niagara Falls (though of course far narrower). A flat 1.2 km trail runs from the parking lot to the foot of the falls, accessible to all. In autumn, the contrast of rock, water and foliage is spectacular. Parking $8 in high season.

Buttermilk Falls State Park, just south of downtown, presents about ten tiered waterfalls in a gorge of 250 meters of elevation. The Gorge Trail (1.5 km) follows the cascades directly on stone steps cut into rock, sometimes on ledges only 20 cm wide—not for those with vertigo. Natural pool at the base, swimming allowed in summer. Parking $8.

The Ithaca Commons is a 3-block pedestrian street right in the center, lined with independent cafés and shops - not a single chain. This is where Moosewood Restaurant (1973) popularized modern American vegetarian cooking with its cookbooks, which have sold 4 million copies.

activities.text: Visit a winery on the Cayuga Lake Wine Trail, the oldest organized wine route in the United States (1983). Sixteen vineyards around the lake, specializing in Riesling—schistous soils and lake microclimate close to Germany's Mosel. Sheldrake Point Winery, 30 minutes away, is among the references. Tasting $5-10, usually credited if you buy a bottle.

Eat at Moosewood Restaurant if the institution appeals to you. Open since 1973, it is one of the birthplaces of vegetarian cooking in the United States. A menu that changes every day, a well-worn bohemian atmosphere. For something simpler, the Ithaca Bakery on Meadow Street makes New York-style bagels and sandwiches all day long.

visits.text: The Two Mississippi Museums opened December 9, 2017 - the state's bicentennial - and the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum is the only state-operated civil rights museum in the country. Its eight galleries run from the Middle Passage through Reconstruction, Jim Crow, and the movement years 1945-1975. At the building's heart, a 12-meter sculpture lights up every 30 minutes with gospel songs that powered the marches; when it activates, it stops people mid-conversation. The Emmett Till section alone justifies the trip: the Bryant's Grocery doors are here, alongside the original Jet magazine pages from 1955 that broke the story open nationwide. Free every Sunday. Allow three hours.

By 1908 one-third of Farish Street was Black-owned - doctors, banks, jazz clubs, a hospital, record studios that would shape American music. Medgar Evers ran the NAACP's state field office from above the Big Apple Inn, the restaurant that's been serving pig ear sandwiches since Mexican immigrant Juan Mora opened it in 1939. The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1980; by 1995 the National Trust listed it among America's Most Endangered Places. Walk the nine-block stretch for the Blues Trail markers and the restored Alamo Theatre. Lunch at the Big Apple Inn - order the pig ears, which Mora invented from a box of butcher scraps he refused to throw away.

Pulitzer Prize-winning author Eudora Welty lived at 1119 Pinehurst Street from 1925 until her death in 2001 - 76 years in the same house, writing nearly all her fiction in the same bedroom. She bequeathed the Tudor Revival home and its entire contents to the State of Mississippi; every wall is still lined with books in the positions she left them. Her mother Chestina designed the garden the same year the family moved in, planting over 40 varieties of camellias that bloom through winter. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 2004. Tours are guided only - reserve ahead. The 3 p.m. tour ends in the garden, which is the right way to close the trip.

activities.text: The Mississippi Blues Trail runs through Jackson with markers most visitors walk right past - the Subway Lounge plaque marks a legendary basement club; the Ace Records marker on Capitol Street celebrates one of the South's most successful independent labels of the 1950s. Download the Mississippi Blues Trail app before arriving, then spend two hours following markers on foot through downtown and out toward the Medgar Evers home site. Each marker is a dense paragraph of verified history; the cumulative walk gives Jackson its full musical and civil rights context before catching a flight.

F. Jones Corner and Johnny T's Bistro & Blues bookend the Farish Street nightlife revival - Johnny T's sits in the same building as the old Crystal Palace, where Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong performed in the 1940s and 1950s. Both venues run live music on weekend nights with a nominal cover. The pineapple vodka at F. Jones Corner is a local institution. This is where Jackson residents actually go on a Friday night, which makes it the more interesting option.

visits.text: Honeymoon Bridge marks the entrance to Jackson with its covered timber frame and narrow roadway. The town identifies it as a Paddleford truss bridge that remains part of village life. Photograph it from a permitted spot without standing in the traffic lane; vehicles continue to cross during visits.

activities.text: At Jackson Falls, the sound of water accompanies a series of rocks and small waterfalls in the heart of the village. This stop complements the covered bridge without adding a long hike to the Mount Washington day. Stay on clearly defined access paths and avoid wet rock slabs, even when the flow seems modest.

places.name: Jackson, WY

visits.text: Settle into Jackson's Town Square, framed by its four elk antler arches. Historic saloons like the Million Dollar Cowboy Bar have kept their saddles bolted to the bar stools since the 1930s. Art galleries and outdoor shops line the square—the capital of the upscale Wild West.

Stop at Snake River Overlook in Grand Teton NP: this is where Ansel Adams photographed the Tetons and the Snake River in 1942. The river meanders in the foreground, and the spires of the Teton Range rise 2,000 m behind it - nothing has changed. Arrive at golden hour. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Reserve an hour and a half for the National Museum of Wildlife Art, carved into the cliff overlooking the National Elk Refuge: 5,000 works dedicated to wildlife—paintings, sculptures, and prints by artists like Bierstadt and Russell. In winter, 6,000 to 8,000 elk winter in the refuge visible from the museum windows.

Be ready: the reflection of the Tetons in Jenny Lake surpasses every photo you have seen. The Jenny Lake Visitor Center occupies a photography studio from the 1920s. Take the ferry (10 min) to reach the foot of Cascade Canyon without the extra 3 km walk. Plan a round trip from Jackson to Jenny Lake before the boat crossing.

Wake early for Schwabacher Landing: this beaver pond 10 km from Moose Junction offers the park's most perfect reflection of the Tetons. Before sunrise, morning mist hangs over the water and moose graze on the banks. The gravel access road is suitable for a regular car. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Settle in at Oxbow Bend, east of Signal Mountain: the quiet meander of the Snake River attracts moose, trumpeter swans, herons and white pelicans. When there is no wind, Mount Moran (3,842 m) is reflected in the water - bring binoculars and a telephoto lens. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Enter Jackson Lake Lodge, built in 1955 and designated a National Historic Landmark - its 18 m high windows frame a direct view of Mount Moran and the Teton Range. Even if you are not staying here, it is one of the most spectacular rooms in the American West. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Choose String Lake for your last morning in the park: between Jenny Lake and Leigh Lake, it is the quietest place to walk along the foot of the Tetons, a few hundred meters from the cliffs. The flat 3 km trail offers direct views of Teewinot Mountain. In summer, the shallow water is warm enough for swimming - a rare luxury in a national park. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Do not miss Mormon Row on Antelope Flats Road: Moulton Barn, a wooden barn from the 1890s, is one of the most photographed farms in the United States, with the snowy Tetons behind it. Arrive before 9 am to have the scene to yourself. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

For this last day in the park, choose Taggart Lake Trail (5.5 km round trip) - less busy than Cascade Canyon, with a gentle climb to a glacial lake framed by moraines. The rock slabs reveal the glaciers that shaped the valley 15,000 years ago. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson to the trailhead, followed by the hike on foot.

activities.text: Float down the Snake River in a raft with a guide. Inside Grand Teton NP, the current is gentle (Class I–II)—perfect for wildlife watching: ospreys, beavers, moose, and occasionally black bears on the banks. The float lasts 2–3 hours. Barker-Ewing and Triangle X are the top-rated operators.

Grab breakfast at The Bunnery on Cache Street—Jackson's most popular restaurant since 1975, ideal before leaving early for the park. Local cuisine revolves around bison, moose, and trout. For dinner, Gather offers a menu focused on Jackson Hole producers.

Take the ferry for Cascade Canyon Trail (8 km from the landing, 19 km on foot) - the signature hike in Grand Teton NP. Beyond the granite canyon, you emerge into an alpine meadow framed by the Tetons. Leave early with water and food to enjoy the quiet before the groups arrive. Plan a round trip from Jackson to Jenny Lake, followed by the boat crossing and the hike.

In the evening, drive up Signal Mountain: the 8 km road leads to a 360° panorama of Jackson Hole valley, the Tetons to the west and the Gros Ventre Mountains to the east. It is the park's best viewpoint accessible by car for sunset. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson.

Take the Jackson Hole Aerial Tram from Teton Village: in 12 minutes, you climb 1,262 m to the summit of Rendezvous Mountain at 3,185 m. The panorama spans the entire Teton range, Jackson Hole valley and, on clear days, as far as Yellowstone. Hiking trails start from the summit. Plan a round trip by road from Jackson to Teton Village, followed by the tram ascent.

In the evening, drive slowly on Antelope Flats Road and Gros Ventre Road at sunset—elk, bison, coyotes, and black bears are regularly spotted at dusk. Stay in your vehicle or keep a distance of 100 m: a park rule and a matter of common sense.

visits.text: Cave Point County Park - Dolomite cliffs plunge straight into Lake Michigan. When wind blows offshore, waves rush into underwater caverns and explode back out through vents with thunderous noise. In calm weather, the water is so clear you can see the bottom at 6-7 meters. This is Door County's most photographed spot - and probably its most spectacular.

Whitefish Dunes State Park - Right next to Cave Point. Lake Michigan's west shore's highest sand dunes (28 meters at the tallest point). The one-kilometer sandy beach is gorgeous for swimming. The Red Trail (4 km) crosses the dunes and cedar forest.
Jacksonport - Small village on the Lake Michigan side, facing sunrises. Quieter atmosphere than Fish Creek or Ephraim on the Green Bay side. A few shops and cafes along the road.

activities.text: Kayaking at Cave Point - Paddle along the cliffs and glide into small caves carved by erosion. Outfitters from Sturgeon Bay or Jacksonport offer guided trips. The lake must be calm - check conditions in the morning.

visits.text: Jacksonville - Florida's Largest City by Land Area: Located 30 minutes from Georgia, this sprawling metropolis spreads across both banks of the St. Johns River, offering urban attractions alongside easy beach access.

Five Points Neighborhood - Where Hip Meets Historic: Browse antique shops, sample craft brews at local gastropubs, and experience Jacksonville's most eclectic district, where Victorian homes neighbor trendy boutiques.

Jacksonville Zoo and Gardens - Face-to-Face with Big Cats: This acclaimed facility features one of the most impressive tiger habitats in the Southeast, allowing visitors remarkable proximity to these magnificent cats.

activities.text: St. Johns River Water Taxi - See the City from the Water: Cruise between attractions while enjoying panoramic views of Jacksonville's skyline reflecting off the river that defines the city.

Jacksonville Beaches - 30 Minutes to Paradise: Neptune Beach, Atlantic Beach, and Jacksonville Beach offer distinct personalities along kilometers of Atlantic shoreline, from family-friendly to surf-focused.

places.name: Jasper, AR

visits.text: Buffalo National River was designated America's first national river on March 1, 1972, ending several decades of dam proposals. The date isn't coincidental: it's exactly 100 years after the creation of Yellowstone, the first national park, that Nixon signed this law. The river flows freely for 135 miles through the park, between white limestone bluffs that sometimes exceed 150 meters in height. It's one of the few undammed rivers in the continental United States - a rarity best appreciated from a canoe. Jasper is the ideal starting point for accessing the central and upper sections.

Hawksbill Crag, also known as Whitaker Point, is Arkansas's most photographed rock promontory: a sandstone outcrop overhanging a forested canyon several hundred meters below. The trail from the parking lot runs about 5.5 km round trip, with some exposed sections approaching the edge. The view embraces miles of forest without a single building visible - plan to be there early morning to avoid weekend crowds.

activities.text: Canoeing the Buffalo River: the Ponca-Kyle's Landing section (about 18 km) is the river's most spectacular stretch - 150-meter bluffs, Class I-II rapids, emerald waters. Outfitters offer canoe rentals and shuttle service from Ponca and Jasper. River flow is most favorable April through June; in summer levels sometimes drop, so check before you go.

Elk viewing in Boxley Valley: a herd of elk was reintroduced to the Boxley Valley grasslands starting in 1981. The park now hosts Arkansas's only wild elk herd. The valley grasslands, visible from the road, are the best place to observe them - arrive at dusk or dawn, especially September through November during the rut.

Lost Valley Trail hike: 3.6 km round trip through a verdant canyon ending in a limestone cave, Eden Falls Cave, at the back of which hides a concealed waterfall. Bring a headlamp - without it, you'll miss the best part. The trail is easy to the cave entrance, then requires ducking for a few yards.

visits.text: Population 1,800 today, versus 30,000 around 1870: Jefferson is Texas's largest inhabited ghost town, once the state's second inland port after Galveston. Big Cypress Bayou allowed steamboat access from the Mississippi via the Red River. In 1873, dynamite blew up a natural logjam 300 km downstream—the water level dropped, steamboats could no longer reach Jefferson, and the city's economy died within a few years. What remains: 56 blocks of intact antebellum buildings, designated historic landmarks. Free walking route.

One of Texas's oldest continuously operating hotels, the Excelsior House opened in 1858—Rutherford Hayes, Ulysses Grant, and Oscar Wilde all slept here. Original woodwork, antique furniture, 1860 canopy bed. Interior tour $5 for non-guests (on request at reception), far better than the modern rooms nearby.

An unreal atmosphere, unique in North America: Caddo Lake is Texas's only natural lake of significant size—formed in the early 19th century by a driftwood logjam on the Red River, exactly the same cause as Jefferson's prosperity. 105 km² of bald cypress draped in Spanish moss, a labyrinth of channels and bayous dotted with duckweed. 25 km east. Canoe rental $25 for two hours, or a guided rowboat tour for $45.

activities.text: An 1860 brick building, a restaurant-saloon with live country music on weekends: Auntie Skinner's Riverboat Club is the classic spot. Otherwise, Riverport BBQ for hickory-smoked barbecue (brisket cooked for 14 hours). Budget $25–35 per person.

days_plan.itin_title: From Jacksonville to Dallas in 15 days, through the Deep South

visits.text: Walk along Jekyll Island's ethereal Driftwood Beach, a surreal landscape where sun-bleached trees twisted into sculptural forms rise from golden sands. The entire island operates as a state park, ensuring conservation and wildlife protection across 2,300 hectares of beaches, marshes, and maritime forests. This otherworldly scenery has attracted filmmakers, featuring in major productions including X-Men and The Walking Dead.

Explore the historic Millionaires' Village where Vanderbilt, Rockefeller, and Pulitzer once gathered in elegant “cottages” that defined Gilded Age opulence. The Georgia Sea Turtle Center rescues and rehabilitates injured sea turtles, offering close encounters with these ancient mariners and their inspiring recovery stories. Passionate guides explain each turtle's journey from injury through rehabilitation.

activities.text: Cycle the scenic island loop past serene marshes, under canopies of moss-draped oaks, and along beaches where dolphins frequently surface offshore. Picnic on windswept dunes while spotting wildlife including deer, alligators, and countless shorebirds in this carefully preserved coastal sanctuary.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Jennette's Pier extends 300 meters out over the Atlantic in Nags Head. Built of wood in 1939, partly destroyed by Hurricane Isabel in 2003, it was rebuilt in concrete and reopened in 2011 by the North Carolina Aquariums. A walk-on pass costs a few dollars, and the pier stays open until 10pm from May to October.

activities.text: If you have never fished at sea, start at Jennette's Pier: a blanket license covers all paying anglers, so no state license is needed. The pier shop rents rods and sells bait, so you can show up empty-handed. Depending on the season, anglers reel in bluefish, Spanish mackerel or drum.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

visits.text: Jenny Lake deserves more than a quick photo between two long drives. The lake fills a glacial basin at the foot of the Tetons, with mountains rising close above its western shore. Start by taking in the scenery from accessible spots in the southern area before choosing your walk. Arrive early enough to find parking and check trail conditions; this stop can also remain a simple stroll if conditions deteriorate.

Hand-dug ditches supplied the fields of Mormon Row long before its barns became photography subjects. Some channels still carry water, recalling the labor behind this agricultural landscape. Explore the Moulton families’ buildings on foot around Antelope Flats Road. Plan this visit as you head toward Jackson from Jenny Lake, and use designated parking areas without driving into the meadows.

activities.text: If the trails are open and the shuttle is running, Hidden Falls followed by Inspiration Point makes for a hike that gradually becomes more challenging from Jenny Lake. The boat drops you off on the western shore; you reach the waterfall before the overlook above the lake. You can stop at Hidden Falls if the climb becomes too demanding. Buy your boat ticket at the dock and check the last return departure: walking back around the lakeshore makes the outing considerably longer.

days_plan.itin_title: Yellowstone and Grand Teton: 12 Days Among Lakes and Mountain Passes

places.name: Jim Thorpe, PA

visits.text: You step into one of the best-preserved Victorian mansions in Pennsylvania. Asa Packer, founder of the Lehigh Valley Railroad and Lehigh University, had this Italianate mansion built in 1861 on the hillside overlooking Jim Thorpe. The interior has remained virtually unchanged since his death in 1879: original woodwork, Victorian wallpapers, period furniture, and personal collections. Jim Thorpe - formerly Mauch Chunk until 1954 - was founded in 1818 as the lower terminus of a gravity railroad transporting anthracite coal from hillside mines to the Lehigh canal. The town became so prosperous that by the late 19th century, it was the second most visited tourist destination in the United States after Niagara Falls. Guided tours last 45 minutes and depart on the half hour; book in advance during the Fall Foliage Festival in October.

The Old Jail Museum is one of the most fascinating visits in the Pocono Mountains. This 1871 penitentiary, still standing with its original cells, is famous for the execution of the Molly Maguires - a secret society of Irish miners who fought against inhumane working conditions in the coal mines during the 1870s. Seven of them were hanged in the prison yard. In cell 17, a handprint on the stone wall, left according to legend by one of the condemned who swore his innocence before being executed, has remained visible despite several layers of paint and plaster. The guides recount the story of the condemned with a level of detail that makes the visit memorable - even skeptics leave troubled.

The Jim Thorpe mausoleum, honoring the Native American athlete considered the greatest American sportsman of the 20th century, stands at the town entrance on Route 903. Thorpe won the decathlon and pentathlon at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics, played Major League Baseball for the New York Giants, and was one of the first NFL players. His wife, Patricia, chose to lay his remains to rest in this Pennsylvania town he had never visited while alive - in exchange for an annuity to fund a memorial. The town, then in economic decline after the mine closures, accepted the offer in 1954 and adopted his name. It's a story of mutual benefit that became legend.

activities.text: The Lehigh Gorge Scenic Railway carries passengers in century-old cars along the Lehigh River, beneath towering cliffs and through tunnels carved into the gorge rock. The rail line is the direct descendant of the Central Railroad of New Jersey, which transported anthracite coal from Carbon County mines to coastal steel mills. In autumn, the gorge slopes transform into a blazing tableau of reds and oranges reflected in the river. The 75-minute journey offers the most spectacular views, particularly at Glen Onoko, a former Victorian resort destination.

The D&L Trail (Delaware & Lehigh National Heritage Corridor) runs along the Lehigh gorge on former 19th-century canal and railroad routes, with the river on one side and remnants of the canal on the other. The trail is virtually flat, as it follows the original railroad route, making it accessible to all levels. Several bike rental shops in Jim Thorpe offer standard and electric bikes. In autumn, this section ranks among the most beautiful cycling routes on the East Coast for fall foliage.

places.name: Jockeys Ridge, NC

visits.text: A slice of desert dropped next to a beach town: Jockey's Ridge State Park holds the tallest active sand dune system on the Atlantic coast. The main dune peaks at around 24 meters, down from about 43 meters in the 1930s, because the sand keeps moving. Wear sandals with straps, as flip-flops get stuck in the sand, and allow 15 to 20 minutes to climb.

activities.text: Take a first hang gliding lesson with Kitty Hawk Kites, based at the foot of Jockey's Ridge for over 40 years. The wind that drew the Wright brothers still blows here, and the school promises flight from the very first lesson. Otherwise, stay at the top for sunset over Roanoke Sound, with a sweater: evenings get cool.
If you want to slide, Jockey's Ridge allows sandboarding on its dunes. Sandboarding requires no permit. Check with the park for the areas open to sandboarding and the conditions that day.

places.name: Joshua Tree, CA

visits.text: The drive from Death Valley to Joshua Tree passes through Barstow in the Mojave. Once in the park, stop at Hidden Valley, a basin surrounded by quartz monzonite rock formations—the characteristic rock type of the park, formed 100 million years ago and sculpted by erosion ever since. The Hidden Valley loop trail is 1.6 km, easy. Continuing east, Skull Rock is a formation whose two cavities carved by erosion suggest eye sockets—the associated trail is 2.7 km.

The Barker Dam trail, about thirty minutes' drive from the town of Joshua Tree, is a 2.7 km loop in the heart of the rock formations. It leads to a small reservoir built by ranchers in the early 20th century to water their cattle - today it stays dry for most of the year and only fills after heavy rain. Along the way you will pass Native American pictographs of the Serrano and Cahuilla peoples painted directly onto the rock.

The Cholla Cactus Garden, nearly an hour's drive from the town of Joshua Tree, is one of the most unusual places in the park: 4 hectares covered in teddy-bear cholla, also called “jumping cactus” because its spiny segments break off and cling at the slightest touch—a formidable dispersal mechanism. The loop is 400 meters long and crosses a transition zone between the Mojave Desert and the Colorado Desert. Touch nothing, wear closed shoes, and go at sunrise to see the chollas glow orange against the low light.

activities.text: Sunset over the rock formations of Joshua Tree is an experience of its own. The quartz monzonite boulders turn pink, orange and red depending on the angle of the light, and the Joshua trees—tree-like yuccas that grow only at this altitude and in this precise geographical area—take on the look of cut-out silhouettes. Settle in at Keys View, about forty minutes' drive from the town of Joshua Tree, at 1,582 meters, for a panorama that takes in the Coachella Valley and, on a clear day, Mexico 145 kilometers away.

In the evening, head to a local bar in the town of Joshua Tree for live music. The town has long attracted artists and musicians—U2 recorded the album 'The Joshua Tree' here in 1987, and the area continues to nurture an active music scene blending desert blues, country, and indie rock.

visits.text: Julian - A Gold Rush Town Famous for Apples: This entire mountain town is a California Historical Landmark, its 1870s gold mining heritage preserved in wooden storefronts and false-front buildings. Unexpectedly, the high altitude creates perfect apple-growing conditions.

Julian Pioneer Museum - Gold Rush to Apple Orchards: This small museum traces the town's evolution from mining camp to apple capital, displaying gold mining equipment alongside Victorian-era artifacts.

Apple Orchards and Cider Mills - Taste Julian's Famous Fruit: Numerous u-pick orchards and farm stands offer the chance to select your own apples from dozens of heirloom varieties, while cider mills press the fresh juice.

activities.text: Julian Apple Pie - The Town's Claim to Fame: Multiple bakeries compete for the title of best apple pie, each guarding their recipes jealously. Warm slices with cinnamon ice cream fuel heated debates about which reigns supreme.

Eagle and High Peak Mine Tour - Descend into Julian's Golden Past: This 1,000-foot tunnel tour reveals the hard-rock mining techniques that drew prospectors to these mountains, with gold veins still visible in the walls.

visits.text: Mendenhall Glacier—20 km from downtown Juneau, accessible by bus or taxi—is the only major glacier in Southeast Alaska accessible by road. The glacier descends from the Juneau Icefield (over 3,800 km²) and has retreated more than 3 km since the 1930s. From the Visitor Center platform, the blue face is in direct view above Mendenhall Lake. The trail to Nugget Falls (1.5 km one-way) follows the shore to the base of the waterfall—one of the most beautiful accessible hikes in Alaska.

The Alaska State Capitol in downtown Juneau is one of the few American capitols without a dome. The building was constructed in 1931 as the Federal and Territorial Building—Alaska wasn't yet a state. It became the seat of state government only after Alaska's admission to the Union in 1959. Free guided tours (45 minutes) show the Senate and House chambers with their Alaska wood inlays, and explain how to govern a 1.7-million-km² state from a capital accessible only by air or sea.

The Last Chance Mining Museum, perched at the end of a narrow road northeast of downtown, occupies the remnants of the Alaska-Juneau mine—one of the world's largest low-grade gold mines at its peak in the 1930s. The steam-powered machinery and partially restored galleries tell how they extracted 17 grams of gold per tonne of rock. The admission is modest and the experience worthwhile.

activities.text: Tracy Arm Fjord, 90 km southeast of Juneau, is one of Alaska's most spectacular fjords—40 km of rock walls covered in waterfalls leading to the twin Sawyer glaciers. Fast boats depart Juneau harbor in the morning and return late afternoon. The fjord is often choked with blue icebergs in summer—the boat weaves between them, just a few meters from glacier faces that calve regularly.

Humpback whale watching in the Inside Passage channels from Juneau is among Alaska's most reliable in summer. Over 100 individuals frequent these waters from June to September to feed. Charters offer 3- to 4-hour trips from the harbor—bubble-net feeding behavior is regularly observed, something few other spots in the world can offer.

days_plan.itin_title: Alaska Adventure - 14 Days Through the World's Most Remote National Parks

activities.text: Movies are a good excuse to explore Kualoa Ranch. The Movie Sites & Ranch Tour travels through Kaʻaʻawa Valley by bus and stops at a former military bunker carved into the mountain: the scenery outshines the movie props. Book the 90-minute tour and arrive as far in advance as your ticket requires.

days_plan.itin_title: Oahu in 3 Days: Honolulu, Pearl Harbor, and the North Shore

visits.text: Kealakekua Bay — Snorkel in this protected bay on the Kona Coast, whose clear waters shelter corals, tropical fish and often spinner dolphins. On the north shore, the white obelisk of the Captain Cook Monument marks where he died in 1779; reach it by boat, by kayak with an authorised operator or via the steep Kaawaloa Trail. The bay is about half an hour's drive south of Kailua-Kona.

Holualoa Coffee Farms — Head up to this artists' village perched on the slopes of Hualalai, at the heart of the Kona coffee belt. Several family farms open their plantations for tours and tastings explaining the growing, picking and roasting of 100% Kona coffee, while the main street is lined with galleries and studios. The village is about twenty minutes' drive above Kailua-Kona.

Kahaluu Beach Park — Snorkel in this shallow bay sheltered by an ancient stone breakwater, an easy spot for beginners on the Kona Coast. Yellow tangs, parrotfish and green turtles move among the corals just a few metres from the shore. The park lies along Alii Drive, south of Kailua-Kona.

Puuhonua o Honaunau National Historical Park — Explore this reconstructed Hawaiian place of refuge where kapu breakers and defeated warriors found sanctuary. The 73-hectare park preserves the royal grounds, fishponds and the Great Wall built around 1550. The park is about forty minutes' drive south of Kailua-Kona.

activities.text: Manta ray night snorkel — Swim with graceful manta rays attracted to plankton illuminated by underwater lights off Kona coast. The 4-meter wingspan giants glide inches from snorkelers in an unforgettable marine encounter.

Kaloko-Honokohau Hike — Explore Kaloko-Honokohau National Historical Park, north of Kailua-Kona, between lava fields and coastline. The trail leads to the ancient Hawaiian fishponds of Kaloko and Aimakapa, to petroglyphs and to Honokohau Beach, where green turtles often rest on the rocks. The terrain is exposed and hot, so set off early in the morning.

Fresh poke bowl dinner — Sample cubed raw fish marinated in soy sauce, sesame oil, and limu seaweed at local markets or restaurants. This Hawaiian staple showcases the islands' Pacific Rim culinary influences.

places.name: Kalamazoo, MI

visits.text: You pass through Battle Creek and understand why this city of 52,000 people proclaimed itself 'Cereal City USA': here John Harvey Kellogg, a Seventh-day Adventist doctor, invented corn flakes in 1894 while seeking healthy food for his sanitarium patients. His brother Will Keith Kellogg founded the Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company here in 1906 - today's Kellogg's, one of the world's largest food groups. Charles William Post, a former sanitarium patient, copied the idea and founded Post Cereals in the same city in 1895. For decades, the smell of toasted cereal drifted across town. Walk the Linear Park Trail beside the Battle Creek River to the Kellogg House gardens: you can admire the exterior of this Prairie-style home, but its interior is not open to ordinary visitors. Allow for a round trip from Kalamazoo for this walk in Battle Creek.

You arrive at the Gilmore Car Museum in Hickory Corners, between Battle Creek and Kalamazoo, and find 90 acres of meadow dotted with historic barns filled with 400 vehicles covering 130 years of American automotive history - the Midwest's largest outdoor collection. Founded in 1966 by Donald Gilmore, heir to a Michigan pharmaceutical fortune, the museum brings together rarities such as the first production Ford Mustang (1964), 1920s Packards, a 1942 Lincoln Continental and dozens of racing cars. The architecture of the restored 19th-century barns housing the collections gives the place a particularly appealing atmosphere: you move between barns as though exploring a village. Open daily from May to October, 9 a.m.-5 p.m.; admission: USD 15 per adult. Allow at least 2 hours. Allow for a round trip from Kalamazoo for this visit to Hickory Corners.

You enter Bell's Brewery's Eccentric Café in Kalamazoo and you're standing in one of the most influential breweries in American craft beer history. Larry Bell opened his first brewery in 1985 in a converted soup kitchen, with a 15-gallon kettle and a detergent pump for hops - making it one of the very first microbreweries in the Midwest. Their Two Hearted Ale, an IPA with pine and grapefruit aromas named after a Michigan river dear to Hemingway, was voted best beer in America by the American Homebrewers Association in 2017. The Eccentric Café, their historic pub, still offers the full range on tap with pub fare in a brick-and-timber space. Open Monday-Thursday 11am-10pm, Friday-Saturday until 11pm.

activities.text: You explore downtown Kalamazoo on foot between several craft breweries. Bell's Brewery is the historic benchmark in the downtown pedestrian district. Kalamazoo is also home to Western Michigan University (23,000 students), which gives the center a particularly lively student atmosphere in the evening.

You enter the Kalamazoo Institute of Arts, a municipal art museum with entirely free admission, and find a permanent collection of 6,000 works spanning 19th-century American art to the present. The museum also organizes public art classes and temporary exhibitions that regularly attract nationally recognized contemporary artists. The building itself, renovated in 2012, integrates naturally lit spaces that highlight collection pieces. A 45-minute break here contrasts nicely with the industrial day between Kellogg's and the Gilmore Car Museum.

places.name: Kanab, UT

visits.text: Kanab bills itself as "Little Hollywood"—over 100 films and TV shows were shot in its surroundings, from John Wayne westerns to Planet of the Apes. The town of 5,000 is a strategic crossroads between Zion, Bryce, Grand Canyon, and Lake Powell. Take a stroll through downtown—the Western storefronts are authentic, not sets.

Around half an hour's drive from Kanab, Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park is a field of pink sand dunes—the only one in Utah. The dunes reach heights of 30 meters. You can walk across them, slide down them or simply admire the contrast between the pink sand and the surrounding red cliffs.

activities.text: Kanab is also the gateway to The Wave (Coyote Buttes North), the Southwest's most famous sandstone formation - but permits are allocated by lottery and are very limited (64 per day).

visits.text: A footbridge lets you watch the Swift River flow through Rocky Gorge without going down to the water’s edge. This site is on the eastern section of the Kancamagus Highway: plan to stop here before Sabbaday Falls when coming from Conway. Walk to the viewpoint from the parking lot and observe the ban on swimming in the gorge.

C. L. Graham Wangan Overlook offers a broader view of the landscape around Kancamagus Pass. After Sabbaday Falls, this overlook adds a stop focused on the mountain terrain as you continue along NH 112 toward Lincoln. Park fully within the designated area and wait for the weather to clear rather than making repeated stops on the shoulder.

activities.text: You’ll reach Sabbaday Falls by a short trail from the Kancamagus Highway. Stairs and railings let you view the waterfall deep in the gorge without searching for a way across the rocks. Check the posted parking requirements and wear shoes with good traction; wet leaves make the steps slippery in fall.

places.name: Kansas City, MO

visits.text: Walk across the glass bridge at the National WWI Museum and look down—beneath your feet are 9,000 red poppies, each representing 1,000 combat deaths. This is America's only federally designated WWI museum, built beneath the 66-meter Liberty Memorial tower that Kansas City erected after 83,000 citizens raised $2.5 million in just ten days in 1919. The 1921 site dedication was the only time the supreme commanders of all five Allied nations stood in the same place. From the top of the tower you get the best panorama of Kansas City. Allow two hours for the museum plus the tower. Paid entry; the Over There Café is accessible without a ticket.

The Arabia Steamboat Museum in the City Market is in its final year—the Hawley family announced its closure in November 2026 after 35 years, so this visit has a deadline. On September 5, 1856, the 52-meter steamboat Arabia hit a tree trunk and sank 10 km west of Kansas City, carrying 200 tonnes of cargo bound for 16 frontier towns. The Missouri River shifted course, and the Arabia lay buried 14 meters underground in a Kansas cornfield for 132 years until treasure hunters dug it up in 1988. The collection is the largest assemblage of pre-Civil War artifacts in the world. Allow 90 minutes.

Four badminton shuttlecocks, each 5.5 meters tall and weighing 2,500 kg, sit on the lawn of the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art as if giants had just abandoned a game. Artists Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen installed them in July 1994, using the neoclassical building as a net and the 9-hectare lawn as the court. The museum itself holds one of the country's great encyclopedic collections—highlights include the ancient Chinese galleries, a Caravaggio, and the photography wing. Free admission; free outdoor access at any hour.

activities.text: Kaw Point Park sits at the confluence of the Kansas and Missouri Rivers on the east side of Kansas City, and a short interpretive loop tells the story of Lewis and Clark's camp here on June 26, 1804. Ten minutes from downtown, often overlooked, and worth the detour—standing at the exact meeting point of the two rivers connects Day 4 directly to the Corps. The park is small, the trail is less than two kilometers long, and the industrial backdrop makes the historical fact feel even starker.

The City Market district surrounding the Arabia Steamboat Museum has operated as a public market since 1857. On weekends, the outdoor farmers' market draws crowds to stalls selling Missouri produce, local charcuterie, and every kind of food. Kansas City's smoked meat culture is distinct enough that a meal here qualifies as cultural research—the tradition of slow, hickory-smoked brisket, burnt ends, and ribs continues in dozens of family-owned establishments within a few kilometers of downtown.

visits.text: Kansas City, Kansas - Where Sports Passion Runs Deep: This side of the metro area delivers world-class sporting experiences, from the roaring crowds at Children's Mercy Park to the thunder of engines at Kansas Speedway.

Children's Mercy Park - One of Soccer's Most Intimidating Venues: Home to Sporting KC, this canopy-roofed stadium has been voted among Major League Soccer's most hostile environments for visiting teams, thanks to the passionate fans who fill its 18,467 seats.

Kansas Speedway - Feel the NASCAR Thunder: This 1.5-mile tri-oval hosts major NASCAR events throughout the year, with the NASCAR Racing Experience allowing visitors to actually drive the track themselves.

Legends Field - Home of the Kansas City Monarchs: Named in honor of the legendary Negro Leagues team that dominated baseball for decades, this stadium hosts the American Association affiliate that continues the proud tradition.

activities.text: NASCAR Racing Experience - Drive the Oval Yourself: Adrenaline seekers can get behind the wheel of a real stock car and experience the thrill of speeds over 240 km/h on the same track where champions compete.

visits.text: From Bluff, take US-163 south. About 15 kilometers from Monument Valley, the road opens onto the Southwest's most famous view—the straight line of asphalt shooting toward the Mittens. This is the exact spot where Forrest Gump stops running in the film. Pull over on the shoulder for the photo.

Monument Valley isn't a national park—it's a Tribal Park managed by the Navajo Nation. The sandstone buttes rise up to 300 meters above the desert floor. The Valley Drive is a 27-kilometer dirt road with 11 numbered stops. You can drive it yourself (allow 2 hours with stops), but the track is rough in places—a high-clearance vehicle is preferable. The Mittens (East and West) and Merrick Butte are the three most photographed formations. According to Navajo legend, these are a giant's hands scattered after a great battle.

The Wildcat Trail is the park's only unguided hike—a 5.2-kilometer loop around West Mitten Butte. Allow 2 hours. You see the butte from every angle, up close, with desert silence all around. Everything else in the park (Mystery Valley, Hunts Mesa, petroglyphs) requires a Navajo guide—outfitters offer Jeep tours from the visitor center.

activities.text: Do not miss sunrise and sunset in Monument Valley. The buttes change color within minutes—from deep red to purple. At night, there is no light pollution—the Milky Way is spectacular.

visits.text: Cape Porpoise, near Kennebunkport, is worth a detour. The harbor still supports an active fishing industry and offers a view toward Goat Island Lighthouse on its island. Stay in the public areas of the wharf to watch the boats; this stop includes neither a crossing to the island nor automatic access to the lighthouse.

activities.text: To get a sense of Kennebunkport beyond its storefronts, explore Dock Square on foot. The local historical society offers walks focused on the houses and streets of downtown. Check available departures before booking; without a guided tour, keep your loop around the wharves and streets near the river.

days_plan.itin_title: New England in Fall: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: The Sun Valley Lodge opened on December 21, 1936, built in seven months on the former 1,573-hectare Brass Ranch for $1.5 million by Union Pacific Railroad chairman Averell Harriman - who also installed the world's first chairlift here, designed by engineer Jim Curran using banana-loading conveyor technology from tropical cargo ships. The four-story, X-shaped building looks today exactly as it did then: concrete poured inside rough-sawn forms and acid-stained to resemble wood. Walk the hallways - they're lined with black-and-white photographs of Clark Gable, Ingrid Bergman, and Marilyn Monroe. In suite 206, Hemingway finished writing For Whom the Bell Tolls in the fall of 1939.

About 2.4 kilometers northeast of the Lodge on Trail Creek Road, a bronze bust by sculptor Robert Berks marks the Hemingway Memorial. It was dedicated on July 21, 1966 - his birthday, five years after his death in nearby Ketchum. The inscription is a eulogy Hemingway himself wrote in 1939 for a friend killed in a hunting accident, ending: “Now he will be part of them forever.” The road closes in deep winter. Trail Creek itself runs below the memorial, clear enough to see the bottom.

On North Main Street, Hemingway's grave in the Ketchum Cemetery sits between two large spruce trees under a flat granite slab - usually decorated with bottles of whiskey left by visitors. He moved to Ketchum permanently in 1959 and died here on July 2, 1961. Nearby, the free Wood River Museum of History and Culture (4th and Walnut, Tuesday-Saturday 11 AM-6 PM) has an exhibit with original artifacts and a vintage typewriter you can use. The museum also covers Sun Valley's ski history and the local mining era.

activities.text: The Pioneer Cabin Trail climbs 7.2 kilometers west of Ketchum to a stone cabin at 2,865 meters, built by Union Pacific in 1937 as a ski hut. 915 meters of elevation gain, mostly in the first two kilometers through shaded pine - the hard part is done early. From the ridge, the Pioneer Mountains open up in every direction. Allow 5-6 hours round trip; late June through September for best conditions. Dogs welcome off-leash.

The Pioneer Saloon on Main Street has been here since Hemingway's era and still displays one of his personal shotguns - a 1953 Winchester Model 21 he used bird hunting on nearby Silver Creek. The Ram restaurant opened in 1938 and is the oldest at the resort. For the full literary cocktail experience, the Sawtooth Club serves the original Hemingway daiquiri recipe brought back from the El Floridita bar in Havana.

days_plan.itin_title: Idaho: Sawtooth Mountains, Sun Valley & Craters of the Moon

places.name: Key Largo, FL

visits.text: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park - America's first underwater park, opened in 1963. It covers 240 km² of Atlantic Ocean along Key Largo. The visitor center houses a 115,000-liter saltwater aquarium—a good preview of the reef if you're not diving. Cannon Beach and Far Beach are the park's two beaches, small but peaceful. Arrive early in the morning—weekend parking fills up fast.

Dagny Johnson Key Largo Hammock Botanical State Park - This park protects one of the last remaining tropical dry hammock forests in the Keys. The main trail (1.5 km round trip) passes through a dense canopy of gumbo-limbo and mahogany trees. You might spot the Key Largo woodrat, an endangered species found only on this island.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Christ of the Abyss - Key Largo's most famous excursion. This 2.6-meter bronze statue, submerged at a depth of 7.5 meters near Dry Rocks, is a replica of the 1954 original placed off Genoa, Italy. Operators within Pennekamp park offer 2-hour 30-minute boat trips—the top of the statue sits 2–3 meters below the surface, visible while snorkeling. Book the day before or that morning.

Kayaking through Key Largo's mangroves - Outfitters offer guided trips through calm mangrove channels, protected from wind. The water is shallow and crystal-clear—you'll see rays, small juvenile lemon sharks, and herons. Ideal in late afternoon when the heat eases off.

places.name: Key West, FL

visits.text: Seven Mile Bridge - The most memorable crossing on the Overseas Highway. This 10.9 km bridge (not 7 miles, though the name has stuck) connects Marathon to the Lower Keys above strikingly clear turquoise water. Beside it, the partially demolished old railroad bridge from 1912 remains visible—its broken arches give the landscape a post-apocalyptic feel. You cannot stop on the bridge, but you can park at either end for photos. From Key West, plan on a round trip in a day.

Bahia Honda State Park - Often ranked among the most beautiful beaches in the United States. The sand is fine, and the water is clear and shallow for dozens of meters. Choose from three beaches: Sandspur Beach (the largest), Calusa Beach (facing the old bridge) and Loggerhead Beach (more secluded). The park has limited capacity—arrive before 10 a.m. in high season or you may find the gates closed. It's approximately 58 km from Key West, a 50-minute drive.

National Key Deer Refuge on Big Pine Key - These miniature white-tailed deer (60–75 cm at the shoulder) live only in the Lower Keys. There are around 700 to 800 of them. The best place to observe them is Blue Hole, an old quarry pit filled with freshwater where alligators coexist with the deer. Drive slowly on Big Pine Key—the speed limit is reduced to protect the deer. From Key West, plan on a round trip in a day.

Ernest Hemingway Home & Museum - The 1851 colonial house where Hemingway lived from 1931 to 1939. This is where he wrote “For Whom the Bell Tolls” and “The Snows of Kilimanjaro”. The real stars are the 50 to 60 cats ruling the property—about half are polydactyl (six-toed), descendants of Snow White, a female cat given to Hemingway by a ship's captain. The 30-minute guided tour (included with admission) also covers the $20,000 pool from 1937, the penny embedded in the ground, and the bar urinal converted into a fountain by his ex-wife.

Southernmost Point - Key West's famous painted concrete buoy (24°33'N), 145 km from Cuba. There is an almost constant line for photos - very early in the morning or toward the end of the day, it is quieter.

Fort Zachary Taylor State Park - The best swimming and snorkeling spot in Key West proper. The brick fort (1845–1866) served as a naval base during the Civil War. The beach is rocky (bring water shoes) but tropical fish are plentiful a few meters from shore. The trees provide shade, rare in Key West.

Key West Cemetery - This 1847 cemetery, right in the middle of town, is one of Florida's strangest. Graves are above-ground (the water table is 30 cm below the surface). Some epitaphs are deliberately comic—the most famous reads “I told you I was sick”. A 30-minute wander is plenty.

Dry Tortugas National Park - Fort Jefferson - Full day devoted to this excursion 110 km west of Key West. The ferry departs at 8 a.m. and returns around 5:30 p.m. (2 hours 15 minutes each way). Fort Jefferson is a massive red brick hexagon set on Garden Key—one of the largest coastal forts ever built in the United States, with walls 2.4 meters thick. Construction began in 1846 and was never completed. During the Civil War it served as a prison—the most famous inmate was Dr. Samuel Mudd, convicted for treating the broken leg of John Wilkes Booth after Lincoln's assassination. The guided fort tour runs 45 minutes.

Duval Street and Old Town - Key West's main street, stretching 2 km between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic. Morning, before the influx of cruise passengers, is the best time to stroll among the wooden Victorian houses, art galleries and cafés. Mile Marker 0 marks the beginning (or end) of US-1, the road linking Key West to the Canadian border in Maine over 3,800 km.

Custom House Museum - This red brick building from 1891, formerly the customs house for the port of Key West, now houses an art and local history museum. Exhibits cover shipwreck salvage (“wrecking”, Key West's main industry in the 19th century), cigar manufacturing, and military history. Handsome Richardsonian Romanesque architecture.

Key West Butterfly and Nature Conservatory - A 465 m² tropical greenhouse housing 50–60 species of free-flying butterflies, flamingos, and tropical birds. Restful after days in full sun—the interior is shaded and humid.

activities.text: Swimming and relaxing at Bahia Honda - Take your time here. The water is the most beautiful in the Keys—turquoise, warm and calm. If you have a mask and snorkel, snorkeling from the beach is decent, with some corals and tropical fish. In the late afternoon, the low sun gives the sand golden hues. It's approximately 58 km from Key West, a 50-minute drive.

Sunset at Mallory Square - Every evening, two hours before sunset, the square transforms into an impromptu festival: jugglers, fire-breathers, musicians, street vendors. Everyone gathers facing west to watch the sun drop into the Gulf of Mexico. Arrive early for a good spot.

Snorkeling at Dry Tortugas - The water around Fort Jefferson is exceptionally clear (visibility of 15–30 meters) and the seabed lies at depths of 1.5 to 4 meters. Snorkeling gear is included with the ferry ticket. You'll see barracudas, sea turtles, groupers, and intact corals—this is one of Florida's best snorkeling spots. Pack waterproof sunscreen—there's almost no shade on the island.

Key lime pie tasting - The Keys' lime pie is THE local dessert. The original recipe uses Key West limes (smaller and more tart than standard limes), sweetened condensed milk, and a graham cracker crust. Sample several to compare—every establishment has its own version. The frozen version on a stick, coated in chocolate, is a street-food classic.

Final sunset or departure - If driving back to Miami (260 km, 3 hours 30 minutes to 4 hours of driving), leave in early afternoon to avoid night driving on the Overseas Highway. Otherwise, Key West airport offers direct flights to Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and other Florida cities.

visits.text: Experience the pristine natural beauty of Kiawah Island, where endless stretches of soft sand meet towering dunes and lush maritime forests untouched by commercial development. Sunlight filters through ancient trees in the most captivating ways, while deer, herons, and dolphins appear regularly throughout the landscape. This barrier island represents coastal South Carolina at its most refined.

Cycle along miles of shaded pathways winding through forests, past lagoons filled with wildlife, and directly onto beaches where firm sand allows extended rides along the shore. The island's world-famous golf courses, including the Ocean Course with its dramatic oceanfront holes, attract players from around the globe seeking championship-caliber challenges amid stunning scenery.

activities.text: Paddle through Kiawah's salt marshes at sunset when the landscape transforms into golden hues reflected across calm waters. Beach days reveal why this island consistently ranks among America's finest, with uncrowded shores and crystal-clear waters. The quiet luxury and naturally wild character create an atmosphere of peaceful exclusivity.

places.name: Kingman, AZ

visits.text: Seligman - Stop here - this is where Route 66 was saved. In 1987, Angel Delgadillo, a local barber, founded the Route 66 Association of Arizona to prevent the Mother Road from fading into obscurity after its decommissioning. The few-block village inspired Radiator Springs in the movie Cars. The Snow Cap Drive-In, founded by Angel's brother in 1953, is a temple of kitsch with gags on the menu ('dead chicken' for chicken) and squirting mustard.

Seligman–Kingman: the most beautiful stretch—The 145 km stretch between these two towns is the best-preserved section of all of Route 66. Two lanes, no traffic, the same road as in 1955 through scrubland and ranches. Take your time.
Hackberry General Store—Stop 50 km east of Kingman—this 1930s former gas station is frozen in time: period pumps, rusted signs, a red Corvette parked out front. It's as authentic as Route 66 gets.

activities.text: Kingman neon lights - If you arrive after dark, Andy Devine Avenue (the local Route 66) lights up with vintage neon. Kingman is also the gateway to the Historic Route 66 toward Oatman - a winding mountain road with wild burros on the pavement.

places.name: Knoxville

visits.text: Market Square has been Knoxville's beating heart since 1854 - when two donors deeded the land to the city, their only condition was that it remain a public market forever. The American Planning Association ranked it among America's best public spaces. Some of the surrounding buildings date back to the 1860s. Linger here for dinner: the outdoor tables stay lively late into the evening.

The Sunsphere Tower rises 81 meters in World's Fair Park - a remnant of the 1982 World's Fair. Go up to the observation deck: the view over Tennessee's wooded hills and Knoxville's skyline is especially beautiful in late afternoon. Admission is free.

activities.text: If you're here on a Saturday between May and November, the Farmers' Market at Market Square opens at 9am. Local producers from eastern Tennessee: cheeses, honey, sourdough breads, charcuterie. It's the best way to see local Knoxville life rather than just passing through.

places.name: Kotzebue, AK

visits.text: The Northwest Arctic Heritage Center in Kotzebue serves as the Visitor Center for three national parks and several monuments—Kobuk Valley, Cape Krusenstern, and Bering Land Bridge. The building itself is a fine museum of Inupiat cultures of northwest Alaska: marine mammal hunting, dog sledding, traditional sewing. Kotzebue is an Inupiat town of 3,000 residents on the Chukchi Sea—one of Alaska's largest Indigenous communities.

Onion Portage, in eastern Kobuk Valley National Park and accessible by air from Kotzebue, is one of Alaska's most important archaeological sites: nine different human cultures have occupied it over 12,000 years, drawn to the same caribou crossing on the Kobuk River. The Inupiat continue the tradition of intercepting caribou here.

activities.text: Bush plane flight from Kotzebue to the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes—the largest active dunes in the Arctic, 25 square miles of sand 100 km north of the Arctic Circle. Summer temperatures climb to 38°C on the sand—an absolute paradox in this context. NASA conducted analog studies here to prepare for Mars missions. In summer, wolf, grizzly, and moose tracks crisscross the sand between patches of spruce.

Floating the Kobuk River by packraft or folding canoe—several Kotzebue operators arrange plane drop-offs upriver, with pickup one or two days later. The river flows through boreal forests and Arctic prairies at a gentle pace, mostly Class I. The permafrost bluffs (up to 45 meters) lining the river contain mammoth and steppe bison fossils visible from the boat.

places.name: Lafayette

visits.text: Welcome to Lafayette, heart of Acadiana and self-proclaimed "Happiest City in America." This morning, head to Vermilionville, a living history museum village on the banks of Bayou Vermilion. This site recreates Acadian life from 1765 to 1890 through 19 restored buildings. Period-costumed artisans demonstrate weaving, wood carving, and Cajun cooking. The on-site restaurant, La Cuisine de Maman, serves gumbo and crawfish étouffée prepared according to traditional recipes.

The Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist, downtown, dates from 1916, and its century-old oak in the forecourt (the Cathedral Oak, estimated to be over 500 years old) is one of Louisiana's most photographed trees. The adjacent cemetery, with its above-ground tombs, recalls those of New Orleans.

Explore downtown Lafayette on foot: Jefferson Street is home to Cajun craft shops, galleries, and colorful murals. The Acadiana Center for the Arts schedules exhibitions and concerts year-round. Lafayette has more restaurants per capita than most American cities—you'll eat well at every meal.

Day trip heading south: drive to Avery Island (50 minutes from Lafayette), birthplace of Tabasco sauce. The McIlhenny family has produced the famous hot sauce here since 1868—same recipe, same place, five generations. Peppers are grown on the island, crushed with local salt, then aged three years in oak barrels (the same ones used for bourbon). The factory tour shows you the entire process, and the shop offers varieties unavailable elsewhere.

Don't leave without exploring Jungle Gardens, 70 hectares of botanical gardens and wildlife sanctuary on Avery Island. The garden was created by Edward Avery McIlhenny in the early 20th century. You'll see Bird City, a nesting colony of snowy egrets he saved from extinction in 1895 by raising 8 young birds. Today, thousands of egrets nest there each spring. The park also features a 12th-century Buddha brought from China and an impressive bamboo grove. Warning: signs indicate the presence of black bears—this is not a joke.

On the way back to Lafayette, stop in New Iberia at Shadows-on-the-Teche plantation. This 1834 red-brick mansion, bordered by oaks on the banks of Bayou Teche, is one of the few plantations managed by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Downtown New Iberia is also worth a look—it's a small, quiet Cajun town with colorful Creole houses.

activities.text: In the evening, look for a Cajun dance or zydeco night. The difference: Cajun music is played on accordion and fiddle, sung in French; zydeco adds the frottoir (washboard) and faster rhythms drawn from blues and R&B. Both are danced with a partner, doing a Cajun waltz or a two-step. Even if you don't know how to dance, locals will show you—that's the spirit of Acadiana.

Return to Lafayette for dinner. Order a dish you haven't tried yet: boudin (spiced rice and pork sausage, 100% Cajun specialty), gumbo (thick soup based on roux, okra, and seafood or andouille), or crawfish étouffée (crawfish simmered in butter-and-spice sauce).

visits.text: Laguna Beach - Where Art Colony Meets Surf Colony: This Orange County gem has nurtured artists since the early 1900s, with over 100 galleries showcasing works ranging from impressionism to cutting-edge contemporary art. World-class waves break just steps away.

Laguna Beach Public Art - Open-Air Museum: The city maintains an impressive collection of outdoor sculptures and murals, from abstract installations on downtown corners to the famous 'Greeter' sculpture welcoming visitors since 1970.

Crystal Cove State Park - 5.1 Km of Preserved Coastline: This protected stretch preserves undeveloped beachfront between Newport and Laguna, with the charming Historic District of 1930s beach cottages tucked into the bluffs.

Thousand Steps Beach - Worth Every Step: Despite the exaggerated name (it's actually about 230 steps), this steep descent rewards beachgoers with tide pools, sea caves, and some of the finest sand in Orange County.

activities.text: Pageant of the Masters - Living Art Like Nowhere Else: Each summer, this unique festival presents 'living pictures' - real people recreating famous artworks in elaborate tableaux that must be seen to be believed.

visits.text: Molokini Crater — Snorkel or scuba dive in this crescent-shaped volcanic caldera rising from the ocean floor to form a natural aquarium. The partially submerged crater is home to 250 species of fish and 38 types of coral in crystal-clear waters with 45 meters of visibility. Access by boat only, on excursions departing from Maalaea Harbor, about half an hour's drive from Lahaina.

Lahaina Historic District — This former whaling village and one-time Hawaiian royal capital was devastated by the August 2023 wildfire, which destroyed most of its 19th-century buildings. The massive Banyan Tree planted in 1873 survived and is putting out new leaves, but its park remains closed: view it from the designated viewpoints along the edge. The historic core is being rebuilt, so respect the fences and do not enter the burned residential areas.

Iao Valley State Monument — Hike to the viewpoints of the 370-meter Iao Needle, a lava remnant sacred to Hawaiians under the name Kuka'emoku. The verdant valley receives abundant rainfall that creates lush tropical vegetation and was the site of Kamehameha's battle in 1790. Allow about forty minutes' drive from Lahaina.

Front Street Lahaina — The waterfront street reopened to traffic on 1 August 2026 between Papalaua Street and Shaw Street, after the 2023 fire. Some businesses have resumed, including the Ulu o Lele Marketplace and Kimo's restaurant, while the north end, around the Lahaina Cannery Mall, has restaurants and shops. The rest of the historic street is still a construction site: come to support the reopened businesses, not to tour the ruins.

activities.text: Whale watching cruise — Spot humpback whales migrating to Hawaiian waters December through April to mate and calve. The 18-meter mammals breach, tail slap, and sing in the warm Pacific, with up to 10,000 visiting annually.

Sunset dinner cruise — Sail along Maui's west coast enjoying Hawaiian music, tropical cocktails, and buffet dinner as the sun sinks into the Pacific. Catamaran cruises offer romantic evening experiences with whale sightings in season.

visits.text: Discover Lake Allatoona, a sprawling 4,800-hectare reservoir surrounded by forested hills and scenic shoreline offering excellent opportunities for swimming, boating, and lakeside relaxation. The crystal-clear waters and numerous sandy beaches make this destination perfect for families seeking outdoor recreation combined with natural beauty. Several marinas provide boat rentals for exploring hidden coves and peaceful inlets.

Explore the historic Allatoona Pass Battlefield, where dramatic red clay cliffs and a remarkable 53-meter-deep railroad cut tell the story of fierce Civil War combat. The strategic gorge and sweeping views over the lake create a striking landscape where history and natural beauty converge. Hiking trails connect key battlefield sites with panoramic overlooks.

activities.text: Hike the Pine Mountain Trail Loop for elevated views over the shimmering lake waters, then camp under the stars at Red Top Mountain State Park. The area offers diverse recreational options from fishing and paddleboarding to scenic picnic areas along the forested shoreline.

places.name: Lake City, FL

visits.text: Your first surprise after leaving I-10: Ichetucknee's water is so clear you can see turtles breathing three meters below the surface. Eight springs feed a 9.6 km river, designated a National Natural Landmark since 1971. Water rises from the aquifer at a constant 22°C—cold when it is 35 outside, lukewarm in winter. The state bought the site from a phosphate company in 1970 for $1.85 million, and nothing has changed since. Entry $6 per car, tube rental $7.50. Arrive before 10 AM in summer: the park closes when it reaches 750 visitors, which happens quickly on weekends. Plan a round trip from Lake City for this visit.

A must-see, Blue Hole Spring takes a little effort—an 800-meter walk from the North Entrance through a cypress forest. A first-magnitude spring, meaning a flow of more than 2.8 million liters per minute. The hole descends 12 meters and opens into 180 meters of underwater caverns explored by technical divers. For an ordinary swimmer with a mask and snorkel, it is already spectacular: sand bubbles up from the bottom like an inverted fountain. Avoid 2–4 PM, when it is the park's only crowded swimming hole. Plan a round trip from Lake City to the park, followed by the walk from the North Entrance.

If Florida and the Civil War seem incompatible, Olustee Battlefield will prove otherwise—February 20, 1864, 10,000 soldiers engaged in total, a Confederate victory, Florida's largest Civil War battle. The site has remained largely intact, with a 1.6 km trail and interpretive signs. Annual reenactment in February, the largest in the Southeast. Free admission, open 8 AM to sunset. Twenty minutes east of Lake City, worth combining with Ichetucknee if you have a full day.

activities.text: Float down the river in a tube from Dampier's Landing—1.2 km, 45 minutes to one hour of gentle drifting among cypress trees and turtles. The current does the work; you just hold on to your tube. Strictly prohibited: food, alcohol, single-use plastic, ice, and non-reusable bottles—everything is inspected at the entrance. Bring sunscreen (apply it 30 minutes before entering the water to avoid pollution), a reusable water bottle, and water shoes. Plan a round trip from Lake City for this activity.

Not exactly a culinary hotspot, Lake City—but Halpatter Brewing Company serves local IPAs and decent burgers in a restored 1902 railroad depot. Locals hang out here until nightfall. For something more rustic, The Patio Place runs a classic Southern buffet (fried chicken, collard greens, mac & cheese) for $14—church cafeteria vibe, and that's exactly why you go.

places.name: Lake Crescent, WA

visits.text: Lake Crescent sets clear water against forested slopes. This glacier-carved lake runs alongside US 101, but designated access points let you leave traffic behind and take in the shoreline. Stop in the Barnes Point area and use the designated parking lots instead of pulling over on the shoulder.

activities.text: Follow the Marymere Falls trail beneath towering trees to reach the waterfall. The route starts in the Storm King area and initially passes through forest; the final approach requires more care on sloping sections. Wear shoes with good traction and plan to return the way you came.

A nearly flat loop offers a change of pace after the waterfall: Moments in Time Trail stays close to Lake Crescent. The interpretive trail passes through old-growth forest and returns to the shore without committing you to a long hike. Take the opportunity to study the trunks and undergrowth; save the walks on the opposite shore for a longer stay.

visits.text: Black Point Estate - This Queen Anne mansion from 1888 was built by beer magnate Conrad Seipp as a summer residence. Accessible only by boat (the cruise is part of the experience). Twenty rooms furnished in period style, verandas overlooking the lake. It perfectly captures the Gilded Age when wealthy Chicago families escaped the city for Lake Geneva's shores.

Riviera Ballroom - This 1932 Art Deco building on the lakefront hosted the great swing-era orchestras. Today it serves as a performance venue and cruise departure point. The architecture is worth a stop even without a show.

Geneva Lake Shore Path - This 34 km trail circles the entire lake passing in front of Gilded Age estates. You don't have to do it all: a 5-8 km section is enough to see the finest properties and enjoy the views.

activities.text: Lake Geneva Cruise - Several cruise types: full lake tour (2h), mail boat cruise (the mailman jumps from the moving boat to deliver mail to lakefront property mailboxes - unique in the world), or sunset cruise.
