visits.text: Lake Ouachita - Arkansas's Crystal-Clear Inland Sea: Spanning 16,000 hectares with over 1,500 kilometers of pristine shoreline, this reservoir consistently ranks among America's cleanest lakes. Created by Blakely Mountain Dam and nestled among the forested Ouachita Mountains, it has impossibly clear waters that reveal depths of up to 12 meters.

Garvan Woodland Gardens - 85 Hectares of Botanical Paradise: Rising from a peninsula on Lake Hamilton, this botanical garden of the University of Arkansas transforms the Ouachita forest into themed displays featuring the magnificent Anthony Chapel, the Asian garden, and the largest bridge of its kind in America - all reflected in tranquil waters. Plan a round trip by car from your stop at Lake Ouachita.

activities.text: Lake Ouachita Water Sports - Dive into Pure Mountain Water: The exceptional clarity supports world-class scuba diving revealing underwater rock formations, while kayakers, sailors, and anglers explore endless secluded coves surrounded by national forest.

Three Sisters Springs - The Historic Springs of Lake Ouachita: Walk to the three springs in Lake Ouachita State Park. Observe their structures and the signs recalling the medicinal properties once attributed to each spring, reminders of the site's spa history.

places.name: Lake Placid, NY

visits.text: Lake Placid is the only small American town to have hosted two Winter Olympics, in 1932 and 1980. The Olympic Center, right in town, houses the original rink of the "Miracle on Ice"—the impossible victory of the US amateur hockey team over the USSR on February 22, 1980. The ice is still there, you can walk on it between training sessions. Adjacent Olympic museum, $15. For sports fans, it's a pilgrimage.

The Intervales ski jumping complex is still used by the US team. The 90- and 120-meter jumps are visible from 10 km away. An elevator goes up the big jump ($50) with 360° views over the Adirondacks. In summer, skiers train on jumps covered with wet synthetic material—surreal to watch them launch in 25°C weather.

Whiteface Mountain peaks at 1,483 meters and remains the only Olympic mountain in the East where you can drive to the summit. The 8-km Veterans Memorial Highway climbs to a parking lot at 1,350 m, then a tunnel and elevator blasted through rock reach the summit in all weather. Built in 1935 under Roosevelt. Clear views to Mount Marcy, the state's highest point (1,629 m). $18 per vehicle.

John Brown Farm, 3 km from downtown Lake Placid, is the farm where abolitionist John Brown lived from 1849 until his hanging in 1859 after the Harpers Ferry raid. His body is buried here, along with those of several sons who fell in combat. State historic site, free. The wooden house remains almost as it was. Surprising to find such history in the heart of the Adirondacks—the region was an active abolitionist hub via the "Timbuctoo" colony.

High Falls Gorge in Wilmington (15 minutes east) features a suspended walkway system over the West Branch Ausable River. Four successive waterfalls, up to 18 meters high, along 800 meters of circuit. Private, $18, open year-round (crampons provided in winter). Photogenic, short, accessible to fragile knees.

activities.text: Take a bobsled run down the Olympic track at Mount Van Hoevenberg. Summer or winter, you can launch at 95 km/h with a pro driver for $125—the same track used by the national team. The experience lasts 50 seconds: brief, but unforgettable in the literal sense. Mandatory online reservation, 48 hours ahead.

Mirror Lake, smaller than Lake Placid but more central, offers a 4-km walk around. Flat trail along the water, ideal in late afternoon. Kayak or paddleboard rental for $25-30/hour at the municipal dock. In winter, the free-access outdoor skating rink lights up until 10 pm—skates loaned for free.

Stop at the Cascade Lakes, 15 minutes from Lake Placid on Route 73. Two narrow lakes squeezed between cliffs, separated by a strip of land where you park by the water, with picnic tables. Upper Cascade Lake, the smaller and more sheltered from the wind, is good for canoeing and fishing, and a rugged path leads to a waterfall tumbling down the mountain between the two lakes. One of the most photographed spots in the Adirondacks in autumn.

visits.text: The lake seems inseparable from the park, yet Lake Quinault belongs to the Quinault Indian Nation. Its shores fall under several management jurisdictions, and forest surrounds this glacier-carved valley. Use a designated public access point to enjoy the view of the water; check the rules separately if you are considering a water activity.

activities.text: Walk beneath the conifers on Quinault Rain Forest Nature Trail without venturing into the long valley farther inland. This interpretive trail on the south shore is part of the Olympic National Forest trail network. Interpretive signs along the way help explain the undergrowth. Save this loop for the morning, before heading toward Olympia.

The shore deserves as much attention as the trees: Quinault Lakeshore Trail alternates between water views and stretches through the forest. This trail is part of the walking trail network south of the lake, allowing a short outing without completing the entire valley loop. Take an out-and-back walk that fits your schedule, and turn around before it delays your departure.

visits.text: Lake Tahoe — Marvel at North America's largest alpine lake spanning 496 square kilometers at 1,897 meters elevation. The impossibly blue waters reach 501 meters deep surrounded by Sierra Nevada peaks straddling the California-Nevada border.

Emerald Bay State Park — Photograph this fjord-like inlet featuring Fannette Island, Lake Tahoe's only island, topped by a stone teahouse. The scenic overlook offers the lake's most iconic vista with crystal waters framed by granite cliffs.

Sand Harbor — Swim in the clearest waters along massive granite boulders creating natural sculptures. This Nevada State Park beach offers white sand and turquoise waters rivaling tropical destinations.

Vikingsholm Castle — Visit this 1929 Scandinavian-style mansion built as a summer retreat, considered one of the finest examples of Scandinavian architecture in the Western Hemisphere. The 38-room castle took 200 workers to build on the shores of Emerald Bay.

activities.text: Lake Tahoe Scenic Drive — Navigate 116 kilometers around the lake passing beaches, vista points, and forest. The route offers constantly changing mountain and water views.
Kayaking on crystal waters — Paddle across transparent waters allowing visibility to 21 meters depth. The lake's purity and dramatic shoreline create unforgettable paddling experiences.
Lakeside dining — Savor fresh trout and steaks at restaurants overlooking the sapphire waters. Tahoe's culinary scene emphasizes mountain cuisine with stunning views.

activities.text: You will wait in Lamar Valley’s parking areas, binoculars in hand, rather than follow the animals. Bison and predators share this open landscape, but no sighting is guaranteed. Stay at least 100 meters from bears and wolves, and 25 meters from other animals; back away if they approach.

visits.text: You enter a 12-acre property that faithfully represents Amish life as it's still practiced today in Lancaster County. The guided tour of this 1840s farm takes you through the sparse rooms of a house without electricity, the forge, the one-room schoolhouse, the barn and its animals. The Amish began settling in this region in 1720, responding to William Penn's invitation that guaranteed religious freedom. Today, approximately 75,000 Amish live in Lancaster County, representing one of the largest communities in America. Book your tour in advance during high season; tours depart every 15 minutes, and allow at least three hours on site to also enjoy the bus tour through the back roads.

The Bird-in-Hand market is one of the most authentic in Amish country: you'll find hand-rolled pretzels, fresh cheeses, homemade jams, hand-stitched quilts, and locally crafted goods sold by Amish and Mennonite vendors. The village name - 'Bird-in-Hand' - supposedly comes from an 18th-century inn sign depicting a bird perched in a hand. On the roads between villages, it's common to pass Amish families in horse-drawn buggies, even on main roads - a sight that reminds you you've entered a different sense of time. The market is open Friday and Saturday year-round, with additional days in summer.

The Strasburg Rail Road is the oldest operating short-line railroad in the United States: its first operations date back to 1832, well before most American railroads existed. Your 45-minute ride aboard a steam locomotive takes you through the fields and farms of Amish country, with views of farmers in the fields and carriages waiting at grade crossings. The ticket includes round-trip from Strasburg station to Paradise, Pennsylvania - and yes, the village of Paradise actually exists. The Railroad Museum of Pennsylvania, right across from the station, houses one of the finest collections of historic locomotives in the country; allow an extra 45 minutes for a quick visit.

activities.text: Aaron & Jessica's Buggy Rides takes you along private paths through non-commercial Amish farms, where cars can't go. The drivers themselves belong to Amish and Mennonite communities, making the encounter direct and authentic. The draft horse, the slow pace, the clip-clop of hooves on asphalt, and the impeccably trimmed hedges around houses without power lines create total immersion in a way of life that 300 years of modernization haven't touched. A stop at a farm allows you to sample homemade cookies and lemonade. Go in the morning to catch the golden light on the fields and families starting their workday.

Kitchen Kettle Village in Intercourse - a village whose name invariably draws smiles from visitors - is the artisanal and culinary heart of Amish country. Since 1954, this collection of specialty shops has sold jams, apple butters, honeys, preserves, ceramics, and textiles made by local artisans. The Amish jam factory, visible from the shop, produces more than 100 varieties. The village also includes an inn, several restaurants, and a cheese shop. It's the best place to bring home authentic local products - prices are reasonable since you're buying directly from producers.

places.name: Lander, WY

visits.text: Ten kilometers southwest of Lander on WY-131, the Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River pulls one of geology's strangest tricks: it disappears into a limestone cavern called “the Sinks” and reappears 400 meters downstream at “the Rise”—taking more than two hours underground to cover those 400 meters. A paved path connects the two sites. At the Rise, a pool holds 4–5-kilogram rainbow trout protected from fishing since 1919; toss in food and the water churns. Humans have used this canyon for approximately 9,000 years. Free admission.

The Fremont County Pioneer Museum in downtown Lander explains the origins of the town: Lander was named for Frederick W. Lander, engineer of the Lander Trail used by thousands of westward emigrants. When the Chicago & North Western Transportation Company chose Lander as the western terminus of its “Cowboy Line” railway in 1906, the phrase stuck—“where the rails end and the trails begin”. It still fits today. Free admission.

Forty kilometers south of Lander, Wild Iris is one of the best sport-climbing areas in North America—over 300 routes in bone-white dolomitic limestone surrounded by aspen groves and wildflower meadows. Todd Skinner and his partners first developed it in 1990. Even without climbing shoes, the drive alone is worth it: the meadows are spectacular in June and July, and Lander's International Climbers' Festival, held every July since 1994, is the oldest climbing festival in the United States.

activities.text: The Canyon Loop Trail in Sinks Canyon crosses the river on a suspension bridge, loops around the Sinks and the Rise, then climbs the north wall for views of the limestone cliffs. The rock type shifts from sandstone to limestone to granite within a few kilometers as the Wind River Range draws closer. Watch for bighorn sheep on the upper cliffs, mule deer in the canyon bottom, and moose near the river in early morning.

Lander's Main Street in the evening has an authentic Western character rare for a town of 7,500. Wild Iris Mountain Sports at 425 Popo Agie St is worth stopping in—the staff have climbed every site in the region and give genuine advice on the Wind Rivers. For dinner, Lander Brewing Company serves local craft beer alongside bison dishes; the Gannett Grill is the other local mainstay.

visits.text: Drive from Landrum to the Caesars Head overlook and gaze across the ridges and valleys of the Blue Ridge Mountains toward the horizon. This granite outcrop offers broad mountain views. Crisp air and sweeping scenery make the overlook a stop for nature lovers. Allow for the return drive to Landrum after your visit.

Drive from Landrum to the Raven Cliff Falls trailhead. This is South Carolina's tallest waterfall, at 128 meters. The roughly six-kilometer round-trip trail leads to an overlook of the falls. The suspension bridge belongs to a separate, longer hike on the Dismal Trail loop: allow more walking time if you want to reach it.

activities.text: Drive from Landrum to Caesars Head State Park. Pass through Devil's Kitchen, a narrow rocky gap leading to the overlook. The park's rugged paths, forests and rock formations reveal the Blue Ridge landscape. After the walk, plan your return drive to Landrum.

Explore Landrum's charming downtown, where rolling foothills, sweeping mountain views, and country roads lined with farms create an idyllic setting. Visit Pearson's Falls, a beautiful 27-meter waterfall tucked into a lush nature preserve, and hike the Blue Wall Preserve for stunning mountain panoramas. The area's equestrian culture adds distinctive character to this hidden gem.

places.name: Laramie, WY

visits.text: Built in 1872 as one of the few federal prisons of its time, the Wyoming Territorial Prison State Historic Site has sandstone walls that still feel oppressive. Of the 44 prisoners admitted during the first two years, 11 escaped. The most famous inmate was Butch Cassidy, held here from 1894 to 1896 for grand larceny. After the prison moved to Rawlins in 1901, the University of Wyoming used the building as an animal experimentation station until 1989—a strange afterlife for a place this grim. The site covers 80 hectares with a nature trail along the Big Laramie River. Admission is charged; open Memorial Day through Labor Day.

A full Apatosaurus skeleton greets you near the entrance of the University of Wyoming Geological Museum—one of the most complete sauropod specimens on display anywhere in the state. The collection covers Wyoming's rich fossil heritage, including dinosaur footprints and Morrison Formation specimens. Free admission. Allow 45–60 minutes; the historic Romanesque Revival campus buildings are worth a walk afterward.

At I-80 Exit 329, 26 kilometers east of Laramie, the landscape breaks open to reveal something that looks structurally impossible: 1.4-billion-year-old Sherman Granite stacked in towers up to 150 meters high. The Arapaho called this place “bito'o'wu”—born of the earth—a name popularized by a University of Wyoming drama professor in 1922. Over 900 climbing routes thread the rock; non-climbers can walk the 5-kilometer Turtle Rock Loop through aspen groves with minimal elevation gain. A day-use fee applies.

activities.text: WY-130 west of Laramie is the day's main event—the Snowy Range Scenic Byway rises to an elevation of 3,306 meters at Libby Flats, Wyoming's second-highest pass. It was designated the second National Forest Scenic Byway in 1988. Lake Marie is the best stop: Medicine Bow Peak (3,662 meters) appears to rise straight out of the water. At Libby Flats, views extend south into Colorado. If you're staying in Laramie tonight, make it an out-and-back; otherwise it's tomorrow's route to Saratoga.

Laramie's historic downtown is worth an evening stroll—locally owned shops, colorful murals, and places like Range Leather Co. (handcrafted leather goods) and the Bent and Rusty (antiques and oddities). The town was born in 1868 when Union Pacific arrived; within months it had a population of several thousand. For dinner, try the Crowbar and Grill for hand-tossed pizza or Sweet Melissa for creative vegetarian dishes a block away.

visits.text: Walk the 122-meter square parade ground and you can see all nine original buildings surrounding you - something no comparable fort in the region can claim. Between 1866 and 1868, Captain A.F. Rockwell replaced the original sod-and-adobe structures with sandstone quarried locally, and every one of them still stands. Seven are open to visitors: barracks, officers' quarters, post hospital, blacksmith shop, commissary, and the commanding officer's quarters, all furnished to their 1860s-1870s appearance. The 10th U.S. Cavalry - one of the first two all-Black cavalry regiments in the Army - was stationed here from 1867 to 1869. Eight kilometers southwest, original Santa Fe Trail wagon ruts remain visible in the prairie grass.

activities.text: Drive west from Lawrence on US-56 and you are on the route that traders followed from 1821 to 1872, moving goods between Missouri and Santa Fe, New Mexico. The land flattens dramatically west of Hillsboro. Consider a 15-minute detour to Pawnee Rock State Park, 14 km northeast of Larned off US-56 - a sandstone prominence where Santa Fe Trail scouts watched for Comanche and Kiowa raiders, now free and open year-round with interpretive panels and views across the Arkansas River valley.

visits.text: Las Vegas Strip — Walk the 6.8-kilometer boulevard lined with mega-resorts recreating world landmarks from the Eiffel Tower to Venetian canals. This entertainment capital features 30 casinos including Bellagio's fountains choreographed to music and the Luxor's 42.3-billion-candlepower sky beam.

Bellagio Conservatory and Botanical Gardens — Marvel at elaborate seasonal displays featuring thousands of flowers, trees, and sculptures. The 13,000-square-meter space transforms five times annually with themes created by 120 horticulturists.

Fremont Street Experience — Discover old Las Vegas under the Viva Vision canopy featuring 12.5 million LED lights creating 360-degree shows. The pedestrian mall in downtown's historic casino district offers vintage neon, street performers, and zip-lining.

Mob Museum — Explore organized crime and law enforcement history in the former 1933 federal courthouse. Interactive exhibits chronicle Las Vegas's mob connections, Prohibition, and the FBI's fight against organized crime.

Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area — About thirty minutes' drive from Las Vegas, take the 21-kilometer scenic loop by car through Mojave Desert landscapes with 900-meter cliffs of red and beige Aztec sandstone. The 78,000-hectare area protects Joshua trees, desert tortoises and climbing routes.

Calico Hills — About thirty minutes' drive from Las Vegas, hike among the swirling patterns of petrified sand dunes laid down 180 million years ago. The multicolored sandstone creates a photographer's paradise, with formations glowing in vivid orange and red.

Valley of Fire State Park — About an hour's drive from Las Vegas, explore Nevada's oldest and largest state park, with 16,000 hectares of Aztec sandstone turned red by iron oxide. The formations date back 150 million years, when dinosaurs roamed the shifting dunes.

Atlatl Rock — In Valley of Fire, about an hour's drive from Las Vegas, admire the prehistoric petroglyphs carved by Ancestral Puebloan and Paiute peoples on this sandstone outcrop. The rock art depicts atlatls—spear-throwing devices—as well as bighorn sheep and geometric patterns.
Neon Museum — Discover the old illuminated signs of Las Vegas casinos and motels gathered in the Neon Boneyard, north of downtown. Night tours let you see several restored signs lit up once again.

Springs Preserve — Explore this site west of downtown, laid out around the springs that gave birth to Las Vegas. Desert botanical gardens, trails and the Nevada State Museum tell the natural and human history of the valley.

High Roller — Ride this observation wheel at the LINQ complex, in the heart of the Strip. Its glass cabins offer views over the casinos, the desert and the surrounding mountains, especially beautiful at sunset.

activities.text: Cirque du Soleil show — Witness acrobatic artistry in one of seven permanent Cirque productions performing on the Strip. The Canadian entertainment company revolutionized Las Vegas shows with theatrical circus performances.
Casino buffet experience — Feast at legendary all-you-can-eat buffets offering cuisines from around the world. Las Vegas pioneered the buffet concept in 1946 to keep gamblers on property.

Fountains of Bellagio show — Watch choreographed water jets dance to classical music and contemporary hits. The 8-hectare lake features over 1,200 nozzles shooting water up to 140 meters high in performances every 15-30 minutes.

Fire Wave Hike — About an hour's drive from Las Vegas, walk 2.4 kilometers to this swirling sandstone formation that looks like frozen waves of red and white rock. The moderate trail reveals one of the most photographed geological wonders of Valley of Fire.
Desert wildlife watching — Spot desert bighorn sheep, chuckwallas, and desert tortoises adapted to extreme Mojave conditions. Early morning and late afternoon offer best viewing opportunities.

Arts District — Stroll through this neighborhood south of downtown, also known as 18b, among galleries, vintage shops and bars. On the first Friday of every month, the First Friday festival brings together artists, musicians and food stalls.
Return to Las Vegas — Complete the Nevada loop returning to the neon oasis. The contrast between wilderness and civilization epitomizes Nevada's diverse character.

visits.text: Lassen Volcanic National Park - The Four Types of Volcanoes: Walk through a geothermal wonderland where the earth bubbles, hisses and steams beneath your feet. This living laboratory features dome, shield, cinder cone and composite volcanoes, all within the park's boundaries.

Bumpass Hell - Three Miles into the Largest Hydrothermal Area in the Cascades: Follow the boardwalk trail past roaring fumaroles, bubbling mudpots, and scalding pools painted in otherworldly hues of orange, yellow, and turquoise. The trail honors Kendall Bumpass, who lost a leg when he broke through thin crust into boiling water.

Sulphur Works - Drive-Up Geothermal Theater: Steam vents and bubbling mud pools mere feet from the road offer the easiest access to the park's volcanic activity. The sulfurous smell announces your arrival before you see the first wisp of steam.

activities.text: Lassen Peak Summit Trail - Climb an Active Volcano: This 5-mile round-trip hike ascends 2,000 feet to the 10,457-foot summit, offering 360-degree views of the volcanic landscape. Lassen Peak last erupted in 1915, creating the devastated area still visible today.

places.name: Laurel, MS

visits.text: If you watch HGTV, you already know Laurel: it's the town from “Home Town” where Erin and Ben Napier have renovated houses since 2016—eight seasons and over 100 restored homes. Before the show, Laurel had dozens of empty buildings in its historic downtown. Today, fans make pilgrimages. The pedestrian downtown packs 80 shops into six blocks: Laurel Mercantile (the Napiers' store), Scotsman Co. (vintage furniture), bookstores, cafes. You can explore it all on foot in 2–3 hours.

An understated Southern treasure, the Lauren Rogers Museum of Art was founded in 1923 by the Rogers family (timber industrialists) in memory of their son who died at 23. Permanent collection: American paintings (Sargent, Whistler, Homer, Cassatt), Dürer prints, the Southeast's largest collection of Native American baskets with 810 pieces. Free admission. The neoclassical marble building is just as worth seeing as the art.

Explore on foot: North 5th Avenue, Magnolia Street, West Oak Street—downtown residential neighborhoods, perfectly restored Victorian houses and Craftsman bungalows, some seen in “Home Town”. The gardens are well tended, the porches occupied in late afternoon. The atmosphere of a real small Southern town, without the tourist fatigue of Charleston or Savannah. Free.

activities.text: Right next to the Napier studio, Pearl's Diner serves breakfast all day—biscuits and gravy, $5 pancakes. Otherwise, Café La Fleur in a renovated old house serves more modern bistro food (mixed salads, gourmet sandwiches). And Slabtown Pizzeria for low-key evenings.

visits.text: Walk six blocks from 6th Street to South Park and you are inside a National Register historic district with 108 contributing properties, most built between 1856 and 1953. At 729-731, the House Building is the only one of the four commercial buildings spared by Quantrill's raid in 1863 that still stands today. The Eldridge Hotel at 701-703 was Quantrill's main tactical target; the current five-story brick building dates from 1928, and every August 21 a white sheet hangs from a window to mark the anniversary. Free State Brewing Company at 636 Massachusetts opened in 1989 as the first legal brewery in Kansas in more than a century.

You enter through the marble foyer of the 1888 Watkins National Bank Building at 1047 Massachusetts Street - marble staircases, stained-glass windows, and mosaic floors intact - and get the most thorough account of Quantrill's Raid in any Lawrence museum. The free permanent collection covers Douglas County history from Bleeding Kansas through the 20th century. James Patti's sculpture of Langston Hughes as a boy is here; Hughes grew up in Lawrence and based his 1930 novel Not Without Laughter on his childhood in this town.

Climb Mount Oread to the KU campus and you are on a National Historic District that opened in 1866 - one year after Quantrill's raid nearly prevented Lawrence from funding the new university at all. The Spencer Museum of Art (over 45,000 objects) and the KU Natural History Museum are both free and both worth at least 30 minutes each. James Naismith, the inventor of basketball and the only KU coach with a losing record, coached here and is buried in Lawrence.

activities.text: Download the free 2.4-km self-guided walking tour from explorelawrence.com and follow Quantrill's path through 10 surviving sites - from South Park, where guerrillas staged their approach, to the Methodist Church that became a makeshift morgue by evening. The raid killed 20 percent of the town's male population and left 85 widows. Quantrill himself had lived in Lawrence under an alias and knew the town intimately before leading 450 men into it at dawn. The Watkins Museum also runs a paid Bleeding Kansas Bus Tour on select summer Saturdays for a wider sweep of the region.

End your day the way Lawrence does: with a pint and a plate on Mass Street. Free State Brewing Company has poured its flagship Ad Astra amber ale - named for the Kansas state motto, “To the stars through difficulty” - since opening in 1989 as the first legal brewery in Kansas in over a century. For dinner, the Mad Greek at 9th and Massachusetts does flaming saganaki tableside. The Granada at 1020 Massachusetts, a Beaux-Arts venue that opened in 1912 with an 11-meter vaulted ceiling, hosts live music most nights under a chandelier the size of a small car.

visits.text: You enter a landscape where the granite is 550 million years old and the animals have been here - with a thirty-year gap - for over a century. The refuge was established July 4, 1901, making it the oldest facility in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service system. On the roads you share space with free-roaming bison, Texas longhorn cattle (established on the refuge in 1927), Rocky Mountain elk (introduced from Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in 1908), white-tailed deer, and prairie dog towns. The Longhorn Trail - a 1.5-mile loop around French Lake - consistently produces bison and longhorn sightings. Drive at 15mph on all refuge roads; bison cross without warning and have the right of way in every sense.

You drive three miles of paved switchbacks to the summit of Mount Scott at 2,464 feet - the highest accessible point in the refuge - and step out into a 360-degree view of the granite-studded prairie below, Fort Sill to the south, and the wind farm on the Slick Hills to the north. The rock beneath your feet is part of the Mount Scott Granite, intruded roughly 530 million years ago. On a clear day you can see the curvature of the land. The drive takes about 20 minutes each way; stay for the full rim walk before heading back down.

You walk through a 66-acre granite complex inside the refuge built by WPA workers in 1934-35 to replicate biblical Jerusalem - Herod's Court, Pilate's judgment hall, the Garden of Gethsemane, watchtowers, and perimeter walls, all quarried from local rock with a $94,000 federal grant. It was built for the “Prince of Peace” Easter passion play, which Rev. Anthony Mark Wallock first staged near Medicine Park in 1926 with five cast members and 200 attendees. Today it's the longest-running Easter pageant in the United States. A mile east, you find Medicine Park - a cobblestone resort village from 1908 where the buildings are faced with rounded granite pulled from local creek beds, and where legend holds that Al Capone kept a cabin. Both are free to visit.

activities.text: You head into 5,000 acres of designated wilderness where interlocking granite boulders and short cliffs have drawn climbers since the 1960s and 70s. The Access Fund and Wichita Mountains Climbers Coalition maintain established routes on the rock faces. If you prefer hiking to climbing, the 2.4-mile Charon's Garden Trail crosses the wilderness from the Sunset trailhead to Treasure Lake - rocky underfoot and worth every step, but bring considerably more water than you think you will need. There is no drinking water on this trail, and the summer heat of southwestern Oklahoma will empty your bottles faster than any mountain path.

You drive to a town of about a dozen people for a burger made with longhorn beef raised in Meers. The Meers Store has been here since 1901, and its “Meersburger” uses this longhorn beef. The building looks as though it was assembled over decades because it was. Meers is open only Thursday through Sunday; arrive before 7 p.m. or expect a wait at the door.

visits.text: Front Street Park — In the heart of Leavenworth, cross this park lined with Bavarian-style facades and stop by the gazebo to watch the activity on Front Street. The downtown shops and restaurants are then easy to explore on foot, with the Cascade Mountains as a backdrop.

Leavenworth Bavarian Village — Stroll this Alpine-themed town transformed in the 1960s with Bavarian architecture, beer gardens, and German restaurants. The former logging town reinvented itself as a tourist destination in the Cascade Mountains.

Waterfront Park — Walk along the Wenatchee River through this landscaped park featuring traditional German gazebos and gardens. The park hosts festivals year-round from Oktoberfest to Christmas lighting ceremonies.

Nutcracker Museum — View over 7,000 nutcrackers from around the world in this unique collection spanning six rooms. Examples range from medieval functional tools to ornate Bavarian figures and modern artistic interpretations.

activities.text: German cuisine sampling — Feast on schnitzel, bratwurst, spätzle, and apple strudel at authentic Bavarian restaurants complete with lederhosen-clad servers. Beer gardens serve German imports and local craft brews in festive atmosphere.

Icicle Gorge Trail hiking — Trek along the cascading Icicle Creek through old-growth forest and granite canyons. The relatively easy 4-mile trail offers swimming holes and dramatic mountain scenery in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

Wine tasting at local wineries — Sample Riesling, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir at tasting rooms surrounding Leavenworth. The Cascade foothills' elevation and temperature variations create favorable growing conditions.

days_plan.itin_title: Washington State Circuit: Seattle and Mount Rainier

visits.text: Stop at Tunnel View (37.7155, -119.6772) when entering Yosemite Valley—this is where the road emerges from the tunnel and El Capitan appears on the left, Bridalveil Fall on the right, Half Dome in the distance. Ansel Adams photographed this exact spot in 1934 and the image is one of the most reproduced in American history. El Capitan's granite monolith measures 2,308 meters and constitutes the world's largest continuous granite face—climbers who have been free climbing it since 2017 (Alexander Honnold) are visible to the naked eye from the parking lot.

Walk to Bridalveil Fall (37.7180, -119.6470) from its parking lot - 5 minutes and a 188-meter waterfall in front of you, constant spray in your face within 30 meters. Lower Yosemite Fall (37.7522, -119.5970) takes 30 minutes round trip from the valley parking lot: a 98-meter drop, and in April-May the flow is so strong that the noise can be heard from 500 meters away.

Head up to Glacier Point (37.7283, -119.5733) if the road is open (generally from May to November, depending on snow cover) - at an altitude of 2,199 meters, a sweeping view down over the entire valley with Half Dome at eye level. This viewpoint radically changes your understanding of the canyon: you realize that the valley is an 11-km glacial U-shaped valley carved between two 1,000-meter granite walls.

activities.text: Travel the Yosemite Valley Loop (37.745, -119.594) by free shuttle or car—a 19 km loop through the valley with views of all the peaks. Yosemite is 3.5–4 hours from San Francisco via I-580 and CA-120. Park admission $35/car for 7 days. Arrive before 10 AM or after 3 PM in high season to find parking in the valley.

Cross Tioga Pass (CA-120 East, a pass at 3,031 meters, the highest road pass in California) to reach Lee Vining in the late afternoon. The road is closed in winter - check its status on nps.gov before leaving. A long drive from the valley, with the landscapes of the high Sierra Nevada gradually opening up.

days_plan.itin_title: The American Far West in 10 Days: San Francisco, Yosemite, Bodie, Death Valley, Las Vegas, Grand Canyon

visits.text: You're wandering through one of Appalachia's best-preserved towns: 236 acres of Lewisburg's heart have been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1978, with Federal and Neoclassical houses dating from the late 18th century. The town was founded in 1782 by the Virginia Assembly, on a site occupied since 1751 by settlers near Lewis Spring. During the Civil War, the Battle of Lewisburg on May 23, 1862, saw Union forces under Colonel George Crook repel the Confederates—you can still see graffiti that soldiers from both sides carved into the walls of a building used as a hospital. In 2011, Frommer's Budget Travel named Lewisburg “America's Most Beautiful Small Town”.

You're walking through the door of one of four Carnegie Halls still operating worldwide—there's of course one in New York, but also here, in an Appalachian town of 4,000 residents. Andrew Carnegie funded this neo-Georgian building in 1902 with a donation of $26,750 for the Lewisburg Female Institute, supplemented by $10,000 from the local community. When the college closed in 1972 and the building was at risk of demolition, residents formed an association in 1983 and raised $3 million to save it. Today Carnegie Hall hosts concerts, exhibitions in three free galleries, and art classes year-round.

You're stopping before this gray stone church built in 1796, considered the oldest church building in continuous use west of the Alleghenies. It survived the Civil War because both armies used it in turn as a field hospital. The cemetery surrounding it dates partly from the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812; several officers from George Washington's army rest here. The interior, simple and white, retains its original oak pews. A quick visit is enough to take in its atmosphere of historic tranquility.

activities.text: You're setting out on one of the longest and most beautiful bike trails in Appalachia: 77 kilometers on the former Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad route, almost flat along the Greenbrier River. You cycle between white limestone cliffs, the meanders of the green river, and horse farms that have produced the famous Greenbrier County beef for generations. The river has been renowned for trout fishing since the 19th century. Red brick railroad tunnels pierce the limestone ridges on certain sections.

You're descending into Lost World Caverns just north of Lewisburg and walking through a 500-meter underground gallery whose ceiling, 400 million years old, is covered with colossal stalactites and stalagmites. The showpiece is a 5-meter-tall stalagmite named “Goliath”, one of the largest known specimens in Appalachia. The region sits on a Devonian limestone plateau riddled with underground caverns linked by active aquifer networks—Lost World Caverns is just one window into this system.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

visits.text: The most historic square mile in America, Jimmy Carter said of Lewiston. A somewhat pompous phrase, but not entirely unjustified for this village 15 minutes north of the falls. First European settlement in western New York State in 1720 (a French trading post called Le Magazin Royal), last stop on the Underground Railroad before crossing to Canada, site of the first American battle of the War of 1812. Center Street, the main street, is lined with 19th-century houses, art galleries, and over 30 restaurants along one kilometer.

The Freedom Crossing Monument, on the Niagara River shore, depicts a family of escaped enslaved people guided by an Underground Railroad agent toward the boat that will take them to Canada. Hundreds of people crossed the river here between 1820 and 1860 to escape slavery. Life-size bronze sculpture, explanatory plaques, free access. Moving, without descending into pathos.

The Niagara Power Vista, free admission, is the visitor center for the Robert Moses Power Plant, the largest hydroelectric plant in the Western world when it opened January 28, 1961 (inaugurated by John F. Kennedy from the White House). 50 interactive exhibits explain how Niagara water is diverted through massive underground tunnels before the falls to power 13 turbines—mainly at night, to preserve the daytime spectacle. A view down into the gorge from the observation deck. One hour is enough, ideal for an educational finale.

activities.text: Whirlpool Jet Boat Tours, departing from the Lewiston dock: flat-bottom boats with 600 horsepower that head up the Class V rapids of the lower gorge to the Niagara Whirlpool. A dry option in a covered boat or a wet option—either way, it's an hour of thrills. Season May through October only; not recommended for children under six.

Final dinner on Center Street: the Brickyard Pub & BBQ for walnut-smoked ribs ($15 half portion), or Tin Pan Alley for more refined American cuisine. Both have been featured on Food Network, deservedly so. An after-dinner walk to the Tuscarora Heroes Monument, celebrating the Tuscarora warriors who saved civilian families during the British burning of Lewiston in December 1813. The journey ends on a strong historical note.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Berkshires to Niagara Falls: 10 Days of Waterfalls, Villages, and Wide-Open Spaces

visits.text: Discover the Davidson County Historical Museum, housed in an elegant 19th-century Greek Revival building that provides an excellent opportunity to learn about Lexington's rich history and culture. The museum's fascinating exhibits chronicle the development of this charming Piedmont community through artifacts and historical displays.

Admire the impressive collection of works at the Bob Timberlake Gallery, celebrating one of North Carolina's most beloved artists. The gallery showcases Timberlake's masterful paintings capturing the essence of Southern rural life and the natural beauty of the Carolina landscape.

activities.text: Experience Lexington's lively winery scene, which offers plenty of opportunities to sample excellent local wines. The serene atmosphere at Childress Vineyards provides the perfect setting for tasting award-winning dry white wines while enjoying the beautiful rolling Piedmont countryside that surrounds this celebrated vineyard.

days_plan.itin_title: North Carolina Road Trip: Coast and Blue Ridge Mountains

places.name: Liberal, KS

visits.text: Liberal - Dorothy's Other Kansas Home: This southwestern Kansas town offers another immersive Wizard of Oz experience, competing with Wamego for fans of the beloved story.

Dorothy's House and the Land of Oz - Follow the Yellow Brick Road: Dorothy herself guides you on a whirlwind tour through this attraction, where you meet the Scarecrow, Tin Man, and Cowardly Lion on the magical path to the Wizard.
Dorothy's Farm - Where the Tornado Struck: Tour the recreated Kansas farm, imagining the moment young Dorothy was swept away to the magical Land of Oz.

Oz memorabilia at Land of Oz - The film at the end of the tour: At the end of the tour of Dorothy's House and Land of Oz in Liberal, discover the Wizard of Oz memorabilia room. Among its exhibits is the original model of Dorothy's house used for the tornado scene in the 1939 film.

activities.text: Pancake Race - Liberal's Quirky Tradition: Each Shrove Tuesday, Liberal hosts an international pancake race, competing against Olney, England, in a tradition dating to 1950.

places.name: Lihue, HI

visits.text: Waimea Canyon — Admire the Grand Canyon of the Pacific, a gorge 16 kilometers long and 900 meters deep carved by rivers and erosion over millions of years. This iconic Kauai site reveals red, brown and green rock layers in spectacular cliffs and valleys. Allow a little over an hour's drive from Lihue to the lookouts.

Na Pali Coast — View this roadless coastline's 1,200-meter sea cliffs, hanging valleys, and sea caves from lookouts or boat tours. The 27-kilometer coastline accessible only by helicopter, boat, or the challenging Kalalau Trail showcases pristine wilderness.

Wailua River Kayak — Paddle upstream on the river, through tropical vegetation and past the ruins of the Hawaiian heiau temple, on this 3.2-kilometer kayak trip. Kayakers are not allowed to land at Fern Grotto, a natural amphitheater dripping with ferns: it is visited on the motorboats that leave from the Wailua Marina.

activities.text: Swimming at Hanalei Bay — Relax on this 3-kilometre crescent beach backed by mountains, taro fields and the historic Hanalei Pier. This North Shore bay offers calm swimming in summer and spectacular surf in winter beneath waterfalls tumbling down the cliffs. Allow about an hour's drive from Lihue.

Island hopper flight return — Fly between Hawaiian islands admiring volcanic peaks, coastlines, and valleys from above. Inter-island flights offer unparalleled aerial views of the archipelago's diverse landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Hawaii Trip: Volcanoes and Dream Beaches

visits.text: The Nebraska State Capitol is unlike any other statehouse in America - deliberately so. Architect Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue won a nationwide competition in 1920 with a design that broke entirely from the dome-on-a-drum template of Washington, D.C. Built in four phases from 1922 to 1932 in Indiana limestone at a cost just under $10 million (paid in full at completion), the 122-meter tower was the first state capitol to incorporate a functional skyscraper into its structure. Goodhue said Nebraska's flat landscape demanded altitude and beacon effect; the tower is visible 30 km away. It was the tallest building in Nebraska until Omaha's Woodmen Tower rose in 1969. Inside, sculptor Lee Lawrie's mosaics and Hildreth Meiere's tile floors trace the Procession of Life from fossils to humans. The unicameral legislature that meets here is the only single-chamber state legislature in the United States. Free guided tours run on the hour.

The Historic Haymarket District - eight blocks of 1880-to-1920 wholesale warehouses just west of downtown - was Lincoln's commercial engine when the jobbing trade here reached into South Dakota, Wyoming and Montana. The Lincoln City Council designated it a landmark in 1982; in 1985 it became the first urban warehouse district in the country to join the National Trust for Historic Preservation's Main Street program. The 1927 Lincoln Station, a neoclassical Burlington depot still operating as an Amtrak stop, anchors the west end. The Saturday Farmers Market (May to October) draws 150 vendors and up to 10,000 shoppers. Walk the loading-dock alleys for original ironwork and hand-painted signs from a century of commerce.

The Sunken Gardens in Antelope Park, first planted in 1930, hold up to 30,000 plants across tiered beds that change three times a year - free to enter. A short drive west brings you to Pioneers Park Nature Center, a 270-hectare grassland preserve where bison and elk roam open pastures: a genuine patch of pre-settlement Great Plains on the edge of the state capital. The nature center has hands-on wildlife exhibits; the trail network is free and open year-round. The two together make for a restorative late afternoon before dinner in the Haymarket.

activities.text: The Sheldon Museum of Art on the University of Nebraska campus holds a quietly impressive collection of American art, with particular strength in 20th-century abstraction and Plains-connected artists. Philip Johnson designed the 1963 travertine-and-glass building, worth seeing in its own right. Admission is free. From the Sheldon, a 15-minute walk through campus along the historic Centennial Mall leads back to the Haymarket.

Spend the evening in the Haymarket for dinner - Nebraska's first brewpub, Lazlo's Brewery & Grill (opened 1991), anchors the district, and the streets stay lively past dark. If you're here on a Saturday morning before departing, the Farmers Market is the right moment to stock up on local honey, aged cheese and smoked meats for the Sandhills drive ahead.

days_plan.itin_title: Nebraska Sandhills & Pioneer Trails: From Omaha to the Rockies

visits.text: Lindsborg - More Swedish Than Sweden: Visitors from Scandinavia themselves say this Kansas town feels more authentically Swedish than modern Sweden, thanks to its traditional festivities and architecture.

Coronado Heights - A Castle Overlooking the Prairie: Climb this 300-foot-tall bluff crowned with a castle-like stone shelter for panoramic views across the Kansas landscape that Spanish conquistadors once traversed.

Wild Dala Horses - A Herd of Painted Wooden Creatures: The Swedish Dala horse tradition inspired these colorful sculptures scattered throughout Lindsborg, each painted with unique designs waiting to be discovered.
Hemslöjd Swedish Gift Shop - Take Home a Piece of Sweden: Browse traditional Swedish crafts, including personalized Dala-shaped house signs, at this authentic Scandinavian emporium.

activities.text: Swedish Heritage Walking Tour - Discover Little Sweden: Explore the architecture, shops, and traditions that have made this Kansas town a living tribute to Scandinavian culture.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Tour: Prairies and the Wild West

visits.text: Litchfield Hills - Connecticut's Most Pristine Countryside: Quiet country roads wind through this rural region where small towns seem lifted straight from a painting. The famous Litchfield town green exemplifies New England charm, surrounded by 18th-century homes and historic churches.

Lake Waramaug - A Glacial Jewel Shared by Three Towns: This idyllic lake stretches across Kent, Warren, and New Preston, its shores lined with forests, farms, and a state park offering swimming, hiking, and spectacular fall foliage viewing.

West Cornwall Covered Bridge - The Most Photographed Span in Connecticut: This beloved 1864 covered bridge carries traffic across the Housatonic River in a scene that defines New England's romantic appeal, especially when autumn colors reflect in the waters below.

activities.text: Housatonic River Paddling - Whitewater to Flatwater Adventures: The Housatonic offers paddling for all skill levels, from challenging rapids at Rattlesnake in Falls Village and Bull's Bridge in Kent to gentle flows through Cornwall's meadows and farms.

Eagle Landing State Park - Winter Wildlife: Allow a day trip from Litchfield to visit this riverside park in Haddam, where bald eagles winter from December to early March and fish along the riverbank.

Connecticut Wine Trail Northwest - Tasting in the Hills: Several wineries dot the Litchfield Hills region. Connecticut Valley Winery offers tastings of its wines amid the rolling countryside; plan a trip from Litchfield to get there.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

visits.text: Day 2 - Pleasant option if the sky is clear: Little Island, a park set on 132 concrete tulips above the Hudson, opened in 2021. Artificial hills, amphitheater, river and Downtown views. Free admission, most often no reservation required. Half an hour suffices to circle it.

Day 2 - From Little Island's heights, you can take in the entire Chelsea waterfront: restored piers, the Whitney Museum just to the south, Hudson Yards towers to the north. Summer brings free or inexpensive concerts and shows in the amphitheater; the schedule is posted at the entrance.

activities.text: Possible detour to the Whitney Museum of American Art, 300 m away, for its tiered terraces facing the city, if you still have the energy.
Walk to the High Line's southern entrance at Gansevoort Street: 800 m, about 10 min.

places.name: Little Rock, AR

visits.text: Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site commemorates one of the most documented civil rights crises in American history. In September 1957, nine Black high school students - the Little Rock Nine - arrived at the entrance of this then all-white high school. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus had mobilized the National Guard to block them. After 18 days of standoff, Eisenhower federalized the guard and sent the 101st Airborne Division to escort the nine students to their classrooms on September 25, 1957. Ernest Green, the group's only senior, graduated there on May 27, 1958 - Central High's first Black graduate. The NPS Visitor Center adjoins the building, which still operates as a high school. The museum traces the crisis day by day with archives and testimonies.

The Clinton Presidential Library occupies a cantilevered building over the Arkansas River, designed to suggest a bridge to the future according to its architect. The library covers the Clinton presidency (1993-2001) with archives, the Oval Office reconstructed identically, and exhibitions on the decade's major issues - NAFTA, Kosovo, DOMA, the Lewinsky affair. Allow at least 75 minutes: the Kosovo war archives and original impeachment trial documents are worth pausing over. It's one of the most-visited presidential libraries in the United States.

The River Market District is the pedestrian quarter along the Arkansas River: the covered market, restaurants, and bars concentrate in a few blocks between the bridge and the Clinton Library. It's the ideal place to end the trip - beer on a terrace facing the river, dinner in the district.

activities.text: Big Dam Bridge: at 1,400 meters, it's the longest pedestrian and bicycle bridge built on a dam in the United States. It connects both banks of the Arkansas River and forms part of an 18-mile network of bike paths and pedestrian trails. The view from the bridge's center embraces the entire valley - sunset recommended.

Pinnacle Mountain hike: the granite summit of Pinnacle Mountain State Park rises about 300 meters above the Arkansas River valley, about twenty minutes from downtown Little Rock. The West Summit Trail runs 2.6 km round trip with about 200 meters of elevation gain. The climb is steep on the final section - kids enjoy scrambling on the bare rock at the summit. Panoramic views across Lake Maumelle and the city.

visits.text: Livermore’s Carnegie Library deserves more than a passing glance through the windshield. Built in 1911, this former library houses the Livermore Heritage Guild’s museum and archives. Use the stop to take a look at the building and, if the museum is open, its local collections; check visiting days before leaving San Francisco.

places.name: Lone Pine, CA

visits.text: The road from Yosemite Valley to Lone Pine crosses Tioga Pass, then passes through Mammoth Lakes, a summer ski resort at 2,400 metres on the slopes of the Sierra Nevada, and on to Bishop, a small ranching town in the Long Valley. Take a break in Bishop - it is the last real town before the desert expanses. After Bishop, the road follows the eastern face of the Sierra Nevada all the way to Lone Pine. The change of landscape is striking: pine forests, then bare granite and high desert.

At Lone Pine, stop at the Alabama Hills, a field of orange boulders sculpted into bizarre shapes at the foot of Mount Whitney. These landscapes have served as backdrops for hundreds of Hollywood westerns since the 1920s—from John Ford films to recent television series. Movie Road lets you drive among the most spectacular formations. Look for natural arches that frame the 4,418-meter Mount Whitney in the background.

activities.text: From Lone Pine, take the Whitney Portal Road up to Whitney Portal, about twenty minutes' drive west of town. The road crosses the Alabama Hills, then climbs in hairpin bends above the Owens Valley to the start of the Mount Whitney trail. Up there, a waterfall tumbles down next to the parking lot and a small pine-fringed pond invites a short walk along the stream. On the way back down, stop at the Museum of Western Film History on Lone Pine's main street: it tells the story of the westerns filmed in the nearby hills, with costumes, posters, and film props. Get up early the next morning: at sunrise, the eastern face of the Sierra Nevada and Mount Whitney glow orange above the town.

days_plan.itin_title: California Road Trip: San Francisco, Yosemite & Death Valley

map_keywords: Badwater Basin Death Valley National Park

visits.text: Reach the summit of Lookout Mountain at Rock City Gardens, a remarkable natural park where ancient rock formations, lush gardens, and whimsical stone pathways lead to Lover's Leap overlook with views extending across seven states. The 55-meter suspension bridge provides an exhilarating crossing above forested ravines while caves reveal fairytale scenes tucked into the mountain's mysterious recesses. Towering sandstone cliffs and carefully cultivated gardens create unforgettable vistas.

Descend into the mountain at Ruby Falls, where an underground pathway leads to a spectacular 44-meter waterfall cascading into an ancient limestone cavern. The illuminated cave formations and thundering waters create a subterranean spectacle unlike anything above ground. Guided tours reveal the geological history of this remarkable natural wonder.

activities.text: Visit the dramatically positioned Covenant College, whose Gothic Revival stone buildings rise castle-like from the clifftops with commanding views across Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama. Sunset Rock offers photographers ideal conditions for capturing the Blue Ridge Mountains bathed in golden evening light.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

places.name: Los Angeles Ca

visits.text: Enter Los Angeles via Santa Monica. The pier, built in 1909, extends 460 meters into the Pacific Ocean and hosts an amusement park with a Ferris wheel. This is where Route 66 ends—a sign at the end of the pier marks it. A few steps away, Venice Beach and its boardwalk are unmissable: skaters, musicians, street artists, and bodybuilders at Muscle Beach on the sand create a perpetual spectacle.

The Getty Center perches on a Brentwood hilltop, 110 acres above the city. Designed by architect Richard Meier and opened in 1997 after 13 years of construction at a cost of one billion dollars, the campus is clad with 16,000 tonnes of travertine quarried near Tivoli, Italy. Admission is free—only parking has a fee. The permanent collection spans European paintings from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, including Van Gogh's Irises painted in 1889. The view of Los Angeles from the terraces alone is worth the visit.

Drive up to Griffith Observatory for the best view of the Hollywood Sign. Built in 1935 with funds bequeathed by Griffith Jenkins Griffith, the building sits at 346 meters elevation on the southern slope of Mount Hollywood. Admission is free—only the planetarium charges a fee. The Hollywood Sign facing you dates from 1923—originally built as 'Hollywoodland' to promote a housing development, shortened to 'Hollywood' in 1949. The observatory has served as a backdrop for Rebel Without a Cause with James Dean (1955) and La La Land (2016).

Beverly Hills means Rodeo Drive and its 300 meters of luxury boutiques, but also residential streets lined with villas reflecting a century of Hollywood wealth. An hour's walk from Rodeo Drive to Greystone Mansion Park—an 18-acre estate with a 1928 stone mansion whose gardens are free to visit—gives a good idea of the city's social geography.

activities.text: Stroll along the Hollywood Walk of Fame, the 2.6 kilometers of star-studded sidewalks lining Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street. More than 2,700 stars have been embedded since 1960, each bearing the name of a film, television, music, or circus artist. Grauman's Chinese Theatre, opened in 1927, is where you'll find star hand and footprints set in concrete.

Visit one of the major Hollywood studios offering guided tours. The visit takes you onto active sound stages, outdoor sets, and behind the scenes of film production. Book online in advance—spots are limited and large groups may be turned away at the last minute.

visits.text: If you pass through during opening hours, the Milliken Museum brings Los Banos to life. The photographs and objects on display trace the history of this agricultural town, notably associated with rancher Henry Miller. Check the afternoon hours before stopping; the museum lends itself to a short visit without turning the drive into a full-day outing.

activities.text: You can unpack your picnic at Pacheco Park before crossing Pacheco Pass. This city park is on Pacheco Boulevard, in the same area as the Milliken Museum: an easy stop along your route. Choose a shady spot in hot weather and keep water within reach for the drive to Monterey.

days_plan.itin_title: San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: Los Olivos, the heart of the Santa Ynez Valley: 1,200 inhabitants, five blocks of tasting rooms within walking distance of the center. Alexander Payne filmed several scenes of Sideways here in 2004, and wine tourism has since surged across the valley. Geography explains the rest: Santa Ynez is a large east–west transverse valley on the American Pacific coast—this axis brings cold Pacific air straight inland, allowing Pinot Noir to grow at a latitude where it would have no chance in a north–south valley.

Andrew Murray Vineyards, Los Olivos: the story of their Roasted Slope cuvée deserves telling. In 1993, the nursery delivered Syrah instead of the Viognier they ordered. Andrew Murray and his father decided to keep the plants rather than uproot everything—and it became their flagship cuvée. The most profitable mistake in Santa Barbara County.

Solvang: village founded in 1911 by Danish immigrants, pseudo-Scandinavian architecture (half-timbering, windmills, thatched roofs), bakeries serving real aebleskivers - sweet dough balls cooked in cast iron molds, Danish Christmas tradition. It's kitsch, but sincere: the founding families really built their community modeled on Jutland. Allow 30 minutes, no more.

activities.text: Lunch at Los Olivos Café, 2879 Grand Avenue: this is where Miles and Maya, in Sideways, share a 1961 Château Cheval Blanc in the back room. The scene isn't marked by a plaque—regulars know, tourists search. The cuisine is Californian Mediterranean, decent without being memorable, but the room is worth the trip for film fans.

Tasting at Beckmen Vineyards (2670 Ontiveros Road, Los Olivos): Rhône varieties, biodynamic viticulture since 2006, one of Santa Barbara County's most serious estates. The Purisima Mountain Vineyard (in the hills above Ballard Canyon) produces Grenache and Syrah that are every bit as good as Paso's. Book online.

days_plan.itin_title: California Wine Country in 10 Days: San Francisco to Los Angeles Through the Vineyards

places.name: Loudonville, OH

visits.text: You place your hands on the stone parapet of the overlook and look down: the Clear Fork Gorge plunges 300 feet below your feet over a width of 1,000 feet, carved into sandstone by the meltwater of the Wisconsin glacier 14,000 to 20,000 years ago. The National Park Service designated this gorge a National Natural Landmark in 1967: the giant hemlocks and native white pines carpeting the walls have survived here since the glaciation, protected by a cool microclimate that Ohio's summer heat never reaches. Legend has it that Johnny Appleseed - John Chapman, the itinerant planter who roamed Ohio from 1800 to 1845 - knew this gorge and planted apple trees along the Clear Fork River. Come at dawn to see the bottom-of-gorge mists rise toward the ridges.

You cross Mohican State Park's covered bridge on foot - a wood and steel structure built in 1969 that spans the Clear Fork River at the bottom of the gorge, replacing a suspension footbridge that the Civilian Conservation Corps had built in the 1930s. You stop in the middle of the deck and look downstream: the river flows between sandstone cliffs on which century-old hemlocks cling, the water is so clear you see brown trout swimming among the blocks. Late afternoon light enters through the bridge's two openings and traces two rectangles of golden sun on the wooden planks - the Mohican photo everyone's looking for. Arrive between 4pm and 5pm for the best light.

You arrive in Loudonville and immediately understand why the town boasts of being the 'Canoe Capital of Ohio': Main Street is lined with canoe outfitters competing for customers with hand-painted signs, and the smell of the river permeates the entire downtown. Yet the town of 2,700 has a discreet and endearing historic center - 1890s commercial facades line the brick sidewalks, and the Mohican River flows silently two blocks away. In spring, when white trilliums and bloodroots bloom on the banks, you understand why locals don't want the rest of the world to discover this corner of Ohio. Settle in for the night at one of the lodges or campgrounds in Mohican State Park 5 miles away.

activities.text: You descend into the gorge on a trail rebuilt in 2020 by Mohican Trails Club volunteers along the original Civilian Conservation Corps route from the 1930s. At the bottom, you follow the Clear Fork River on its south bank between dripping sandstone cliffs and century-old hemlocks whose roots grip the walls - the river is so clear you see the pink sandstone bottom through the water. Then you climb back up the north wall on a switchback trail, and emerge at the stone observation terrace: the green river 300 feet below, the opposite cliffs, the hemlock canopy at eye level. Every meter of elevation is worth ten on the descent. Hiking boots required - wet rocks at the gorge bottom don't forgive smooth soles.

You paddle on the Mohican River and enter the Ohio few travelers see: transparent water over a pale pink sandstone bottom, sycamores whose branches meet above you in a vegetal tunnel, great blue herons motionless on gravel banks taking off unhurriedly as you approach. In places you glimpse rainbow trout swimming upstream in the shaded sections. The 8-mile section between Clear Fork and Brinkhaven is the wildest - you'll only encounter local fishermen. Ask your outfitter for the return shuttle rather than backtracking: Mohican Canoe Livery, Loudonville Canoe Livery, and Mohican Adventures all offer this service, shuttle included in the price.

days_plan.itin_title: Interior Ohio Loop - From Columbus to Mohican Gorges

places.name: Louis Armstrong House, NY

visits.text: Day 3 - optional: On an ordinary street in Corona, the Louis Armstrong House preserves the home where Satchmo lived from 1943 until his death in 1971 exactly as it was: a turquoise lacquered kitchen, a bathroom with gold-framed mirrors, an office filled with recording tapes. Guided tours are mandatory, groups are small, and booking is advised. Deeply moving in its simplicity.

Day 3 - optional: Across from Louis Armstrong's house, the Armstrong Center, opened in 2023, displays trumpets, manuscripts, and recordings. The world's most famous musician chose this working-class Queens neighborhood and never moved away: the place tells the story of that loyalty better than any biography.

activities.text: Corona is a Latino stronghold: arepas, tacos, or an Italian ice from the Lemon Ice King of Corona on your way out, a neighborhood institution since the 1940s.
To the Unisphere: 1.7 km, 25 min walking through Corona, or one 7 line stop to Mets-Willets Point, about 15 min.

places.name: Louisville, KY

visits.text: Start at Churchill Downs - and don't just peer through the gates. The track has been operating since 1875, and those twin spires that became Kentucky's symbol were built in 1895. The first Kentucky Derby ran here on May 17, 1875: African American jockey Oliver Lewis won aboard Aristides. The Kentucky Derby Museum on-site shows a 360° screen film that recreates the two-minute race. Off-season access to the grandstands costs $3.

Three stories on the Ohio River tell one life: the Muhammad Ali Center is dedicated to a local kid, born here in Louisville in 1942. It's not just about boxing - the museum dwells on his refusal to join the army in 1967, his civil rights activism, his improvised poetry. You can practice shadow boxing against a projection of the champion. Allow 90 minutes to do it justice.

Outside, a 36-meter, 31-tonne baseball bat leans against the brick façade of the Louisville Slugger Museum & Factory - you can see it from the end of the street. Inside, the production line runs live and you can touch Babe Ruth's bat. More than a third of professional baseball clubs in America still use wood made here.

Old Louisville is the largest Victorian residential district in the United States - 48 blocks of red brick mansions built between 1880 and 1910, larger than San Francisco's. Plan an hour walking around Saint James Court and Central Park: the private gardens are often immaculate and the atmosphere feels worlds away from the busy downtown.

Spend your morning at the Frazier History Museum on Museum Row: it's also the official Welcome Center for the Kentucky Bourbon Trail. Four floors of Kentucky history, thoroughly documented military collections, and a solid introduction to bourbon culture before heading out to distilleries. If you're only visiting one history museum in Louisville, make it this one.

The 21c Museum Hotel, a few blocks away, is a special case: it's a luxury hotel whose lobby and hallways function as a contemporary art museum, open free 24/7. The golden David statue at the entrance, flanked by giant red penguins, sets the tone. Even if you're not staying here, wandering the public spaces is worth half an hour.

Look up as you walk Main Street: the second-largest concentration of cast-iron façades in America after New York's SoHo. These 19th-century arcaded buildings were built for river port warehouses. Each façade has different cast-iron details - flowers, lion heads, columns with capitals. An hour is enough to take it all in.

activities.text: If you're only doing one bourbon tasting in Louisville, do it at Angel's Envy on Whiskey Row. Their whiskey is finished in port wine barrels - slightly fruity, very different from standard bourbon - and the tasting room is one of the most polished downtown. Figure $25 and 90 minutes. Book online.

For dinner, head to NuLu (East Market Street), Louisville's foodie district. If you want to try the Hot Brown - an open-faced roast turkey sandwich with bacon and Mornay sauce invented in 1926 - the Brown Hotel that created it is a 10-minute walk toward downtown. NuLu's craft breweries often have food trucks out in the evening.

Cross the Big Four Bridge early in the morning - a former railroad bridge converted to a pedestrian walkway over the Ohio River. The low-angle light hits the river and Louisville's skyline behind you makes for great photos from mid-span. On the other side, Jeffersonville, Indiana has a few cafés for breakfast.

The Belle of Louisville is a Mississippi-style steamboat still in service, built in 1914 and run by the city. Two-hour public cruises head up the Ohio River. Dinner and jazz cruises run in the evening during the season. Check the schedule at belleoflouisville.org.

days_plan.itin_title: Louisville, Mammoth Cave & Congaree - Caves and Swamps of the Deep South

map_keywords: Main Street Cast Iron Facades Louisville

visits.text: The journey south from the Porcupine Mountains first skirts the forests of the Upper Peninsula, then crosses the invisible boundary into the Lower Peninsula to reach Manistee—a 19th-century town on the banks of the Manistee River, a few hundred meters from Lake Michigan. Its Victorian red-brick commercial blocks have been listed on the National Register of Historic Places; the Riverwalk promenade runs along the old pine timber loading dock that made Manistee one of Michigan's wealthiest cities in the 1880s. Stop for coffee and cherry pie before continuing to Ludington.

Ludington State Park borders the mouth of Hamlin Lake with 4 kilometers of sandy beach along Lake Michigan—one of Michigan's best state parks for swimming and sunsets. The Big Sable Point lighthouse (1867) is accessible via a 5-kilometer trail from the park's north parking lot; its 34-meter-tall black-and-white striped tower is one of Michigan's most photographed. This is your last evening facing Lake Michigan before crossing it tomorrow morning.

The SS Badger dock is a few blocks from downtown Ludington. On the evening you arrive, watch the ferry return to port—125 meters of riveted steel backing into its slip with surprising precision for a 1952 vessel. The pier and loading sheds still have railroad tracks embedded in the lower deck, vestiges of the era when the Badger transported C&O Railway cars from shore to shore.

activities.text: Book your crossing on ssbadger.com if you have not already done so - the ferry has been designated a National Historic Landmark since 2016. The Badger carries up to 620 passengers and 180 cars on a single trip. Arrive at the dock 45 minutes before departure for vehicle boarding: the ferry loads through the stern, and watching your car disappear into the belly of the ship is an experience in itself.

Stearns Park beach, a ten-minute walk from downtown, faces due west over Lake Michigan. In July and August, the sun sets directly on the water—a rare sight on the Great Lakes where the lake's eastern shore offers sunrises over water, not sunsets. Tomorrow morning at 9 am, you'll take the ferry in this same direction, heading to Manitowoc.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Lakes Grand Loop: Chicago, Milwaukee, Door County, Sleeping Bear, Mackinac, Pictured Rocks - 12 Days

places.name: Luray, VA

visits.text: You enter Shenandoah National Park through the Front Royal entrance at milepost 0 and start along one of America's most famous scenic roads: 169 kilometers along the ridge at 35 mph, with 75 overlooks facing the Shenandoah Valley to the west and the Piedmont to the east. The road was built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps, a New Deal program employing thousands of unemployed workers; President Roosevelt inaugurated it in 1936. On this northern section, stop at Hogback Overlook (milepost 21) for a 270° panorama over five counties, and pass through Mary's Rock Tunnel at milepost 32—cut through billion-year-old granite. Set off before 9 a.m. to see deer grazing in the meadows before the midday heat. Allow for a round trip by car from Luray to reach the Front Royal entrance.

You're descending beneath the Shenandoah Valley floor into the largest caverns in the eastern United States, discovered in 1878 by Andrew Campbell and Benton Stebbins. Beneath your feet: a network of galleries carved through limestone over millions of years, adorned with giant stalactites and stalagmites—some reaching 4 meters high. The showpiece is the Stalacpipe Organ, a one-of-a-kind organ built in 1956 whose 37 notes are produced by gentle strikes on stalactites chosen for their resonance across 14 acres of caverns. The caverns maintain a constant temperature of 12°C year-round—bring a cardigan even in midsummer.

You stop at the exact halfway point of Skyline Drive: Big Meadows is the park's largest open meadow—around twenty hectares of pasture at an elevation of 1,070 meters, surrounded by oak and hickory forests. This meadow existed long before the park: mountain families dispossessed in the 1930s to create Shenandoah had grazed their livestock here for generations. Today it is one of the best places in the park to watch white-tailed deer at dusk. The adjacent Byrd Visitor Center recounts the park's human and geological history through permanent exhibits. Allow for a round trip by car from Luray to reach Big Meadows.

activities.text: You climb toward the park's second-highest summit—1,235 meters—along a trail through cliffs of columnar basalt formed by lava flows 570 million years ago. From the summit you take in the entire Shenandoah Valley at a glance, and on clear days the Blue Ridge stretches 100 kilometers to the south. The trail starts at Skyland Resort, the park's oldest site: Stony Man Camp, as it was then known, was already welcoming vacationers from Washington and Baltimore in 1888. Arrive early—the Skyland parking lot is among the first to fill in summer. Allow for a round trip by car from Luray to reach the trailhead at Skyland Resort.

You descend along a 1.4-kilometer round-trip trail to Dark Hollow Falls, which plunge 21 meters over basalt rocks formed 570 million years ago. It is the closest waterfall to a road anywhere in the park, and therefore the busiest—come early in the morning to enjoy the quiet and the light filtering through giant tulip trees. The climb back up is steep but short: around 20 minutes of effort. Wear shoes with treaded soles; the wet rocks near the falls are unforgiving of smooth soles. Allow for a round trip by car from Luray to reach the trail parking lot on Skyline Drive.

days_plan.itin_title: West Virginia Loop - From the Appalachians to New River Gorge

map_keywords: Skyline Drive Front Royal entrance Shenandoah

visits.text: On July 6, 1898, the Mackinac Island city council voted to ban automobiles after a first 'horseless carriage' had terrorized local horses. Michigan made it state law in 1960. You step off the ferry onto Main Street in an intact 1898 Victorian town: horse-drawn carriages, cobblestones, Grand Hotel on its hill with its 201-meter veranda - the world's longest. Plan to take the ferry from Mackinaw City midday after the drive from the Porcupine Mountains - the crossing lasts 20 minutes.

Arch Rock is a natural limestone arch with a 15-meter opening suspended 46 meters above Lake Huron. For the Ojibwa, it was a sacred place where the spirits of the lake came to rest. The trail from Main Street leads there in 20 minutes on foot; if you're on a bike, it's accessible from the ridge path on the east side. Don't expect solitude in July—but the formation remains spectacular.

activities.text: M-185 circles the entire island in 13 kilometers—it's technically a state highway, and the only one in the American network where automobiles have been illegal from the outset. You share it with horse-drawn carriages, horseback riders and other cyclists. The view of the Mackinac Bridge to the south—8 kilometers of suspension bridge opened in 1957—gradually opens up from the west shore. Allow a leisurely 1 hour and 30 minutes, stopping at viewpoints.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Lakes Grand Loop: Chicago, Milwaukee, Door County, Sleeping Bear, Mackinac, Pictured Rocks - 12 Days

places.name: Macon, GA

visits.text: Seventeen thousand years of human habitation. That's what Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park represents—one of the most continuously inhabited places in North America, right on the edge of Macon. The Great Temple Mound, 17 meters tall, was built around 900 CE by Mississippian people. Over 2,000 artifacts dating from 10,000 BCE onward are in the visitor center museum. Thirteen kilometers of trails run through 750 hectares. The Earth Lodge—a partially reconstructed council chamber with an original clay floor from around 1015 CE—is easy to overlook; don't. Free admission, open daily.

In 1969, the Allman Brothers Band signed with Capricorn Records in Macon and rented a Tudor-style house at 2321 Vineville Avenue—several members living communally at a time, from 1970 to 1973. That's the Big House. It's a museum now, every room filled with instruments, costumes, setlists, and recordings from the years that produced “At Fillmore East” and “Eat a Peach.” The unsettling part is that the rooms still look like rooms—kitchen, bedrooms, living room—not like display cases in a gallery. Paid entry.

Perched on Coleman Hill at 934 Georgia Avenue, the Hay House is the most ambitious building in antebellum Georgia—1,670 square meters, 24 rooms, Italian Renaissance Revival style, built between 1855 and 1859 by William Butler Johnston after a three-year European honeymoon. Italian craftsmen brought to Macon did the work. It had hot and cold running water, central heat, gas lighting, a speaking-tube system, and a French elevator—extraordinary for the 1850s. National Historic Landmark since 1974, managed by the Georgia Trust since 1977. Paid entry.

activities.text: The bronze statue of Otis Redding moved in 2025 from Gateway Park to the corner of Cotton Avenue and Cherry Street, in front of the Zelma Redding Amphitheater at the new Otis Redding Center for the Arts. The two-meter figure shows him seated on a dock, guitar in hand—the image of “(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay,” recorded three days before his plane crashed on December 10, 1967. He was 26. Redding had grown up in Macon after his family moved from Dawson, Georgia, when he was five. The Otis Redding Museum at 339 Cotton Avenue, steps away, is free to enter.

Rose Hill Cemetery opened in 1840 on the Ocmulgee River. When the Allman Brothers arrived in Macon in 1969, they adopted it immediately - walked the paths at night, wrote music here, found names for songs in the stones. 'In Memory of Elizabeth Reed' takes its title from a grave they found. Duane Allman died on October 29, 1971, at the corner of Hillcrest and Bartlett. Berry Oakley died one year later, three blocks from the same spot. Both were 24. Gregg Allman joined them in 2017. The three graves are together on Carnation Ridge. Free, open daily.
