visits.text: Hammonasset Beach State Park - Connecticut's Largest Shoreline Park: This pristine 2-mile stretch of protected coastline draws beachgoers to sunbathe on sandy shores, swim in Long Island Sound's gentle surf, and stroll the historic boardwalk. The park's network of walking paths, fishing piers, and wildlife viewing areas remain open year-round.

Meigs Point Nature Center - Where Land Meets Sea: Located on the park's southern end, this facility features a turtle habitat and ten themed gardens showcasing native plant species. The surrounding wetlands and tidal pools provide excellent birdwatching opportunities.

activities.text: Long Island Sound Sunset - Nature's Nightly Masterpiece: The park's western-facing shoreline offers spectacular sunset views across the sound, with colors reflecting off gentle waves as day turns to dusk.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

visits.text: Stroll through Madison's remarkably preserved antebellum district, where grand 19th-century mansions line oak-shaded streets virtually unchanged since the Civil War. Sherman's army famously spared this elegant town during the March to the Sea, preserving architectural treasures including Heritage Hall and the historic Rogers House. Manicured gardens, decorative fountains, and refined Southern storefronts create timeless elegance.

Visit Rose Cottage, built by Adeline Rose after she gained her freedom, offering moving insights into African American history in the antebellum South. The Steffen Thomas Museum showcases bold folk art in striking contrast to the town's refined classical architecture. Antique shops throughout the walkable historic district contain fascinating treasures from centuries past.

activities.text: Experience Madison's genteel Southern hospitality while exploring the town's carefully preserved heritage spanning two centuries of American history. The intimate scale and exceptional preservation make this one of Georgia's most photographically rewarding destinations for lovers of historic architecture.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Olbrich Botanical Gardens - 6.5 hectares of gardens beside Lake Monona. Under its glass pyramid, the Bolz Conservatory houses 750 tropical plants from 550 species and an indoor waterfall. Outside, do not miss the Thai garden and its sala pavilion. Admission to the outdoor gardens is free.

Wisconsin State Capitol - Its white granite dome dominates central Madison, set on an isthmus between lakes Mendota and Monona. Free guided tours. If you are there on a Saturday morning (April-November), the Dane County Farmers' Market circles the entire building - it is the largest producer-only farmers' market in the United States.

State Street and UW Campus - The pedestrian street connects the Capitol to the University of Wisconsin campus. Bookstores, restaurants, cafes, and student atmosphere. At the end, the Memorial Union Terrace on Lake Mendota is where locals drink beer in the evening facing the sunset.

activities.text: Biking Along the Lakes - Madison is one of America's most bike-friendly cities. The Capitol City Trail circles Lake Monona (20 km) on separated paths. Bike-share rentals (B-cycle).

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: Day 2 - The day starts in Chinatown, at the Mahayana Buddhist Temple, set at the foot of the Manhattan Bridge. Past the two golden lions at the entrance, a Buddha nearly 5 m tall sits enthroned amid the scent of incense. Free admission, one dollar to draw a small fortune slip. Ten minutes outside time.

Day 2 - Around the Mahayana temple, Chinatown wakes early: roast ducks in Mott Street windows, stalls selling unfamiliar fruits, traditional herbal shops. It's one of the last corners of Manhattan where you can eat heartily for under $15. Follow the lines of locals rather than the illuminated signs.

activities.text: Morning dim sum in a teahouse on Mott or Bayard Street: carts loaded with steamers, brisk service, a small bill.
Walk to the Tenement Museum: 700 m via Canal Street then Orchard Street, about 9 min through the Lower East Side.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

visits.text: Getty Villa—Explore this spectacular recreation of a 1st-century Roman villa housing J. Paul Getty's collection of Greek and Roman antiquities. The 44,000 works displayed in the peristyle gardens and galleries evoke Herculaneum.

El Matador State Beach — Descend the steep stairs to this wild cove hidden between sculpted cliffs and rock arches. The geological formations create sea caves and natural pools at low tide, a photographer's paradise.

Malibu Pier—Stroll along this historic 230-meter pier built in 1905, a focal point of Malibu's surfing lifestyle. Malibu Farm restaurant serves farm-to-table cuisine while dolphins and sea lions patrol the crystal-clear waters.

Adamson House — Visit this 1929 Spanish-Moorish residence adorned with 3,000 colorful Malibu Potteries ceramic tiles. The artisanal azulejos decorate fountains, stairs and patios of this property listed as a historic monument overlooking Surfrider Beach.

activities.text: Hiking at Solstice Canyon — Explore the shaded trails of this coastal canyon leading to the romantic ruins of the Roberts Ranch House destroyed by fire in 1982. The Tropical Terrace Trail crosses an unexpected tropical oasis with waterfalls and ferns.

Seafood lunch at Nobu Malibu—Savor chef Nobuyuki Matsuhisa's Japanese-Peruvian fusion cuisine on the glass-enclosed terrace directly overlooking the Pacific. The miso black cod is legendary and the people-watching opportunities are unmatched.

Surf session at Surfrider Beach—Learn to surf at this legendary spot with long, consistent waves, the birthplace of modern California surfing in the 1960s. Local schools provide equipment and coach beginners on this beach designated a World Surfing Reserve.

days_plan.itin_title: California Road Trip: Pacific Coast Highway

visits.text: Mammoth Hot Springs looks like a staircase that water keeps rebuilding without consulting visitors. The springs deposit travertine, a type of limestone whose terraces change with the flow of water; some surfaces may be dry while others remain active. Explore the Lower Terraces and look for contrasts around Palette Spring and Liberty Cap. Stay on the boardwalks: a pale crust is never an authorized shortcut.

Before rangers, soldiers protected Yellowstone: Fort Yellowstone gives this history a tangible presence. The Army took charge of the park in 1886 to combat poaching and damage. The red-roofed buildings still serve as offices, housing, and visitor facilities. Follow the outdoor tour route, then check the information at the Albright Visitor Center; working buildings are not freely open to visitors.

activities.text: Head to the Upper Terraces to view Mammoth Hot Springs from above, following open paths. The short Upper Terrace Drive provides access to other formations, including Orange Spring Mound, and lets you alternate stops with walking without repeating the entire lower route. Pay particular attention to the difference between terraces receiving water and dried-out slopes. Check local closures before heading up and bring water: the exposed stretches offer little shade.

days_plan.itin_title: Yellowstone and Grand Teton: 12 Days Among Lakes and Mountain Passes

visits.text: Mammoth Mountain - California's Legendary Ski Destination: This volcanic peak rises to 11,053 feet, receiving an average 400 inches of annual snowfall that fuels one of America's longest ski seasons, often extending into June or July.

Devils Postpile National Monument - Nature's Perfect Geometry: These 60-foot columns of basalt, formed by cooling lava 100,000 years ago, display hexagonal symmetry so precise it appears artificial. The 101-foot Rainbow Falls completes this geological wonderland.

Mammoth Lakes Basin - Alpine Paradise at 9,000 Feet: Five crystal-clear lakes fill glacier-carved bowls beneath towering Sierra peaks, offering swimming, fishing, and hiking amid some of California's most pristine mountain scenery.

activities.text: Mammoth Mountain Gondola - Rise Above the Sierra: Even in summer, the gondola whisks visitors to 11,053 feet for 360-degree views spanning from the White Mountains to Yosemite's high country.

Hot Creek Geological Site - Geothermal Springs Meet Trout Stream: Hot springs bubble up through a creek renowned for fly fishing, creating swirling patterns where cold and hot water mix against a backdrop of jagged peaks.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Mammoth Spring State Park - Where 9 Million Gallons Surge Hourly from the Earth: One of America's largest springs creates an instant river from a 10-acre basin of impossibly blue water. The Mammoth Spring discharges enough crystal-clear flow every day to supply a city of 300,000 people, maintaining a constant 58°F year-round.

Historic Frisco Depot - Gateway to the Ozarks: This restored 1886 railway station recalls the era when Mammoth Spring served as a resort destination for Victorian travelers seeking the spring's legendary waters. The depot now houses exhibits on regional history and railroad heritage.

activities.text: Spring Lake Dam & Spillway - Watch a River Being Born: The spring's outflow creates Spring River, famous for trout fishing. Walk the dam and watch millions of gallons cascade over the spillway every hour, feeding one of the Ozarks' finest cold-water fisheries.

Spring River Water Trail - Float the Ozarks' Clearest Stream: Beginning at the spring's outlet, this designated water trail offers gentle paddling through pristine Ozark scenery, past towering bluffs and through swimming holes.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Manhattan and the Flint Hills - Gateway to America's Last Tallgrass Prairie: This university town serves as the perfect launching point for exploring the vast grasslands that once covered 69 million hectares of North America.

Flint Hills Discovery Center - Interactive Gateway to the Prairie: This state-of-the-art facility immerses visitors in the ecology, history, and culture of the Flint Hills through hands-on exhibits, films, and programming.

Konza Prairie Biological Station - Hike Through Living History: A network of nature trails crisscrosses this 3,500-hectare research prairie, offering intimate encounters with the tallgrass ecosystem that once dominated the continent.

Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve - 11,000 acres of protected prairie: Allow for a day trip from Manhattan. Ranger-led tours and the Southwind Nature Trail take visitors through this remarkable preserve towards bison pastures and scenic overlooks, one of the last places to discover what pioneers encountered when crossing the Great Plains.

Flint Hills National Scenic Byway - 47 miles of prairie splendor: Allow for a day trip from Manhattan. This designated scenic route winds through pastoral landscapes where cattle and cowboys still roam, as they have for more than a century.

activities.text: Council Grove and the Santa Fe Trail - In the footsteps of travelers to the West: Allow for a day trip from Manhattan. In Council Grove, discover the Kaw Mission, a former stone school building, and the historic sites of the Santa Fe Trail to understand the town's role in journeys across the prairie.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Tour: Prairies and the Wild West

visits.text: Turtle Hospital - Founded in 1986, this marine turtle treatment center is entirely dedicated to sea turtles. The guided tour (1 hour 30 minutes) takes you into the surgical rooms and rehabilitation pools. You will see green turtles, loggerheads and hawksbills undergoing treatment. Reservations are required - slots fill up quickly.

Crane Point Hammock - This 25-hectare site protects a hammock forest and houses a natural history museum of the Keys. The trail passes remnants of a late 19th-century Bahamian settlement. Less crowded than the beaches, it offers a good contrast with its natural setting.
Sombrero Beach - One of the few genuine sand beaches in the Keys, complete with palms, picnic areas, and calm water. Free admission. Perfect for a late-day swimming break.

activities.text: Visit Pigeon Key by sightseeing train - This small island beneath the old Seven Mile Bridge served as a base camp for the workers who built the bridge between 1908 and 1912. The wooden barracks have been restored, and a museum traces the history of the Overseas Railroad. The sightseeing train leaves from the Pigeon Key Visitor Center on the Marathon side.

days_plan.itin_title: Florida Keys Road Trip: Key Largo to Key West
South Florida in 8 Days: A Road Trip from Miami to the Keys

visits.text: Marathon - This village of 400 souls in the middle of nowhere is an improbable but charming stop. The Gage Hotel (1927), built by a rancher as a way station, has been tastefully restored: leather furnishings, terracotta floors, a courtyard planted with cacti. Even if you're not staying, grab a drink at the bar or have dinner at the restaurant (Texan and Mexican cuisine).

Gage Gardens - Behind the hotel, stroll through these arid gardens cultivating desert-adapted plants. Roses, herbs, and cacti in a peaceful setting. If you're an early riser, have breakfast here—it's the most pleasant spot in Marathon.

Marathon galleries - Step into the two or three small art galleries exhibiting works inspired by the Big Bend desert. If you're looking for a souvenir, the local crafts (pottery, silver jewelry) are quality and reasonably priced.

activities.text: Stargazing - Marathon sits in one of the darkest spots in the United States. Step outside the hotel after dinner and look up: the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye, shooting stars are frequent. If you have binoculars, bring them.

days_plan.itin_title: Far West Texas Circuit: Big Bend and Ghost Towns

places.name: Marfa, TX

visits.text: The Chinati Foundation, established in 1986 by Donald Judd on 140 hectares of a former military base (Fort D.A. Russell), is one of the world's most distinctive contemporary art sites. The centerpiece: 100 untitled works in mill aluminum (1982-1986), all with identical exterior dimensions (104 × 130 × 183 cm) but each with a unique interior configuration. Judd installed these 100 boxes in two former artillery sheds, which he transformed by replacing garage doors with long gridded glass walls and doubling the buildings' height with arched roofs. Chihuahuan Desert light streams through these windows and constantly shifts the reflections on the aluminum. Allow at minimum 2.5 hours for the full collection - guided tours are recommended.

Prada Marfa is a 2005 installation by the artists Elmgreen & Dragset, set on Route 90 about 56 km by road northwest of Marfa, near the village of Valentine. A fake Prada boutique in the middle of the desert: a real window display of items from the autumn-winter 2005 collection (genuine bags and shoes), but a door that does not open. You can pull over on the roadside at any time - access is free, and the best photo is at sunrise with the empty desert behind.

Downtown Marfa, population 1,700, centers around the Presidio County Courthouse (1886) in red brick, visible from a distance. The Judd Foundation, distinct from Chinati, manages Donald Judd's studios and libraries in former airplane hangars downtown. A guided tour (2 hours) provides access to the artist's working and living spaces - a dive into the methods of a man who refused to separate art from the space where it exists.

activities.text: The Marfa Lights are mysterious lights observed in the plain at the foot of the Chinati Mountains since at least 1883. A purpose-built viewing platform on Route 67, 15 km east of Marfa, lets you watch for them at night. Their origin remains debated - atmospheric refraction, mineral phosphorescence, or other optical phenomena. Arrive after 9pm on a moonless, cloudless night to maximize your chances. Bring a sweater: it gets cold even in summer once the sun goes down.

days_plan.itin_title: Far West Texas Circuit: Big Bend and Ghost Towns
Desert Parks of Texas and New Mexico: Big Bend, Carlsbad, White Sands, and Guadalupe
Desert to Alamo: West Texas & Big Bend - 10 Days from El Paso to San Antonio

visits.text: Your first sight of Yosemite comes at Tunnel View - a viewpoint built in 1932 at the exit of the Wawona Tunnel, bored in 1933 through solid granite with 230 tonnes of dynamite. This is where Ansel Adams immortalised the valley: El Capitan on the left (900 metres of vertical wall), Bridalveil Fall on the right, Half Dome in the background. The viewpoint is about 65 km from Mariposa, a 1-hour drive. Arrive early in the morning - before 8am if possible - to avoid the crowds and enjoy the low-angled light on the granite. Don't leave without walking to the El Capitan meadows to look up at the climbers: from below, they look like tiny dots inching up a wall as smooth as glass. A classic ascent takes between seven and ten days.

The Lower Yosemite Fall loop is the busiest trail in the park, and for good reason: in twenty minutes round trip from the car park, you find yourself at the foot of a waterfall that drops 739 metres in total (upper and lower falls combined). The car park is a little over an hour's drive from Mariposa. The lower fall alone is 98 metres - the equivalent of a 30-storey building. It is at its peak in April-May with the snowmelt; in summer, it can almost disappear. Allow 30 minutes on the trail.

To see Half Dome head-on without leaving the valley, head to Sentinel Bridge, the bridge that crosses the Merced River in the middle of Yosemite Valley. The dome rises at the end of the river and is reflected in the calm water in the late afternoon. Half Dome tops out at 2,693 metres and its northwest faces show a verticality of 93% - making it the sheerest cliff in North America. Native Americans called it Tis-sa-ack, “the split rock”. Continue on foot into Cook's Meadow, the neighbouring meadow, to have it as a backdrop with Yosemite Falls on the other side.

activities.text: Late in the day, return to the Valley Loop Trail for sunset. When golden light strikes El Capitan's granite, the face shifts from grey to orange-pink in minutes. Find a quiet spot in the meadows - it's one of the park's simplest yet most striking spectacles. Bring a torch for the return.

days_plan.itin_title: California National Parks Road Trip: Yosemite, Sequoia, and Death Valley
San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

activities.text: Follow Grizzly Giant Loop among the trunks of Mariposa Grove. The 3.2 km loop passes Grizzly Giant and California Tunnel Tree in a forest with more than 500 mature giant sequoias. Use the shuttle when it is running and check its last departure; when it is out of service, reaching the grove adds a long walk before you even begin the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: Head out to the Black Rocks at the tip of Presque Isle Park: 1.7-billion-year-old basalt cliffs dropping 3 meters into Lake Superior. It's Marquette's unofficial cliff-jumping spot—the water reaches 15–18°C in August. The park is a 131-hectare peninsula with forest trails, a beach, and views of the iron ore docks. Arrive early.

Sugarloaf Mountain is a 45-minute climb from the parking lot. At the summit, 143 meters above Lake Superior, three observation platforms give you 360-degree views of the city, the lake, the ore docks, and the forest. The steep trail up the front or the gentle route around the back—both lead to the same panorama. Free, open year-round.

activities.text: Dead River Falls is 10 minutes from downtown. A half-mile trail follows the river to a series of waterfalls cascading into pools of polished granite. The currents are treacherous—stay on the rocks at the edge. The setting—spruce, moss, dark water—captures the stark beauty of the Upper Peninsula.

days_plan.itin_title: Minneapolis, Voyageurs, Isle Royale & the Upper Peninsula

visits.text: Mashantucket Pequot Museum & Research Center - The Largest Native American Museum in the World: This tribally owned 308,000-square-foot complex brings the story of the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation to life through immersive multisensory experiences. The incredibly realistic Pequot Village recreation transports visitors to pre-contact New England life.

185-Foot Glass and Stone Observation Tower - Views Across Southern New England: Rise above the surrounding landscape for panoramic views of the Connecticut wilderness, wetlands, and coastline stretching to Long Island Sound (reopening early spring 2025 after renovations).

Permanent Galleries and Dioramas - 10,000 Years of History: Two levels situated below ground house extensive exhibits on regional Native American history, from the Ice Age to the present, through films, interactive programs, archival materials, and meticulously crafted dioramas.

activities.text: Connecticut Wine Trail - Sample Award-Winning New England Wines: Thirty-three member wineries spread across the state offer tastings of varietals uniquely influenced by Connecticut's terroir. Saltwater Farm Vineyard near Stonington adds briny coastal notes to its wines, while farms like Bishop's Orchards combine vineyards with markets and bakeries.

days_plan.itin_title: Connecticut Circuit: Maritime Heritage and Ivy League

visits.text: Day 1: McCarthy Road - The 60-mile gravel route from Chitina to McCarthy follows the abandoned Copper River & Northwestern Railway bed, crossing the Kuskulana and Gilahina trestle bridges. This adventurous drive takes approximately 3.5 hours and requires vehicles permitted for unpaved roads, passing through pristine wilderness with views of surrounding glaciers and peaks.

Day 1: McCarthy Historic District - This remote outpost at the end of the road was once a bustling supply town for the Kennicott copper mines. Today the small community maintains its frontier character, accessible only by footbridge across the Kennicott River, with no running water, limited electricity, and a population that swells slightly in summer.

Day 2: Kennicott Mines National Historic Landmark - This remarkably preserved ghost town represents one of the most significant early 20th-century copper mining operations in North America. The fourteen-story concentration mill and surrounding structures cling to the mountainside above the Kennicott Glacier, abandoned in 1938 when ore deposits were exhausted. Ranger-led and private tours explore the industrial complex's haunted red buildings.

Day 2: Root Glacier - A short hike from Kennicott leads to one of Alaska's most accessible glaciers, where visitors can walk onto the ice without technical equipment. The glacier's surface features crevasses, meltwater streams, and ice caves that shift and change throughout the summer season.

activities.text: Day 1: Air Taxi from Chitina - Bush planes offer a scenic 30-minute alternative to the rough road, flying over glaciers, peaks, and abandoned railway infrastructure before landing on the gravel strip near McCarthy. This aerial approach provides stunning perspectives on Wrangell-St. Elias's vast wilderness.

Day 2: Guided Glacier Hiking - Naturalist guides lead excursions onto Root Glacier, providing crampons and instruction for safe travel across the ice. Extended trips venture deeper into the glacier's blue ice formations and seracs.
Day 2: Ice Climbing - The glacier's features provide natural climbing terrain, with professional guides offering instruction for beginners and challenging routes for experienced climbers.

Day 2: Wrangell-St. Elias Scenic Flight - Aerial excursions reveal the staggering scale of the park, with countless glaciers and active volcanoes visible from above. Flights may include glacier landings for an immersive wilderness experience.
Day 2: Nizina River Rafting - Whitewater and scenic float trips explore the wild rivers draining the Wrangell Mountains, passing through canyons and along glacial moraines rarely seen by visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alaska Circuit: National Parks and Glaciers

visits.text: Effigy Mounds National Monument—Iowa's only national monument. Across 1,000 hectares along the Mississippi, 206 Native American mounds are preserved, including 31 shaped like animals: bears and birds, all with their heads pointing downstream. The oldest date to 500 BC. Start at the visitor center, then take the Fire Point Trail (5 km round trip)—it passes the Little Bear Mound and leads to a viewpoint 90 m above the Mississippi. The view is breathtaking.

Pikes Peak State Park—Nothing to do with Colorado's Pikes Peak. This state park offers Iowa's highest overlook above the Mississippi: a 152 m vertical bluff. A boardwalk trail leads to Bridal Veil Falls, a cascade tumbling into a wooded ravine. From the main overlook, you see the confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers—a panorama stretching for several kilometers.

River Bluffs Scenic Byway—This scenic route follows the bluffs above the Mississippi between McGregor and Guttenberg. Views of the river and deciduous forests rank among the Midwest's finest, especially in fall when the maples turn red.

Guttenberg - Plan a round trip from McGregor to this village on the Mississippi, founded by German immigrants who named it after Gutenberg (with a single T, corrected later). The municipal lookout offers an unobstructed view of the river and locks. Walk along the levee - it is peaceful.

Motor Mill Historic Site—Located 15 km west of Guttenberg, this limestone mill dating from 1869 stands beside the Turkey River; allow a day for the round trip from McGregor. Six stories, walls 1 m thick—it is one of the largest stone mills in the Midwest. It was never profitable and closed after only two years of operation. The ruins are photogenic.

activities.text: Late in the day, head down to McGregor—this tiny riverside village has antique shops and cafés lining its streets in 19th-century buildings. The atmosphere feels timeless.
If you're curious, stop at Spook Cave—a cave you tour by boat on an underground river. The entrance is a hole in the bluff just wide enough for the boat. Kitschy but fun.

places.name: Medicine Lodge, KS

visits.text: Gypsum Hills Scenic Byway - Red Rock Country in Kansas: This 42-mile route reveals a landscape of flat mesas, deep canyons, and rust-colored buttes complementing green cedar trees and prairie grasses—scenery that defies Kansas stereotypes.

Carry Nation Home - The Hatchet-Wielding Temperance Leader's Story: In Medicine Lodge, learn about the remarkable woman who smashed law-breaking saloons across Kansas and beyond in her crusade against alcohol.

Lake Coldwater - An oasis in the Red Hills: Allow for a day trip from Medicine Lodge. Cool off by swimming, boating and fishing in this scenic lake, watching for wintering bald eagles, migrating white pelicans and ospreys.
Gyp Hills Guest Ranch - Authentic Ranch Experience: Ride horses across hilly pastures, assist with livestock chores, catch fish, or simply absorb the dramatic Red Hills scenery.

activities.text: Red Hills Photography - Capture Kansas's Hidden Landscape: The rusty tones of the Gypsum Hills create stunning photographic opportunities, especially during golden hour when the rocks seem to glow.

places.name: Medora, ND

visits.text: Drive the 58-kilometer Scenic Loop Road through Theodore Roosevelt National Park's South Unit. The herd of roughly 300 bison often walks straight across the road; wild horses roam the southwestern section; prairie dogs pop up at Skyline Vista. Roosevelt came here in September 1883 to hunt bison and left co-owning the Maltese Cross Ranch. He came back after devastating personal loss in 1884, and it was riding alone through these formations that his grief turned into purpose. The park is the most direct physical evidence of how a place can change a person. Paid entry.

Stop at the Maltese Cross Cabin, just outside the South Unit visitor center. Ranch managers Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield built it during the winter of 1883-84 at Roosevelt's request - a story-and-a-half ponderosa pine log structure with three rooms and wooden floors, considered a “mansion” by badlands standards. After Roosevelt's presidency the cabin was exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair and the 1905 Lewis and Clark Centennial in Portland before ending up on the Bismarck capitol grounds - it didn't arrive at its current location until 1959. Free with park admission; ranger tours in summer.

Cross the river to visit the Chateau de Mores, a 26-room wood-frame house built in 1883 by French aristocrat Antoine de Vallombrosa, the Marquis de Mores. His plan: slaughter cattle in Medora, ship dressed meat east in refrigerated railcars, bypass Chicago, get rich. He bought over 17,800 hectares and named the town after his wife Medora von Hoffman. The whole enterprise collapsed in 1886 - overgrazing, falling beef prices, and the brutal winter of 1886-87 killed it. The original furnishings survive intact. Paid entry; open May-September.

activities.text: Hike the Wind Canyon Trail - a short, steep 650-meter out-and-back from the Scenic Loop Road that puts you on a sandstone promontory above a bend in the Little Missouri River. The view is one of the best in the park: badland formations in every direction, the river cutting a green corridor through pale rock, and usually complete silence. Do it early morning before the heat builds; the wind at the top is usually strong enough to explain the name.

Drive 11 kilometers east on I-94 to the Painted Canyon Visitor Center overlook at exit 32. It's the first real view most people get of the North Dakota badlands - the canyon drops away in layers of red, gray, and cream banded rock with no warning from the flat prairie above. The overlook is accessible day and night; the visitor center is seasonal. Free access. Use this stop to grasp the scale before heading into the park itself.

visits.text: Copper Falls - The tea-colored water of the Bad River (stained by tannins, not copper) plunges 9 meters down 1.2-billion-year-old black lava. The falls twist through several tiers in a canyon so narrow the walls rise 20-30 meters on either side. Wooden walkways and stone stairs bring you up close.

Brownstone Falls - Just downstream, the Tyler Forks River joins the Bad River by plunging 12 meters over a red lava shelf. This is often the most photogenic of the two falls, especially after rain when the flow explodes.

Devil's Gate - Further down the gorge, this massive rock formation creates a natural gateway over the river. Stone stairs (built by the CCC in the 1930s) descend to the water's edge. The place is impressive in its scale.
Observation Tower - At the end of the CCC trail, this tower offers views across the forested hills of the Penokee Range to the north and, on clear days, Lake Superior on the horizon.

activities.text: Doughboy's Nature Trail - This 2.7 km loop around the gorges is the heart of the park. Budget 2 hours if you take your time at the six viewpoints. The trail is named for the WWI veterans who built the first suspension bridges here in 1922. No pets allowed on this trail.
Swimming at Loon Lake - After the hike, head down to the lake for a swim in clear water surrounded by forest. The sandy beach is well-maintained.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

places.name: Memphis, TN

visits.text: At 450 Mulberry Street, the pale turquoise facade of the Lorraine Motel looks nearly unchanged since April 4, 1968. A wreath hangs on the second-floor balcony outside Room 306 - the spot where Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated while talking to Jesse Jackson below. Walter Bailey had bought and renamed the hotel in 1945 after his wife Loree and the jazz song “Sweet Lorraine”; during segregation it hosted Aretha Franklin, Otis Redding, and Ray Charles, all passing through to record at nearby Stax. The National Civil Rights Museum opened here in 1991 and was overhauled in a $27.5 million renovation in 2013-2014. Budget two and a half hours minimum - the 260-artifact span covers five centuries of civil rights history. Arrive before 10 a.m. on weekdays to beat school groups.

The building at 706 Union Avenue is shockingly small - a converted windshield repair shop that Sam Phillips rented in 1950 for $150 a month. He opened Memphis Recording Service on January 3 that year, ripped out the tin roof, replaced it with acoustic tiles, then spent weeks clapping across every inch of the room to map its echo. That obsession produced the “slapback” reverb on Elvis Presley's July 5, 1954 recording of “That's All Right (Mama).” In March 1951, Jackie Brenston and his Delta Cats recorded “Rocket 88” here - widely considered the first rock 'n' roll single. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 2003, the studio still records at night. Tours run daily; book online - they sell out on weekends. You get to touch the same microphone Elvis used.

Jim Stewart and Estelle Axton - a brother and sister - bought an old movie theater on McLemore Avenue in 1959 and installed their recording equipment. From 1960 to 1974, a string of hits followed that still stop you cold: Otis Redding's 'Try a Little Tenderness', Booker T. & the M.G.'s 'Green Onions', Isaac Hayes' Academy Award-winning 'Theme From Shaft.' Of the 900 singles recorded here, 167 charted in the pop top 100. The original building was razed after Stax went bankrupt in the 1970s; the current museum opened May 2003, rebuilt on the same site, with over 2,000 exhibits including Hayes' gold-trimmed 1972 Cadillac Eldorado. The recreated Studio A alone is worth the trip. Give yourself two hours.

Beale Street was founded in 1841, and by the 1920s it had become the main artery of Black Memphis - barber shops, blues clubs, churches, and a 2,000-seat park auditorium where President Theodore Roosevelt spoke in 1902. W.C. Handy moved here from Clarksdale in 1903 and wrote “Beale Street Blues” in 1916; a young Elvis Presley absorbed the sound by hanging around the clubs in the 1950s. Congress recognized it as the “Home of the Blues” in 1977. Today the three-block entertainment district runs live music every night. Arrive early evening to walk the street before the crowds arrive, then stay for a set at B.B. King's Blues Club or the Rum Boogie Cafe.

activities.text: Every day at 11 a.m., a red carpet unrolls in the Peabody Hotel lobby and five North American Mallards ride the elevator down from their rooftop Duck Palace - a $200,000 marble enclosure with a bronze fountain. The tradition started as a tipsy prank in 1933 when general manager Frank Schutt put live hunting decoys in the lobby fountain after a hunting trip; by 1940, former circus trainer Edward Pembroke had formalized the march and served as Duckmaster for 50 years. The Peabody at 149 Union Avenue has been the social hub of Memphis since 1925. Arrive 20-30 minutes before 11 a.m. to claim a front-row spot along the red carpet.

An evening blues walk starting at Beale and Second, working east through the neon-lit blocks, is the right way to end a Memphis day. Stop at the W.C. Handy statue in Handy Park, then duck into a bar for a live set - cover charges are typically under $10 and bands rotate all night. The street stays open until 5 a.m. on weekends. For the most authentic sound, look for smaller venues away from the main tourist drag; Thursday through Saturday brings the best bands.

places.name: Meridian, MS

visits.text: An incredible concentration of talent for a state of three million inhabitants: Elvis Presley, B.B. King, Faulkner, Eudora Welty, Oprah Winfrey, Tennessee Williams, Robert Johnson, Morgan Freeman—all born in Mississippi. The Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Experience (The MAX) opened in 2018 to tell this story, a 5,700 m² building combining interactive exhibits and live performances. $15, budget two hours.

The Gustav Dentzel carousel turns here in Highland Park, with its original paintings from 1896. Twenty-eight hand-carved animals (horses, giraffe, deer, tiger), with a wooden pavilion built for it in 1909. Designated a National Historic Landmark, restored for $700,000 between 2014 and 2017. Rides $1, open on weekends from May to September.

Completed in 1929 just before the crash, the Threefoot Building rises 16 stories and 57 meters—it was originally Mississippi's tallest building, and remains the tallest in eastern Mississippi today. Polychrome glazed terra-cotta facade (red, orange, green, white) on the first two levels, brick above. Commissioned by the Threefoot family (Jews of German origin, their name anglicized from Dreyfus), wholesalers ruined by the Depression six months later. Empty for decades, restored as a Marriott Tribute hotel in 2021. You can go up to the lobby for coffee; the interior has retained its original woodwork.

activities.text: Mississippi's oldest continuously operating restaurant, Weidmann's opened in 1870—formerly frequented by train travelers (Meridian was a major rail junction). Original mahogany bar, pressed-tin ceilings. Classic Southern cuisine, comfort food, decent wine list. Budget $35-45 per person.

visits.text: A crater that did not come from a volcano: Meteor Crater provides a counterpoint to Sunset Crater, seen earlier. The impact dates back about 50,000 years, and viewing platforms let you appreciate its shape without descending to the bottom. Start with the panoramic view and keep your hat secure when the wind picks up.

Meteor Crater’s Discovery Center & Space Museum connects geology with space exploration. The exhibits cover impacts, meteorites, and the site’s links to Apollo astronaut training. Enjoy this indoor portion before the guided walk and check what your ticket includes to avoid unnecessary purchases.

activities.text: You will follow a guide along a section of Meteor Crater’s rim, provided the tour runs under that day’s conditions. The explanations help you identify evidence of the impact and understand the research conducted at the site. Confirm the departure at the front desk; the program includes neither a full circuit of the crater nor a descent to the bottom.

places.name: Metropolitan Museum, NY

visits.text: Day 4 - The Metropolitan Museum of Art lines up 5,000 years of art: Egyptian Temple of Dendur reassembled stone by stone, armor, Impressionists, entire wings by continent. $30 ticket, free under 12, valid 3 days and including the Cloisters. Target three or four departments, no more.
Day 4 - One tip at the Met: enter on 81st Street rather than by the grand staircase, as the lines are shorter there. It's open late on some evenings until 9 PM; check which days.

activities.text: Break on the Fifth Avenue steps, food truck sandwich in hand: the neighborhood regulars' ritual.
Walk to the Guggenheim: 500 m up Fifth Avenue along the park, about 6 min, on Museum Mile.

places.name: Miami, FL

visits.text: Art Deco Historic District — Stroll Ocean Drive admiring 800+ pastel-hued buildings from the 1920s-1940s representing the world's largest concentration of Art Deco architecture. Streamline Moderne hotels feature terrazzo floors, porthole windows, and geometric facades in pink, turquoise, and yellow.

Vizcaya Museum and Gardens — Explore this Italian Renaissance-style villa built 1914-1922 for industrialist James Deering. The 34-room mansion overlooks Biscayne Bay surrounded by 10 acres of formal European gardens featuring fountains, sculptures, and natural stone grottos.

Wynwood Walls — Discover this outdoor museum showcasing large-scale murals by international street artists on repurposed warehouse walls. The 50+ artworks transformed a warehouse district into Miami's most Instagrammed neighborhood since 2009.

Pérez Art Museum Miami — Visit this striking waterfront museum designed by Herzog & de Meuron featuring contemporary and modern art. The hanging gardens and bay views complement collections focusing on 20th and 21st-century international art.

Blue Spring State Park — Watch manatees from the boardwalk beside the 22 °C spring, where they spend the winter from November to March. During this period, the spring and its run are closed to swimming and other water activities to protect the animals. The 2,600-acre park preserves their habitat amid cypress swamps.

Daytona International Speedway — Tour the World Center of Racing where the Daytona 500 has crowned NASCAR champions since 1959. The 2.5-mile tri-oval banking rises 31 degrees, creating the thrilling high-speed racing that made Daytona legendary.

Daytona Beach — Drive or walk on 37 kilometers of hard-packed sand where cars have raced since 1903. The wide Atlantic beach permits vehicle access while offering swimming, surfing, and iconic fishing pier views.

activities.text: Cuban lunch in Little Havana — Savor authentic ropa vieja and café cubano at family-owned restaurants along Calle Ocho. This vibrant neighborhood pulses with salsa music, cigar shops, and domino parks where Cuban exiles recreate Havana's atmosphere.

South Beach sunset — Relax on white sand beaches backed by Art Deco hotels as the sun sets over the Atlantic. The wide beach draws sunbathers, volleyball players, and people-watchers to America's most famous oceanfront.

Lincoln Road evening stroll — Browse this pedestrian mall designed by Morris Lapidus in 1960, featuring outdoor cafes, boutiques, and Art Deco cinemas. Street performers and al fresco dining create a European boulevard atmosphere under swaying palms.

Fresh citrus at roadside stand — Sample sweet Florida oranges, tangerines, and grapefruit at family-run fruit stands. The state's famous citrus industry offers fresh-squeezed juices and homemade preserves from grove to glass.
Return drive to Miami — Cruise south through Florida's diverse landscapes from Atlantic beaches to inland wetlands. The journey reveals the state's natural beauty and development contrasts.

visits.text: Indiana Dunes National Park - The United States' 61st national park since 2019, it protects 24 km of Lake Michigan shoreline. Its biodiversity is the 7th richest of all National Park Service sites: more than 1,400 plant species and 370 bird species across 6,000 hectares. The dunes formed 11,000 years ago from the retreating Wisconsin glacier.

Indiana Dunes State Park - Plan a round trip by car from Michigan City. Enclosed within the national park, this state park established in 1925 contains the three highest dunes: Mount Tom (58 m), Mount Holden (56 m) and Mount Jackson (54 m). Trail 8, known as the “Three Dune Challenge”, climbs all three in a single route - it is steep, but the view of Lake Michigan from the ridges is expansive.

Mount Baldy - This "wandering" dune advances 1 to 3 meters per year southward, swallowing trees in its path. Summit access is by ranger-guided tour only - check schedules on the park website. From the top, you'll see Chicago's skyline on clear days.

Michigan City Lighthouse - At the end of the Michigan City pier, this 1858 lighthouse guards the harbor entrance. The pier promenade offers an open panorama of the lake. The small Old Lighthouse Museum, in the old lighthouse on shore, traces local maritime history.

activities.text: Swimming and beach time on Lake Michigan - West Beach or Kemil Beach are the most accessible; plan a round trip by car from Michigan City to your chosen beach. The sand is fine and the water is cold (15-20°C in summer), but the view is spectacular. Beware of rip currents - follow the flags and warnings.

Cowles Bog Trail hike - Plan a round trip by car from Michigan City to the trailhead. A 7.5 km loop through marsh, prairie and forest, designated a National Natural Landmark for its plant diversity. You may encounter carnivorous plants (purple pitcher plants) and wild orchids depending on the season.

days_plan.itin_title: Indiana Road Trip: Dunes, Caves, and Cities

visits.text: Middleton Place claims the oldest landscaped gardens in the United States, begun in 1741 by Henry Middleton. The layout follows the principles of André Le Nôtre, the gardener of Versailles, with terraces and two butterfly-wing-shaped Butterfly Lakes dug by enslaved people. Aim for March-April for the azalea bloom and avoid the humid summer heat.

activities.text: Continue to the Middleton Place Stableyards, where blacksmiths, potters and weavers give demonstrations among heritage breeds, including water buffalo. The "Beyond the Fields" program and Eliza's House tell the story of the people enslaved on the plantation. Allow 3 to 4 hours on site; the house museum tour costs extra.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

places.name: Miles, MT

visits.text: You pull up to the Range Riders Museum on the west end of Main Street, built on the site where General Nelson Miles constructed Fort Keogh's Cantonment No. 1 on July 22, 1876, in the immediate aftermath of the Little Bighorn. Founded in 1939 by actual working range riders, the museum now covers 13 buildings and over 3,500 square meters across 5 hectares. The Bert Clark Gun Collection runs to over 400 firearms. Walk the replica frontier street with eleven period shops, and spend time with the L.A. Huffman photography collection - Huffman documented plains life in the 1880s and 1890s with a directness no studio photographer could match. Fee applies; closed Tuesdays.

Stop at the WaterWorks Art Museum, housed in the city's 1910 water pumping station on the Yellowstone River. The brick industrial building was repurposed as a community arts center with rotating exhibitions of regional artists and year-round classes. During the Bucking Horse Sale in May, WaterWorks hosts a Quick Draw competition where artists create and auction a piece in 30 minutes flat. Free admission to the main gallery.

Walk into the Montana Bar on Main Street - one of the best-preserved historic saloon interiors in the state, operating continuously since 1902. The Victorian back bar with carved wood and mirrored glass is exactly the kind of furniture that cattle barons and cowboys drank at in the 1880s, when Miles City was the largest horse market in the world. No museum fee, just the price of a drink.

activities.text: Drive to Pirogue Island State Park on the Yellowstone River north of Miles City and spend an hour by the water. The park occupies an island shaded by cottonwoods in the Yellowstone — ideal for fishing (flathead catfish, walleye), walking along the bank, and watching the current that carried steamboats through here in the 1870s. Miles City was founded in 1877 near the confluence of the Tongue and Yellowstone rivers; General Miles was to control the crossing after Custer's defeat. Free access.

If you're here the third full weekend of May, the World Famous Miles City Bucking Horse Sale fills every hotel within 80 kilometers. Started in 1951 when livestock yard owner Les Boe inherited 35 unruly horses and didn't know what to do with them, the event has grown to nearly 20,000 visitors and an estimated $18-22 million for the local economy. The 75th edition runs May 14-17, 2026, with a PRCA Xtreme Broncs Match (32 riders, $57,000 purse), wild horse races, and a Saturday parade where horse entries outnumber motorized floats. Fee applies for rodeo events.

visits.text: Milledgeville was Georgia's capital for 64 years, from 1804 to 1868, and the Old Governor's Mansion is the building that explains why. Completed in 1839 in the High Greek Revival style—imposing columns, grand proportions—it served as the executive residence for over three decades before Atlanta took over. On November 23, 1864, General Sherman made it his headquarters during the March to the Sea. It's a Smithsonian affiliate now. Guided tours run Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Paid entry.

Three kilometers north of downtown, Andalusia Farm is a modest white farmhouse where Flannery O'Connor lived with her mother from 1951 until she died of lupus on August 3, 1964. She was 39. She wrote most of her stories and both novels here—“A Good Man Is Hard to Find,” “Wise Blood,” “Everything That Rises Must Converge.” Every rural Southern landscape in her fiction begins on this porch. The farm became a National Historic Landmark in 2022; the interpretive center opened in 2023. A peacock named Astor still roams the grounds. Tours Tuesday–Saturday from 10 a.m., suggested donation $7.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Beyond Atlanta: Music, Gardens & the Deep South

places.name: Millinocket, ME

visits.text: Baxter State Park is 209,644 acres of boreal wilderness donated to Maine by Governor Percival Baxter in parcels between 1930 and 1962, each gift bound to a single condition: the land must be kept “forever wild.” No paved roads, no Wi-Fi, no gift shops. At the center rises Mount Katahdin - 5,267 feet, Maine's highest peak, and the northern terminus of the 2,190-mile Appalachian Trail since 1937. Baxter Peak's meaning to the Penobscot people comes through the name: Katahdin means 'the Greatest Mountain.' Every summer, several thousand thru-hikers arrive from Georgia to touch the wooden summit sign. Reserve a Katahdin Trailhead Pass at baxterstatepark.org well in advance.

Sandy Stream Pond lies half an hour's walk from the Roaring Brook Campground car park, itself nearly an hour's drive from Millinocket, the last stretch on a dirt road. The pond ranks among the most reliable moose-watching sites in New England. Moose wade into the shallow pond to feed on aquatic plants - bulls can stand six feet at the shoulder and weigh over 1,400 pounds. The pond offers the classic postcard view: Katahdin reflected in calm water at dawn, a moose in the foreground. The park issues “Moose Passes” for three-hour visits on a first-come, first-served basis from the Togue Pond gatehouse.

The Knife Edge Trail links Baxter Peak to Pamola Peak along a glacial arête - 1.1 miles of narrow ridge with drop-offs on both sides, some sections barely two feet wide. In clear summer weather it is demanding but doable for fit hikers comfortable with exposure. In rain, wind or fog it becomes genuinely dangerous; the park advises turning back immediately if conditions change. The full loop via the Helon Taylor Trail and the Cathedral Trail is over 10 miles and should be started no later than 7 a.m. from Roaring Brook, nearly an hour's drive from Millinocket, the last stretch on a dirt road.

activities.text: The Hunt Trail - the official route to the Appalachian Trail's terminus - starts at Katahdin Stream Campground, nearly an hour's drive from Millinocket, the last stretch on a dirt road, and gains 4,188 feet over 5.2 miles to the summit. It follows Katahdin Stream through spruce forest before emerging above the treeline at around 3,500 feet, where iron rungs bolted into the rock help you up the steepest boulder sections. At the top, the weathered wooden sign marks the end of the trail. In August, you may share the moment with long-distance hikers arriving from Georgia with tears in their eyes.

The Penobscot West Branch runs class V rapids below Ripogenus Dam, about 25 miles north of Millinocket on the Golden Road. Northern Outdoors and New England Outdoor Center both run guided trips on this stretch - considered the most technical commercially rafted whitewater in the Northeast. NEOC's base camp is right in Millinocket, making it practical to book a morning trip before checking in.

places.name: Milwaukee, WI

visits.text: Between 1840 and 1860, thirty-five breweries opened in Milwaukee, fueled by the wave of German immigration seeking the same ingredients here as in Bavaria: grain within reach, cold water, and a thirsty clientele. The Pabst complex is what remains of that empire—16 Victorian red-brick buildings saved at the last moment from demolition, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, converted into apartments, hotels and restaurants. Jacob Best had founded the brewery in 1844; his son-in-law Frederick Pabst, a former steamship captain on the Great Lakes, turned it into the world's largest brewery by the end of the 19th century. The Blue Ribbon Hall on site still serves ice-cold Pabst Blue Ribbons in a setting that's remained unchanged since the brewery's centennial in 1944.

The Milwaukee Art Museum, inaugurated in 2001 with its Santiago Calatrava extension, has become an architectural icon: two white concrete wings open and close like the wings of a seabird twice daily, at noon and at closing. This mechanism—the Burke Brise Soleil—weighs 90 tonnes and covers 200 square meters. But don't overlook the collection either: 30,000 works, including one of the Midwest's finest rooms of works by Georgia O'Keeffe, and remarkably well-documented collections of 19th-century American and European art. The entrance faces Lake Michigan—one of the few American museums located directly on the shore of one of the Great Lakes.

The Third Ward is Milwaukee's converted Victorian warehouse district, wedged between the harbor and downtown. You'll find art galleries, restaurants, and the Milwaukee Public Market—a permanent covered market with local Wisconsin producers. Cream City's red-brick facades are the best preserved in the city here; its characteristic pale yellow brick is made from Menomonee River clay. Stroll in late afternoon: the neighborhood comes alive with beer bar patios and galleries opening their doors for Thursday evening exhibition openings.

activities.text: An hour in Pabst's old executive offices, beer in hand. The guide starts by recounting the bombshell of 1871: the Great Chicago Fire destroys all the city's breweries, and Schlitz urgently ships barrels by steamship from Milwaukee—that's where the slogan “The Beer That Made Milwaukee Famous” comes from. The tour passes through the Blue Ribbon Hall, the VIP reception room, and the old factory infirmary, with vintage advertising films as the soundtrack. To understand Milwaukee, there's no better starting point.

The Milwaukee River runs through downtown alongside 5 kilometers of landscaped riverwalk—kayaking from the Third Ward, you paddle under historic bridges toward Beertown, with views of the facades of converted former warehouses and the patios of craft breweries that have replaced the industrial giants. Lakefront Brewery, founded in 1987 in a former power plant, offers tours on the waterfront. The kayak session lasts about 1 hour and 30 minutes before you paddle back upstream against the gentle current to the starting point.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Lakes Grand Loop: Chicago, Milwaukee, Door County, Sleeping Bear, Mackinac, Pictured Rocks - 12 Days

map_keywords: Best Place at the Pabst Brewery Milwaukee

visits.text: Mill City Museum—Built into the ruins of the Washburn A Mill, once the world's largest flour mill. In 1878, the mill exploded—flour dust is more combustible than gunpowder—killing 18 workers. Rebuilt, it operated until 1965 before a 1991 fire left only the walls standing. The museum, opened in 2003, rises from these ruins: an eight-story glass façade emerges from the charred walls. Go up to the roof for the view over the Mississippi and St. Anthony Falls.

Stone Arch Bridge—This 1883 railroad bridge, with its 23 limestone arches, spans the Mississippi just above the falls. It's the second-oldest bridge still standing over the river. Now reserved for pedestrians and cyclists, it offers the best vantage point of the falls, the mill ruins, and Minneapolis's skyline. Cross it late in the day when the light hits just right.

Guthrie Theater—Even if you're not catching a show, step inside for the building itself. The cantilevered walkway (the Endless Bridge) juts out over the river—the panoramic view from inside is free and open to the public.

Minneapolis Sculpture Garden—You're standing in the largest urban sculpture garden in the United States: 40 artworks spread across 4.5 hectares. Look for Spoonbridge and Cherry, a 16 m spoon crowned with a cherry—it's the classic Minneapolis photo op. Next door, the Walker Art Center showcases contemporary art in a Herzog & de Meuron building. Visit on Thursday evenings or the first Saturday of the month for free admission.
Minneapolis Institute of Art—More than 90,000 works spanning 5,000 years, from Asian art to the Impressionists. Admission is free. Allow at least 90 minutes for the main collections.

Chain of Lakes—Minneapolis has 22 lakes within its city limits. The 21 km loop around Bde Maka Ska, Lake Harriet, and Lake of the Isles is one of the city's most trafficked trails. Stop at the Lake Harriet Bandshell for sunset—in summer, free concerts play here almost nightly.

Minnehaha Falls—Walk down to the base of this 16 m waterfall, the one Longfellow immortalized in The Song of Hiawatha in 1855. A trail follows Minnehaha Creek all the way to the Mississippi. Come in spring when the flow is thunderous. In winter, the falls freeze solid—a spectacle in its own right.

American Swedish Institute—Step through the door of this 33-room Tudor Revival mansion, built in 1908 by a Swedish press magnate. Inside: hand-carved woodwork, Swedish tile stoves, and exhibits on Nordic culture. A modern glass addition houses rotating exhibitions.

Midtown Global Market—Inside a converted 1920s Sears department store, this covered market gathers about 40 stalls serving global cuisines: Somali, Hmong, Mexican, Ethiopian. Minneapolis is home to the largest Somali-American community in the United States—you'll feel it in the diversity of this space.

Glensheen Mansion—This 39-room lakeside mansion was built in 1908 for an iron magnate. The gardens descend to the lake. The house is also known for an unsolved double murder in 1977—guides discuss it during the tour. Allow an hour.

Enger Tower—Climb the steps of this 24 m stone tower on the heights above Duluth. The 360-degree view takes in Lake Superior, the harbor, and the forested hills—it's the best panorama of the city. Bring a picnic for the surrounding park.

activities.text: Wander through North Loop, a former warehouse district transformed into restaurants, breweries, and galleries. It's Minneapolis's liveliest neighborhood after dark. If you're here on a Saturday, the Mill City Farmers Market unfolds beneath the museum's canopy—local producers, street food, and a laid-back vibe.
Push on to Uptown, the bohemian quarter south of the lakes. Vintage shops, independent record stores, and bar patios—you'll find a miniature Portland atmosphere here.

Try a Juicy Lucy—the burger where cheese is sealed inside the beef patty (not on top) is the subject of fierce rivalry between two historic city bars. Be warned: that first bite releases molten cheese hot enough to burn.
Have dinner on Eat Street (Nicollet Avenue)—you'll find Minneapolis's greatest culinary diversity packed into a few blocks: Vietnamese, Ethiopian, Mexican, Thai. Follow your nose.

Before heading back to Minneapolis (2 hours 45 minutes of driving), drive Skyline Parkway, a 40 km scenic road that follows the ridgeline above Duluth. The views of the lake and the city below are spectacular. Plan for photo stops.
The return drive to Minneapolis via I-35 cuts through forests of birch and pine. Stop in Hinckley for the local specialty: giant cinnamon rolls from the historic roadside diner—a Minnesota tradition.

visits.text: Flathead Lake — Follow the shores of Montana's largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi, covering 490 square kilometers. This glacier-carved lake offers cherry orchards, Wild Horse Island, and the Flathead cherry harvest in summer. Allow for a round trip by car during the day from Missoula to reach the lake.

National Bison Range—Watch 350–500 bison roaming 7,600 hectares of Palouse grassland and Mission Valley meadows. Established in 1908, this reserve protects these icons of the American West along with moose, pronghorn, and bighorn sheep. Allow for a round trip by car from Missoula to reach the reserve.

University of Montana campus — Visit this public university founded in 1893 featuring Gothic Revival architecture on 89 hectares. The campus sits in the Missoula Valley surrounded by five mountain ranges.

Smokejumper Visitor Center — Learn about elite firefighters who parachute into remote wildfires at this active smokejumper base. Exhibits explain training, equipment, and the dangerous work protecting Western forests.

activities.text: Downtown Missoula—Explore this vibrant college town featuring breweries, farm-to-table restaurants, and outdoor gear shops. The pedestrian downtown reflects Montana's recreation culture.

Clark Fork River walk — Stroll along riverside trails through Missoula's heart watching fly fishermen cast for trout. The Clark Fork flows through town creating green corridors and recreation opportunities.
Montana craft beer—Sample local brews in Missoula's thriving brewery scene. The city claims more breweries per capita than most American cities, celebrating Montana grains and water.

days_plan.itin_title: Montana Tour: Glacier National Park and Yellowstone

visits.text: Loess Hills Scenic Byway—This scenic route follows the loess hills, geological formations found in only two places on Earth: here in western Iowa, and in China's Yellow River valley. Loess is soil made of dust deposited by the wind at the end of the last ice age, 14,000 to 24,000 years ago. The hills sometimes rise 60 m above the plain—rolling prairie landscapes you won't see anywhere else in the United States.

Preparation Canyon State Park - Plan a round trip from Missouri Valley to this wild park without electricity or running water, tucked away in the loess hills. Its name comes from a religious community that broke away from the Mormons and settled here in the 1850s before dispersing. The trails cross tallgrass prairies and wooded ravines - you will probably have them to yourself.

activities.text: Hiking in Loess Hills State Forest—Allow a day for the round trip from Missouri Valley. Several marked trails cross the forest and prairies. The contrast between the steep slopes on the Missouri River side and the gentle valleys to the east is striking. Bring water—there is no place to replenish your supplies.

days_plan.itin_title: A Different Side of Iowa: From Glacial Lakes to Mississippi Bluffs

places.name: Moab, UT

visits.text: Park Avenue—Right at the park entrance, this first trail immerses you in the atmosphere. Sandstone walls 100 m high line the path like skyscrapers on an avenue—hence the name. The descent is 1.6 km (shuttle or out-and-back). It's quick and gets you into the spirit of the place.

Balanced Rock—You can't miss it from the road. This 3,500-tonne boulder perched on an eroded sandstone pedestal rises to a height of 39 m. Its “little brother,” a similar rock called Chip Off the Old Block, collapsed during the winter of 1975–76. A short 500 m trail circles it.

Windows Section—Three massive arches grouped together: North Window, South Window, and Turret Arch. A 1.6 km trail links all three. Walk through North Window for the framed view of the desert—it's one of Utah's most reproduced images. Just nearby, Double Arch forms two nested arches you can walk beneath. The parking lot is often full after 10 AM—arrive early.

Devils Garden (early morning)—An ambitious day: you combine the rest of Arches with Canyonlands and Dead Horse Point. It is feasible if you leave at dawn, but the pace is demanding—around 2 hours of driving in total between the three sites. At the end of the Arches scenic road, 29 km past the entrance. The main trail leads to Landscape Arch, 1.3 km away, the longest natural arch in North America: an 88 m span, barely 2 m thick at its thinnest point. In 1991, blocks broke away from its base—nobody knows how long it will last. The trail is easy and flat. Along the way, take the two short detours to Pine Tree Arch and Tunnel Arch. Allow time for the drive from Moab to the trailhead, followed by the walk.

Canyonlands - Island in the Sky—45 minutes from Moab, this isolated mesa towers 300 m above a labyrinth of canyons carved by the Colorado and Green Rivers. First stop: Mesa Arch. The short 800 m loop leads to an arch perched at the cliff edge—at sunrise, light reflects off the rock below and the arch glows red and gold. If you go at dawn, arrive 45 minutes before sunrise to get a spot.

Grand View Point—At the end of the Island in the Sky road, a 3 km round-trip trail follows the edge of the plateau. The view extends over hundreds of kilometers of canyons, mesas and buttes. Here you grasp the scale of Canyonlands—the park covers 1,366 km², three times the size of Zion. Below, you can see White Rim Road, a 160 km track winding 300 m beneath you. Plan a round-trip drive from Moab to the trailhead, separate from the hike.

activities.text: Delicate Arch hike—Utah's most famous arch, the one featured on the state license plates. The 5 km out-and-back trail starts at Wolfe Ranch (a ranch dating from 1898) and gains 150 m in elevation over exposed slickrock—no shade, bring at least 2 liters of water per person. At the end, you emerge into a natural rock amphitheater where Delicate Arch stands alone, 16 m tall, with the La Sal Mountains as a backdrop. Leave in late afternoon for the golden light at sunset—it's magical, but bring a headlamp for the return. Along the way, make the short detour to see the Ute petroglyphs near the ranch.

Dead Horse Point State Park - Right beside the entrance to Canyonlands, this state park offers one of Utah's finest viewpoints. Legend says cowboys corralled wild mustangs on the narrow point - unable to find the way out, the horses died of thirst with the Colorado 600 m below. The view looks down on a bend in the river framed by blood-red cliffs. Below, you can see pools of an unreal turquoise blue - evaporation ponds belonging to a potash mine. Go for sunset. Plan a round-trip drive from Moab for this visit.

Back in Moab for the evening, soak up the laid-back vibe of this town of 5,000 that serves as base camp for two national parks. Stroll down Main Street - galleries, bars, and patios buzz all season long.

visits.text: Day 1: Discover Mobile's cosmopolitan soul along Dauphin Street, where wrought-iron balconies and French Quarter-style architecture recall the city's time as capital of French Louisiana. Boutiques overflow with antiques, local art, and quirky curiosities, while the street's name honors the Dauphin, the French crown prince whose flag once flew over these Gulf shores. Pause at shady Bienville Square and intimate Cathedral Square to watch Mobile life unfold.

Day 1: Follow the colorful Oyster Trail past a dozen whimsically painted oyster sculptures scattered through downtown, each transformed by a different artist into a marine-themed masterpiece. Beyond their charm, the sculptures raise awareness about the oyster gardening program that helps restore Mobile Bay's crucial mollusk populations. Download the map to find them all.

Day 1: Seek out Mobile's vibrant street art scene, from the Heart of Mobile mural perfect for selfies to colorful works tucked down alleys and along warehouse walls. The arts district around Wintzell's Oyster House offers particularly rich hunting grounds for photographers. Each mural adds another layer to this city's creative story.

Day 1: Immerse yourself in the sequined, feathered extravaganza of Mardi Gras at the Mobile Carnival Museum, celebrating the city's claim as the original American home of Mardi Gras festivities since 1703. Three floors of galleries showcase impossibly elaborate gowns worn by carnival queens, towering float designs, and the traditions that distinguish Mobile's celebrations from New Orleans' more famous party. The self-guided audio tour brings the magic to life year-round.

Day 1: Savor Gulf Coast cuisine with a view at Dauphin's, perched on the 34th floor of a downtown tower where floor-to-ceiling windows overlook the city, the port and the bay. The Gumbo Z'herb arrives rich with greens, local Conecuh sausage and smoked meats in a bowl that defines comfort food. Pair it with the Power Greens Salad and fresh thyme-scented lemonade for balance.

Day 2: Peek behind the columns of the Condé-Charlotte Museum, an elegant downtown mansion that served first as courthouse and jail before becoming a gracious family home filled with antiques and Southern refinement. Guided tours reveal how Mobile's elite lived during the antebellum era, with formal parlors, ornate furnishings, and gardens offering a window into Gulf Coast gentility.

Day 2: Trace Mobile's layered history at the History Museum of Mobile, where the exhibits range from dollhouse-style miniature rooms to the elaborate tableware from historic Mardi Gras balls. The accessible galleries suit all ages.

Day 2: Enter a world of moss-draped elegance at Historic Oakleigh House, an 1830s Greek Revival masterpiece rising from the heart of the Oakleigh Garden neighborhood. Cotton broker James Roper built this gracious home amid ancient oaks, and hourly tours guide you through rooms preserved with period furniture, family portraits, and stories of Mobile's leading families. The surrounding Washington Square epitomizes Southern charm.

Day 2: Climb aboard the mighty USS Alabama at Battleship Memorial Park, where a WWII-era warship that served in the Pacific now rests as a floating museum. Explore multiple deck levels from the engine room to the bridge, gaining respect for the sailors who lived and fought in these steel corridors. The adjacent USS Drum submarine offers claustrophobic thrills for those brave enough to squeeze through its hatches.

Day 2: Examine military aircraft spanning decades of American air power in the Medal of Honor Aircraft Pavilion, where fighters, bombers, and reconnaissance planes tell stories of aerial combat and technological evolution. Tanks and artillery pieces arrayed outdoors complete this comprehensive tribute to those who served.

activities.text: Day 1: Satisfy your sweet tooth at the Moon Pie store, where the marshmallow-and-chocolate treats beloved as Mardi Gras throws come in every flavor imaginable. These Southern snacks originated in Tennessee but found their spiritual home in Mobile, where catching one flung from a parade float brings pure joy. Stock up on assorted flavors and Moon Pie merchandise.

Day 1: End your day at Wintzell's Oyster House, the legendary original location where Mobile has slurped bivalves since 1938. The Oysters Rockefeller arrive bubbling with spinach and rich butter sauce, while the West Indies Salad showcases sweet Gulf crab in a simple oil-and-vinegar bath that lets the seafood shine. Quirky signs and decades of character cover every surface.

Day 2: Drive through Mobile's historic districts to admire architectural styles spanning centuries, from French Colonial cottages to grand Italianate mansions draped in cast-iron lacework. The Mobile Historic Development Commission maps several driving routes that guide you past the city's best-preserved neighborhoods. Keep your camera ready for columned porticos and flower-filled gardens.

places.name: Mobridge, SD

visits.text: From Mobridge, cross to the other bank of the Missouri and join SD-1806 to reach a quiet bluff overlooking the river. This is where Sitting Bull's remains were reburied in 1953, beneath 20 tonnes of steel and concrete to prevent further disturbance. The bust was sculpted by Korczak Ziolkowski, the same artist who began the Crazy Horse memorial. Beside it stands a monument to Sacagawea, funded by Mobridge schoolchildren in the 1920s. Lewis and Clark met the Arikara people just downstream here on October 8, 1804; Clark noted their earth-lodge villages and cornfields in his journal. Admission is free; the view of the Missouri from the bluff is worthwhile.

visits.text: Day 3 - MoMA brings together modern art from around the world: Van Gogh's The Starry Night, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Monet's Water Lilies, Warhol. Tickets are $28 online ($30 on site), free for children under 16. Start on the 5th floor and work your way down: two hours already provide a very good overview.

Day 3 - MoMA's sculpture garden, Rodin and Picasso between pools, has free access even without a ticket: few visitors know. Friday evening, admission becomes free for New York State residents: big crowds guaranteed, avoid this slot if you're paying full price.

activities.text: If the day is running long, set aside 45 min just for the museum's 5th floor: most of the masterpieces hang there.
To Roosevelt Island and Four Freedoms Park: 2.2 km. Most memorable is the Roosevelt Island Tramway from 59th Street and Second Avenue, at subway fare ($2.90); otherwise F train, about 20 min.

visits.text: The Old Monroe County Courthouse was built in 1903 at a cost that nearly bankrupted Monroe County. Harper Lee watched her father, attorney A.C. Lee, try cases from the balcony upstairs throughout her childhood. When Hollywood came to film To Kill a Mockingbird in 1962, the courtroom was still an active court. Art director Henry Bumstead flew to Monroeville, photographed and measured every detail, and rebuilt the entire room on a California soundstage - winning an Academy Award for it. The exhibits cover Lee's life and her friendship with Capote, who moved next door in 1930 at age six. Paid admission. A stage production of the novel runs in this very courtroom every April and May; tickets at tokillamockingbird.com sell out months in advance.

places.name: Monterey, CA

visits.text: Bixby Creek Bridge is on Highway 1, about 29 km south of Monterey, a 30-minute drive - 714 metres long, 260 metres above the canyon, built in 1932 during the Great Depression with 45,000 sacks of cement carried by hand onto cable-suspended platforms. When it was built, it was the longest concrete arch on the California highway network. Today it is one of the most photographed bridges in the United States. Park in the lot on the north side before the bridge - that is where the classic shot with the ocean in the background comes from. Don't stop on the bridge itself: it has no pavement and traffic is fast.

Point Lobos State Natural Reserve, just south of Carmel, is one of the California coast's richest nature reserves: sea lions, sea otters, cormorants, and underwater waters ranked among the world's most biodiverse. Coastal trails run along wild coves with surprisingly transparent water. Allow at least 1.5 hours for a partial circuit. Come in the morning - parking fills quickly.

Cannery Row in Monterey: the old sardine cannery district, made famous by John Steinbeck's 1945 novel. The factories closed in the 1950s when the sardine schools disappeared, and the buildings were converted into restaurants, galleries, and an aquarium. The Monterey Bay Aquarium, opened in 1984 in the former Hovden Cannery, is one of the world's most important - its open bay directly connected to the ocean is unique.

activities.text: Sunset walk along Monterey's waterfront between Cannery Row and Fisherman's Wharf. Monterey Bay has been a national marine sanctuary since 1992 - otters lounge a few meters from shore and pelicans dive-bomb right in front of you. It's one of the rare places where marine wildlife is this close without needing to take a boat.
