places.name: Montgomery, AL

visits.text: Day 1: Step into the Jazz Age at the Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald Museum, the only museum dedicated to America's most glamorous literary couple, set in the Montgomery home they rented during the 1930s. Letters between Scott and Zelda reveal their passionate, turbulent romance, while Zelda's vibrant paintings showcase talents often overshadowed by her husband's fame. The museum captures both the dazzling promise and tragic unraveling of two bright stars of the Roaring Twenties.

Day 1: Stroll Montgomery's riverfront district, where the Alabama River winds past historic wharves that once bustled with cotton bales bound for Mobile and beyond. The strategic bluff that gave Montgomery its prominence still offers commanding views across the water. Wander up Commerce Street to Court Square Fountain, built on the site of both the city's original water source and, more grimly, its slave market.

Day 1: Prepare your heart for the National Memorial for Peace and Justice, a profound tribute to the thousands of African Americans terrorized and killed by lynching across the American South. As you walk through the memorial, the ground slopes away until 800 weathered steel columns hang overhead, each inscribed with names of victims from a single county, the weight of injustice made physical and inescapable. The memorial's stark beauty offers space for grief, reflection, and reckoning.

Day 1: Continue the emotional journey at the Legacy Museum, housed in a warehouse where enslaved people were once held before auction, now transformed into a searing examination of how slavery's legacy persists. From video testimonies of modern prisoners to holographic figures of enslaved mothers separated from their children, the exhibits draw unflinching connections between past and present injustice. Photography is forbidden, making this an experience to be fully present in and carry with you.

Day 1: Climb Dexter Avenue to the gleaming white dome of the Alabama State Capitol, where the Confederacy was briefly born and where, a century later, Dr. King addressed 25,000 marchers demanding voting rights. The Greek Revival monument offers tours through legislative chambers, the old Supreme Court, and the soaring rotunda. Outside, the Avenue of Flags representing all 50 states surrounds a replica Liberty Bell.

Day 1: Complete your civil rights pilgrimage at Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. served as pastor from 1954 to 1960, just steps from the seat of Alabama's segregationist government. From this pulpit he launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott after Rosa Parks' arrest, and within these walls strategies for nonviolent resistance took shape. Tours reveal the sanctuary, a powerful mural, and the parsonage where King's family lived.

Day 2: Find refuge in art at the Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts, set amid lush green lawns just outside downtown where galleries showcase everything from American masters to shimmering art glass. The colorful children's gallery and activity area make this an ideal family stop, while the outdoor sculpture garden invites contemplation among bronzes and blooms. Free admission and parking remove any barrier to cultural enrichment.

Day 2: Give in to pecan paradise at Priester's, a roadside institution a good half-hour's drive south of Montgomery, where every imaginable pecan creation fills the shelves and display cases. Grab a bag of freshly roasted nuts, a slice of dense pecan pie, or spoonful after spoonful of praline-studded ice cream before settling into a rocking chair on the shaded porch. Just remember that the correct pronunciation is pe-CAHN, not PEE-can, if you want to blend in with the locals.

activities.text: Day 1: Fuel up on smoky, tender ribs at Dreamland BBQ, a Montgomery institution where families pack communal tables to devour platters of pit-smoked meats. Even if you're watching your waistline, the Smokehouse Cobb salad arrives heaped with enough pulled pork to satisfy your BBQ cravings. The sweet-tangy sauce that made Dreamland famous comes bottled to take home.

Day 1: Discover Montgomery's contemporary culinary scene at Central, a sophisticated yet approachable destination in the historic Alley warehouse district. The smoked pork belly with tangy peach chutney bridges traditional and modern Southern cooking, while the iconic wedge salad loaded with bacon, candied pecans, and blue cheese dressing is a meal unto itself. The buzzing room draws everyone from lawmakers to artists.

Day 1: Live your Jazz Age fantasy at the Fitzgerald Museum's Zelda Suite, one of two atmospheric apartments available above the museum through vacation rentals. Fall asleep beneath a portrait of the golden-haired beauty herself, surrounded by reproductions of her paintings and framed love letters to Scott. The 1930s decor feels like visiting a stylish grandmother's home, with spacious living areas and a vintage kitchen.

Day 2: Enjoy a quiet morning exploring the calmer corners of Montgomery before the scenic drive south. The extra time allows for an unhurried browse through the vast gift shop at Priester's, a good half-hour's drive south of Montgomery, where pecan candies, flavored coffees and Southern cookbooks make perfect edible souvenirs. The rocking chairs practically urge you to sit for a while.

places.name: Montrose, CO

visits.text: Drive the 11 km South Rim Road, stopping at each viewpoint - Black Canyon of the Gunnison is not America's largest canyon, but its most terrifyingly vertical. At Warner Point, the walls drop 830 m and the canyon floor is just 12 m wide. The gneiss and schist are 1.7 billion years old - among the oldest rocks exposed at the surface in North America. Plan a round trip by road from Montrose.

Painted Wall, Colorado's tallest cliff, rises 686 m in granite streaked with pink pegmatite veins. You can see it from several viewpoints along South Rim Road - go early in the morning or late in the afternoon: the colors of the streaks change completely with the angle of the sun. Plan a round trip by road from Montrose.

Stop at Chasm View: the canyon's width (330 m) is less than its depth (680 m) - mathematically dizzying. The Gunnison River below drops 43 m per mile, compared with 2.3 m for the Colorado in the Grand Canyon. In calm weather, its roar rises all the way to the rim. Plan a round trip by road from Montrose.

activities.text: Follow the Oak Flat Loop Trail (3 km, moderate), which descends 120 m below the canyon rim through pine forests clinging to the slope. You are inside the canyon without truly descending into it - the views of the walls from below are radically different. Be aware: it is often 10°C warmer in the canyon. Plan a round trip by road from Montrose to the trailhead, followed by the hike on foot.

Black Canyon is designated a Dark Sky Park - stay after sunset if you arrive late in the afternoon. On a moonless night, the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye from the South Rim viewpoints. You probably will not see as many stars anywhere else on the trip. Plan a round trip by road from Montrose.

visits.text: From the terrace of the Monument Valley Visitor Center, shadows define the buttes long before their details become visible. West Mitten, East Mitten, and Merrick Butte form the panorama in a park administered by the Navajo Nation. The location chosen for this stop is in Arizona, although Monument Valley also extends into Utah. Check the terrace's closing time before counting on a late photo session.

activities.text: You will head down the Wildcat Trail to appreciate the scale of the buttes from ground level, instead of viewing them only from the terrace. The trail circles West Mitten and includes sandy stretches that are more tiring on the way back than on the way out. Confirm the accessible route at the visitor center and register your departure as requested by the park. Start early, bring water, and shorten the hike if the heat makes the climb back difficult.

If you want to explore Valley Drive without subjecting your rental car to the dirt road, book a tour with an authorized Navajo guide. The 17-mile loop, approximately 27 km, brings you closer to the buttes and offers a variety of views. Access to additional areas depends on the tour you choose, rather than the entrance ticket alone. Ask for details about the route, included fees, and meeting point; transportation provided by the guide is included in this activity.

visits.text: Day 3 - An optional gem well worth considering: the Morgan Library, banker J.P. Morgan's private library. Three levels of antique bindings, a Gutenberg Bible, and manuscripts by Mozart and Dickens beneath a painted rotunda. An hour is enough and offers a break from the skyscrapers; check which days it is closed before going.

Day 3 - Visiting Morgan's office, hung with red damask, feels like stepping into a scene from a novel: a hidden safe, Renaissance paintings, a monumental fireplace. The Morgan Library also hosts specialized temporary exhibitions, and its café beneath the glass atrium offers a proper, peaceful break.

activities.text: If the place doesn't appeal to you, head straight to Grand Central: an hour saved on a packed day.
Walk to Grand Central Terminal: 500 m up Madison or Park Avenue, about 6 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

places.name: Morris Jumel Mansion, NY

visits.text: Day 4 - An option for history buffs: the Morris-Jumel Mansion, the oldest house in Manhattan (1765), perched on the heights of Washington Heights. Washington set up his headquarters here in 1776; Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote part of Hamilton here. The house is closed for restoration: you can see it from the outside from the surrounding Roger Morris Park, a peaceful garden with very few people.

Day 4 - The cobblestone lane of Sylvan Terrace, below the Morris-Jumel Mansion, is lined with wooden houses from 1882: one of Manhattan's most improbable settings. Bear in mind: this area and the Cloisters are far to the north. Set aside a separate half-day for them if Day 4 is already too full.

activities.text: Photo in Sylvan Terrace, deserted on weekdays: ten identical wooden houses, zero cars, feels like 1900.
Subway to the Cloisters: 3.4 km, A line to 190th Street, about 20 min, then climb through Fort Tryon Park.

visits.text: Mount Magazine State Park - Standing Atop Arkansas's Rooftop: At 2,753 feet, Arkansas's highest peak commands views spanning 50 miles across the Petit Jean River Valley to distant blue ridges. The dual summits-Signal Hill and Mossback Ridge-frame a highland plateau of rare flora, hang-gliding launches, and endless sky.

Cameron Bluff Overlook - The Grandest View in the Natural State: Gaze across a sea of forested ridges from this heart-stopping precipice where the mountain drops away into the void. On clear days, visibility extends to the Boston Mountains of the Ozarks.

activities.text: Hang Gliding Capital of the Mid-South - Soar with Eagles: Consistent thermals rising from the valley floor make Mount Magazine legendary among pilots. Tandem flights offer beginners the chance to experience human flight above spectacular terrain.

Rim Trail System - 15 Miles of Cliff-Edge Adventure: Multiple interconnected paths trace the mountain's dramatic edges, ranging from easy strolls to rugged backcountry routes through boulder fields and communities of rare endemic plants.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Mount Nebo State Park - The Flat-Topped Giant with Endless Views: Rising 1,350 feet above the Arkansas River Valley, this isolated mesa offers rim trails skirting dramatic cliff edges with unobstructed panoramas across the valley to distant mountain ranges. Originally developed as a resort escape in the 1880s, the mountaintop retains its peaceful, time-forgotten atmosphere.

Sunrise Point & Sunset Point - Bookend Your Day with Spectacle: Strategic overlooks on opposite sides of the mesa capture the valley's transformation from dawn's first light to twilight's final glow, as mist rises from the river far below.

activities.text: Bench Road Trail - Walk the Historic Rim: This 3.5-mile path circles the mountain's edge, originally carved as a carriage road for Victorian-era visitors, now offering continuous cliff-edge views and access to rustic CCC-built structures.

Gum Springs Trail - Descend toward the Spring: In Mount Nebo State Park, follow this trail built by the CCC between the waterfall overlook and Gum Springs. Descend the stone steps through the forest and observe the seasonal waterfall along the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Mount Rainier National Park — Paradise — Hike wildflower meadows beneath the 4,392-meter active volcano dominating the Cascade Range. The Paradise area receives 17 meters of average annual snowfall and offers stunning views of Rainier's 26 named glaciers.

Paradise Inn — Visit this 1916 National Historic Landmark built from Alaska cedar with massive exposed beams and stone fireplaces. The rustic mountain lodge exemplifies National Park Service architecture designed to harmonize with natural surroundings.

Nisqually Vista Trail — Walk this 1.2-mile loop offering close views of the Nisqually Glacier descending from Rainier's summit. Interpretive signs explain glacial geology and climate change impacts on these shrinking ice rivers.

Reflection Lakes — Photograph Mount Rainier mirrored in alpine lakes along the Stevens Canyon Road. On calm days, the 4,392-meter peak creates perfect reflections framed by subalpine fir and mountain hemlock.

activities.text: Wildlife watching — Scan meadows for black bears, mountain goats, and marmots while keeping eyes skyward for Clark's nutcrackers and gray jays. The park protects 65 mammal species and 182 bird species.

Visit to the Sunrise viewpoint — This viewpoint in Mount Rainier National Park, at 1,950 meters, offers panoramic views of the Cascade volcanoes. On clear days, Mount Adams, Mount Hood and Mount Baker appear on the horizon. In 2026, Sunrise Road remains closed to cars for the rest of the season; access is limited to pedestrians and cyclists.

Evening campfire program — Attend ranger-led programs explaining Rainier's volcanic history, glacial dynamics, and ecosystem. The evening talks occur in amphitheaters throughout the park during summer months.

places.name: Mount Washington, NH

visits.text: At approximately 1,917 meters, Mount Washington can have very different conditions from the valley. Take in the ridgelines from accessible areas around the summit without continuing onto an exposed trail. The Sherman Adams center and its museum close at the end of the season: check their calendar before counting on their services.

activities.text: Drive up the Mount Washington Auto Road only if its operator confirms that it is open. The toll road reaches the summit via the eastern slope and requires you to descend on the same side. Check vehicle restrictions and the weather before setting out; on the descent, use an appropriate gear rather than continually applying the brakes.

places.name: Mountain View, AR

visits.text: Blanchard Springs Caverns lies 15 miles northwest of Mountain View in the Ozark National Forest - the only cave system managed directly by the U.S. Forest Service. It is called a “living” cave: its calcite formations are still growing. Two levels are open to the public. In 2026, guided tours run from May to October; the Discovery Trail opens after Memorial Day. The Dripstone Trail (about 800 m, 1 hour) takes an elevator 65 meters underground and crosses two vast rooms filled with stalactites, stalagmites and soda straws - including the Cathedral Room, large enough to hold three football fields. The Discovery Trail (1.9 km, 1 hour 30 minutes) is more demanding - 700 steps - and follows galleries carved by the underground river where the first explorers rappelled down through the natural entrance. The cave stays at 58°F year-round: bring a light jacket. Book tickets ahead, as tours often sell out in peak season.

Ozark Folk Center State Park is the only state park in the United States devoted entirely to preserving a regional folk culture. Period-costumed artisans demonstrate skills dating back to the first Ozark settlers: blacksmithing, weaving, pottery, luthiery. Musicians play live fiddle, banjo, and guitar. It's less a museum than a living village - let the artisans engage you, they're there to talk.

activities.text: Live music on Mountain View town square: the town bills itself as the Folk Music Capital of the World, and evenings on the central square make it credible. Circles of local musicians - fiddle, banjo, guitar, upright bass - form spontaneously on public benches from April to October, especially Friday and Saturday nights. Bring a folding chair, settle in, and no one will ask you to leave. It's free and authentic.

Trout fishing on the White River: the river is fed with cold water from releases from Bull Shoals Dam, maintaining trout-friendly temperatures year-round - browns and rainbows. Local fishing guides offer full-day or half-day outings. An Arkansas fishing license is required - available online or at local retailers.

visits.text: Day 2 - Little Italy now consists mainly of Mulberry Street: three blocks of trattorias, garlands, and checkered tablecloths, squeezed between an expanding Chinatown and a rising NoLIta. More stage set than neighborhood, but an espresso at the counter of Ferrara, a pastry shop opened in 1892, sets the record straight.

Day 2 - In September, Mulberry Street becomes the Feast of San Gennaro: eleven days of grilled sausages and processions. The rest of the year, push on to the old St Patrick's Cathedral, two blocks up on Mott Street, in Scorsese's childhood neighborhood. Peaceful courtyard, red brick, no lines.

activities.text: Cannoli to go from Ferrara or Caffè Palermo, to enjoy as you walk.
Walk to SoHo: 700 m via Broome or Spring Street, about 9 min.

visits.text: Tahquamenon Falls - On your way to Munising, make the detour to this 20,000-hectare state park. The Upper Falls are the third most powerful waterfall east of the Mississippi, after Niagara Falls and Cohoes Falls: 60 meters wide, a 15-meter drop, and up to 190,000 liters of water per second at the spring peak. Locals nickname them “Root Beer Falls” because of their amber-brown color - it isn't pollution but cedar tannins leached from the swamps upstream. A 500-meter paved trail leads to the overlook, then 94 steps take you down to the edge of the falls for a close-up view.

Lower Tahquamenon Falls - 6 km downstream, five smaller cascades (5 to 6 meters high) frame an island accessible by a pedestrian footbridge installed in 2022. You can also rent a rowboat to paddle between the falls. The atmosphere is calmer than at the Upper Falls - in summer, people swim in the pools. Longfellow mentioned the Tahquamenon River in his poem “The Song of Hiawatha” (1855).

Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore - Miners Castle - Created in 1966, Pictured Rocks is the very first National Lakeshore in the United States. It stretches for 67 km along Lake Superior. Start at Miners Castle, the park's best-known rock formation - a sandstone turret perched above the lake. It had two turrets until 2006, when one collapsed into the lake from erosion. From the observation platform, you'll see sandstone layers colored by minerals: iron produces red and orange, copper yields blue and green, manganese creates brown.

Miners Beach - A few minutes' drive from Miners Castle, this sandy beach on Lake Superior is the perfect spot for a break. Warning: even in summer, Lake Superior's water rarely exceeds 10-12°C. The beach is long and uncrowded on weekdays - ideal for a peaceful walk along the shore.
Miners Falls - A short 1.2 km forest trail leads to this 12-meter waterfall plunging into a steep-sided hollow. The trail runs through a boreal forest of birch, sugar maple and hemlock.

Munising Falls - On your way back to town, stop at the Munising Falls visitor center, at the junction of Washington Street and Sand Point Road. The trail to this 15-meter waterfall has been closed since a storm washed it out in April 2025, and rebuilding work is not expected to be finished before the end of 2027: the falls cannot be seen until then. The visitor center remains open. Panels tell the site's industrial history: in the 19th century, a blast furnace (the Schoolcraft Blast Furnace) stood here and produced up to 20 tonnes of pig iron a day. Then carry on to the Sand Point beaches, at the end of Sand Point Road, facing Grand Island.

Pictured Rocks Cruise from Munising - This is the best way to see the cliffs: from the water. Operators offer 2- to 3-hour cruises departing from Munising's municipal dock. You'll cruise along 15 km of sandstone cliffs rising 15 to 60 meters above Lake Superior. You'll pass Lovers' Leap, Rainbow Cave, the Battleship Rocks, Grand Portal (an arch that continues to erode), and Spray Falls, a waterfall that drops directly into the lake. The oldest visible rocks here date back one billion years. Book ahead in summer - cruises often sell out.

Grand Sable Dunes - At the eastern end of the park, near Grand Marais and more than an hour's drive from Munising on H-58, these large parabolic dunes slope down to Lake Superior. Formed 4,000 to 6,000 years ago by post-glacial rebound, they offer a landscape very different from the sandstone cliffs. On the beach below, you will find trunks bleached by storms - the “driftwood” of Lake Superior, a reminder of the power of the winter waves (up to 12 meters high).

activities.text: Wildlife Watching on M-123 - On the drive between Paradise and Munising, keep your eyes open. The park harbors black bears, deer, otters, porcupines, and bald eagles. Newberry, the neighboring town, is Michigan's “Moose Capital” - sightings are regularly reported along M-123, especially in wetland areas.

Evening Exploration in Munising - Settle in for the night in this small Upper Peninsula town, gateway to Pictured Rocks. Stroll the lakefront in late afternoon. Light pollution is nearly nonexistent here - if the sky is clear, you'll be treated to a spectacular star show.

Chapel Loop hike (short version) - If you still have energy, carry on to Chapel Falls, a 24-meter waterfall about 5 km from the parking area (one way). This parking area is inside the park, more than half an hour's drive from Munising. The full loop is 16 km and also passes Chapel Rock and Chapel Beach, but you can simply hike out and back to the waterfall. Bring water and snacks - there is nothing along the trail.

Kayaking Along the Cliffs (Weather Permitting) - For total immersion, outfitters offer guided sea kayak tours along the Pictured Rocks cliffs. You enter narrow sea caves and approach the multicolored mineral seeps at water level. Trips run only on calm days - Lake Superior can produce waves exceeding 10 meters, and the water temperature makes any capsize dangerous. Outfitters cancel in high swell conditions.

Glass Bottom Boat Shipwreck Tour - An alternative to the standard cruise: glass-bottom boats let you see shipwrecks beneath Lake Superior's surface. You'll pass over the Bermuda, a wooden schooner built before the Civil War and sunk in 1870, still intact just a few meters below the surface - Lake Superior's cold water (averaging 4°C at depth) dramatically slows decomposition. The tour lasts about 2 hours, also passes the cargo ship Herman H. Hettler (sunk in 1926), a historic lighthouse, and Grand Island.

places.name: Murfreesboro

visits.text: Crater of Diamonds State Park sits on an ancient lamproite volcanic pipe emplaced about 106 million years ago. It's the only place in the world where the public can search for diamonds in their original volcanic source and keep what they find. The 37.5-acre field is plowed regularly to bring stones to the surface. More than 37,000 diamonds have been registered since the State of Arkansas purchased the site in 1972 - the average is two diamonds found per day. The largest ever discovered here is the Uncle Sam, 40.23 carats, found in 1924, now at the Smithsonian. Arrive early in the morning and preferably after rain: rain washes diamonds clean and brings them up in the low-lying areas.

The Ka-Do-Ha Indian Village Museum presents artifacts of the Caddo civilization that occupied this territory since 1000 AD. The site has a small dig area where visitors can search for crystals and arrowheads planted in the ground - fun for kids after a morning of diamond hunting.

Cossatot River State Park Natural Area protects one of the wildest river segments in Arkansas: the Cossatot drops in waterfalls and Class III-IV rapids through sandstone gorges. For non-paddlers, the walk along the banks from the Cossatot Falls picnic area offers a direct view of the falls - impressive even on foot. The river takes its name from a Caddo word meaning 'skull crusher' - an honest description of its waters in flood.

activities.text: Diamond digging in the volcanic field: rent shovel, screen, and bucket at the Diamond Discovery Center entrance, or bring your own gear. Three techniques exist: surface searching (for trained eyes), dry screening (loose soil), and wet screening (most productive, especially in low areas after rain). Raw diamonds have a slightly greasy, metallic luster, different from quartz. If you find something suspect, the center staff will identify and certify it for free. Plan for sun protection - the field is completely exposed.

places.name: Myrtle Beach, SC

visits.text: Experience the vibrant energy of Myrtle Beach, where golden sands stretch for miles along the Atlantic and the famous boardwalk pulses with vacation excitement. The iconic SkyWheel observation wheel provides panoramic views of the coastline, while sunrise paints the sky in cotton-candy hues above the rolling waves. This classic American beach destination delivers sun-soaked fun for visitors of all ages.

Explore Broadway at the Beach, a large entertainment district with waterside attractions, performance venues and a range of places to eat. The complex offers family activities, from aquarium visits to interactive experiences. In the evening, the walkways come alive with arcades and shops.

activities.text: Drive from Myrtle Beach to North Myrtle Beach, birthplace of the Shag dance, where this regional tradition remains alive. The Beach Shaggers National Hall of Fame celebrates its history, while venues around Ocean Drive keep the tradition going. Barefoot Landing offers waterside shops and restaurants. Plan the return drive to Myrtle Beach after your visit.

visits.text: Gillette Castle State Park - A Medieval Fantasy Overlooking the River: Explore the extraordinary 24-room mansion of Connecticut-born actor William Hooker Gillette, with 47 unique doors, each designed by the eccentric performer and made by local craftsmen. This medieval-style stone castle offers superb terrace views of the Connecticut River winding through the valley below. Allow for a round trip by car from Mystic to visit this park.

Mystic Seaport Museum - America's Leading Maritime Museum: Step aboard the country's largest collection of historic vessels, from majestic tall ships to humble tugboats, in this 19-acre living history museum. Working craftsmen demonstrate traditional boat-building techniques in authentic 19th-century buildings recreating a New England coastal village.

Mystic Aquarium - Encounter Ocean Life Up Close: Meet beluga whales, penguins, sea lions, and thousands of marine species in this world-renowned facility dedicated to ocean education and conservation. Interactive exhibits and animal encounters bring the underwater world to life.

Mystic River Bascule Bridge - Engineering Marvel Since 1922: This historic drawbridge rises regularly to allow tall-masted vessels passage along the Mystic River, a spectacle that has defined the town's character for over a century.

activities.text: Downtown Mystic - 80+ Independent Shops and Galleries: Wander the charming downtown district filled with clothing boutiques, artisanal candy stores, art galleries, and waterfront patios offering views of the harbor.

Mystic Pizza - The Setting That Launched a Thousand Pies: This actual pizzeria inspired the 1988 Julia Roberts romantic comedy of the same name. Browse film memorabilia while enjoying the famous pies that put this small town on the Hollywood map.

places.name: Nags Head, NC

visits.text: Go to where it all began. On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright took off from level ground in a 27 mph wind and flew 120 feet in 12 seconds. The fourth flight of the day covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Granite markers pinpoint the exact landing spots. The 18-meter monument atop Big Kill Devil Hill and the museum—with a full-scale replica of the 1903 Flyer—are open year-round. Rangers give talks at fixed times: don't miss them.

The Bodie Island Lighthouse, 7 miles south of Nags Head, has worn its famous horizontal black and white bands since 1872—it's the third built at this location, the second having been dynamited by Confederates in 1861. Its first-order Fresnel lens, supplied by Barbier et Fenestra of Paris in 1871, is one of the few still active on the East Coast. Climb the 214 steps, available from mid-April to Columbus Day.

Jockey's Ridge State Park offers you a view few people get: Roanoke Sound to the west and the Atlantic to the east, at the same time, from the top of the tallest natural dunes on the US East Coast - about 30 meters. These are exactly the conditions that drew the Wright brothers here.

Roanoke Island, 20 minutes from Nags Head, is the place you must see if American history interests you. It was the site of the first English colonization attempt in North America—the colony founded in 1587 vanished mysteriously before 1590, and was never found. The Roanoke Island Festival Park in Manteo recreates the ship Elizabeth II. Budget 90 minutes.

The NC Aquarium on Roanoke Island is quieter and more affordable than big urban aquariums—and its collections hold a surprise for you. Its 285,000-gallon central tank hosts bull sharks and rays. Don't miss the collections on the "Graveyard of the Atlantic"—the dozens of shipwrecks littering these waters for centuries. Plan 90 minutes.

Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge, on Route 12 about thirty minutes' drive south of Nags Head, is a major migratory stopover - more than 365 bird species recorded. The boardwalk trails let you get within a few meters of herons, avocets and diving ducks. In autumn, between September and November, the migrations are particularly spectacular.

activities.text: Jockey's Ridge is the hottest kite flying and hang gliding spot on the East Coast—and you need zero experience to jump. Schools offer introductions from the dunes, the 15 to 25 mph winds and soft sand make this site ideal for a first flight. Kitty Hawk Kites has operated here since 1974. Budget $75 to $100 for 2 hours.

Nags Head's beaches stretch along Route 12, with more than 30 free access points. Just to the south begins Cape Hatteras National Seashore, one of the few wild, undeveloped barrier islands on the East Coast. In the late afternoon, head to the shore of Roanoke Sound for sunset: the reflections on the water are spectacular.

Rent a kayak or stand-up paddleboard to explore Pamlico Sound—the shallow, calm waters are ideal for beginners. Go out early in the morning for wildlife and reflections. Several rental outfits on Route 158, around $25 to $35 for a half day. Avoid summer afternoons when the southeast wind picks up.

The Lost Colony, at Waterside Theatre in Manteo, is the oldest outdoor drama still performed in the United States—created in 1937, it tells the fate of the vanished colonists of 1587 with the bay as backdrop. Book your seats in advance: performances Monday through Saturday in summer season, between $15 and $30. Duration about 2 hours.

Managed by The Nature Conservancy, it is one of the largest maritime forests still standing on the East Coast, with 8 trails through wooded dunes, ponds and marshes, and more than 550 plant species. visits.text: Nantucket, 30 miles offshore from Cape Cod, smells of salt and roses the moment you step off the ferry. Start at the Nantucket Whaling Museum, housed in a former 1847 spermaceti candle factory: its nine galleries present over 1,000 objects, including a 46-foot sperm whale skeleton suspended from the ceiling. Nantucket was the whaling capital of the world until the mid-19th century—the sinking of the Essex, rammed by a sperm whale in 1820, inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick.

Take the bike toward Siasconset, on the island's east side—the Wampanoag name means "near the great whale bone." Its 17th- and 18th-century wooden cottages, former whale-watchers' shelters, are now covered in climbing roses. Sankaty Head Lighthouse (1849), perched on the bluff, dominates the Atlantic. The Sconset Bluff Walk follows the cliffs with direct ocean views.

Main Street Nantucket descends from the hill to the harbor paved with granite slabs—stroll it slowly: 36 blocks designated a National Historic Landmark, including the former homes of 19th-century whaling merchants. At the harbor entrance, Brant Point Lighthouse accompanies you on the return: tradition has it that you toss a coin into the water from the ferry to ensure you'll return to the island.

The Jethro Coffin House, built in 1686, is Nantucket's oldest house—step inside to see what a Colonial timber frame preserved in near-original condition looks like. The Old Mill (1746), a few streets away, is the oldest working windmill in the United States. Both sites are managed by the Nantucket Historical Association.

activities.text: Rent a bike right off the ferry and ride to Siasconset via Milestone Road (7 miles) or via Polpis Road, wilder, along the coastal moors. Sandy paths between the dunes provide access to Surfside, Cisco, or Madaket beaches—budget a full day to properly appreciate several.

Cisco Brewers, just south of downtown, is a brewery-distillery-winery on a former ranch. The open-air campus comes alive with food trucks and weekend concerts—it's where islanders gather late afternoon. Last Nantucket-Hyannis ferry (Hy-Line) around 6pm in high season: check hylinecruises.com.

visits.text: Napa Valley - The World's Most Famous Wine Destination: This 48-kilometer valley produces wines that have triumphed over French competitors in blind tastings, forever changing global perceptions of California viticulture. Over 400 wineries, 95% family-owned, dot the landscape from valley floor to mountain slopes.

Silverado Trail - The Quieter Path Through Wine Country: This scenic alternative to Highway 29 winds past historic estates and boutique producers, offering a more intimate wine country experience away from the crowds.

Oxbow Public Market - Napa's Culinary Heart: This indoor marketplace showcases the region's artisanal food producers, from oyster bars to olive oil specialists, chocolatiers to charcuterie masters, all celebrating Northern California's bounty.

activities.text: Hot Air Balloon Over the Vineyards - Drift Above a Patchwork of Vines: Balloons launched in the morning float silently over mist-shrouded valleys as the sun illuminates thousands of hectares of perfectly aligned grapevines stretching to distant mountain ridges.

Napa Valley Wine Train - Vintage Rails Through Vintage Vines: This restored 1915 Pullman dining car travels 58 kilometers through the heart of wine country, offering multi-course meals paired with local wines as the landscape glides past mahogany-framed windows.

visits.text: Naples Pier — Go to Naples Beach to see the historic pier and the Gulf of Mexico. The pier itself is closed to the public while it is rebuilt: do not plan to walk or fish on it. From the shore, watch the seabirds and the sunset.

Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary — Plan a round trip by car from Naples. Follow a 3.7-kilometer boardwalk through the largest remaining old-growth bald cypress forest, with trees more than 500 years old. This Audubon sanctuary protects wood storks, alligators and the endangered Florida panther.

Fifth Avenue South — Browse upscale boutiques, galleries, and sidewalk cafes in this Mediterranean-style shopping district. Royal palms and flowering plants line the pedestrian-friendly streets of Naples' cultural heart.

Naples Botanical Garden — Explore 170 acres showcasing plants from tropical climates worldwide, including Caribbean, Brazilian, and Asian gardens. Water features, orchid displays, and butterfly gardens create serene landscapes designed by renowned landscape architects.

activities.text: Shell collecting on Sanibel Island — Plan a round trip by car from Naples to look for shells on the island's beaches. Sanibel's east-west orientation helps shells accumulate, including junonias and lion's paws.

Sunset dolphin cruise — Glide through calm Gulf waters watching bottlenose dolphins feed and play during golden hour. Captains navigate to prime viewing spots while explaining marine ecosystems and local history.

Fresh Gulf seafood dinner — Dine on grouper, snapper, and stone crab at waterfront restaurants serving daily catches. Naples' culinary scene combines Florida seafood with sophisticated preparations and Gulf sunset views.

days_plan.itin_title: Florida Road Trip: Everglades and Miami Art Deco

visits.text: Naples - The Paradise Coast Lives Up to Its Name: Sugary white sand, glimmering blue-green water, and spectacular sunsets define this sophisticated Gulf Coast destination.

Naples Botanical Garden - 170 Acres of Global Flora: This world-class garden showcases plant communities from around the world, from Brazilian rainforest to Caribbean islands, across beautifully designed landscapes.

Historic Naples Pier - The Center of Sunsets: Naples' historic pier is closed for reconstruction. To watch the sunset over the Gulf, settle on an open section of beach in Naples; do not plan to walk or fish on the pier.
Fifth Avenue South - Sophisticated Strolling: Naples' premier shopping and dining district features upscale boutiques, galleries, and restaurants along a beautifully landscaped promenade.

activities.text: Access to Everglades City - Gateway to the Ten Thousand Islands: Allow for a round trip from Naples. This nearby outpost offers boat access to the western Everglades, where a maze of mangrove islands shelters manatees, dolphins, and countless bird species.

places.name: Nashville, TN

visits.text: Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum — Explore the history of country music through artifacts, recordings, and exhibits spanning 350,000 square feet. The $37 million facility opened in 2001 houses Elvis's gold Cadillac, Hank Williams's Martin guitar, and Taylor Swift's rhinestone stage outfits.

Ryman Auditorium — Tour the Mother Church of Country Music, an 1892 tabernacle turned concert hall that hosted the Grand Ole Opry from 1943 to 1974. The intimate 2,362-seat venue offers unparalleled acoustics and preserves pews where legends performed.

Broadway Honky Tonks — Experience live music pouring from three-story bars lining lower Broadway. The neon-lit strip features Tootsie's Orchid Lounge, Robert's Western World, and other venues offering free country music from 10am to 3am.

Parthenon in Centennial Park — Marvel at this full-scale replica of the Athens Parthenon built for Tennessee's 1897 Centennial Exposition. The permanent concrete structure houses an art museum and 13-meter statue of Athena Parthenos.

Grand Ole Opry — Attend a performance at country music’s most famous stage, broadcasting live since 1925. The show moved to the Opry House in 1974 but maintains traditions of introducing artists and mail-order sponsorships.

Johnny Cash Museum — Discover the Man in Black's life through the world's largest collection of Cash artifacts. The museum chronicles his musical career, activism, and personal struggles across 18,000 square feet.

Frist Art Museum — Explore rotating exhibitions in this Art Deco former post office built in 1934. The museum presents diverse art from antiquities to contemporary without maintaining a permanent collection.

Tennessee State Capitol — Tour this 1859 Greek Revival building designed by William Strickland who is buried in its walls. The National Historic Landmark sits prominently on a hill above downtown offering city views.

Grand Ole Opry — Explore backstage at this Nashville venue on a guided tour. Walk through the areas used by performers and get close to the stage where country musicians play. This tour complements the show scheduled earlier in the itinerary.

Andrew Jackson's Hermitage — Tour the mansion and plantation of the seventh US president who lived here 1804-1845. The 445-hectare estate preserves Greek Revival architecture, slave quarters, and Jackson's tomb.

Belle Meade Plantation — Explore this antebellum plantation famous for thoroughbred horses and bourbon. The 1853 Greek Revival mansion offers tours explaining Southern plantation life and horse breeding.

activities.text: Hot chicken experience — Taste Nashville's signature dish featuring fried chicken coated in cayenne-laced oil at Prince's Hot Chicken Shack or Hattie B's. The spice levels range from mild to shut-the-cluck-up hot.
Music Row exploration — Drive past recording studios where countless hits were produced on this concentrated strip. RCA Studio B, where Elvis recorded over 200 songs, offers tours.

Live music at the Bluebird Cafe — Catch songwriters performing original material in this intimate 90-seat venue. The listening room launched careers of Garth Brooks and Taylor Swift with its famous writers-in-the-round shows.
Gulch neighborhood — Browse boutiques, murals, and restaurants in this revitalized warehouse district. The trendy neighborhood features Instagram-worthy street art and upscale Southern cuisine.
Pedal tavern tour — Join a party bike cruising Nashville streets while sampling local beers. The 15-passenger cycles powered by pedaling passengers create rolling happy hours.
Final Nashville evening — Return to Broadway for last night of honky-tonk music and people-watching. The street comes alive after dark with boot-scootin' crowds and live bands.
Farewell Southern dinner — Celebrate with meat-and-three, fried catfish, or hot chicken one last time. Tennessee cuisine embodies Southern comfort food traditions.

visits.text: Unmatched in the South, Natchez is perched on a 60-meter bluff above the Mississippi—600 designated historic antebellum properties, more than any other American city. Why here? Before the Civil War, Natchez had more millionaires (in pre-1860 dollars) per capita than any city in the country except New York. The city surrendered without a fight in 1862, which explains why nothing was destroyed. Walk along the bluff at sunset, with views stretching 50 km. Free.

You'll find the South's strangest mansion on the southeast outskirts: Longwood—octagonal, a 27-meter Oriental dome, six stories. Construction began in 1860 under planter Haller Nutt, but the Northern workers (all abolitionists) fled when war was declared in 1861, abandoning tools and materials inside the house. Only the ground floor was finished. The upper five floors have remained unfinished for 165 years—tools, ladders, and wood shavings exactly as in 1861. Guided tours only, $30, budget 75 minutes. Unsettling.

At the opposite extreme, Stanton Hall downtown is the most opulent antebellum mansion still intact—completed in 1857 by merchant Frederick Stanton at a cost of $83,000 ($3 million today). Drawing rooms with six-meter ceilings, Bohemian crystal chandeliers, French mirrors ordered directly from Paris. The furniture is largely original. $25, one-hour guided tour.

Deliberately understated, Forks of the Road, 2 km northeast of downtown, was a slave market—its activity peaked in 1820–1860, with tens of thousands of people sold here. Today it is an empty plot with a few interpretive panels and a simple memorial. The decision to avoid spectacle is explicitly upheld. An essential place to understand the darker side of the antebellum wealth admired elsewhere in town. Free, accessible 24 hours a day.

Rare testimony of a free African American life in the antebellum South, the William Johnson House preserves the home of "the Barber of Natchez"—a freed Black man, who became a property owner and himself an enslaver, murdered in 1851. His journal kept for 16 years (2,000 pages) is one of the few such writings to survive. Federal site managed by the National Park Service, free admission.

Managed by federal rangers, Melrose Estate is the flagship unit of Natchez National Historical Park—and what makes it unique is that the rangers give as much weight to the history of enslaved people as to that of the owners. A 33-hectare estate, an 1845 Greek Revival mansion, and six original slave cabins preserved and studied. The McMurran family owned 25 enslaved people at the estate, 700 across their five Louisiana plantations—the rangers hide nothing. Free guided tour, 1.5 hours, reserve at the Visitor Center.

An engineering masterpiece of the early 19th century, Auburn House's central hall spiral staircase is built without a central support—copied throughout the South afterward. First known example of Greek Revival architecture in Mississippi (1812), located in Duncan Park. Estate donated to the city in 1911, public park open 24/7 around the house. Interior tour $15.

On Homochitto Street, Dunleith Historic Inn is one of the few mansions with 26 Corinthian columns on four sides—visible in "Showboat" (1951) and "Beauty Queen" (2001). Built in 1856 by Charles Dahlgren, brother of the inventor of the Dahlgren cannon used during the Civil War. Today a luxury hotel (rooms $250-400), but interior tours $25 for non-guests, by reservation.

activities.text: Sunset nearly mandatory at Magnolia Grill, beneath the bluff at river level—wooden deck facing the Mississippi, river fish (fried catfish), gumbo, crawfish étouffée. $30-40 per person. For something less touristy, Magnolia Sushi & Grill serves surprisingly well-executed Vietnamese-Southern fusion.

At twilight, walk along Broadway Street atop the bluff—benches, cast-iron lampposts, views down onto barges passing on the Mississippi. The historic “Under the Hill” below (the former district of saloons, prostitution, and brawls during the steamboat golden age, 1830–1860) is quiet today: three bars remain.

You see the city from the river, as in the steamboat era—a paddlewheel boat cruise from Natchez Landing, two hours for $35 (Riverside Magnolia, local operator). The historical commentary during the cruise is honest about the city's economic underside (cotton trade and slavery). In summer, sunset departures.

Natchez's oldest standing building, opened in 1789: King's Tavern built from recycled steamboat wood, low ceilings, period fireplaces. Also Mississippi's oldest restaurant. Current cuisine: wood-fired pizzas, salads, wines by the glass. Budget $40-50 per person. Reservations recommended.

places.name: Natchitoches, LA

visits.text: Learn the pronunciation before arriving; locals will correct you otherwise: “NACK-uh-tish”. Natchitoches is the oldest city founded by the French in Louisiana—1714, four years before New Orleans. The historic downtown along the Cane River (actually a former bend of the Red River, now a lake) has 33 blocks of Creole, Spanish, and antebellum houses. Paved Front Street runs along the river for 1 km: wrought iron on the balconies, old lampposts, terraces. This is where “Steel Magnolias” was filmed in 1989 (Julia Roberts, Sally Field, Dolly Parton, Shirley MacLaine), and the town still lives off it.

Exact reconstruction of the 1716 French fort on its original site, Fort St. Jean Baptiste stands on the riverbank—cypress-post palisade, barracks, chapel, powder magazine. Costumed demonstrations on weekends, you learn that the garrison never exceeded 30 soldiers and they survived through trade with the Caddo and Natchitoches peoples. $4, Wednesday-Sunday.

What the Cane River Creole National Historical Park preserves is unique in the world—two Creole plantations 15 km south on Cane River Road: Oakland (1818) and Magnolia (1830). The term “Creole” takes its technical meaning here: descendants of French colonists and their enslaved Africans, forming a free, property-owning caste before the Civil War. Magnolia has 21 original outbuildings, including the only intact mule-powered cotton press in the United States. Free admission, parking at both sites, budget three hours.

Marie Thérèse Coincoin (1742–1816), an enslaved woman born in Natchitoches, freed in 1778 by her French partner Claude Thomas Pierre Metoyer and the mother of ten children, became a landowner and slaveholder. The 911-hectare land grant that would become Melrose Plantation was awarded in 1796 to her son Louis Metoyer, who built the Big House there. The Metoyer family, together with other freed people, formed the Isle Brevelle community; they were the country's wealthiest free family of color in the 19th century. Cook Clementine Hunter, born here around 1887, became a major painter of American naïve art in the 1950s without ever learning to read. Guided tour $12, 30 km south.

activities.text: Taste Natchitoches meat pies, the city's official specialty since 1967 (proclaimed by the Louisiana legislature)—fried turnover stuffed with spiced beef and pork, sold at Lasyone's Restaurant on Second Street since 1967. $4 each, $8 with sides. Texture between a samosa and empanada, family recipe never published.

If you visit between the Saturday before Thanksgiving and January 6, you will encounter the “Christmas Festival of Lights”—300,000 bulbs illuminating the historic downtown, one of the oldest year-end light displays in the United States, begun in 1927. Outside the season, dinner on the terrace at Mama's Oyster House on Front Street facing the river: gumbo, jambalaya, and fried-oyster po-boys, $30–40 per person.

places.name: Natural History Museum, NY

visits.text: Day 4 - A suspended 28 m blue whale, T. rex skeletons, century-old dioramas: the American Museum of Natural History enchants visitors of all ages. Admission is around $28 for nonresidents. The recent Gilder Center and its organic architecture in sculpted stone are worth a look in their own right.

Day 4 - Let's be honest: you don't seriously visit both the Museum and the Met the same day. Choose by taste, dinosaurs or fine arts, and give three hours to the winner. With family, the Museum almost always wins. If you choose the Met, content yourself here with the façade and Theodore Roosevelt Park.

activities.text: Inside the museum, head straight to the fossil exhibits on the 4th floor when it opens: the dinosaur halls lose much of their appeal in the noon crush.
Central Park crossing to the Met: 900 m via the 79th Street path, about 11 min walk.

visits.text: New Glarus - Wisconsin's 'Little Switzerland.' Founded in 1845 by 108 immigrants from the Canton of Glarus, this town has taken its Swiss heritage all the way: flower-decked chalets, German signage, cheese factories, and bakeries. The historical museum recreates a nineteenth-century Swiss village.

New Glarus Brewing Company - Wisconsin's most cult brewery. Their Spotted Cow (a creamy farmhouse ale) is sold only in Wisconsin - making it a prized contraband item for Illinois neighbors. Free tour of the exterior and beer garden. Tastings at the bar.
Historical Museum - Several reconstructed buildings: chalet, cheese factory, forge, school. The story of Swiss immigration to Wisconsin is well told.

activities.text: Sugar River State Trail - This former railway converted into a cycle path runs for 39 km through rolling countryside between New Glarus and Brodhead. It crosses several bridges. Bicycle rentals are available in the village.

Local Cheese Tasting - Wisconsin is America's top cheese producer. Around New Glarus, several artisan cheese factories offer tastings of gruyère, aged cheddar, and fresh cheese curds (the famous 'squeak-squeak' that squeaks under your teeth).

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: New Harmony - This village of 690 inhabitants on the Wabash River was the setting for two successive utopias. In 1814, German pastor Georg Rapp settled his community of separatist Lutherans here - in ten years, they built 180 buildings. In 1825, Welsh industrialist Robert Owen bought the entire town and tried to create a “community of equals”. The experiment failed within two years, but the intellectuals he had brought in (the “Boatload of Knowledge”) founded the first free public school in the United States here. Start at the Atheneum, the visitor center designed by Richard Meier (1979) - an angular white block that stands out in the rural landscape. Then walk to Philip Johnson's Roofless Church (1960): a roofless brick enclosure with the sky as its ceiling, gilded bronze gates at the entrance and a statue by Jacques Lipchitz beneath the inner dome. Finish at the Harmonist Labyrinth, a hedge maze suited to contemplation.

Lincoln Boyhood National Memorial (Lincoln City) - Plan a round trip by car from New Harmony to visit this site where Abraham Lincoln lived from the age of 7 to 21. His mother Nancy is buried here - she died of “milk sickness” poisoning in 1818 after drinking milk from a cow that had eaten snakeroot. A reconstructed farm shows the living conditions of the pioneers of that time.

activities.text: Walk through the Harmonist Labyrinth and New Harmony gardens - The hedge labyrinth, inspired by the one created by the Harmonists in the 19th century, invites a contemplative stroll. The surrounding gardens, maintained by the local club, conceal a “Tree of 40 Fruits” (a grafted tree bearing 40 varieties of stone fruit).

places.name: New Haven, CT

visits.text: Yale University - One of America's Oldest and Most Prestigious Institutions: Founded with roots dating to the 1640s, this Ivy League campus spans 200 acres featuring buildings from three different centuries. Free student-led walking tours reveal Gothic treasures like Sterling Memorial Library and the iconic Harkness Tower rising 216 feet above the historic campus.

Yale University Art Gallery - The Nation's Oldest University Art Museum: Open since 1836, this world-class institution houses over 300,000 works spanning ancient civilizations to contemporary masters, all with free admission in a stunning Louis Kahn-designed building.

Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History - Newly Renovated Wonder: After four years of extensive renovations reopening in 2024, this museum showcases extraordinary collections including the famous Age of Reptiles mural and dinosaur specimens that have educated visitors for generations.

Marsh Botanical Garden - Eight Acres of Living Laboratory: This university-managed garden features greenhouses, outdoor collections, and research facilities supporting both scientific study and public enjoyment of horticultural diversity.

activities.text: New Haven Pizza Trail - Birthplace of American Pizza Perfection: This college town claims America's finest pizza tradition, with legendary establishments perfecting thin-crust pies since the early 1900s. The famous 'white clam pie' has achieved national recognition, while multiple pizzerias have earned spots on 'best in America' lists.

Louis' Lunch - Where the Hamburger Was Born: This tiny establishment claims to have served America's first hamburger sandwich, still prepared on original vertical cast-iron grills using a century-old recipe that draws pilgrims from around the world.

Long Wharf Food Truck Paradise - Latin American Street Food Hub: A cluster of vendors along Long Wharf Drive serves authentic tacos, empanadas, Cuban plantains, and other Latin American specialties from mobile kitchens.

visits.text: Avery Island Tabasco Factory—Tour the source of Tabasco hot sauce, produced on this salt dome island since 1868. The McIlhenny Company factory processes peppers grown on-site into the iconic sauce shipped to 195 countries worldwide.

Jungle Gardens—Wander through 67 hectares of botanical gardens featuring a 900-year-old Buddha statue, bamboo groves, and lagoons. The sanctuary on Avery Island protects snowy egrets nearly hunted to extinction for their plumes in the 1890s.

Shadows-on-the-Teche — Explore this 1834 plantation home preserved by the National Trust for Historic Preservation on Bayou Teche's banks. The Classical Revival mansion retains original furnishings and documents four generations of the Weeks family.

Konriko Rice Mill — Discover how rice is processed at America's oldest operating rice mill and company museum. The 1912 facility explains Louisiana's rice industry history while demonstrating milling equipment still producing Konriko brand rice.

activities.text: Paddling on Bayou Teche—Kayak or canoe down this historic Louisiana waterway winding through moss-draped cypress swamps. This scenic 201-kilometer bayou offers wildlife viewing and access to Cajun culture along its banks.

Boudin trail food tour — Sample different boudin recipes at specialist shops and gas stations along this unofficial culinary trail. Each establishment claims the best recipe for this essential Cajun sausage served hot from steamers.

New Iberia Main Street — Browse antique shops and cafes in this historic downtown preserving 19th-century commercial buildings. The compact Main Street reflects South Louisiana's French-Spanish heritage in its architecture and culture.

days_plan.itin_title: Louisiana Road Trip: New Orleans and Cajun Country
Deep Louisiana Road Trip: Jazz and Bayous

visits.text: Start at Jackson Square, the heart of the French Quarter since 1721. This 1-hectare plaza, modeled after Paris's Place des Vosges, witnessed Louisiana's transfer from France to the United States in 1803 during the Louisiana Purchase. At the center stands an equestrian statue of General Andrew Jackson dating from 1856. Around you: artists display their work along the wrought-iron fence (200 artists authorized each year), jazz musicians perform on the sidewalks, and tarot readers offer their services—all in a cheerful jumble typical of New Orleans.

Facing the square, St. Louis Cathedral is the oldest continuously active Roman Catholic cathedral in the United States. The current building dates from 1789, rebuilt after the great fire that devastated the French Quarter in 1788. On either side stand the Cabildo (former seat of Spanish government, now a Louisiana history museum) and the Presbytère (Mardi Gras museum). Cathedral admission is free—take a look at the rococo-style altar.

Cross Decatur Street to the French Market, the oldest public market in the United States (operating since 1791). You'll find stalls selling local produce, Cajun spices, hot sauce, and souvenirs. At the market's end, the old U.S. Mint building houses the New Orleans Jazz Museum—it's the only building in the U.S. to have served as a mint for both the United States and the Confederacy.

Walk up Royal Street—the French Quarter's street of art galleries and antique shops, much quieter than Bourbon Street. The wrought-iron balconies adorned with ferns are a sight in themselves. Look for the initials engraved in the railings: they identify the Creole families who built these houses in the early 19th century.

Take the St. Charles Avenue streetcar from Canal Street—the oldest continuously operating streetcar line in the world, designated a National Historic Landmark in 2014. The wooden cars date from 1923-1924, with no air conditioning—open windows are part of the charm. The ride costs $1.25 (exact change required). Get off at Washington Avenue to enter the Garden District.

The Garden District is the neighborhood of grand mansions built by wealthy Americans after the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Unwilling to live with the Creoles in the French Quarter, they built their own palaces on the other side of Canal Street. You'll see Greek Revival, Italianate, and Queen Anne-style homes, shaded by century-old oaks draped with Spanish moss. Stroll along Prytania Street, Coliseum Street, and First Street for the finest facades.

Lafayette Cemetery No. 1, at the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street, is one of New Orleans' famous “cities of the dead” cemeteries. Its marble and brick tombs are built above ground. The cemetery dates from 1833 and has appeared in several films and television series. The cemetery is closed to unguided visitors while work is underway: to explore its paths, book an authorized guided tour with the Preservation Resource Center.

Head down to Magazine Street, parallel to St. Charles Avenue, for 10 km of independent shops, galleries, and restaurants. This is the best spot for non-touristy shopping: antiques, vintage clothing, bookstores, contemporary art galleries. If you're hungry, po'boys (giant sandwiches stuffed with fried seafood or meat) are the specialty to order here.

Start the morning at Mardi Gras World, a huge warehouse on the banks of the Mississippi where carnival floats are built. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour, and you will see artisans working on giant papier-mâché and fiberglass sculptures—some more than 6 meters tall. Mardi Gras in New Orleans attracts more than a million visitors each year, and the floats you see here parade along St. Charles Avenue during carnival season (January through February or March, depending on the date of Mardi Gras).

Head to the National WWII Museum, ranked among the best museums in the United States. It was founded in 2000 in New Orleans because this is where Andrew Higgins designed the landing craft used on D-Day. The museum occupies several buildings, and you could spend an entire day here—allow at least 2 to 3 hours for the main exhibitions. The aircraft and tanks on display are authentic.

Late afternoon, ascend to Vue Orleans, the observation deck on the 34th floor of the former World Trade Center. The 360-degree view covers the Mississippi, French Quarter, Superdome, and Lake Pontchartrain. The interactive exhibit on the same floor traces the city's history through its various colonial periods.

Head back to New Orleans, but not via the interstate. Take US-90 eastbound then branch onto LA-1 along Bayou Lafourche, nicknamed “the longest cul-de-sac in the world”—a straight road following the bayou for dozens of kilometers, lined with houses on stilts and shrimp boats moored along the banks. Stop in Thibodaux, a small Cajun town on the bayou, for coffee and a photo of the historic downtown.

As you reach the New Orleans area, make a detour to the Barataria Preserve in Jean Lafitte National Historical Park (free admission, 30 minutes south of NOLA). The visitor center and trails are currently closed for construction, except for Twin Canals Trail. Keep your walk to this trail to observe the preserve's wetlands and waterbirds; the boardwalk route through the swamp is unavailable during this closure.

Last day in New Orleans—spend it on what you've missed. If you haven't been to City Park yet, now's the time. This 530-hectare park (larger than New York's Central Park) features 800-year-old oaks, the New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), and the Sydney & Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden—an outdoor contemporary sculpture garden among cypress trees and lagoons, free and open to all.

Take the Canal Street streetcar (City Park/Museum line) to get there—it's another historic line that crosses Mid-City, a residential neighborhood undergoing a revival, with good restaurants and local bakeries.

activities.text: At the end of the day, settle onto the terrace of one of the cafés lining Jackson Square for café au lait and beignets—the local specialty served here since the Civil War. Beignets are squares of fried dough covered in powdered sugar, always served in threes.

In the evening, head to Frenchmen Street (not Bourbon Street—locals will tell you). This is where the city's real jazz clubs are concentrated. You can listen to live music in several clubs without paying a cover charge—just walk from bar to bar and follow what you like. Jazz was born here in New Orleans in the early 20th century, and Frenchmen Street is its beating heart today.

Continue by streetcar to Audubon Park (Calhoun Street stop). This 140-hectare park lined with century-old oaks borders the Mississippi River. You can walk, jog, or simply sit beneath the trees. Audubon Zoo is at the back of the park if you're traveling with children.

Return downtown by streetcar for a free evening. If you want to explore the Creole culinary scene, restaurants in the Warehouse District (between the French Quarter and Garden District) offer a good balance of local cuisine and an atmosphere less touristy than Bourbon Street's.

Make a detour through the Tremé neighborhood, the oldest African American neighborhood in the United States. This is where enslaved people gathered on Sundays at Congo Square (now in Louis Armstrong Park) to play music and dance—a site considered one of jazz's birthplaces. The neighborhood gave its name to the HBO series.

Last evening in NOLA: if you haven't done it yet, take a stroll down Bourbon Street for the atmosphere (loud, touristy, but it's a must at least once). Bars are open around the clock and you can walk with your drink in the street—it's legal here, unlike most American cities.

Return to New Orleans in the late afternoon. Take advantage of this last evening to explore the Bywater neighborhood, east of the French Quarter. This is the city's creative district: giant murals, alternative galleries, cocktail bars in former warehouses. The atmosphere is less touristy than in the French Quarter—this is where the city's artists and musicians live.

Final hours in NOLA: return to the French Quarter for one last café au lait, one last beignet, one last jazz tune in the street. Louis Armstrong Airport (MSY) is 25 minutes by car from downtown. If you're returning your rental car, allow some extra time—traffic on I-10 can be heavy during rush hour.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden, NY

visits.text: Day 4 - optional: The New York Botanical Garden covers about a hundred hectares in the Bronx, including an old-growth forest that has never been cut down, crossed by the Bronx River. The grand Victorian Haupt Conservatory, with palms and seasonal exhibitions, is the highlight of the ticket. Allow half a day; a small train within the garden covers the distances.

Day 4 - optional: The Bronx Zoo, right next to the botanical garden, ranks among the world's largest urban zoos: combining the two fills an entire day, so choosing one is more reasonable. The garden traditionally offers some weekday pay-what-you-wish slots for its outdoor areas: check before coming.

activities.text: About ten minutes away on foot, Arthur Avenue serves as the Bronx's real Little Italy: hand-stretched mozzarella, a covered market, cannoli without tourist lines.
To Yankee Stadium: about 5.3 km, D line subway south through the Bronx, count 25 min.

visits.text: Three Capes Scenic Loop — From Newport, set aside a day trip for this 64-kilometer coastal loop taking in Cape Meares, Cape Lookout and Cape Kiwanda. Headlands, sea stacks and century-old Sitka spruce forests line the route. Allow for the return drive to Newport.

Oregon Coast Aquarium — Discover Pacific Northwest marine life in exhibits featuring sea otters, seals, sharks, and jellyfish. The Newport aquarium played a crucial role in rehabilitating Keiko, the orca from Free Willy.

Yaquina Head Outstanding Natural Area — Climb Oregon's tallest lighthouse standing 28 meters and visit tide pools at Cobble Beach. The basalt headland jutting into the Pacific offers seal and whale watching opportunities.

Historic Bayfront — Explore Newport's working waterfront featuring seafood markets, restaurants, and sea lion docks. The fishing fleet and marine science facilities maintain the harbor's maritime character since the 1860s.

activities.text: Whale watching — Spot gray whales migrating along the Oregon coast from December through May, with resident whales visible year-round. The headlands offer prime viewing as 20,000 whales pass during spring migration.

Watching sea lions — Look for sea lions on the docks of Newport's Bayfront, near the Yaquina Bay Bridge. When they are present, watch them from public areas without approaching the animals. Their calls and movements bring the waterfront to life.
Clam chowder tasting — Sample Oregon's famous seafood at Bayfront restaurants serving award-winning chowder made with fresh local clams. Many establishments claim the best chowder on the coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Oregon Natural Wonders: Crater Lake to Pacific Coast Road Trip

visits.text: Chatham merits 30 minutes en route to Newport: the 1808 lighthouse at the tip of the peninsula offers one of Cape Cod's clearest views of the barrier beaches stretching offshore. The village is intact, without the tourist excess of Hyannis.

In Hyannis, the JFK Hyannis Museum (397 Main Street, ticket $12, 1 hour) displays rare photos and archival footage of Kennedy in the village where he was born. The Kennedy Compound on Marchant Avenue remains inaccessible—private property. You can see its shoreline from a boat, but the view from the road reveals nothing.

Sandwich is Cape Cod's oldest village (1637) and least visited. The Sandwich Glass Museum (129 Main Street, ticket $10, 45 minutes) traces a thriving 19th-century glass industry, before Midwestern coal rendered it economically obsolete. A more spacious alternative: Heritage Museums and Gardens (100 hectares of gardens, ticket $22).

The Breakers (44 Ochre Point Avenue) cost $7 million in 1895—roughly $350 million today. Cornelius Vanderbilt II wanted a fireproof summer residence after losing the previous one in an 1892 fire: no structural wood, steel and stone throughout, marble from Italy and Africa. 70 rooms, a Grand Hall with a 15-meter ceiling. What you learn on a visit: Vanderbilt died in 1899, four years after completion, having enjoyed the palace for only four summers. His widow Alice spent 35 consecutive summers there until 1934. During World War II, The Breakers served as an official air-raid shelter for the city of Newport.

William K. Vanderbilt gave Marble House (596 Bellevue Avenue) to his wife Alva for her 39th birthday in 1892—$11 million, with $7 million for marble alone, dining room entirely gilded in 24-karat gold leaf. What the brochure omits: this is where Alva locked up her daughter Consuelo, 18, for several days to force her to marry the Duke of Marlborough in 1895. Consuelo loved someone else, refused, was threatened with disinheritance. She wore a dark veil during the ceremony. The affair is documented in Consuelo's correspondence. Alva, repentant, became a women's suffrage activist in the 1910s and funded the campaigns that succeeded in 1920.

Belcourt of Newport (657 Bellevue Avenue, ticket $40) is the most eccentric of the mansions: Oliver Hazard Perry Belmont had it built in 1891–1894 with the horses on the ground floor and his own quarters on the upper floors. He married Alva Vanderbilt in 1896—the same Alva, divorced from William—the scandal of the season. Belcourt has been managed by a private owner since 2012 rather than the Preservation Society, and restoration is ongoing. Less visited, more unusual.

activities.text: Drive via I-195 and US-1 to Newport, 3 hrs from Provincetown with these stops. Arrival in the late afternoon in this port of 24,000 inhabitants. A first stroll along Thames Street to get your bearings.

The White Horse Tavern (26 Marlborough Street) is the oldest restaurant in the United States still in operation, founded in 1673. Half-timbered house, original fireplace, refined American cuisine at $60–100 per person—and an atmosphere that merits booking 1 to 2 weeks ahead in season.

The Preservation Society's combination ticket for 5 mansions costs $49.50 at newportmansions.org ($29 per mansion individually). Two hours per mansion for a thorough visit—three mansions make a full day. Start with The Breakers as soon as it opens at 10 a.m., before the groups arrive around 11 a.m.

The Cliff Walk follows Newport's cliffs for 5.5 km, behind the Bellevue Avenue mansions—open to the public free of charge from Memorial Boulevard. Cliffs 20 to 30 meters high, a direct view of the Atlantic, the backs of the palaces on the left. Two hours round-trip, no equipment needed. Dinner at Black Pearl on Bannister's Wharf—an institution since 1972, award-winning clam chowder, $40–70.

New England in 8 Days: Boston, Salem, Cape Cod, Newport, Providence

visits.text: Without Frederick Law Olmsted, who designed Central Park, Niagara Falls would today be an amusement park surrounded by factories. Niagara Falls State Park, created in 1885, is the oldest state park in the United States, and it saved the site from industrialists competing for it in the 19th century. The three falls (American Falls, Bridal Veil, Horseshoe) together discharge 168,000 cubic meters of water per minute at peak hours, 90% over Horseshoe alone on the Canadian side.

The Prospect Point Observation Tower gives the first overview, 86 meters above the gorge. Built in 1961, it juts directly over the cliff and offers the best American-side perspective on American Falls and, beyond, the great crescent of Horseshoe. It's also where the elevator departs for the Maid of the Mist dock.

Goat Island, accessible by car or on foot via a bridge, separates American Falls from Horseshoe. Three Sisters Islands at the tip, a statue of Nikola Tesla (inventor of alternating current, whose patents enabled Niagara's hydroelectric development starting in 1895), and above all Terrapin Point: the only American-side spot where you stand literally at the edge of Horseshoe, a few meters from where the water pours over. Deafening noise, spray guaranteed.

Second day, cross the Rainbow Bridge on foot ($1 Canadian for pedestrian passage, passport required) to see the falls from the Ontario side. The view is radically different: you face all three falls aligned, and Horseshoe reveals itself across its entire 792-meter curve. Queen Victoria Park, free admission, runs along the shore for two kilometers. This is the classic postcard angle.

Journey Behind the Falls, Canadian side: elevators descending 38 meters into the rock, then tunnels carved behind the Horseshoe curtain. The two portals in the cliff face open directly onto the reverse side of the falls—you see only a wall of white water, but you hear and feel it. Outdoor platform below for the view from the falls' base. Open year-round; gloves and hats in winter for the icy walkways.

The Whirlpool Aero Car, a cable car designed by Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo and inaugurated August 8, 1916, has never had a serious accident in over a century. The cabin crosses the river about 76 meters above the whirlpool, on 520 meters of cable, and crosses the U.S.-Canada border four times in a single round trip because of the gorge's bend. The whirlpool below, more than 500 meters wide, forms where the river makes a 90-degree turn in the gorge.

activities.text: For 178 years, this boat has been taking visitors to the base of Horseshoe Falls—Maid of the Mist has sailed since 1846. The current boats, electric since 2020, carry 600 passengers each. Twenty minutes total, including five in the permanent mist at the falls' base; the provided blue poncho will be soaked to the last centimeter. Season: mid-April to early November. Book online; on-site lines reach 1.5 hours in summer.

Cave of the Winds, American side: you descend by elevator into the gorge then climb wooden walkways to within six meters of the base of Bridal Veil Falls. The Hurricane Deck, the final platform, sits under the falls—wind, water, pressure, thrills guaranteed. The walkways are dismantled each winter then rebuilt in spring, which is why the visit is only possible May through October.

If night falls while you're on the Canadian side, stay: the falls have been illuminated since 1925, in changing colors controlled by the Niagara Falls Illumination Board. An LED system has been in use since December 2016, consuming 82% less energy than the old xenon system. The display runs until 2 a.m. most of the year. Free show; the best viewing spot remains Table Rock right at the edge of Horseshoe. In summer, fireworks on Friday and Sunday evenings.

A meal in the Skylon Tower, a 160-meter observation tower built in 1965. The revolving restaurant completes a full rotation in one hour, with 360-degree views of the falls, Toronto's skyline in the distance on clear days, and the Sir Adam Beck power station below. Classic Canadian cuisine, tourist prices, but the experience makes up for them. Book online with elevator access included.
