visits.text: Snoqualmie Falls (47.5417, -121.8390), 6501 Railroad Avenue SE, drops 82 meters into a forested gorge—taller than Niagara, and almost nobody around in misty weather. For the Snoqualmie people, the mist at the base of the falls represents the prayers of ancestors rising toward the sky, a sacred site long before David Lynch discovered it. The underground hydroelectric plant visible on the gorge wall has been generating local electricity since 1898, still in operation. The Salish Lodge & Spa (47.5417, -121.8388) crowns the cliff above—the facade of the Great Northern Hotel in Twin Peaks. Two freely accessible viewpoints, a 2 km trail between them.

Drive 5 minutes south to Twede's Cafe (47.4952, -121.7857), 137 W North Bend Way. The building dates to 1941—formerly the Mar-T Cafe, the famous Double R Diner from the series. In 2017, HBO production renovated the interior to shoot Season 3 on location, and the decor stayed. Order the cherry pie and coffee: it's exactly what you imagined, and that's a good thing. One hour on site, two if you're a fan. $15-25.

Find the Reinig Road Bridge (47.5410, -121.7795) without signage—it's the bridge where Ronette Pulaski flees bloodied in the Twin Peaks pilot, freely accessible. The "Welcome to Twin Peaks" sign from the opening credits never physically existed: it was created for filming and destroyed afterward. The topographic map of Mount Si displayed in the Sheriff's office is, however, a real USGS map of the area—Lynch liked true details.

activities.text: Mount Si (47.4878, -121.7174) gives the twin peaks their name in the title. From the Mount Si Trailhead (47.4878, -121.7242), the trail climbs 1,100 meters of elevation gain over 8 km round-trip—between 3 and 5 hours depending on fitness, summit at 1,270 meters with panoramic views of the valley and Mount Rainier to the south. For those who prefer to stay in the valley mist, the rainforest trails around the falls are well worth the afternoon.

Sleep at Salish Lodge (47.5417, -121.8388) if budget allows—$450-900/night, but waking in morning fog above an 82-meter waterfall has no equivalent on this trip. Simpler B&Bs in North Bend for $130-220.

days_plan.itin_title: 9-Day Pacific Northwest: Uncovering Hidden Gems and Cult Locations

places.name: North Conway, NH

visits.text: Cathedral Ledge offers a grander perspective without requiring a long climb. A short road leads to the summit, where views stretch across the Saco Valley toward the White Mountains. Check that the gate is open before driving up; at the overlook, stay behind the barriers along the cliff edges.

activities.text: For a train ride that fits this short stop, choose Conway Scenic Railroad’s Valley Train. This heritage excursion lasts about 1 hour and returns to North Conway station. Book a departure that leaves time to enjoy the surrounding scenery; the Mountaineer is a different, longer outing.

The calm waters of Echo Lake reflect the cliffs of White Horse Ledge, near North Conway. A trail circles the lake, letting you enjoy the forest without taking the routes that climb to the cliffs. Be sure to choose Echo Lake State Park in North Conway: another Echo Lake lies farther along, at Franconia Notch.

places.name: North Platte, NE

visits.text: You pull off the highway in North Platte and suddenly understand why the city exists: Bailey Yard spreads in every direction across 1,155 hectares - 13 km long and 3 km wide at its widest point - making it the largest railroad classification yard on earth, recognized in the Guinness Book of Records in 1995. Union Pacific handles 14,000 rail cars through this yard every 24 hours, 365 days a year. The Golden Spike Tower and Visitor Center, shaped like a railroad spike and opened in 2008, lets you ride to the 8th floor for a panoramic view of the endless rows of cars, the two 'hump' sorting mounds, and 507 km of interlocking track. Former railroaders staff the observation decks and can walk you through exactly how a car gets from an incoming train to its correct outbound route. Paid entry; plan 60 to 90 minutes.

activities.text: While in North Platte, stop briefly at the site of the North Platte Canteen marker downtown - from 1941 to 1946, local women organized to meet every troop train that passed through, sometimes more than 20 a day, providing free coffee, sandwiches and a moment of warmth to over six million soldiers during World War II. The story is told inside the Golden Spike Tower visitor center. If you have an extra 30 minutes, Buffalo Bill's Scouts Rest Ranch - his actual working ranch north of town, where he launched his Wild West Show touring operation - is a state historical park with the original 1886 mansion open for tours.

places.name: Nouvelle Orleans, LA

visits.text: Let's clear up a misconception first: what they call the "French Quarter" isn't actually French. The French founded New Orleans in 1718, then two fires in 1788 and 1794 burned everything to the ground. The Spanish rebuilt it all—bricks, interior courtyards, wrought-iron balconies. The architecture everyone photographs is Spanish. Start at Jackson Square and St. Louis Cathedral (1789, the oldest continuously active cathedral in the United States) to get your bearings: the square's always packed with street musicians, fortune tellers, and tourists who haven't figured out where to go yet.

To the left of the cathedral, the Cabildo deserves an hour. This is where the Louisiana Purchase was signed on December 20, 1803: Napoleon sold 2.1 million square kilometers to the United States for $15 million—about 4 cents per hectare—because he needed cash to finance his wars and Saint-Domingue had just slipped from his grasp. One of the most lopsided real estate deals in history. Now the Louisiana State Museum, $10 admission.

Before dinner, give Bourbon Street 20 minutes—no more. The bars are open 24/7, the smell of beer and fried food is permanent, and you'll quickly understand why locals never set foot here. For music worth hearing, you'll need to go to Frenchmen Street tonight. Royal Street, on the other hand, shows colonial houses at their best—art galleries, antique dealers, preserved facades.

At 1140 Royal Street, an ordinary red brick house—private property, no official plaque. It's the most infamous house in the American South. Marie Delphine Macarty, high-society Creole hostess, kept enslaved people on the upper floors alive in horrific conditions. On April 10, 1834, a fire deliberately set by the cook—who'd been chained to her own stove for years—forced firefighters to break down the doors. They found 7 enslaved people suspended by their necks, wearing spiked iron collars. Madame LaLaurie fled to Paris on the ship Poland on June 24, 1834, was never tried, and died in Paris in December 1849. The current house is an 1837 reconstruction. Ten minutes from the sidewalk, and you leave with something difficult to name.

The Voodoo Museum (724 Dumaine Street, $10) is kitschy, cramped, and a bit dusty—but it's useful for untangling Louisiana voodoo from its Hollywood versions. Marie Laveau (1801-1881), the "Voodoo Queen of New Orleans," was a real person: a free woman of color, hairdresser to high society which gave her access to everyone's secrets, recognized voodoo priestess, and a figure who aided the poor and enslaved. Not a legend—a person documented in parish records.

In St. Louis Cemetery #1 (499 Basin Street, mandatory guide since 2015, $25 ticket), the dead have rested above ground since 1789—the water table sits at 30 centimeters and coffins would float back up after rains. A family tomb receives the body for a year and a day, Louisiana heat does its work, then the bones are pushed to the back for the next deceased. The same tomb serves indefinitely, generation after generation. Marie Laveau's tomb is here, regularly adorned with offerings. As is the white 2.7-meter pyramid that a still-living Nicolas Cage bought himself in 2010, inscribed with the Latin "Omnia Ab Uno." The reasons for this purchase remain unclear—even to him, it seems.

Board the St. Charles streetcar at Canal Street for $1.25—the oldest continuously operating streetcar in the world since 1835, century-old wooden cars, 45 minutes under a canopy of giant oaks. Ride it standing on the running board if you can: wind in your face, branches brushing past, and you'll understand why Tennessee Williams used to take this route for nothing, just to watch.

Lafayette Cemetery #1 (1416 Washington Avenue, 1833), closed to the public since 2019, can no longer be entered freely: it reopens on October 1, 2026 for guided tours only, run by the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans, the sole authorized operator, in groups of 16 people at most and with no ghost tours. Book your place. Anne Rice set several scenes of her Vampire Chronicles here. The whitewashed above-ground tombs overgrown with vegetation, the silence five minutes from the crowded terraces of Magazine Street: it is one of those places you leave with regret.

The Garden District is the neighborhood where Protestant Americans wanted to distinguish themselves from the Catholic Creoles of the Vieux Carré—each to their own territory in the 19th century. On Prytania Street, Coliseum Street, and Camp Street, the Greek Revival mansions from the 1850s are still inhabited. Anne Rice lived at 1239 First Street, Rosegate—a plaque marks it. Nicolas Cage owned the neighboring house, which he sold during his bankruptcy. He's said since that living in two haunted houses back-to-back seemed, in retrospect, an error in judgment.

At the end of the St. Charles line, Audubon Park spreads across 142 hectares designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, creator of Central Park. The live oaks are 300 years old, including the "Tree of Life" whose branches touch the ground in ten places. Locals run here, picnic, let their kids roam. Free, peaceful, and guide-free.

John Cummings, a white New Orleans attorney, bought this former sugar plantation in 1999, invested $10 million of his own money over 15 years, and opened Whitney Plantation on December 7, 2014—the first American museum entirely devoted to slavery from the enslaved people's perspective. Founded in 1752, the property counted 101 enslaved people in 1860. What you need to know before entering: the life expectancy of a newly arrived enslaved person on a Louisiana sugar plantation was 7 years. Historians call Louisiana "the human-devouring machine." Ticket $25, audio guide in French included, plan minimum 3 hours. Online reservation recommended.

Three memorials to see in the grounds of Whitney. The Allées Gwendolyn Midlo Hall engrave the names of 107,000 enslaved people of Louisiana with their birthplace and skills, reconstructed by the historian after whom they are named - the scale of the figure takes a while to sink in. The memorial to the 1811 German Coast uprising shows 63 ceramic heads on spikes, by the artist Woodrow Nash: a reminder of the largest slave revolt in the United States, crushed within a few days and followed by a repression whose heads were planted along 100 km of the River Road. The memorial to enslaved children lines up 40 life-size statues, their faces individualised from real testimonies of the Federal Writers' Project (1930). These children have names.

Oak Alley (3645 Highway 18, Vacherie, 15 min west of Whitney, $32 ticket)—not for the quality of the tour, but for the contrast. The alley of 28 live oaks planted in 1700, before the house even existed, forms a 240-meter plant tunnel that served as backdrop for Interview with the Vampire (1994) and Django Unchained (2012). The tour remains mostly devoted to the planter's house, slave cabins relegated to the end of the route. Doing both in the same day means understanding two American memories that haven't finished arguing with each other.

Mark Twain said of Baton Rouge's Old State Capitol (300 North Boulevard, free) that it was "one of the most grotesque architectural crimes America has ever committed." The 1847 neo-Gothic building, with its turrets and stained glass, eventually won people over—everyone except Twain. It's now a museum of Louisiana political history, and the building itself is worth the detour.

In Louisiana, people still love Huey Long. "The Kingfish," populist governor nicknamed the Robin Hood of the Delta, had the New State Capitol (State Capitol Drive, free) built in 14 months in 1932—137 meters, the tallest state capitol in the United States, because he wanted to surpass New York's. He was shot twice in this marble corridor on September 8, 1935, between the Senate chamber and his office. A floor plaque marks the exact spot where he fell. He died 30 hours later. Louisianans still stop over it in silence.

The USS Kidd (305 S. River Road), a Second World War destroyer launched in 1943 and in service until 1964, is not in Baton Rouge at the moment: it left in 2024 for restoration at a shipyard in Houma, could not make its way back up the Mississippi in 2026, and is not expected back before spring 2027. The shoreside museum remains open, with its collections and a room devoted to the kamikaze attack the ship suffered off Okinawa in 1945. Check usskidd.com to see whether the ship is back before making the detour.

activities.text: At Café du Monde on Decatur Street, an institution since 1862 and open 24/7, three fried beignets under an avalanche of powdered sugar cost $6-8 with chicory café au lait. The line is almost constant—arrive at 7am or accept the wait. It's not really about taste: it's an entry ritual into the city.

Frenchmen Street in the Faubourg Marigny, a 10-minute walk from the French Quarter, is where locals go. The Spotted Cat, Snug Harbor, Three Muses: live jazz from 9pm, free entry, drinks recommended. It's loud and crowded—and infinitely more honest than Bourbon Street, which feels like a carnival midway.

For lunch, Dooky Chase's Restaurant (2301 Orleans Avenue) is worth leaving the French Quarter. Leah Chase cooked here until age 95, Obama, Clinton, and Martin Luther King ate here—and the Creole African-American cuisine served since 1941 is on another level from what you find on Bourbon Street. Expect $30-50.

Evening in Tremé, the oldest African-American neighborhood in the United States: free Black people founded it in the 18th century, before slavery even ended. On weekends, brass bands erupt in the street without warning—"second line parades" pull the whole neighborhood behind them with a fanfare and jubilation that belongs only to New Orleans. No tickets, no schedule. Just be there.

New Orleans takes Sunday brunch very seriously—more seriously than dinner in most other cities. Commander's Palace (125 Washington Avenue, $50-90, reservation essential) is the historic Creole address in the Garden District: dress code at table, impeccable service, gumbo and bananas Foster in the dining room. More casual, Coquette (2800 Magazine Street, $35-60) offers contemporary market cuisine without ceremony.

Magazine Street stretches 10 kilometers and concentrates the best of the Garden District beyond the houses: independent shops, galleries, antique dealers, cafés that locals actually frequent. More lively than Royal Street, less touristy. Return by streetcar to downtown.
Between Whitney and Oak Alley, the villages of Wallace and Vacherie have a few unpretentious Cajun restaurants—take what's open and local, $15-25. Most of the day is spent on foot at both sites.

To return to NOLA, take Highway 18 rather than the interstate—the Great River Road runs along the levees, passes refineries, village cemeteries, painted wooden chapels, centuries-old oaks. The Mississippi is on the left, invisible behind the levee, but you can sense it from the width of the sky.

Lunch in Baton Rouge before getting back on the I-10 towards NOLA: downtown, around Third Street, a short walk from the Old State Capitol, you will find po'boys and plates of red beans and rice ($15-25) - ordinary, authentic Louisiana cooking, far from the tourist trail.

Return to New Orleans on the I-10 (about 130 km, 1 hour 15 by road from Baton Rouge), drop the car off at MSY. Total car budget for the whole stay: $300-400 for 5-6 days of an automatic sedan. Return flight to Paris via Atlanta or Charlotte, 14-16 hours in total.

visits.text: A stop at the Cowboy Museum in Oakdale adds context to the drive through farmland. The museum preserves the history of ranching and rodeo in the Central Valley: behind the Western imagery, it also tells the story of work and livestock raising. Check its hours before setting off, and keep the visit short so you can reach Yosemite before dark.

days_plan.itin_title: San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: The drive from San Francisco to Yosemite passes through Mariposa, a small town that was one of the most active during the 1850s Gold Rush. Its wooden courthouse, built in 1854, is the oldest still in operation in California. Stop for 30 minutes to walk the main street—the period architecture is remarkably well preserved.
The Mariposa Museum and History Center traces the region's history from the Miwok people to the Gold Rush. Small but well documented—allow 45 minutes to an hour to see everything.

As soon as you enter the valley, a little over an hour's drive from Oakhurst, Bridalveil Fall comes into view: a 189-meter waterfall that flows all year round—one of the few in the park that never dries up completely. In strong winds the water is blown sideways, which earned it its English name. The Ahwahneechee, the Native American people of the valley, called it “Pohono,” the spirit of the puffing wind. The access trail is 800 meters round trip from the parking lot, a 15-minute walk.

El Capitan is one of the world's largest granite walls: 914 meters of vertical rock rising from the valley floor. The first free climb was completed in 1993 by Lynn Hill—a performance that stunned the global climbing community. From Tunnel View as you enter the valley, you get the classic frame with El Capitan on the left, Half Dome in the distance, and Bridalveil Fall on the right.

Yosemite Falls is one of the highest waterfalls in North America: 739 meters in total over three sections. The Lower Yosemite Falls trail is an easy 1.6 km return walk that leads to the base. In spring, during snowmelt, the flow is spectacular—in summer, the fall can be almost dry.

activities.text: Near Oakhurst, the Yosemite Mountain Sugar Pine Railroad offers steam train rides on narrow-gauge tracks that were used from 1899 to 1931 to haul timber from the sequoia forests. The 6-kilometer journey winds through pine forests and offers a glimpse of Sierra Nevada country before entering the park. Check seasonal schedules.

Drive up to Glacier Point for sunset—it's the park's most famous viewpoint. The overlook sits at 2,199 meters elevation, 975 meters above the valley floor. From here, you have Half Dome directly in front of you, Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall below, and the High Sierra peaks stretching to the horizon. Ansel Adams captured some of his most iconic photographs here. Plan for an hour's drive from the valley and arrive 45 minutes before sunset to secure a spot.

days_plan.itin_title: California Road Trip: San Francisco, Yosemite & Death Valley

Sierra California Road Trip: Sequoia and Kings Canyon

visits.text: Oakland - San Francisco's Cooler, More Rebellious Sister: This diverse city across the bay has emerged as a cultural powerhouse, with thriving arts scenes, innovative cuisine, and proud communities that celebrate authenticity over pretension.

Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) - The State's Story Under One Roof: This unique institution weaves together California's art, history, and natural sciences through immersive galleries and rotating exhibitions exploring the Golden State's identity.

Lake Merritt - America's First Official Wildlife Refuge: This tidal lagoon in the heart of downtown Oakland, designated in 1870, provides sanctuary for migrating birds while offering residents jogging paths, gardens, and waterfront relaxation.

activities.text: Children's Fairyland - Where Storybooks Come to Life: This beloved theme park, opened in 1950, inspired Walt Disney to create Disneyland. Whimsical sets bring fairy tales and nursery rhymes to three-dimensional life for young visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Northwest Kansas Rock Formations - Kansas's Best-Kept Natural Secrets: For decades, travelers sped past these otherworldly geological treasures, but today these Niobrara chalk formations rank among Kansas's most remarkable attractions.

Little Jerusalem Badlands State Park - A mile-long city of stone: Allow for a day trip from Oakley. Nestled in a valley between Scott City and Oakley, the state's largest Niobrara chalk formation features rock faces and pillars 100 feet high. A scenic trail circles the imposing formations that gave the park its biblical name.

Monument Rocks - 70-foot chalk pillars rising from the prairie: Allow for a day trip from Oakley. The surrounding expanse of shortgrass prairie makes these Niobrara chalk pillars and natural arches even more dramatic, geological sentinels standing guard over the Kansas plains.

Fick Fossil & History Museum in Oakley - Fossils and the history of the plains: Discover marine fossils found in the region, including shark teeth and remains of large prehistoric fish. The collections and reconstructed buildings also tell the story of Oakley, the railroad and the people of the plains.

activities.text: Chalk Pyramids Trail - Walk Among Ancient Seabed Remnants: These 80-million-year-old formations were deposited when an inland sea covered Kansas, leaving behind the shells and skeletons of marine creatures compressed into chalk.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Tour: Prairies and the Wild West

visits.text: Rainbow Springs State Park - Florida's Fourth Largest Spring: Allow for a round trip from Ocala. Crystal-clear water in seemingly impossible shades of blue and green flows from one of Florida's most beautiful springheads. The spring-fed Rainbow River maintains a consistently cool temperature all year.

Tubing on Rainbow River - Float Through Paradise: Allow for a round trip from Ocala. Drift downstream on this crystal-clear, spring-fed river beneath canopies of live oaks, with fish clearly visible swimming above the sandy riverbed below your tube.

activities.text: Paddling on Rainbow River - Kayaking Through Vivid Colors: Allow for a round trip from Ocala. The remarkable clarity of this spring-fed river reveals an underwater world of fish, turtles, and aquatic plants that makes every paddle stroke a discovery.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

visits.text: On the way, stop at Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, on Hatteras Island, across the ferry from Ocracoke - the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, 60 meters and 257 steps. Built in 1870, it was moved in one piece 880 meters inland in 1999 to save it from the erosion threatening its base. An $11.8 million operation, a 23-day move on rails. The climb is closed in 2026 for restoration; the grounds remain open.

Free ferry from Hatteras to Ocracoke, 60-minute crossing, departures every hour. Arrival on an island 26 kilometers long and 1 kilometer wide, with a single village. Ocracoke was a pirate refuge in the 18th century - this is where Blackbeard (Edward Teach) was killed on November 22, 1718, in a fierce duel that lasted several hours. The cove where he perished is still called Teach's Hole. One thousand permanent residents, no chains, no traffic lights.

Ocracoke Lighthouse, whitewashed since 1823, is the oldest operating lighthouse in North Carolina. Small (only 23 meters) but authentic. You cannot climb it, but access to its base is free. The wooden boardwalk crosses the salt marshes from the parking lot.

activities.text: Swim at Ocracoke Beach, ranked America's number 1 beach by Dr. Beach (Stephen Leatherman) in 2007. 25 km of wild beach, no visible buildings, access via paths through the dune. The water is warmer than at Nags Head (the Gulf Stream is closer) and the swell gentler. Lifeguards in summer on the guarded beach just north of the village; elsewhere, swim at your own risk.

Visit Ocracoke's wild horses - presumed descendants of Spanish horses stranded in 16th-century shipwrecks. Today they are kept in a 73-hectare reserve for their safety (they once roamed the main road). Viewing platform about 11 km north of the village, overlooking the herd. Free.

days_plan.itin_title: Washington to Miami in 16 Days Along the American East Coast
US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

visits.text: Manes in the wind behind a fence along NC 12: this is the Ocracoke Pony Pen. The Banker Ponies are thought to descend from Spanish horses that survived shipwrecks, and the National Park Service has kept them in an enclosure since the 1950s. They don't run on the beach: stop at the roadside viewing area, a few kilometers from the Hatteras ferry.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

visits.text: At Perkins Cove, boats and footbridges frame the scene around a small harbor. This part of Ogunquit also preserves the memory of its artists’ colonies, featured on the town’s historical tours. View the docks from public areas and park before entering the narrowest streets.

Paintings are only part of the pleasure at the Ogunquit Museum of American Art: the ocean is part of the setting. Opened in 1953 by artist Henry Strater, the museum continues the coast’s artistic story through paintings and sculptures. Check its opening season before buying tickets; indoor visits are not available year-round.

activities.text: Follow the coast along Marginal Way, the maintained path connecting the area near the village to Perkins Cove. Its roughly two kilometers bring the rocks and the Atlantic into view without a long hike. Plan to walk back or arrange another way to return, and stay off exposed rocks when the sea is rough.

days_plan.itin_title: New England in Fall: 11 Days on the Road

places.name: Ohiopyle, PA

visits.text: Fallingwater is the most admired architectural work in the United States - American Institute of Architects members voted it 'best all-time work of American architecture' in 1991, and UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2019. Frank Lloyd Wright, then 67 and late in his career, designed this house in 1935 for Edgar J. Kaufmann, owner of Pittsburgh's Kaufmann department stores. The commission was simple: a weekend forest retreat. The result stunned the architectural world: a 490-square-meter house built in cantilever directly over a waterfall on Bear Run creek, with reinforced concrete balconies that appear to float without visible support. The interior incorporates a natural rock as the fireplace hearth, polished local stone floors reflect the nature outside, and corner windows without posts open onto a 360° forest. Book tickets online several weeks in advance - spaces sell out quickly, admission: $30 adult for the standard guided tour.

Ohiopyle Falls - a six-meter cascade spanning the full width of the Youghiogheny River - is the park's visible heart and the starting point for whitewater navigation. The Visitor Center observation platform offers a direct view of the falls from inside the building, allowing you to admire the spectacle even in rain. It was here that George Washington passed in 1754 during the Seven Years' War and considered - then abandoned - the idea of using the river as a military supply axis, the rapids being too violent. In summer, dozens of rafts and kayaks run the Class III-IV rapids just downstream from the falls - a sight in itself from shore.

A few minutes' drive from Ohiopyle, Cucumber Falls is one of Pennsylvania's most photographed waterfalls: a nine-meter bridal veil plunging into a natural pool framed by moss-covered rock walls. The access trail from the Chalk Hill Road parking lot is short, flat, and accessible to all. The unique feature: you can walk behind the falls between the rock wall and the water curtain, offering a rare and slightly damp perspective. Arrive early in the morning - it's one of the park's most visited spots in summer - or late afternoon when tour buses have left.

activities.text: The Youghiogheny River at Ohiopyle is one of the best rafting rivers on the East Coast. The Lower Yough, Class III-IV over seven miles, attracts thousands of amateur and experienced paddlers each summer. Local outfitters - Wilderness Voyageurs, White Water Adventurers - provide wetsuit, helmet, and life jacket, and prepare groups with a safety briefing before departure. The name Ohiopyle comes from a Lenape word meaning 'it turns white' - a direct reference to the rapids' foam. Even if you don't paddle, watching groups run the rapids from shore is a free and lively spectacle all summer.

The Great Allegheny Passage is a 244-kilometer rail trail linking Pittsburgh with Cumberland, Maryland, entirely laid out on converted former railway lines. The stretch from Ohiopyle follows the Youghiogheny gorge through dense woodland of hemlocks and maples. The path is almost flat, making it accessible to riders of all abilities. In autumn, red maples and golden beeches turn the GAP Trail into a tunnel of color.

days_plan.itin_title: Pennsylvania Loop: From Amish Country to the Appalachians - 12 Days

map_keywords: Great Allegheny Passage GAP Trail Ohiopyle

visits.text: Enter the Okefenokee Swamp, a 177,000-hectare wilderness where crystal-clear blackwater channels wind through ancient cypress and tupelo forests draped in Spanish moss. This vast wetland, one of the largest intact freshwater ecosystems in North America, supports over 600 species including American alligators, river otters, and countless wading birds. The mysterious, primordial atmosphere creates a hauntingly beautiful landscape unlike anywhere else in the country.

Walk the elevated Chesser Island Boardwalk to an observation tower providing panoramic views across endless prairies of floating peat islands and wildlife-rich marshlands. The preserved homestead reveals how hardy pioneers once survived in this watery wilderness. The visitor center explains the swamp's unique ecology and cultural history.

activities.text: Glide through mirror-calm waters on guided boat tours where experienced naturalists point out alligators basking on logs, herons stalking fish, and turtles sunning on cypress knees. The earthy, mossy scent of the wetlands and calls of countless birds create a sensory immersion in one of America's last great wild places.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: You walk between the two bronze Gates of Time: 9:01 on one side for the last moment of ordinary life, 9:03 on the other for the first moment of aftermath. Between them, 168 bronze chairs stand in nine rows - one per floor of the Murrah Building - nineteen of them smaller to mark the children from the day care center. The Reflecting Pool occupies what was Fifth Street, where McVeigh parked the Ryder truck. The Survivor Tree, an American elm that stood next to the building, absorbed the full force of the blast and still grows at the east end of the memorial. Inside the museum, you hear the actual audio from a water board meeting taking place across the street when the bomb went off - then the explosion itself, mid-sentence. Allow at least two hours.

You enter through a foyer dominated by James Earle Fraser's 18-foot-tall plaster “End of the Trail” - a lone Native American slumped on a weary horse, cast in 1915 and reproduced more widely than almost any other American sculpture. Chester Reynolds of Kansas City campaigned in the early 1950s for a national Western institution; Oklahoma City won the bid by donating property on Persimmon Hill, and the museum opened in 1955. The 220,000-square-foot building holds 28,000 artworks and artifacts, the world's largest collection of American rodeo photography, and the Prosperity Junction gallery - a full-scale replica turn-of-the-century Western town you walk through. Plan two and a half hours.

You stand in front of the only state capitol in America that ever had working oil wells on its grounds. When oil was struck south of downtown in December 1928, drilling crept north until derricks surrounded the building itself; one well was slant-drilled from across the street to tap reserves directly beneath the Capitol. Production ended in 1986. The dome you see today was added in 2002 - the original building opened without one in 1917 because funds ran out. The Capitol is also one of only two state capitols on the historic Route 66 alignment. Free tours run on weekdays.

You walk down Exchange Avenue and hear an auctioneer's rapid-fire chant drifting through the morning air - the Oklahoma National Stockyards, founded October 3, 1910, still runs cattle auctions on Mondays and Tuesdays, and by the early 1980s had become the world's number-one stocker-feeder cattle market handling over a million animals per year. The half-mile of Exchange Avenue is a living Western district: Langston's Western Wear has been here since 1913, Little Joe's Boots has sold handmade cowboy boots since 1950, and Cattlemen's Steakhouse has been open since 1910. Stockyards City is on the National Register of Historic Places and still smells exactly like what it is.

You step into a building whose design references the Mississippian mound culture - the central 109-foot “Sky Journey” tower rises above a complex opened in September 2021 after two decades of planning, built to represent Oklahoma's 39 federally recognized tribal nations on land that was once Indian Territory. The permanent galleries cover 12,000 years of continuous Native presence in what became Oklahoma, from pre-contact civilizations through the forced removals of the 1830s, the allotment era, and the present. The Harvest Moon Café inside serves food influenced by tribal food traditions - stop for lunch if the timing works.

You finish the trip at the 17-acre Myriad Botanical Gardens in the heart of downtown - an easy walk from the memorial and Bricktown. The Crystal Bridge Tropical Conservatory is a 224-foot glass cylinder housing a rainforest and desert ecosystem side by side; it opened in 1988 and is still one of OKC's stranger buildings in the best sense. The outdoor gardens are free and open daily; the Crystal Bridge carries a small admission fee. If the weather holds, it's a calm, unhurried end to seven days on the road.

activities.text: Tonight you walk the mile-long Bricktown Canal, opened in July 1999 as part of the MAPS voter-approved program that transformed what had been an abandoned 1890s warehouse district into Oklahoma City's main entertainment draw. The red-brick buildings date from 1898 to 1930; their facades now house restaurants, bars, and live music. The Chickasaw Bricktown Ballpark - home of the Triple-A OKC Dodgers - opened in 1998 right on the canal. For dinner, Vast on the 49th floor of the Devon Energy Center gives you the full Oklahoma plains panorama on a clear night, or stay canal-level at any of the restaurants along the water.

You find sculptor Paul Moore's bronze panorama at the south end of the canal - dozens of life-size figures in full gallop, capturing the April 22, 1889 Land Run when 50,000 settlers charged simultaneously across the border into unassigned Indian Territory. Some claimed 160-acre plots within an hour. The full monument was completed in 2008 and spans a city block. It's free, it's lit at night, and it takes about fifteen minutes to walk the full length of it.

You board the water taxi at the canal dock and spend forty minutes cruising the mile-long Bricktown Canal - passing the Land Run Monument, Chickasaw Bricktown Ballpark, and converted 1890s-1930s warehouse fronts that now house restaurants and bars. The canal opened in July 1999 as part of the MAPS program; the guides on board recount the district's transformation from abandoned warehouses to a leading city attraction. The taxi operates year-round when weather permits, with schedules varying by season.

You close out the trip at a table in Bricktown, where the red-brick walls and the canal outside do most of the atmosphere work for you. Mickey Mantle's Steakhouse at 7 Mickey Mantle Drive sits right on the canal and has been an OKC staple since 1995, the year of the bombing - the city rebuilt around it. If you want something lighter, the Bricktown Brewery has been on E. Sheridan since 1992 and serves its own beer in a 1903 building. Either way, you're eating in a place that was boarded up twenty years before you arrived and has been alive ever since.

visits.text: Arnolds Park Amusement Park—This 8-hectare park on the shore of West Lake Okoboji has been operating since 1889. Its wooden roller coaster, The Legend, dates to 1927—it's the 13th-oldest wooden roller coaster still operating in the world. Park admission is free—you pay only for the rides. Ride the Ferris wheel for the best view of the lake.

Iowa Great Lakes Maritime Museum—Right next to the amusement park, this small museum showcases antique wooden boats and traces the history of the lake region. If you have time, head one block farther west to the Abbie Gardner Cabin—this 1856 cabin is tied to the Spirit Lake Massacre, a violent chapter in pioneer history.

Gull Point State Park—On the north shore of West Lake, this park offers a sandy beach, shaded trails, and picnic areas under the oaks. It's quieter than Arnolds Park—perfect for a calm morning by the water.

Visit Spirit Lake, Iowa's largest natural lake (2,300 hectares). The small town of the same name has the charm of a Midwestern small town, with its tree-lined streets. Nothing spectacular, but the atmosphere is authentic.

activities.text: Boat trip on West Lake Okoboji - The Queen II, an excursion boat, offers 1-hour-15-minute cruises with commentary on the lake's bays and properties. The water is indeed a deep blue thanks to the lake's depth (41 m) and its spring-fed water supply.

Biking the Spine Trail—This 22 km bike path links the communities around the lakes. The stretch between Arnolds Park and Milford hugs the shoreline with open views of the water. Bike rentals available on-site.
In the evening, enjoy the sunset from the west shore of the lake—locals gather with coolers and folding chairs. The atmosphere recalls seaside resorts from another era.

visits.text: Despite its name, Old Faithful does not erupt like clockwork at fixed times. Eruption predictions are posted at the Visitor Education Center and shared in the NPS app. Waiting is part of the experience: the hissing grows louder, the steam thickens, and then the jet shoots upward. Check the next prediction before planning your walk, and leave a buffer rather than scheduling something immediately afterward.

Black Sand Basin brings the colors down to eye level, away from the towering jet everyone awaits at Old Faithful. The boardwalks lead to Rainbow Pool, Sunset Lake, and Cliff Geyser, among other features, beside Iron Spring Creek. The visit focuses on these small thermal scenes rather than a single eruption. Use the dedicated parking lot or designated trails from Upper Geyser Basin, and respect the barriers even when a pool seems calm.

activities.text: Follow the paths through Upper Geyser Basin beyond Old Faithful, adjusting your loop to the available predictions. Castle, Grand, Daisy, and Riverside are among the geysers whose eruptions staff can regularly predict; the others keep their own rhythm. The appeal lies in comparing jets, cones, and pools without rushing from bench to bench. Ask at the visitor center for updated predictions and information on accessible sections, then return along open routes.

visits.text: Olympia’s Legislative Building offers a monumental break between two mountain regions. Its rotunda, marble interiors, and public spaces reveal a seat of government still in use, rather than a mere historic backdrop. A free guided tour lasts about fifty minutes. Choose a departure that fits your arrival time and stick to areas open to the public if the galleries are unavailable.

activities.text: The sound of lapping water replaces road noise at Percival Landing on Olympia’s harbor. The promenade follows the waterfront at the southern end of Puget Sound, near downtown. It offers a way to end the day without heading out on another excursion. Save this walk for late afternoon and bring a jacket in case the wind picks up.

days_plan.itin_title: Olympic, Rainier and North Cascades: 11 Days in Nature

visits.text: You step into the Old Market and it takes a moment to register that these cobblestone streets and cast-iron canopies have been here since the 1880s, when the district was the engine of Omaha's wholesale produce trade. Bounded by 10th and 13th Streets and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the neighborhood was nearly demolished in the 1960s until Sam Mercer converted his family's red-brick warehouses rather than tear them down - his first move was opening a French restaurant in the former Gilinsky Fruit Company building in 1968. Today, over 45 restaurants, galleries and boutiques fill the ground floors of what the Register recognizes as one of the most intact 19th-century warehouse districts in the Midwest. The Saturday Farmers Market (May to October) draws 150 vendors and up to 10,000 shoppers. Don't leave without ducking into the Old Market Passageway - a covered arcade of small shops that most visitors walk straight past.

The Durham Museum occupies Omaha's former Union Station, an Art Deco building designed by Gilbert Stanley Underwood - the same architect behind the lodges at Bryce Canyon and Zion - and opened in 1931. At its peak the station served eight railroad lines, ranking Omaha as the fourth-largest rail center in the United States; it closed in 1971 and was donated by Union Pacific to the city two years later. Congress designated it a National Historic Landmark in December 2016. Inside you'll walk through restored 1940s storefronts, board full-size train cars on Track 1, and examine the Byron Reed coin collection, assembled in the 1880s and donated to the city at his death. The working soda fountain in the lobby is original - order a phosphate at the counter.

The Joslyn Art Museum was a gift to Omaha from Sarah Joslyn, who donated more than $3 million in 1928 as a memorial to her husband George - at the time the richest man in Nebraska. The 1931 Art Deco building, clad in Georgia marble and designed by John and Alan McDonald, was ranked among the 100 finest buildings in the United States seven years after opening. The collection of over 12,000 objects spans 5,000 years; the museum stewards one of the country's most important Karl Bodmer painting holdings in its Western Studies center. Ed Ruscha donated over 40 works in 2018. A 3,900 m² addition opened in September 2024. General admission is free.

activities.text: Henry Doorly Zoo covers 65 hectares and has been rated the world's best zoo by TripAdvisor and No. 1 in the U.S. by USA Today multiple years running. The Desert Dome is the world's largest indoor desert - 7,800 m² across two levels under the largest glazed geodesic dome on earth, housing three desert ecosystems side by side. Below it, Kingdoms of the Night is the world's largest nocturnal exhibit. The Lied Jungle is North America's largest indoor rainforest. Arrive at 9 a.m. when the gates open, start at the Desert Dome, and work back toward the entrance.

In the evening, walk across the Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge - a 915-meter cable-stayed span over the Missouri River linking Nebraska and Iowa. The view back toward Omaha from the Iowa side is the best free panorama of the city, and the bridge is lit after dark. Return to the Old Market for dinner: Plank Seafood Provisions for oysters, Le Bouillon for modern French, or Ted & Wally's scratch-made ice cream to finish. The First Friday gallery walk (first Friday each month) keeps Old Market galleries open late with free entry.

visits.text: Blue Spring State Park - Summer Swimming, Winter Manatee Watching: This remarkable spring offers completely different experiences by season. Summer visitors swim in water at a constant 22°C, while winter brings hundreds of manatees seeking warmth as ocean temperatures drop.
Manatee Viewing Boardwalks - Gentle Giants by the Hundreds: Elevated boardwalks offer extraordinary views of Florida's beloved marine mammals during the peak season (November-March).

activities.text: Spring Diving Competition - Local Kids at Play: Watch (or join) as children compete to see who can freedive deepest into the spring's blue depths, a centuries-old tradition at this beloved swimming hole.

visits.text: PEZ Visitor Center - 370 Square Meters of Candy Nostalgia: Explore the colorful history of the iconic candy brand, first created in 1927 and now producing around 5 billion sweet treats annually. The self-guided tour reveals a product packaging line, the world's largest PEZ dispenser, and an extensive collection of themed dispensers spanning decades of pop culture.

activities.text: Interactive PEZ Experience - Sweet Fun for All Ages: Engage with games throughout the facility, browse the extensive gift shop, and learn how this Austrian-born candy conquered American hearts. The convenient highway location makes it a perfect road trip stop.

visits.text: Kennedy Space Center — Plan a round trip by car from Orlando to explore NASA's visitor complex, including the space shuttle Atlantis and the Saturn V rocket. Interactive exhibits trace the history of space exploration; viewing points offer glimpses of the launch pads at Cape Canaveral.

Rocket Garden — Walk among actual Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo rockets standing vertically as they did before launch. These historic spacecraft carried America's first astronauts into orbit during the 1960s space race.

Astronaut Encounter — Meet veteran astronauts who share firsthand accounts of living and working in space. Q&A sessions offer unique insights into spacewalks, zero gravity, and life aboard the International Space Station.

activities.text: Surfing at Cocoa Beach — Plan a round trip by car from Orlando to try surfing on this 10-kilometer beach where eleven-time world champion Kelly Slater learned to ride the waves. Consistent Atlantic swells and warm water offer conditions for beginners and experts alike.

visits.text: If the wind dies down, Mount Moran is reflected in a branch of the Snake River at Oxbow Bend. The NPS also notes possible sightings of swans, otters, or beavers, with no guarantees. Stay at the designated overlook with your binoculars; do not go down toward an animal to reduce the distance.

visits.text: Discover Padre Island National Seashore, the longest undeveloped barrier island in the world, stretching over 110 km along the Gulf of Mexico with pristine beaches untouched by commercial development. The protected coastline provides critical nesting habitat for endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtles, with public releases of hatchlings creating unforgettable wildlife encounters during nesting season. The island's wild, windswept beauty offers a serene escape into coastal wilderness.

Explore the diverse ecosystems where Gulf waters meet coastal dunes, grasslands, and tidal flats supporting remarkable biodiversity. The Malaquite Visitor Center provides orientation to the park's natural and cultural history, including the shipwrecks that dot the treacherous coastline. Designated sections allow four-wheel-drive vehicle access to remote beach areas far from crowds.

activities.text: Experience world-class bird watching opportunities, as Padre Island lies along the Central Flyway migration route, attracting hundreds of species throughout the year including rare shorebirds and raptors. Fishing enthusiasts can cast into the surf for red drum, speckled trout, and other Gulf species along kilometers of accessible shoreline. Swimming, shell collecting, and camping under starlit skies provide classic coastal recreation in an unspoiled natural setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Texas: An Epic Journey from Metropolises to Wild Canyons

visits.text: Horseshoe Bend is 10 minutes from Page. The trail is 2.4 km round-trip from the parking lot and ends at a viewpoint on the edge of a 300-meter drop. Below, the Colorado traces an almost perfect horseshoe meander through red sandstone. No guardrails along most of the rim—stay cautious, especially with children. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon for the light and to avoid crowds.

Push on to Upper Antelope Canyon, the world's most photographed slot canyon. Sunlight pierces openings above and creates beams that illuminate sandstone streaked with pink, orange, and purple. The visit is only with a Navajo guide (the canyon is on Navajo land) and lasts about 1 hour. Book weeks in advance in high season. The noon slot offers the best light beams in summer. Lower Antelope Canyon is a cheaper and more adventurous alternative (stairs, ladders).

Late in the day, check out Glen Canyon Dam—this 216-meter-high dam holds back Lake Powell, a reservoir 300 km long with 3,100 km of shoreline (more than California's entire Pacific coast). The visitor center offers a view down over the dam and canyon below.

For your second day in Page, explore what most tourists miss. Wahweap Overlook offers panoramic views of Lake Powell and Navajo sandstone cliffs. It's free, little-known, and the morning light is superb.

If you are looking for solitude, Stud Horse Point is an off-the-beaten-path viewpoint; plan a day trip from Page. Access is via a dirt track requiring a high-clearance 4WD vehicle. It leads to a promontory with a 360° view of the desert streaked with red and white. Very few visitors—the place is a local secret.

activities.text: If you have time, a boat excursion on Lake Powell gives you access to flooded side canyons and isolated red sand beaches. Outfitters offer half-day trips from Wahweap Marina.

If you didn't do Antelope Canyon yesterday, now's the time. Otherwise, spend the morning kayaking on the Colorado between Glen Canyon Dam and Lees Ferry—red sandstone cliffs plunge directly into turquoise water. Outfitters offer half-day trips.

visits.text: Palm Springs - Midcentury Modern Paradise in the Desert: This Sonoran Desert oasis has attracted Hollywood celebrities since the 1930s, its clean-lined architecture and year-round sunshine creating an aesthetic preserved in over 800 documented modernist buildings.

Palm Springs Aerial Tramway - 10 Minutes from Desert Floor to Alpine Forest: The world's largest rotating tramcars climb nearly 6,000 vertical feet to Mount San Jacinto State Park, where temperatures drop 40 degrees and pine forests replace palms.

Palm Springs Art Museum - World-Class in the Desert: This respected institution houses significant collections of modern and contemporary art, Native American artifacts, and glass sculpture, with a satellite architecture museum downtown.

activities.text: Midcentury Modern Architecture Tours - The World's Finest Concentration: Preservation groups offer tours of homes designed by legends like Richard Neutra, Albert Frey, and Donald Wexler, many still privately owned but viewable from the street.

Joshua Tree National Park - Where Two Deserts Meet: Just an hour away, this otherworldly landscape of twisted Joshua trees and boulder piles spans both the Mojave and Colorado deserts, offering world-class rock climbing and surreal photography opportunities.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Marvel at Palo Duro Canyon State Park, known as the Grand Canyon of Texas, featuring dramatic landscapes of colorful rock formations, steep mesa walls, and hiking trails stretching over 190 km long and up to 32 km wide. The canyon's geological formations display a vivid palette of red, orange, and white hues that are especially striking at sunrise and sunset. As the nation's second-largest canyon, this natural wonder offers breathtaking vistas at every turn.

Hike the Lighthouse Trail to reach the iconic Lighthouse Peak, a towering hoodoo formation that has become the symbol of Palo Duro Canyon. The moderate trail winds through varied terrain showcasing millions of years of geological history carved by the Prairie Dog Town Fork of the Red River. The panoramic views from this landmark reward hikers with some of the most spectacular scenery in all of Texas.

activities.text: Explore the CCC Trail, which traces the remarkable work of the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, when it built much of the park's infrastructure during the Great Depression. Wildlife enthusiasts can observe various bird species and other native animals. The Pioneer Amphitheater within the park hosts concerts, theatrical performances and special events throughout the season.

places.name: Panama City Beach, FL

visits.text: The resort strip that defines Panama City Beach ends at St. Andrews State Park's gate. Behind it: 485 hectares of former military reservation purchased from the U.S. government in 1947 for $2.50 an acre, protecting one of the last stretches of intact coastal scrub in Northwest Florida. The War Department emplaced two 155mm guns in the dunes here in 1942 for harbour defence - one original gun mount still stands near the jetty, shaded by a pavilion. Two and a half kilometres of Gulf beach, a calm lagoon, two nature trails. Fee applies.

Shell Island exists because of the Army Corps. In the 1930s they dredged a pass between St. Andrews Bay and the Gulf; the spoil sand accumulated into an 11-kilometre undeveloped barrier island with no buildings, no roads, no cars. Spanish explorers, pirates, and the U.S. Navy all passed through here at different points; the island kept washing their traces away. Today you cross by shuttle from St. Andrews - a 15-minute ride to a beach that feels completely removed from the resort town behind you. Sea turtles nest here May through October. Take the first crossing at 9 a.m.

Gator Lake Trail and Heron Pond Trail at St. Andrews thread through coastal scrub communities that used to cover this entire coastline before development. Alligators sun on the Gator Lake banks, herons stalk the shallows, white-tailed deer browse the dune edges at dusk. These trails pull a fraction of the crowd that hits the beach parking lot. Weekday mornings give you the boardwalks to yourself.

activities.text: The St. Andrews jetty has been creating an artificial reef since the 1930s - flounder, sheepshead, rays, and the occasional sea turtle moving through the pass. Snorkel the Gulf side of Shell Island at high tide: visibility regularly hits 9 metres in calm conditions, and the colour of the water over white sand at that depth is something you won't forget. Gear rents at the park concession or from the shuttle operator.

Thomas Drive, five kilometres east of the resort zone, is where the local fish houses are - places buying direct from the Panama City Beach fleet for decades. Gulf red snapper filleted the same day it was caught tastes nothing like what arrives frozen on Front Beach Road. Ask your server if the catch is local; in the right season, it always is. Go at sunset, find a deck with a water view.

places.name: Paradise, WA

visits.text: If clouds hide the summit, the Henry M. Jackson Visitor Center helps you understand what you will see later at Paradise. Its exhibits and film introduce Mount Rainier and the park’s environments; staff also provide information about snow remaining on the trails. Stop here before choosing your hike, then divide your walks between your arrival afternoon and the following full day.

Still water sometimes reflects Mount Rainier at Reflection Lakes. These small subalpine lakes line Stevens Canyon Road near Paradise, and enjoying the designated viewpoints does not require a strenuous hike. The reflection depends on the light and the water’s surface and is never guaranteed. Make this stop as you leave Paradise for Enumclaw, without adding an out-and-back drive.

activities.text: A rocky valley draws your eye toward the ice on Nisqually Vista Trail. This loop at Paradise offers viewpoints of Nisqually Glacier and the valley it shaped while crossing subalpine meadows. The route is shorter than Skyline, but snow can change its difficulty. Save it for your arrival afternoon and stay on established paths to avoid damaging the flowers.

Devote the full day to Skyline Trail, which climbs from Paradise toward panoramic views of Mount Rainier and Nisqually Glacier. The loop also passes through the Myrtle Falls area, so there is no need to schedule a second visit to this waterfall. Meadows gradually give way to rockier terrain. Set out with water, food, and sun protection; turn back if snow or visibility makes it unclear whether you can safely continue.

places.name: Paris, TX

visits.text: A good-natured battle among the six U.S. cities named Paris: ours, in Texas, has its 20-meter Eiffel Tower with a 1.5-meter red cowboy hat installed at the top in 1998, as a reply to the Eiffel Tower in Paris, Tennessee, which had dared raise its own to 18 meters. Population 25,000, and yes, this is exactly the kind of thing you photograph on a road trip. Free, accessible 24/7, on Jefferson Road.

Built in 1866–1868 by Samuel Bell Maxey, a former Confederate general (trained at West Point) who became a two-term U.S. senator, the Sam Bell Maxey House is one of the few fully preserved 19th-century Texas homes. High Victorian Italianate style: tall windows with cornices, a portico, and a rooftop belvedere. The family lived there for 99 years, until donating it to the city in 1966. Over 10,000 original objects preserved. Tours $8, Wednesday–Saturday.

The South's most unexpected funerary sculpture: Willet Babcock's grave at Evergreen Cemetery (founded in 1866) is topped by a 4.6-meter monument depicting a Christ-like figure… wearing cowboy boots. Babcock, originally from Ithaca, New York, a former Union lieutenant during the Civil War, owned a furniture and coffin factory in Paris whose ground floor also served as a 1,200-seat opera house. He commissioned his monument from German sculptor Gustave Klein in 1880, eight years before his death. Nicknamed “Jesus in Cowboy Boots”, it's now Texas's most photographed tomb—some question the identification: no beard, a feminine face, and the figure leans on the cross instead of carrying it. Perhaps a mourning angel. Free, sunrise to sunset.

activities.text: A house cheeseburger at Jaxx Gourmet Burgers, or barbecue at Rib Crib, on the Downtown Square (the town's central square, as in all Texas towns). The square itself merits a stroll: Confederate monuments, a fountain, and restored commercial buildings from 1900.

places.name: Park, UT

visits.text: Park City nearly died twice: when the silver ran out, then when the mountain burned in 1898. Everything you see on Main Street was rebuilt after that fire. George Hearst—the press baron's father—made his fortune here with the Ontario Mine, bought for $30,000 and yielding over $50 million. The street is now lined with 200 shops and restaurants in those century-old buildings. Walk to the top: the view of the Wasatch is worth the climb.

Head down to the basement of the Park City Museum to see the 19th-century territorial jail cell—intact, bars and all. The museum occupies the old courthouse and traces the town's history from the silver boom to the 2002 Olympics. It's compact, well-done, and in one hour you'll understand why Park City survived when so many mining towns around it vanished.

Ten minutes north of Main Street, the Utah Olympic Park still hosts athletes training on the ski jumps and bobsled runs from the 2002 Olympics. You can watch from the stands for free. The Joe Quinney Museum traces Utah's Olympic history since the 1930s. Summer bobsled rides and zip-lining cost extra but are worth it if you're game.

activities.text: Take the Town Lift from Main Street—it drops you right onto Park City Mountain's trails. As soon as the snow melts (usually May-June), over 640 km of marked trails open for mountain biking and hiking. Rent a bike at the bottom of the street or come on foot: even an hour up high completely shifts your perspective on the town.

High West Saloon occupies a former 1906 stable on Park Avenue, one block from Main Street—originally Utah's first legal distillery since 1870. Order a Rendezvous Rye at the bar. If you want a guided tour and tasting at the current distillery, it is outside central Park City: plan a separate trip. With the mountains behind it, the saloon is a pleasant place to end the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Salt Lake City to Great Basin Road Trip: Desert, Salt & Stars

map_keywords: Park City Main Street Historic District

visits.text: Tablas Creek Vineyard, 9339 Adelaida Road: co-founded in 1989 by the Perrin family (Château de Beaucastel, Châteauneuf-du-Pape) and Robert Haas, an American importer. The Rhône varieties—Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Roussanne, Viognier—were imported directly from Beaucastel after mandatory quarantine. The estate is certified organic and biodynamic, and was the first American estate certified Regenerative Organic (2021). If you visit only one estate in Paso Robles, this is it—it's the region's most serious project.

Eberle Winery, 3810 Highway 46 East: Gary Eberle founded the winery in 1979, after helping with the first soil mapping in Paso for UC Davis. Paso Robles' first wine caves are here—about 1,500 m² of tunnels carved into the rock under the vines, accessible during the tour. A rarity in California today: tastings are free and will remain so as a matter of winery policy.

L'Aventure Winery, 2815 Live Oak Road: Stéphan Asseo, a Bordeaux winemaker, left Saint-Émilion in the late 1990s to settle in Paso with the idea of making blends without appellation constraints. The Estate Cuvée and Optimus have become Westside benchmarks. Visits by appointment only.

activities.text: Exploring downtown Paso Robles: downtown around City Park is less polished than Healdsburg or St. Helena. Independent cafes, secondhand shops, cowboy art galleries, a craft beer bar. It's California wine country before big money arrives—this probably won't last. The Saturday morning market is one of the Central Coast's liveliest.

Dinner at Les Petites Canailles, Paso Robles: French bistro run by French people, classic bistro cuisine (steak-frites, mussels, entrecôte), wine list mostly from Paso. The anachronism is delicious - eating French in Paso after a day of California Rhône Grenache. Reservation recommended on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: California Wine Country in 10 Days: San Francisco to Los Angeles Through the Vineyards

visits.text: Pawleys Island bills itself as "arrogantly shabby" - the official slogan since the 1980s, expressing a deliberately old-fashioned local aesthetic. It's one of America's oldest beach resorts, frequented as early as 1690 by rice planters fleeing inland mosquitoes. Six kilometers of beach, no seawall, no high-rise hotels. The famous Pawleys Island hammocks were invented here in 1889 by a riverboat captain, and are still hand-woven at the local Hammock Shops Village.

Brookgreen Gardens, 15 minutes north, is the world's largest garden of American figurative sculpture - 1,400 sculptures by 430 artists across 3,900 hectares of former rice plantations. Founded in 1931 by Anna Hyatt Huntington (herself a sculptor) and her husband Archer Huntington. Adjacent zoo with local fauna, bobcats, alligators, deer. Plan half a day. $22, ticket valid 7 days.

Myrtle Beach, about 44 km to the north, 40 minutes' drive, lacks the charm of Pawleys but is worth a look for the contrast: 100 km of wooden promenade, the Family Kingdom amusement park, a 60-meter SkyWheel ($180 per private gondola), and the kitsch aesthetic of 1960s neon signs. It is the Atlantic City of the South, to be seen for what it is. Spend 1-2 hours at most on the Boardwalk.

activities.text: Picnic at Huntington Beach State Park - 3 kilometers of flat sand, dunes planted with sea oats. The Moorish castle of Atalaya, built in 1931 by the Huntingtons (the same family behind Brookgreen) in the middle of the dune, can be toured for $2 and remains one of the coast's strangest residences. Park entrance $8.

Washington to Miami in 16 Days Along the American East Coast
US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

places.name: Pea Island, NC

visits.text: Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge has recorded more than 370 bird species on its thin strip of barrier island. At the visitor center, fixed spotting scopes point at North Pond, where thousands of ducks, geese and swans stop over in fall and winter. For raptors, aim for the fall migration: bald eagles and peregrine falcons pass through regularly.

activities.text: Walk the 800 meters of North Pond Wildlife Trail, from the Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge visitor center to a two-level observation tower. Along the way, a boardwalk crosses a pond full of freshwater turtles. Dogs are not allowed on this trail, and bring mosquito repellent if you continue around the pond.
