visits.text: Step back nearly 1,000 years at Pecos National Historical Park, where substantial ruins of Pecos Pueblo and a Spanish colonial mission church reveal centuries of cultural interaction and conflict in the American Southwest. The park preserves one of the largest and most important archaeological sites in the region, where the Pecos people built a thriving trade center connecting Plains and Pueblo cultures.

Walk among the massive adobe walls and reconstructed kiva structures that once housed a population of over 2,000 people at the height of Pueblo civilization. The adjacent mission ruins demonstrate Spanish colonial efforts to convert indigenous peoples, creating a layered historical landscape of profound significance for understanding the region's complex heritage.

activities.text: Explore the park's trails connecting archaeological sites with natural landscapes that supported human habitation for thousands of years. Interpretive exhibits explain the daily lives, spiritual practices, and eventual abandonment of this once-great pueblo, whose descendants now live among the Jemez Pueblo people.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Ancient Pueblos, White Sands and Ancestral Volcanoes

visits.text: A day's road trip through the countryside of central Iowa. First stop: Winterset, John Wayne's birthplace and above all Iowa's covered bridge capital; allow for a round trip by car from Pella, the overnight stop. Six bridges survive in Madison County, built between 1868 and 1884. Roseman Bridge is the best known—it features in the 1995 film with Meryl Streep and Clint Eastwood. Robert James Waller's novel sold 50 million copies. You can cross the bridge on foot and read the messages visitors have left on its interior walls.

Holliwell Bridge, the longest of the six (33 meters), spans the Middle River amid rolling prairie. Allow for the round trip by car from Pella. If you have time, also visit Cutler-Donahoe Bridge, which you can reach from Winterset's City Park without driving on a dirt road.

In downtown Winterset, visit the John Wayne Birthplace Museum; allow for the round trip by car from Pella. You can tour the modest four-room house where Marion Robert Morrison (his real name) was born in 1907, along with the adjacent museum, which holds personal belongings, film costumes and a collection of photographs.

Drive 1 hour 15 minutes east to Pella, a Dutch town transplanted to Iowa. The Vermeer Mill, built in 2002 by craftsmen from the Netherlands, is North America's tallest working windmill—37 meters. It still grinds grain. The Molengracht Canal downtown, with its gabled houses and tulips (in May), will make you feel like you've landed in the Netherlands. The Tulip Time Festival in May attracts 150,000 visitors.

activities.text: End the day with a Dutch pastry at one of Pella's bakeries—the letterbanketen (almond paste puff pastry sticks) and stroopwafels are homemade.

days_plan.itin_title: Iowa and Midwest Road Trip: Great Plains
A Different Side of Iowa: From Glacial Lakes to Mississippi Bluffs

places.name: Pensacola, FL

visits.text: 32,500 square metres. 150 aircraft. 4,000 artefacts. Free. The National Naval Aviation Museum at NAS Pensacola is the largest of its kind in the world, and it earns the title. NAS Pensacola opened in 1914 as the first naval air station in the United States - every Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard aviator has trained here. The NC-4 that crossed the Atlantic in 1919 is here. The only surviving aircraft from the Battle of Midway is here. In the Blue Angels Atrium, four A-4 Skyhawks hang in diamond formation above you. Since early 2026, public access has been limited to weekends - confirm the current policy before visiting.

Fort Pickens was completed in 1834, came through the Civil War without Confederate capture, and took on a darker role from 25 October 1886, when Geronimo and 15 Apache warriors stepped off a train in Pensacola under escort. Local businessmen had lobbied the government to send the prisoners here rather than to St. Augustine - for tourism. In February 1887, 459 visitors on a single Sunday paid 50 cents to stare through the bars of the casemate. Geronimo was moved to Alabama in 1888 and died at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, in 1909, still a prisoner. Part of Gulf Islands National Seashore; entrance fee applies, National Park pass accepted. The fort is less than an hour's drive from downtown Pensacola.

Palafox Street is where Pensacola's layered history shows up most clearly. A Spanish expedition landed near here in 1559 - 46 years before Jamestown - making this one of the oldest European-settled sites in North America. The five-block corridor mixes Spanish Colonial buildings with 19th-century commercial architecture; the Seville Quarter at the south end turns historic warehouses into live music venues after dark. Walk north to Christ Episcopal Church, then south toward the bay at sunset. The light on the brick in late afternoon is worth timing your day around.

activities.text: The western section of Santa Rosa Island - Fort Pickens Road inside Gulf Islands National Seashore, less than an hour's drive from downtown Pensacola - gives you 11 kilometres of protected Gulf beach with no resort buildings in sight. The quartz sand here was ground down from the Appalachian Mountains and carried south by rivers over millions of years; by mid-afternoon it turns white in a way that makes every other Florida beach look beige. Swim, walk the whole length, or rent a bike at the park entrance and ride the dune-line road along the Gulf.

The Fish House on Pensacola Bay has been sourcing local Gulf catch for 30 years and has a deck directly over the water. Last meal on the Panhandle: Gulf red snapper, local shrimp, maybe oysters from one of the farms rebuilding the region's shellfish culture. Get there before 6 p.m. to watch the sun drop behind the Pensacola Bay Bridge - a fitting end to a coast that started at a spring pumping 1.5 billion litres a day and finishes at the bay where naval aviators have been taking off since 1914.

days_plan.itin_title: Florida Panhandle: Tallahassee to Pensacola on the Emerald Coast

map_keywords: Fort Pickens Gulf Islands National Seashore

visits.text: Petit Jean State Park - Arkansas's First and Most Beloved State Park: Perched atop a flat-topped mountain bearing the name of a legendary French explorer's disguised lover, this park offers 95-foot Cedar Falls plunging into a misty canyon, ancient Native American rock shelters, and Seven Hollows Trail winding through otherworldly geological formations.

Cedar Falls - The Crown Jewel Cascade: Descend into Cedar Creek Canyon to witness water plummeting nearly 100 feet into an emerald pool surrounded by towering bluffs. The 2-mile round-trip hike rewards adventurers with one of Arkansas's most photographed natural wonders.

Rock House Cave & Native American Rock Shelters - Windows into Ancient Arkansas: Explore shallow caves where indigenous peoples sought shelter thousands of years ago, their presence still visible in mysterious petroglyphs etched into stone walls.

activities.text: Seven Hollows Trail - Journey Through a Wonderland of Stone: This 4.4-mile loop traverses seven distinct geological formations, from narrow canyons to natural bridges, through a primeval landscape that feels untouched by time.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

visits.text: Bands of pink and red fill the horizon at the Painted Desert overlooks in the northern section of Petrified Forest. The eroded landforms make the landscape’s layers immediately apparent. Stop here as you enter the park, then continue south; a few well-chosen viewpoints are enough without making repeated stops for similar views.

Puerco Pueblo is a reminder that Petrified Forest also preserves traces of human settlement amid its rocky landscapes. The short developed trail runs alongside the remains of an ancestral Pueblo village and offers views of petroglyphs. Walk to the southern part of the trail to look for them, without touching the carvings or climbing on walls or boulders.

If you enjoy spotting details, stop at the Newspaper Rock overlook in Petrified Forest. You can make out the carvings from the observation point, at a distance from the rocks that bear them. Bring binoculars instead of trying to get closer: the appeal is spotting several designs without entering the protected area.

From fossils to their original landscape, Rainbow Forest Museum places petrified logs within the park’s natural history. The paleontology exhibits complement what you have just seen outdoors and offer a break from the sun. Stop here before Giant Logs and leave enough time to exit the park before the gates close.

activities.text: You will descend into Blue Mesa’s bluish terrain on a 1.6 km loop. The banded clay hills and fragments of petrified wood change the perspective you had from the road. Save some energy for the final climb and bring water; the short distance does not eliminate the slope or sun exposure.

A forest with no standing trees: Crystal Forest displays its mineralized logs at ground level. The 1.2 km loop lets you get a close look at their colors and the crystals that gave the area its name. Observe the pieces where they lie, without collecting anything; photographing a fragment is the right way to take it home with you.

You will finish your journey through the park with a walk on Giant Logs, just behind Rainbow Forest Museum. The short loop features particularly massive petrified logs, including one nicknamed Old Faithful. There are steps along the trail: keep them in mind if you are traveling with a stroller or have difficulty walking, then head to Holbrook via the south exit.

days_plan.itin_title: Navajo Country in 10 Days: Sedona and Monument Valley

places.name: Philadelphia, PA

visits.text: You step inside the most important building in American history. It was in this room - the Pennsylvania State House, completed in 1753 - that 56 delegates signed the Declaration of Independence on August 4, 1776, and where the United States Constitution was adopted in 1787. Architect Andrew Hamilton, assisted by master builder Edmund Woolley, designed this red brick building in the Georgian style: symmetry, classical proportions, wooden steeple. Today a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, the building is managed by the National Park Service. Ranger-led tours last 30 minutes and depart every half hour - book online in advance, as morning slots fill quickly in high season.

The Liberty Bell is one of the most historically charged symbols of the United States, and its famous crack tells more than any text ever could. Commissioned in 1751 by the Pennsylvania Assembly to commemorate the 50th anniversary of William Penn's Charter of Privileges, the bell weighs 900 kilograms and bears an inscription from Leviticus: 'Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants Thereof.' It cracked permanently on George Washington's birthday in 1846 and has never rung since. It was the abolitionists of the 1830s who gave it the name 'Liberty Bell,' adopting its inscription as a banner against slavery. The Liberty Bell Center is open daily from 9am to 5pm, admission is free - arrive before 10am to avoid the security line.

Housed since 1893 in the former Reading Railroad train shed, this covered market is one of America's oldest operating food markets. Walk past more than 80 stalls run by local producers, Pennsylvania Dutch butchers, Amish bakers and food vendors from many different backgrounds. Amish vendors - present Wednesday through Saturday - sell pies, homemade pretzels, fresh cheese and preserves. The market is open daily from 8am to 6pm, with free admission. Arrive when it opens for a hot Philly cheesesteak before the lines grow long.

The Philadelphia Museum of Art is one of the largest museums in America, with more than 240,000 works covering 5,000 years of art history. Its monumental staircase, made world-famous by the 1976 film Rocky, has become a pilgrimage site in its own right - a bronze statue of Sylvester Stallone stands at the foot of the steps. Founded in 1876 for the Centennial Exposition, the Greek marble building dominates the city from atop Fairmount Hill. Its Impressionist collection - featuring Cézanne, Renoir, Duchamp - is among the best outside Europe. The museum is open Wednesday to Monday from 10am to 5pm, closed Tuesday; admission: $25 adult, online booking recommended on weekends.

The Mütter Museum is one of the most fascinating and most disturbing medical museums in the United States - a collection founded in 1858 by Dr. Thomas Dent Mütter, pioneering reconstructive surgeon, to train medical students in anatomy and pathologies. You discover anatomical specimens preserved in jars, wax casts of medical anomalies, the megacolon of a man who died from chronic constipation weighing 28 kilograms, thousands of skulls measured by physician-anthropologist Samuel Morton in the 19th century, and a histological slice of Einstein's brain. The museum is open daily 10am to 5pm, admission: $22 adult - booking strongly advised on weekends as admission is limited.

The 9th Street market, known as the Italian Market, is the oldest continuously operating outdoor market in the United States, established in the late 19th century by southern Pennsylvania Italian immigrants. Across six blocks of South Philly, fruit and vegetable stands, butchers, cheese shops, delicatessens, and bakeries succeed one another under metal awnings. The market was made world-famous by a scene in the 1976 film Rocky, where the boxer runs among the stalls at dawn. Today, Italian vendors neighbor Mexican, Vietnamese, and African groceries, faithfully reflecting the demographic evolution of South Philadelphia. Come in the morning for fresh produce.

The National Constitution Center, opened in 2003, is the only museum in the world devoted to the United States Constitution, signed three blocks away in 1787. Its interactive exhibitions trace the Founding Fathers' debates, the history of each amendment, and major American constitutional crises since 1791. Signers' Hall features life-size bronze statues of the 42 delegates who signed the Constitution, in their positions and with their supposed expressions at the moment of signing - you can photograph yourself among them. The permanent '1787' exhibition uses immersive technologies to recreate Constitutional Convention debates. Admission: $16 adult, open daily 9:30am to 5pm.

activities.text: The walk through Old City and Society Hill is the best way to understand what Philadelphia was before it became a metropolis. You stroll along Elfreth's Alley - 32 brick houses built between 1702 and 1836, designated a National Historic Landmark - then the cobbled streets of Society Hill, the residential quarter of 18th-century merchants and notables. Christ Church (1744) was the parish of George Washington and Benjamin Franklin. Go in late afternoon to catch the warm light on the brick facades and nearly deserted alleys.

Eastern State Penitentiary, opened in 1829, was the most famous - and most controversial - prison of the 19th-century America. Its architect, John Haviland, designed a seven-spoke radial plan allowing a single guard to monitor all corridors from a central point, a revolutionary concept at the time that influenced hundreds of prisons worldwide. Inmates were held in total isolation - a reformist method meant to encourage redemption. Al Capone was briefly incarcerated here in 1929; his cell has been reconstructed to show the relative comfort enjoyed by the mobster. Today partially in ruins, the prison offers audio-guided tours through cells overgrown with vegetation.

Rittenhouse Square, one of five original squares traced by William Penn on his 1682 plan, is the residential and cultural heart of bourgeois Philadelphia. The square is surrounded by some of the city's finest architectural facades - Second Empire buildings, brownstone mansions, and 1900s Beaux-Arts buildings. On weekdays, the square is the lunch spot for professionals from surrounding law firms and offices; on weekends, farmers markets and outdoor concerts animate it. The 20th Street art galleries concentrate some of Pennsylvania's best private galleries.

South Street has been Philadelphia's alternative artery since the 1960s, when rock and funk artists and musicians made it their reference neighborhood against urban renewal policies threatening the south side. Today, the street mixes vintage shops, outsider art galleries, world street food restaurants, bars, and clubs. The most singular attraction is Philadelphia's Magic Gardens (1020 South Street), a monumental mosaic created since 1994 by artist Isaiah Zagar on the facades, courtyards, and basements of a half-block, using tiles, mirrors, bottles, and found objects. Open Thursday-Monday 11am to 5pm, admission: $10.

visits.text: Start at the Desert Botanical Garden, set within Papago Park across 55 hectares. More than 50,000 plants fill the grounds, including multi-century-old saguaros and rare species you won't find anywhere else. Plan at least two hours to explore the trails—go early in the morning, before the heat sets in.

The Heard Museum (2301 North Central Avenue) deserves a half-day on its own. Its collection of over 40,000 objects—Navajo and Zuni jewelry, Hopi kachina dolls, textiles—traces the history of Southwestern Native peoples with rare precision. Don't miss the dance performances held on select evenings.

Roosevelt Row, the downtown arts district, is the best place to grasp Phoenix's creative energy. Giant murals, independent galleries, and local designer boutiques line the neighborhood. If you're there on the first Friday of the month, the First Friday Art Walk transforms the district into a street festival running until 10 p.m.

If you have time before returning the car, Taliesin West in Scottsdale is worth a detour: Frank Lloyd Wright built this winter camp in the Sonoran Desert starting in 1937, and it remained his main studio until his death in 1959. A visit shows how Wright integrated architecture into the desert landscape - angles, local materials and natural light shaped by the terrain.

Old Town Scottsdale, about twenty minutes from Phoenix, concentrates Western art galleries, turquoise shops, and a few blocks of early 20th-century adobe architecture. The district is pedestrian in the afternoon and pleasant to wander before heading back toward Phoenix.

activities.text: Late afternoon, climb Camelback Mountain via the Echo Canyon Trail—3.2 km with 270 m of elevation gain—for a panoramic view over the Phoenix basin before sunset. Bring water: the climb is short but steep.

In the evening, stay in Roosevelt Row for dinner. The neighborhood concentrates many of downtown's best restaurants, with cuisines ranging from Middle Eastern to Mexican influences—true to Arizona's melting pot.

The Japanese Friendship Garden (Ro Ho En) in downtown Phoenix is one of the city's most tranquil addresses: 3.5 acres of Japanese garden with koi ponds, waterfalls, and a tea house, designed in tribute to Phoenix's sister city, Himeji. A peaceful interlude before concluding the circuit.

places.name: Pierre, SD

visits.text: The South Dakota Cultural Heritage Center on Governors Drive is built into a hillside in the shape of a Lakota winter camp structure, and the architecture signals that this museum takes Indigenous history seriously. Exhibits run from 12,000-year-old Clovis points through the Lakota Nation to the Lewis and Clark passage in September 1804 — when the Corps had a tense armed standoff with Lakota warriors over upriver passage near present-day Fort Pierre. Out-of-state paid entry; South Dakota residents free. Plan 90 minutes.

Eight kilometers north of Pierre on Route 1804—literally named for the expedition—the Oahe Dam Visitor Center tells the story of the fourth-largest man-made reservoir in the United States. Construction ran from 1948 to 1962, when President Kennedy dedicated it; the dam displaced entire Lakota communities and submerged traditional lands beneath a 372 km reservoir stretching north to Bismarck. A small exhibit connects the dam to Lewis and Clark's river passage. The center is free, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Farm Island Recreation Area, 6 km east of Pierre on the Missouri, has the Lewis and Clark Family Center—a hands-on interpretive site open from Memorial Day to Labor Day where you can examine dugout canoe replicas and animal hides, and walk on the ground where the expedition camped. Across the river, a monument on the Fort Pierre levee marks the September 1804 confrontation with Chief Black Buffalo—an encounter that almost ended the expedition before it reached the Mandan villages.

activities.text: The South Dakota State Capitol grounds have the 1910 building at the center—47 hectares with an artesian-fed lake, the Fighting Stallions Memorial, and the Flaming Fountain veterans' memorial. The capitol interior has murals, tile work, and a rotunda that rewards a 30-minute self-guided walk. Everything on the grounds is free and accessible daily. Pierre is one of the least-visited state capitals in the country—the lack of crowds makes the building more accessible, not less interesting.

Lake Oahe stretches 372 km from Pierre north to Bismarck, and the Missouri River access points near Pierre offer some of the best walleye and northern pike fishing in the Great Plains. Shore fishing from Oahe Downstream Recreation Area is free. The 42 km Lewis and Clark Bicentennial Trail runs from Pierre along the river through rolling prairie and cottonwood groves—a gravel and dirt multi-use path where you're more likely to see white-tailed deer than another person.

days_plan.itin_title: Lewis & Clark Trail: St. Louis to Great Falls, Retracing the 1804 Expedition

map_keywords: South Dakota Cultural Heritage Center Pierre

visits.text: Dollywood — Experience Dolly Parton's theme park celebrating Appalachian culture with rides, shows, and craft demonstrations. The 60-hectare park features world-class roller coasters, traditional music, and Southern food opened in 1986.

Roaring Fork Motor Nature Trail — From Pigeon Forge, travel via Gatlinburg to drive this 9-kilometer one-way loop through old-growth forest, past log cabins and a mill. The narrow road follows mountain streams and gives access to short waterfall hikes. It closes in winter.

Grotto Falls — From Pigeon Forge, drive via Gatlinburg to the trailhead, then hike 4.3 kilometers round trip to the park’s only waterfall you can walk behind, with an 8-meter drop. The trail passes rhododendron thickets and hemlock forest. The access road closes in winter.

activities.text: Moonshine tasting — Sample legal Tennessee moonshine at Ole Smoky Distillery or others lining Gatlinburg's main strip. The clear corn liquor once made illegally in mountain stills now drives tourism.
Smoky Mountain pancake breakfast — Fuel up with buttermilk pancakes, country ham, and red-eye gravy at Pancake Pantry or similar institutions. The hearty Southern breakfast tradition sustains hikers.
Pigeon Forge evening show — Attend dinner theater featuring country music, comedy, or magic. The resort town offers family entertainment rivaling Branson, Missouri.

days_plan.itin_title: Tennessee Music & Mountains Road Trip: Nashville to Great Smoky Mountains

places.name: Pinedale, WY

visits.text: Detour to Fremont Lake, 7 km from Pinedale: the 7th deepest lake in the United States (212 m) and 2nd largest natural lake in Wyoming. Its translucent waters reflect the granite ridges of the Wind River Range. The marina overlook offers a panorama of peaks exceeding 4,000 m—a quick stop but a memorable one.

Take Skyline Drive from Pinedale: 23 km to the Elkhart Park Trailhead at an elevation of 2,750 m. The overlook just before the road ends offers the best car-accessible panorama of the Wind River Range—Fremont Peak (4,191 m) and seven other summits over 4,000 m identified on an interpretive sign. In autumn, the aspens turn gold in September.

days_plan.itin_title: Colorado-Wyoming Road Trip: National Parks, Rockies & Wide Open Spaces

map_keywords: Skyline Drive Elkhart Park Pinedale Wyoming

visits.text: Pinnacle Mountain State Park - The Pyramid Rising from the Valley: This striking 308-meter cone-shaped summit dominates the horizon west of Little Rock, offering two distinct trails to its rocky apex. The West Summit Trail challenges hikers with a boulder-scrambling adventure, while the East Summit provides a gentler ascent through 800 hectares of pristine Arkansas wilderness.

activities.text: Sunset Summit Experience - Watch the River Valley Ignite in Golden Light: Time your ascent to reach the exposed rock summit as daylight fades, witnessing the Arkansas River Valley transform into a canvas of amber and crimson stretching to distant mountain ridges.

Arboretum & Nature Trails - 28 Hectares of Botanical Discovery: Wander through diverse ecosystems from wetlands to hardwood forests, where interpretive trails reveal the flora that earned Arkansas its “Natural State” designation.

days_plan.itin_title: Arkansas Road Trip: Ozark Mountains and Hot Springs

places.name: Pittsburgh, PA

visits.text: The two Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh occupy the same monumental building on Forbes Avenue, built starting in 1895 thanks to philanthropy from Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish immigrant who became Pittsburgh's steel magnate. The Museum of Art holds more than 34,000 works emphasizing contemporary art and photography - it's considered America's first contemporary art museum. The Museum of Natural History is famous for its dinosaur collection, including several specimens discovered during expeditions financed by Carnegie himself in the late 19th century. The minerals and gems hall, the Ancient Egypt section, and the public paleontology lab ('Paleolab') are among the most popular attractions. Buy the combo ticket online in advance; allow 3 to 4 hours for both museums.

The Strip District is Pittsburgh's liveliest and most authentic neighborhood, wedged between the Allegheny River and a railroad track. In the 19th century, it was the industrial quarter par excellence: Andrew Carnegie launched his first steel mills here, ALCOA began its commercial aluminum production here, and George Westinghouse built his first air brake workshops here. Since the 1990s, the Strip has converted into an international food and cultural market: Primanti Brothers (legendary sandwiches with fries included in the bread), Wholey's Fish Market, Pennsylvania Macaroni Company, and dozens of ethnic groceries line Smallman Street. The Heinz History Center, Pennsylvania's largest history museum, is also located here. Come on a Saturday morning for maximum atmosphere.

The Andy Warhol Museum is the largest American museum dedicated to a single artist - seven floors presenting the work of Andrew Warhola, born in Pittsburgh in 1928 to Slovak immigrant parents. The collection of 900 paintings, 77 sculptures, and 4,000 photographs covers Warhol's entire career: Campbell's soup screen prints, portraits of Marilyn Monroe and Mao Zedong, his experimental films, and multimedia installations. The museum also displays Warhol's personal archives - his notebooks, polaroids, notes - revealing the lesser-known side of this Pittsburgh native who remained attached to the city until the end. Open Wednesday-Sunday 10am to 5pm, admission: $20 adult.

The Heinz History Center is Pennsylvania's largest history museum and a Smithsonian Institution affiliate - a rare affiliation that guarantees collection quality and rigor. Installed since 1996 in a former refrigeration plant in the Strip District, on the very street where Andrew Carnegie started his first steel mills in the 1870s, the museum covers 250 years of regional history on six floors. The permanent exhibition traces the rise of the steel empire, the period of mass immigration (Pittsburgh welcomed successive waves of Irish, Poles, Italians, and African-Americans between 1870 and 1940), and inventions that came out of the city - radio, aluminum, polio vaccine. The section dedicated to Pittsburgh sports culture (Steelers, Pirates, Penguins) is equally remarkable. Admission: $18 adult.

The Phipps Conservatory, built in 1893 in the Oakland neighborhood, is one of the finest Victorian greenhouses in the United States, gifted to Pittsburgh by businessman Henry Phipps, Andrew Carnegie's associate. Its metal and glass architecture - 2,300 square meters of glazed surfaces - houses themed greenhouses of tropical plants, desert cacti, orchids, giant ferns, and carnivorous plants. Seasonal floral displays change several times per year and attract photographers from around the world. The conservatory is also one of the most sustainable museums in the United States, LEED Platinum certified for its environmental initiatives. Admission: $20 adult, open daily 9:30am to 5pm.

The Mattress Factory is a contemporary art museum installed in a former mattress factory in Pittsburgh's Mexican neighborhood - and it's one of the most original art museums in the United States. Since 1977, it has invited artists to create permanent or temporary installations in its industrial spaces, some of which have become worldwide references. Yayoi Kusama's 1996 permanent installation, 'Repetitive Vision,' is one of the first 'Infinity Rooms' the Japanese artist has created worldwide - and one of the few accessible to the public in a permanent museum context. The institution presents about ten immersive installations simultaneously in its three interconnected buildings. Admission: $25, open Wednesday-Sunday 10am-5pm.

activities.text: The Duquesne Incline is one of two funiculars still operating in Pittsburgh - cables pulling up the hillside that transported residents from the lower industrial quarter to Mount Washington's residential neighborhoods since 1877. From the summit, the panoramic view of the 'Confluence of the Three Rivers' - Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio - is Pittsburgh's most famous, and for good reason: it's precisely this strategic triangle of land that the French and English fought over in the 18th century, giving birth to Fort Duquesne then Fort Pitt. Go at sunset for the city lights coming on over the bridges.

Point State Park occupies the exact point where the Allegheny and Monongahela join to form the Ohio - one of the most strategic geographic points in all of pre-colonial North America. It was here that the French built Fort Duquesne in 1754, the English renamed it Fort Pitt in 1758, and this position became the pivot of control over the entire continental interior. The monumental fountain at the point's end, active May through October, propels water 40 meters high. The Fort Pitt Museum in the park displays models of the original fortifications and Seven Years' War artifacts.

Pittsburgh is home to one of Pennsylvania's most active craft brewing scenes, with more than 20 independent breweries throughout the city. Church Brew Works, installed since 1996 in Lawrenceville's Saint John the Baptist Church (1902), is probably the most visually impressive: shiny copper vats sit beneath Gothic vaults, barrels occupy the side naves. East End Brewing, in industrial warehouse mode in Pittsburgh's East End strip, is the local reference with its seasonal ales and lively outdoor courtyard. City Brew Tours organizes 3-hour guided minibus tours with tastings at several breweries - online booking required.

Pittsburgh has 446 bridges, and seeing them from the water is a rewarding way to explore the city. Gateway Clipper Fleet runs sightseeing cruises from Station Square along the banks of the three rivers, under the city's distinctive yellow bridges and past views of Mount Washington from water level. The daytime cruise lasts two hours; the Friday and Saturday evening cruise includes a musical performance.

places.name: Porcupine Mountains, MI

visits.text: Park the car at the end of the forest road and walk ten minutes to the overlook. Lake of the Clouds opens up before you: a mountain lake perched in a forest clearing in the Porcupine Mountains, ringed by maples, beeches and birches. The state park preserves 15,000 hectares of old-growth forest untouched by logging since the pre-industrial era—one of the last tracts of primary forest east of the Mississippi. In autumn, when the maples turn red, this panorama ranks among the Midwest's finest. Arrive early in the morning to catch the mist on the lake.

The Presque Isle River tumbles in a succession of waterfalls and rapids before pouring into Lake Superior - five named cascades in a few kilometers, connected by a 3 km loop trail with suspension bridges over the gorges. You cross Manabezho Falls, Manido Falls, Nawadaha Falls - Ojibwe names, like all the toponymy of this region. The water is tinted tannic brown by decomposing leaves, making the rapids resemble a Scottish river under stormy skies. Don't miss the suspension bridge at the mouth where the river meets the lake - the contrast is striking.

The trail descending from the Lake of the Clouds overlook to the Big Carp River crosses 5 kilometers of old-growth forest without crossing a road—trees over 300 years old, spongy ground covered in moss and ferns, no sound except the wind and birds. Here you understand why the Porkies, as locals call them, are among the few true wilderness areas in the eastern United States. Black bears frequent the park—rangers recommend making noise while hiking.

activities.text: Summit Peak is the highest point in the Porcupine Mountains. The observation platform at the summit offers a 360° panorama: old-growth forest in every direction, Lake Superior to the north like a sea without a horizon, and, on a clear day, Wisconsin visible in the distance. The northern lights can be observed from this spot on around ten nights a year in autumn and winter - the Upper Peninsula lies at the edge of the magnetic zone where they become frequent.

The Porcupine Mountains park preserves 15,000 hectares of old-growth forest untouched by logging since the pre-industrial era—one of the last tracts of primary forest east of the Mississippi. The maples, beeches and basswoods grow too wide to wrap your arms around. The Union Spring Trail leads in 3 km to a natural mineral spring that's been gushing from a rock fissure for millennia. Leave early in the morning to hear woodpeckers and owls before the sun climbs higher.

places.name: Port Alsworth, AK

visits.text: Port Alsworth is a hamlet of about fifty residents perched on the shore of Lake Clark—it's the only inhabited center in the national park and the logical starting point for exploring the surrounding 4 million acres. The NPS Visitor Center is here, with rangers available to orient your hikes. Stop in as soon as you arrive: terrain conditions change quickly and rangers know which areas have active bears.

Tanalian Falls—a 9-meter cascade tumbling over ancient lava flows through birch forest—is accessible via a 6.5-km round-trip trail from Port Alsworth. The path cuts through birch groves that turn golden in autumn and dense conifer forests in summer. Lake Kontrashibuna on the return loop offers perfect reflections of the Chigmit Range on calm days.

Lake Clark stretches 67 km against a backdrop of snow-capped peaks and active volcanoes—Mount Redoubt (3,108 m) and Mount Iliamna (3,053 m) dominate the southern horizon. The park was designated in 1980 in part to protect the salmon spawning grounds that constitute one of the most important sources in the Bristol Bay basin. From the shore at Port Alsworth, the reflections of the Chigmit Range in the turquoise water are worth the flight alone.

activities.text: The coastal areas of Silver Salmon Creek and Chinitna Bay, accessible by floatplane from Port Alsworth, are among Alaska's best spots for observing coastal brown bears. In spring and summer, bears dig in the mud for clams or graze on salt marsh grasses. Local operators from Port Alsworth run day trips—expect 3 to 5 hours on-site.

Kayaking on Lake Clark from Port Alsworth—rent on-site or through lodges. Waters are usually calm in the morning, allowing you to approach wild shorelines where moose and bald eagles are common. For anglers, arctic char, rainbow trout, and arctic grayling abound in the Tanalian River, 200 meters from the lodge.

visits.text: Olympic National Park — Hurricane Ridge — Allow about a 45-minute drive from Port Angeles to reach this viewpoint at 1,631 meters, with panoramic views of the Olympic Mountains and the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Wildflower meadows bloom from July to August while black-tailed deer graze on the alpine slopes.

Olympic National Park Visitor Center — In Port Angeles, visit the Olympic National Park Visitor Center to find trails at Hurricane Ridge and wooded valleys accessible from the city. Exhibits introduce the park’s temperate rainforests, mountains and coast before you set out on the trails.

Madison Falls — From Port Angeles, head into the Elwha Valley and walk from the Madison Falls parking area to this waterfall at the foot of a wooded cliff. The short trail lets you see the river and damp vegetation of Olympic National Park without crossing the entire peninsula.

activities.text: Sol Duc Hot Springs — Soak in natural mineral pools ranging from 37-40°C surrounded by old-growth forest. The three developed pools fed by underground springs offer relaxation after hiking Olympic trails.

Lake Crescent scenic drive — Navigate the winding highway along this glacially-carved fjord-like lake reaching 190 meters deep. The crystalline blue waters reflect surrounding peaks and forests in this pristine alpine setting.

Port Angeles waterfront dinner — Sample fresh halibut and clam chowder with views across the Strait of Juan de Fuca to Vancouver Island's mountains. The working port town serves as gateway to Olympic National Park.

places.name: Port St Joe, FL

visits.text: Dr. Beach ranked it number one in the United States in 2002. Under the rules of that ranking, the title can't be awarded twice - so St. Joseph Peninsula quietly dropped off the list and stayed little visited. The park is a little over half an hour's drive from Port St. Joe. Sixteen kilometres of white quartz sand, tall dunes, no high-rise buildings. The 1,098-hectare park at Cape San Blas also protects more than 240 bird species, three species of nesting sea turtles and the endangered St. Andrews beach mouse. Hurricane Michael cut the peninsula in two in 2018; the breach has since filled in and a new road links the two halves again. Book the cottages months ahead - spring weekends sell out from January.

The bay side of St. Joseph Peninsula is a different beach from the Gulf side - calm, shallow, protected, the water over seagrass beds so clear it looks unreal. The 45-minute Maritime Hammock Trail connects the campground to a sheltered cove where bay scallops feed in the grass at your feet. In late summer and early fall, local boaters anchor here specifically for scalloping season. Eagle Harbor concession rents kayaks and canoes seasonally. Low tide gives the best underwater visibility.

Port St. Joe's Constitution Convention Museum State Park stands on the site where Florida's first constitution was drafted in 1838, seven years before the state joined the Union. It is one of the first two museum buildings constructed by the Florida Park Service - the other is the Gorrie Museum you saw yesterday in Apalachicola. A short stop that weaves a coherent thread through the political history you began at the Capitol in Tallahassee. Small admission fee; thirty minutes is enough.

activities.text: Fifteen kilometres of paved path run the length of Cape San Blas, connecting the state park at one end to the Cape San Blas village at the other. At certain points the peninsula is barely 180 metres wide - you look left at the Gulf of America, right at St. Joseph Bay, and see two different blues simultaneously. Bikes rent at Scallop Cove near Eagle Harbor. Go in the morning before the heat.

Between May and October, loggerhead and green sea turtles haul up onto this Gulf-side beach to nest. Rangers mark every nest and monitor every emergence. The rule is absolute: no artificial lights on the beach at night - flashlights, phone screens - because the glow disorients nesting females and hatchlings making their run to the sea. Check the park website for ranger-led turtle watches on select summer evenings. They fill quickly.

visits.text: The Old Port's cobblestone streets run down to the water, and the smell of low tide and lobster rolls hits you before you reach Commercial Street. This district - a working waterfront flanked by 19th-century brick buildings on the National Register of Historic Places - burned to the ground in 1866 and rebuilt almost overnight. Today Fore, Middle, and Exchange Streets pack in fishmongers, breweries, and galleries with barely a chain in sight. If you're staying the night, Tommy's Park at Middle and Exchange has the city's visitor information booth.

Founded in 1882, the Portland Museum of Art holds a collection of works by Winslow Homer - Homer spent the last 27 years of his life at Prouts Neck, just along the coast, and the museum owns 17 of his paintings. The main building was designed in 1983 by I.M. Pei, a striking granite cube linked to the McLellan House of 1801. The Payson Collection on the upper floor brings together works by Renoir, Degas and Monet. Closed on Mondays and Tuesdays; allow 1.5 to 2 hours.

Drive 15 minutes south to Fort Williams Park in Cape Elizabeth and you will find yourself at the foot of Portland Head Light, commissioned by George Washington in 1787 and first lit in January 1791. It is the oldest lighthouse in Maine. Edward Hopper painted it in 1927; that watercolour now hangs in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts. The tower itself opens to the public only once a year (Maine Open Lighthouse Day in September), but the grounds and the museum in the former keeper's house are open from spring to autumn.

Victoria Mansion on Danforth Street is the finest surviving example of Italian villa-style architecture in the United States - built between 1858 and 1860 for hotelier Ruggles Sylvester Morse, and untouched since. Original frescoed ceilings, stenciled walls, carved woodwork, and Gustave Herter-designed furniture give you a complete snapshot of high Victorian taste. Even the draperies are original. Tours run about 45 minutes and cover details no placard can convey.

Portland Observatory on Munjoy Hill is the only surviving maritime signal tower in the United States, built in 1807 by Lemuel Moody to alert merchants to incoming ships. From the octagonal cupola - 86 steps up - the view sweeps across Casco Bay, the harbor islands, the White Mountains on a clear day, and the full Portland peninsula below. The tower is engineered from a single continuous piece of interlocking timber.

The Eastern Promenade on Munjoy Hill is Portland's great waterfront park - 78 acres of lawn, trails, and shoreline overlooking Casco Bay. The paved trail runs 2.5 miles from the Old Port along the waterfront to Back Cove, with benches facing east toward the ocean. This is where Portland comes to watch the sun rise over the harbor islands and the lobster boats go out. In summer the park hosts free Concerts at the Promenade.

activities.text: Portland runs on lobster and craft beer, and the Old Port puts both within easy reach. Eventide Oyster Co. on Middle Street helped put Portland on the national food map - their brown butter lobster roll, served on a Chinese bao bun, has been called the best in New England. Around the corner, Fore Street restaurant has been sourcing from Maine farms since 1996 and wood-fires almost everything. Book well in advance for both, especially July and August.

Casco Bay Lines runs a ferry service from the Old Port to the archipelago of islands in the bay - Peaks Island is the closest, 20 minutes away, with bikes for hire and a small museum devoted to Civil War history. The Great Chebeague ferry takes about 45 minutes and drops you on an island with a tiny general store. Check the timetable before setting off: departures become much scarcer outside the summer season.

Portland's food scene goes well beyond lobster rolls, although those remain compulsory. The Public Market House on Monument Square brings together local vendors selling Maine cheese, charcuterie and bread. Around it, the Congress Street Arts District is lined with independent restaurants, and a few blocks further south Eventide serves its brown-butter lobster on Middle Street. For a last-night dinner, Fore Street's wood-fired menu has set the standard for Maine farm-to-table dining since chef Sam Hayward opened it in 1996.

Portland's craft brewery scene is worth an afternoon of its own. Allagash Brewing on Industrial Way, one of the breweries that put American craft beer on the map with its Belgian-style White Ale, offers free tours Friday through Sunday. Bissell Brothers on Thompson's Point fills a converted industrial space and keeps roughly 15 beers on tap. Both are a short drive from downtown.

places.name: Portland, OR

visits.text: On May 18, 1980 at 8:32am, a magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggers the largest landslide ever recorded, instantly depressurizing Mount St. Helens' magma chamber. The lateral blast—never scientifically observed before that day—levels 600 km² of forest in minutes: thousands of trees ripped out and piled like matchsticks, all pointing in the same direction. The ash column rises to 24 km altitude in 15 minutes. 57 dead. David Johnston, 30, USGS volcanologist, transmits at 8:32: “Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!” Body never recovered. Harry Truman, 83, lodge owner on Spirit Lake, refused to evacuate: “If the mountain goes, I'm going with it.” Buried under 50 meters of mud with his 16 cats. Body never recovered. Since May 2023, Johnston Ridge Observatory (north side) has been closed following a landslide—check fs.usda.gov before departure.

Enter Ape Cave (46.1097, -122.2106) at a constant 4°C, headlamp mandatory. This 3,970-meter lava tube—the 3rd longest in North America—formed 2,000 years ago when a flow hardened on the surface before draining from the interior. The walk takes an hour and a half, silence and cold are absolute. Permit $5 + reservation on recreation.gov—mandatory and often booked out the day before for the next day.

Multnomah Falls (45.5762, -122.1158) in the Columbia River Gorge drops 189 meters in two tiers—the 2nd tallest year-round waterfall in the United States. The 1914 stone bridge spans the first tier at mid-height and gives the best view of both falls simultaneously. The Columbia Gorge (45.6917, -121.9092) stretches 130 km between 1,200-meter basalt cliffs. Free access, parking $5.

Enter Powell's City of Books (45.5232, -122.6817), 1005 W Burnside Street, through any door and get lost—it's the intended effect since 1971. The world's largest independent bookstore sprawls across 6,600 m² and a million new and used books mixed together in nine color-coded rooms. Portland is a city that reads, and Powell's is the most convincing physical proof. Two hours minimum if books hold you.

Cross through Lan Su Chinese Garden (45.5253, -122.6726), 239 NW Everett Street—65 artisans from Suzhou built this garden in 2000 on 0.4 hectares in the heart of Portland. Ponds, pavilions, calligraphy, authentic Suzhou architecture. A perfect anachronism in a neighborhood of industrial brick. Ticket $14.

End at Voodoo Doughnut (45.5226, -122.6731), 22 SW 3rd Avenue—offbeat donuts since 2003 (Bacon Maple Bar with real grilled bacon on top, Captain My Captain with Cap'n Crunch, explicit phallic shapes). Portland institution, guaranteed line, $3-7 per donut. It's the most fitting trip ending for a circuit that began in Seattle's mist.

activities.text: Mount St. Helens now measures 2,549 meters—400 meters less than before the eruption, the summit blown off in seconds. A lava dome reformed between 2004 and 2008 inside the crater, proof the volcano remains active. Geologists consider a future eruption likely within the century. Allow three hours minimum between the lava tube, viewpoints, and the Forest Learning Center (46.3164, -122.5881) en route, free, with excellent films on the 1980 eruption.

Reach Portland via I-5 (2h from St. Helens), or make the one-hour detour via the Historic Columbia River Highway—Vista House at Crown Point (45.5394, -122.2416) gives a view over the Columbia 230 meters below from a circular lookout built in 1918, one of the trip's finest perspectives.

Have lunch at Cart Blocks in central Portland: this food cart pod hosts several vendors who left the former SW 10th & Alder site after it closed. Look over the counters before choosing lunch and take a seat there. It is a way to experience Portland's food cart culture without searching for a pod that no longer exists.

Return the car at PDX (45.5887, -122.5969), 20 minutes from downtown. Total car budget for the stay: $700-1,000 for 7 days one-way rental Seattle-Portland, $40-100 one-way drop fee included depending on rental company.

places.name: Portsmouth, NH

visits.text: Strawbery Banke Museum consists of houses that remain on their original lots, rather than an entirely relocated village. This open-air museum tells the story of the residents, trades, and changes that shaped the Puddle Dock neighborhood. Check the day’s schedule to choose between exploring on your own and taking a guided tour, then leave time for the gardens.

If historic interiors interest you, book a visit to Moffatt-Ladd House & Garden. The tour considers both the lives of the owners and those of the enslaved people who also lived in the house. The advertised guided tours last forty-five minutes; days and arrangements differ on weekends, so check before visiting.

activities.text: Finish your stop at Prescott Park, on the banks of the Piscataqua River. Its gardens occupy land acquired by the Prescott sisters and later bequeathed to the city for public use. Stroll among the flower beds and wharves; fall blooms vary, but the river views remain the main appeal of this break.

visits.text: In 1783, the American government fit inside a university building: Nassau Hall hosted the Congress of the Confederation. This Princeton facade therefore deserves more than a photo stop between two cities. View it from the public areas of campus; don’t count on an interior visit without checking access options.

If you want a quieter break from the highway, the Princeton University Art Museum offers a free stop in the heart of campus. Its collections bring together works from several continents and eras, making it far more than a gallery just for students. Choose a few galleries; on Sundays, the museum is open from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m.

visits.text: Marvel at Providence Canyon, Georgia's 'Little Grand Canyon' where vivid walls of red, orange, pink, and white sandstone rise dramatically above wildflower-lined trails and pine forests. Poor farming practices in the 1800s triggered erosion that carved these spectacular formations, transforming agricultural failure into geological wonder. The Canyon Loop Trail winds through the colorful gorges offering photographers extraordinary compositions.

Discover rusted vintage automobiles from the 1950s along the quirky White Blaze Trail, abandoned relics slowly being reclaimed by the surrounding forest. Backcountry camping sites allow overnight visitors to see canyon walls glowing golden at sunrise and sunset. This unexpected Southwestern landscape feels transported from Arizona to rural Georgia.

activities.text: Hike through pine-scented woods to remote backcountry campsites where crackling campfires beneath starry skies create unforgettable wilderness experiences. The park's dramatic terrain changes character throughout the day as shifting sunlight paints the multicolored canyon walls in ever-changing hues.

places.name: Providence, RI

visits.text: Benefit Street, nicknamed the "Mile of History," displays one of the greatest concentrations of Colonial and Victorian houses in the United States on a single stretch. Walk it slowly: the First Baptist Church in America (1775) is the third church built by the congregation founded in 1636 by Roger Williams, Providence's founder. Brown University, founded in 1764, was the first American college to admit students regardless of religious affiliation.

The RISD Museum deserves more than a quick pass—devote at least an hour to it. Its 100,000 works span antiquity to the present in a building adjoining the campus of the nation's most prestigious design school. Asian ceramics, French Impressionism, American industrial design: the quality far exceeds what you'd expect from a city this size.

Before departing for the Cape, climb to Prospect Terrace Park for the best view of Providence: a statue of Roger Williams contemplates the city from College Hill. Five minutes, no more—then hit the road.

activities.text: Don't miss WaterFire if the dates align: at sunset, more than 80 braziers ignite in the middle of the Woonasquatucket, Moshassuck, and Providence rivers, carried by silent torchbearers on boats. Created by Barnaby Evans (Brown, class of 1975) in the 1990s, the event attracts nearly a million visitors per year. Calendar of "full lightings" on waterfire.org—May through November.

End the evening on Federal Hill, a 10-minute walk from downtown: pasta restaurants, delis, and cafés under string lights await you in Providence's Italian neighborhood. The arch at the entrance to DePasquale Square bears the pigna, a pinecone symbol of welcome from Naples.

Prospect Terrace Park Providence Rhode Island

visits.text: At Plimoth Patuxet Museums (137 Warren Avenue, combined ticket $38, allow 3 hrs), two worlds face each other on the same grounds. On one side, a reconstructed 1627 Pilgrim village with actors speaking Elizabethan English who refuse to acknowledge anything later than 1627. On the other, a reconstruction of a Wampanoag village with Native Americans who speak in the role of their ancestors. What is often forgotten: only 53 of the 102 Mayflower passengers survived the first winter of 1620-1621, the others carried off by scurvy, pneumonia and malnutrition. The Thanksgiving of November 1621 celebrated the first successful harvest - made possible because the Wampanoag had taught the survivors how to farm.

The Mayflower II at Pilgrim Memorial State Park is an exact replica of the 1620 ship, built in 1955 in England and sailed across the Atlantic in 1957. 27 meters long, 7 meters wide—seeing it in person makes you realize how improbable it is that 102 people crossed the Atlantic aboard it in November. Ticket $18, 45 minutes.

Plymouth Rock is probably the most documented tourist disappointment in the United States. The rock is small, cracked since it was broken in 1774 during an attempt to move it, and no historical evidence confirms that the Pilgrims actually stepped on it. Two minutes under the neoclassical dome is enough—but those two minutes are necessary, if only to understand what Americans do with their founding myths.

Few people know the Pilgrims landed in Provincetown first—on November 11, 1620—before deciding to continue south to Plymouth. The Pilgrim Monument on High Pole Hill commemorates this landing: 77 meters of solid granite, the tallest granite structure in the United States, built between 1907 and 1910. You climb via 120 steps and ramps. A 360° view over Cape Cod and Massachusetts Bay, and on clear days Boston, 60 km away. Ticket $20 (includes the museum at the base), allow 1 hour.

North of Provincetown, the Province Lands cover 6,000 hectares of shifting dunes protected since 1961 within Cape Cod National Seashore. Race Point Beach: 20 km of white sand, 30-meter dunes, and between May and October, humpback whales visible from the beach—no boat needed, just binoculars. The Province Lands Visitor Center has a panoramic terrace overlooking the dunes. Park admission $25/car/day.

Commercial Street stretches for 5 km—Eugene O'Neill performed his first plays here in the 1910s, Jackson Pollock painted here, Tennessee Williams lived here every summer. It's the best place for people-watching in New England, and the most colorful stop on the circuit.

activities.text: Lunch at Plymouth harbor at Wood's Seafood—clam chowder and lobster roll, $25–40. Then drive toward Cape Cod via US-6 to the Sagamore Bridge (1935) over the Cape Cod Canal: a view of the canal from the bridge deck as you enter the peninsula. Cape Cod extends 100 km into the Atlantic in the shape of a bent arm—the Outer Cape at the tip, for the dunes and the light that inspired Edward Hopper.

Arrive in Provincetown in the late afternoon: 3,000 residents in winter, 60,000 in summer, a major art scene since the early 20th century and New England's gay capital. Get your bearings along Commercial Street, which runs for 5 km along the harbor. Spiritus Pizza on the harbor, open late, $15–25—simple and good.

Dolphin Fleet Whale Watch from MacMillan Pier: 4 hours at sea heading to the Stellwagen Banks, 40 km offshore, with commentary from naturalists. Humpback whale sightings are nearly guaranteed between May and October. $70 per adult, departures every 2 hours. If you've never seen whales, Cape Cod offers one of the highest sighting rates in the world—hard to find a better opportunity.

Alternative or addition: the Cape Cod Rail Trail, whose nearest access point is about thirty minutes' drive from Provincetown - 35 km of bike path on the former railway line through forests, ponds and villages. Bike rental $35-50/day at P-Town Bikes. Lunch in Provincetown at The Lobster Pot (321 Commercial Street), open since 1979, lobster bisque and baked stuffed lobster, $30-60 - a line is guaranteed but the price is fair.

visits.text: The North Carolina State Capitol in downtown Raleigh deserves a quick stop on your route to Charlotte. This gray granite building in neoclassical style completed in 1840 houses, in its rotunda, a copy of the Washington statue by Houdon. Raleigh was founded in 1792 specifically as the state capital, on neutral ground chosen for its central location in North Carolina.

Fayetteville Street, a one-kilometer thoroughfare between the Capitol and the Convention Center, is the backbone of Uptown Raleigh. Have lunch in the area before getting back on the road: The Pit serves North Carolina-style vinegar barbecue there.

places.name: Rangeley, ME

visits.text: Stop at Height of Land on Route 17, about thirty minutes' drive south of Rangeley, and the view opens up without warning: Mooselookmeguntic Lake and Upper Richardson Lake stretch far below, hemmed in by wooded ridges reaching west to the White Mountains on the New Hampshire border. It is the highest point of any numbered state road in Maine. The Appalachian Trail crosses right here - on summer days you will find long-distance hikers in the parking area, with huge packs, heading north. Stone seats and interpretive panels make it a stop in its own right, not just a windscreen view.

Off Dodge Pond Road, the Wilhelm Reich Museum sits on the hilltop property called Orgonon, where Austrian psychiatrist Wilhelm Reich studied what he called “orgone energy” - a universal life force he believed permeated all living matter and the atmosphere. The FDA seized and destroyed his books and equipment in 1956; he died in federal prison in 1957. The 1949 stone observatory and his second-floor study, library, and laboratory look exactly as he left them - original mid-century furniture and scientific apparatus. Trails lace the largely forested 175-acre property, with views over Rangeley Lake.

The Outdoor Heritage Museum near Oquossoc preserves the sporting history of the Rangeley Lakes region: a reconstructed log sporting camp from 1900, exhibits on the brook trout (10-12 lb.) caught here in the 1880s, the famous Rangeley boat (a locally designed rowing craft), and a gallery devoted to fly tier Carrie Stevens, whose streamer flies in the 1920s spread Rangeley's fishing fame across New England. Free exhibits on the front lawn invite a stop even when the museum is closed.

activities.text: Saddleback Mountain's summit sits at 3,985 feet, reached via the Appalachian Trail in about 4 miles from the trailhead on Saddleback Mountain Road - not the ski area, a different GPS entry. Above treeline for the last mile, the open ridge walk between the main summit and The Horn is one of the finest in western Maine. Budget 5-7 hours round trip. The ski area at the base reopened in 2020 after a long closure.

Rangeley Lake at 1,516 feet of elevation, surrounded entirely by forest, rewards a morning on the water. Canoe and kayak rentals from Ecopelagicon Nature Store on Pond Street put you on Haley Pond with direct paddling access to the main lake. Loons are common; bald eagles occasionally circle the western shore. The town beach on Main Street has a free boat launch.

places.name: Rapid, SD

visits.text: Drop your bags, then head straight to the Museum of Geology on the South Dakota School of Mines campus—and don't let the university address put you off. The Cretaceous and Oligocene fossil collections here rank among the most comprehensive in the country, and admission is completely free. Plan for 1 hour 30 minutes, and you'll leave with a genuine understanding of what you're about to see in the Badlands tomorrow.

Seven painted concrete dinosaurs watch over you from Skyline Drive—built in 1936 as part of a WPA public works program, proudly kitsch and beloved by locals. Walk up from the parking area: the view across the entire city with the Black Hills as backdrop beats most paid overlooks in the region. 30 minutes total.

Head downtown for the “City of Presidents”: since 2000, a life-sized bronze statue of every American president has occupied a street corner along Main Street. Some stand, others sit, a few look like they're hailing a cab. Download the map from the city website and turn it into a game—which one will you find first?

Before leaving, step inside Prairie Edge Trading Company at the corner of Main Street and 6th. Pendleton blankets, handcrafted turquoise jewelry, moccasins, Lakota drums—this is one of the finest selections of contemporary Native American art in the United States. Come to understand, not necessarily to buy, though you'll rarely leave empty-handed.

Before returning the car, detour to the Chapel in the Hills, in a wooded neighborhood on the outskirts. It's an exact replica of Norway's 12th-century Borgund Stave Church, built in 1969 by a Lutheran pastor struck by the connections between Dakota's Scandinavian immigrants and their homeland. Free entry. The adjacent museum on Dakota's Scandinavian heritage is worth 30 minutes.

If you have time before your flight, the Journey Museum & Learning Center offers a good overview of everything you've just traveled through: Black Hills geology, 10,000 years of Lakota culture, gold rush, pioneers. Nothing you haven't already seen firsthand, but put into context clearly. Plan for 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: Rapid City has a solid craft beer scene for a city of 80,000. Hay Camp Brewing is known for seriously funky sours; Firehouse Brewing, the oldest in South Dakota, operates from a converted fire station—go for the architecture as much as the pint. Expect under $8 per glass, and take time to chat with locals.

Finish the evening at Main Street Square, the pedestrian heart of downtown. In summer, free outdoor concerts happen several nights a week—check the schedule on the city website. Choose a restaurant on the surrounding streets and eat outside if weather permits: you've got a big day ahead tomorrow.

Take time for a real breakfast downtown before heading to the airport—several coffee shops and brunch spots open early around Main Street Square. Take one last walk among the presidential statues. It's the kind of morning you'll remember for a long time.

visits.text: Pull off I-80 in Rawlins for the Wyoming Frontier Prison - Wyoming's first state penitentiary, 80 years in operation from 1901 to 1981, roughly 13,500 inmates including Big Nose George. Guided tours run through the dungeon, solitary confinement cells, and the gas chamber where 14 executions took place. One-hour tours run year-round. The building is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Step into the Carbon County Museum a few blocks away - free admission, 30,000 artifacts, and the only place in the world where you can see shoes custom-made from the skin of outlaw Big Nose George Parrot after his 1881 hanging. Exhibits also cover Thomas Edison's visit to the Rawlins area, where he reportedly found inspiration for his lightbulb filament while fishing, and Wyoming women's history. Allow 30-45 minutes.

places.name: Red Lodge, MT

visits.text: Cowboys fill the display cases, but miners built the Carbon County Historical Society & Museum. The building was their Labor Temple, erected in 1909; its collections cover rodeo and mining, among other subjects. Check opening hours before you arrive, then take time to look at the facade as well as the objects displayed inside.

Carbon County Arts Guild & Depot Gallery brings the mountains into a former train station. Paintings, photographs, and other works by regional artists fill the Rocky Fork and Cooke City Railway depot. The tourism office lists admission as free; check the gallery’s own hours, which differ from those of the information center.

activities.text: You’ll walk along Broadway Avenue in Red Lodge, taking in downtown facades after the switchbacks of the Beartooth Highway. The historical society offers guided walks on select dates, providing insight into the history of local businesses and former residents. Check its schedule; without a guided tour, stick to a short walking loop.

visits.text: Redding - California's Sunniest Secret with 300+ Days of Brilliance: This underrated gateway to Northern California's wilderness basks in more sunny days than almost anywhere in the state. The striking Sundial Bridge, a gleaming white cable-stayed span designed by Santiago Calatrava, serves as the world's largest working sundial.

Shasta Dam - The Second-Largest Concrete Dam in America: Rising 602 feet above the Sacramento River, this engineering marvel created the spectacular Shasta Lake with its 365 miles of shoreline. Free tours descend into the dam's interior.

activities.text: McArthur-Burney Falls Memorial State Park - 'The Eighth Wonder of the World': President Theodore Roosevelt's famous description still holds true. Watch 100 million gallons of crystal-clear water cascade down 129 feet daily, emerging from underground springs that keep the falls flowing all year. Allow for a round trip during the day from Redding.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Redwood National Park - Where Earth's Tallest Living Giants Touch the Sky: Stand humbled beneath trees that were ancient when Rome was young. These coastal redwoods soar over 350 feet, creating cathedral-like groves where filtered light streams through canopies that have witnessed millennia. A UNESCO World Heritage Site protecting some of the most magnificent forests remaining on Earth.

Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park - Drive Through a Living Tunnel of Green: Navigate the legendary Howland Hill Road as it winds through old-growth forest so dense that the canopy forms a continuous emerald ceiling. Some trees here sprouted before the pyramids were built. Allow for a round trip during the day from your stop in Redwood.

Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park - Where Roosevelt Elk Roam Free: Encounter herds of majestic elk grazing in meadows surrounded by towering redwoods. Fern Canyon, with its 50-foot walls draped in seven species of ferns, served as a filming location for Jurassic Park.

activities.text: Avenue of the Giants - 31 Miles of Breathtaking Wonders: This legendary scenic road winds through the world's largest contiguous old-growth redwood forest. Numerous pullouts invite you to get out and look up at the sky in disbelief.

visits.text: Wilbur D. May Center — Visit this museum in Rancho San Rafael Regional Park, northwest of downtown Reno, which displays objects brought back from around the world by traveler and rancher Wilbur D. May. The adjoining arboretum and botanical garden features plants adapted to the high-desert climate.

Midtown District — Stroll through this neighborhood along South Virginia Street, south of downtown Reno, where older buildings house independent shops, cafés and bars. Many of its façades are covered with murals painted by local artists.
Wingfield Park — Head to this park set on an island in the Truckee River, right in the center of Reno. The engineered pools of the Truckee River Whitewater Park draw kayakers and swimmers in summer.

National Automobile Museum — Discover 200 vintage cars including Elvis's 1973 Cadillac and John Wayne's Corvette in this world-class collection. The museum showcases automotive history from horseless carriages to modern supercars.

Nevada Museum of Art — Explore contemporary art with focus on landscapes and environment in this architectural landmark. The museum houses the Center for Art + Environment documenting land art and environmental themes.
Truckee Riverwalk — Stroll along this urban trail following the river through downtown past shops, galleries, and public art. The revitalized corridor connects parks and cultural attractions.
Fleischmann Planetarium — Learn about astronomy and space exploration at University of Nevada's planetarium. The facility offers star shows and exhibits explaining the cosmos.

activities.text: Desert scenic drive — Cross Nevada's vast basin and range topography under endless skies. The journey reveals the state's emptiness with occasional ghost towns and roadside diners.
Reno Arch photo — Snap pictures beneath the famous arch proclaiming The Biggest Little City in the World. The neon gateway has welcomed visitors to downtown Reno since 1926.

Casino dinner and gaming — Try your luck at Reno's casinos offering a more relaxed atmosphere than Las Vegas. The original Nevada gaming destination maintains old-school charm with affordable table limits.
Downtown Reno revival — Explore the revitalized downtown featuring murals, breweries, and the RiverWalk District. The city reinvented itself beyond gaming with arts and outdoor recreation focus.

Basque cuisine dinner — Savor family-style Basque meals at restaurants preserving sheepherder traditions. Reno's Basque community maintains culinary heritage with multi-course dinners served communally.

places.name: Richmond, VA

visits.text: Few American buildings have played as many roles—and you can walk through them all in a single visit to the Virginia State Capitol. Designed by Thomas Jefferson after the Roman temple of the Maison Carrée in Nîmes, it housed the Confederate Congress from 1861 to 1865. Don't miss the rotunda: the marble statue of Washington by Houdon—commissioned in 1784 and considered the most faithful portrait of the general—deserves a few minutes on its own. Free admission.

Spend at least two hours at the American Civil War Museum at Tredegar Iron Works. The Tredegar foundry produced approximately 1,100 cannons for the Confederacy—nearly half of its domestic artillery production. The museum tells the war from three perspectives: Confederate, Union, and freed slaves. The 19th-century brick warehouses are beautifully restored.

The White House of the Confederacy on East Clay Street survived the war intact when the rest of Richmond burned—visit it to understand just how comfortably the Confederate government lived while its soldiers died. Jefferson Davis resided here as president from 1861 to 1865. Lincoln himself toured it on April 4 and 5, 1865, two days after the city fell. Guided tour of 45 minutes.

Take time to wander Hollywood Cemetery, on the heights overlooking the James River. Jefferson Davis, James Monroe, John Tyler, and 18,000 Confederate soldiers rest here—the latter grouped around a granite pyramid erected in 1869. The views over the river rapids are among Richmond's finest. Open from sunrise to sunset.

Shockoe Bottom, a stone's throw from downtown, is the place many visitors pass without stopping—wrongly. It was the second-largest slave market in the United States between 1830 and 1865: more than 350,000 people were bought and sold here. The Richmond Slave Trail connects the major sites over 3 miles along the canal.

activities.text: Don't leave Richmond without walking the Canal Walk: 1.25 miles along the James River and Kanawha Canal, with 19th-century locks and panels telling the city's industrial and slavery history. In the evening, Shockoe Slip is packed with restaurants in former warehouses.

If you're here on a Saturday between May and November, the South of the James market gathers the best local producers. Otherwise, hit a seafood bar in Shockoe Bottom for Chesapeake Bay oysters—mignonette sauce or straight up—before hitting the road.

visits.text: Women's Rights National Historical Park in Seneca Falls — Allow for a round trip from Rochester. Visit the birthplace of the American women's rights movement, where the first Women's Rights Convention was held in 1848. Wesleyan Chapel and Declaration Park commemorate Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, and 100 signatories.

George Eastman Museum — Explore the world's oldest museum dedicated to photography and film in Kodak founder George Eastman's 1905 Colonial Revival mansion. The collection spans 400,000 photographs and 28,000 films documenting the evolution of visual media.

High Falls — Stand at the edge of this 29-meter waterfall on the Genesee River that powered Rochester's 19th-century flour mills and breweries. The gorge's Silurian dolostone layers reveal 400 million years of geological history.

Strong National Museum of Play — Discover the world's only collections-based museum devoted solely to play, housing the National Toy Hall of Fame. Interactive exhibits celebrate video games, dolls, and classic toys across 14,000 square meters.

activities.text: Public Market browsing — Sample local produce, artisan breads, and ethnic specialties at this indoor-outdoor market operating since 1905. Over 300 vendors gather on Saturdays offering everything from hydroponic greens to Nicaraguan pupusas.

Genesee Riverway Trail cycling — Pedal along this 39-kilometer paved trail following the Genesee River through parks, wetlands, and historic districts. The route passes three waterfalls and connects downtown Rochester to Lake Ontario.

Charlotte Beach sunset — Relax on this sandy Lake Ontario beach where the Genesee River meets the Great Lake. The historic 1905 Dentzel Carousel and pier offer family entertainment as the sun sets over Canadian waters.

places.name: Rock Harbor, MI

visits.text: Isle Royale receives around 25,000 visitors a year—compared to 3 million for the Grand Canyon. Accessible only by boat or seaplane, the 72-km-long island is home to a wolf and moose population that's been continuously studied since 1958: the longest study of a predator-prey system in the world. Start at the Rock Harbor Visitor Center to plan your days on the island.

Rock Harbor Lighthouse, built in 1855 of red sandstone, is the oldest on the island. It now houses exhibits on the maritime history of Lake Superior - nine shipwrecks lie in the waters around the park. From Rock Harbor, access is by boat to Edisen Fishery, then on foot to the lighthouse. The NPS guided tour includes nearby Edisen Fishery, a family operation restored to its 1940s condition.

Scoville Point is 3 km from Rock Harbor via the Stoll Memorial Trail, under a canopy of spruce. The rocky point overlooks Lake Superior—on clear days, you'll spot freighters on the horizon and sometimes the Canadian shoreline. Leave at 5:30 a.m. for sunrise over the lake; you'll have it to yourself.

The Greenstone Ridge Trail is the island's backbone: 64 km from east to west, from Rock Harbor to Windigo, through boreal forests and exposed ridges. At minimum, hike the segment to Mount Franklin—6 km from Rock Harbor, 300 m of elevation gain—for views of Canada and Lake Superior's north shore. Waterproof boots essential.

Suzy's Cave is a sea arch carved into rock by the waves of a prehistoric Lake Superior whose water level was higher than today's. It's a 2-km walk from Rock Harbor. Water now disappears into a crevice plunging into the island's interior—the geology is as striking as the visual spectacle.

activities.text: Rent a canoe or kayak at the Rock Harbor Lodge dock to paddle in Tobin Harbor, the sheltered arm of the lake just north of Rock Harbor. Loons, herons, mergansers, and subboreal vegetation trailing into the water. The quiet feels almost unsettling compared with the mainland.

Attend the evening program led by NPS rangers at Rock Harbor: wolves, moose, Ojibwe history, or Canadian Shield geology depending on the schedule. The rangers live on the island for the entire season and know every corner of the park. Free, no reservation needed.

Take the MV Sandy from Rock Harbor Lodge to Raspberry Island for a ranger-guided walk through the spruce bog. The island is only accessible by private boat or this NPS tour. A boardwalk crosses an ecosystem of sphagnum moss and stunted spruce—fragile, silent, mesmerizing. The tour lasts 2.5 hours total.

Fishing for lake trout and salmon is excellent in the cold waters around Isle Royale. Rock Harbor Lodge organizes half-day charter fishing trips with a captain—all gear provided, license included. The Lighthouse Restaurant at the lodge will cook your evening catch if you ask. Book in advance.

visits.text: Day 3 - Rockefeller Center is worth visiting for its Art Deco complex: gilded Prometheus above the ice rink in winter, murals in the 30 Rock lobby, rows of flags on the plaza. If you didn't go up the Empire State Building this morning, this is where to get up high: Top of the Rock, from $45, open from 8 AM to midnight.

Day 3 - Top of the Rock looks out over Central Park and the Empire State Building; aim for the slot 45 min before sunset, booked several days ahead. The 70th floor, with no glass panels, is a delight for photographers. Reminder: there is no point paying for two observatories on the same day.

activities.text: A drink up high to end the day: the rooftop at 230 Fifth, at 27th Street, serves drinks with the Empire State Building filling the view, without an observatory ticket; blankets are provided in winter.
Walk to St Patrick's Cathedral: 200 m, it faces Rockefeller Center on Fifth Avenue, 3 min.

visits.text: You wander through 5 hectares of koi-filled ponds, waterfalls, winding gravel paths, and meticulously pruned Japanese maples along Spring Creek. Every rock placement, tree position, and water feature was designed by master craftsman Hoichi Kurisu, who has been involved with the gardens since 1978. The layout is dense enough to fill 90 minutes without retracing your steps. The on-site Fresco at the Gardens café serves an Asian-inspired lunch using local produce. Admission charged.

activities.text: Downtown Rockford's Burpee Museum houses Jane, one of the most complete juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex fossils ever discovered, unearthed in South Dakota in 2001. The permanent dinosaur gallery built around Jane has won national recognition for its interpretive approach to fossil science. The museum sits a 10-minute drive from Anderson Gardens. Admission charged.
