places.name: Rockport, TX

visits.text: Aransas National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1937 on 115,000 acres of coast and marshland, is the only wintering site for the last remaining wild population of whooping cranes in the world. The species had fallen to just 15 individuals in the 1940s - the 2024-2025 season count reached a historic 557 cranes. These birds stand five feet tall, have a 7.5-foot wingspan, and migrate each fall from Wood Buffalo National Park in Canada, over 2,500 miles. The best way to see them is from the refuge's auto tour route or by boat tour from Rockport, between November and March. Outside this period, you can still observe over 400 bird species in the refuge.

Fulton Mansion, built in 1877 by General George Fulton, was ahead of its time: running water, hot-air central heating and ventilation in every room - all rarities in Texas at the time. The Second Empire-style house, with its mansard roofs and corner tower, has survived several major hurricanes. If you're passionate about 19th-century architecture, the guided tour is truly worthwhile - it tells how the Fulton family built their fortune in the Texas cattle industry.

The Big Tree at Goose Island State Park is a live oak (Quercus virginiana) estimated to be over 1,000 years old with a trunk circumference of roughly 35 feet. It's one of the most massive trees in Texas. Push on to the park - it's a quick 20-minute stop that leaves a lasting impression.

activities.text: Operators offer kayak outings in Aransas Bay, among the seagrass beds and sandbars. The waters are calm and shallow, ideal for observing dolphins and brown pelicans at very close range. From November through March, boat tours allow you to skirt the refuge's east shore to watch whooping cranes feeding in the salt marshes less than 150 feet away.

places.name: Roswell, NM

visits.text: Embrace the extraterrestrial atmosphere of Roswell, world-famous for the alleged 1947 UFO incident that transformed this agricultural town into a mecca for alien enthusiasts and curious travelers. The International UFO Museum and Research Center presents exhibits examining the incident, government investigations, and broader questions about extraterrestrial life. The entire downtown district celebrates its otherworldly reputation with themed attractions and memorable photo opportunities.

Discover alien-themed street lights, murals, and memorabilia throughout downtown Roswell, where the community has embraced its unique place in American pop culture. The town offers a lighthearted exploration of one of the most persistent mysteries in modern history, regardless of personal beliefs about what actually occurred in the New Mexico desert.

activities.text: Explore beyond the alien attractions to discover Roswell's genuine history as a ranching and agricultural center in southeastern New Mexico. Museums and historic sites document the region's development from frontier territory to modern community, offering context for understanding how an isolated desert town became internationally famous.

visits.text: Explore the Person County Museum of History, where comprehensive artifact exhibitions provide a detailed and engaging account of Roxboro's fascinating past. This welcoming museum offers visitors the opportunity to understand the heritage and development of this delightful Person County community through carefully curated displays and historical documents.

activities.text: Relax in the open spaces of Longhurst Park, an ideal setting for outdoor recreation with hiking trails and sports facilities. The park provides a refreshing escape where visitors can enjoy the small-town atmosphere that makes Roxboro so charming.

Experience downtown Roxboro's lively social atmosphere, where the family-friendly Kirby Cultural Arts Complex hosts entertaining stage performances. Browse for unique treasures at local shops while engaging with friendly locals proud to share their community's heritage and hospitality.

visits.text: Waves roar behind the driftwood logs at Ruby Beach. Below the coastal forest, sea stacks stand isolated in the water while the shoreline changes with the tides and storms. Wear sturdy shoes for the walk down; never settle on a log that the surf could move.

activities.text: At low tide, Ruby Beach’s tide pools offer a closer look at the coast. Marine organisms shelter in rocky pools between high tides, revealing more than the sweeping views of sea stacks. Check the day’s tides before heading down, observe without collecting anything, and always keep a clear route back.

places.name: Sabbathday Lake, ME

visits.text: Twenty miles north of Portland, down a quiet country road in New Gloucester, Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village has been here since 1783. It is the last active Shaker community in the world - a 1,750-acre working farm with 17 historic buildings, a museum, and as of late 2025, three members: Brother Arnold Hadd, Sister June Carpenter, and newly-received novice Sister April Baxter. At its peak in 1850, the worldwide Shaker movement had 5,000 believers. The celibate faith limited membership by birth, and the Canterbury, New Hampshire community - the last other active one - closed in 1992. Guided tours of the buildings run May through October; the Shaker Store sells herbs grown in gardens cultivated here since 1799.

visits.text: Sacramento - America's Farm-to-Fork Capital: California's capital city sits at the confluence of the Sacramento and American Rivers, surrounded by the most productive agricultural region on Earth. The historic Old Sacramento Waterfront district preserves Gold Rush-era architecture along wooden boardwalks.

California State Capitol - Where the Golden State Governs: This stunning neoclassical building, completed in 1874, anchors a 40-acre park filled with memorials, gardens, and trees from around the world. Free tours reveal legislative chambers adorned with California history.

Crocker Art Museum - The West's Oldest Public Art Museum: Founded in 1885, this institution houses one of the finest collections of California art, European master drawings, and international ceramics, all within a striking contemporary expansion adjoining the original Victorian Italianate gallery.

activities.text: Old Sacramento Historic District - Return to the Gold Rush Era: Wooden sidewalks, horse-drawn carriages and restored buildings from the 1850s create an immersive journey into California's most transformative era. The California State Railroad Museum houses a collection of locomotives and railway cars.

Sacramento Mural Trail - Urban Art Gallery Without Walls: Over 600 murals transform the city into an open-air museum, with new works constantly appearing on buildings throughout downtown and surrounding neighborhoods.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Houmas House (40136 Highway 942, Darrow) is probably the most beautiful architecture of all the River Road plantations—Greek Revival style, 38 hectares of gardens, house built between 1810 and 1825. The guided interior tour lasts 90 minutes ($30 ticket) and doesn't fall into the usual nostalgic trap. The Latil's Landing restaurant on-site serves honest Southern cuisine in an antebellum setting without kitsch—$40-70, and better than eating on the road.

Nottoway (31025 Highway 1, White Castle), built in 1859 and long presented as the largest antebellum house in the South, no longer exists: a fire destroyed it on May 15, 2025 and the site can no longer be visited. In Saint Francisville itself, Rosedown Plantation State Historic Site (12501 Highway 10) tells the same story. Daniel and Martha Turnbull had their house built there in 1834-1835, with a fortune drawn from cotton and from the labor of some 450 enslaved people in the best years. Guided tour of the house every hour, then about 11 hectares of formal gardens created by Martha Turnbull, beneath century-old oaks. The scale of the estate makes tangible a fortune built on hundreds of enslaved people in a way that figures alone cannot.

Saint Francisville, founded in 1809 and too small for tour buses, is the kind of stop you regret only allowing an hour. Commerce Street with its antique dealers and gallery, Grace Episcopal Church (1858) in its shaded cemetery—several headstones from the 1860s document the yellow fever epidemics that decimated the region. In 1853, New Orleans had lost 8,000 inhabitants in three months; the river villages hadn't been spared.

activities.text: The Great River Road between Darrow and Saint Francisville drives easily in 2 hours. You run along the levees, cross Acadian villages, see sugarcane fields and country chapels that nobody's repainted in a long time. At the levees, stop: the Mississippi is wider than you imagine from a map.

Saint Francisville's antebellum B&Bs often serve dinner to guests by reservation—crawfish étouffée, fried green tomatoes, gumbo. Otherwise, Magnolia Café on Commerce Street will do for $25-40. It's a quiet evening after a full day, and that's exactly what's needed.

places.name: Saint Paul, MN

visits.text: Minnesota State Capitol - Do not miss this building by Cass Gilbert (who also designed the Woolworth Building in New York), completed in 1905. Look up: the marble dome rises to 67 m and is the world’s second-largest self-supporting marble dome after St. Peter’s in Rome. Above the south entrance, look for the gilded quadriga by Daniel Chester French. Guided tours are free.

Cathedral of Saint Paul—You'll see it from a distance: this granite cathedral, completed in 1915, dominates the city from St. Anthony Hill. The copper dome rises 93 m, and the interior seats 3,000. Architect Emmanuel Masqueray drew inspiration from St. Peter's in Rome. Step inside—it's free and the acoustics are remarkable.

Summit Avenue—From the cathedral, walk down this 7 km avenue lined with 373 Victorian mansions. It's the longest continuous stretch of intact Victorian homes in the United States. At 240 Summit, the James J. Hill House (1891) is a 36,000-square-foot sandstone mansion—the railroad magnate who built the Stone Arch Bridge lived here.

Science Museum of Minnesota—On the banks of the Mississippi, this interactive museum appeals to families. The Omnitheater (a domed IMAX screen) is worth the ticket. The exhibits on dinosaurs and Minnesota geology are well executed.

Landmark Center—Enter this former federal courthouse from 1902, built in pink sandstone. The five-story atrium is worth the visit alone. Know that gangster John Dillinger stood trial here in 1934. Admission is free.

Historic Fort Snelling—At the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers, this 1825 fort is one of the oldest military posts in the American West. Period costume re-enactments immerse you in the lives of 19th-century soldiers and civilians. The fort's history also includes the 1862-63 Dakota internment camp—a painful chapter told with honesty.

activities.text: End the day on Grand Avenue, which runs parallel to Summit. You'll find shops, cafés, and restaurants in brick buildings—the atmosphere is quieter than Minneapolis, more residential.

Como Park Zoo & Conservatory - If you are travelling as a family, this free zoo and botanical garden (donations suggested) are an excellent stop. The tropical garden under glass is worth seeing, especially when it is cool outside.

places.name: Salem, MA

visits.text: Salem has thoroughly transformed its 1692 trials into a tourism industry—a police department with brooms on its cars, a sports team called the Witches, thirty crystal shops. It's kitsch across 90% of the area. But behind all that, three places hold out. First: the Salem Witch Trials Memorial on Liberty Street, a small stone memorial behind the Old Burying Point Cemetery. Twenty benches engraved with each victim's name and last words. Sarah Good, condemned to death: “I am no more a witch than you are a wizard.” Rebecca Nurse, 71: “I am innocent as the child unborn.” George Burroughs recites the Lord's Prayer perfectly from the scaffold—theologically impossible for a witch—the crowd cries out that this is a miscarriage of justice, but the execution proceeds anyway. Dedicated in 1992, free admission.

In the neighboring Old Burying Point Cemetery (1637), the grave of John Hathorne, a judge at the 1692 trials, bears no plaque of regret - because he never expressed any. His great-great-grandson Nathaniel Hawthorne added the “w” to his name to distance himself from his ancestor, then wrote The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851) as acts of symbolic reparation. The family guilt still had a long memory two centuries later.

The second place that holds out: Proctor's Ledge Memorial on Pope Street. This is the exact site of the 19 hangings, identified only in 2016 by the University of Virginia through a GIS study cross-referenced with court archives and testimony from 1692. The memorial was dedicated in 2017. It sits in an ordinary residential neighborhood, next to a Walgreens, with no signs directing visitors there from downtown. A small circle of stones, 19 names engraved, almost no one. Families had retrieved the bodies at night in secret—touching witches' bodies was illegal—to bury them in secret cemeteries. Twenty minutes on site, and you understand why this is infinitely more powerful than the Salem Witch Museum.

The Witch House (310 Essex Street, ticket $8) is the only house still standing in Salem with a direct link to the trials: Judge Jonathan Corwin lived here and held his pre-trial examinations here in 1692. Built in 1675, period furniture, audio guide included. The House of the Seven Gables (115 Derby Street, ticket $18, 1 hr) inspired Hawthorne's novel (1851) - the author's birthplace, moved to the site in 1958, is attached to it.

The Salem Witch Museum (19 Washington Square North, ticket $18) is a little kitsch - wax scenes and 1970s narration - but gives the overview of the trials in 30 minutes before you head to the sites. Useful for context, not for depth.

activities.text: Turner's Seafood at Lyceum Hall (43 Church Street) occupies the former Lyceum Hall where Alexander Graham Bell gave the first public demonstration of the telephone on February 12, 1877—a commemorative plaque is in the room, between two tables. Chowder, lobster roll, $30–50. In October during Haunted Happenings, evening ghost tours led by costumed guides ($25, 1 hour) are excellent—book ahead.

In October during Haunted Happenings, evening ghost tours led by costumed guides ($25, 1 hour) are excellent—historical characters portrayed, real sites, no haunted house with special effects. If you're there specifically for Halloween, be aware that October 31 brings one million people to a city of 45,000 residents: book accommodations 6 to 12 months ahead.

visits.text: Salina - Kansas's Emerging Arts Capital: Even longtime locals discover something new with each visit to this booming downtown, where fresh attractions, murals, and revitalized streetscapes continue transforming the city's core.

Mural at the Mill - 100 Feet of Monumental Art: Australian artist Guido van Helten's stunning work wraps three sides of a flour mill, the first of many murals coordinated by the Salina Kanvas Project that have transformed the city into an open-air gallery.

Salina SculptureTour - 20 Works Adorn Downtown Sidewalks: This rotating outdoor exhibition changes every spring, with pedestrians voting for their favorite sculptures among the works displayed throughout downtown.

The Stiefel Theatre - Art Deco Splendor Under a Neon Spire: This beautifully restored 1931 showpiece hosts live performances beneath its distinctive illuminated tower, a beacon of culture on the Kansas plains.

activities.text: Downtown Salina Walking Tour - Art at Every Turn: Wander the revitalized streetscape discovering murals, sculptures, and the creative energy that has made Salina a destination for art lovers.

visits.text: Guadalupe Mountains National Park - This park protects an ancient Permian reef dating back 265 million years, now raised to an elevation of 2,667 m. El Capitan, the limestone cliff marking the park's southern entrance, has served as a landmark for travelers for centuries. Stop at Pine Springs Visitor Center for maps and trail conditions. Allow for a round trip by car from Salt Flat.

Frijole Ranch - This former 19th-century farm, 3 km from the visitor center, houses a small museum about the region's pioneers and Native Americans. The spring supplying the ranch attracts varied wildlife - you may see elk or wild turkeys. Allow for a round trip by car from Salt Flat.

activities.text: Guadalupe Peak hike - If you are fit, this is THE challenge: climbing to the highest point in Texas (2,667 m). The trail is 14 km round trip with 975 m of elevation gain. Allow 6 to 8 hours. At the summit, a stainless-steel pyramid marks the “roof of Texas”. Set off at dawn and take at least 3 liters of water. If that is too long, Devil's Hall Trail (7 km, 2 hours 30 minutes) is a shorter alternative descending into a spectacular canyon. Allow for a round trip by car from Salt Flat to the trailhead, in addition to the hike.

places.name: Salt Lake, UT

visits.text: Four days after arriving in the valley in July 1847, Mormon pioneers planted a cross on the exact spot where Temple Square stands today. The temple took 40 years to build (1853-1893), and its granite walls are still 2.7 m thick at the base. It remains closed during renovation; public tours of its interior are planned from April to October 2027, by reservation. The 1867 Tabernacle (8,000 seats) hosts free organ recitals: check the schedule before visiting.

If you don't love dinosaurs, you're about to. The Natural History Museum of Utah displays more than 30 reconstructed skeletons along a spiral ramp—including a Utahraptor found in Moab and the world's only collection of 14 Ceratopsian skulls. Utah is one of the richest fossil states on the planet, and this museum proves it meter by meter. Head up to the 5th-floor terrace afterward for views across the entire valley. Book tickets online, especially in summer.

From the terrace of the Utah State Capitol (1916), the logic of Salt Lake City becomes crystal clear: streets are numbered based on their distance from the temple—'200 South' means two blocks south. Brigham Young designed the entire city around that building in 1847. The dome is inspired by Washington's. Free entry, and the rotunda is worth a five-minute stop.

Red Butte Garden sits right next to the natural history museum—21 hectares of gardens tucked into the foothills of the Wasatch, with 4 miles of trails winding into the hills. In spring, it explodes with tulips and irises. In summer, the outdoor amphitheater hosts top-tier concerts. Check the schedule at redbuttegarden.org before you go.

activities.text: If you are here on a Saturday morning between June and October, don't miss the Pioneer Park market (8 a.m.–2 p.m.). More than 150 certified local vendors sell Brigham City peaches, artisan cheeses, Utah honey and sourdough bread. It is the city's largest outdoor market and a real glimpse into its food culture. Arrive before 9 a.m.—it gets crowded later.

In the evening, walk down to The Gateway from Temple Square—ten minutes. After 7 p.m., the terraces come alive, food halls open and craft breweries put out their menus. The atmosphere is relaxed and local. Try Squatters Pub if you prefer to stay downtown.

places.name: San Antonio, TX

visits.text: The Alamo is the chapel of Mission San Antonio de Valero, built around 1718 by Franciscans. The building entered history on March 6, 1836, at the end of a 13-day siege: between 183 and 257 Texan defenders (including Davy Crockett, former Tennessee congressman, and Colonels Bowie and Travis) held out against General Santa Anna's army before being killed to the last man. This defeat became the symbol of Texan resistance - six weeks later, Sam Houston crushed Santa Anna at San Jacinto to the cry of "Remember the Alamo!" Free entry, but crowds are massive during the day - arrive at opening.

San Antonio Missions National Historical Park protects four 18th-century Franciscan missions: Concepción (1755, the best preserved), San José (dubbed the "Queen of the Missions"), San Juan, and Espada. Together with the Alamo, San Antonio's five missions were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on July 5, 2015 - the first Texas site to achieve this status. The park's four missions remain active Catholic parishes. Biking is the best way to connect them via the Mission Reach Trail along the river.

Market Square (El Mercado) is the largest open-air Mexican market in the United States. The two main halls offer crafts, ceramics, textiles, and food products imported from Mexico. Push to the back of the halls - the most authentic and least touristy stalls are in the second row. The surrounding neighborhood comes alive in the evening with restaurants and outdoor music.

The King William Historic District is a neighborhood of Victorian and Neoclassical mansions from the 19th century, built by German merchants enriched through cattle and cotton trade after the Civil War. The name comes from King Wilhelm I of Prussia - the German founders named their main street after him. Some thirty homes are preserved; several are open to visitors. It's San Antonio's most elegant and peaceful residential quarter - stroll in the morning, when the streets are nearly deserted.

The Japanese Tea Garden was landscaped in 1917 in an abandoned limestone quarry north of downtown. Pools fed by natural springs, terraced gardens, and artificial waterfalls make it an unexpected refuge in the heart of San Antonio. Free admission - ideal early morning before the heat rises.

The Briscoe Western Art Museum occupies a 1929 Neoclassical building facing the River Walk. Its collection focuses on the art and culture of the American West: paintings, sculptures, embroidered saddles, posters, and vintage photographs - a more nuanced reading of the Western myth than you might expect. The view from the terrace over the River Walk is a bonus.

activities.text: The San Antonio River Walk (Paseo del Río) is a 24-kilometre network of pedestrian paths one level below street grade, along the San Antonio River. The Museum Reach section, toward the Pearl District, is quieter and greener than the commercial downtown stretch. Water taxis shuttle between neighborhoods. Even if you've seen photos, the descent a few metres below the city streets always surprises.

The Pearl District occupies the buildings of the former Pearl Brewery (1883), converted into a culinary complex, hotel, and farmers market. The Saturday morning farmers market is one of the city's most active, with Hill Country cheeses, smoked meats, vegetables, and preserves.

Natural Bridge Caverns are the largest commercial caves in Texas, about thirty minutes' drive north of downtown San Antonio, in Comal County. Discovered by students in 1960 and open to the public since 1964, they take their name from a 27-metre natural bridge spanning the entrance. The temperature inside is a constant 21°C - welcome in the height of the Texas summer. The standard guided tour (1 hr 15) passes beneath formations tens of millions of years old in chambers up to 30 metres high.

The Mission Reach Trail is a completely flat 13-kilometre bike path connecting the national park's four missions along the San Antonio River, from downtown to Mission Espada. It's the most pleasant way to see all the missions without a car. You'll find bike rentals at the Pearl District or at Mission Concepción.

visits.text: San Diego - America's Finest City: Year-round perfect weather, 110 kilometers of beaches, and a relaxed vibe distinguish California's second-largest city. From world-class attractions to legendary surf breaks, San Diego delivers coastal California at its best.

San Diego Zoo - One of the World's Largest Zoos: This 40-hectare facility in Balboa Park houses over 12,000 animals representing 650 species, many in innovative open-air habitats that have set the standard for modern zoos.

Balboa Park - The Smithsonian of the West: This 485-hectare urban cultural park houses 17 museums, performing arts venues, and the zoo within stunning Spanish Colonial Revival architecture built for the 1915 Panama-California Exposition.

USS Midway Museum - Walk the Deck of a Floating City: This decommissioned aircraft carrier served from 1945 to 1992, and now offers guided tours through living quarters, engine rooms, and a flight deck lined with historic aircraft.

Gaslamp Quarter - Victorian Splendor Meets Urban Energy: Sixteen blocks of restored Victorian architecture house San Diego's premier dining, entertainment, and nightlife district, all walkable from the convention center and waterfront.

activities.text: La Jolla Cove - Sea Lions, Seals, and Snorkeling: This small beach flanked by sandstone cliffs offers some of Southern California's clearest water, with sea lions lounging on nearby rocks and garibaldi (California's state fish) flashing orange in the shallows.

Coronado Beach - Where the Beach Meets the Grand Dame: The iconic Hotel del Coronado has anchored this beach since 1888, its distinctive red turrets rising above some of the finest sand in California.

Cabrillo National Monument - Where European Exploration Began: This point at the tip of Point Loma marks where Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo became the first European to set foot on the West Coast in 1542, with tide pools and panoramic views as bonuses.

Craft Beer Capital of America - 150+ Breweries and Counting: San Diego has emerged as America's premier craft beer destination, with pioneering breweries producing styles from hop-forward IPAs to innovative barrel-aged creations.

places.name: San Luis Obispo, CA

visits.text: Hearst Castle—Explore the extravagant palace with 56 rooms and 61 bathrooms, built between 1919 and 1947 for newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst. Architect Julia Morgan created this Spanish-Moorish fantasy perched on La Cuesta Encantada, the enchanted hill. Allow for a round trip from San Luis Obispo to the visitor center, then take the tour shuttle to the palace.

Elephant Seal Vista Point—Observe the colony of northern elephant seals lounging lazily on the beaches of Piedras Blancas. These marine mammals, which can weigh up to 2 tonnes, have gathered here to molt and breed since 1990. Allow for a round trip within the day from San Luis Obispo.

Morro Rock — Contemplate this 176-meter volcanic dome emerging majestically from the ocean. Formed 23 million years ago, this volcanic neck sacred to the Chumash shelters nesting peregrine falcons and marks the entrance to the bay.

Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa — Visit this mission founded in 1772 by Father Junípero Serra, fifth in the chain of California missions. Its museum traces the tumultuous history of interactions between Franciscans and the native Chumash population.

activities.text: Stroll through the Farmers Market—Wander through the Thursday evening farmers market that has transformed Higuera Street into a lively street festival since 1983. Local producers, street musicians and barbecue vendors create a typically Californian festive atmosphere.

Wine tasting in Edna Valley—Explore the rolling vineyards planted with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in this renowned wine appellation. Family-run tasting rooms offer food and wine pairings in a bucolic setting 8 kilometers from downtown.

Hiking to Bishop Peak — Climb to the summit of this 474-meter volcanic peak, highest point of the Nine Sisters. The steep 6.5-kilometer trail rewards the effort with panoramic views of the valley and sparkling ocean.

visits.text: Hearst Castle layers decorative styles like a collector unwilling to choose. The Grand Rooms Tour takes you through the sitting rooms of Casa Grande, the dining room, the billiard room, and the theater in the home Julia Morgan designed for William Randolph Hearst. Choose this tour for a first visit and book a time that works with your arrival. Check in at the visitor center, since access to the castle is arranged as part of the tour.

activities.text: Snorts and lumbering movements catch your attention at Piedras Blancas Elephant Seal Rookery. From the viewing paths, you will see elephant seals resting, molting, or breeding, depending on the season; their presence is not a show scheduled for a set time. Use binoculars to observe their behavior without getting closer. Stay behind the site's boundaries and never attempt to go down among the animals.

A walk at William Randolph Hearst Memorial Beach nicely complements a visit to the castle. After rooms filled with objects, this San Simeon beach draws your gaze back to the bay and coastal landscape; it is part of the protected sites within Hearst San Simeon State Park. Simply follow the accessible shoreline and choose a spot sheltered from the wind for a break. Follow the posted signs that day, especially around access to the pier.

visits.text: You enter the Cedar Point peninsula, a 7-kilometer sand spit battered by the waters of Lake Erie where the first amusement park opened in 1870—the second oldest operating park in the United States after Lake Compounce. What began as a beach with a refreshment stand and dance floor has become the largest roller coaster complex in North America, with 18 coasters including the Millennium Force (93 meters high) and the recent Siren's Curse, opened in 2025 as North America's tallest and fastest tilt coaster. At the peninsula's tip stands the Cedar Point lighthouse, built in 1862, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984 and the park's oldest permanent structure. The main season runs from May to September, with Halloween-themed days in October.

Aboard the Jet Express from Sandusky harbor, you reach the largest American island in Lake Erie in 20 minutes - 11 square kilometers of vineyards, forests, and polished limestone beaches. The island is famous for its Inscription Rock, sandstone slabs on which the Erie Native Americans carved petroglyphs centuries ago, and for its Glacial Grooves - grooves carved into limestone rock by passing glaciers during the last ice age about 18,000 years ago, among the most accessible in the United States. The island's center is easily explored by rental bike from the dock. Avoid July-August weekends for a quieter experience.

Sandusky is one of Ohio's cities richest in military history: during the War of 1812, Sandusky Bay served as a supply base for Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry's fleet, which defeated the British navy on September 10, 1813, at the Battle of Lake Erie, 40 kilometers northwest toward Put-in-Bay. Earlier, in the 1850s, Sandusky was one of the last stops on the Underground Railroad that helped slaves cross Lake Erie to Canada. The Sandusky Maritime Museum, on the waterfront, traces these stories with documents and ship models. In the evening, the Jackson Street Pier promenade offers remarkable sunsets over the bay.

activities.text: Put-in-Bay is the main town on South Bass Island, 6 kilometers from the American coast, known as a major site associated with the American naval victory of 1813. Access is by boat from Sandusky. Perry's Victory and International Peace Memorial—a 107-meter Doric column inaugurated in 1915—towers over the island and is visible from the shore. The island also has Crystal Cave, carved out by groundwater, with walls lined with celestite crystals.

Cedar Point Beach extends over a kilometer along the peninsula's north shore, facing Lake Erie - the same white sand beach that attracted the first visitors arriving by steamboat from Sandusky in the late 19th century. Lake Erie, though the shallowest of the Great Lakes with an average depth of 19 meters, warms faster than its neighbors and offers pleasant swimming temperatures from July to September. In the evening, after the park closes, the beach remains accessible and the sunset over the water is one of the region's finest.

days_plan.itin_title: Pittsburgh to Detroit: Steel, Rock & Motown - 9 Days on the Great Lakes

visits.text: Old Mission Santa Barbara — Discover the queen of California missions founded in 1786, the only one to have remained under continuous Franciscan administration. The neoclassical church with its double-tower facade houses a golden altarpiece and Chumash wall frescoes.

Santa Barbara County Courthouse — Admire this Spanish-Moorish architectural masterpiece completed in 1929 after the destructive 1925 earthquake. The El Mirador clock tower offers a 360° view of the red tile roofs and sparkling Pacific.

State Street — Stroll the main palm-lined shopping artery where designer boutiques, art galleries and fusion restaurants sit alongside Spanish colonial style buildings. The uniform architecture creates a Mediterranean atmosphere unique in California.
Stearns Wharf — Walk along California's oldest wooden pier built in 1872. Artisan shops and the Sea Center aquarium occupy the historic buildings while fishermen and pelicans share the docks.

activities.text: Wine tasting on the Urban Wine Trail — Explore the thirty or so tasting rooms concentrated in the Funk Zone, a former industrial district converted into an urban wine paradise. Winemakers from Santa Ynez Valley present their award-winning vintages in renovated warehouses.

Beach bike ride—Pedal along the bike path that follows 5 kilometers of palm-lined golden sand beaches. Stop at East Beach for an impromptu beach volleyball match or a surfing session in the gentle waves.

Sunset at Butterfly Beach — Settle in on this exclusive Montecito beach where celebrities blend incognito with locals. The sun plunging into the Pacific behind the Channel Islands creates memorable flaming skies.

visits.text: Santa Cruz - California's Original Surf City: This laid-back university town at the northern tip of Monterey Bay has shaped surf culture since the sport arrived on the mainland in 1885. The world-famous break at Steamer Lane draws elite surfers while beginners learn on gentler waves at Cowell's Beach.

Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk - California's Last Remaining Seaside Amusement Park: This 1907 landmark operates two National Historic Landmarks: the 1924 Giant Dipper wooden roller coaster and the 1911 Looff Carousel. Free admission lets visitors soak up the vintage atmosphere without riding.

Natural Bridges State Beach - Where Monarchs Meet the Sea: This coastal park features a dramatic natural arch emerging from the surf, and from October through February, eucalyptus groves shelter thousands of migrating monarch butterflies.

activities.text: Mystery Spot - Where Gravity Gets Confused: This roadside attraction has baffled visitors since 1939 with optical illusions and seemingly impossible physical phenomena in a small patch of redwood forest. Kitsch or science experiment? You decide.

visits.text: Marvel at Saint Francis Cathedral Basilica, a magnificent Romanesque Revival structure whose beautiful interior and stunning stained glass windows create an atmosphere of profound peace and artistic grandeur. The cathedral stands as the spiritual heart of Santa Fe and represents one of the finest examples of ecclesiastical architecture in the American Southwest.

Visit the Loretto Chapel, renowned for its mysterious spiral staircase that appears to defy architectural principles, constructed without any central support and using only wooden pegs. Legend attributes its creation to a mysterious carpenter who appeared to answer the sisters' prayers and vanished without payment upon completion. The tiny chapel and its miraculous staircase draw visitors from around the world.

activities.text: Stroll around Santa Fe's central Plaza, the historic heart of the city, surrounded by superb adobe architecture, lively street artists and exceptional craft galleries. The plaza has served as the city's commercial and cultural center since its founding in 1610, making it one of the most historically significant public spaces in the United States.

Explore the Railyard Park district, where preserved railway heritage meets contemporary arts and culture in a revitalized urban space. Old railway details and industrial architecture provide atmospheric backdrops for galleries, markets, and community gatherings that celebrate Santa Fe's creative spirit.

places.name: Santa Monica, CA

visits.text: Wigwam Motel (Rialto/San Bernardino) - 19 concrete teepee-shaped rooms, built in 1949, surrounded by vintage cars. One of Route 66's most photographed motels. If you're not staying overnight, a photo from the parking lot is enough.

Santa Monica Pier—The “End of the Trail” sign (installed in 2009) marks the official end of Route 66. You've driven 3,940 km from Chicago. The Pacific is before you. Take your photo near the sign, then turn around: the Pacific Park Ferris wheel, the historic 1922 carousel, and the arcade are there. It's the end of the journey and the beginning of California.
Venice Beach - Walk 3 km south of the pier to Venice Beach, California's wildest boardwalk: outdoor bodybuilders, street performers, skateboarders and vendors selling anything and everything.

activities.text: Pacific sunset - You've crossed the Illinois plains, Texas, the New Mexico and Arizona deserts, the Mojave. Sit on the Santa Monica sand and watch the sun descend into the Pacific. It's the perfect ending.

visits.text: Sarasota - Where Beach Vibes Meet Big City Culture: This Gulf Coast gem combines laid-back coastal living with world-class cultural institutions, creating an unusually sophisticated beach destination.

The Ringling - A Museum Complex Celebrating Art and the Circus: John Ringling's legacy includes his extensive art collection, the Circus Museum, and Ca' d'Zan—his lavish Venetian Gothic mansion overlooking Sarasota Bay.

Siesta Key - America's Best Beach Sand: The quartz crystal sand of Siesta Key Beach stays remarkably cool even in blazing heat, a unique quality that has earned it 'best beach' titles from numerous publications.
Lido Beach - Siesta's Quieter Neighbor: Less crowded but equally beautiful, Lido Key offers a more laid-back alternative with the same stunning Gulf water.

St. Armands Circle - Upscale Shopping in a Garden Setting: This circular shopping district features upscale boutiques, galleries, and restaurants arranged around a beautifully landscaped central park.

activities.text: Siesta Key Village - Beachside Bohemia: Browse surf shops, sample local brews at low-key bars, and soak up the relaxed atmosphere of this beloved beach community.

visits.text: Taste the water before you judge. Eighteen naturally carbonated springs rise in Saratoga Spa State Park, and the water is drawn straight from the fountain. Metallic, salty, truly distinctive—but it has been the tradition since the 19th century. The park itself, laid out in 1935 in the Beaux-Arts style, houses the Roosevelt Baths, where you can still take a hot mineral bath just as in the old days. Book the baths online; weekend slots sell out ten days in advance.

A month after the Battle of Gettysburg, on August 3, 1863, a former bare-knuckle boxing champion named John Morrissey staged thoroughbred races on Union Avenue. That was the birth of Saratoga Race Course, one of the oldest racetracks in the country. The Travers Stakes, the oldest major thoroughbred race in America, has been run here every year since 1864. Outside the season (mid-July to Labor Day), you can visit the stables and the National Museum of Racing just across the street  -  livelier than it looks, with the saddles, boots and trophies of the champions.

Congress Park, right downtown, houses the Canfield Casino—a former gambling house from 1870 turned local history museum. Upstairs, the original gaming room remains intact with its gilding and grand mirror. Five-dollar admission, and many skip it: a mistake, as it's a rare reminder of the city's Victorian golden age, when Saratoga rivaled Newport as a vacation destination for the Vanderbilts and Whitneys.

activities.text: A stroll along Broadway, the main street lined with restored Victorian façades. Mrs. London's Bakery is the local Viennese institution: kouign-amann, cardamom scones, brown-butter brioche. For breakfast or an afternoon snack, it works any time of day and there's often a line on Saturday mornings.

Truman Capote, Sylvia Plath, and Aaron Copland all worked here. Yaddo Gardens, on the east side of town, has hosted artist residencies in its grand Victorian mansion since 1900—the house itself is closed to the public, but the terraced gardens with their classic diamond-patterned rose garden are open and free. Peak bloom in June, and rarely crowded even then.

places.name: Saratoga

visits.text: In Saratoga's City Park on Walnut Street, a public mineral hot spring remains open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, free of charge—the Hobo Hot Pool. Its temperature ranges from 41°C at its coolest end to 48°C at the “Lobster Pot”. The current pool was discovered in 1917 after a flood eroded the banks of Spring Creek. Native Americans had used the original springs here as neutral territory for centuries; the town was named Saratoga in 1884 after an Iroquois word meaning “place of miraculous water in the rock”. Restrooms and changing facilities are on site.

The Hotel Wolf on Bridge Street has been operating since the late 19th century and remains the social hub of the North Platte Valley. The bar and restaurant serve some of the best steaks in the region. Sit down for lunch and listen to the tables around you—ranchers, fishing guides, and visiting fly anglers talking about water levels and insect hatches. This is what Saratoga is really like.

Eight kilometers north of town on WY-130/230, the Saratoga National Fish Hatchery raises several trout species for federal and state hatcheries nationwide and runs a captive breeding program for the endangered Wyoming toad. Free to visit; a short self-guided tour explains the operation. Context worth knowing: the North Platte at Saratoga holds over 4,000 catchable wild trout per mile and has not been stocked since 1979.

activities.text: A guided float trip on the Upper North Platte is the full-day option—113 kilometers of blue-ribbon water holding over 4,000 wild trout per mile (brown and rainbow trout averaging 33–43 cm), unstocked since 1979. The section from Bennett Peak via Treasure Island to Saratoga runs through canyon scenery and cottonwood-lined banks. Mid-June to early August is peak season, when snowmelt runoff clears. Reserve at least a week in advance in summer.

Twenty minutes south of Saratoga lies Encampment, and from there Battle Highway (WY-70) heads west to “Aspen Alley”—a half-kilometer stretch of dirt road where tall aspens form a complete canopy overhead, glowing gold in late September. The Grand Encampment Museum covers the 1890s–1900s copper mining boom with over a dozen original buildings; free admission. A 2–3-hour loop that shows a completely different face of Carbon County.

places.name: Savannah, GA

visits.text: Owens-Thomas House & Slave Quarters brings two social realities together in a single visit. The reception rooms and the quarters of enslaved people reveal the relationships between those who owned the house and those who kept it running. The focus shifts from domestic comfort to the labor that made it possible. Reserve a tour time, then arrive early so you don’t miss the group’s departure.

Forsyth Park deserves more than a photo stop. Its 1858 fountain marks the northern end of a park whose lawns, paths, and recreation areas extend the downtown streets. This is as much a space for everyday use as a setting for photographs. Continue beyond the fountain basin to appreciate the park’s scale, then choose a bench in the shade; save long stretches without shade for the cooler hours.

Step inside the Cathedral Basilica of St. John the Baptist when visits are permitted, leaving the pace of the street outside. This Savannah cathedral remains an active place of worship, and tourist visits are arranged around that role. A quiet visit gives you time to observe the interior without disturbing worshippers. Check the guidelines at the entrance and come back later if a service is underway.

Bonaventure Cemetery reveals another side of Savannah’s landscape, on high ground above the Wilmington River. The cemetery occupies the grounds of a former plantation; today, its graves and trees make for a visit in which the landscape matters as much as the monuments. It remains a place of remembrance, not a setting for unrestricted use. Pick up a map at the entrance, stay on the paths, and give families priority.

For a change from Bonaventure’s landscapes, the Telfair Academy offers a break devoted to art. This former neoclassical residence displays American and European works, including paintings, sculptures, and decorative arts. Two rooms furnished in 19th-century style recall its origins as a home. Explore the galleries at your own pace and save this indoor visit for the hotter hours before returning to River Street.

activities.text: If you put the map away for a few moments, you can also discover Savannah Historic Landmark District from square to square. These leafy squares break up the street grid and offer natural pauses as you walk between historic houses. Here, open space contributes as much to the cityscape as the facades. Choose a short loop around the area you have already visited and use designated crossings, without turning your stroll into a race to see monuments.

Walk along River Street to return to Savannah’s waterfront after exploring its streets and squares. The promenade follows the Savannah River, which connects the city to the water. The difference in elevation from the neighboring streets makes the transition tangible as you move from downtown to the wharf. Wear sturdy shoes and identify an access route suited to your mobility before heading down to the river.

You will return to Savannah to finish the trip and head to Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport. Returning from Tybee Island brings you back to the starting point for your airport transfer without changing bases again. Arrange your rental car return according to your reservation and allow enough time for your flight.

places.name: Scottsbluff, NE

visits.text: Coming from Alliance, you'll spot Chimney Rock from 50 km away - a 100-meter spire of Brule clay and volcanic ash rising from the North Platte River valley like a stone needle. Stop here first, 35 km before reaching Scottsbluff. Between 1843 and 1869, historians found that 95 to 97 percent of westward emigrants who kept journals mentioned Chimney Rock by name, making it the single most-referenced landmark on the entire Oregon, California and Mormon trail system. Erosion and lightning strikes have reduced it by an estimated 30 meters since pioneer days. Congress designated it a National Historic Site in 1956. The Abbott Visitor Center in Bayard has exhibits and a trail film; since August 2023, the Walk to the Rock trail lets you approach across 146 hectares of protected prairie on a 1.3 km accessible path.

Scotts Bluff National Monument, 3 km west of Gering, towers 244 meters above the North Platte River - the second-most-mentioned landmark in pioneer diaries after Chimney Rock. Over 250,000 emigrants passed between 1843 and 1869; after 1850, most funneled through Mitchell Pass, so narrow that 300,000 people and their wagons all crossed the same strip of ground, carving deep parallel ruts still visible and walkable today. The Oregon Trail Museum at the base holds the world's largest collection of William Henry Jackson's artworks - paintings and photographs of the westward migration made in the 1860s and 70s. Drive the 2.6 km Summit Road to the top: on a clear day you can see Chimney Rock 30 km east and Laramie Peak 145 km west.

The Legacy of the Plains Museum in Gering tells the agricultural history of the North Platte Valley - from Oregon Trail emigrants who first broke ground here to the irrigation systems that made western Nebraska productive farmland. The collection spans pioneer wagons, farm equipment and oral history archives of the families who settled the valley from the 1880s onward. It is the quieter daily-life counterpart to Scotts Bluff's epic landscape: the story of what happened after the covered wagons stopped. Paid entry; plan 45 to 60 minutes.

activities.text: Hike the Saddle Rock Trail at Scotts Bluff - 2.6 km one way, climbing 133 meters from the visitor center to the summit. The trail passes through two hand-dug tunnels blasted by Civilian Conservation Corps crews in the 1930s; the top opens onto a 360-degree view of the North Platte valley, the Wyoming border, and the flat Nebraska plains reaching east to the horizon. Then walk the 800-meter Oregon Trail Pathway from the wagon display at the base - the actual ruts carved by 300,000 emigrants are visible as parallel troughs in the dry grass. You can stand in them.

After the bluff, explore downtown Scottsbluff and nearby Gering in the North Platte Valley. Walk along Broadway in Scottsbluff, then visit downtown Gering separately. For dinner, the historic district along Broadway in Scottsbluff has independent steakhouses and Mexican restaurants serving the ranching community of western Nebraska.

visits.text: Peter Weir didn't build a set for The Truman Show. He found one. Seaside - planned in 1981 by Robert Davis following New Urbanism principles - was already so perfectly ordered that the film crew barely needed to intervene when they arrived in 1997. Pastel cottages, brick streets, white picket fences, a town square with a working grocery store (Modica Market, family-run since 1988). The Truman House is at 31 Natchez Street, still a private home. Walk to the Tupelo Street gazebo where Jim Carrey's awakening scenes were shot - it still stands, still circles the same roundabout.

Grayton Beach State Park interrupts the planned villages of 30A with 898 hectares of dune and scrub habitat and a beach that regularly ranks among the best in the country. The real draw is Western Lake behind the dunes: a rare coastal dune lake that periodically breaks through its sand barrier and connects directly to the Gulf. Take the one-kilometre nature trail to the viewpoint above the lake before heading to the beach. Entrance fee applies; arrive before 10 a.m. in summer.

Scenic Highway 30A runs 38 kilometres between Inlet Beach and Dune Allen, threading a sequence of planned coastal villages each with its own architectural identity. Rosemary Beach leans Caribbean; Alys Beach is all white stucco and shadow; WaterColor breaks up the rooflines with Florida vernacular. Between the villages the road passes through scrub pine and past the coastal dune lake corridor that makes this stretch unlike anywhere else in Florida. No admission - drive it, stop where something catches you, eat when you're hungry.

activities.text: The 29-kilometre paved bike path along 30A requires no athletic ambition - flat and mostly shaded, it links Seaside to Rosemary Beach and Alys Beach in one continuous thread through the scrub pine woods and past the dune lakes. Rentals on Seaside's central square cost less than an hour's parking at the resorts. Set off early on a weekday before traffic builds on the road alongside.

Seaside's Central Square fills at sunset around the food truck vendors that have anchored the community's social life since its early years. Tacos, flatbreads, fresh-churned ice cream, cold beer - the square runs on its own logic, and the best table is no table at all. After dark, take the Coleman Pavilion walkway down to the beach: the same shore where Truman Burbank stood at the edge of his manufactured world and realized something was wrong.

places.name: Seattle, WA

visits.text: Since 1907, Pike Place Market (47.6097, -122.3422) has occupied the same block on 1st Avenue without succumbing to the sanitized renovation that killed off markets of its era. Employees have been tossing salmon 5 meters over the counter since 1986, a nearly constant tourist performance that ends up feeling oddly natural. The original Starbucks (47.6101, -122.3401) stands at 1912 Pike Place since 1971, sporting a more explicit mermaid logo than the current one, with a guaranteed line—the coffee's no better than elsewhere, but this is where it all began. Head downstairs to the Gum Wall (47.6086, -122.3412): 2 million pieces of chewing gum stuck here since 1993, covering the entire wall, with a sweet and faintly chemical smell. Pure kitsch, yet you'll linger longer than planned.

Ascend the Space Needle (47.6205, -122.3493) early enough to beat the tour groups—the observation deck at 152 meters rotates in 47 minutes, and since the 2018 renovation the floor is transparent glass: you're looking at Seattle through your own feet. Built for the 1962 World's Fair at 184 meters tall, it hasn't lost any relevance in the skyline. On clear days, Mount Rainier appears to the south, far larger than you'd expect. Ticket $38.

Right next to the Space Needle, Chihuly Garden and Glass (47.6206, -122.3505) showcases the monumental works of Dale Chihuly, Tacoma-born glass sculptor. Enter the central gallery: a 30-meter glass ceiling gives the impression of standing beneath a giant luminous jellyfish. The outdoor garden features flower-sculptures reaching 3 meters tall among the shrubs. The combined Space Needle + Chihuly ticket costs less than buying separately—check at the counter first.

Head underground at Pioneer Square (47.6019, -122.3340) to understand why Seattle is built 6 meters above its original level. A fire in June 1889 destroyed 30 hectares of the founding district; during reconstruction, the city raised its streets to solve water drainage problems—and buried 19th-century Seattle beneath modern Seattle. The Underground Tour (614 1st Avenue, $25, 1h) covers 3-4 subterranean blocks with intact storefronts and sidewalks. The storytelling leans humorous rather than academic, but the quality is excellent.

The MoPOP building (47.6212, -122.3479), 325 5th Avenue North, stops people in the street—deconstructivist crumpled titanium designed by Frank Gehry in 2000, a metallic mass that appears to have been wrinkled and dropped there. The interior collection is serious: Nirvana and the grunge movement, Jimi Hendrix (born in Seattle in 1942), science fiction and horror. Nothing of the souvenir museum you might fear. Ticket $38, minimum two hours.

Rem Koolhaas designed the Seattle Central Library (47.6065, -122.3326), 1000 4th Avenue, in 2004—cantilevered floors, deconstructed glass and steel structure, a spiral ramp across four archive levels. Entry is free and the building is open to the public. Thirty minutes for the architectural tour, or longer if you settle in with a book in the suspended reading room.

activities.text: Dine in Capitol Hill (47.625, -122.318) rather than the tourist center—this alternative neighborhood to the northeast shows a Seattle that Pike Place doesn't. Independent bars and restaurants, historic LGBTQ scene, bookstores still open evenings. 20 minutes by cab or Uber from the market.

End the evening at a craft brewery in the Pike Place area—Pike Brewing Company (47.6097, -122.3415) or one of its neighbors. Seattle has been a craft beer capital since the 1980s, and local brews deserve more than a single round. $25-45 per person.

Visit Viretta Park (47.6310, -122.2826)—a small ordinary park in Capitol Hill, except for one bench covered in graffiti, dried flowers, and letters that have accumulated for 30 years. Kurt Cobain was found dead on April 8, 1994, in his Lake Washington Boulevard home (47.6309, -122.2828), a private property just steps away. Nobody officially maintains the bench: it maintains itself. The self-guided Court Cobain Walk (3 km) links MoPOP to Capitol Hill and passes significant addresses from his Seattle life.

End the day at Olympic Sculpture Park (47.6166, -122.3553) along Puget Sound—monumental outdoor sculptures, views of the Olympic Mountains if the sky cooperates. Free, permanently open. Pick up the car tomorrow morning: Seattle works without one, and downtown parking costs $40-60/day.

places.name: Sedona, AZ

visits.text: Hike back up from Havasupai (16 km, pre-dawn start), then drive 4.5 hours to Sedona. You'll arrive tired—that's normal. Go straight to Airport Mesa for sunset: this 360° viewpoint overlooks Sedona's red sandstone formations with the green mountains of Coconino National Forest in the background. The parking lot is small—arrive 30 minutes before sunset.
If you still have energy, visit Tlaquepaque Arts & Shopping Village—an artists' village built in Mexican colonial style, with galleries, pottery studios, and restaurants under sycamore trees.

Cathedral Rock is THE Sedona hike. The trail is 1.8 km one-way (short but steep—230 meters of elevation gain), with sections where you scramble on all fours up sandstone. From the “saddles” at the top, the view of Sedona's red formations and Oak Creek valley is spectacular. Start early—the parking lot fills before 8 a.m.

In the afternoon, do the Bell Rock & Courthouse Butte loop (6 km, easy). Bell Rock is a perfectly bell-shaped formation—you can climb its lower slopes. Courthouse Butte is more massive and the trail circles it. It's one of Sedona's “vortexes.”

Take AZ-89A north to drive through Oak Creek Canyon—nicknamed the “Grand Canyon's little cousin.” The road winds for 20 km between red cliffs covered in pines. Stop at Slide Rock State Park—a natural 24-meter waterslide in sandstone polished smooth by Oak Creek water. Kids (and adults) love sliding in the icy water.

Heading back to Sedona, stop by the Chapel of the Holy Cross—a church embedded in a red sandstone cliff, built in 1956. The architecture is striking: a 27-meter cross integrated into the glass and concrete façade, with red rock as the back wall. The view from the parking lot is already beautiful, but go inside—the light-flooded interior is worth the visit.

activities.text: Sedona is known for its "vortexes"—points where earth energy is supposedly concentrated. The four main vortexes are at Airport Mesa, Cathedral Rock, Bell Rock, and Boynton Canyon. Whether you believe in them or not, they're also Sedona's best hiking spots.

If you want another hike, Devil's Bridge Trail (6.4 km round-trip) leads to Sedona's largest natural sandstone bridge—16 meters wide and suspended over a drop. The photo on the bridge went viral on social media. The trail isn't difficult but the Dry Creek Road parking lot fills fast.

The Red Rock Scenic Byway (AZ-179) between Sedona and Village of Oak Creek is one of Arizona's most beautiful scenic roads—12 km with Bell Rock, Courthouse Butte, and Cathedral Rock as a backdrop. Drive it in late afternoon when the sun casts low-angle light on the red formations.

visits.text: Angel & Vilma Delgadillo's Route 66 Gift Shop brings together much more than road-trip souvenirs. Angel Delgadillo, a Seligman barber, played a major role in preserving Route 66 after the town was bypassed. Look at the documents on display and check the shop’s opening hours before planning your stop.

activities.text: You’ll explore Seligman Commercial Historic District on foot, among old storefronts, signs, and vehicles displayed along Route 66. The scene recalls the economy of small towns that motorists passed through before the major highway bypasses. Park once, cross at designated places, and keep this stop short before Kingman.

visits.text: Stand at the west end and look across. The Edmund Pettus Bridge arches high enough that from the starting point you can't see what's on the other side - the 600 marchers on March 7, 1965 had no idea what waited for them until they reached the crown. Then they saw it: 150 state troopers and possemen, some on horseback, stretched across Route 80. They were given one minute's warning, then charged. John Lewis suffered a skull fracture. Amelia Boynton was beaten unconscious; the photograph of her lying on the roadway ran on front pages worldwide. The bridge is 380 meters long. The name across the crossbeam belongs to Edmund Pettus, Confederate general and Grand Dragon of the Alabama KKK. National Historic Landmark since 2013. Always open, always free.

Six blocks from the bridge, the twin Romanesque towers of Brown Chapel AME Church rise above the surrounding houses. This is where the congregation organized in 1866, one year after Emancipation - the 1908 building by Black builder A.J. Farley is the only surviving work he's known to have built. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke from this pulpit on January 2, 1965, urging registration. On March 7, 600 marchers gathered on these steps and walked two-by-two through downtown. Brown Chapel provided food, shelter, and organizing space throughout the entire 1965 campaign. National Historic Landmark 1997. Tours by appointment: (334) 874-7897.

A few blocks from the Edmund Pettus Bridge, the Selma Interpretive Center marks the beginning of the Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail, a federal trail following the 1965 march. The center is closed for construction. During the closure, National Park Service rangers welcome visitors at the Selma Welcome Center, 14 Broad Street, near the bridge: ask there about voter registration campaigns and the three marches.

activities.text: The Selma Civil Rights Heritage Trail links the bridge, Brown Chapel, the Old Depot Museum, and the National Voting Rights Museum on Water Avenue - all on foot, about 1.6 km, flat ground. At the foot of the bridge, the Voting Rights Museum holds oral histories from marchers who were present on Bloody Sunday. The signage on the trail is clear; no guide is needed. Small admission fee at the Voting Rights Museum.

Drive east on US-80 to the Lowndes County Interpretive Center, a free NPS site about 32 km out on the historic march route. Lowndes County is where marchers camped in open fields on Day 3 of the third march under National Guard protection, and where Viola Liuzzo - a white civil rights worker from Detroit - was shot and killed by KKK members on March 25, 1965, as she drove marchers back to Selma after the march reached Montgomery. The center tells that story without softening it. Free admission.

places.name: Seneca Rocks, WV

visits.text: From afar, you spot a white quartzite spire bursting from the forest like a sawtooth—Seneca Rocks rises nearly 280 meters above the confluence of Seneca Creek and the North Fork of the South Branch Potomac. It's the only rock face in the eastern United States whose summit is inaccessible without roped climbing techniques. During World War II, in 1943 and 1944, the U.S. Army's 10th Mountain Division trained here in alpine climbing before fighting in Italy's Apennines; the soft iron pitons they left in the rock are still visible on certain routes. The trail from the Discovery Center climbs 1.3 km to an observation platform overlooking the valley from 700 meters above it—accessible to all fitness levels.

You drive 70 km north of Seneca Rocks and set foot on the highest plateau east of the Mississippi—Dolly Sods extends across 17,371 acres at elevations between 800 and 1,257 meters in the Monongahela National Forest. The name comes from an 18th-century German family, the Dahles, who used these mountain meadows to graze their sheep. The flora resembles that of the Canadian tundra: dwarf birches, sphagnum moss, wild blueberries, and spruces twisted into flag shapes by relentless winds. The trails around Bear Rocks offer spectacular views of the wooded gorges of the Alleghenies—bring water, as there are no sources of drinking water on the plateau.

You're visiting one of the region's oldest intact farms: the Sites House, built in 1839 by a German immigrant family named Seitz (Anglicized to Sites), still stands a few hundred meters from the Discovery Center. It was built on land that German families began claiming in 1761, attracted by fertile soil and cheap land. Germany Valley, which extends around Seneca Rocks, actually takes its name from these settlers. The NPS has restored the wood and stone house; the interior is open during summer open-house days.

activities.text: You're strapped into a harness at the base of a wall of hard, rough quartzite—ideal for beginners because it offers good holds even on the first routes. Seneca Rocks has over 400 routes rated from 5.0 to 5.14b, but beginner routes already let you reach intermediate ledges with striking valley views. Seneca Rocks Climbing School, founded in 1971, is one of the oldest climbing schools in the United States and has trained several generations of East Coast climbers.

You explore Dolly Sods on 47 miles of trails, many following old logging railroad tracks from the early 20th century, when the region was completely stripped by loggers. The fires that followed burned through even the humus, leaving only bare rock—hence the slowly recovering vegetation that still resembles Canadian heathland a hundred years later. Red Creek Trail follows a crystal-clear stream and offers some of the wildest backcountry camping spots on the entire East Coast. On weekdays and outside the peak season, you will have the plateau to yourself. Allow for a round trip by car from Seneca Rocks to reach the hiking trailhead at Dolly Sods.

visits.text: Day 1: Alaska SeaLife Center - This marine research facility and public aquarium in Seward provides close encounters with Alaska's marine wildlife, including Steller sea lions, harbor seals, sea otters, and seabirds like puffins and murres. The center conducts important research on marine ecosystems and wildlife rehabilitation.

Day 1: Exit Glacier - The only road-accessible portion of Kenai Fjords National Park features trails leading directly to the face of this actively retreating glacier. The 0.8-mile trail to the glacier face passes markers showing the ice's position in previous years, dramatically illustrating glacial recession. The strenuous Harding Icefield Trail climbs 3,500 feet over 8.2 miles to views of the vast ice field feeding Exit Glacier and dozens of others.

Day 1: Seward Historic Waterfront - This picturesque port town at the head of Resurrection Bay was established in 1903 as the ocean terminus of the Alaska Railroad. The small marina, galleries, and historic buildings reflect the community's fishing heritage and role as a gateway to Kenai Fjords.

Day 2: Kenai Fjords National Park - This 670,000-acre park protects the Harding Icefield, one of the four largest ice caps in the United States, and the spectacular coastal fjords carved by its glaciers. Tidewater glaciers calving into the sea create a landscape of extraordinary beauty and remarkable ecological richness.

Day 2: Holgate Glacier and Aialik Bay - Full-day cruises venture deep into the park's fjords to witness massive tidewater glaciers actively calving icebergs into the sea. The thunderous crack and splash of ice breaking from glacier faces create one of nature's most dramatic spectacles.

Day 2: Northwestern Fjord - Extended cruises reach this remote arm of the park, where multiple glaciers flow from the Harding Icefield and wildlife viewing opportunities multiply with distance from Seward.

activities.text: Day 1: Resurrection Bay Kayaking - The protected waters of the bay offer excellent paddling with mountain and glacier views, wildlife observation opportunities, and access to remote beaches and coves.

Day 2: Kenai Fjords Wildlife Cruise - Half-day and full-day boat tours explore the park's coastal ecosystems, with regular sightings of humpback whales, orcas, sea otters, Steller sea lions, and harbor seals. Seabird colonies host thousands of puffins, cormorants, and kittiwakes on rocky islands and cliffs.

Day 2: Fishing Charters - The nutrient-rich waters of Resurrection Bay and the adjacent Gulf of Alaska support excellent fishing for halibut, salmon (kings, silvers, and sockeye), ling, and rockfish throughout the summer season.

places.name: Shark Valley, FL

visits.text: In an almost flat marsh, a single tower changes your sense of scale: the Shark Valley Observation Tower rises above the grasses of the Everglades. The National Park Service lists its height as approximately 21 meters. Visit it on the tram tour; the stop at the tower is included in the route, and you cannot reach it by private car.

activities.text: Take the Shark Valley tram along the roughly 24-kilometer loop through the freshwater marsh. The open landscape makes birds and alligators easier to spot, though sightings are not guaranteed on every trip. Book the tour and arrive before departure; the tower stop is part of this excursion.

The planks echo underfoot on Bobcat Boardwalk, between marshland and denser vegetation. This short trail begins near the Shark Valley Visitor Center and complements the tower panorama with a view close to the water. Check at the visitor center to see whether it is open, and keep your distance from wildlife.

places.name: Sheridan, WY

visits.text: Plan a round trip from Sheridan to reach the Medicine Wheel parking lot. Forest Road 12 off US-14A leads to a lower parking lot, from which you must walk along a 2.4-kilometer gravel road to the Medicine Wheel: white limestone blocks arranged in a circle 25 meters in diameter, 28 radial spokes extending from a central cairn, and six outer cairns around the edge. All of this stands at an elevation of 2,939 meters and has been visited by Native Americans for at least 7,000 years. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1970, it remains an active ceremonial site used by tribes from across the Northern Great Plains - negotiations over the 1996 historic preservation plan involved representatives of 16 tribes. If a ceremony is underway when you arrive, stay back and observe in silence. The site is normally accessible from mid- or late June to mid-September, depending on snow cover.

King's Saddlery at 184 N. Main Street is a working shop, not a museum—the smell of leather, power tools, artisans making saddles and lassos. Don King opened it in 1963 after learning his trade riding cattle trails through Texas, Arizona and California as a child; his custom saddles are in the Cowboy Hall of Fame and the ProRodeo Hall of Champions. Behind the shop is the Don King Museum—free to enter—with historic saddles, wagons, photographs, and leatherworking tools spanning a century of Western craftsmanship. Ask the staff if you can watch them work.

The Historic Sheridan Inn at 856 Broadway Street opened in 1893 - built by the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad and designed by Thomas Kimball after a Scottish hunting lodge. It was the first building in the area with electric lights and bathtubs, and was said at opening to be the finest hotel between Chicago and San Francisco. Buffalo Bill Cody was a part-owner who auditioned Wild West show performers from the wraparound front porch. Reopened in 2015 after a 50-year closure; walk in for a meal or a drink without staying.

activities.text: The descent toward Sheridan along the Bighorn Scenic Byway (US-14) from Burgess Junction to Dayton offers a worthwhile stop: Steamboat Point, where a steep trail leads to a viewpoint with 360-degree views over the valley. US-14 is suitable for all vehicle types - US-14A is not.

Sheridan's Main Street in the evening is worth lingering on—the 1923 WYO Theater at 42 N. Main still hosts live performances in a building that newspapers called “Wyoming's wonderful movie palace” when it opened. A few blocks away, the Mint Bar has been a gathering spot since 1907: ranchers, rodeo cowboys, and passing travelers on the same barstools. No show for tourists; just a real Western town doing what it does.

visits.text: Behold Tsé Bitʼaʼí (Shiprock), a dramatic volcanic rock formation rising over 450 meters above the surrounding desert plain on Navajo Nation land. This sacred site holds profound spiritual significance to the Navajo people, who consider it a place of great power and cultural importance. The jagged peak and radiating dikes create one of the most distinctive natural landmarks in the American Southwest.

Learn about the geological and cultural significance of this ancient volcanic neck, the eroded remnant of a volcano that erupted approximately 27 million years ago. The formation's English name derives from its resemblance to a 19th-century clipper ship, while Navajo traditions associate it with a great bird that carried their ancestors to safety. Photography from surrounding viewpoints captures the monument's dramatic presence against endless desert skies.

activities.text: Experience the vast landscapes of the Navajo Nation, the largest Native American reservation in the United States, where traditional culture and natural beauty interweave across millions of acres of high desert terrain. Respect for sacred sites and Navajo customs enriches any visit to this remarkable region.

places.name: Shreveport, LA

visits.text: October 16, 1954, Shreveport Municipal Auditorium: Elvis Presley takes the stage for his first paid concert, age 18, at the venue for “Louisiana Hayride”, a country radio show broadcast nationally every Saturday. He would return 50 times over 18 months. Hank Williams had debuted there in 1948, Johnny Cash in 1955. Art Deco building from 1929, a 3,200-seat hall still in use. Guided tour $10 by appointment, mornings only.

A surprise of the trip and an absolute must-see: the R.W. Norton Art Gallery is the best-kept secret of Texas and Louisiana—a private collection bequeathed to the city in 1966 by an oil tycoon. Forty hectares of botanical gardens, plus a Frederic Remington collection (135 works, the world's largest collection of this artist of the American West) and works by Charles Russell. A rare-book library with 5,000 old volumes. Free admission.

Both folk art and historical testimony, the Louisiana State Exhibit Museum's 26 dioramas, arranged in a semicircle, were built in the 1930s by the WPA under Roosevelt—illustrating Louisiana life (sugarcane harvesting, bayou fishing, a Creole forge), and restored in 2010. On Greenwood Road. Free, Tuesday–Friday.

activities.text: Pierre Avenue, a little wooden shack: Herby-K's Restaurant has been open since 1936 and the house specialty is found nowhere else—the “Shrimp Buster”, shrimp pounded between two sheets of wax paper to half a millimeter thick, then grilled. $22. Brusque but cordial service, as it should be. A line at lunchtime.

You finish the day at the Strand Theatre, a fully restored 1925 theater—country, blues, Broadway. Check the schedule (strandtheatre.com); many nights have no concert. Otherwise, an open mic at Noble Savage Tavern, a bar with local beers and local musicians until 1 AM.

places.name: Sioux City, IA

visits.text: The Sergeant Floyd Monument stands on a bluff overlooking the Missouri—a 30-meter Egyptian-style obelisk of Kettle River sandstone completed in 1901 and among the first 92 sites designated as National Historic Landmarks in the United States in 1960. Floyd's remains are sealed at its base. He died on August 20, 1804, at age 22, likely from a ruptured appendix—the only member of the Corps of Discovery to perish during the entire expedition. His last words to Clark were: “I'm going away and I want you to write me a letter.” The grave was twice washed away by Missouri River erosion before the Floyd Monument Association secured permanent burial here. Free site; the view over the river valley is the reason to linger.

The Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center on the riverfront levee goes deeper into the Great Plains section of the 1804 journey than almost any other stop on this trail. Interactive exhibits cover the Lakota tensions near present-day Pierre, Floyd's death, the natural history the Corps documented, and the Missouri as the highway of the interior. The center sits in a converted pavilion with direct views of the river bend the expedition navigated. Paid entry; open daily.

Built in 1918, the Woodbury County Courthouse at 7th and Douglas is a National Historic Landmark — designed by William Gray Purcell and George Elmslie, two protégés of Louis Sullivan, in the organic Prairie style. The exterior terra cotta ornament and the central rotunda are among the most elaborate public interior spaces in the upper Midwest. Free to enter during business hours. The Sioux City Art Center, three blocks away, holds regional and contemporary works with free admission and is worth a 30-minute stop.

activities.text: Stone State Park in the northwest corner of Sioux City has bluff trails reaching an elevation of 300 meters with views of the Missouri Valley and three states simultaneously—Iowa, Nebraska, and South Dakota. The Dorothy Pecaut Nature Center inside the park runs natural history programming and exhibits on the Missouri River ecosystem the Corps navigated. The Sergeant Floyd River Museum at the south end of town doubles as the city visitor center and has a 19th-century sternwheeler on display.

The Historic Fourth Street District two blocks from the river is Sioux City's restaurant and entertainment corridor. The city has a strong Czech and German immigrant food culture that persists in family-owned bakeries and supper clubs. If you're arriving in the evening, Fourth Street is where you eat — several restaurants specialize in grilled Midwest beef and the craft beer scene on this block has grown considerably in recent years.

visits.text: Head to Sioux Falls, South Dakota's largest city. Falls Park is the heart of town: the Big Sioux River cascades over pink quartzite formations 1.7 billion years old. In season, 14,000 liters of water per second rush over the rocks. Climb the observation tower (5 stories) for an overview, then descend onto the walkways at water level. The ruins of an old 1881 stone mill add a photogenic touch to the scene.

Downtown Sioux Falls has completely reinvented itself in recent years. SculptureWalk is an outdoor trail of over 60 contemporary sculptures installed along the sidewalks—they change annually. Phillips Avenue is the main street, with pink quartzite buildings (the same stone as the falls) converted into restaurants, galleries, and bars.

activities.text: In the evening, sample Sioux Falls' food scene—the city has exploded gastronomically with chefs highlighting Great Plains products: bison, sweet corn, wild berries. For local beer, downtown craft breweries abound.
