places.name: Skaneateles, NY

visits.text: The lake water is so clear it supplies Syracuse, 30 km north, with minimal treatment—one of the few large American lakes in this situation. Skaneateles (pronounced skin-ee-AT-lus) borders the north shore, with a center spanning just two streets: Genesee Street and Jordan Street, lined with white Federal-style houses from the early 19th century. Clift Park, free admission, opens directly onto the lake with its wooden dock. Best toward the end of the day, with golden light on the nearly still water.

Saint James' Episcopal Church (1873), at the corner of West Genesee Street, deserves a quick stop for its dark wood interior and stained glass windows. Free entry on weekdays; ask at the parish office next door. The church hosts an organ festival each summer, with detailed programs posted at the entrance.

John D. Barrow Art Gallery, above the municipal library, displays the paintings of the eponymous landscape artist (1824–1906) for free. He spent his life painting the lake under every kind of light. Small gallery, 30 minutes is enough, but it's a valuable record of American landscape painting in the Hudson River School tradition.

activities.text: Lake cruise with Mid-Lakes Navigation, a family operation since 1968. Two options: the classic one-hour outing aboard the Judge Ben Wiles (1985 boat), or the three-hour mail cruise aboard the Barbara S. Wiles, a wooden steamboat launched in 1937. The latter follows the actual mail delivery to residences inaccessible by road—about a dozen families still depend exclusively on the boat for their mail. A continuous tradition since the 19th century, except during both World Wars.

Tasting at Anyela's Vineyards, five kilometers southwest of the village, on the slopes overlooking the lake. The estate treats its Riesling and Vidal Blanc with Germanic rigor. Wooden terrace, views across the vines sloping toward the water. Complimentary glass with bottle purchase.

Monumental and experimental works facing the water, free admission from sunrise to sunset. The do-it-yourself spirit of Queens, a world away from yesterday's museums.

Day 3 - optional: Right next to Socrates Sculpture Park, the Noguchi Museum showcases Isamu Noguchi's studio and sculptures in a converted factory: one of the city's most serene museums. Together, the two make Astoria a real afternoon destination for art lovers.

activities.text: In summer, there's a farmers market and outdoor movie screenings in the park: check the schedule; everything is free.

places.name: Soho Cast Iron, NY

visits.text: Day 2 - SoHo has the world's highest density of cast-iron façades, painted in shades from almond green to deep black. Look up above the shops: Corinthian columns, zigzag fire escapes, Greene Street cobblestones. The neighborhood is best enjoyed early, before the stores open and the tide of shopping bags arrives.

Day 2 - At 488–492 Broadway, the 1857 Haughwout Building was one of the first buildings equipped with an Otis elevator: cast iron already made it possible to build tall. Art galleries have largely migrated to Chelsea, but a few hold on upstairs in SoHo. Admission is free; don't hesitate to go in.

activities.text: A proper break or some window-shopping: Mercer and Greene Streets, quieter than Broadway, hide cafés and bookstores where you can catch your breath for twenty minutes.
Walk to Washington Square Park: 1 km heading north, about 12 min.

places.name: South Bend, IN

visits.text: You enter the Notre Dame campus along its main avenue and the Golden Dome catches your eye before you even park - a 21-meter gilded dome topped by a statue of the Virgin Mary, crowning the Main Building rebuilt in 1879 after a fire. The Basilica of the Sacred Heart, consecrated in 1888 and made a minor basilica by Pope John Paul II in 1992, houses a collection of 19th-century French-style stained glass - imported directly from France in the late 19th century. The organ added in 2016 cost USD 4 million. The Notre Dame Grotto - a one-seventh-scale replica of the Massabielle grotto in Lourdes - is lit by candles at all hours of the day and night. Campus access is free; free guided tours leave from the Eck Visitor Center on weekdays.

You climb the steps of the Studebaker National Museum and find yourself facing 150 years of American industrial history, from the Conestoga wagon to the last car model off the lines in 1963. The most historically charged piece sits on the ground floor: an unassuming carriage - the four-horse landau that carried Abraham Lincoln from his hotel to Ford's Theatre in Washington on the evening of April 14, 1865, hours before his assassination. The Studebaker family began building Conestoga wagons for western pioneers in 1852, converted to automobiles in 1902, and delivered 275,000 jeeps to the US Army during World War II. Open Monday-Saturday 10am-5pm, Sunday noon-5pm; admission: $15 combined with The History Museum.

You follow the St. Joseph River until you see the white foam of the rapids from the footbridge—you are looking at the East Race Waterway, the first artificial whitewater course built in the United States using this hydraulic technique, created in 1977 in a branch of the river. The 450-meter course served as an official course for the kayak World Cup in 1979. In the evening, the River Lights, inaugurated in 2015, illuminate the St. Joseph River until midnight—the riverside walk between East Race and downtown South Bend takes 20 minutes on foot and is worth a detour after dinner.

activities.text: You approach Notre Dame Stadium and look up: a monumental 28-meter mosaic depicts Christ with his arms raised - fans have nicknamed it 'Touchdown Jesus' because it resembles a referee's signal. Opened in 1930 with 59,000 seats and renovated in 1997 and 2017 to reach 80,795 spectators, the stadium has hosted teams among the most decorated in NCAA history. Outside game days, the forecourt is freely accessible for photos in front of the mosaic. On fall game days, the campus atmosphere from early morning turns South Bend into the capital of American college sports - book well ahead.

You push open the door at South Bend Chocolate Company—an artisan chocolatier founded in 1991 that makes its bars and confections in its own workshops. A small free museum traces the history of cacao from the Maya to 20th-century industrial chocolatiers, with a collection of antique molds and vintage advertisements. The main store adjoins downtown and serves as a gathering place for Notre Dame fans before home games. Hot chocolate made to order is the winter specialty; salted butter caramel is sold year-round and is the company's best-known house-made product.

places.name: South Padre Island, TX

visits.text: Sea Turtle Inc. is a nonprofit organization founded in 1977 by Ila Fox Loetscher, known locally as 'The Turtle Lady of South Padre Island'. Initially created in her backyard garden to protect Kemp's ridley turtles - a species on the brink of extinction - the organization moved in 1999 to its current facility and now treats over 100 turtles per year. During the great Texas freeze of February 2021, Sea Turtle Inc. rescued several thousand hypothermic turtles in a matter of days. You can visit Tuesday through Sunday; the daily 'Turtle Talks' at 11:30 AM are highly informative. If you're there in summer, inquire about baby turtle releases on the beach.

Isla Blanca Park occupies the southern tip of South Padre Island, with a fishing pier, a well-equipped beach and a direct view of the Brazos Santiago Pass - the channel through which large ships enter Laguna Madre. It's also one of the best kitesurfing and windsurfing spots on the Texas coast thanks to steady Gulf winds.

Palo Alto Battlefield National Historical Park, around twenty kilometers north of Brownsville, preserves the site of the first battle of the Mexican-American War, fought on May 8, 1846. Plan a round trip from South Padre Island for this visit. General Zachary Taylor's 2,300 US troops faced 3,700 Mexican soldiers here. The battle marked the beginning of a conflict that led Mexico to cede a third of its territory to the United States, a war that deeply divided American opinion. The NPS visitor center offers an effective introductory film; do not miss the battlefield map showing the troop movements.

Brownsville, on the Rio Grande, faces Matamoros on the Mexican side. Plan a round trip from South Padre Island to visit the city. Its nineteenth-century historic center retains Spanish colonial houses and shaded squares that recall its prosperous past as a border town. You can walk along the riverbank; the Rio Grande here is surprisingly narrow, scarcely wider than a canal.

activities.text: South Padre Island's beach offers 34 miles of fine white sand and turquoise waters at 82-86°F from June through September. The island's north section, less crowded than the city's waterfront, gives a sense of what Padre Island looked like before development. Arrive early in the morning to have the beach to yourself before 10 AM.

Laguna Madre, a 130-mile-long hypersaline lagoon separating South Padre Island from the mainland, is one of the few hypersaline lagoon systems in the world. Operators offer kayak or stand-up paddle outings in this calm, shallow water frequented by dolphins, stingrays and brown pelicans. Leave early - dolphins are most active between 7 and 10 AM.

Operators from South Padre Island run boat tours to observe bottlenose dolphins in the Brazos Santiago channel, the passage between the island and the coast. These dolphins are permanent residents of the lagoon and channel - observation odds exceed 90% according to local operators. Late afternoon, the raking light on the water makes for easier photography.

The bay-side sunset on South Padre Island is one of the most beautiful day's endings on the Texas coast. Laguna Madre takes on orange and pink hues for 20 to 30 minutes before turning violet. Head to the island's west side (Bay Side) an hour before official sunset - in summer, count on around 8 PM. It's the perfect place to wrap up this 9-day road trip before heading to Harlingen airport (40 min) or McAllen (1h) the next morning.

visits.text: Discover downtown Spartanburg's revitalized urban core, where recent development has created a walkable district suited to relaxed exploration. The compact downtown divides into distinct neighborhoods, each offering its own character and dining options. Historic architecture mixes with contemporary additions in this evolving Upstate community.

activities.text: Experience the Hub City's emerging cultural scene, where local establishments reflect regional tastes in comfortable settings. The downtown area has transformed into a destination for travelers seeking authentic small-city Southern atmosphere. Spartanburg's position along major routes makes it an ideal stopping point between coastal and mountain destinations.

visits.text: A long drive west through the Iowa prairies—3½ hours of corn and soybean fields stretching as far as the eye can see. You arrive at the Iowa Great Lakes, the state's lakeside resort area. West Okoboji Lake is known for its clear water. Settle in on the beach at Arnolds Park in the early afternoon.

Arnolds Park Amusement Park, open since 1889, is Iowa's oldest operating amusement park. This isn't Disneyland—it's a retro lakeside carnival with wooden roller coasters, vintage rides, and a "1950s American summer" vibe. Next door, the Iowa Great Lakes Maritime Museum traces the region's nautical history.

activities.text: Late in the day, drive around the lake or rent a pontoon to cruise the water. The sunset over West Okoboji is one of Iowa's most beautiful—locals compare it (with considerable enthusiasm) to those of Lake Como.

places.name: Spring Green, WI

visits.text: Taliesin - Frank Lloyd Wright's residence, studio, and 320-hectare estate in the Driftless Area hills. The name comes from Welsh meaning "shining brow" - Wright built his house on the hillside, not the summit, because "if you build on top of the hill, you lose the hill." Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, it's Wisconsin's only publicly accessible UNESCO site. Budget 2-4 hours depending on the tour chosen.
Hillside Home School (1903) - The school Wright designed for his aunts, with its enormous assembly hall and diamond-paned windows. Later became the Taliesin apprentice architects' workshop.
Romeo and Juliet Windmill (1896) - One of Wright's early commissions. The structure of interlocking diamond and octagon was so bold his uncle bet it wouldn't stand. It's still there, 130 years later.
Riverview Terrace Café - Wright's last restaurant design in the world. Panoramic windows overlooking the Wisconsin River. Local cuisine, relaxed atmosphere. Make it a lunch stop.

activities.text: Taliesin Guided Tour - Four tour options, from 1h to 4h. The 'Highlights' tour (2h) offers the best time-to-content ratio: you visit the school, Wright's residence, and studio. The 'Estate' tour (4h) covers the entire grounds including Midway Barn and gardens. Booking essential.

visits.text: Zion Canyon Scenic Drive—This 10 km road runs up the canyon and is served by a free shuttle (mandatory from March to November). Navajo sandstone cliffs rise 600 m on either side. First stop: Court of the Patriarchs, three monoliths named Abraham, Isaac and Jacob by a Methodist minister in 1916. The view from the platform is one of the park's most photographed.

Emerald Pools—Three cascading pools fed by springs seeping through the sandstone. The Lower Pool is an easy 20-minute walk. If you have the energy, continue to the Upper Pool—the waterfall drops from a 30 m ledge into a red rock amphitheater. Allow 1.5 hours for the full loop.

Continue by shuttle to the Temple of Sinawava at the end of the road. This natural temple takes its name from the Paiute coyote god. Here the canyon narrows to just 6 meters wide with walls 600 m high—the transition to The Narrows. The Riverside Walk, a paved 1.6 km trail along the Virgin River, leads you to the canyon entrance. Even without entering the water, the walk is worth the detour.

Angels Landing OR The Narrows—Today is built around a choice. Both hikes are long and demanding; doing both in one day is only realistic for very fit hikers. Choose the one that suits you. Option 1: Angels Landing. The trail gains 450 m in elevation over a 4 km round trip. Walter's Wiggles, 21 switchbacks carved into the rock in 1926, haul you up to Scout Lookout. From there, the final section follows a narrow ridge with chains as the only safety measure and sheer drops on both sides—a 450 m fall. A permit is mandatory (online lottery). If you don't have a permit or suffer from vertigo, Scout Lookout already offers spectacular canyon views. Start early in the morning.

Weeping Rock—After the exertion of Angels Landing, this short 800 m trail leads to a rock overhang where water seeps constantly. The water you see dripping is actually rainfall from 1,200 years ago, filtered slowly through the sandstone. It's cool, relaxing, and takes 20 minutes.

activities.text: At the end of the day, wander through the village of Springdale. Art galleries and outdoor patios line the road leading to the park entrance. If you're planning to do The Narrows tomorrow, stop by a rental shop to pick up neoprene shoes, a walking stick, and waterproof pants—essential if the water is cold or the current strong.

Option 2: The Narrows from the bottom—If you prefer canyons to heights, or if you don't have an Angels Landing permit, enter The Narrows from the Temple of Sinawava. You'll walk directly in the Virgin River between walls 600 m high just a few meters apart. No permit is needed for the bottom-up out-and-back route—go as far as you like and turn around. Allow 3 to 5 hours depending on your ambition. Warning: flash floods are deadly; don't attempt this hike if a thunderstorm is forecast. If you're a seasoned hiker and leave at dawn, you can attempt both—but plan for a 10-hour day and bring plenty of water.

If you have time at the end of the day, take the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway eastward. The 1.7 km tunnel carved through the sandstone between 1927 and 1930 is an engineering feat—windows cut into the rock offer dizzying views into the canyon. On the other side, don't miss Checkerboard Mesa, a sandstone dome striped with horizontal and vertical lines that resembles a giant chessboard.

visits.text: Begin your Appalachian Trail experience at Springer Mountain, the legendary southern terminus of the 3,525-km footpath stretching to Maine. Georgia's 127-km section winds through misty forests, wildflower meadows, and rhododendron tunnels, and offers spectacular panoramic overlooks. Standing at the bronze plaque marking Kilometer Zero creates a profound connection to one of America's greatest hiking traditions.

Climb Blood Mountain, the highest point on Georgia's Appalachian Trail at 1,359 meters, where the ruins of an old stone shelter and sweeping ridge views reward determined hikers. The challenging terrain passes through diverse ecosystems supporting black bears, deer, salamanders, and countless songbirds. Backcountry camping sites offer stargazing far from light pollution.

activities.text: Visit the legendary Mountain Crossings outfitter at Neel Gap, the only building the Appalachian Trail passes directly through. The famous 'shoe tree' outside displays worn-out hiking boots left by through-hikers, many containing handwritten notes and memories. Detour to misty Long Creek Falls for a serene waterfall tucked into the forest.

visits.text: Gemini Giant (Wilmington, IL)—This 9-meter fiberglass giant holding a Gemini rocket is the first of the “Muffler Men” you will encounter along the Route. Built in the 1960s to attract motorists. A quick photo stop.

Pontiac Murals - Don't pass through without stopping - this small Illinois town has transformed its walls into an open-air gallery. Over 20 murals tell the story of Route 66. The Route 66 Hall of Fame Museum is right next door - free admission.

Abraham Lincoln Home (Springfield) - The only house Lincoln ever owned, preserved by the National Park Service. Pick up a free ticket at the visitor center for the guided tour - first come, first served. The entire neighborhood is preserved as it was in the 1860s.

activities.text: Lunch at the Cozy Dog Drive In - This is where the corn dog (deep-fried cornmeal-battered sausage on a stick) was invented in 1946. The restaurant is still run by the same family and the walls are covered with Route 66 memorabilia.

places.name: Springfield

visits.text: Get to Wilson's Creek before you do anything else in Springfield. On August 10, 1861, on this hill 16 km southwest of town, 5,400 Union soldiers held off 12,000 Confederates for five hours. General Nathaniel Lyon died here—the first Union general killed in combat during the war. Around 2,330 men fell that day. The 8 km auto tour loop is well marked, and the 1852 Ray House is open in summer. Take time to walk on Bloody Hill—the interpretive panels are good and the terrain has changed little.

Wonders of Wildlife sits right against the wall of the original Bass Pro Shops—both occupy the same city block. It's the most awarded aquarium in the United States, and it shows: sea turtles in rehabilitation, sharks, river otters, and full-scale recreations of North American landscapes spreading across multiple floors. Block out at least two hours. If your kids drag their feet at the entrance, mention the shark tank.

The History Museum on the Square is worth 45 minutes even if local museums bore you. Its Route 66 gallery tells how the highway's name was proposed from Springfield by telegram on April 30, 1926—Cyrus Avery and John Woodruff wanted the future major national highway to run through here. Original neon signs, a 1957 Chevrolet, and archives from the Rail Haven motel where Elvis slept in 1956. Free admission.

activities.text: Springfield's Bass Pro Shops covers 46,500 m², and even if you buy nothing, it is a spectacle. Giant aquariums run through the fishing departments, a vivarium houses alligators, and Hemingway's Restaurant looks like a safari trophy room. The NRA National Sporting Arms Museum is housed in the building. Allow an hour just to walk around.

Park Central Square brings together the best places for an evening out in downtown Springfield. This is a college town—Missouri State University has 24,000 students—and it changes the vibe: less kitschy than Branson, more affordable. Order a cocktail at Golden Girl Rum Club or have dinner at Civil Kitchen. Set aside the next morning for Branson.

places.name: St Augustine, FL

visits.text: Saint Augustine is the oldest city of European origin in the United States, founded by the Spanish on September 8, 1565 - 42 years before Jamestown, 55 years before the Mayflower landed at Plymouth. The historic center retains its 16th-century layout, with whitewashed single-story houses built of coquina (local limestone made of oyster shells). Saint George Street, pedestrianized, crosses the quarter for 1.5 kilometers. Avoid weekend afternoons when it's packed.

The Castillo de San Marcos is the oldest masonry fortification in the United States - built by the Spanish from 1672 to 1695. Its stone is coquina (shell limestone), so porous it absorbed cannonballs rather than shattering. No siege ever succeeded in taking it. Four star-shaped bastions, dry moat, Spanish flag still hoisted. Self-guided tours, $15, cannon-firing demonstrations in period costume on weekends.

Flagler College occupies the former Hotel Ponce de Leon, opened in 1888 by railway magnate Henry Flagler. It is one of the first large buildings in the United States to be fully electrified - Thomas Edison himself supervised the installation. The Spanish Renaissance interior - carved wood, Tiffany stained glass, frescoed dining room - has remained intact. 1-hour tours led by students, $12.

The Fountain of Youth Archaeological Park marks the spot where Juan Ponce de León supposedly discovered the Florida coast in 1513 - the "fountain of youth" story is probably a 19th-century legend, but the site is genuinely authentic. Artesian spring (slightly sulfurous water, taste without illusions), reconstructed Timucua village, archaeological remains of the first Spanish mission. $19.

activities.text: Try the datil pepper, a chilli grown almost exclusively in Saint Augustine since the 18th century (introduced by Minorcan settlers). Heat comparable to a habanero but fruitier. Datil B Good's sauce goes with every local dish.

Evening stroll through the neighborhood during Nights of Lights, an illumination of 3 million white bulbs covering the historic center from mid-November to late January. National Geographic ranked it among the 10 most beautiful holiday light displays in the world. Off-season, the streets at dusk by period gas lamp retain their charm.

places.name: St Charles, MO

visits.text: At Bishop's Landing on the Missouri River, the Lewis & Clark Boat House and Museum keeps the full-scale operational replicas of the keelboat and both pirogues that carried the Corps out of this town on May 21, 1804. The keelboat was built by volunteers from the Discovery Expedition of St. Charles using period tools and methods reconstructed from the expedition's journal descriptions—the original construction plans were never preserved. Clark's journal entry that day is brief: the crew had partied until 5 a.m. the night before and could only manage a few kilometers upriver. Open Monday to Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., Sunday from noon to 5 p.m.; paid entry. The 4.5-meter bronze sculpture of Lewis, Clark, and Seaman just outside is the tallest Lewis and Clark monument on the entire trail.

Federal-style brick buildings line Historic Main Street, and the one at 200 South Main deserves particular attention: the First Missouri State Capitol, where the new state's legislature met from 1821 to 1826 before Jefferson City was ready. A guided tour of the 11-room building covers the debates over slavery, states' rights, and taxation that shaped early Missouri — all while commerce hummed in the Peck Brothers dry goods store downstairs. Free admission; tours run throughout the day.

South Main Street runs directly alongside the Missouri River, and the Katy Trail—a 386 km converted rail corridor—begins right here. Even if you only walk one kilometer north from Frontier Park, you're on the same riverbank the Corps navigated along in 1804. The trail is packed dirt and crushed limestone, flat and easy, with cottonwoods overhead and the river in earshot. Bike rentals are available from local outfitters near the trailhead; a one-hour ride in either direction rewards you with Missouri plains scenery.

activities.text: Historic Main Street has more than 25 restaurants, and the area from South Main to Second Street offers everything from traditional Missouri cuisine to riverside patios. Eat dinner outside if the weather allows—this is one of the few spots on the trail where you can watch the Missouri River while you eat. Lewis and Clark were guests of honor at dinners here the night before departure; several restaurants stay open past 9 p.m. on weekends.

Route 94 west of St. Charles follows the Missouri River to Defiance and Augusta through Missouri wine country, with hillsides planted with Norton, Vignoles and Traminette. Lewis and Clark passed through this very landscape in 1804. Chandler Hill Winery in Defiance and Sugar Creek Winery are two tasting rooms; the scenic round trip takes about 90 minutes with one stop. The road itself matters as much as the wine.

places.name: St Francisville

visits.text: The Myrtles Plantation was built in 1796 by General David Bradford, a Whiskey Rebellion insurgent who fled Pennsylvania after George Washington ordered his arrest. The Creole cottage-style house, its 22 rooms and long veranda draped with oaks covered in Spanish moss make it one of the most frequently cited places in American paranormal tourism guides. The legend of the enslaved woman Chloe—whose ear was allegedly cut off before she poisoned her owners' family—isn't historically documented, but guides on candlelit nighttime tours readily tell it. The only verified murder on the property is that of William Winter in 1871, shot on the veranda and said to have died while climbing the 17 steps of the staircase.

Rosedown Plantation, built in 1835, is among the South's best-preserved with its 28 acres of French-style formal gardens—oak avenues, camellia beds, and cast-iron statues imported from Paris. The main house and its period outbuildings remained in the same family for five generations before being purchased by the State of Louisiana in 2003. If you visit in spring, the blooming azaleas and camellias make these gardens among the Deep South's most beautiful.

The Audubon State Historic Site is home to Oakley House, the plantation where naturalist John James Audubon lived and worked from June to October 1821, during which time he drew 32 of the birds in his monumental Birds of America. The surrounding woods are still frequented by the species he observed there—bring binoculars and allow 30 minutes to walk the trails behind the house, where birdlife is particularly abundant at daybreak.

activities.text: Hiking in Tunica Hills on the Clark Creek trail: 6 km of trails wind through wooded gorges with waterfalls and deep ravines. The site is in Mississippi; plan to drive from St Francisville to the Pond Store Road parking lot, then continue on foot. The best of this scenery is concentrated in the first 3 kilometers from the Pond Store Road parking lot.

visits.text: A pioneer town in the middle of the desert: Historic Downtown St. George preserves this contrast between historic buildings and an arid horizon. Downtown’s public spaces offer an urban break before Zion’s trails. Take a short walking loop, then have lunch here before heading to Springdale.

activities.text: Red sandstone warms the colors of Pioneer Park, just above St. George. Rounded boulders and passages between the rocks create a setting for a walk with the city below. Stay on the easy paths and avoid narrow crevices if they make you uncomfortable.

days_plan.itin_title: Las Vegas in 10 Days: Zion, Bryce, and the Grand Canyon

visits.text: Robert Mondavi Winery, Oakville: the California mission-style architecture is a calling card, but what matters most lies elsewhere. Mondavi reshaped American wine tourism in the 1960s and coined the term “Fumé Blanc” in 1968 to rebrand Sauvignon Blanc. The To Kalon vineyard (plantings dating to 1868) is one of Napa's oldest—the tour that includes a walk through the vineyard plots explains better than any lecture what makes Oakville Cabernets distinctive.

Inglenook in Rutherford, owned by Francis Ford Coppola since 1975: the director of The Godfather bought the winery founded by the Niebaum family in 1879 and fully restored it. Rubicon remains the estate's flagship wine.

Beringer Vineyards, St. Helena: founded in 1876, it's Napa Valley's oldest continuously operating winery. The Rhine House, a Victorian mansion built in 1884 by Frederick Beringer for his brother Jacob and modeled on their childhood home in Mainz, is a designated historic building. Even if you don't taste here, the exterior justifies the stop.

Hall Wines, St. Helena: the modern architecture contrasts with the neighboring Victorian style. A rabbit sculpture by Lawrence Argent—“Bunny Foo Foo”, 11 meters tall in chrome-plated steel—is visible from the road. It was installed in 2010 and has become a visual landmark on Highway 29. Inside, the contemporary art collection hangs among the barrels. Tasting $75.

activities.text: Lunch at Gott's Roadside, St. Helena: founded in 1949 as Taylor's Refresher, it's an outdoor drive-in serving burgers and milkshakes made with local ingredients. Don't turn your nose up at it—it's the quintessential local institution, and the ahi tuna burger is better than expected. Fast-moving line; eat standing up or in the car, $15–20 per person.

A drive along Highway 29 from St. Helena to Calistoga at golden hour: the 15 km separating the two towns run alongside century-old vineyards, discreet estates, and wineries that don't display their names. Driving this stretch just before dinner, without stopping, gives you a sense of the landscape that tastings alone don't provide.

days_plan.itin_title: California Wine Country in 10 Days: San Francisco to Los Angeles Through the Vineyards

visits.text: Charlevoix - A driving day with three stops, covering about 200 km total between Traverse City and St. Ignace. First stop: Charlevoix, a harbor town wedged between Lake Michigan and Lake Charlevoix, 45 minutes from Traverse City. It's worth the detour for its “Mushroom Houses” - 28 stone cottages with undulating roofs and whimsical mushroom shapes, built between 1919 and 1973 by Earl Young, a self-taught builder who never obtained an architecture degree. He worked without blueprints, using limestone blocks and boulders hauled from Lake Michigan. Pick up a walking tour map at the visitor center on Mason Street - the finest examples cluster along Park Avenue and Clinton Street.

Petoskey - Gaslight District - Continue on US-31 to Petoskey, a resort town perched on Little Traverse Bay. The historic Gaslight District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, contains 278 period buildings and about 170 shops and restaurants. Look for the Ernest Hemingway statue - he spent summers here in his youth and frequented the City Park Grill, which still operates today. Don't leave without collecting a “Petoskey stone” from the beach - this 350-million-year-old coral fossil is Michigan's official state stone.

Mackinac Bridge - After Petoskey, reach Mackinaw City to cross the Mackinac Bridge, nicknamed the “Mighty Mac.” Opened in 1957, this suspension bridge measures 8 km total (26,372 feet). Its suspension span between anchorages (8,614 feet) makes it the longest suspension bridge in the Western Hemisphere by this measure - though its main span between towers (3,800 feet) ranks third in North America, behind the Golden Gate and Verrazzano-Narrows. Engineer David Steinman designed it to withstand violent strait winds: the deck can shift laterally 10 meters under extreme gusts, and the roadway surface is open-grated to let wind pass through. Five workers died during the 42 months of construction. The crossing takes about 10 minutes by car - enjoy views of Lake Michigan to the left and Lake Huron to the right.

Mackinac Island - Take the ferry from St. Ignace (15-minute crossing) to reach this island where cars have been banned since the 1920s. Everything happens on foot, by bicycle, or in horse-drawn carriages. The island welcomes nearly a million visitors per year but counts only 600 permanent residents. Upon docking, you'll arrive in a Victorian-fronted village lined with fudge shops - it's been the local specialty for over a century.

Grand Hotel - Perched on a bluff overlooking the straits, this 1887 hotel boasts the world's longest porch: 200 meters long, lined with rocking chairs. Five U.S. presidents have stayed here. Thomas Edison gave the first public demonstration of his phonograph here. The film “Somewhere in Time” starring Christopher Reeve was shot here in 1980. At minimum, climb up to the porch for the view - a small admission fee is charged if you're not a hotel guest.

Fort Mackinac - This fort built by the British in 1780 towers over the harbor from a limestone bluff. It played a role in the War of 1812 between Americans and British. You'll find 14 restored period buildings, cannon-firing demonstrations in season, and panoramic views of the straits and Mackinac Bridge in the distance.

Arch Rock - Continuing around the island on foot or by bike, don't miss this natural limestone arch perched 45 meters above Lake Huron. Formed by erosion, it measures roughly 15 meters across. A 207-step staircase leads up from the coastal road.

activities.text: Petoskey Stone Hunting at Petoskey State Park - Before leaving the area, stop at Petoskey State Park. The beach pebbles hide Petoskey stones - hexagonal Devonian coral fossils. Wet the stones to reveal the pattern - it shows up better on a damp surface. Allow 30 to 45 minutes for a beach stroll.

Bike Loop Around the Island - The coastal road runs 13 km and traces Lake Huron around the island's entire perimeter. It's flat, easy, and the scenery alternates between limestone cliffs, forest, and beaches. Bike rentals are available near the dock. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours without stops.

Sunset from Straits State Park - Back in St. Ignace, head to this small state park to watch the sun set behind the towers of Mackinac Bridge. The silhouette of the illuminated bridge at twilight is one of Michigan's most photogenic images.

places.name: St Louis, MO

visits.text: One hundred and ninety-two meters of stainless steel form a curve above the Mississippi, and you feel it before you see it—the Gateway Arch pulls the eye skyward from the moment you step into Gateway Arch National Park. Designed by Eero Saarinen in 1948 and built between 1963 and 1965, it remains the tallest arch in the world, equal in height and width. At its base, the Museum of Westward Expansion connects the Arch directly to the Lewis and Clark Expedition, which launched from this region in 1804. Book tram tickets to the observation deck well in advance—the tiny capsule ride is part of the experience, and views stretch 50 km on a clear day.

The green dome of the Old Courthouse is impossible to miss from the Arch, and the building merits a stop in its own right. On April 6, 1846, Dred and Harriet Scott filed for their freedom in this building—one of more than 300 freedom suits filed here before 1860. Their case reached the Supreme Court in 1857, where Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that enslaved people were not citizens—a decision many historians believe accelerated the Civil War. The courthouse, completed in its current form in 1864, is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. with free admission. The mock trial program run by rangers brings the Scotts' case back to life.

Cross the Mississippi to Hartford, Illinois, and you're standing at the spot where the Corps of Discovery spent the winter from December 1803 to May 14, 1804. The Lewis & Clark State Historic Site holds a full-scale replica of the 17-meter keelboat, cut away on one side so you can see exactly how more than 200 bundles, barrels, and boxes were stacked for the journey. Six galleries in the 1,300 m² interpretive center cover the preparation phase in detail that the Arch museum doesn't match. Allow at least 45 minutes—the confluence viewing area outside, where the Missouri meets the Mississippi, is worth lingering at.

activities.text: Walk the levee along the Mississippi south of the Arch after dark and you get the full scale of Saarinen's curve lit against the sky. During the day, Gateway Arch Riverboats run one-hour narrated cruises on replica paddlewheelers — a gentle way to see St. Louis from the water and understand why this bend in the river made the city. Boats depart from the levee just north of the Arch; check the schedule as departures vary by season.

The City Museum is not a museum—it's a multi-story playground built from salvaged architectural fragments, with caves, tunnels, a rooftop Ferris wheel, and a ten-story slide. Created by artist Bob Cassilly in a former shoe factory, it opened in 1997 and has no equivalent anywhere else in the country. Three kilometers from the Arch; open until midnight on weekends. If you're traveling with kids or simply want to end Day 1 somewhere genuinely strange, allow two hours.

places.name: St Patricks Cathedral, NY

visits.text: Day 3 - Wedged between towers, St Patrick's Cathedral displays its white neo-Gothic architecture opposite Rockefeller Center: spires about 100 m tall, a rose window, over 2,000 seats. Free admission, daily services, relative quiet despite the stream of visitors. Fifteen minutes are enough, but the contrast with Fifth Avenue makes it worth a stop.

Day 3 - St Patrick's crypt houses New York's archbishops and Pierre Toussaint, a formerly enslaved man on the path to canonization. Look up at the great organ and its thousands of pipes. The cathedral reopened in 2015 after a major restoration: the stone regained its original whiteness.

activities.text: Fifth Avenue window-shopping between 49th and 59th Streets: Saks, Tiffany, the Apple glass cube. Free as long as you don't go into any of the stores.
Walk to MoMA: 300 m via 53rd Street, about 4 min.

visits.text: St. Petersburg - The Sunshine City: This bayside community combines the relaxed feel of a beach town with an increasingly sophisticated arts scene.
The Dalí Museum - The Salvador Dalí Collection: This striking waterfront museum houses more than 2,400 works by the surrealist master, including seven of his 18 monumental 'masterpiece' paintings.
St. Pete Murals - An Open-Air Gallery: Over 700 murals transform the city into one of America's largest outdoor art exhibitions, with new works constantly appearing on buildings throughout downtown.
The Don CeSar - The Pink Palace of St. Pete Beach: This iconic 1928 resort, painted its distinctive Pepto-Bismol pink, has hosted everyone from F. Scott Fitzgerald to Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Fort De Soto Park - Five Interconnected Islands of Paradise: Allow for a round trip from St. Petersburg. This 460-hectare park at the southern tip of Tampa Bay offers camping, fishing, hiking, and some of Florida's most beautiful beaches.

activities.text: St. Pete Beach Water Sports - Gulf Coast Adventures: The calm, warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico provide ideal conditions for paddleboarding, parasailing, and kayaking.

visits.text: Explore St. Simons Island, the largest of Georgia's Golden Isles, where wide golden beaches, moss-draped oaks, shimmering salt marshes, and a charming village atmosphere create quintessential coastal Georgia scenery. The historic lighthouse dating to 1872 offers panoramic views from its tower, reached by climbing 129 steps. Over 48 km of bike paths wind past tree spirits carved into ancient oaks by local artists.

Visit Fort Frederica National Monument, the substantial ruins of a colonial-era British fortification established in 1736 to defend against Spanish incursion from Florida. The moss-covered walls and archaeological excavations reveal 18th-century military life on the frontier. Cannon's Point Preserve offers hiking through wild maritime forest where salty marsh aromas drift on ocean breezes.

activities.text: Relax on sunlit East Beach, browse boutiques and galleries in the charming Pier Village, and watch spectacular sunsets paint the marshlands in brilliant colors. The island's laid-back atmosphere invites visitors to slow down and embrace the gentle rhythms of Georgia's coast.

places.name: Stanley, ID

visits.text: Stanley has a permanent population of roughly 70 people but three designated national scenic byways converge here, and on summer weekends the population multiplies tenfold. The town sits at 1,908 meters in a bowl-shaped basin below the Sawtooths - 57 peaks over 3,000 meters filling the western sky. This bowl shape is also why Stanley records overnight lows below freezing on average 294 days a year and was measured as the coldest place in the contiguous U.S. more often than any other weather station between 1995 and 2015. The Stanley Historical Museum, housed in the 1933 Valley Creek Ranger Station, gives the historical context in 20 minutes.

Eight kilometers south on Highway 75, Redfish Lake spreads out at 1,981 meters below the serrated granite of the Sawtooth range - one of the clearest alpine lakes in the American West, fed almost entirely by snowmelt. The Redfish Visitor Center and Gallery at the lake's edge is the oldest National Forest visitor center in the contiguous United States, built in the early 1960s. In late summer and fall, sockeye salmon complete a 1,450-kilometer migration from the Pacific to spawn here. The Redfish Lake Lodge runs a sunset wine-and-appetizer lake cruise in summer - reserve a seat in advance, it sells out.

In December 2017, the Central Idaho Dark Sky Reserve became the first of its kind in the United States - 3,666 square kilometers encompassing the entire Sawtooth NRA, from Ketchum to northwest of Stanley. The designation requires that area businesses and municipalities limit light pollution, which means that on clear moonless nights over Stanley, the Milky Way appears as a textured band with visible lanes of intergalactic dust. No equipment needed. Just get away from the streetlights.

Eighteen kilometers west on Highway 21, the Iron Creek Trailhead is the launch point for the Sawtooth Lake Trail - arguably the best single day hike in the range. The route climbs 6.9 kilometers through open forest and then granite scree to Sawtooth Lake, the largest alpine lake in the Sawtooth Wilderness, sitting under the sheer face of Mount Regan. The Sawtooth Wilderness was established in 1972 and covers 88,660 hectares; Thompson Peak at 3,277 meters is the highest point. Expect snow on the upper trail before mid-June. The parking area fills before 9 AM on summer weekends.

The 5-kilometer side road to Stanley Lake branches off Highway 21 and dead-ends at one of the most photographed lakes in the Sawtooths - a glacially carved basin directly below 3,005-meter McGown Peak, whose reflection dominates the surface on calm mornings. Motorized boats are limited here, so the water is quiet. This is also the spot, at kilometer 188 on Highway 21, where the Sawtooth peaks first come into view for drivers approaching from Boise - a good indicator of what's been visible behind you all day.

Forty-eight kilometers south of Stanley on Highway 75, the Galena Summit pullout at 2,652 meters gives the best single view on this entire route: the Sawtooth Valley unrolling northward below, the Salmon River as a thread of silver at the valley floor, and on clear days, a wall of peaks extending to the horizon in every direction. The overlook is named for Senator Frank Church and his wife Bethine - Church championed the 1980 Central Idaho Wilderness Act that protected much of what you're looking at.

activities.text: Join one of the Stanley-based outfitters for a half-day on the Salmon River. The Upper Salmon runs Class III and IV rapids through a canyon flanked by the Sawtooths; June brings the highest water (snowmelt-fueled Class IV), while July and August mellow to Class III. Sawtooth Adventure Company runs full-day guided paddle-raft and inflatable kayak trips for all ability levels. At 684 kilometers, the Salmon is one of the longest free-flowing rivers in the lower 48 - this stretch is its headwaters.

Snake Pit Hot Spring sits at the edge of town and costs nothing - rock pools fed by a thermal spring, with a view of the valley and the Sawtooth peaks. A small herd of deer routinely wanders through at dusk. Several other springs are within a 30-minute drive on Highway 75 toward Ketchum; the Mountain Village Lodge in Stanley also has access to commercial hot spring pools if you want facilities and privacy.

Rent a kayak or paddleboard at Redfish Lake and spend the morning on the water. The Bench Lakes Trail begins on the west shore and leads to four smaller alpine lakes in about 6.5 kilometers round trip. For something different, the Redfish Lake Corrals - operated by Mystic Saddle Ranch since 1969 - runs guided horseback rides through the Ponderosa pines along the lakeshore and into the wilderness above. Either way, plan to be back at the lake by late afternoon when the alpenglow hits.

Stanley's handful of restaurants punch well above their weight. The Stanley Baking Co. handles breakfast and lunch, with cinnamon rolls that are discussed with unusual seriousness by people who have driven three hours for them. The Stanley Supper Club handles dinner. After eating, the Stanley to Redfish Lake Trail - an 8-kilometer paved and gravel path built with Sawtooth Society grant funds - makes a good evening walk.

places.name: Staten Island Ferry, NY

visits.text: Day 1 - optional: The Staten Island Ferry is New York's best free deal: 25 min crossing, frequent departures 24/7, with the Statue of Liberty on one side and the skyline receding on the other. Position yourself on the outer deck, right side outbound. At sunset, the crossing becomes the day's highlight: aim for that window.

Day 1 - optional: At the St George terminal on Staten Island, don't immediately turn back like most passengers. The renovated waterfront and esplanade facing the harbor deserve an hour, and the neighborhood around the terminal has its cafés. Departures run all day: no pressure for the return.

activities.text: Photo tip: on the return to Manhattan, position yourself at the front of the upper deck; the skyline grows shot by shot, striking at blue hour.
Bus S40 from St George terminal to Snug Harbor: 2.5 km, about ten minutes.

visits.text: Day 1 - On Liberty Island, your first view of the Statue of Liberty is from her feet: 46 meters of green copper, 93 with the pedestal, facing Manhattan. Budget 1 to 1.5 hours on the island, with an audio guide included in the ticket. Pedestal or crown access must be reserved weeks, sometimes months in advance, for a few dozen cents more.

Day 1 - The Statue of Liberty Museum, opened in 2019, displays the original 1886 torch; admission is included in the ferry ticket. The best photo spot is at the back of the island, statue and skyline in the same frame. Don't linger too long: Ellis Island awaits and the last ferries leave early.

activities.text: Go up to the pedestal if you've booked: 215 steps or an elevator, a second security check on site, an unobstructed view over the entire bay, and a much shorter wait than for the crown.
Ferry to Ellis Island: 1.2 km, about 15 min for the crossing plus the wait at the dock. All ferry services from Battery Park stop at both islands on the same ticket.

places.name: Steamboat Springs, CO

visits.text: Steamboat Springs owes its name to early French explorers who, hearing a spring bubbling along the Yampa River, thought they glimpsed the paddle wheels of a steamboat. The spring disappeared during railroad construction in 1908, but the town retains its character as a real Colorado mountain town—not a ski-resort boutique village, but a real town with locals' bars on Lincoln Avenue.

Strawberry Park Hot Springs, 10 km north of town, are set into the rock, with water at 71°C at the source that cools naturally to 38-42°C in the pools. The setting is wild - forest, rocks and steam in the cold air. Reservations are required for all visits, including weekends.

visits.text: Stillwater - Founded in 1843, the town invites you to walk down Main Street towards the St. Croix River, past 19th-century brick buildings now home to bookshops, antique shops and restaurants. Do not miss the Stillwater Lift Bridge (1931), a lift bridge still in operation across the river to Wisconsin.

Walk down to the banks of the St. Croix—this clear-running river, a tributary of the Mississippi, is designated a "Wild and Scenic River." The forested bluffs on both sides give the valley the feel of a miniature fjord.

activities.text: Canoe or kayak the St. Croix River—outfitters offer rentals right on the water. The current is gentle, the banks wild. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a relaxed float.
Stillwater is known for its bookstores. Step inside one—some occupy vaulted brick cellars. If you're a wine enthusiast, several wineries have set up in the valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Minnesota in 10 Days: Twin Cities, Lakes, and Lake Superior's North Shore

visits.text: Without the museum, Stockbridge would be just another Berkshires village. With it, it's worth a stop. Norman Rockwell spent the last 25 years of his life here, and the museum holds 574 original paintings and drawings—the world's largest collection—plus archives containing 100,000 photographs, letters, and sketches. His studio was dismantled and reconstructed stone by stone on the museum grounds; it is open May through October, with brushes and books left exactly as they were. Allow a solid two hours, and avoid Wednesdays when the museum is closed.

Rockwell painted this street exactly as it stands in Stockbridge Main Street at Christmas in 1967—same Red Lion Inn façade, same lampposts, same maples. The inn has stood here since 1773 and still operates today: massive porch, wicker chairs, the smell of wood smoke starting in September. Even if you're not staying overnight, coffee on the terrace gives you a sense of the Berkshires' discreet high society.

Chesterwood, three kilometers west, was the summer residence of Daniel Chester French, the sculptor who created the seated Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. His studio preserves preparatory models at different scales—enlightening if you've seen the finished statue. The 50-hectare estate features gardens and wooded trails with contemporary art installations in summer. Open only late May through late October.

activities.text: On August 5, 1850, during a thunderstorm, two writers took shelter in a cave at the summit of this hill. They'd never met before that impromptu picnic. The first was Nathaniel Hawthorne, the second Herman Melville—and in the weeks that followed, Melville returned to work on Moby-Dick, ultimately dedicating it to Hawthorne. Monument Mountain Reservation, five kilometers south of Stockbridge on Route 7, offers two trails climbing to the summit (Peeskawso Peak, 500 meters) via the Hickey Trail. Count on 2 hours round trip. Sweeping views across the Housatonic Valley.

Dinner at the Red Lion Inn, either in the main dining room (pricey but solid) or downstairs in the Lion's Den—a pub with a simpler menu and live music almost every night. The chicken pot pie hasn't changed since the 1950s. On tap, beers from Berkshire Brewing Company, brewed in South Deerfield 40 minutes away.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Berkshires to Niagara Falls: 10 Days of Waterfalls, Villages, and Wide-Open Spaces
Boston to Niagara Falls in 13 Days, Through New England and New York State

visits.text: To understand Stowe’s culture, the Vermont Ski & Snowboard Museum provides a useful complement to your walks. At the intersection of Routes 100 and 108, its collections and exhibitions explore the role of skiing and snowboarding in local life. It’s a good choice for a rainy stretch of the day; check opening days and the current exhibition before planning the rest of your day around the museum.

If the road is open and visibility is good enough, continue to Smugglers’ Notch. The pass narrows between Mount Mansfield and Spruce Peak, with rock walls and large boulders that completely change the scale of the landscape. Then return to Stowe before continuing south the next day. Check the restrictions that apply to your vehicle: this narrow road requires advance checks before you use it as a connecting route.

activities.text: Follow the Stowe Recreation Path on foot or by bike, taking time to enjoy the valley views. This greenway connects the village to the Mountain Road area and offers several options for a walk without having to cover the entire route. Choose your starting point and distance before setting out; when cycling, slow down near pedestrians and plan to return along the same route.

At Barnes Camp Boardwalk, the wetlands open up a view toward the mountains at the entrance to the Smugglers’ Notch area. The boardwalk lets you observe this landscape without committing to a summit hike; it complements the drive with a lower viewpoint at vegetation level. Stay on the boardwalk and check access conditions, especially after heavy rain or the first freezes.

days_plan.itin_title: New England in Fall: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: You pull up to a sandstone building that is literally made from Route 66 itself. Roy Rives bought the entire supply of sandstone scraped up during the road's own paving for five dollars and used it to build this cafe, which opened August 4, 1939. It served as a 24-hour Greyhound bus stop through World War II and kept going through decommissioning, a 1999 tornado, and a 2008 fire that gutted everything but the stone walls. Current owner Dawn Welch, who took over in 1993, inspired the character of Sally Carrera - the blue Porsche attorney - in Pixar's 2006 film Cars, after the research team stopped here in 2001. The original neon sign, restored in 2025, still glows over the entrance.

You continue west to Arcadia, where farmer William Harrison Odor built a perfectly round barn in 1898 using native bur oak boards soaked while still green and bent into the curves needed for the walls and rafters. His son later explained the design: “My father figured if they had something round, it would hit and go around it instead of through it.” When Route 66 came through Arcadia in 1926, the barn became a landmark. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1977 and restored in 1992, it's free to enter and open daily. Half a mile west, POPS opened in 2007 with a 66-foot LED soda bottle sign weighing 4 tons - over 700 varieties of bottled soda on glass shelves arranged by color, plus burgers and milkshakes.

days_plan.itin_title: Oklahoma Route 66 & Native Heritage: Tulsa to OKC

visits.text: Old Sturbridge Village recreates life in an 1830s New England village. It's the largest living history museum in the Northeast: 40 period buildings relocated and reassembled across 80 hectares—blacksmith, farm, school, tavern, all functioning. The costumed interpreters actually work—the blacksmith forges, the farmwife milks. Touristy but well done, and far more instructive than typical demonstrations. Budget half a day. Entry $32, valid for two consecutive days.

Sturbridge Common is the town center—a classic New England triangular green with its white steepled church. Small, but representative. The neighboring Publick House Historic Inn has been serving since 1771—an inn operating since colonial times, where you can grab coffee or spend the night in a room with exposed beams.

If you still have time, Route 20 is lined with several antique shops, including Sturbridge Antique Shops, which gathers more than 75 dealers on two floors, and Past to Present Antiques. Shaker furniture, old earthenware, oil lamps: this is the classic hunting ground of New York decorators on weekends.

activities.text: Taste local maple syrup at a sugar shack if you come between mid-February and early April, the harvest season. Otherwise, several Massachusetts producers sell their syrup all year round, sorted into color grades. Grade A dark has a caramelized taste you won't find in industrial syrups.

visits.text: Sturgeon Bay - Door County's 'gateway' is also a shipbuilding town. The canal cutting the peninsula in two connects Green Bay to Lake Michigan. Downtown is pleasant with art galleries, restaurants, and shops.

Door County Maritime Museum - The history of shipbuilding and Great Lakes navigation. Models, tools, and shipwreck stories (Door County owes its name to the dangerous currents of 'Death's Door,' the passage between the peninsula and Washington Island).

Cana Island Lighthouse - Allow for a round trip from Sturgeon Bay. Cross the gravel causeway (sometimes flooded) to this 4-hectare island. The 27-meter lighthouse dates from 1869. Climb its 97 steps for the view. Door County has 11 lighthouses in all - more than any other Wisconsin county.

activities.text: Wine and Cider Tasting - Door County has several wineries and cideries. The peninsula's cherries produce fruity wines and easy-drinking ciders. Ask to try cherry wine, the local specialty.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

visits.text: Bonito Vista offers an overview of the dark lava flow at Sunset Crater without a long hike. The short developed path crosses volcanic ash and helps you distinguish the volcanic features around you. Use this viewpoint to understand the terrain before walking; stay on the designated surface, as the lava flows are fragile.

activities.text: You will walk at the base of Sunset Crater on the Lava Flow Trail, among black blocks and the solidified shapes of the Bonito lava flow. The loop is 1.6 km long; a developed upper section offers a shorter route. Wear closed-toe shoes: the lava is sharp, and leaving the trail damages this fragile environment.

days_plan.itin_title: Navajo Country in 10 Days: Sedona and Monument Valley

visits.text: Prepare for the day's hike to Havasupai—one of the most spectacular and hardest-to-reach places in the United States. From Hualapai Hilltop, the trail first descends 800 meters in 2.4 km of switchbacks, then follows a sandy wash for 11 km to the village of Supai—the country's most isolated town, with 700 residents, accessible only on foot, on horseback, or by helicopter. Mail still arrives by pack mule.

Two kilometers past the village, Navajo Falls appears on your left—a series of turquoise waterfalls amid red sandstone. Then Havasu Falls, the star: a 30-meter blue-green waterfall tumbling into a pool surrounded by travertine. The color comes from calcium carbonate dissolved in the water. This is the image you've seen all over Instagram—and in person, it's even better.
The campground is just past Havasu Falls, along Havasu Creek. Set up your tent anywhere in the designated area—first come, best spot. The creek water is 21°C year-round.

Hike down to Mooney Falls, 800 meters from the campground. It's Havasupai's tallest waterfall—a 60-meter free fall. To access it, you descend through a passage in the rock with chains and metal ladders bolted to the wall. It's steep, slippery, and dizzying—but the turquoise pool at the bottom is worth the effort.

Third day at Havasupai—savor it. Explore Fifty Foot Falls, a less conspicuous waterfall between the village and Havasu Falls, often overlooked by hurried hikers. The pool is smaller and more intimate. The rest of the day, swim in Havasu Creek, read by the water, photograph the changing light on the cliffs. This is why you came.

activities.text: A permit is mandatory—3-night minimum, about $455 per person. Reservations open February 1 and sell out in minutes. No day hiking allowed. Leave before dawn to avoid heat—carry at least 3 liters of water. No services on the trail. This is true backcountry.

If you're a strong hiker, continue 5.5 km beyond Mooney Falls to Beaver Falls—a series of terraced waterfalls with natural swimming pools. The trail follows Havasu Creek with several stream crossings. Allow 4 hours round-trip from the campground. The rest of the time, swim in the pools—the water at 21°C is perfect after hiking.

Mentally prepare for tomorrow: the climb back to Hualapai Hilltop is 16 km with 800 meters of elevation gain. Be sure to leave before dawn—heat in the wash is brutal after 9 a.m. Some hikers book a helicopter for the ascent ($80 per person), but seats are limited and flights don't start until 10 a.m.

places.name: Superior, WI

visits.text: Big Manitou Falls - Wisconsin's highest waterfall awaits you 20 minutes south of Superior. The Black River plunges 165 feet (50 meters) into a basalt gorge carved 1.2 billion years ago by lava flows. Native Americans called it 'Gitchee Manitou' - the voice of the Great Spirit. Multiple viewing platforms offer unobstructed views from both sides of the gorge. Arrive early morning to beat the crowds and catch the best light.

Little Manitou Falls - 2.5 km upstream, the river splits into two channels and drops 9 meters across a wide basalt shelf. Less dramatic than its big sister, but more accessible: you can scramble down to the pool to feel the spray. Watch for slippery rocks.

Interfalls Lake and Beach - Between the two falls, the Black River slows and forms this man-made lake bordered by pines and spruces. The sandy beach (trucked in from Lake Superior shores in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps) makes for a pleasant swimming break.

CCC Buildings - The Civilian Conservation Corps transformed this park between 1935 and 1941. The cut-stone shelter, nature center, and former bathhouse still stand. Interpretive signs tell the story of these young workers who came primarily from Illinois.

activities.text: Big Manitou - Little Manitou Loop Trail - This 6.5 km trail follows the Black River and passes both waterfalls. Moderate elevation gain (65 m). In fall, maples and birches frame the gorge in red and gold.

days_plan.itin_title: Wisconsin's Essential Wonders

map_keywords: Big Manitou Falls Pattison State Park

visits.text: Talkeetna Historic District - This charming frontier village at the confluence of three rivers has served as the traditional base camp for Denali climbers since the early 1900s. The compact Main Street preserves authentic gold rush-era architecture, with original wooden storefronts now housing local artisans and outfitters. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the town offers an authentic glimpse into Alaska's pioneering heritage.

activities.text: Denali Flightseeing - Experience breathtaking aerial views of North America's highest peak and the surrounding Alaska Range. Small aircraft circle massive glaciers, navigate between towering granite peaks, and offer perspectives of Denali's 20,310-foot summit that few ever witness. Weather permitting, glacier landings provide the opportunity to step onto ancient ice fields.

Susitna River Rafting - Float through pristine wilderness where the Susitna, Talkeetna, and Chulitna rivers converge. These glacier-fed waterways wind through boreal forest with views of the Alaska Range, offering opportunities to spot moose, eagles, and salmon depending on the season.

Talkeetna Zipline Tours - Soar above the Talkeetna River valley on aerial cables stretching through old-growth spruce forest, with panoramic mountain views serving as the backdrop to this elevated wilderness experience.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alaska Circuit: National Parks and Glaciers

visits.text: Two buildings share the same address in downtown Tallahassee: the 22-story New Capitol completed in 1977 and, directly in front of it, the original 1845 structure it almost replaced. The Florida Historic Capitol Museum is that survivor - restored to its 1902 appearance after a citizens' campaign saved it from demolition. Under the stained-glass dome, you move through the restored Governor's Suite and Supreme Court chambers where Florida's political battles were fought. Tallahassee was chosen as capital in 1824 because it sat precisely halfway between St. Augustine and Pensacola - two commissioners walked toward each other from opposite coasts and met in the middle. Free admission; allow 75 minutes.

FSU English professor Laura Jepsen bought a three-acre pasture on High Road in 1956 because she fell in love with a tree. The live oak at Lichgate is estimated at 300 years old, its branches sweeping the ground like a billowing skirt, and everything she built - Tudor-style cottage, labyrinth, gardens - was designed to protect it. The granite came from the same Georgia quarry as the Old State Capitol steps; the cypress panelling from Tallahassee swamps. On the National Register of Historic Places since 2006, maintained by volunteers, it's free and open dawn to dusk. Find the driveway by the two white posts on High Road - most locals have never been.

Fifty-two acres of live oak forest on the edge of town hold one of Florida's most unusual museums. The Tallahassee Museum combines restored 19th-century cracker buildings with habitats for live animals - Florida panthers, red wolves, black bears and otters along boardwalk trails that wind through the forest. Founded in 1957 as a junior science museum, it holds national accreditation. The Tree-to-Tree Adventures zip-line courses fly over the canopy for those who want some altitude with their ecology. Buy timed tickets online for weekends.

activities.text: 25 km south of Tallahassee on Highway 267, one of the world's deepest and largest freshwater springs pumps 1.5 billion litres a day from the Upper Floridan Aquifer. The water stays 21°C year-round; the vent drops 58 metres, perfectly clear to the bottom. Board the flat-bottom riverboat at Edward Ball Wakulla Springs State Park and keep your eyes on the banks - manatees have been regular here since 1998. Hollywood discovered the place: Tarzan's Secret Treasure filmed in 1941, Creature from the Black Lagoon in 1954. The 1937 Spanish lodge restaurant serves breakfast. Book the riverboat tour the evening before.

Railroad Square Art District began as a World War II industrial warehouse park and became the city's creative hub without ever trying to look like one. More than seventy galleries, studios and restaurants fill the converted sheds. The art walks on the first Friday of each month draw locals drifting between wood-fired pizza, craft beer and hand-thrown pottery. First night, no plans: this is where you go.

days_plan.itin_title: Florida Panhandle: Tallahassee to Pensacola on the Emerald Coast
From Jacksonville to Dallas in 15 days, through the Deep South

visits.text: Marvel at Tallulah Gorge, a dramatic 3-km-long canyon plunging nearly 300 meters deep where five magnificent waterfalls cascade over ancient rock formations. A suspension bridge spans the gorge 24 meters above the rushing Tallulah River, providing dizzying views of the canyon walls and roaring cascades. Free permits allow adventurous hikers to descend to the gorge floor for an intimate encounter with this geological wonder.

Explore over 32 km of hiking and biking trails radiating from the gorge rim, each offering different perspectives of the dramatic landscape carved over millennia by rushing waters. The park's historic dam and interpretive center document the area's role in pioneering hydroelectric development. Overlooks along the rim trail provide photographers with stunning compositions of waterfalls and canyon walls.

activities.text: Experience the exhilarating natural waterslide at Sliding Rock, where smooth granite channels lead visitors into refreshing pools surrounded by moss-covered boulders and echoing canyon walls. The nearby lake beach offers calmer swimming for those seeking relaxation after gorge adventures.

days_plan.itin_title: Georgia Road Trip: From the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Golden Isles

visits.text: Tampa Bay - Where Theme Parks Meet Championship Sports: This Gulf Coast metropolis combines world-class attractions with a thriving dining scene that rivals any city in Florida.

Busch Gardens Tampa Bay - A World-Class Theme Park and Zoo: This unique combination of African wildlife preserve and thrill ride destination features one of the country's best roller coaster collections alongside remarkable animal habitats.

Historic Ybor City - Tampa's Latin Quarter Since 1885: Once the cigar capital of the world, this national historic district preserves Cuban, Spanish, and Italian heritage through architecture, restaurants, and the ongoing cigar-rolling tradition.
Tampa Riverwalk - 4.2 Kilometers of Waterfront Wonder: This continuous pedestrian path connects downtown museums, parks, restaurants, and attractions along the Hillsborough River and Tampa Bay.

activities.text: Tampa Craft Beer Trail - Florida's Brewing Capital: Pioneering breweries like Cigar City and Coppertail have established Tampa Bay as a craft beer destination, with dozens of beer bars offering local brews.
Tampa Bay Sports - Championship Caliber: Home to the NFL's Buccaneers and NHL's Lightning—both recent champions—the region offers professional sports events year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Florida: Barrier Islands and the Keys

places.name: Taos, NM

visits.text: Experience Taos Pueblo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with over 1,000 years of continuous habitation, representing one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in North America. The remarkable multi-story adobe structures, some reaching five stories, have been home to the Tiwa-speaking Puebloan people since before European contact. Visitors can explore the living village and learn about traditions that have survived for a millennium.

Discover the charming mountain town of Taos, nestled beneath breathtaking peaks and surrounded by an artistic heritage that has drawn creative spirits for more than a century. The Wheeler Peak Wilderness Area offers challenging hikes and skiing opportunities, with stunning views from New Mexico's highest summit at 4,013 meters. It is reached via Taos Ski Valley, around forty minutes' drive from Taos, and the summit can only be reached on foot, at the end of a full-day hike.

activities.text: Experience the thrill of rafting down the Rio Grande through rugged, wild terrain where the river has carved dramatic gorges through the volcanic landscape. Outfitters offer trips ranging from gentle floats to challenging whitewater adventures through some of the most spectacular canyon scenery in the Southwest. The Rio Grande del Norte National Monument protects this remarkable landscape for future generations.

days_plan.itin_title: New Mexico Odyssey: Ancient Pueblos, White Sands and Ancestral Volcanoes

map_keywords: Rio Grande del Norte National Monument

visits.text: Temecula Valley Wine Country - Southern California's Napa: Nearly 50 wineries grow over 30 grape varieties in this warm-climate region, producing distinctive wines that have earned national recognition. Rolling hills dotted with oaks create a surprisingly Tuscan atmosphere.

Old Town Temecula - The Real Old West: This six-block historic district preserves 1880s wooden storefronts where cowboys once hitched their horses. Today, antique shops, restaurants, and wine tasting rooms fill the authentic buildings.

Temecula Valley - Tastings Among the Vines: Visit the wine region's estates to discover their wines in tasting rooms. Vineyards form a patchwork across rolling hills dotted with oaks; visits offer a chance to observe this landscape and taste the different grape varieties grown in the valley.

activities.text: Hot Air Balloon Sunrise Flights - Float Over Wine Country at Dawn: Balloons launched in the morning year-round drift over patchwork vineyards as mist rises from the valleys, with traditional champagne toasts following upon landing.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

places.name: Tenement Museum, NY

visits.text: Day 2 - The Tenement Museum can only be visited on a guided tour, and that's its strength: you enter real immigrant apartments at 97 Orchard Street, frozen in time between 1863 and 1935. Each tour tells the story of a real family, German, Italian, or Eastern European Jewish. Booking online is essential; slots fill up fast.

Day 2 - Allow 1 to 1.5 hours per Tenement Museum tour, in English only. The bookstore and gift shop, which you can enter for free, is worth a detour for its books on working-class New York. The contrast with the galleries and wine bars that have colonized the Lower East Side is part of the experience.

activities.text: Pastrami at Katz's Delicatessen, 400 m away on Houston Street: 1888 institution, enormous sandwich to share, and carefully guard the ticket given at entrance, it's used to pay on exit.
Walk to Mulberry Street and Little Italy: 600 m due west, about 8 min.

places.name: Terlingua, TX

visits.text: Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive - This 50 km road crosses the heart of Big Bend, descending toward the Rio Grande. Stop at Sotol Vista for a 180° panorama of the desert and the mountains of Mexico. Farther down, Tuff Canyon offers a short trail above a canyon carved into volcanic rock. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua.

Santa Elena Canyon - The Rio Grande flows into a canyon with 460 m high walls. A 2.5 km trail crosses Terlingua Creek (sometimes by wading when the water is high) and follows the base of the cliff. The Mexican wall is within calling distance on the other side of the river - you are literally on the border. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

Terlingua Ghost Town - Leaving the park, stop in this abandoned mining town. The 1900s adobe ruins now serve as a backdrop for a few bars, restaurants, and galleries. The atmosphere at sunset, with raking light on the ruins and desert, is unique.

Chisos Basin - Follow the winding road uphill (11 km, 520 m of elevation gain) to this mountain basin nestled in the heart of Big Bend. At an elevation of 1,700 m, the temperature is 10°C cooler than in the desert below. The visitor center is here, as is the park's only lodge. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua to Chisos Basin.

Window Trail - From Chisos Basin, this 8 km round-trip trail descends into a canyon to an opening (the “window”) framing the desert below. The view through this gap in the rock is Big Bend's signature photo. Set off in the late afternoon to see the sunset through the window. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

Rio Grande Village - Take the nature trail (1 km) up a small hill. From the top, you will see the river below and the Mexican village of Boquillas del Carmen on the other side - the border has never seemed so close. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

Boquillas Canyon Trail - This 2.2 km trail descends toward the Rio Grande and follows the base of a canyon with 300 m high walls. The hike is easy, but the heat can be intense - set off early. From the bank, you may spot residents of Boquillas offering handicrafts from the opposite shore. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

activities.text: Grab a drink on the terrace of one of Terlingua's bars at sunset—the locals, a mix of desert misfits and adventurous retirees, are welcoming, and their stories are worth the stop.

Lost Mine Trail - If you prefer climbing to descending, this 8 km round-trip trail climbs along a ridge with panoramic views of the Chisos basin and the Rio Grande desert. It is the park's highest-rated hike - set off early to avoid the heat. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

Big Bend is a certified Dark Sky Park - at night, the total absence of light pollution makes the Milky Way appear like a river overhead. Step outside after dinner and let your eyes adjust to the darkness for 20 minutes.

Hot Springs Trail - This 1 km trail leads to a natural hot spring (40°C) beside the Rio Grande. You sit in a stone pool with Mexico across the river. It is one of the few places in the world where you can soak in a hot spring while looking at another country. Go early in the morning or late in the day - it is too hot in full sun. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua, in addition to the walk.

If the border crossing is open (check at the visitor center), you can cross the Rio Grande in a rowboat to visit the Mexican village of Boquillas del Carmen - a passport is required. It is a tiny village of 150 residents. Otherwise, enjoy your last evening in the Terlingua desert. Allow for a round trip by car from Terlingua to the border crossing, before crossing by rowboat.

visits.text: Day 4 - At the northern end of Manhattan, the Met Cloisters brings together elements from five European cloisters transported stone by stone to Fort Tryon Park, above the Hudson. The Unicorn Tapestries alone justify the climb. Admission is included in the Met ticket, valid for 3 days. Allow 1.5 hours.

Day 4 - The Cloisters gardens grow plants depicted in medieval manuscripts, amid Romanesque colonnades and Gothic chapels. The place feels outside time and away from the tourist crowds; it's also the most out-of-the-way stop of the trip. If you're getting tired, replace the climb with a quiet late afternoon in Central Park, without guilt.

activities.text: Before leaving, walk to Fort Tryon Park's linden terrace: a view down over the Hudson and the Palisades cliffs.
Head to the optional stop in the Bronx: Wave Hill, in Riverdale, is about 4.1 km away. Take connecting buses or a taxi; allow about twenty minutes.

places.name: The Forks, ME

visits.text: The drive from Millinocket to Rangeley runs over 3.5 hours without stops - so The Forks is the natural break. This is where the Dead River meets the Kennebec, and where Northern Outdoors launched commercial whitewater rafting in Maine in 1976, turning these Class III-IV rapids into a 60,000-rafter-a-year industry. Even if you're not rafting today, stop for lunch at the Kennebec River Pub & Brewery and walk to the river confluence - two powerful rivers coming together in granite walls is genuinely dramatic. The full-day Kennebec trip is one of the best rafting experiences in New England for mixed groups and families.

Moxie Falls drops 90 feet over a granite ledge in a narrow gorge, a 15-minute hike from the trailhead off Lake Moxie Road. It's one of the highest free-falling waterfalls in New England and a well-kept secret compared to better-marketed waterfalls elsewhere in Maine. The trail is largely flat with a short steep descent near the base.

days_plan.itin_title: Inland Maine: Moosehead Lake, Mount Katahdin & the North Woods
