places.name: Thermopolis, WY

visits.text: You can smell the minerals at Hot Springs State Park from the parking lot. The Big Spring—Wyoming's first state park since 1897—discharges more than 6.8 million liters of water per day at a constant 53°C, flowing over rainbow-colored travertine terraces in layers of orange, white, and rust. The free public Bath House at the heart of the park is a condition of a treaty signed that year with the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho, who sold the land on the condition that the waters remain free. The Bath House, cooled to 40°C, limits soaks to 20 minutes. Cross the suspension footbridge over the Bighorn River for the best view of the terraces.

In 1993, fossil hunters found dinosaur bones weathering out of the hills on Warm Springs Ranch ten minutes from downtown Thermopolis. The Wyoming Dinosaur Center grew from that discovery and now houses 58 mounted skeletons and over 20,000 bones from the Thermopolis bonebeds - including the Thermopolis Specimen of Archaeopteryx, one of the most complete ever found. Watch scientists at work in the preparation lab year-round; the Dig for the Day program (late May through mid-September) puts you on a real excavation site with actual paleontology tools. Book in advance.

Six kilometers south on US-20, Wind River Canyon closes in around the road—sheer walls, the Wind River running alongside, rock layers exposing more than 2.5 billion years of geological history in one of the most complete sequences visible anywhere in Wyoming. Keep your eyes on the upper ledges for bighorn sheep. The canyon runs about 22 kilometers; allow 20–30 minutes with stops.

activities.text: For a soak longer than the Bath House's 20-minute limit, Hellie's Tepee Spa charges admission but offers waterslides, several pools and no time limit - supplied by the same mineral waters. The State Bath House allows a second 20-minute session if you wait two hours between sessions.

Northwest of Thermopolis, plan a round trip from town to visit the Legend Rock Petroglyph Site, whose sandstone cliffs bear the work of three prehistoric cultural groups, dating from roughly AD 500 to the 19th century—hundreds of meters of images. From October to April, collect the gate key at the State Bath House before leaving town; from May to September, no key is needed. Admission is free. The road turns to gravel for the final kilometers. Bring water: this is an exposed high-altitude desert.

days_plan.itin_title: Wyoming Beyond Yellowstone: Cowboys, Hot Springs & Bighorn Medicine Wheel

Wind River Canyon Scenic Byway Wyoming

places.name: Three Rivers, CA

visits.text: The General Sherman Tree is the largest living tree on the planet - by trunk volume. It stands 83.8 metres tall, measures 11 metres in diameter at the base and contains 1,487 cubic metres of wood. It is between 2,200 and 2,700 years old, which means it was already a young tree when Rome was founded. It is neither the oldest (that title goes to a bristlecone pine) nor the tallest, but no other tree rivals its mass. A special feature: it keeps growing every year, adding the equivalent of an 18-metre tree in new wood. The car park is about 40 km from Three Rivers, a 55-minute drive. The trail from the car park is paved and descends 500 metres to the tree - the way back is uphill, so take your time as the 2,100-metre altitude makes itself felt.

Moro Rock is a granite dome that rises out of the sequoia forest like the prow of a ship, about an hour's drive from Three Rivers. The stone staircase cut into the rock climbs 300 steps to the summit at 2,050 metres - allow 20 minutes. The 360° view over the Great Western Divide and the Kings Canyon gorge is worth every step. Don't miss the Tunnel Log on the Crescent Meadow road either: a sequoia that fell naturally in December 1937, through which park staff cut a tunnel in 1938 to let cars pass - it is 2.4 metres wide and 8 metres high.

activities.text: Stop by the Giant Forest Museum before leaving the forest. The building dates from 1928 and houses exhibits on giant sequoia ecology - why they resist fires (their bark can reach 60 centimetres thick and doesn't burn), how they reproduce only through fire, and what we know about their shallow roots that intertwine with neighbouring trees to share stability. In 2021, a fierce wildfire threatened the General Sherman - rangers wrapped its base in reflective fire-retardant sheeting normally reserved for structures. The tree survived undamaged.

Take the Congress Trail starting from the General Sherman: a 5-kilometre loop that passes through dozens of giant sequoias, several with diameters larger than your living room. The forest is silent, the ground soft beneath the needles, and the light filtered through the canopy is photographically rare. Allow 2 hours for the complete loop.

visits.text: Day 3 - Times Square needs no introduction: ten-story screens, constant crowds, costumed characters who charge for photos with them. Spend ten minutes taking it in, preferably at nightfall when the neon takes over. Climb onto the red steps above the TKTS booth for an overview.

Day 3 - Times Square's TKTS booth sells tickets for that evening's Broadway shows at 20 to 50% off; the line starts forming in midafternoon, and ticketing apps offer an alternative. If you feel like seeing a musical during these 5 days, this is where to decide. The surrounding restaurants cater to tourists: eat elsewhere.

activities.text: For dinner, aim for 46th Street called Restaurant Row, or better Ninth Avenue: two blocks suffice to escape the neon traps.
Walk to Rockefeller Center: 600 m up Sixth Avenue, about 8 min.

days_plan.itin_title: New York in 5 Days: The Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood Itinerary

places.name: Toledo, OH

visits.text: You enter one of the few major U.S. museums offering completely free admission—a tradition rooted in the institution's very founding in 1901 by Edward Drummond Libbey, Toledo's glass magnate. The 1912 Greek Revival main building, with its Ionic columns, sits alongside the Glass Pavilion, opened in 2006—a building made entirely of curved glass designed by Japanese firm SANAA, the first American project by this architecture firm, which would receive the Pritzker Prize in 2010. Since Toledo has been nicknamed the “Glass City” because of its glass industry dating back to the 19th century, this pavilion is both a showcase for the historic glass collection and an architectural demonstration of what the material can achieve. The museum holds works by Van Gogh, Rembrandt, Picasso, and Cézanne among its 30,000 pieces.

On the Maumee River, Fort Meigs is the largest reconstructed wooden stockade fort in the United States. Here, in May 1813, General William Henry Harrison (the future president in 1841) withstood a siege lasting more than a week by British forces and their Native American allies led by Tecumseh. The American victory, together with the Battle of Lake Erie in September 1813, firmly established American sovereignty over northern Ohio. Guides in period costume recreate life in the fort.

Located in Toledo on the banks of the Maumee River, this museum tells the story of the five Great Lakes—a 244,000-square-kilometer basin that holds 20% of the world's surface freshwater. The centerpiece is the Col. James M. Schoonmaker, a real 182-meter lake freighter launched in 1911 that you can board to visit the pilothouse, engine room, and crew quarters. The permanent exhibition traces the history of commercial navigation on the Great Lakes from the first Native American canoeists to the Edmund Fitzgerald disaster in November 1975.

activities.text: Toledo's botanical gardens extend over 18 hectares with collections of roses, aromatic herbs, hydrangeas, and a deciduous forest whose fall colors are spectacular. Founded in 1964, they're managed as a community space with public art programs—sculptures and installations line the walkways between flower beds. The medicinal herb garden, inspired by medieval monastic gardens, is particularly well documented with panels explaining each plant's use by settlers and Native Americans.

The Toledo Museum's Glass Pavilion regularly offers live glassblowing demonstrations in its studio open to the public - you watch artists shape works from molten glass at 1,000°C. In 1962, it was in a garage on the museum's very site that Harvey Littleton organized the first studio glassblowing workshop that launched the global Studio Glass Art movement. Toledo claims to have triggered a worldwide artistic revolution from a garage, and this studio continues that tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: Pittsburgh to Detroit: Steel, Rock & Motown - 9 Days on the Great Lakes

map_keywords: Toledo Museum of Art Glass Pavilion
Toledo Museum of Art Monroe Street
National Museum of the Great Lakes Toledo

visits.text: The O.K. Corral is the site of the most famous gunfight in American history. On October 26, 1881, around 3 p.m., Wyatt Earp, his brothers Virgil and Morgan, and Doc Holliday confronted the Clantons and McLaurys. Thirty seconds of gunfire: three dead on the outlaw side—Billy Clanton, Tom McLaury, and Frank McLaury—and two Earps wounded. The complex today includes reconstructed period stables, C.S. Fly's photo gallery, and the Historama—a multimedia presentation narrated by Vincent Price—included with admission. Reenactments are performed several times daily.

Boothill Graveyard sits on a small hill at the north entrance to town. About 300 people were buried here between 1878 and 1884, including Billy Clanton, Tom McLaury, and Frank McLaury, who fell during the gunfight. The epitaphs are often terse, sometimes sardonic—"Hanged by mistake," "Murdered in the streets." Entry is free. Allow 30 minutes.

The Tombstone Courthouse State Historic Park, built in 1882, is the town's best museum for understanding the mining and legal history of Cochise County. Wyatt Earp's razor is on display, along with the rifle of Ed Schieffelin, the prospector who discovered silver in the area in 1877 and founded the town in 1879. A courtroom mock-up and a reconstructed jail cell give a concrete sense of frontier justice.

The Tombstone Epitaph is Arizona's oldest newspaper, still published today. Its museum, free and located behind the Crystal Palace Saloon on Fifth Street, displays the original front page from October 27, 1881, covering the gunfight, printed on an old Washington hand press. The paper was founded by John Clum—Tombstone's reformist mayor, who had recruited the Earps to maintain order in town.

activities.text: Allen Street is Tombstone's main drag, entirely preserved in its 1880s state and closed to traffic. Actors in period costume roam all day. Order a sarsaparilla (a typical Wild West non-alcoholic beer) at the Crystal Palace Saloon, founded in 1879, and watch souvenir vendors offer photos in western costume. Kitsch, yes—but remarkably effective for time travel.

Several underground mine tours are offered around Tombstone—notably the Good Enough Mine, which produced silver during the 1880s boom. The circuit lasts about an hour and descends into the original shafts. It's a solid introduction before the more in-depth visit to the Queen Mine in Bisbee the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Arizona: Tucson, Tombstone & Bisbee

visits.text: You walk into Monroe Elementary, a two-story Italian Renaissance Revival brick building from 1926 that was one of four segregated schools serving Topeka's African American children. Oliver Brown and 12 other parents filed suit in 1951, the Supreme Court consolidated their case with four others, and on May 17, 1954 it ruled that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” The school closed in 1975, nearly went to auction, and was saved by the Trust for Public Land before opening as a National Historic Site in 2004 on the decision's 50th anniversary. Ranger-led programs and an orientation film deepen the visit.

Look up from the rotunda and you are 93 meters below the tip of a copper dome that stands taller than the one in Washington, D.C. (88 meters), though with roughly half the diameter. Construction ran from 1866 to 1903 - 37 years for $3.2 million. John Steuart Curry's 1930s second-floor murals include Tragic Prelude, depicting an oversize, raging John Brown flanked by flames and a tornado - the only portrait of a convicted traitor in any U.S. state capitol. The dome tour climbs 296 steps with no elevator; reserve your spot in advance.

Stroll into the Reinisch Rose Garden and you are surrounded by over 4,500 rosebushes in 180 varieties, laid out in 1930 by Chicago landscape architect Emmett Hill on land donated by the heirs of Civil War veteran Guilford Gage in 1899. The garden is one of 23 All-America Rose Selections test gardens in the United States, which means serious horticultural work happens here alongside the wedding photos. The Topeka Zoo within the same 65-hectare park houses a walk-through tropical rainforest, one of the first in the U.S. The 1908 carousel still runs to its original Wurlitzer band organ.

activities.text: Walk through 2,800 m² of Kansas history and you will pass a full-sized Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe locomotive, a Southern Cheyenne-style tipi, a reconstructed 1950s diner, and a strong section on the Bleeding Kansas era that many historians consider the true opening of the Civil War. The Oregon and Santa Fe Trail galleries are particularly well done, and the overall arc - from prehistoric times through the 20th century - gives good context for everything you have seen and will see on this loop.

Pick up the free map at the Brown v. Board visitor center and follow Topeka's civil rights geography beyond Monroe School. Constitution Hall at 429 S. Kansas Avenue - called the “Free State Capitol” - is where Free State supporters drafted the Topeka Constitution in 1855 rejecting slavery; it also served as a stop on the Underground Railroad and reopened as a museum in late 2025 after extensive restoration. A community mural painted by volunteers faces the park from across the street. Topeka's Brown v. Board site was added to the U.S. Civil Rights Trail in 2021.

visits.text: Fruita Historic District—As you enter Capitol Reef, you suddenly pass through a ribbon of green in the middle of the red desert. It's not a mirage: it's Fruita, a village founded in the 1880s by Mormon pioneers who planted orchards along the Fremont River. No more than 10 families ever lived here—the last resident left in 1969. The National Park Service now maintains over 2,700 original fruit trees: cherry, apricot, peach, and apple trees. From June through October, you can pick the fruit yourself (self-service weighing and payment at orchard entrances).

Gifford Homestead - This restored farm among the orchards sells homemade fruit pies, ice cream and artisan jams. Do not leave without tasting the cherry or peach pie - it is one of the best-kept secrets of Utah's national parks. Open from mid-March to late November.

Fremont Petroglyphs—Along Highway 24, a wooden boardwalk leads to a panel of petroglyphs carved by the Fremont people 1,000 to 2,000 years ago. You'll see bighorn sheep, human figures, and geometric shapes. Access is easy and free—it's 2 km east of the visitor center.

Capitol Reef Scenic Drive—This 13 km road runs along the western face of the Waterpocket Fold, a 160 km geological fold that cuts through the entire park from north to south. The name “Capitol Reef” comes from the white Navajo sandstone domes that resemble the Capitol in Washington, and the impassable cliffs that explorers compared to reefs blocking ships. The road passes walls of red Wingate sandstone 200 m high—pull over often, each turn reveals a new vista.

Grand Wash Trail—At the end of a dirt road accessible by car, this flat 3.6 km trail threads through a canyon with vertical walls that narrow in places to just a few meters. It's one of only four passages through the Waterpocket Fold. Easy and spectacular.

Hickman Bridge—This natural sandstone bridge with a 40 m span is accessible via a 1.6 km trail from Highway 24. The climb is short but steep. Along the way, you'll pass the ruins of an ancient Fremont granary, perched in an alcove.

activities.text: Cohab Canyon Trail—This 3 km out-and-back trail climbs quickly above Fruita and offers a view down over the orchards and the Waterpocket Fold cliffs. The name comes from “cohabitation”: according to local lore, Mormons practicing polygamy hid here to evade federal marshals in the 1880s. The ascent is steep at first, but the canyon at the top is beautiful.

Capitol Gorge Trail—Before the modern road was built in 1962, this narrow canyon was the only vehicle route through the Waterpocket Fold. Travelers in wagons and later cars passed through here, and many carved their names in the rock—you'll see the “Pioneer Register” with inscriptions dating to the 1870s. The trail is 3 km out and back, flat and easy. If you continue a bit farther, you'll reach the “water pockets,” natural potholes carved in the sandstone that hold rainwater for months.

At the end of the day, stop at the base of Chimney Rock, an isolated sandstone pillar visible from Highway 24. Capitol Reef is a certified Dark Sky Park—if you stay after sunset, the low light pollution makes it one of Utah's best stargazing spots.

visits.text: Front Street and Historic Downtown Traverse City - Start with a stroll down Front Street, the main thoroughfare lined with Victorian buildings converted into shops and tasting rooms. Along the way, spot the City Opera House at No. 106: built in 1891, it was the city's first building to have electricity and still hosts performances today. Traverse City is dubbed the “Cherry Capital of the World” - the surrounding five counties produce 40 to 50 percent of the nation's tart cherry harvest. If you're here in July, the National Cherry Festival has been running since 1925 with eight days of festivities, including a parade and pie-eating contests.

Old Mission Peninsula - Head north along this 29-km finger of land that separates the two arms of Grand Traverse Bay. The lighthouse at the peninsula's tip sits almost exactly on the 45th parallel - halfway between the equator and the North Pole. All along the drive, you'll pass cherry orchards and vineyards - the sandy soil and Lake Michigan's microclimate are perfect for riesling and pinot gris. Stop at one of the wineries for a tasting.

Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore - Thirty minutes west of Traverse City, this national park protects 56 km of Lake Michigan shoreline, established in 1970. The name comes from an Ojibwe legend: a mother bear fleeing a fire in Wisconsin swam across the lake with her two cubs. The cubs drowned from exhaustion and became North and South Manitou Islands. The mother, asleep on the bluff waiting for them, was covered in sand by the Great Spirit. The “perched” dunes rise 140 meters above the lake - formed 12,000 years ago as glaciers retreated.

Pierce Stocking Scenic Drive - This 12-km loop winds through forest before emerging at spectacular overlooks. At Overlook #9, you'll discover the dunes' dizzying plunge toward Lake Michigan's blue-green waters, with the Manitou Islands on the horizon. Pierce Stocking, a land speculator who fell in love with the area, created this drive in the 1960s before the park was officially designated.

Dune Climb - This is the park's most popular attraction: a vast 40-meter sand ramp you can scramble up on foot. If you have the energy, continue beyond the crest - a 5.5-km trail leads all the way to Lake Michigan through forest and dunes. Stay on marked paths: vegetation is fragile and protected.

Glen Haven Historic Village - This restored lakeside hamlet once housed a maritime rescue station in the 19th century. You'll find the Coast Guard building, a blacksmith shop, and D.H. Day's original general store, all telling the story of Great Lakes maritime and timber commerce. Admission is free.

activities.text: Sunset at Clinch Park Beach - Settle in facing Grand Traverse Bay to watch the sun sink over Lake Michigan. The water turns shades of turquoise striking enough for a freshwater lake. Pack a picnic with local cherry products - jam, sausage, or pie.

Walk along the Boardman River - Follow the pedestrian trail that traces the river through downtown. In late afternoon, light filters through the trees and the atmosphere turns peaceful. The main section takes about 30 minutes.

Empire Bluff Trail Hike - This short loop (2.5 km round-trip) climbs through hardwood forest to a stunning panorama over South Bar Lake, Lake Michigan, and the dunes. Best in late afternoon for golden light. Moderate difficulty, allow 45 minutes.

visits.text: Perrot State Park - Limestone bluffs rise 150 meters above the Mississippi. The name "Trempealeau" comes from French "la montagne qui trempe à l'eau" - the mountain that soaks in the water - an isolated peak rising from the floodplain like an island. From the bluff tops, the view across the Mississippi Valley is vast: meanders, wooded islands, and transport barges.

Trempealeau Mountain - This isolated rock island rises at the confluence of the Trempealeau and Mississippi rivers. View it from the Brady's Bluff trail in Perrot State Park: as you climb the bluff, you see the mountain surrounded by water and the Mississippi Valley. Access to the mountain itself is by boat from the park boat launch.
Trempealeau River Confluence - At the mountain's base, the river joins the Mississippi in a calm meander. Marshy area good for birding.

activities.text: Kayaking Trempealeau Bay - Paddle through backwaters and channels of the Mississippi. The water is calm here, lined with willows and populated by herons and bald eagles. Outfitters rent kayaks at the water's edge.
Bluff Hiking - Brady's Bluff Trail (2.5 km round-trip, 150 m elevation gain) is the most popular trail. The climb is steep but short, and the summit reward is worth it.

places.name: Tuba City, AZ

visits.text: Tuba City's history deserves a stop: the Explore Navajo Interactive Museum places the landscapes in the context of a living culture. The exhibits introduce traditions, history, and ways of living in this territory. Plan a weekday stop and confirm opening hours before you arrive, as the museum may close during the lunch break.

Tuba Trading Post continues the museum visit with a stop at a place of trade on Main Street. Their proximity lets you combine a cultural introduction with items offered for sale, without adding a driving detour. Ask about the origin and maker of any pieces that interest you; a decorative label is no substitute for information from the seller.

places.name: Tucson, AZ

visits.text: Mission San Xavier del Bac rises in brilliant white about fifteen kilometers south of downtown, on Tohono O'odham Nation land. The current building was constructed by Franciscans between 1783 and 1797—the Jesuits, who had founded an earlier mission on this site in 1692, had been expelled from Spain in 1767. It's the oldest intact European structure in Arizona. The interior is covered with baroque murals and sculptures that have earned it the nickname “the Sistine Chapel of North America.” Arrive early in the morning to avoid school groups.

The Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum, west of Tucson beside Saguaro National Park, is neither quite a zoo nor quite a botanical garden - it is both, outdoors. Rattlesnakes, river otters, Mexican wolves and 300 plant species from the Sonoran Desert share its 21 hectares. Allow at least two hours. In hot weather, come when it opens - the animals are active in the morning.

Perched on Tucson's eastern edge, the Pima Air & Space Museum houses more than 300 aircraft across 80 hectares—one of the largest private aviation collections in the world. You'll encounter an SR-71 Blackbird, B-29s, and Cold War prototypes. The site adjoins Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, where 4,000 decommissioned military aircraft rust in the open desert—the infamous “Boneyard.”

The Barrio Histórico, an adobe neighborhood downtown, contains some of Tucson's oldest houses, built from the 1850s onward. The earthen walls have retained their vivid colors—ochre, turquoise, salmon. This is where el Presidio San Agustín del Tucson once stood, the Spanish fort founded in 1775. The walk is brief (30 minutes on foot) but gives an honest sense of what the city was like before the railroad arrived.

activities.text: Saguaro National Park West runs along the Tucson Mountains just behind the Desert Museum—it's the densest area for saguaros, those cacti that can exceed 12 meters in height and live 150 years. The Bajada Loop Drive (12 km of gravel) lets you see everything without walking in extreme heat. If you prefer hiking, the Valley View Overlook Trail (2.4 km round-trip) offers a panorama across the plain at sunset.

Tucson is the first American city designated a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy—and that shows on the plate. Devote your evening to dinner in the Fourth Avenue district or around Mercado San Agustín to explore border cuisine: tacos al pastor, chiles en nogada, Sonoran hot dogs (in a grilled bolillo roll, with beans, onions, and crema). The Mexican restaurants here are often run by families from Sonora, not chains.

places.name: Tucumcari, NM

visits.text: Cadillac Ranch (Amarillo) - Cross the field (400 meters from the parking lot) to see ten Cadillacs planted nose-first in the ground, all covered in multicolored graffiti. This 1974 installation, financed by eccentric millionaire Stanley Marsh, pays tribute to the evolution of the Cadillac tail fin. Bring spray paint - this is one of the few places in the world where graffiti is encouraged. You'll need to walk 400 meters across the field from the parking area.
MidPoint Cafe (Adrian, TX) - You're exactly halfway between Chicago and Los Angeles: 1,139 miles on each side. The sign in front of the cafe confirms it. Try the Ugly Crust Pie - the house specialty.

Blue Swallow Motel (Tucumcari) - Arrive at dusk: the blue neon swallow promising '100% Refrigerated Air' is the most beautiful lighted sign on all of Route 66. This 1939 motor court, listed on the National Register, has garages attached to each room - standard back when every traveler wanted to keep an eye on their car. If you can book a room (reserve 2 months ahead in summer), it's the ultimate Route 66 experience.

activities.text: Walk through Tucumcari's neon lights - Over two dozen vintage neon signs illuminate the main street after dark. The Blue Swallow is the star, but also look for the Palomino Motel, Safari Motel, and Teepee Curios. Walk slowly - it's an open-air museum.

visits.text: You walk into one of America's great concentrations of Zigzag Art Deco architecture, every facade paid for by oil money between 1927 and 1939. The Philcade Building at 511 S. Boston, built by oil tycoon Waite Phillips in 1930, has a lobby shaped like a “T” for Tulsa - a mix of Art Deco and Art Nouveau that drew national architectural attention at the time. Two blocks south, the Boston Avenue Methodist Church from 1929 rises like a limestone rocket; designated a National Historic Landmark in 1999, it was one of the few major Art Deco buildings in America designed by a woman, art teacher Adah Robinson. Tulsa's deco spans three distinct phases: Zigzag, PWA Moderne, and Streamline. Book the Saturday morning walking tour by Tulsa Tours for inside access to locked lobbies.

You look up at a 1929 limestone tower that National Historic Landmark status since 1999 has still not fully rendered ordinary. Adah Robinson, an art teacher rather than a licensed architect, drove the design - making this one of very few major Art Deco structures in the world with a woman as primary creative force. Step close to the entrance terracotta reliefs: stylized wheat, the cross, and elongated human figures all push skyward in the Zigzag manner. Guided tours of the interior run on Sundays after the 11am service and on most weekday mornings - call ahead to confirm timing before you drive over.

The Gilcrease Museum is closed while preparations continue for its announced reopening in early 2027. To see part of its collection now, visit the Helmerich Center for American Research on the museum grounds in Tulsa. The exhibition “Indigenous Independence: America at 250,” running through December 17, 2026, brings together treaties, peace medals and historic maps that shed light on the role of Indigenous nations during the American Revolution. Walk through the gallery and see how these documents tell the story of the era's alliances and territories. Check opening days before setting out: the center welcomes visitors on weekdays.

You walk into a neighborhood that, by 1921, had two newspapers, multiple theaters, a hospital, hotels, and scores of Black-owned businesses - all built within a segregated system that left residents no other choice. In eighteen hours on May 31-June 1, 1921, white mobs burned 1,256 homes and killed a death toll historians place between 100 and 300; 10,000 people were left homeless and 6,000 spent days under armed guard at the fairgrounds. The massacre was erased from local history for decades, recognized by an Oklahoma state commission only in 1997. The Greenwood Cultural Center and the Black Wall Street Memorial anchor this walk through a rebuilt neighborhood that carries the weight of what happened here.

You step into a 72-room Italian Renaissance villa built in 1927 for oil magnate Waite Phillips, who surprised Tulsa in 1938 by donating the entire estate - and 23 acres of formal gardens - to the city as an art museum. It opened October 25, 1939. The permanent collection runs to 16,000 objects, with particular depth in Native American art: Phillips had asked the museum to “perpetuate the culture of people to whom Oklahomans are especially indebted,” and more than half the holdings reflect that charge. The 2004 garden renovation cemented a reputation as the most beautiful place in Oklahoma. Plan at least two and a half hours - the grounds alone earn the trip.

You walk into a 100-acre riverside park that, when it opened September 8, 2018, set a U.S. record as the largest private gift ever made to a community park - $465 million from the George Kaiser Family Foundation. The land sits on what was Muscogee Nation territory; the main trail was renamed the Tuckabache Trail to honor the Muscogee medicine man to whom it was originally allotted. Over 3 million people came in year one alone, tripling every projection. The Chapman Adventure Playground, ONEOK Boathouse, skate park, and wetlands trail give the park enough range that two hours here still feels like you've only scratched it. Entry is free.

activities.text: You'll spend two hours inside four Art Deco lobbies - one of them normally locked to the public - hearing stories about the oil barons who commissioned these buildings and learning to read three distinct phases of the style. Your guide explains why Zigzag Art Deco arrived in Tulsa just two years after its 1925 Paris debut, and why typically conservative utility companies embraced the most flamboyant style of the Roaring Twenties. AARP named it a top-10 walking tour in America. Book online at tulsa.tours at least a few days ahead - Saturday morning slots fill quickly.

Tonight you eat and drink in the Tulsa Arts District - formerly the Brady Arts District - a stretch of red-brick warehouses just north of the railroad tracks that has been Tulsa's cultural engine since the 1990s revitalization. You'll find the Woody Guthrie Center here (Guthrie was born in Okemah, Oklahoma, in 1912), the Bob Dylan Center, and Cain's Ballroom, which has hosted touring acts since 1930 and is still one of the best small venues in the country. The First Friday Art Crawl fills the streets on the first Friday of each month. For dinner, Restaurant Basque and Amelia's Wood Fired Cuisine both earn consistent local praise.

You set off from the ONEOK Boathouse on Peggy's Pond, a park pond where kayaks, canoes, and pedal boats are available to rent. You paddle under the Williams Crossing pedestrian bridge - completed on Labor Day 2024 - for a view back toward the park skyline. The boathouse operates seasonally; weekday mornings are the quietest times on the water. It's an easy but rewarding extension of your time in the park before you head out for the evening.

If your second night in Tulsa falls on a first Friday, you're in luck - galleries, studios, and museums across the Tulsa Arts District stay open into the evening with free or reduced admission, and the streets fill with locals and visitors moving between venues. On any other evening, the district's restaurants and bars draw a crowd until late. The Woody Guthrie Center displays rotating exhibits on Guthrie's life and the folk tradition he shaped; the Bob Dylan Center opened in 2022 and documents six decades of Dylan's archive. Cain's Ballroom at 423 N. Main has hosted touring acts continuously since 1930 and almost always has something on.

places.name: Tusayan, AZ

visits.text: On the route to the Grand Canyon via US-89, stop at Cameron Trading Post, a trading post founded in 1916 on Navajo lands, beside the Little Colorado River. Its Navajo craft gallery—rugs, silver and turquoise jewelry, pottery—is one of the region's most comprehensive. The suspension footbridge behind the trading post offers a plunging view of the river's orange gorges.

Enter the park through the east entrance and first get a sense of the canyon from Desert View—the stone tower built in 1932 by architect Mary Colter on the South Rim stands at 2,280 meters. From there, the view extends some 30 kilometers of canyon, with the Colorado visible below. Then continue west on the Desert View Drive, stopping at Lipan Point: the river describes a curve rarely seen from such heights.

Mather Point is the South Rim's most frequented viewpoint—and for good reason: at 2,170 meters elevation, it plunges more than 1,370 meters above the Colorado, and on clear days you can see up to 96 kilometers west. It's named after Stephen Mather, the first director of the National Park Service. Arrive at dawn to watch the walls ignite—and to avoid the crowds that arrive by 9 a.m.

Walk along the Rim Trail to Yavapai Geology Museum (1.1 km from Mather Point), built in 1928 from local limestone and ponderosa pine to blend into the landscape. Its panels trace 1.8 billion years of geological history—each meter of the canyon wall represents roughly one million years. The view through the museum's picture windows is among the South Rim's widest.

Continue west on the Rim Trail to Grand Canyon Village Historic District: the stone buildings constructed by Mary Colter in the 1930s (El Tovar Hotel, Lookout Studio, Bright Angel Lodge) are all designated historic landmarks. Step inside Lookout Studio, perched at the cliff's edge since 1914—the architecture plays with the rocks to the point where it's hard to tell where the building ends and the rock face begins.

activities.text: Position yourself at Mather Point or Yavapai Point for the golden hour and sunset—the canyon walls successively turn from yellow to blood red to orange depending on the light. If you arrive in late afternoon, it's not uncommon to see the colors shift within twenty minutes. Plan to be there 45 minutes before sunset.

Descend a few hundred meters along the Bright Angel Trail to experience the canyon from within—the first switchbacks reveal rock layers you couldn't see from above. Don't go beyond Havasupai Gardens (a 14.5 km round trip, too ambitious for a single day in intense heat).

From March to November, take the free Hermit Road shuttle (Red Route) to Hermits Rest west of the village—11 km of viewpoints, including stops such as Pima Point and Monument Creek Vista. The shuttle lets you alternate between walking and riding the bus.

places.name: Tuskegee, AL

visits.text: Moton Field sits just off I-85 and the airport runway is still active - you may hear a small plane overhead as you walk into Hangar 1. Inside, a canary-yellow PT-17 Stearman biplane is the first thing you see: that is where it began, primary flight training for men the Army had decided would probably fail. Between 1941 and 1946, 992 Black pilots were trained here and at nearby Tuskegee Army Air Field. The park is free and open Monday through Saturday. Walk through both hangars: Hangar 1 covers the training, the Double V campaign - victory abroad against fascism, victory at home against racism - and includes a WWII-era flight simulator. Hangar 2 centers a restored P-51 Mustang. Climb the three flights to the original control tower for a 360-degree view of the airfield.

A ten-minute drive brings you to the Tuskegee University campus and the George Washington Carver Museum. The building served as the school's laundry until 1938; Carver himself largely funded its conversion into a museum, opened in 1941 by Henry Ford. Inside are his laboratory equipment—he started with one microscope—alongside more than 300 industrial products he developed from peanuts, sweet potatoes and local clays. His paintings, which mattered to him as much as his chemistry, are also displayed. The museum is open Monday through Saturday, 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call ahead to confirm the hours.

A few hundred meters from the Carver Museum on the same campus, The Oaks—Booker T. Washington's home—is currently closed for restoration. Washington founded the school in 1881 with almost nothing, building it literally brick by brick with student labor, then recruited Carver from Iowa State in 1896. The small campus cemetery nearby holds the graves of Washington and Carver. Walk through it: it takes ten minutes and is quietly moving. The campus itself—its brick buildings and live oaks—was built largely by students learning a trade while earning an education.

activities.text: The Tuskegee Human and Civil Rights Multicultural Center, on Franklin Road in downtown Tuskegee, documents the 40-year Tuskegee Syphilis Study - in which the U.S. Public Health Service monitored the progression of untreated syphilis in 399 Black men who were told they had “bad blood.” The study ran from 1932 to 1972, long after penicillin was available and known to be effective. President Clinton formally apologized in 1997. Check hours before visiting.

If you have energy in the evening, the Tuskegee University campus invites a quiet walk after hours. The 1922 Booker T. Washington Monument - sculptor Charles Keck's bronze depicting Washington lifting the veil of ignorance - stands near the main entrance. The campus has been a National Historic Landmark since 1966, the first HBCU to receive that designation.

places.name: Twentynine Palms, CA

visits.text: Joshua Tree National Park lies on the boundary between two deserts - the Mojave to the north, cooler, where Joshua trees grow (tree-like yuccas that can live 500 years), and the Colorado Desert to the south, hotter, home to cholla and ocotillo. Hidden Valley is its geological heart: an enclosed amphitheatre of quartz monzonite boulders that have been emerging from the ground for millions of years. The site is about 35 km from Twentynine Palms, a 35-minute drive. Local legend has it that it was a cattle rustlers' hideout in the 19th century. Today it is above all a climbing paradise - more than 8,000 routes recorded in the park, many of them starting here. The 1.6-kilometre nature loop is accessible to all and passes at the foot of spectacular formations.

Skull Rock, reached directly from the parking area on Park Boulevard, is one of the most photographed rocks in the park - hollows carved by water erosion give it the look of a skull. It is about twenty minutes' drive from Twentynine Palms. A 2.7-kilometre nature trail starts here and passes several remarkable formations, with information panels on desert geology. It is a good introduction if you haven't done Hidden Valley.

activities.text: In the late afternoon, head down to the Cholla Cactus Garden on Pinto Basin Road - a transition zone between the two deserts where thousands of “teddy bear” cholla cover 4 hectares. The site is about 32 km from Twentynine Palms, a 30-minute drive. Don't be fooled by their fuzzy appearance: their hollow spines lodge in the skin at the slightest brush and curl once in contact with moisture, making them extremely hard to remove. Stay on the trail and wear closed shoes. The late-day light creates a golden halo around each cactus - the ideal time for photos.

Joshua Tree is one of the American West's finest parks for stargazing - a certified Dark Sky Park with no significant light pollution for dozens of kilometres in any direction. Park in one of the park's isolated parking areas after nightfall and look skyward. Tour operators offer guided astronomy outings from Twentynine Palms.

places.name: Twin Falls, ID

visits.text: At the rim of the Snake River Canyon, Shoshone Falls drops 65 meters - taller than Niagara - across a horseshoe-shaped cliff nearly 305 meters wide. The canyon itself was carved in a matter of weeks during the Bonneville Flood roughly 14,000 years ago, when Lake Bonneville released 4,583 cubic kilometers of water in a catastrophic overflow. Thomas Moran, who had already painted Yellowstone, came here in 1900 for the Pan-American Exposition. See it in spring: by summer, irrigation diversions on the Snake can reduce the flow to a trickle. Admission is $5 per car from March 30 through September.

The I.B. Perrine Bridge is 457 meters long and its deck hangs 148 meters above the Snake River - the only man-made structure in the United States where BASE jumping is legal year-round without a permit. On most weekends, jumpers step off the east side and deploy their parachutes two seconds into a five-second freefall, drifting to the canyon floor. Evel Knievel's 1974 steam-rocket launch ramp is still visible on the south rim, 2.6 kilometers east of the bridge. The pedestrian walkway is free.

From the south rim of the Snake River canyon, follow the rim trail for views of Perrine Bridge and the river below. To reach the water, drive down to Centennial Waterfront Park, where you can rent a kayak and paddle under the bridge. Blue Heart Springs are not on this stretch; kayakers reach them near Banbury Hot Springs on a separate outing. Treat the rim walk and the kayak trip as two separate activities.

activities.text: TandemBASE, based in Twin Falls, runs commercial tandem jumps off the Perrine Bridge - you're strapped to a qualified instructor and fall 148 meters in about five seconds before the parachute opens. Minimum age 18; fee applies. If that's a firm no, the canyon walls below the bridge have bolted sport climbing routes, and the visitor center at the south end of the bridge points you to current access.

Magic Valley - the agricultural region around Twin Falls - produces more than 70% of all commercial trout eaten in the United States, raised in spring-fed farms whose water comes out of the canyon walls at a constant 15°C year-round. Rock Creek Restaurant and Snake River Brewing both serve it well, alongside local dairy cheese and Magic Valley potatoes. The Thursday summer farmers' market on Shoshone Street (June through October) is one of the better ones in southern Idaho.

visits.text: Escape to Tybee Island, Savannah's laid-back beach retreat where wide sandy beaches, rolling dunes, and tranquil marshlands create a carefree coastal atmosphere. The historic lighthouse, Georgia's oldest and tallest, has guided mariners since 1736 and offers panoramic views from its observation deck, reached by climbing 178 steps. The island maintains nostalgic beach-town charm with colorful cottages and relaxed local culture.

Explore the imposing Fort Pulaski National Monument, a masterpiece of 19th-century military engineering whose massive brick walls were breached by rifled cannon during the Civil War, forever changing the course of the war. The moated fortification and surrounding marshlands offer walking trails rich with birdlife and historical significance. Interpretive programs bring the fort's dramatic history to life.

activities.text: Swim and sunbathe at lively South Beach, spot dolphins offshore, and watch pelicans diving for fish as the sun sets over the Atlantic. The Tybee Pier and Pavilion area buzzes with activity while quieter stretches of shore provide peaceful escapes. Over 200 bird species make this island a rewarding destination for wildlife observation throughout the year.

visits.text: One-fifth of all roses grown commercially in the United States comes from East Texas counties—a legacy of the early 20th century, when local nurserymen replaced peach trees decimated by the freezes of 1907 with rose bushes. Tyler Municipal Rose Garden, on 5.7 hectares, has 35,000 rose bushes and 500 varieties: North America's largest public rose garden. Peak bloom in May and October. Free, open year-round.

Adjacent to the garden, the Tyler Rose Museum explains why this East Texas sandy soil suits roses (acidic soil, mild climate), how seven million cuttings were shipped nationwide each year in the 1950s, and the annual Texas Rose Festival tradition since 1933—the second weekend in October, 100,000 visitors. $3.50, budget 45 minutes.

If you're here in late March or early April, it's the absolute peak: the Tyler Azalea District showcases 16 km of streets lined with azaleas planted in the 1920s by residents themselves. Self-guided route by car or on foot, map available at the Visitor Center. Off-season, the houses remain beautiful but without the spectacle.

activities.text: Locals' favorite burger since 1979, that's Jucy's Hamburgers—not haute cuisine, but the local institution. Otherwise, Rick's on the Square downtown serves elegant Southern cuisine (steak, Gulf fish) in a former 1916 bank whose marble vault has been preserved.

places.name: Unisphere, NY

visits.text: Day 3 - optional: At the center of Flushing Meadows-Corona Park stands the Unisphere's 43 m steel globe, a relic of the 1964 World's Fair. Fountains in summer, skaters, families from around the world: the park is the city's true melting pot. Free access; the fair's abandoned pavilions add a touch of melancholy.

Day 3 - optional: Around the Unisphere, Flushing Meadows brings together the Queens Museum and its Panorama, a model of the entire city at a scale of 1:1,200 with nearly 900,000 buildings, plus the US Open courts and Arthur Ashe Stadium. Allow half a day if you go into everything, two hours for the essentials.

activities.text: The Queens Museum, which charges a modest admission fee, deserves 45 min just for the Panorama: you can look for your neighborhood as you would on a giant map.
End of Day 3. For Central Park tomorrow morning: 7 line subway to Manhattan then transfer toward Upper West Side, about 11 km and 50 min.

visits.text: Oak Alley Plantation - The avenue of 28 three-hundred-year-old live oaks leading to the mansion is the most famous image of Louisiana. Planted between 1725 and 1750, these trees form a 250-meter tunnel of greenery. The house, built in 1837 by Jacques Télesphore Roman (brother of the governor), is a square measuring 21 meters on each side, surrounded by 28 columns—as many as there are oak trees. Allow at least 2 hours. Don't miss the slavery exhibit in the reconstructed cabins: it's there you learn that an enslaved man named Antoine grafted the first commercial pecan trees in 1846.

Whitney Plantation - Twenty minutes from Oak Alley, this is the only Louisiana plantation entirely dedicated to the history of slavery. No romantic narrative here—the guided tour (mandatory) focuses on the lives of enslaved people, with testimonies carved in stone. Count on 1.5 hours.

activities.text: Drive the River Road - The road hugging the Mississippi between New Orleans and Baton Rouge passes a dozen plantations. The stretch between Vacherie and Donaldsonville is the most spectacular—old mansions, sugar cane fields, and century-old oaks.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Louisiana Road Trip: Jazz and Bayous

visits.text: Day 1: Worthington Glacier State Recreation Site - Located along Thompson Pass at an elevation of 2,800 feet (about 45 km from Valdez, a 45-minute drive), this glacier descends from the Chugach Mountains to within easy viewing distance of the Richardson Highway. A paved trail leads to the viewing platforms, while more adventurous visitors can take the two-mile Worthington Glacier trail for closer access to the ice.

Day 1: Bridal Veil Falls - This spectacular 900-foot waterfall plunges down the sheer cliffs of Keystone Canyon, visible from the roadside pullouts and accessible via a one-mile trail leading to a viewpoint. The waterfall is most impressive during the spring melt and after summer rains. Keystone Canyon is less than half an hour's drive from Valdez.

Day 1: Keystone Canyon - The Richardson Highway runs through this dramatic gorge carved by the Lowe River, with towering rock walls and multiple waterfalls creating one of the most scenic roads in Alaska. The historic remains of the failed Trans-Alaska Railway attempt are visible along the canyon walls. The canyon is less than half an hour's drive from Valdez.

Day 2: Valdez Harbor and Waterfront - This ice-free port at the head of a fjord serves as the terminus of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and a major fishing harbor. The downtown area rebuilt after the 1964 earthquake offers views of surrounding peaks rising directly from the water.

Day 2: Prince William Sound - This island-studded waterway encompasses 15,000 square miles of protected waters, tidewater glaciers, and abundant marine wildlife. The sound's deep fjords and sheltered bays create ideal conditions for viewing sea otters, seals, sea lions, and whales.

activities.text: Day 1: Thompson Pass Scenic Drive - The approach to Valdez crosses this 2,678-foot pass through the Chugach Mountains, an area that receives some of the heaviest snowfall in North America. The pass is about a forty-minute drive from Valdez. In summer, the alpine meadows burst with wildflowers while glaciers cling to the surrounding peaks.

Day 2: Glacier Cruise - Day cruises venture into Columbia Bay to witness Columbia Glacier, one of Alaska's largest tidewater glaciers. These journeys navigate through floating icebergs while naturalists explain glacial geology and point out wildlife including puffins, kittiwakes, and marine mammals.

Day 2: Sea Kayaking - Guided paddling excursions explore the fjords and bays surrounding Valdez, offering intimate access to marine ecosystems inaccessible by larger vessels. Multi-day expeditions reach remote glaciers and beaches for camping.

Day 2: Wildlife Viewing - Prince William Sound's nutrient-rich waters support abundant marine life, with sea otters, harbor seals, Steller sea lions, humpback whales, and orcas regularly observed. Seabird colonies host thousands of puffins, cormorants, and eagles.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Alaska Circuit: National Parks and Glaciers

places.name: Valentine, NE

visits.text: The Niobrara National Scenic River Visitor Center on Highway 20 in Valentine is where you orient yourself to one of the most biologically surprising places in the Great Plains. Congress set aside 122 km of the Niobrara for preservation in 1991; six distinct ecosystems converge in this single river valley - northern boreal forest, western coniferous forest, eastern deciduous forest, tallgrass prairie, mixed-grass prairie, and Sandhills prairie - a botanical crossroads found nowhere else on the continent. In October 2023, the Niobrara became the first river in the United States designated a Quiet Trail by nonprofit Quiet Parks International, recognized for the near-total absence of human-made noise. Rangers here are knowledgeable; ask them to sketch the best float route before you head to the river.

Fort Niobrara National Wildlife Refuge, 6 km east of Valentine on Highway 12, protects 7,745 hectares of prairie and canyon on the site of an 1880 military fort built to shield settlers from Sioux raids. A free driving tour winds through bison and elk pastures - herds of roughly 300 bison and several dozen elk are reliably visible from the road, often within 15 meters. The refuge launch site is the standard put-in for the most scenic Niobrara float: 42 km of Class I-II water to Smith Falls, passing more than 90 side-canyon waterfalls and sandstone cliffs lined with paper birch and ponderosa pine.

Smith Falls State Park, east of Valentine via Highway 12, protects Nebraska's highest waterfall; allow for a drive from Valentine to reach it. Smith Falls drops about 19 meters into a narrow side canyon before joining the Niobrara below. It is named for Frederic Smith, who settled this land in the 1880s; the site became a state park in 1992. A footbridge across the Niobrara and an accessible boardwalk through a canyon of birch and pine lead to the foot of the falls. You hear the water well before seeing it. This is also the main takeout for canoe trips from Fort Niobrara.

activities.text: Rent a canoe or kayak in Valentine and float the Niobrara from Fort Niobrara to Smith Falls; set aside half a day on the water and arrange the return shuttle with your outfitter. Fed by the Ogallala Aquifer, the river runs cold and clear year-round, passing waterfalls, fossil-bearing sandstone cliffs and canyon sections where the trees meet overhead. Several outfitters in Valentine supply equipment and shuttle service. It is a highlight of the Sandhills region.

In the evening, drive south on US-83 for 15 km to take in the full scale of the Sandhills at dusk - 50,000 km² of grass-stabilized sand dunes, the largest such formation in the Western Hemisphere, rolling to every horizon. The wind almost never stops. Merritt Reservoir, 42 km southwest of Valentine, is a designated International Dark Sky Park; the Milky Way here on a clear night is as vivid as anywhere in the contiguous United States.

places.name: Valley Of Fire, NV

visits.text: At Atlatl Rock, look at the rock faces as closely as the landscape: the carvings give the red rocks a human history. Valley of Fire’s petroglyphs bear witness to ancient habitation in the desert. View them from the designated access area without touching the carved surfaces, then return to your vehicle before the heat sets in.

A short stop at Valley of Fire Visitor Center is better than choosing a hike at random in the sun. The exhibits connect geology, wildlife, and human presence in these red sandstones, formed from ancient sand deposits. Confirm which trails and road access routes are open that day before continuing toward Mouse's Tank.

activities.text: You’ll follow Mouse's Tank Trail through a sandy corridor lined with carved rocks to a natural basin that sometimes holds water. This short trail shows how the desert preserves subtle traces of those who passed through. Carry water from the parking lot, stay on the trail, and skip the walk in extreme heat.

places.name: Vicksburg, MS

visits.text: Established February 21, 1899, the Vicksburg National Military Park protects 730 hectares of battlefield where Grant besieged Confederate defenders for 47 days - May 18 to July 4, 1863. When Vicksburg surrendered, the Confederacy was split in two and the Union held the entire Mississippi River. The park's 1,325 monuments and markers are second in number only to Gettysburg's, with 32 kilometers of reconstructed trenches and 144 emplaced cannon. Drive the 26-kilometer tour road first, then walk the key positions - the sight lines explain the siege more clearly than any text panel ever could.

The USS Cairo is a Civil War ironclad gunboat, and it stands under a shelter inside the military park, looking exactly as battered as you would expect after 102 years submerged in the Yazoo River. Confederate forces sank it on December 12, 1862 with an electrically detonated mine (the first American warship ever lost to a floating mine); it went down in 12 minutes. It was raised in 1964 and transferred to the National Park Service in 1972. The adjoining museum holds thousands of crew belongings recovered from the wreck: boots, combs, pocketknives, remarkably intact after a century in the mud. Allow 60 minutes.

General Pemberton reportedly watched Union naval attacks on the Mississippi from the bell tower of the Old Court House during the siege - and when Vicksburg fell on July 4, 1863, Grant's troops marched in and raised the Union flag from the same roof. The Greek Revival building at 1008 Cherry Street was constructed between 1858 and 1860 by enslaved craftsmen; it nearly came down in 1939 before historian Eva Whitaker Davis rallied the community and saved it, reopening it as a museum in 1948. Inside: Civil War newspapers printed on wallpaper when paper ran out, the tie Jefferson Davis wore at his Confederate presidential inauguration, and Native American Mississippian-culture ceramics. National Historic Landmark since 1968.

activities.text: Along Vicksburg's floodwall, artist Robert Dafford's 32 life-sized murals run for several hundred feet, first unveiled April 12, 2002. They depict the city's history from Native American settlement through the Civil War, the steamboat era, and the 20th century. Walk the entire length - each panel has a text plaque, and the Mississippi River overlooks at Louisiana Circle or Navy Circle off South Washington Street are among the most dramatic on the entire river. Lincoln called Vicksburg 'the key' to winning the war; standing above the water on the bluffs, you see why.

Solly's Hot Tamales on Washington Street has been open since 1939 - Vicksburg's version of the Delta tamale, made to a three-generation recipe that's subtly different from Greenville's. Dinner here or at one of the other restaurants along Washington Street closes a dense Civil War day with food that's rooted in the living culture of the region. The walkable stretch of Washington Street near the park has several good local options.

places.name: Virginia Beach, VA

visits.text: To see the Cape Henry Lighthouse, the first lighthouse authorized by the U.S. Congress (Lighthouse Act of 1789) and the first public work of the new federal government, operational in 1792—you'll need to pass through military security. The lighthouse sits on Fort Story base: Gate 8, photo ID required, then free shuttle. Right next to it, a cross marks the First Landing site, where English colonists set foot on April 26, 1607, before sailing upriver to Jamestown.

First Landing State Park, north of Cape Henry, covers 2,888 acres of coastal forest with 19 miles of trails. Walk them early in the morning before the heat—the subtropical forest at this latitude is a rarity on the East Coast, with its live oaks and canopies that exist nowhere else in northern Virginia.

activities.text: Walk or bike the Virginia Beach boardwalk in the evening—5 kilometers along the Atlantic, seafood restaurants on both sides, waves as your soundtrack. The beach stretches 35 miles long: one of the world's longest urban beaches.

The Virginia Aquarium & Marine Science Center on General Booth Boulevard is worth 2 to 3 hours of your time: more than 10,000 marine animals and an outdoor re-creation of the Chesapeake marshes. Less crowded and cheaper than the National Aquarium in Baltimore.

places.name: Virginia, NV

visits.text: Virginia City — Step into this authentically preserved 1860s mining boomtown perched on Mount Davidson's slopes. The National Historic Landmark preserves boardwalks, Victorian buildings, and saloons from when Comstock Lode silver discovery created Nevada Territory.
The Way It Was Museum — Explore the mining equipment, minerals and artifacts that explain how the Comstock Lode produced 500 million dollars in silver and gold.

Chollar Mine — Descend into a real silver mine with original 1860s square-set timbering still supporting tunnels. Guided tours explain mining techniques that extracted precious metals from 300 meters underground.

St. Mary in the Mountains Catholic Church — Visit this 1876 Gothic Revival church built with mining wealth featuring Italian marble and stained glass. The cathedral replaced an earlier church destroyed in the Great Fire of 1875.

activities.text: C Street walking tour — Stroll the main street lined with saloons, shops, and museums occupying original 1860s buildings. Wooden boardwalks and Victorian storefronts recreate Wild West atmosphere.
Virginia & Truckee Railroad ride — Board vintage steam trains running the historic route built in 1869 to haul Comstock ore. The scenic journey passes mining ruins with mountain views.
Saloon experience — Sample local beers at authentic Old West saloons with swinging doors and antique bars. Some establishments maintain 1860s character serving spirits to modern visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Nevada's Great Contrasts: Las Vegas Neon to Red Rock Desert Silence

map_keywords: St. Mary in the Mountains Church

visits.text: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park — Witness ongoing volcanic activity at Kilauea, one of the world's most active volcanoes. The 1,348-square-kilometer park encompasses the summit caldera, lava tubes, steam vents, and barren lava fields from recent eruptions.

Thurston Lava Tube — Walk through this 150-meter tunnel formed 500 years ago when lava drained leaving a hollow tube. Ferns and native plants surround the entrance while the interior reveals smooth walls created by flowing molten rock.
Chain of Craters Road — Drive 30 kilometers down from the summit to the sea across vast lava fields. The scenic road passes extinct craters, petroglyphs and the Holei Sea Arch.

Uēkahuna Overlook — Take in the Kilauea caldera from this bluff on the crater rim, where the Jaggar Museum and the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory buildings stood until their demolition after the 2018 earthquakes. A line of stones from the former columns marks the museum's footprint, and the restored terrace overlooks Halemaʻumaʻu crater. During eruptive episodes, the lava glow is visible at night; stay behind the stone walls.

activities.text: Punaluu Black Sand Beach — Walk on volcanic sand formed by lava shattering on contact with cold ocean water. Endangered green turtles bask on the black beach beneath the coconut palms in this remote spot in the south of the island, about half an hour's drive from Volcano.

Kaʻū Coffee Farm Visit — Discover Kaʻū coffee, grown on the slopes of Mauna Loa, at the Kaʻū Coffee Mill near Pāhala. The estate offers tours and tastings explaining the growing, harvesting and roasting of this Hawaiian coffee. It lies on the road to Punaluu: plan a half-day round trip from Volcano.

Kilauea Iki Trail — Descend through tree-fern rainforest to the floor of Kilauea Iki crater, a lava lake frozen since the 1959 eruption. The crossing of the cracked crater floor, where steam still rises from fissures, passes beneath Puʻu Puaʻi, the cone built by the lava fountains, before climbing back to the crater rim.

days_plan.itin_title: Hawaii Trip: Volcanoes and Dream Beaches

places.name: Waco, TX

visits.text: Dr Pepper Museum: in 1885 - one year before Coca-Cola - a pharmacist named Charles Alderton was mixing fruit extracts in the back room of the Old Corner Drug Store in Waco. The drink was initially called 'Waco' before his boss renamed it Dr Pepper. The 1906 bottling plant that now houses the museum is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Three floors of archives on the soda industry, a vintage soda fountain, and the chance to concoct your own soda in a workshop.

Waco Mammoth National Monument: in 1978, two men out collecting Indian arrowheads discovered a mammoth femur protruding from a ravine. What they found after 19 years of excavation is the only nursery herd of Columbian mammoths ever uncovered in the United States: 23 individuals, nearly all females and juveniles, likely victims of a Bosque River flood 70,000 years ago. The bones remain in place in their original positions - you tour them with a ranger under a large covered shelter.

Magnolia Market at the Silos: the former grain silos transformed into an urban market by the Gaines couple popularized the concept on the TV series Fixer Upper. Whether you're a fan of the show or not, the site is worth a stop—manicured gardens, food trucks with outdoor seating, shops and a bakery. Allow an hour: it's larger and livelier than you'd expect.

activities.text: Tasting at Balcones Distilling: founded in 2008, Balcones is the distillery that put Texas craft whiskey back on the world map. Their True Blue, made from Hopi blue corn grown in Texas, has won multiple international awards. Guided tours let you see the copper stills and understand the cold-distillation process unique to their method.

days_plan.itin_title: Texas Triangle: Dallas, Austin, San Antonio & the Hill Country - 8 Days

visits.text: Great Eddy Covered Bridge frames the Mad River with its timber structure at the end of Bridge Street in Waitsfield. The bridge still carries road traffic, with restrictions posted by the town. Park before approaching it and observe its construction from pedestrian areas without stopping in the roadway to take a photograph.

activities.text: Leave the car behind to explore Bridge Street and Main Street in downtown Waitsfield. These streets bring together cafés and artisan galleries around the historic heart of the Mad River Valley. Look for open storefronts and take a break by the river before continuing south on Route 100.

days_plan.itin_title: New England in Fall: 11 Days on the Road

places.name: Wall, SD

visits.text: The billboards start appearing 500 km before Wall. Dorothy Hustead came up with the idea in 1936: her pharmacy was dying on the edge of US-16, so she put up signs promising free ice water, and cars started stopping. Today, 2 million visitors a year pour into these 7,000 m² of madness—a 25-meter dinosaur, giant jackalope, mini chapel, Texan cafeteria. Coffee is still 5 cents. Water is still free. It's kitsch, unapologetic, and thoroughly American.

From Wall, plan a same-day round trip to visit Minuteman Missile National Historic Site. Rangers go down with you into the underground Delta-01 launch control center and explain how it really worked. Book on Recreation.gov before you leave: places sell out the day before.

From Wall, plan a same-day round trip to the Ben Reifel Visitor Center. Enter via I-90 exit 131 and head straight to the center before doing anything else. Not out of obligation—but because understanding what you are about to see changes everything. The layers of the Badlands Wall record 75 million years of geological history: a Cretaceous inland sea, Oligocene savanna, volcanic ash. The buttes erode by 2.5 cm a year. In 500,000 years, none of this will remain.

Big Badlands Overlook awaits just beyond the east entrance; from Wall, plan a same-day round trip. There, you understand why the Lakota called this place Mako Sica, “bad land.” The wall of buttes and pinnacles stretches as far as the eye can see, separating two prairies at different elevations. The town of Wall took its name from this natural cliff. Stop for 20 minutes; the late-afternoon light turns everything into blocks of amber.

From Wall, plan a same-day round trip to the Fossil Exhibit Trail. It runs for 800 meters past replicas of fossils in situ—prehistoric rhinoceroses, camelids, giant tortoises. This is not a theme park: the real fossils are still in the rock around you, but the NPS does not allow you to take them. The Badlands contain the world's richest collection of Oligocene mammal fossils. Wheelchair accessible.

Door Trail—do not skip it. From Wall, plan a same-day round trip to the trail. Door Trail (800 m round trip) takes you literally through a gap in the Wall and into the formation's inner labyrinth. Bring water, a hat, sunscreen—the sun beats down mercilessly.

Roberts Prairie Dog Town borders the road, and it's better than its name suggests. These social rodents live in organized underground cities with sentries, tunnels, and nurseries—John James Audubon described them as “the noisiest creature on the Great Plains.” Stay in your car, approach slowly: they fear nothing and let you photograph them from 3 meters away.

Finish at Pinnacles Overlook, at the western end of the park, where the pinnacles - slender columns isolated by erosion - take their most spectacular form. We are not saying this is a cheerful place - but we are saying it is a powerful one.

activities.text: From Wall, plan a same-day round trip to Notch Trail. Notch Trail (2.4 km round trip) is the park's most spectacular trail—and few people hike it because it begins with a rope ladder fixed in a crack in the Wall. Get past that point: on the other side, a narrow canyon opens onto a panoramic terrace overlooking the White River Badlands. Closed-toe shoes, hat, water. Set off before 8 a.m. in summer.

An hour before sunset, get back on the Badlands Loop Road (SD-240) and drive slowly, windows down. The buttes turn orange then brick red, bison and pronghorn come out to graze. Park at whichever overlooks you happen upon and listen: wind through the rock formations, sometimes a coyote in the distance. It's the best time of day.

visits.text: Wamego OZ Museum - Where a Kansas Farm Girl Became a Hollywood Legend: This whimsical museum houses over 2,000 artifacts telling the story of how L. Frank Baum's children's novel about a Kansas girl swept away by a tornado became one of the most-watched films in cinema history.

OZ Museum Collection - Original 1939 Movie Artifacts: Browse signed photographs by the film's stars, original L. Frank Baum books, and production memorabilia from the beloved 1939 movie that made 'There's no place like home' an American catchphrase.

activities.text: Downtown Wamego - Small Town Charm on the Prairie: Explore the charming main street of this Kansas community that has embraced its connection to one of America's most beloved stories.
