places.name: Washington Dc

visits.text: Smithsonian Institution Building (The Castle) - Your museum marathon begins with the Smithsonian's founding building, but be aware: the Castle has been under renovation since February 2023 (its first major renovation in 50 years) and its interior is not open during construction. This red sandstone neo-Gothic castle, designed by James Renwick Jr. (the same architect as St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York), was completed in 1855. It houses the crypt of James Smithson, the British scientist who never set foot in the United States and who left his entire fortune to found what has become the largest museum complex in the world. His remains were brought back from Genoa in 1905. Admire the exterior facade and use the virtual visitor center on si.edu to plan your visits.

Enid A. Haupt Garden - Right behind the Castle, this 4-acre garden is a little gem many visitors miss. Since 1987, it has featured brick walkways, fountains, and meticulously maintained flower beds. The underground entrances to the African Art Museum and the Asian Art Museum are located here. It's the perfect spot to map out your program before tackling the museums.

National Museum of American History - This is where you'll see the Star-Spangled Banner, the original 9-by-10-meter flag that flew over Fort McHenry in 1814 and inspired the national anthem. This wool and cotton flag, sewn by Mary Pickersgill in Baltimore, is preserved in a special chamber with floor-to-ceiling glass walls. Note that photography is prohibited in this room. The museum houses 1.7 million objects - you won't be able to see everything in one day.

National Air and Space Museum - One of the world's most visited museums holds the planet's largest collection of aircraft and spacecraft: approximately 60,000 objects. Right from the entrance, the Boeing Milestones of Flight Hall puts you face-to-face with the showstoppers. Plan for at least 3 to 4 hours, and book your free timed-entry pass online - it's required.

National Museum of Natural History - The world's most visited natural history museum welcomes you with Henry, a 4-meter-tall, 11-ton mounted African elephant that has stood in the rotunda since 1959. The museum is larger than 18 football fields and houses the world's largest natural history collection. Free admission, no reservation required.

National Museum of African American History and Culture - Opened in 2016, this is the only national museum entirely devoted to African American history. The 10-story building (5 above ground, 5 below) is clad in a pierced bronze crown inspired by West African decorative metalwork. With more than 45,000 objects in its collection (3,500 on display), plan for a full day. Book your free timed-entry pass online - it's essential, as the museum often sells out.

National Museum of the American Indian - This building with golden limestone curves, designed to evoke natural rock formations, houses collections devoted to the indigenous peoples of the three Americas. The architecture itself deserves attention: prismatic windows cast light onto the interior walls, and a 36-meter-high central dome crowns the entrance hall. The outdoor space recreates a wetland landscape with plants used by indigenous nations.

National Museum of African Art - This underground museum, accessible from the Haupt Garden, is the only American national museum devoted exclusively to African art. You'll discover wood and bronze sculptures, textiles, ceremonial masks, and ceramics spanning millennia of artistic creation. The contemporary African collections are particularly strong - don't expect only ancient art.

National Museum of Asian Art (Freer Gallery and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery) - Connected by an underground passage, these two galleries form the Smithsonian's Asian art museum. The Freer Gallery holds the world's most important collection of Whistler's works, including the Peacock Room: a London reception room entirely decorated by James McNeill Whistler in 1877 - blue-green and gold walls, life-size painted peacocks, transported from London piece by piece. The Sackler Gallery displays Chinese ritual bronzes dating from the Shang Dynasty (around 1500 BC), Japanese ceramics, Mughal Indian miniatures, and calligraphy. Don't miss the Moongate Garden between the two buildings - a circular Chinese-inspired garden perfect for a break.

Smithsonian American Art Museum - Housed in the former Patent Office Building (an 1836 Greek Revival structure), this museum traces three centuries of American art. You'll see canvases by Georgia O'Keeffe, Edward Hopper, Winslow Homer, and Hudson River School artists. The folk art collection is one of the most important in the country. On the 3rd floor, the Luce Foundation Center displays more than 3,300 objects in glass cases - a visible storage facility open to the public.

National Portrait Gallery - In the same building (both museums share the Patent Office Building), the National Portrait Gallery displays portraits of significant figures in American history. Each president has their official portrait here. The interior courtyard covered by a Norman Foster-designed undulating glass roof is a perfect place to catch your breath between galleries.

Renwick Gallery - A stone's throw from the White House, this branch of the Smithsonian American Art Museum occupies an elegant 1859 Second Empire building, also designed by James Renwick Jr. It is devoted to contemporary American craft: blown glass, carved wood, textiles, ceramics and metalwork. Monumental installations often fill entire rooms - the Grand Salon on the second floor is worth a look on its own.

National Postal Museum - Right across from Union Station, this often-overlooked museum is a gem. Housed in the former Washington main post office (a 1914 Beaux-Arts building), it traces the history of the American postal service from Pony Express riders to mail planes. You'll see stagecoaches, historic mailboxes, mail planes suspended from the ceiling, and one of the world's largest stamp collections. A playful museum, perfect if you're visiting with children.

Union Station - Even though it's not a museum, Washington's main train station deserves a stop. Inaugurated in 1907, it's a Beaux-Arts masterpiece with a 29-meter-high gilded coffered vault inspired by Rome's Baths of Diocletian.

Smithsonian's National Zoo - The National Zoo spans 66 hectares in the Woodley Park neighborhood, right in the heart of the city. Founded in 1889, it's one of the oldest zoos in the United States. It houses approximately 2,200 animals from 400 species, one-fifth of which are threatened. Like all Smithsonian sites, admission is free - but you must book a timed-entry pass online. Take the Metro (Woodley Park or Cleveland Park stations, red line).

Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center (Chantilly, Virginia) - The only excursion outside Washington on this itinerary, and it is well worth it. This giant 70,000 m² hangar near Dulles Airport, about 44 km from central Washington, 40 minutes by road, is the annex of the Air and Space Museum - it houses the craft too large for the museum on the Mall. You will see the Space Shuttle Discovery (39 space missions in 27 years of service), the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird (capable of flying at more than Mach 3.3), the B-29 Enola Gay that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and an Air France Concorde. Admission is free, parking costs $15. To get there by public transport, take the Metro Silver Line to Innovation Center, then the Fairfax Connector 983 bus, which drops you at the door.

Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden - This concrete cylinder, 70 meters in diameter and raised on four piers 4 meters above the ground, is the Smithsonian's museum of modern and contemporary art. Designed by Gordon Bunshaft and opened in 1974, it holds more than 12,000 works. The collection grew from the 1966 gift of 6,000 pieces by collector Joseph H. Hirshhorn. You will see works by Picasso, Warhol, Rothko, de Kooning and Hopper. The visit flows naturally - you follow the circle on each floor.

Arts and Industries Building - Right next to the Castle, this Victorian-style building completed in 1881 is the oldest museum on the Mall. Designed by Adolf Cluss (who had already renovated the Castle after the 1865 fire), it hosted President Garfield's inaugural ball before it was even finished. After years of closure, it reopens intermittently for temporary exhibitions. The interior architecture is worth the trip: wrought-iron structure, vast halls of natural light, and decorative columns.

The National Mall memorials - For your last day, step out of the museums and take time to visit the monuments. The Lincoln Memorial (1922) with its 6-meter-high marble statue is at the west end of the Mall - this is where Martin Luther King delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech in 1963. The Washington Monument, a 169-meter obelisk completed in 1884, offers a panoramic view of the entire city (book free tickets online). The Vietnam Veterans Memorial (a black granite wall bearing the 58,318 names of soldiers killed) and the Korean War Veterans Memorial complete the circuit.

activities.text: Get your bearings on the National Mall - Use this first day to walk along the Mall and scout out the museums you'll visit in the coming days. From the Lincoln Memorial to the Capitol, you have about 3 km of walkway lined with free museums. Pass by the Washington Monument and the memorials to get an overview before diving into the collections.

Explore the pop culture collections - On the 3rd floor, you'll find the famous ruby slippers Dorothy wore in The Wizard of Oz, Abraham Lincoln's top hat, Muhammad Ali's boxing gloves, and Duke Ellington's sheet music. The Entertainment Nation gallery brings together 60 objects from American pop culture in 670 square meters. Don't miss Julia Child's kitchen either, reconstructed piece by piece.

Browse the presidential and First Ladies galleries - The American Presidency exhibition traces the history of presidents through personal and official objects. Right next door, the First Ladies gallery showcases the inaugural gowns worn at inaugural balls. You'll also see the desk on which Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence.

See the icons of aviation - The 1903 Wright Flyer stands at the center of its gallery: it's the very first powered aircraft to fly. During its 4th test at Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903, piloted by Wilbur, it covered 852 feet (255.6 meters) in 59 seconds. Just above, Lindbergh's Spirit of St. Louis hangs suspended - the cockpit door is slightly ajar, at Lindbergh's own request. You'll also see the Blériot XI that crossed the English Channel in 1909.

Explore the conquest of space - You'll be able to touch a real piece of lunar rock brought back by the Apollo 17 mission. The suit Neil Armstrong wore during his first steps on the Moon is displayed here. Also look for John Glenn's Mercury Friendship 7 capsule (first American in orbit, 1962), the Apollo lunar module, and the F-1 engine from the Saturn V rocket. If you have time, the planetarium and IMAX theater are worth a visit.

Marvel at the Hope Diamond and the gem collection - In the Janet Annenberg Hooker Hall of Geology, Gems and Minerals, you'll see the Hope Diamond: a 45.52-carat deep blue diamond. This diamond was part of the French Crown Jewels under the name "Blue Diamond" since its purchase by Louis XIV in 1668. It was stolen during the French Revolution, recut, and changed hands several times before being donated to the Smithsonian in 1958. The hall also displays the Star of Asia sapphire, the Gachala emerald, and more than 7,500 individual gems. A sample from the asteroid Bennu is also on display.

Explore the Deep Time Hall of Fossils - The David H. Koch Hall of Fossils spans nearly 2,900 square meters and traces 4.6 billion years of Earth's history. You'll see 46 complete dinosaur specimens, including a T. rex and a Triceratops. The paleontology lab is visible from the gallery - you can watch scientists extract fossils in real time. Head up to the Sant Ocean Hall to see a life-size replica of a North Atlantic right whale.

Descend into the underground history galleries - The museum is visited from bottom to top, moving forward chronologically. On the underground levels, you'll traverse the history of slavery with a cabin from an Edisto Island plantation (South Carolina), Nat Turner's Bible (who led a slave rebellion in 1831), a segregated railroad car, and a guard tower from Angola Prison in Louisiana. You'll also see remnants of the São José, a slave ship discovered off the coast of South Africa.

Explore the culture and sports galleries - On the upper floors, the tone shifts. You'll find the shawl Queen Victoria gave to Harriet Tubman, Chuck Berry's red Cadillac, Gabby Douglas's leotard, Jesse Owens's spikes (1936 Olympics), and nine Olympic medals from Carl Lewis. The Musical Crossroads gallery traces African American influence from blues to hip-hop. The piano from August Wilson's play The Piano Lesson is also on display - a piano on which an enslaved man had carved his family's history.

Browse the exhibitions on indigenous nations - The Americans exhibition traces the presence of Native Americans in popular culture: sports team names, films, brands, place names. If you're going with children, the imagiNATIONS space offers interactive activities. The permanent collections feature more than 800,000 objects ranging from the Arctic to Tierra del Fuego.

Lunch at the Mitsitam Café - This is probably the best cafeteria of all the Smithsonian museums. The menu offers dishes inspired by indigenous culinary traditions, with five themed stations (North, South, Great Plains, Forests, Meso-America). A real meal, not just a sandwich break.

Compare artistic traditions from two continents - Take advantage of this day to observe parallels between African and Asian art: Benin bronzework versus Chinese ritual bronzes, Congolese Kuba textiles versus Japanese silks. Both museums are less crowded compared to the Mall's giants - you'll have peace and quiet.

Wander through the Penn Quarter neighborhood - Leaving the museum, you're in one of Washington's liveliest neighborhoods. Take the opportunity to explore the area's art galleries and Chinatown, whose grand entrance arch is just steps away. It's also a good neighborhood for dinner.

View the White House from Lafayette Square - Leaving the Renwick, cross the street: you're facing the White House. Lafayette Square offers the clearest view of the north facade. Take time to walk around via the Ellipse on the south side for another perspective. You can't go inside, but the proximity is striking.

Stroll along Pennsylvania Avenue - From the White House to the Capitol, Pennsylvania Avenue is Washington's ceremonial artery. This is where presidential motorcades pass on inauguration day. Along the way, you'll pass the Old Post Office, the FBI Building, and the National Archives (where the Declaration of Independence and Constitution are displayed - free admission).

Explore the Capitol Hill neighborhood - From Union Station, head toward the Capitol through residential streets lined with Victorian brick houses. This is locals' Washington, far from the touristy Mall. The Eastern Market (open Saturdays and Sundays) is a good spot for fresh produce, crafts, and street food.

See giant pandas Bao Li and Qing Bao - The two pandas, who arrived from China in October 2024, have been the zoo's stars since their public debut in January 2025. Bao Li (born August 4, 2021) is the grandson of Mei Xiang and Tian Tian, who lived here for 23 years. Qing Bao (born September 12, 2021) is more independent - you'll often find her perched in trees. The Smithsonian's panda program has lasted more than 50 years and helped move the species from "endangered" to "vulnerable" status.

Walk the Asia Trail and other exhibits - The Asia Trail brings together seven Asian species: sloth bears, red pandas, clouded leopards, otters, and more. Continue to the great apes, Asian elephants (in the Elephant Trails habitat opened in 2013), big cats, and the aviary. Plan for the morning - animals are more active before noon.

Climb the Donald D. Engen observation tower - From the top, you have a panoramic view of Dulles Airport runways and surroundings. It's also a chance to watch planes take off and land - a spectacle that fascinates children and adults alike.

Watch historic aircraft restoration - The Mary Baker Engen Restoration Hangar is visible from a glass-walled balcony. You can watch Smithsonian specialists restore historic aircraft - precision work that sometimes takes years per plane.

Visit the sculpture garden - The 5,300-square-meter Sculpture Garden, sunken 2 to 4 meters below street level, is a space unto itself. You'll find Rodin's Burghers of Calais - one of twelve original castings of this 1889 bronze sculpture depicting six notables offering their lives to save their city during the Hundred Years' War. Also look for Alexander Calder's mobiles and stabiles, Henry Moore's organic forms, and sculptures by Matisse, Giacometti, and Jeff Koons.

Discover Barbara Kruger's permanent installation - On the lower level, Belief+Doubt covers walls, floors, and staircases with black, white, and red texts that question power, consumption, and beliefs. It's one of Washington's most photographed installations.

Taste Washington's culinary specialties - Use this second-to-last day to explore DC's food scene. The half-smoke is the emblematic local sausage, half pork and half beef, served grilled with mustard and onions. Mumbo sauce (a sweet and spicy condiment typical of DC) goes with fried chicken wings. And if you have not yet tried Ethiopian food, the area around U Street has many Ethiopian restaurants - the injera and spicy stews there are remarkable.

Stroll through the Mall gardens - The Mary Livingston Ripley Garden (between the Hirshhorn and the Arts and Industries Building) and the Katherine Dulin Folger Rose Garden (behind the Castle) are two small gardens often overlooked. In late afternoon, the Mall empties out and the golden light on museum facades is superb.

Walk around the Tidal Basin - If you're visiting between late March and mid-April, the cherry blossoms around the Tidal Basin are an extraordinary sight - approximately 3,000 trees gifted by Japan in 1912. Even out of season, the loop around the basin (about 3 km) passes the Jefferson Memorial, the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, and the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial. Allow 1.5 hours to see everything at a relaxed pace.

Final Mall pass at sunset - The Mall is even more beautiful in late afternoon. The low light on the Capitol at one end and the Lincoln Memorial at the other creates a panorama you won't forget. It's the best way to conclude 15 days at the heart of American history and culture.

visits.text: Day 2 - Washington Square Park's marble arch opens onto the heart of Greenwich Village: outdoor grand pianos, chess games, NYU students sprawled around the fountain. It's the neighborhood living room, free and loud. Sit for half an hour, the show comes on its own.

Day 2 - Around Washington Square, the Village is a place to wander without an agenda: MacDougal Street's brick houses, historic jazz clubs like the Blue Note, tiny, winding Minetta Street. It's the day's planned breather; let yourself get lost for an hour before heading up to Chelsea.

activities.text: Detour through Washington Mews, cobbled alley of former stables behind the arch, then coffee on MacDougal Street, where young Bob Dylan made his debut.
Walk to Chelsea Market: 1.5 km via Sixth Avenue then 15th Street, about 19 min; otherwise one subway stop (A/C/E lines to 14th Street).

places.name: Washington Street Dumbo, NY

visits.text: Day 5 - Brooklyn's most-recreated photo is taken at the intersection of Washington Street and Water Street in Dumbo: the Manhattan Bridge framed by brick buildings, with the Empire State Building visible in the arch. Come before 9 AM; otherwise, the wait for a spot in the middle of the street runs to tens of minutes.

Day 5 - There's more to Dumbo than its cobblestone street: galleries in former warehouses, a large neighborhood bookstore, and Jane's Carousel from 1922 inside its glass enclosure by the water. Brooklyn Bridge Park then stretches its lawns to the bridge, with skyline views all the way.

activities.text: Lunch at Time Out Market, 55 Water Street: about twenty selected counters and a 5th-floor rooftop facing Manhattan, no reservation.
Walk to Brooklyn Heights Promenade: 1.1 km along Brooklyn Bridge Park then climbing to the Heights, about 14 min.

visits.text: You walk through mist before you see where it's coming from. The Gorge Trail at Watkins Glen follows Glen Creek through a gorge carved over 12,000 years since the last glacier's retreat. 19 waterfalls, 3.2 kilometers, 400 feet of descent, over 800 stone steps laid by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s. At Cavern Cascade, you literally pass behind the falls. The park, one of the most visited in New York State, has been open to the public since 1863 and managed by the state since 1906. Trail accessible mid-May through late October only.

The Suspension Bridge spans the gorge 26 meters above the creek, built in 1870 and still in service after two generations of renovations. It connects the Rim Trails on each side and offers the best view down onto Central Cascade, the park's tallest waterfall. Not for those afraid of heights.

You see it for two seconds while crossing the Route 414 bridge, ten minutes north of Watkins Glen. Hector Falls measures 50 meters total, but only 15 are visible from the road—the rest drops downstream on private property, visible only from a boat. No particular amenities, just a shoulder and the roar of water plunging directly into Seneca Lake (a rare case; most Finger Lakes waterfalls have carved gorges upstream). Especially spectacular in spring after snowmelt.

activities.text: One-hour narrated cruise on Seneca Lake with Captain Bill's, departing from Watkins Glen harbor. Seneca is the deepest of the Finger Lakes—188 meters at the bottom—and the U.S. Navy has been testing submarine sonars here since 1962 on a platform near Dresden on the west shore. The captain mentions the Seneca Guns along the way, unexplained dull detonations sometimes heard from the lake, with no scientific consensus on the cause.

The Seneca Lake Wine Trail has about thirty wineries, many within ten minutes' drive of downtown. If you can only visit one, Lamoreaux Landing sets a high bar with dry Rieslings that follow German benchmarks. $10 tasting, terrace facing the lake. A « permis de bouche » or taxi is recommended.

places.name: Wave Hill, NY

visits.text: Day 4 - optional: In the far northwest of the Bronx, Wave Hill is an 11-hectare estate perched above the Hudson, facing the Palisades cliffs. Manicured gardens, a pergola framing the views, intimate greenhouses. Mark Twain and the Roosevelt family lived in the house. A modest admission fee, with free admission during certain morning slots.

Day 4 - optional: Wave Hill offers a side of New York few people associate with the city: lounge chairs on the lawn, silence, the river below. The affluent, wooded neighborhood of Riverdale seems light-years from Times Square. A green interlude before heading back down to the southern Bronx.

activities.text: Coffee at the visitor center, then reading under the pergola: a proper, peaceful break before the next two stops.
To the New York Botanical Garden: about 4.9 km; take connecting Bronx buses or a taxi, and allow about twenty minutes.

visits.text: Explore picturesque Waynesville, nestled between the Great Smoky Mountains and the Blue Ridge Mountains. This charming little town in Haywood County captivates visitors with sublime mountain views and a welcoming atmosphere that embodies the spirit of Southern Appalachian hospitality.

Catch an entertaining live performance at Haywood Arts Regional Theater, where talented local and regional artists showcase their skills. This celebrated venue brings cultural enrichment to the mountain community and offers visitors an authentic taste of Appalachian arts and entertainment.

activities.text: Experience downtown Waynesville's bustling atmosphere featuring an eclectic mix of galleries, antique shops, and local boutiques. Visit Haywood's Historic Farmers Market to meet hospitable locals, sample fresh farm produce, and discover unique heritage crafts that make perfect mementos of your mountain visit.

visits.text: Take exit 4 off I-80 and drive north. Suddenly, nothing—just white as far as you can see. The Bonneville Salt Flats cover 120 km², a salt crust left by the evaporation of ancient Lake Bonneville 15,000 years ago. Since 1914 people have been setting speed records here; in 1970 someone hit 1,001 km/h. In dry weather you can drive right onto it. In wet weather, it becomes a perfect mirror reflecting the sky to infinity. No services on-site—grab water in Wendover first.

A few kilometers away, the Historic Wendover Airfield Museum preserves the memory of one of World War II's most secret bases. This is where the 509th Composite Group trained before dropping the atomic bombs in 1945. At its peak: 20,000 people on this base in the middle of the salt desert. You can climb the control tower and see a replica of the Little Boy bomb in the hangar.

places.name: West Branch, IA

visits.text: Herbert Hoover National Historic Site—The 31st U.S. president was born in this tiny two-room house in 1874. His father was a blacksmith. The tiny original cottage gives a tangible sense of his modest beginnings. Around it, a tallgrass prairie has been recreated to show the landscape Hoover saw as a child.

Herbert Hoover Presidential Library & Museum—The museum traces the life of a man who lived many lives: mining engineer in Australia and China, humanitarian relief coordinator during World War I, then president during the Great Depression. The Depression exhibit is especially well done.

Explore the site on foot—the blacksmith shop, Quaker meetinghouse, and the grave of Herbert and Lou Hoover, on a wooded hill overlooking the site, can be visited in 30 minutes. The grounds are peaceful and well-maintained.

activities.text: Stroll through the recreated tallgrass prairie—In summer, the grasses reach shoulder height and wildflowers attract butterflies and birds. Walking the marked trail around it takes 30 minutes.

visits.text: Glacier National Park — Enter this 4,100-square-kilometer wilderness preserving pristine ecosystems from prairie to alpine peaks. The Crown of the Continent features 700 lakes, 25 active glaciers, and abundant wildlife including grizzlies, wolves, and mountain goats.

Going-to-the-Sun Road — Drive this engineering marvel crossing the Continental Divide at 2,026-meter Logan Pass. The 80-kilometer scenic road completed in 1932 hugs cliff faces with stunning glacier and valley views.

Lake McDonald—Photograph the park's largest lake, stretching 16 kilometers with mountains reflected in pristine waters. The lake of glacial origin reaches a depth of 141 meters and is surrounded by old-growth cedar and hemlock forests.

Trail of the Cedars — Walk this wheelchair-accessible trail through an ancient rainforest with 500-year-old western red cedars. The 1.1-kilometer loop crosses Avalanche Creek on a suspension bridge. Allow for a round trip by car from West Glacier to reach the start of the walk.

Logan Pass — Hike from the crest of the continental divide, where snow lingers until July. The alpine visitor center offers exhibits and access to the Hidden Lake Trail through wildflower meadows frequented by mountain goats. Allow for a round trip by car from West Glacier via Going-to-the-Sun Road.

Hidden Lake Overlook — Walk 4.8 kilometers round trip for spectacular views of turquoise Hidden Lake surrounded by peaks. The trail crosses alpine tundra, revealing bighorn sheep and hoary marmots. From West Glacier, drive to Logan Pass before the hike and allow for the return journey.

Jackson Glacier Overlook — View one of Glacier's most accessible glaciers from this roadside overlook. The ice field has retreated considerably but remains impressive against the continental divide. Allow for a round trip by car from West Glacier via Going-to-the-Sun Road.

St. Mary Falls — Hike 2.6 kilometers through the forest to this 10-meter waterfall cascading over bedrock. The trail follows Rose Creek through wildflower meadows with mountain views. From West Glacier, allow for a round trip by car via Going-to-the-Sun Road to reach the trailhead.

Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park — Tour Montana's largest known limestone cavern featuring stalactites, stalagmites, and helictites. The 90-minute guided walk descends into chambers carved by water over millions of years.
Gates of the Mountains — Boat through this section of the Missouri River where limestone cliffs rise 370 meters. Lewis and Clark named the formation in 1805 during their expedition upriver.
Historic downtown Helena—Explore Montana's capital, with its Victorian architecture from the prosperous gold rush era. Last Chance Gulch preserves 1880s buildings housing shops and restaurants.

activities.text: Wildlife watching—Scan meadows and roadsides for grizzly bears, black bears, bighorn sheep, and mountain goats. Early morning and evening offer the best viewing opportunities along Going-to-the-Sun Road.
Apgar Village exploration — Browse visitor center exhibits, rent boats, and dine at this lakeside village. The park's west entrance hub offers services and lake access.

Scenic boat tour—Cruise across pristine lakes aboard historic wooden boats while listening to naturalist guides explain the park's history and geology. Tours operate on Lake McDonald and St. Mary Lake.
Evening ranger program — Attend talks about grizzly bears, glaciers, or night skies at park amphitheaters. Rangers share ecological knowledge and conservation challenges.
Blueberry treats—Sample Montana's signature berry in ice cream, pie, or jam at park lodges. Wild blueberries ripen in late summer throughout Glacier's forests.
Scenic return drive—Navigate mountain passes and valleys back to Glacier through the heart of the Rockies. The journey showcases Montana's vast wilderness and big sky.
Montana farewell dinner—Celebrate the journey with a bison sirloin steak or grilled trout at a mountain lodge. Montana cuisine emphasizes wild game and locally raised meats.

places.name: West Palm Beach, FL

visits.text: West Palm Beach - Florida's Emerging Cultural Capital: This rapidly developing city has cultivated world-class dining, entertainment venues, and high-end shopping while maintaining easy access to pristine Atlantic beaches.

Palm Beach - Billionaire's Row: Across the Intracoastal Waterway, Palm Beach proper showcases some of America's most valuable real estate, with beachfront mansions owned by the nation's wealthiest families.

John D. MacArthur Beach State Park - Preserved Paradise: This barrier island park protects one of the last remaining undeveloped stretches of the Palm Beach coast, with hiking trails, kayaking, and swimming on a pristine Atlantic beach.

Norton Museum of Art - World-Class Collection in the Tropics: This recently expanded museum houses significant European, American, and Chinese art collections in stunning galleries designed for natural light.

activities.text: Jupiter - Palm Beach's Best-Kept Secret: This small northern town offers outstanding beaches, historic lighthouse tours, and a laid-back atmosphere that contrasts with Palm Beach's formality.
Delray Beach and Boca Raton - Atlantic Avenue Strolling: These neighboring beach communities offer vibrant downtown districts filled with restaurants, boutiques, and galleries steps from the ocean.

activities.text: Catching a trout and then cooking it without taking it off the hook: Fishing Cone, in West Thumb Geyser Basin, was once used for this unusual demonstration. visits.text: Experience White Sands National Park, where the world's largest gypsum dune field creates a surreal landscape of brilliant white waves stretching across 712 km² of the Tularosa Basin. The pristine white dunes, constantly shifting with the wind, provide an otherworldly environment unlike anywhere else on Earth. This rare ecosystem supports uniquely adapted plants and animals found nowhere else.

Walk the Interdune Boardwalk and Dune Life Nature Trail to discover how life persists in this seemingly barren landscape of pure white gypsum crystals. Interpretive signs explain the geological processes that created this remarkable feature and the adaptations that allow plants and animals to survive in such an extreme environment.

activities.text: Sled down the pristine white dunes on specially designed sand discs available at the visitor center, creating unforgettable memories in one of the most photogenic landscapes in America. Sunset transforms the white sands into a canvas of pink, orange, and purple hues, offering photographers extraordinary opportunities for capturing the desert's ethereal beauty.

visits.text: Start in downtown Whitefish. Central Avenue is lined with art galleries, shops and restaurants in an authentic mountain town setting. Do not miss the Whitefish Depot, the old railway station where Amtrak’s Empire Builder (the Chicago–Seattle route) still stops. The small museum inside traces the town’s history, which began with the railroad in the early 20th century.

Head down to City Beach, the public beach at the end of Whitefish Lake. The lake stretches 11 km long by 4 km wide, with a maximum depth of 68 meters. The water runs clear and the beach is lifeguarded in summer—you'll see families, paddleboarders, and kayakers. If you prefer a wilder setting, push on to Whitefish Lake State Park on the west shore.

Last big hiking day: rise early to tackle the Iceberg Lake trail, one of the finest hikes in all of Glacier National Park. The trailhead sits behind Swiftcurrent Motor Inn in the Many Glacier valley. Figure 16 km round-trip with 390 m elevation gain—it's rated moderate and doable in 5 to 6 hours. The trail crosses fir forests, wildflower meadows, and follows the Ptarmigan Wall, a 450-meter-high ridge carved by glaciers. At the end, Iceberg Lake awaits at 1,858 m elevation, wedged between 900-meter cliffs—ice blocks float on its surface even in midsummer because sunlight almost never reaches the water. If you're brave, dip your feet—the water is frigid but invigorating.

The Many Glacier area is the park's best spot for observing grizzly bears. The Iceberg Lake trail corridor is particularly active in summer when huckleberry bushes are loaded with berries. Make noise while walking, keep your bear spray accessible (not in your backpack), and hike in a group if possible. If the trail is closed for bear activity (this happens regularly in July-August), fall back on the Cracker Lake Trail (19 km R/T) whose intensely turquoise lake is worth the effort.

Your last morning in Whitefish before departure. If your flight leaves late in the day, take the gondola to the summit of Whitefish Mountain Resort (15 minutes by car from downtown). In summer, the resort offers scenic lift rides, a zip line course, alpine slides and a network of mountain bike trails. From the Summit House at the top, the view takes in the entire Flathead Valley and the mountains of Glacier Park in the distance.
If you prefer to stay in town, the Living Wetlands Interpretive Nature Trail is an easy, short loop—perfect for a final peaceful walk through the wetlands.

activities.text: Spend the evening touring downtown's craft breweries. Whitefish has several microbreweries that close at 8pm (Montana law for craft breweries). Sample the huckleberry specialties—this wild local berry shows up in beers, ice creams, and even vodkas.

Pack your gear for the coming days: buy bear spray at one of the downtown outdoor shops (figure around forty dollars), verify your camping reservations if you're camping, and note that gas isn't available inside Glacier National Park.

After the hike, treat yourself to ice cream at the Swiftcurrent Motor Inn—you'll have earned it. Then take the road back to Whitefish via US-89 south and US-2 west (about 2.5 hours driving). Enjoy the evening dining at one of Whitefish's downtown restaurants. The town is known for its culinary scene—several local chefs have earned James Beard Foundation Award nominations.

Make a final tour of Central Avenue's shops to pick up souvenirs—Montana t-shirts and huckleberry products are the classics. Glacier Park International Airport (FCA) is only 15 minutes' drive from Whitefish, giving you plenty of margin to enjoy the morning.

visits.text: You cross one of two cable-stay pedestrian bridges - each shaped like a bow and arrow - to reach the 5-tonne steel figure that Kiowa-Comanche artist Blackbear Bosin donated to the city in 1974. The plaza around the base describes Plains Indian ways of life through interpretive panels. Bosin designed the piece in 1968 and lived only six years after its dedication before dying in 1980. Access is free around the clock until midnight, and the nightly Ring of Fire makes the after-dark visit worth planning for.

Step onto the dirt roads of this 9-hectare open-air museum and you are in Wichita between 1865 and 1880, when the Chisholm Trail ran right through here. Over 60 buildings line the grounds - more than 40 of them fully furnished - and costumed interpreters demonstrate blacksmithing, printing, and carpentry in real time. Established in 1952, it holds accreditation from the American Alliance of Museums, a distinction fewer than 3 percent of U.S. museums earn. Go on a weekday morning to avoid school groups.

You ride a glass elevator past Ivan the T. rex skeleton to reach three floors of a restored 1914 brick warehouse in Old Town, where an Egyptian mummy, a 10-meter Tylosaurus fossil from the Kansas Cretaceous sea, Roman emperor coins, and a section of the Berlin Wall share the same building. The museum opened in 2001 as the Museum of Ancient Treasures, moved to this Old Town address in 2003, and now draws around 45,000 visitors a year. It specializes in nothing - and that eclecticism is the whole point.

The largest art museum in Kansas opened in 1935 on an endowment left by Louise Caldwell Murdock, who in 1915 instructed that her estate fund an American art collection in memory of her husband. Today the permanent collection exceeds 10,000 works - Edward Hopper, Georgia O'Keeffe, Winslow Homer, Mary Cassatt, and Charles Russell among them. General admission to the permanent collection is free, and the Art Garden with outdoor sculpture by Tom Otterness and Henry Moore is open 24 hours.

You walk into a $62 million building that Canadian architect Moshe Safdie designed specifically to sit on the banks of the Arkansas River - the geometric toroid shape is a deliberate response to the waterfront site. The museum opened April 1, 2000, and Safdie later applied lessons from it to the Crystal Bridges Museum in Bentonville and the Kauffman Center in Kansas City. Inside, the “Design, Build, Fly” exhibit lets you rivet an airplane wing, test landing gear, and design an aircraft seat - Wichita-specific content for a city where Cessna, Beechcraft, and Learjet all built their planes. The Boeing Dome Theater shows films on an 18-meter, 360-degree screen; dome tickets can be purchased separately.

Step into the museum adjacent to the Keeper of the Plains and you are looking at 39 original works by Blackbear Bosin - the Kiowa-Comanche artist who created the sculpture outside. The permanent collection also includes traditional Plains Indian beadwork, ceremonial objects, and historical photography. The museum itself was the direct result of community organizing by Native residents of Wichita through the 1960s, who lobbied the city for a gathering space where all Plains tribes could share their culture.

Cross the Arkansas River to Delano, which was founded in the 1870s just outside Wichita's city limits precisely so that gambling, brothels, and saloons could operate without interference from Wichita lawmen. Train-masters who visited the establishments are said to have carried their red caboose lanterns, which is where the expression “red-light district” comes from. Wichita annexed Delano in 1880. Today it is an eclectic stretch of independently owned shops, galleries, and restaurants along West Douglas Avenue, with public art celebrating the Chisholm Trail throughout.

activities.text: Walk the brick-lined grid of Old Town after dinner and you are in one of the American Planning Association's 'Great Places in America' - a designation it received in 2008 for its adaptive reuse of late-19th-century warehouses. The Hotel at Old Town was the Keen Kutter brand warehouse in 1906, billed at the time as the largest warehouse in the world, and its lobby still displays the largest authentic Keen Kutter collection in existence. Start at River City Brewing Co. or Nortons Brewing Co. before working your way through more than 100 businesses in the district.

Follow the trail markers embedded in the sidewalks and you are walking the original Chisholm Trail, which ran along the east side of Wichita from 1867 to 1871. Jesse Chisholm, for whom the trail is named, established a trading post here in the 1860s; Wichita was incorporated in 1870 and became a Texas cattle railhead in 1872. Pick up the self-guided map at the Wichita-Sedgwick County Historical Museum, housed in the original 1890 City Hall with its 52-meter clock tower.

Rent a kayak or a bike from Boats and Bikes on the river and you can reach the five Museums on the River institutions (Exploration Place, the Wichita Art Museum, Old Cowtown Museum, Botanica Wichita and the Mid-America All-Indian Center) on a 4 km paved loop. The cable-stayed pedestrian bridges crossing both rivers to the Keeper plaza were specifically designed in the shape of bows and arrows, as part of the 20 million dollar restoration completed in 2007. The loop is free to use all year round; Boats and Bikes operates from late May to October.

Choose your farewell meal from three Wichita institutions. Old Mill Tasty Shop at 604 E. Douglas has been running its marble soda fountain counter since 1932, with daily specials that change every day and hand-mixed malts. NuWay Burgers on West Douglas Avenue has been serving its signature “crumbled” ground beef patty, unique to the chain, since 1930. In the Douglas Design District, east of downtown, Hopping Gnome Brewing brews small-batch beers in its taproom on East Douglas. All three are easy to reach from ICT airport for an early departure.

places.name: Williamsburg, VA

visits.text: Colonial Williamsburg isn't a theme park—it's a real colonial town reconstructed on 301 acres that you'll explore on foot all day. It contains 89 original 18th-century buildings and hundreds of faithful reconstructions, thanks to funding from John D. Rockefeller Jr. since 1927. Buy your ticket in advance: it grants access to buildings and demonstrations.

At the Colonial Williamsburg Capitol, a costumed guide explains why Virginia outpaced the entire nation. On May 15, 1776—50 days before the national Declaration—the Virginia delegation here received orders to vote for independence. The burgesses' chamber, with its wooden benches, is faithfully reproduced.

The Governor's Palace deserves as much time for its 10-acre French-style gardens as for the interior—plan at least 90 minutes for both. Seven royal governors resided here, then Patrick Henry and Thomas Jefferson as the first elected governors. Jefferson's library, recreated identically, is a detail that stands out.

Bruton Parish Church on Duke of Gloucester Street may be an original 1715 building, but it still welcomes worshippers today—enter to see the pews where Washington and Jefferson prayed. The parish register goes back to 1662. Free admission, volunteer guides on site.

Step through the door of the Raleigh Tavern—rebuilt on its original foundations—to understand where revolutionary decisions were really made. Members of the House of Burgesses gathered here after the royal governor shut down Parliament to silence them. Next door, the Raleigh Tavern Bakery still serves period gingerbread cakes.

activities.text: Spend time with Colonial Williamsburg's artisans: blacksmith, printer, cooper, wigmaker. These aren't extras—they're true masters working with 18th-century tools. Try some tasks if the opportunity arises. The musket-firing demonstration on Market Square is particularly striking.

In the evening, book a table at one of the four historic taverns—Chowning's, King's Arms, Shields, or Christiana Campbell's. Colonial menu: crab stew, cider chicken, sweet potato pie, beeswax candles. Reservations required, especially in summer. Budget $35 to $50 per person.

places.name: Williston, ND

visits.text: Forty kilometers southwest of Williston, right on the North Dakota–Montana border, Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site rises from the floodplain with its white palisade walls and red-roofed towers exactly as the original looked in 1851. John Jacob Astor's American Fur Company built Fort Union in 1828, and for 39 years it controlled the buffalo robe and fur trade across a vast Northern Plains territory—over 25,000 robes and $100,000 in merchandise changing hands annually. Assiniboine, Crow, Blackfeet, Mandan, and six other nations traded here. The reconstructed Bourgeois House holds museum exhibits; rangers in period dress staff the trade room. Free admission.

Three kilometers downstream, Fort Buford State Historic Site marks where the U.S. Army dismantled Fort Union in 1867—using its timber and stone to build Buford—and where Sitting Bull surrendered on July 19, 1881, famously handing his rifle to his young son first before giving it to the commander. A small museum holds the original surrender document. The Missouri-Yellowstone Confluence Interpretive Center, one kilometer farther on, stands at the exact meeting point of the two rivers where Lewis arrived on April 26, 1805, calling it the most remarkable river junction in North America. Free state park entry.

The drive back to Williston from Fort Union follows Route 1804 through Missouri River bottomland that looks much as Karl Bodmer painted it during his 1833 journey up the river with Prince Maximilian of Wied. The cottonwood gallery forests, oxbow ponds, and sandbar configurations remain relatively intact through this corridor. Williston itself was the epicenter of the 2010s Bakken oil boom; the Frontier Museum on 2nd Avenue West—an open-air village of restored farm buildings from the 1800s to the 1950s—and the James Memorial Art Center document the territory's earlier history.

activities.text: The Missouri River bottomlands around the Fort Union–Fort Buford corridor are some of the least-disturbed riparian habitats remaining on the Upper Missouri—cottonwood gallery forests, oxbow ponds, and sandbars that look much as they did in 1805. Walk the park trails from Fort Union toward the river in the early morning and you'll likely see white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and migrating waterfowl. Bald eagles are common year-round in the cottonwood groves.

The annual Fort Union Rendezvous in June draws hundreds of buckskinners and mountain-man reenactors to the site for two days of demonstrations of 19th-century fur trading, flintlock shooting and period camp life. If your dates coincide, it is one of the most historically vivid events along the entire Lewis and Clark route. Otherwise, Williston's Saturday farmers market runs throughout the summer and serves both the oilfield and ranching communities, with unusually good produce for this latitude.

visits.text: Stop on the way in Beaufort (about 169 km northeast of Wilmington, 2 hours' drive) - a colonial port founded in 1709, the third oldest in North Carolina. The historic center has more than 100 houses built before 1820. It was here that Blackbeard's ship, the Queen Anne's Revenge, was found in 1996 at a depth of 7 meters - the recovered pieces are at the North Carolina Maritime Museum, free. Opposite, the wild horses of Carrot Island graze in a reserve reachable by kayak.

The USS North Carolina Battleship is permanently moored in the Cape Fear River across from downtown Wilmington. A 1941 battleship, 220 meters long, nine 406 mm guns, crew of 2,339. She participated in every major Pacific operation between 1942 and 1945, without losing a single man in combat - a remarkable fact for a vessel of this importance. Self-guided 1.5 to 2-hour tour, access to 9 levels. $16.

The Wilmington Riverwalk runs 1.6 kilometers along the Cape Fear, restored 19th-century industrial wharves turned promenade. The city has increasingly served as a Hollywood backdrop since the 1980s (Dawson's Creek, One Tree Hill, The Crow, and more recently numerous series) - nickname: "Hollywood East." Historic center of 230 preserved blocks, one of the largest in the South.

activities.text: Sunset at Wrightsville Beach, 20 minutes east. Six-kilometer urban beach ranked among the best family beaches in the United States. Sweetwater surf shop rents boards and wetsuits ($25 half-day), the waves from October to April are the most consistent. Simpler option: Bluewater restaurant offers direct views of Banks Channel and returning boats.

visits.text: Wilson Lake - The Clearest Lake in Kansas: Red sandstone cliffs and pillars interrupt the shoreline of this remarkably clear reservoir, creating scenery more reminiscent of the Southwest than the Great Plains.

Wilson State Park - Where Smoky Hills Meet Crystal Waters: Lake lovers fish, paddle, boat, and swim while mountain bikers conquer the 25-mile Switchgrass Trail that snakes through canyons carved into the surrounding Smoky Hills.

activities.text: Switchgrass Trail - 25 Miles of Mountain Biking Adventure: This challenging trail system winds through Smoky Hills canyons, offering technical terrain and scenic views rarely associated with Kansas.

Boating on Wilson Lake - The waters of the Smoky Hills: At Wilson State Park, head to the shores of Wilson Lake for an outing on the water. From a boat, observe the red sandstone cliffs and the reservoir's coves in the rolling landscape of the Smoky Hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Kansas Tour: Prairies and the Wild West

visits.text: New England Air Museum - The Largest Aviation Collection in the Northeast: Explore an extraordinary assemblage of aircraft, helicopters, engines, and memorabilia spanning the entire history of flight. Highlights include the oldest surviving aircraft in America (a hot air balloon basket) and the oldest Connecticut-constructed airplane.

Historic Aircraft Collection - From Pioneers to Jets: Walk among vintage fighters, bombers, and experimental aircraft in massive hangars, with knowledgeable volunteer docents—many former pilots and aviation professionals—ready to share stories behind each machine.

activities.text: Redbird Flight Simulator - Take the Controls: Experience the thrill of piloting through this realistic simulator, while younger visitors can build paper airplanes and participate in family-friendly aviation scavenger hunts throughout the facility.

places.name: Winslow, AZ

visits.text: El Rancho Hotel (Gallup, NM) - This 1937 motel, nicknamed the 'Playground of the Stars,' hosted Hollywood stars during western film shoots in the 1940s-50s. Each room is named after a star - John Wayne, Katharine Hepburn, Ronald Reagan. Even if you don't stay overnight, the lobby and its hunting trophies are worth a look.

Petrified Forest National Park—Don't miss this park protecting the world's largest concentration of petrified wood: 225-million-year-old tree trunks transformed into colorful quartz crystals. The 45 km scenic drive also crosses the Painted Desert—hills striped with red, purple, and white. Don't take anything: it's illegal and the park estimates it loses 12 tonnes of petrified wood annually to visitors.

Standing on the Corner Park (Winslow, AZ) - 'Take it easy, take it easy / Standing on the corner in Winslow, Arizona...' - the 1972 Eagles song saved this town from decline. A bronze statue and mural mark the street corner. Five-minute photo stop, but the song will stick in your head all day.

activities.text: Stay at La Posada (Winslow) - If you can book a room at this 1929 former Harvey House hotel, designed by architect Mary Colter, it's the most beautiful lodging on the entire Route 66. The Turquoise Room restaurant serves refined Southwest cuisine. Even without staying overnight, visit the gardens and lobby.

visits.text: You arrive at a 565-square-meter museum that opened in May 2015, standing less than 30 meters from the modest four-room house where Marion Morrison was born on May 26, 1907. Inside, you find the world's largest public collection of John Wayne memorabilia—film costumes, original scripts, his personal station wagon, and 24 authentic seats recovered from Grauman's Chinese Theatre at a 2013 auction. Budget 75 minutes to take in both the museum galleries and the adjacent birthplace home, where a guide shares stories of the Duke's early years. Admission charged; open daily 10 a.m.–5 p.m.

You drive a few kilometers west of Winterset to the Roseman Bridge, built in 1883—the most photographed of Madison County's six surviving covered bridges and the one featured prominently in the 1995 film. Cross it slowly. Take your time. This is what Iowa's backroads look like at their finest. Free access, open year-round.

activities.text: You wander the Winterset Historic Square, designated a National Historic District in 2015. At its center stands an 1870s limestone courthouse crowned with a distinctive dome, ringed by locally-owned shops and cafes. Pick up lunch here before heading east to Des Moines. The Iowa Quilt Museum and the old county jail - now home to the 1st Avenue Collective gallery - both sit within a block of the courthouse square.

days_plan.itin_title: Iowa Backroads: From the Missouri Cliffs to the Mississippi Bluffs

visits.text: Upper Dells Sandstone Gorges - The Wisconsin River carved these canyons through 500-million-year-old Cambrian sandstone. The walls rise 30-40 meters and take spectacular shapes: columns, arches, mushroom rocks. The only way to see them is by boat - the shores are private and protected.

Witches Gulch - Accessible only from the cruise, this narrow gorge is carpeted with moss and ferns. A wooden walkway winds between sandstone walls so close together there's almost never direct sunlight. Photographer H.H. Bennett discovered and named it in the 1860s - his photos launched tourism at Wisconsin Dells.

Stand Rock - An isolated sandstone pillar facing a cliff. Since 1886, a trained dog has jumped the gap between cliff and rock to recreate Bennett's legendary photograph. It's Wisconsin's most iconic image.

activities.text: Upper Dells Cruise - The 2-hour tour goes upriver between sandstone cliffs, with two land stops: Witches Gulch and Stand Rock. The guide tells Native American legends, raftsmen (log floaters) history, and canyon geology. Departs from downtown.
Lower Dells Cruise (optional) - The 1-hour tour goes downriver passing Hawk's Bill, the Rocky Islands, and other formations. Less spectacular than the Upper Dells but complementary.

places.name: Wolf Point, MT

visits.text: Wolf Point is the largest town on the Fort Peck Indian Reservation, home to Assiniboine and Sioux communities who have lived along the Missouri since before Lewis and Clark passed through in May 1805. The Wild Horse Stampede, held each July, is the oldest rodeo in Montana—running since 1915. Outside of rodeo season, the town has a small regional museum and the Missouri River access points used by the expedition. Fuel up, stretch, and spend 20 minutes by the river before continuing west.

places.name: Woodstock, VT

visits.text: A family home can also tell the story of forest management: that is the focus of Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park. The estate connects the history of its owners with that of conservation, offering tours of the residence and outdoor trails. Book your indoor visit before you arrive; services and programs do not operate every day. The parking lot shared with Billings Farm makes it easier to organize both visits.

A working dairy farm is part of Billings Farm & Museum, at the foot of Mount Tom. The visit connects farming practices with Vermont’s rural history, going beyond a collection of objects. Check the schedule to see which demonstrations are offered that day. Parking is shared with the neighboring historical park, but their visits and tickets are separate.

activities.text: You will climb through Mount Tom Forest to look out over Woodstock from South Peak, following a route shown on the park map. The trails and former carriage roads pass through a managed forest, where forestry is part of the landscape’s history. Download the map before setting out and adjust your loop to the available daylight. Plan to return before access closes at dusk.

places.name: Wright Brothers National Memorial, NC

visits.text: Twelve seconds and 37 meters: the first flight doesn't look like much, and that is what strikes you at the Wright Brothers National Memorial. On December 17, 1903, Orville took off here, and granite markers still show the landings of that day's four flights. Then climb Big Kill Devil Hill, five minutes up a gentle slope, to the monument over 18 meters tall. Paid entry, free for ages 15 and under.

The Wright brothers spoke of "Kitty Hawk": the town of Kill Devil Hills did not exist yet in 1903. At the Wright Brothers National Memorial, the renovated visitor center displays a replica of the 1903 Flyer in its Flight Room, and the brothers' hangar and living quarters have been rebuilt. Open daily 9am to 5pm; leashed dogs allowed outside, not in the buildings.

visits.text: Walls without inhabitants do not mean a place has no presence: Wupatki Pueblo remains an ancestral site for several Indigenous communities. The route reveals rooms clustered around the landform, a ball court, and a natural air vent. Pick up the guide at the visitor center and examine the masonry without climbing on it.

Wukoki Pueblo resembles a small tower set on a rocky base, isolated in the open landscape. Its name means “big house” in Hopi; the NPS notes that this place remains connected to descendant communities. Walk around it only on the designated path, and step back to understand its setting rather than using the walls as footholds.

Nine rooms were enough for Lomaki Pueblo, whose sandstone and limestone walls overlook a fissure in the plateau. The small structures at Box Canyon round out this combined visit and recall the presence of a farming community. Follow the route to the end without leaving the trail; its uneven surface requires more attention than a sidewalk.

days_plan.itin_title: Navajo Country in 10 Days: Sedona and Monument Valley

visits.text: Yakima River Canyon — Follow scenic SR 821 from Yakima between the rocky walls framing the Yakima River. Stop at access points along the road to see the bends in the river, the dry slopes and birds of prey above the canyon.

Yakima Greenway — Follow this developed path on foot beside the Yakima River, through parks and natural areas accessible from the city. Stop by the water to observe riverside trees and birds, then continue along the paved trail.

Yakima Valley Museum — Visit this Yakima museum to discover the history of the valley, its communities and its agriculture. Explore the galleries devoted to local heritage, then head to the nearby parks to continue your visit to the neighborhood.

Yakima Valley wine country — Drive through Washington's premier wine region producing 40% of the state's grapes. The rain shadow of the Cascades creates ideal conditions for Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Chardonnay.

activities.text: Wine tasting tour — Visit family-owned wineries and tasting rooms sampling award-winning Washington wines. Many vineyards offer tours explaining viticulture practices and the valley's unique terroir.

Drive along scenic SR 821 — From Yakima, take the Yakima River Canyon road along the river, between cliffs, dry slopes and bends. Pullouts let you view the canyon and reach the river access points before returning to Yakima.

Farm-to-table dinner — Savor cuisine featuring Yakima Valley produce including hops, apples, cherries, and wine. The agricultural region supplies ingredients to restaurants throughout the Pacific Northwest.

visits.text: Day 4 - optional: In the Bronx, Yankee Stadium is home to baseball's most decorated franchise. A game during the season, April through October, remains very affordable: inexpensive upper-level seats, a hot dog, singing during the seventh-inning stretch. In the offseason, there are guided tours of Monument Park and behind the scenes. The atmosphere is well worth it in its own right.

Day 4 - optional: Even without a ticket to Yankee Stadium, the plaza and shops give you a feel for the South Bronx, now undergoing a revival. Purists miss the old 1923 stadium, demolished just across the street; others appreciate the comfort of the new one, opened in 2009. The view from the elevated subway already makes a great photo.

activities.text: Buy game tickets in advance on the official website or through resale on the day: for a weekday game against a lesser team, you can get in for the price of a movie ticket.
End of Day 4. For Williamsburg tomorrow morning: Bronx to Brooklyn subway, about 13.3 km, count 1 to 1.25 hours with transfers.

places.name: Yankton, SD

visits.text: Yankton sits at the base of Gavins Point Dam, the smallest of the six main dams on the Missouri but the one that creates Lewis and Clark Lake—a 40 km reservoir over what was open river in September 1804. The dam visitor center connects the engineering to Lewis and Clark's passage. Yankton's 1924 Meridian Bridge, a swing-span structure over the Missouri with a pedestrian walkway, gives you the same view across the river that expedition members would have known. It's 130 km north of Sioux City—a worthwhile break before the long Plains stretch to Pierre.

days_plan.itin_title: Lewis & Clark Trail: St. Louis to Great Falls, Retracing the 1804 Expedition

visits.text: Fishing Bridge Visitor Center frames Yellowstone Lake through its very architecture of stone and wood. Completed in 1931, the building was designed to let visitors look through it toward the water, so the exhibition begins before you reach the display cases. You can also ask about local trail conditions at the visitor information areas. Check the museum’s seasonal opening dates and bring a warm layer for stepping out onto the shore, even in clear weather.

A fishing bridge where fishing is no longer allowed: Fishing Bridge kept its name after the 1973 ban. The measure was intended to protect cutthroat trout, once caught here in large numbers. Today, you can watch the river flowing out of Yellowstone Lake and look for fish from the pedestrian areas. Do not cross the barriers or stop in the roadway to get a better view.

activities.text: You will walk to Natural Bridge from the Bridge Bay area, through a landscape very different from the thermal basins. Bridge Creek eroded the rhyolite to form this natural arch, whose top stands about sixteen meters above the creek. The detour offers a look at another way water shapes rock. Ask whether the trail is open, stay on the marked route, and do not cross the arch itself.

days_plan.itin_title: Yellowstone and Grand Teton: 12 Days Among Lakes and Mountain Passes

visits.text: Explore York's traditional Southern downtown, where the historic York County Courthouse and commercial buildings line streets that retain their nineteenth-century character. Part of South Carolina's Olde English District, the town is connected to Revolutionary War history. In a brick building, the McCelvey Center houses the Southern Revolutionary War Institute, devoted to research and educational programs.

activities.text: Drive from York to Anne Springs Close Greenway, a large nature area and return to York after your visit. You can hike, ride horses or watch wildlife there. Trails cross different habitats and make for a peaceful walk. This nature excursion complements a visit to historic York.

days_plan.itin_title: South Carolina Road Trip: From Lowcountry Beaches to the Blue Ridge Mountains

visits.text: Yorktown Battlefield is the scene of the last major battle of the Revolutionary War. On October 19, 1781, Cornwallis surrendered here to Washington's troops and Rochambeau's French forces; cross Surrender Field, then visit the Moore House, where the terms were negotiated. Two driving tours total about 26 km: do at least the first one.

Every 30 minutes, the film "Liberty Fever" sums up the weeks of the 1781 siege at the American Revolution Museum at Yorktown. Outside, a recreated Continental Army encampment and a period farm complete the visit. The museum recommends three to four hours: if you are short on time here, choose between the museum and the battlefield.

activities.text: Board Yorktown's tall ship at Riverwalk Landing Pier, from April to late October. The sail runs past the battlefield, and the sunset cruise sometimes lets you spot dolphins. Back on shore, look up at the Yorktown Victory Monument: in 1942, lightning knocked the head and arms off its Lady Liberty statue.

days_plan.itin_title: US East Coast: Washington to Savannah in 15 Days

visits.text: Yosemite National Park - America's Cathedral of Stone and Water: Sheer granite walls rise 3,000 feet from the valley floor as waterfalls plunge from heights that dwarf skyscrapers. This UNESCO World Heritage Site inspired the conservation movement and continues to humble millions of annual visitors.

El Capitan - The World's Most Famous Big Wall: This 3,000-foot vertical granite monolith draws elite climbers from around the globe attempting multi-day ascents of routes like The Nose. Even from the valley floor, watching climbers as tiny specks on the face is mesmerizing.

Half Dome - Yosemite's Iconic Sentinel: This distinctive granite dome, cleaved as if by a giant's axe, rises 4,737 feet above the valley floor. The cables route to the summit remains one of America's most sought-after hiking achievements.

Yosemite Falls - A Waterfall in Three Tiers: Water plunges 2,425 feet in three tiers, creating a spectacle visible throughout Yosemite Valley. Peak flow occurs in May and June when melting snow transforms the falls into a thundering curtain of white.

activities.text: Tunnel View - The Most Photographed Vista in America: This overlook presents El Capitan, Half Dome, and Bridalveil Fall in a single striking panorama that has graced countless postcards, calendars, and wallpapers.

Glacier Point - Stand 3,214 Feet Above the Valley: This dramatic overlook provides bird's-eye views of Yosemite's greatest hits, with Half Dome at eye level and the High Sierra stretching to the horizon.
Mariposa Grove - Walk Among Giant Sequoias: Over 500 mature giant sequoias populate this ancient forest, including the 1,800-year-old Grizzly Giant with its 96-foot circumference.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of California: From Redwoods to Deserts

visits.text: Granite suddenly fills the windshield at Tunnel View. El Capitan frames the left side, Bridalveil Fall marks the opposite slope, and Half Dome appears in the distance: this overlook helps you make sense of the valley before driving through it. Take time to identify these landmarks instead of leaving after a photo. Park only in designated spaces and cross carefully, as vehicles emerge directly from the nearby tunnel.

Binoculars completely transform a stop at El Capitan Meadow. From the edge of the meadow, the rock face looks smooth at first; watch longer, and you may make out the routes climbers follow and their tiny movements. The NPS recommends this area for viewing El Capitan and Cathedral Rocks. Stay on designated paths: crossing the meadow to gain a few meters damages a fragile habitat without improving the view much.

Long before visitors arrived by car, Miwok and Paiute peoples lived in this valley. The Yosemite Museum puts their history at the center of the visit, with artifacts and exhibits devoted to Indigenous cultures. After the cliffs and waterfalls, this stop connects the landscape with names and ways of life. Check the hours on-site; craft demonstrations depend on the schedule and should not be considered guaranteed.

activities.text: Follow Cook’s Meadow Loop to see Yosemite from meadow level. The route offers views of Yosemite Falls, Half Dome, Sentinel Rock, and Royal Arches, showing them together rather than isolating each one like a postcard. Boardwalks keep you from trampling wetlands and lead to different perspectives as the light changes. Leave your car parked and reach the trailhead on foot or by the valley shuttle.

On Lower Yosemite Fall Trail, you hear the roar before you see the waterfall, especially in spring. The trail leads to the base of the lower fall, close enough to feel the spray when the flow is strong; by late summer, the same spot may be quiet and almost dry. Stay on open paths and keep off rocks beyond the trail, even if other visitors are sitting there. Wet surfaces quickly become slippery.

Its name promises a lake, yet Mirror Lake can become a meadow. This small, shallow pool gradually recedes during summer, exposing sand and vegetation at the foot of the cliffs. The trail remains an interesting place to study the landscape, even without a reflection of Half Dome. Take the shuttle to the trailhead, then follow the designated pedestrian route; choose a short out-and-back walk and bring water, without counting on a swim.

days_plan.itin_title: California Road Trip: San Francisco, Yosemite & Death Valley
San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road
San Francisco, Yosemite, and Big Sur: 11 Days on the Road

visits.text: Yountville, 3,000 inhabitants and more Michelin stars per capita than anywhere else in the United States—the figure is quoted everywhere, it's true, and it says it all. The village is compact, everything is walkable, and the architecture is that of an old 19th-century California town that wine money has carefully preserved. The main street is home to several Thomas Keller restaurants and galleries worth stopping for. Bouchon Bistro for lunch: classic French cuisine, waiters in white aprons, prices less traumatizing than the neighboring French Laundry.

Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, 5766 Silverado Trail: this is where everything changed. On May 24, 1976, in a blind tasting in Paris organized by Steven Spurrier, this winery's 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon beat Mouton-Rothschild, Haut-Brion, and Montrose. The winning bottle is now at the Smithsonian in Washington in the “Objects that Made America” collection. The FAY Outlook & Visitors Center (designed by Barcelona architect Javier Barba) offers a view of the historic FAY Vineyard. The underground cellar has over 3,000 m² of tunnels, with a suspended Foucault pendulum—one of 50 in the world. The S.L.V. cuvée is the direct heir to the 1973. Reservations required.

Domaine Chandon (1 California Drive, Yountville): the first venture by a French Champagne house into California, founded in 1973 by Moët & Chandon. The 1970s architecture has aged well, the gardens are well-maintained. It's not the highlight of the wine tour, but California's traditional-method wines deserve a 30-minute stop between appointments. Tasting $30–45.

activities.text: Comparative tasting in the Stags Leap District AVA: after Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, a second stop at Shafer Vineyards or Clos du Val in the same AVA helps you grasp what defines the terroir - Cabernets with tight structure and more precise fruit than in the rest of Napa. Don't attempt more than two serious tastings in a day if you want to stay clear-headed.

Cycling in Yountville: the town is flat, distances are short, and several hotels lend or rent bicycles. The Vine Trail follows the Napa River for a few kilometers and lets you reach Napa Town to the south without a car. Ideal in the late afternoon when the heat eases.

visits.text: You cross the world's only Y-shaped bridge - and you could end up on the same side of the river as you started, depending on which of its two branches you took. Zanesville's Y-Bridge has spanned the confluence of the Licking and Muskingum rivers since 1814, when the first wooden bridge was inaugurated by architect Rufus Scott. The current bridge - the fifth of its kind - was built in 1984 in steel and concrete to replace the fourth (1902), itself a pioneer of reinforced concrete in its time. The structure is so unique that aviator Amelia Earhart declared that Zanesville was 'the most recognizable city in the country' seen from the air. Ripley's Believe It or Not immortalized the bridge with the formula: 'the only bridge in the world you can cross and stay on the same side of the river'. Park at Putnam Hill Park for the overhead view.

You climb to the Putnam Hill overlook and suddenly find spread before you the only panoramic view of the entire Y-Bridge and the confluence of the two rivers. From this hill, you understand at once why the engineers of 1814 built a Y-shaped bridge rather than two separate bridges: the two waterways meet at almost a right angle, and a single three-branched structure solved the problem in one go. What you don't see from below, you see here: the strange intersection that emerges in the middle of the waters. Local anecdote: in 1810, Zanesville was briefly Ohio's capital - it replaced Chillicothe for two years before Columbus became the permanent capital in 1816. This park is perfect for a picnic with a view.

You push open the doors of the Zanesville Museum of Art and discover a town that was briefly the world capital of art pottery: local clays and coal energy from Muskingum County gave birth in the early 20th century to manufacturers like Weller Pottery, Roseville Pottery, and J.B. Owens Pottery - Weller alone produced three train cars of pottery per day, making it the world's largest manufacturer. You walk through the galleries admiring the matte and satin glazes in shades of moss green, earth brown, and olive that the Art Nouveau of the 1900s made famous. These pieces today fetch thousands of dollars at auction in major houses. Arrive on Tuesday: admission is free.

activities.text: You glide on the Muskingum River and pass your first lock manually operated by a state lockmaster - the 11 locks of the Muskingum are the only ones in the United States still manually operated, a system dating from the 19th century. You paddle between red-orange sandstone cliffs whose reflections dance on the calm water, you pass great blue herons motionless on gravel banks, and corn belt farms descend to the water's edge with their rusty silos. The river is still unknown to travelers outside Ohio - you'll mostly encounter local brown trout fishermen. Ask your outfitter for the downstream section toward McConnelsville: the wildest and most peaceful of the entire route.

You drive on the National Road - the first federally funded road in America, built between 1811 and 1837 from Cumberland, Maryland, to Vandalia, Illinois - and realize that today's US Route 40 follows exactly the original route. It reached Zanesville in 1826 and the Y-Bridge immediately became the most strategic passage on its Ohio route. You look for period buildings along the road: the entrance to the National Road/Zane Grey Museum in Norwich, the stone arches of the old stagecoach stations in Gratiot. For enthusiasts, the 1812 Norfolk Inn in Norwich is one of the rare intact National Road buildings still standing in this section of Ohio.
